review_text:
This game is like a room full of mirrors - there isn't any real depth, just reflections to make it seem bigger and grander than it actually is. The graphics is beautiful, the main quest line is interesting - but that's about it. 

The game is over-bloated with the most sacrificial, shallow and bland secondary quests I've seen in a long time. From the first hour of playing right till the very end, you see the same pattern: 

1. Bring something to someone. 
2. Travel across the map to fetch it. 
3. Turns out the person doesn't have it/lost it/it was stolen. 
4. Travel across the map in the other direction to retrieve it. 
5. Boring fight/search sequence. 
6. Bring it back.

It's just so repetitive, so mundane. Other key points about this game: 

- Voice acting is terrible (apart from a few exceptions, such as Capon). 
- The equipment you can get is pretty much the same as in the first game - variety is so poor! - Random forest-roaming bandits wearing some of the most expensive pieces of armour.
- Invisible walls.
- Weird narrative choices and not-so-subtle enforcement of modern political views.
- Hunting doesn't really serve a purpose.
- The world is huge but empty - those places that are more lively (like settlements) are very static, there's nothing really going on. 
- Choices have no real impact on anyone but the main protagonist.

There's an annoying lack of consistency with historical accuracy - some elements are hyper-accurate (equipment, locations, the general setting etc), and others are fitting the time/place premise very loosely (such as the whole thing with Capon getting imprisoned - it's just ridiculous).

In the end, this game isn't hugely improved from KCD 1. It looks and runs better - but it also repeats a lot of the predecessor's mistakes and misses out on easy wins and improvements. It's fun to play at times - but other times, it's anything but fun. Can't recommend.

review_text:
I have to come to the conclusion that this game has an incredibly well targeted market, with it having such amazing reviews all around. 

I gave it a good shot, but honestly a bit shocked by how unpolished, badly written and animated, and clunky and buggy this game is. It looks absolutely stunning (though the sky and weather are awful, but everything else is just.. wow). But the writing and quest design are just mediocre at best and incredibly dated and ridiculous at worst. I was excited for this, and don't mind the slow pace, and love just going about experiencing the world, but there's just very little to it imo, and it's not exactly well made (people's reactions and the world's interaction with you are often buggy and nonsensical, sometimes just plain broken, and every single thing is clunky). The systems, complicated as they may be, add very little to my experience overall, and the role-playing experience is also very much taking the back seat overall. You have very little agency and the character is whatever it is regardless. Acting, unfortunately, is also not very good and often leans towards the silly side.

I reckon you'll know if you'll like this. It's not a horrible game, it's just a mediocre game with quite some scale and old school features added in (which can appeal to some). I'm genuinely a bit baffled by the reception of this game. Feels like if it were released by Bethesda or Obsidian or someone, people would go mild on it as dated, unpolished, and poorly written, but since it's sort of an indie game the reception is completely different.

review_text:
tl;dr: The game has its flaws yet I can't stop playing it. Fun (but repetitive) gameplay with great customisation. 

Few games let premium features be accessible to free-to-players, but in this case, SEGA has shown some generosity.
There are numerous ways of getting the Star Gems currency to access things like the premium battlepass and renting extra storage space for materials. If you're a new player, I'd advise saving the Star Gems on Material Storage Rental, your inventories can get cluttered quick, having a button to deposit the crafting materials all at once in the storage is handy.

My biggest gripe so far is that character slots are limited unless you are willing to spend real money, and I'm the kind of person that likes having multiple different characters/styles for roleplaying. You can somewhat work around this by having set "looks" be bookmarked for easy switching between several styles. There are also salon passes and color passes which are trivial to obtain, so you're free to experiment as much as you like. I also wish performance was just a little better, it takes a painful amount of time to log in and loading into new regions can get tiresome with how often/long the game halts. With that said, apparently performance was in a worse state before I got in, so I suppose I should be thankful the game runs at all.

Core gameplay is very fun and engaging with parries and dodging, however it can also be repetitive, especially so when seeing the same enemies you've fought in the tutorial still lurking around far later into the game. The small amount of the special moves that the weapons are provided doesn't help with this problem either. The toolkit you get is the toolkit you will have for the rest of the game, except you may get an extra whistle or two to shake up the gameplan, e.g: A counter attack when you dodge an attack, or you unlock a meter to build up with attacks that can be spent on a heavy hitting attack. 

The amount of customisation and options at the player's disposal can be overwhelming and that's a good thing, there is so much to experiment with and sink your teeth into here. However you will also have to work for your drip, auction house prices are high and you'll have to work on your dailies/weeklies to earn enough for the gear you want. With that said there's also a free gacha accessible every day alongside a gacha accesible via star gems.

review_text:
Here is the deal. As someone who started playing PSO2 on the original Japanese servers back in 2014, I can't help but feel disappointed with NGS. The charm of PSO2 was in its randomly generated stages and central hub. PSO2 captured the essence of being on a home ship and embarking with your team on missions. Emergancy missions were awesome as the matchmaking allowed for a full team of 12 players. The game offered numerous quality-of-life features that benefited free-to-play players, and the vibrant economy thrived due to accessible trading and item exchanges. 

Sadly, NGS's shift to an open-world format and alterations to the PSO2 formula appear to be Sega's strategy to increase monetization, pushing players to spend more. Each update feels like a regression, especially with the current power system acting as a barrier to boss encounters, the most enjoyable activity in PSO2. The open-world design and player distribution sometimes result in vast empty areas, particularly outside the main hubs, having the game feel like your playing solo. The removal of friend bots sucks. It always felt like you were playing with your friends even if they where offline. With the current average of 1,557 players on Steam, it seems PSO2 has days have long since peaked.

review_text:
A perfect example of beautiful idea and poor execution. Bioshock manages to really wow with its graphics, animations and water effects unseen before. Despite its prowess in these areas the game proves that it is more style than substance as the player is constantly thrust into a reptitve slog of combat moving from one locked area to the next. Now to say that the combat is not fun would be doing this game a disservice, but once you have used all the gadgets and have fought all the enemies in the same manner for two hours it does not impress anymore. There is not enough variety to the gameplay here as you explore the mysterious city. The gameplay mechanics do not evovle or add to the FPS genre in an engaging way like Half-Life or Portal. The lack of proper pacing here makes every session a drag, especially if you decide to finish the game in one fell swoop. 

The story in the game is commendable, but given everything you hear in the logs it frankly leaves too much to the imagination and you cannot help but feel that it would have been more fun to play during the downfall rather than coming in well after the collapse. The voice actors do a good job of keeping you engaged, but their faceless characters like the story logs make it difficult to sympathise with their plight. This makes the connection feel very weak and keeping track of them all a chore as the cast builds over time. The idea to keep the player in the game rather than interrupting the gameplay with story cutscenes was a good one, however with the amount of information thrown at the player it simply does not work.

As universally lauded as this title, the flaws are overlooked by most. In a genre where innovative gameplay and impeccable story-telling are key to differentiate from the over-saturated market Bioshock does little to shake the foundations.

review_text:
Yakuza 5's responsiveness in combat is horrible.

Not seldom have I experienced only initiating a single light attack, only for my character to automatically execute a second or third attack as well. Somehow, the game sometimes mistakes light attacks for heavies, which screwed me over several times. And, when playing Saejima, often, the charge attack fails to execute after a rush combo.

All these issues mentioned above I've never once experienced during my playthroughs of Yakuza 3 and 4. These games use an older version of Yakuza 5's engine and share the same Movesets.

Let's talk about graphics. It's a big step up and almost looks as good as Yakuza 0 already. Depth of field still sucks, though, and won't work through transparent textures.

Storywise, from what I've seen, it's Yakuza (Good). I'm not yet finished, so I can't judge this portion of the game properly.

I have mixed feelings about the abilities system in this one. I've liked that in Yakuza 4, you have a list of abilities to learn from and are not restricted to choose either a Soul, Tech, Body or Heat ability. To me, it feels like a step-down back to Yakuza 3's ability system.

To end this off, I'd like to talk about the taxi minigame. In my honest opinion, it's the worst minigame in all of Yakuza. Never in my life have I seen such horrible artificial intelligence. There's a penalty called 'Contact' that triggers when your taxi touches something. That wouldn't be so bad if it weren't for pedestrians to be so awfully coded that even when you're already driving over a crosswalk, they'll still attempt to cross the road. review_text:
I hate to say this, Sega, but you fucked up, big time.

NGS is a technical and visual upgrade to PSO2. In many ways, this game is better than PSO2 - however, PSO2 worked because of an overabundance of content and small, unobtrusive, largely socially focused hub. Part of the issue - in my opinion - is that they did not commit to a direction, but weakly reached in many directions. The Combat is easier and fancier, but with less options. The world is bigger and more beautiful, but lacking in any kind of meaningful content, and most importantly of all, the Fashion aspect is as egregious as it ever was. - admittedly, the final bit is owing to the utter destruction of the original market, and the fact that the global ships always had a worse economical basis than the JP servers, owing to a larger stock due to more customers (and the fact that JP had more things in the FUN scratch, and more things in the regular scratches, too.)

The character creation and customization is amazingly good, As is the combat. The problem is, it's always the same combat.

In PSO2, combat felt weighty. moving around was slow in comparison - you used abilities to move meaningfully most of the time, and combat was alot more rigid and reflexive. In NGS, you have a dedicated dash button and can climb even the harshest mountains with ease - and these would not be problems were it not for the fact that it seems like they did not plan for this at all in map design.

That is what I mean when I say they did not commit to a direction. None of the systems compliment each other. Movement is fast, but as a result, anything else that causes the character to move feels slow. Why would I use a hoverboard if my dash is easier to control, to jump with, and I can more easily attack out of it? why would I use a movement skill if my dash is faster? why would I attack normally, when the dash attack deals more damage (this one's more situational, really, but I feel like it's still a valid point)
The above, mixed with... a horrifically disappointing stream of content. (it took them a *year* to release 10 minutes worth of gameplay, not counting time wasting, soul-sucking grinding, and another year to release a goddamn festival.) and the game is, understandably, dying in player count - or at least, it feels that way to me.

So, I can't recommend this game. Because while I have a soft spot for PSO2 base game, with the release of NGS, they completely abandoned it, and no newcoming hotfixes that try to pump the dead heart of this game series is going to resuscitate it unless they release an altogether new game - and no, not another attempt at NGS. To get people who were fans and are now disgruntled interested again - to get ME interested again. they'd have to make a free MMO that's generous about it's items and content, like the Japan-server PSO2 was, and is supported handily, like said game was back in it's day.

Goodnight, PSO, May they not desecrate your corpse for long - for it is too late for them to not have done it at all.

review_text:
-- The Short Review --
This is going to be long-winded, and probably expanded upon much like my MW5:M review as I play more. The TL;DR is that yes, I think this game is a fun time if you like sci-fi horror and melee-focused action games. However, going in to this game expecting a 'true' survival-horror experience will set you up for disappointment. Graphically impressive and with some tense moments, an open-minded person will still have a good time as long as they feel the price for admission was worth it. For ~$20, I'd say go for it.

-- The Long Review --
To get the technical stuff out of the way: the game is visually stunning. The fidelity of the environments, character models, gore, monsters, etc. is truly impressive and maybe it is partially due to not being 'current' on modern blockbuster-esque games but the graphics alone have left much more of an impression on me than I ever thought they would. The animations have lots of nuance and fluidity and look amazing. I love looking at this game and taking in the carnage of the environments as I walk and run and fight around them. The sound is great as well; I've not noticed any bad or out-of-place effects and sounds are appropriately powerful or guttural for the weapons and monsters respectively. The music has been good, not 'put this in my playlist' good but also the game would lack something without its presence. After close to two years since its release, I have not had any performance issues apart from the weirdness that can happen from running a game on native LInux with Proton. Honestly its ran far better for me than RE4R despite possibly being the more demanding game.

Now, we can get into the real issues.

The monster design is cool! They are gross and mean-looking and are definitely not out-of-place in sci-fi horror. But... they're not scary. I know that I'm also not all of the way through this game and probably haven't seen everything, but I had to start this review because it just doesn't scare me. Sure it has tense moments and some environments are genuinely creepy, but the horror element is severely let down by the mechanics of the game. The game sets you (Jacob) up as a surprisingly durable killing machine, that can swiftly dodge and dismantle the creatures that set upon you. Against a player that can handle the combat system, these creatures don't stand a chance. You will beat the ever-living shit out of them until they are convulsing in a pile of broken bones and mangled flesh and then you stomp on them some more to let them know how pathetic they are (and to get your loot drops of course).

In a real survival-horror game, combat is a gamble. Is the cost of resources worth the investment of dealing with this threat? (ex. Zombies in RE2R) Can I even deal with this threat? (ex. Mr. X or the Ubermorph) Or, for the more apt comparison of Dead Space (2008) or Dead Space 2 (2011), will I be able to deal with the enemies before they ever get close to me? In my opinion, survival-horror is at its best when you can technically deal with the threats before you, but at the same time you are sacrificing something to do so, while also not wanting these creatures to ever even think about touching you because the consequences are severe.

Conversely in Callisto, when I see an enemy I buckle up and charge in to start beating the ever-living shit out of them with a big smile on my face. The combat system isn't even that technically deep like a Souls-like game or a fighting game, but I find it to be quite satisfying. This is the complete opposite feeling I should have about combat in a game that wants to be a horror game, where the game clearly wants you to fear the creatures that you are fighting. While I enjoy Dead Space combat, I don't necessarily *want* to be in combat in Dead Space. I do everything I can to deal with the necromorphs as quickly as possible so that I can stop being in danger. Callisto has for better or worse, turned you into the danger. I am actively looking for fights because ironically that is the safest place to be in as well as the point when I'm having the most fun. Dodging is simple and easy enough to pull off, and is almost completely safe when doing so. Ranged enemies still pose a threat as your dodge animation only saves you from the enemy you are currently engaged with, but management of ranged enemies or the environment will reduce that risk. Getting grappled does not instantly deal damage to you with all enemy types as far as I can tell, or does not deal enough damage to be a big factor because of the ease of dodging. There is at least a balance issue if I'd rather be grabbed than block an attack because blocking feels like I take more damage from bleed-through. At risk of repeating myself, we'll leave it at that until my inevitable comment-extensions.

My only other major complaint is that the first three chapters of the game and somewhat into the fourth, I was drowning in items with not enough places to offload them. We don't have storage this time around so you have to sell or use what you don't need, but you can't pick up everything because the game starts you off with a measly SIX INVENTORY SLOTS. With how much stuff there was to pick up, this was incredibly frustrating. Instead of being relieved that I found another health injector or ammo for the pistol, I had to play the "Do I have enough space for this item?" game every couple of minutes. What added insult to injury was instead of being able to back-track reasonable amounts to pick up items I had to leave behind, the game pushes you forward several times with permanently locked doors or sequences that cannot be undone due to the game's linearity. Dead Space managed this finite balance well, and offset some of the pressure by allowing you to store items for later when in an excess, so that if you ever found yourself in a drought you could address it. What I will say is that I have so far found the ammunition for the pistol to be a pretty good balance of 'just enough'. Once I'm further into the game that may change.

What about the story? Oh yeah, it's there. I'm enjoying the characters enough and I'm engaged because it does feel like a horror-movie story but its not the 'best story ever told'. When thinking about Callisto's story I'm reminded of The Belko Experiment, which while I had fun with that movie it wasn't a movie I'd rush home to tell everybody about.

Despite my issues with the game, I am still having a good time and have been trying to fit it into my busy schedule. Will it hold up on repeat playthroughs? Higher difficulties? I'll know soon enough. More thoughts TBA as I get further along. Although...

Game is simple but difficult at the same time. It is easy to become frustrated with the mechanics and gameplay due to repetitive actions. For some it may be the constant hacking, others the constant attacks from machines, splicers, big daddies, turrets, etc....also I personally found the audio recordings and radio chatter cumbersome. 

For those who simply enjoy looking at walls, environment, and soaking up the atmosphere maybe this game is for you but I was overall disappointed with the storytelling, hacking, and frequent battles. You would think exploration would be the central focus of this game but its not...exploring often ends in a death animation as you're attacked from every direction. Nothing really provides you with motivation to continue other than random strangers talking to you on a radio. The game presents itself as a mystery to be solved but the truth is nearly everything you need to know about Rapture is presented in the first 10 minutes of the game.

I did not enjoy playing this game it felt like a grind, like a chore, and when I finally got to the end the conclusion was a letdown. The game is polished, it is AAA in every way but overall not for me!

review_text:
Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun, developed by Mimimi Games and released on Steam in 2016, is a masterclass in stealth tactics that revitalizes a genre many had written off as dormant. Channeling the spirit of classics like Commandos and Desperados, this game blends old-school real-time strategy mechanics with modern design sensibilities and a unique Edo-period Japanese setting. What emerges is an experience that is both demanding and rewarding, a thinking player’s game where every move must be deliberate, and every mistake is an opportunity to learn.

Set in the early Edo period, Shadow Tactics places players in control of a team of five uniquely skilled characters, each offering a distinct tactical utility. The story follows a ragtag group of operatives—led by the stoic samurai Hayato—who are tasked with rooting out a shadowy conspiracy threatening the Shogunate. Joining Hayato are characters like the cunning ninja Yuki, the deceptive and alluring Aiko, the mighty samurai Mugen, and the mysterious marksman Takuma with his loyal pet tanuki. Each mission unfurls against the backdrop of beautiful hand-crafted environments, from snowy fortresses to coastal towns and ancient temples, with a level of care in visual detail that complements the precision of the gameplay.

The core gameplay loop is pure tactical stealth. Missions are large, open-ended playgrounds with multiple infiltration routes, enemy patrols, traps, and environmental hazards. Players must scout the terrain, study guard movements, and execute synchronized actions using the “Shadow Mode” mechanic, which allows simultaneous commands to be issued to multiple characters. There are no overpowered tools or brute force solutions here—combat is rarely viable, and detection usually leads to swift death. Instead, players are encouraged to use observation and timing to create windows of opportunity: distract one guard with a whistle, lure another with a sake bottle, and quietly take down a third when no one is watching. The satisfaction comes from the chain of perfectly executed moves leading to the seamless elimination of threats.

Each character’s toolkit reinforces the need for coordination and forethought. Hayato is a classic ninja—capable of silent kills and throwing shuriken—but he lacks the raw strength of Mugen, who can carry bodies and dispatch multiple enemies in a single sweep. Yuki’s traps and agility make her ideal for luring and isolating targets, while Aiko can disguise herself and sow confusion from within enemy ranks. Takuma’s sniper rifle has devastating range but limited ammunition, and his frailty makes him best kept at a distance. Success in Shadow Tactics isn’t just about mastering individual characters; it’s about understanding how they complement one another and using them in harmony.

The game’s challenge is formidable, but it is rarely unfair. Every guard, line of sight, and patrol route is clearly communicated, and the quick-save/quick-load system allows for rapid iteration. The game encourages experimentation and rewards creative thinking, but it demands patience and planning. There is immense joy in finding your own path through a heavily guarded area and executing it flawlessly, especially when your plan involves clever use of the terrain—such as dropping a boulder, cutting a rope bridge, or using noise to create a distraction. Few modern games offer this kind of cerebral, rewarding tension.

Visually, Shadow Tactics uses an isometric perspective with painterly detail that brings feudal Japan to life. The environments are vibrant and filled with subtle touches that add to immersion—villagers go about their business, guards chatter, and the weather changes the mood of a level. Characters are stylized but expressive, and the animations are smooth enough to give every action a tangible sense of weight and consequence. The game also features a strong Japanese voice cast that adds authenticity, although the English dub is serviceable for those who prefer it.

Narratively, the game is stronger than one might expect for a tactics-focused title. While the story of political intrigue and rebellion isn’t groundbreaking, it is well-executed, with thoughtful character development and dialogue that highlights each member’s personality. The dynamics between the team members evolve throughout the campaign, especially as secrets come to light and personal motivations clash with duty. These interactions give emotional stakes to what could otherwise be a purely mechanical experience. The final missions in particular have real emotional weight, driven by the characters’ arcs and the culmination of everything you've learned.

Beyond the main campaign, Shadow Tactics offers a high level of replayability. Optional badges challenge players to complete missions in specific ways—such as avoiding kills or never using certain abilities—encouraging experimentation and mastery. The level design supports this flexibility, offering multiple solutions to every problem. For those who crave additional challenge, higher difficulties crank up enemy awareness and reduce margins for error, making success feel even more hard-won.

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a rare gem—an expertly crafted tactical stealth game that respects the player’s intelligence and rewards methodical thinking. It stands out not only for its mechanical precision and elegant design but also for its dedication to atmosphere, character, and cultural authenticity. It’s a love letter to a forgotten genre, modernized just enough to feel fresh without sacrificing the depth that made those earlier games great. Whether you’re a veteran of Commandos or a newcomer to the world of real-time tactics, Shadow Tactics is a brilliant, deeply satisfying experience that demands and deserves your full attention.

Rating: 9/10

a third when no one is watching. the satisfaction comes from the chain of perfectly executed moves leading to the seamless elimination of threats. each character s toolkit reinforces the need for coordination and forethought. hayato is a classic ninja capable of silent kills and throwing shuriken but he lacks the raw strength of mugen, who can carry bodies and dispatch multiple enemies in a single sweep. yuki s traps and agility make her ideal for luring and isolating targets, while aiko can disguise herself and sow confusion from within enemy ranks. takuma s sniper rifle has devastating range but limited ammunition, and his frailty makes him best kept at a distance. success in shadow tactics isn t just about mastering individual characters it s about understanding how they complement one another and using them in harmony. the game s challenge is formidable, but it is rarely unfair. every guard, line of sight, and patrol route is clearly communicated, and the quick-save quick-load system allows for rapid iteration. the game encourages experimentation and rewards creative thinking, but it demands patience and planning. there is immense joy in finding your own path through a heavily guarded area and executing it flawlessly, especially when your plan involves clever use of the terrain such as dropping a boulder, cutting a rope bridge, or using noise to create a distraction. few modern games offer this kind of cerebral, rewarding tension. visually, shadow tactics uses an isometric perspective with painterly detail that brings feudal japan to life. the environments are vibrant and filled with subtle touches that add to immersion villagers go about their business, guards chatter, and the weather changes the mood of a level. characters are stylized but expressive, and the animations are smooth enough to give every action a tangible sense of weight and consequence. the game also features a strong japanese voice cast that adds authenticity, although the english dub is serviceable for those who prefer it. narratively, the game is stronger than one might expect for a tactics-focused title. while the story of political intrigue and rebellion isn t groundbreaking, it is well-executed, with thoughtful character development and dialogue that highlights each member s personality. the dynamics between the team members evolve throughout the campaign, especially as secrets come to light and personal motivations clash with duty. these interactions give emotional stakes to what could otherwise be a purely mechanical experience. the final missions in particular have real emotional weight, driven by the characters arcs and the culmination of everything you've learned. beyond the main campaign, shadow tactics offers a high level of replayability. optional badges challenge players to complete missions in specific ways such as avoiding kills or never using certain abilities encouraging experimentation and mastery. the level design supports this flexibility, offering multiple solutions to every problem. for those who crave additional challenge, higher difficulties crank up enemy awareness and reduce margins for error, making success feel even more hard-won. shadow tactics blades of the shogun is a rare gem an expertly crafted tactical stealth game that respects the player s intelligence and rewards methodical thinking. it stands out not only for its mechanical precision and elegant design but also for its dedication to atmosphere, character, and cultural authenticity. it s a love letter to a forgotten genre, modernized just enough to feel fresh without sacrificing the depth that made those earlier games great. whether you re a veteran of commandos or a newcomer to the world of real-time tactics, shadow tactics is a brilliant, deeply satisfying experience that demands and deserves your full attention. rating 9 10

review_text:
I really really really wanted to like this game.  I love the Rimworld, Dwarf Fortress, ONI, etc type games, and I've always liked tower defense games, so I found the concept of this game quite intriguing.  And there is a lot of game here... lots of buildings and upgrades, interesting world map concept and global perks/xp, migrating people from your starting town outwards to start new towns... all this plus tower-defense style planning.  What's not to like?

Alas, it never really came together for me in a way that was actually fun.  You can tell there's a lot going on under the hood, but the UI is frustratingly opaque and uninformative; I frequently found myself unable to get the information I wanted, or unable to do anything with the information once I had it.  There's a ton of buttons, windows, menus, and lists, but there's no tech tree or tutorial to unlock them in a logical order.  So the initial experience is a little overwhelming, but I rapidly got to the point of knowing which buildings were important, which towers were needed, and what order to build things in, at which point... there was nothing to do.  I found myself just sitting there, watching the game flicker by at a fast speed, occasionally upgrading buildings/towers, and wondering what to do next.  There are no real goals, no obvious way to interact with the world, no significant advantage in expanding; nothing to really plan or strategize or think about.  Even bad things that lead to people dying can be mostly ignored, since your people are almost instantly replaced by nomads with no discernible penalty that I could detect (there probably is a penalty of some sort... but that gets back to the opaque UI).   I rapidly ran out of interesting decisions to make and ended up just marking time until I could migrate out more people to create a carbon copy of my village all over again.  Which after the first few times, really isn't very interesting or challenging anymore.

And a personal pet peeve.... dogs barking.  You eventually get dogs to join your village.  And they bark.  Non-stop.  Literally hours of a background sound track of bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark bark.  With no way that I could find to turn off their barking or get rid of them, without also turning off the "something important happened!" type sounds.  This won't bother everyone, but for me it was the final straw.

review_text:
I want to love this game, after waiting 4 years beating Arizona, and pumping this game up to many others; im left feeling dissapointed. 
Ok, i'll start with the bad:
Bugs - Shit tons of them. Weapon atachements/mods is a broken system. All mods look the same,so if you accidentally drop an old one, then pick it up, and try to replace the current one on the weapon, you cant tell which is new or old. 
You can collect and buy mods for weapons you dont own yet, and they look similar to ones you think you can use, but the game doesn't stop you from trying to bolt-on to other weapons. The mechanics of selection/assembly of weapon modifications is broken. 
Lobby / Multiplayer - The division of the difficulty levels and actual maps doesn't really work; most people choose easy and this reduces the chance of playing harder levels. Cross platform barely works, i've discconnected more than I finish maps, and the lag can be unreal most of the time. Its also broken.
The reloading mechanics on Valve index are disjointed; ive only tried the auto reload feature, even though it halves the amount of harvest you get, I cant figure out how to change it to manual. The game resets the player height and other variables each time you play, but not the reload option-strange. But the auto reload only works 50% of the time. Ive even tried swapping Index controllers, and it didnt help. 
Actual multi-player match making is broken, it seems to put players with teamleaders who are AFK or not really in the lobby, this happens all the time; and the game stalls, and you cant do anythig except look for another team.
There are so many annoying kids playing that flair / speed run to get achievements, the little story/plot of the game gets lost in the shuffle. 
The Good 
The maps are fun, when they work, and the spawn points, locations of the breed are great; the game is challenging and fun in that regard.
The concept of snow breed, and the survivor/resistance culture and feel is somewhat unique, and I think thats cool too
Like I said, I want to love this game, but honestly, why the fuck this game took 4 years is beyond me. In its current state Id consider it MAYBE EA, but def. not final products. 
The bosses are fun, and challenging, but repeptitive, and ive litterally played the game less that 5 hours in total.

review_text:
Nearly a year later and we still have empty promises and no updates. 

The whole idea of bonelab was built around modding and we still haven't gotten the SDK update or workshop support. The whole selling point and main campaign idea was that you could mod the game. Even before bonelab released, the devs were hyping up the fact that this game could be the Gmod for VR. It's not like the developers are trying hard to save their game. They've been nearly radio silent since the game came out, relying on the communities false sense of hope and underdeveloped mods to keep the game going. 

Onto the actual game itself; It was disappointing. It was hardly a sequel to boneworks. Half of the campaign was just a tutorial for the new characters, while the other half is just linear. Boneworks' biggest selling point was that you could beat the game however you wanted. There wasn't one true way to beat a level. This is especially true on the level Warehouse. Furthermore nearly all the new enemies in bonelab are just reskinned boneworks NPC's. If there is a simple way to describe the gameplay of bonelab, it would be "Boneworks 0.5" as it felt like more of a downgrade than anything else.

I tried to love Bonelab more than anything, but seeing what it is now and the fact that the once respect Stress Level 0 developers have adopted the "Launch now, fix later" ideology and not make any improvements to the game for nearly a year hurts. I don't understand how this was the same company that made something as good as Boneworks. 

TL;DR: Don't buy this game. The gameplay isn't fun and the devs abanonded it. If you want an actual fun campaign try "Boneworks", "Vertigo 2", or "Half Life Alyx". If you want a fun sandbox try "Blade and Sorcery" or "Hot dogs Horseshoes and Hand Grenades".

review_text:
Relic Hunters Legends is like if the Destiny and Borderlands series had a Saturday morning cartoon child.

The game overall is a charming game filled with a mix of 2D with 3D environments/weapons, a very unique visual style. Each character are different and has their own special abilities to suit different playstyles from Tank, Support, DPS! The replayability for this game is quite massive as there are plenty of characters to level and even a mode that queues you up with players that need assistance through the story or mission (and also get rewarded special currency for it!)

As an Early Access game for the price of $10 (When it was discounted, normally $15) -- It is very well worth the price as there is so much content and story filled inside it to fulfill those needs. Story Quests, Multiple characters to play as, Hard Mode, Endgame content, and many more. It is a looter-shooter at heart with plenty of RPG elements such as leveling up characters, gearing up, and collecting a variety new/unique weapons. I personally can't wait to see this game grow more and more once the full version of the game launches.

With Early Access games comes many negatives of course, as there are plenty of glitches that happen in the game. For the hours that I have played, I've mainly ran into more visual glitches than anything entirely game-breaking worthy so it wasn't too much of an issue for me. Thankfully, the devs added a Bug Report button/system so players can assist the devs in finding out the glitches they can possibly fix!

I highly recommend Relic Hunters Legend if you are itching for a looter-shooter with a more laid back top-down style game.

review_text:
While it's definitely not a perfect game, I definitely still recommend it. The description does say it's the first of a two part series - something very apparent by the time you reach the end. It's clear it's not a complete story.

I feel the '80 hours of romance' is a huge overstatement on several fronts. Even though it is necessary to play through multiple times to really get the full story (and it can be fun to uncover all the different moments available based on the choices you make), there's a lot of repeating what you've already read.

The art is hontestly flat out *gorgeous* on all fronts, though. All sprites are well designed, including the side characters. CGs are also beautifully done.

The 'extras' in the cast do have a bit of no-eyes syndrome going on but the protagonist, at least, has a face when she appears in CGs so that's a definitely plus – and it makes the no-eyes extras more forgivable.

There are also a lot of really gorgeous backgrounds. A lot. Because the scenery changes quite a bit, there's a huge variety of different environments and a lot of small details that really add to the experience (such as showing a simple ceiling BG when the protagonist is lying in bed.) It feels like they went to a lot of lengths to ensure the game was visually appealing. The fight sequences are also well done, and are set up in a way that makes them more engaging than just looking at static sprites on static backgrounds. 

The simple animations definitely enhance the experience. And the lip-synch animation is actually done much better than a lot of visual novels. So props there. 

All the love interests I've played so far have distinct personalities. While some characters have similar traits, each one is still unique enough to stand out from the others, which is really nice in a game with so many potential love interests. I think the characters are interesting and, for the most part, likeable. Some characters have clear and interesting development as well, which makes the story fun to read.

The writing, from a technical standpoint, is well done. Things are written clearly, they're easily understandable, though there are a few typographical errors here and there.

But…as I mentioned above. '80 hours'? I just don't see it. 

First of all, there's not much 'romance' to speak of - much less 80 hours of it. Most of this part of the story focuses on the political goings on around the protagonist so she actually spends comparatively little time with whatever specific love interest you're pursuing. What scenes she does have tend to be more on the platonic side - there are exceptions and some routes have more obvious hints at romance than others. These moments are often short and don't really go far beyond hints until the latter chapters of a few routes.

But  I just struggle to see how there's 80 hours of content at all, due to the sheer amount of re-reading previously read content. It seems extremely exaggerated at best (unless the 80 hours refers to parts one and two together. In which case, it seems misleading to list the complete amount what is only part of the story).

Personally, I find the story to be the weakest part of this visual novel. While the characters are interesting, fun, cute, and often intriguing…

They frequently get a bit lost in a story that's trying to juggle too many events, too many sub-plots and a too-huge time scale. Characterization and relationship development often suffer while the story tries to cram a huge amount of historical upheaval into a fairly condensed game experience.

To be safe, I'll put the rest below spoiler tags:

[spoiler]The amount of time this game covers is at least four years. That means a lot of time skips –often months at a time, over really a really short amount of play time. This rapid jumping through time causes a sort of strange situation where the story both feels like it's moving way too fast and dragging on way too slowly. 

For instance, many characters (including the protagonist, frankly) show relatively little character development despite the amount of time that passes. Even though they're aging four years - sometimes going from child to adult - there is not much emotional maturing that happens. The MC is as naive and innocent four years later, as she is when she first joins the Shinsengumi. And that is after living alongside seasoned samurai, helping out on missions and being surrounded by death.

There are other issues with the time scale not seeming to match up with story development. It's hard to believe that hints of romance developing in her first months with the Shinsengumi remain mere hints four years later. How does a relationship not develop at all during that amount of time?

There's also a lot of ambiguity as to what exactly she's doing during that four years. She clearly isn't learning to use her sword (she's as useless in battle during the final chapters as she is at the start.) Some routes indicate she is acting as a medic but this isn't addressed at all if you focus on other characters. And either way, she's never really shown acting as a medic. It mostly happens off-screen or in conversation.  Like other things, it feels glossed over and cast to the side in favor of focusing on the upheaval and struggles of the Shinsengumi as a whole.

The story just didn't seem to be able to balance the events going on with actual character development. 

The demon/fury sub-plot kind of comes out of left field. As if historical fiction wasn't interesting enough on its own so they had to make the main character special by being not human - and throw some Vampires in for dramatic effect. Some aspects of it aren't handled extremely well, particularly in some routes. It typically only surfaces when it seems convenient for stirring up some drama. I also felt that some elements of this plot struggled to find any sort of internal logic to follow and were a bit all over the place.

This is another plot that is handled better when you focus on some love interests than on others. But the fact that some routes feel so much better balanced while others are lacking gets a bit frustrating at times.[/spoiler]

All these elements together cause the story to sometimes buckle under its own weight. I found myself really dissatisfied, at times, with how sluggish things were moving and at others I was frustrated because it felt like I was just skimming the surface of what could be a really detailed story.

All of that may seem like a serious gripe but this visual novel definitely has parts that are enjoyable. There are some fantastically lovable characters, and it's definitely a joy to just look at. Seriously. The art's [i] really[/i] beautiful.

For those thinking of buying the game, I recommend waiting until it's on sale. Lovely as it is, I don't think the story content warrants the full price. Despite its length, it very much feels like a prologue or set up to a longer story. Which explains the skips through time and glossing over of certain story elements and the lack of development in some areas. It feels very much like it's just prepping you for what's to come. 

All of that's fine, honestly. But I wouldn't personally pay full price for something that doesn't really read like a full game/story.

review_text:
i have 600 hrs on steam, but I also had about 300 hrs on SEA server way back then, and 1,200 hrs on JP before NGS.
Base PSO2.. I loved the game. the combat felt great and rarely felt repetitive even though it objectively was. the bosses were great and had a lot of variety to them, both mechanics and design-wise. 

rather than a review, the following is a rant. skip to bottom for actual review and why the recommend.

the only things I really hated about base pso2 was the obtuse and unnecessarily complicated affixing system, and the gazillion types of currencies. NGS solved those and also brought shiny new graphics and an open world, but at what cost? pretty much everything else. what used to be a more customizeable and varied combat experience is now so watered down that all classes feel almost the same. gone are the highly varied and epic boss designs and fight mechanics (except maybe the dark falz and retem worm). the monsters are all same-y not just in aesthetics, but in mechanics as well. Base PSO2 had the many Dark Falz's, Red Dragon, Masquerade, Yamato, AIS space fight, ep6 final boss, all accompanied by the epic scenarios, all play very differently from each other. 
NGS profoundly (hehe) confuses me. PSO2 was already great! all it needed was some trimming of abandoned features and reworking the affixing system, i think. ok, new combat mechanics, open world, new story, cool! why not a full sequel instead? maybe they wanted to carry over the loads of cosmetics, tie them together and stuff, maybe a way to cover the licensing issues with the collabs idk? a way to reuse the assets and save workload? but they still had to remaster all those anyway???? ok, maybe just the idea of having all your stuff from base onto a new world is cool. i think it is. but then it effectively kills the player market for base PSO2?? was base PSO2 really meant to be left alone and abandoned?? Why even join them in the first place?????

I could probably go on forever on all the stuff that Base PSO2 had that just got lost in NGS for forever and all the other questionable decisions put into the game, but at this point, it's all been said by others.

----------------------

WHY THE RECOMMENDATION:
Now, all that are negatives and just me ranting my disappointment on what the game has become and how base PSO2 was meaninglessly killed off. So why the recommend?

well, taking for what the game is, NGS is, well, fine. It has solid gameplay in its foundation. there's a sizeable amount of content to enjoy. It's not objectively "bad" per se, it's still pretty fun to play for a while actually! If you're a newcomer, I recommend playing it with a few friends casually. Base PSO2 is still also technically playable too and it's pretty good for what it is. It's got the advanced classes and infinitely better boss encounters, although of course it's also a decade old game, so expect it to feel rather bloated/overwhelming for a while.

as a veteran player though, I just.. I'm never playing this game again. NGS, what it's become and becoming, the death of base pso2... there's just too much heartbreak and disappointment for me now. most of the things i really liked just arent in NGS anymore. and they dont seem to be coming back either. Maybe if the Etoile class comes back and we get more bosses as fun as those i mentioned, I'll reconsider it. idk. I'm really just a pso2 boomer now i guess.

review_text:
"Look around you. This horrible bunch of psychopaths are all begging to join up with me, but unfortunately for them, I only take the best. And today, best means whoever can kill you. Come on out lads. It's initiation time."

[i]Batman: Arkham City[/i] is an action-adventure game developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment.

[b]Story[/b]
I suggest playing through Arkham Asylum first, as events from that game are used as a setup to setting of this one.

Arkham City takes place 18 months after Arkham Asylum events. Taking credit for stopping Joker's siege, director Sharp becomes a Mayor of Gotham City. Declaring Asylum no longer suitable, he creates immense prison enclosure known as Arkham City inside Gotham's slums, taken care of by mysterious Hugo Strange while monitored by private military firm TYGER Security. Our protagonist, Bruce Wayne, opposes that idea and ends up in a titular prison himself. Here as Batman he wants to find out more about mysterious Protocol 10 and real intentions behind the prison.

[b]Gameplay[/b]
If you played Arkham Asylum, you already know what to expect as City builds up upon gameplay from previous game, providing third person open world venture where you will investigate, explore, stealth and brawl through the prison as our favourite Caped Crusader, searching for truth (and few faces to soak your fists in).
First thing you will experience is the main dish of the game- combat. Punch, kick, smack thugs before they smack you to avoid a dreadful fate of watching villians laugh in your face as you lose and reload a checkpoint. Counter or dodge incoming attacks, chain up combinations to gain speed and power, utilize plenty of gadgets to surprise your opponents. Game provides improved version of the "Freeflow" combat system, meaning you can now perform more moves, such as option to counter multiple attacks at once or being able to chain combinations for long enough to unleash deadly special attacks. Enemies can be armed with different armor and weapons, forcing you to adjust your moves accordingly.

Sometimes you get a chance to resolve encounters silently. Similar scenario as with first game, utilize vantage points, environment, detective vision and your gadgets to eliminate enemies without them noticing you. Watch as fear strikes their minds and heartpulse keeps rising with each performed takedown on their buddies, but just like in combat, thugs are a bit more Bat-proof this time so they come with more firearms, jammers and extra tools that will make your life harder, as tides can quickly shift back and forth. Know when to strike and when to wait for opportunity, or just create your own!

Arkham City opens up the area, providing way more space to explore. Glide, grapple and sprint around looking for collectibles that expand the narrative and lore, side activities, or just seek out local thugs waiting for a fight! (Or to be knocked out silently by a sneaky Bat.) Fans favourite Riddler returns with his trophies and riddles, while other villians make an appearance in side quests spread all over the prison, unlockable as you progress through the story. Same applies to gadgets, so you might have to wait a bit to obtain a tool or two before you can enter certain buildings or collect specific trophies. No pressure, you can always return to every area you visited.

Combat and exploration grant you experience points, earn enough to level Batman up and unlock new skills, moves, or improve gadgets.

[b]Playtime, other modes[/b]
It took me roughly 13 hours to complete everything in Arkham City. After beating the story you unlock New Game Plus where you can utilize everything you have unlocked with increased overall difficulty to balance it out. Additionally there is "Riddler's Revenge" mode, where you tackle on different challenge maps and campaigns for medals! Fair to say you can spend a bit more time in City than you might think at first glance, if interested. Especially as this version comes with extra DLC, Catwoman content, and extra characters in RR mode.

[b]Impressions[/b]
Out of the gate I will go out with a very bold claim- Arkham City is probably the best sequel I ever had a pleasure to play. A textbook definition of how they should be made. It's not a revolution, but an evolution. If you played Asylum you feel right at home almost instantly as game keeps same great controls and fantastic core gameplay allowing you to quickly get into action, increasing and opening up the location where game takes place, addition of side quests and expanded lore make it feel like an entirely new experience. Already great combat is now reaching superb levels, it's smooth, it's intuitive, with very tight controls and top notch precision when it comes to inputs as if game knows which thug you want to hit before you even do. Some annoying moments from Asylum where Batman in the middle of combination would decide to punch ghosts are gone, combined with new moves and gadgets it practically makes you beg for as many enemies on screen as possible to go wild.

But game knows when to slow down, when to give you a stealth section to showcase pretty solid enemy AI, allowing you to fully lean into Batman's strategic side with various gadgets, careful planning and utilization of environment to his advantage. Quite frankly it's a shame that because game is no longer as linear as first title, plus complete change of area where game takes place so it's almost impossible to just give you a stealth section in the middle of the city, it doesn't actually have that many of those section. But when you get them, it's an absolute treat to play.

Asylum no doubt had it's own unique atmosphere, but City is no slouch in that department either. Prison filled with crime in the middle of gang wars, with secrets on top of secrets, the mash of destroyed slums with iconic locations, freedom you get to explore it and encounter many more and lesser known villians across short yet satisfying side quests, it hits right. Fortunately game never feels too long, it doesn't drag on, even if you decide to dive into the madness that is collecting those forsaken trophies.
Fantastic audiovisual side, strong art direction, top of the game performance from voice actors and animators, game even today looks fairly impressive. Forgot to even mention expanded extra side mode of the game in which you can spend plenty hours, if running around Arkham City gets boring for you.

If there something...mixed, I can say about this game, it would probably be about the story. In my book the main villian in this one was a bit..disappointing? Especially as he was pretty much a "main face" when it came to promoting the game. I expected a better conclusion of certain arcs and felt like it could have focus on just one story, instead of jumping around and trying to have two main storylines branching out and at least for me, that never really worked. So yeah, story is enjoyable but I would like it to go into a different direction.

Nonetheless, Arkham City is simply superb. Easy recommendation. Combat feels great, explorating feels enjoyable, still holds up visually and it's a treat for fans of DC/Batman.

[b]Final words and conclusion[/b]
Said it before, gonna say it again, GOTY Edition comes with everything released so you get all the fun stuff- alternative costumes, post-main game DLC and extra characters- in one pack!

Batman: Arkham City improves pretty much everything from first game while still focusing on core strenghts- fantastic combat, great audiovisuals and intriguing exploration. Buy it, play it, enjoy it.

review_text: This game is a chore to play. I don't wanna say I didn't enjoy it but it is very very lacking. The stealth is shit, camera's spot you without you even knowing where they are, the handler gets very very annoying if you keep restarting, you have to rely on quick saves that 9 out of 10 times put you in a spot you don't want to be and the fact that you have to watch the briefing every single fucking time when you play a contract is extremely annoying. The story is a cluster fuck that wants me to care about the people I kill while I cant even pronounce their names. The sniping is decent but without a good silencer you cant really snipe up close which is not an issue, but while I was playing this game I found myself not really relying on my sniper instead I went for close quarter kills with my knife and pistol. The assault rifles are lazily added to the game without reason. The only AR that felt somewhat good was the AK but the rest of the guns have to much recoil making them unreliable. All sniper rifles feel the same with small variations there are some rifles who are impossible to use because of their lack of noise suppression. For someone who almost only used a silence pistol in his first playthrough they feel like dog shit. They are good if you want to take one guy out but the second you shoot your second shot it feels wrong like it isn't finished. The DLC feels outrages having to pay for extra guns (that are not viable) and cosmetics you probably don't use because they look awful on your weapon The game doesn't feel finished I can understand that people might like this game but for someone who expected a stealthy sniper shooty shooty assassin game I am disappointed. Just get sniper elite this game isn't worth the price it currently has. Anyone who doesnt think this game is a 4 out of 10 clearly doesn't have any experience with games in this genre, the fact that this game is mostly positive is beyond me. After finishing the game I tried going for a 100% run but quickly found out the challenges are either very very easy or just down right annoying to complete. I tried only killing the target in the first mission to find out after completing that dumb ass challenge that it didn't even register. I have also encountered numerous game breaking bugs like trying to hide in a locker to find myself stuck on the outside unable to move. The AI is abysmal either spotting you from across the map or not seeing you when you are standing right in front of them. Throwing rocks sometimes doesn't work revealing your location. When a single enemy saw you and you don't kill him quick enough the whole area suddenly know's your exact fucking coordinates. I really really tried to like this game but its borderline unplayable. The ending was super predictable if you interrogated all of your targets and was just sequel bait for another broken mess of a game. This game is incredible short only having six levels that blend together. There are only two variants between the levels and the only big difference between them is that you can swim without slowly dying of hypothermia in the green foresty area. This game is not finished and it will never be finished the second game should have been part of this game instead of a completely separate game.

review_text:
When this first released (as early access) it was fun, very fun. There were some issues but not that many. It honestly felt more complete than most other games I have played despite being early access.
A lot of changes have happened since then.


CLASSES & WEAPONS
Each of the 6 classes start out with the same weapon. The signature weapon for each class is locked behind this leveling. And now the weapons themselves have levels to grind!

If I change weapons, I lose all the customization, ammo type, scope type, I had on the previous weapon, have to re-add it all. And again there are like 6 classes you gotta do this on over and over. Sometimes I just click on a weapon to view it's stats (which I sometimes feel there are too many of) and ooopss. There goes your loadout customization you had before.

Rocket Launchers - who doesn't like rocket launchers? There used to be situations in nearly all game modes where you or your teammates would get some. They were fun and really helped when overwhelmed by large ranged enemies in the distance. I have not seen any at all in a looong time.

Weapons that are not fully auto besides sniper & pistol really wear our your mouse click finger. There are a lot of bugs. That means a lot of clicking if your weapon is not fully auto.

GAME SYSTEMS
"Re-Enlistment" which is basically Prestige did not mention I would lose all the weapons I had already unlocked. They are wiped out. I am starting over - AGAIN. I am literally uninstalling the game after writing this review.

Carnage system is great for immersion but it reallly seems like there are wayyy less enemies on hard mode than I saw before.

GAMEPLAY
There are new events like grenader bombardments from space - if you are out doing an objective you cannot defend yourself from them or mitigate the damage. They come from straight above you so you cannot see it coming. You get blown away from your team. If someone comes to revive you, now you both die in the bombardment that happens after that because the timing is just right. 
I would rather be vaporized.
Sometimes you get blown away down a cliff and someone with a jet pack revives you then scales that huge cliff with their jet pack. Well I don't have one...I gotta walk way around this huge cliff. What feels like 20min later I am back in the game. 
Again I would rather be vaporized.

Walls are not preventing enemies from coming through before they are destroyed.

MENUS
I used to be able to choose the game mode and difficulty very easily but now I can only choose from a preset list of certain mode & difficulty combinations, but not all combinations.

Horde mode is MIA and when I do see it, nothing happens when I click on it. This was my favorite game mode.

SUMMARY
Yes it is early access, I knew that going in. I am sure a lot will improve. My opinion on the game as swung back and forth between positive and negative a lot. Ultimately the design decisions for the classes, weapons, and prestige system are what annoyed me the most. I have played this game for soooo many hours, and because of these systems I have only used 3 weapons: The basic rifle, the Saw, and the grenade launcher. Because everything is locked behind leveling, or eliminated on prestige, or eliminated in a patch, I can't even experience the others. Weapon variety was the biggest complaint when this first released. It has been addressed, but in the worst way.

review_text:
This game is a huge disappointment. Gameplay is mostly about grinding.

The levels look completely uninteresting and empty, nothing is interactive, just completely static environment. And level design is also lacking, mostly because of random placement of key objects like chests.

I think the key gameplay mechanics can be described in just a few sentences in the design document, something like "run, shoot and dodge" which is very sad. Enemy AI is absolutely trivial, they either run around trying to find a way to you or just stand slightly away shooting projectiles. Combine all this with limited equipment which does not give you any strategic options.

review_text:
Awesome game. Definitely can feel the inspiration from games like Silent Hill, Dead Space, Resident Evil, etc. The atmosphere is unnerving and gradually gets more and more demented the farther you get into the story. 

Performance wise, no issues and seems well optimized. Ran great on my PC and the visuals look awesome. I did not encounter any bugs and it never crashed on me.

Combat feels good. If you enjoy those games I mentioned above, you will like this. Resource management is important and getting comfortable with the charge mechanic of some of the weapons is important to increase damage and cut down on ammo usage. There are several weapons and utility items to choose from. You can also use the environment to your advantage in many situations.

The game follows a linear path, though it does seem to promote exploration within. A lot of upgrade resources and other items will be missed if you do not stray from the beaten path at times and find the codes, keys, etc. to access certain areas. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of the genre, as not only does it provide more than other similar games released over the years, it will also have you coming back for more with every update, eager to see what new features await... and perhaps do "just one more" [quick] run into another 20+ hr campaign.

Overall, extremely disappointing. It may have potential but I'm not sticking around to find out. Developer should look to games like the original Sonic or Mirror's Edge, and see how the game could be done right.

review_text:
This is a very mixed review.

This game has atrocious onboarding and UI.  It loves to break conventions and does a terrible job of making it clear to players what is happening and why.

Despite this, the unique genre combo is quite enjoyable.  City builders can feel aimless, but having to tower defend provides a purpose for expansion.  The introduction of god powers means that you always have some action that you could be taking to improve your game.  The end result is a surprisingly addictive game that's quite fun for ~40 hours if you can get past the initial roadblocks.

Unfortunately, in the late game, the flaws in this unique combo start to show.  Much of the game is structured as a god game where you're not supposed to have insight into hard numbers or mechanics.  This is fine until you realize that enemy difficulty scales infinitely (practically).  When you know you're guaranteed to lose, the only fun is in seeing how far you can get - yet the game doesn't track records and optimizing runs is frustrating when every mechanic is opaque.  The game feels incongruous to me; I think it would be vastly improved if it picked a side between casual god game and deadly tower defense.

Ultimately, if you can accept poor UI and can handle intermittent frustration, this game has a solid amount of fun to offer.  Just don't expect the same amount of depth and replayability as many other city builders.

review_text:
There are aspects of this game that work okay, but by and large the balance feels really off in a way that's kind of uncomfortable. This game is still in beta right? It feels like it is. With the aging aspect, there's no reason to get to know anyone or feel close to anyone, they're going to die pretty soon (including your character), and you can turn that off, but people are still going to die in your own (idk if this is a bug, since you can turn off both player and general aging, but they will still die). 

On top of that, gifting seems a bit misleading or broken. Characters will have dialogue that says things like 'wouldn't it be nice to work where (X character) works and get Bread wherever you want! Mm' (or something like it). Suggesting that it's that character's favourite food. It's not. It's a tooltip hidden in dialogue: Go to that shop for bread. But because liked gifts are vague and often buried you can go through 10 dialogue / talk options to get to something that *sounds* like a gift that isn't one. Needless to say I gave that character Bread and they were mad at me, lmao. 

There's no sprinkler system, and the watering can doesn't water larger areas as you upgrade (it just holds more water). Be prepared to waste nearly half of your day or more purely on watering if you want to make a decent profit and have access to food. 

It's *hard* to get access to basic building components. There's a limited amount of wood you can get per day, a limited amount of resources, an extremely limited amount of stone (until you get an ultimate tool upgrade). As far as I can tell, without the extremely expensive *ultimate* steel pickaxe, you have to buy basically all your raw building resources re: mining from characters that are only intermittently available (and who will die, and be replaced by others over time). As someone who has had the satisfaction of mining from Spring onwards in every single other game, this just feels really bizarre and limiting, especially since even with making farming and fishing as easy as possible through the Options, it's just a hard grind to ever have enough gold to do what you need to do. 

In terms of the balance specifically feeling off, as an example, I am mostly only catching gold fish now and getting high gold/silver crops in Summer of Year 1 (the endless grind for resources), yet still don't have a Barn or Coop, because I keep sinking money into raw materials like nails for storage options (which are stingy and cost a lot). 

Likewise, cooking to recipes is both time consuming (you can, at least, leave the pot to cook on its own), and extremely resource consuming. Expect to be using more than 4 pieces of meat (which costs more than your basic tools) for example, plus 15 units of other ingredients, for a single meal. As a result, my cooking skill is still on like 1 or 2 and I live off mostly raw and gifted foods. There's no balance to the way the different skills grow, because you'll be so desperate for food and coinage that things like the extraordinarily resource hungry cooking (where even some "basic" meals require fruits from fruit trees that take a long time to grow), and resource hungry crafting, just fall by the wayside. I can sort of see how they've thought a lot about late game rewards re: cosmetics, but I don't know if the team who have created this game have realised how much of an absolute slog it is to even get there in the first place. Every drying rack, preservative maker etc. takes an inordinate amount of labour, grind and gold to acquire, and does not pay itself back investment-wise for a looooong time. In some cases you're better off NEVER getting some of these things, and just buying them outright in trade, which sort of ruins the reason for / joy of crafting - that you can do stuff so much cheaper and easier and faster than buying it outright. 

There's some niggling annoyances re: QOL like targeting not working properly (i.e. I cannot tell you how many times I've clicked on a storage item or sign and walked straight past it because I didn't get exactly in the yellow box in the perfect way). I wish the game had more signposts or the ability to earn more signposts (maybe that exists, I don't know). As for the Pillars (think Community Centre Stardew Valley but different), there should be an ability to see what you've completed/achieved in your main (possibly Family) section so you don't constantly have to go into the particular section (which involves a lengthy time-wasting walk with no resources along the way) just to remember where you're at. The Community Centre achievements had a nice menu-accessible option which would solve a lot of QOL issues on that front in this game. 

The pros: Despite everything it is playable. The art style is nice, and the characters are cute. The grumpy characters are so grumpy you will almost look forward to killing them (or them dying), which is not something I ever thought I'd say. The fact that ships can visit (inc. pirate ships) is cool. Resource gathering can be enjoyable. You don't have to worry about romance at all aside from getting married to make sure you get some of that sweet sweet child labour both before and after you die, and you won't have to worry about remembering anyone's gifts because every character is transient and they won't clearly tell you what they like most of the time anyway (TL;DR I have maxed friendship for multiple characters just by talking to them so often and *never finding out what they like from them or others talking about them* lmao - me: trying to find out their liked gifts, them: actually talking is fine). The gifting mechanic re: characters gifting you is pretty generous. The lighthouse and ocean locations are great, and the sound effects are well sourced. It hasn't crashed for me, though there's been a few visual glitches, none has stopped me from playing the game. 

I have turned off a lot of mechanics in the game to make it more liveable / enjoyable for me personally, I definitely recommend going into the Options of your game, though try it unaltered first to see what you like and don't like. 

I wish this game had been tested a bit more before launch since a lot of this stuff could have been quickly picked up, especially around targeting, QOL, a more generous watering system, the gifting mechanic, and the unbalanced levelling between skills (I've never seen a stingier cooking system in my life. I could make these foods in *real* life using less ingredients. The reality is that you can buy an iron watering can - a later stage tool - or make one (1) dario burger). 

Farm games are my thing, I've been playing them for over a decade, I've picked up almost every indie one I could get my hands on, and have sunk over 1000 hours (each) into the ones I love most. I was determined to give this at least 10 hours of my time to see what it's like, and started wanting to give up around hour 6. I think I'll keep going just to see out all the seasons, but the appeal of getting close to no one while being able to randomly poison or cough on characters to kill them, is just not that fun for me.
