Before talking about act 2, im gonna make a resume of chpater 1's pros and cons.
Hiveswap act 1 was an absolute fucking joke of a game, most hidden acchievements were bullshit, that 2nd snake puzzle was also bs, the game lacked a LOT in the comedic field and you did not have any good or fulfilling reward for clicking on stuff. There was one (currently) impossible acchievement and the songs were (mostly) trash and ABSOLUTELY unfit for the occasions. Xefros was an absolute loser and the game was overral trash (i have made a review about act 1 already, check it out for a more eloquent review).

Act 1 was awful and a joke of game that was as unfunny as the god awful jokes it tried to land (which obviously failed incredibly). Act 2 on the other hand, is an absolute MASTERPIECE of point-n-click games. Most of the first game problems were fixed in this one, with the best addition to the game being autosave.

PROS:

When you are in the game's menu, there is a recap button, which shows a visually incredible recap of act 1, the devs and artists were amazing on this one.
There is a lot of homestuck's charm here, like not writing we're correctly (they usually forget the '), the songs resemble Andrew Hussie's godlik soundtrack in its quality, Toby Fox and James Roach really overacchieved themselves this time. There are 8 bit music, orchestras, trap (matuê) and many other music genres.
The game manages to FLAWLESSLY time the expository dialogue (like when they explicitely say that you have to switch characters for  some puzzles) and intertwines it with mysteries and some deep thinking in order to make a great experience for the player. The game has many long dialogues and textboxes, however they effectively tell the story and don't make them pointless with unfunny gags.
The game also really makes Xefros a character with depth (even though he is 2d), like how he simoutaneously finds it wrong to just go inside some troll's cave but at the same time doesn't give much of a fuck about breaking in the bee house. I'm not going to give spoilers about very important parts of the game so rest assured, you can enjoy Xefros being much better for yourself if you buy the game
For the comedy, it was a MASTERPIECE of the genre, there is Marvus, there is an amongus reference, there are moments where Xefros goes XXD (which is a super awesome thing to say XD), there is a super duper funny dialogue when you are in the bee house where they say "it's a lamp" (still makes me lol everytime XDDDD), the acchievements are EPIC references (i might not have understood many of them, but they were XD awesome either way), in the last car of the train, they play the mlg horn (which is super awesomeeeee), there is an acchievement for getting catfished multiple times, and many more INCREDIBLE comedic gags. If you are looking for a good laugh, buy this game.
About the characters, the most notable one has to be Marvus, he has great dialogue (such as "cum n prove ur innocence", it's SO funny [because he says cum]), doesn't have a speech pattern like other trolls and is overrall the best character in the game, with more detailed animations then Xefros (the guy that you are with for the entire game). Tegiri is also a notable one, with him being a huge anime fan and being awesome with his chuuny side during the jade's car. Chixie is another great one, being a rapper that speaks in verses, which unfortunatelly didn't have the form well translated, making an unnatentive viewer think she only puts random slashes on her speeches.
The game has an overrall solid structure and good enough storytelling. You can't run and there is no fast travels, which i don't like, however allows you to VERY CAREFULLY analyse the ambients the artist team put so uch effort on building. You also can't make the text quicker, allowing you to read the textboxes EXTREMELY ATTENTIVELY. The story is great and has GENIUS plotpoints, like the ticket part, which happened because silly Joey tried getting a ticket without much thought and ended up on the ordeal to aquire 2 tickets for both xefros and herself.
There is a bee rythm game that was easy and fun, definetely a treat to play and a fun side challenge for you. The autosave function does a lot of heavy lifting for the game and does a good job at saving on occasional important parts of the game. Marvus basically gives you a mini spoiler to break the 4th wall. Most acchievements are not secret anymore. There is definetely no reused animations (DEFINETELY). Bazli wears a sad emoji mask. All of these sweeten the experience even more, being great details.

CONS:

No bubsy
You still can't run/go faster

review_text:
Scorn is a pretty unique experience. The bleak and hostile world that you explore is art direction at its finest. It showcases a very depressing and gruesome imagery of a world that is clearly on the brink of collapse just by observing its surroundings. One of the standout features to me at least is the fact that the entire game is seamless. Once you start first chapter and later the final chapter, you won't encounter a single loading screen at all. The only drawback to this is that you'll encounter some stuttering since the game is rendering new environments as you progress. As for the soundtrack, it helps amplify the experience with its ambiance and eeriness. It further highlights Scorn's tone and visuals to a T. So that alone, Scorn wins in the audio and visual department.

The story for Scorn if you can call it that, doesn't really lead you in on any details. This is mainly due to the fact that you get no exposition, no narrations, or any context for what is going on. All you know is that you wake up and you're on way to your objective. The rest is all left to the world building, the journey, and what you take from it. This leaves Scorn's story up for interpretation and open discussion which in my opinion works well.

In fact, the gameplay itself is minimal too with the information such as your health and ammo only being shown when you have your weapon drawn or how many healing items you have by looking down at your view model. While it adds to the immersion, it goes overkill with the fact that there are some puzzles in the game that are annoyingly difficult to figure out. Then there's the combat which is just ok. Now granted, most encounters can be avoided so you wouldn't even have to engage, but sometimes you are forced into combat since some of the battles with the creatures are in corridors where avoidance really isn't an option. Plus fighting the same enemy type over and over again gets real tedious.

Thankfully once you get through the worst, Scorn gets kicking into high gear towards the end which you need to see for yourself if you haven't already. Now the campaign is very short and there's no bonus content whatsoever. My hours and 100% achievements are proof of that. And while normally there would be cause for complaints for this, I think it works in the game's favor since:

A: Combat is annoyingly tedious and repetitive, 
B: You've just finished a bunch of frustratingly long puzzles do you really want to spend another 30 minutes on another one?

So really, the game ends right before Scorn's shtick gets stale and that's honestly the best way to finish it. 
Would I recommend Scorn? Absolutely.  It's a game you should play at least once... But it is not for everyone. Just be prepared for some of the hard knocks you'll face in its runtime. Also $40 is pretty high considering the campaign's length so grab it while it's on sale. 

TL;DR
Scorn is a masterclass in art direction, world building, and it's soundtrack. The combat is meh and puzzles can be cryptic. It's not that long, but overall a solid experience.

review_text:
It's a scammy, gimmicky, buggy (Pun intended), mess, and poorly optimised.

 All characters can clip through walls and be damaged by parts clipping through walls,
and parts clipping through walls can be damaged too.
The game's aesthetic is very clay-like.
The movements of the characters, bugs and people alike, are all very stiff.
The game is very jittery and laggy, the more players join a lobby the worse it becomes.
All of these issues aside from the art-style were not present before the release update.

The clipping and/or stiff art-style wouldn't be so bad but all of those things together break the keystone experience.
The gameplay.
Also, I personally hate the bugs that shoot you. They interrupt the gameplay loop of shooting bugs before they get too close. I also feel like the "Gunner" bugs just break immersion, they don't feel like bugs, or anything from Starship Troopers. They feel like, aliens with assault rifles.
If i wanted to play something like that, I would.
I want to play a Starship Troopers FPS.
Instead I played this scammy, dead on arrival building simulator.

Get Helldivers 2 instead, same price way better experience.

I really wanted this game to work, but even the aesthetic is lazy and can't be taken seriously.
This franchise has been a major let down for more than 2 decades now, the original film and PC game were good.
The sequel films were bad, 'Starship Troopers 3: Murauder' especially.
The 3D C.G. anime spin-offs were okay.
The only good game I imagine is the RTS, but there hasn't been a decent first person bug shooter since the old Starship Troopers game, and that was a singleplayer, linear, experiences based on the '97 film.

review_text:
A metroidvania that feels like it was made by a small team which has some truly awful combat.  You can equip one special item and two weapons, but early enemies are either slow and plodding or have ranged attacks that they let off in quick succession.  Many fights were 'hold shield to block projectile, move up, block projectile, move up, block projectile, strike, wait, block projectile, wait, block projectile, strike...'

Arial combat causes you to stop moving and drop as you swing.  You can equip a special item to slightly help, but this is in place of better options like a damage booster.  Other items are misleading, such as a 'slingshot' not being a weapon but instead an item that improves the damage of a limited number of consumable thrown grenades.  Magic is already powerful and if you have MP you can waste difficult enemies. 

The thing that made me end up refunding the game so early on is the save system.  You can save at a small number of computer stations and you automatically save when you encounter a statue.  But you can't autosave at the same statue until you've saved at another one.  This feels like an attempt to make a slower, more deliberate form of gameplay but it feels overly restrictive along with the other issues.  It seems average at best and even watching a few videos showing where the story will go did not make me want to continue.  The cadence of combat just isn't worth the frustration to me, but I'm dead certain that it will 'click' for the right people and be an enjoyable (but too short) experience.

review_text:
I have finished the game now, so here are my complete thoughts on it:
I really want to like this game, but there were a lot of things that put me off of it.

Quality of life is worse than KCD1. They added more systems to take away from player time, resources, and fun. For example, herbs can now expire like food.

Combat is worse than KCD1 IMO. Early level combat feels impossible, more impossible than any low level combat that I encountered in KCD1. Even at level 14 with master strike and training, it's nigh impossible to take on two armored bandits with my dog. Having now completed the game, it feels like the game is centered around late-game combat even though it only takes up a small portion of the game.

'For Whom the Bells Toll' is the single-worst quest design that I've ever encountered. I hated that quest and I hated monastery in KCD1. Stealth from one end of this place to the other, oh I need this thing that's back from where you started, go all the way back then come all the way back to me. 

There are a lot of bugs and crashing for me personally. One of the worst bugs is that I'm getting trespassed in rooms that I already paid for, effectively taking my money and rescinding on the paid service. In the second region, I've crashed half a dozen times. Throughout the game I also encountered floating NPCs, combat camera getting stuck looking anywhere except the enemy, locking onto enemies not working properly, and one specific guard on a mission spotting me from behind a wall, 40ft away, behind him, when you proc him with proximity to move for a certain quest.

It feels impossible for me to know what level I should be or what level of equipment I should have before I invest way too much of my time in a quest that I'll just have to reload 10 saves before to finish later (INHALE) because my stats/equipment aren't up to par. Ultimately I think this comes down to the game focusing too much on end-game play and not enough on early-level fun. 

I will say that the game was much more fun late-game for the reasons I mentioned before about it feeling focused around that. The story got much better towards the end. I felt invested in my companions and allies towards the end of the game, and their personalities each shown through. I had a lot more fun with the combat and skills late-game.

review_text: There is so much that I could go on about regarding this game, but I'll try to keep this as short and as sweet as possible. This game is as close to the ideal hockey management sim there has ever been, by a long shot, and that can probably be seen in my hours played lol. The amount of detail and customization available in this game is staggering, and the ability to pick any league/team is refreshing, as taking over junior teams is one of my favourite features. The drafting/scouting system is very well thought out, and even acts like real life, with players falling/rising and teams drafting based on positional needs rather than BPA. Free agency can be a little iffy at points, with many core/superstar players all available at once. The salary cap rises very slowly from year to year, which is another issue, but it's a fun challenge to go along with building a dynasty. Developing prospects requires patience and playing them in the right spots, and it really is rewarding to develop a superstar, or watch a 6th round pick grow into a key player. Trading is good as well, as there will be times where you get 'ripped off' and others where you come off with a steal - asset management is a big thing in this game. The only complaints I have, albeit minor, is that if you draft well, the game gets easy very quickly, as you just trade good players for picks, let them develop, and repeat. As well, if you don't know hockey that well, the game may be a bit tricky to begin with, but the tutorials help with that. Additionally, the custom roster/logo//facepacks that come along with the game are very well done. I would highly recommend this to any hockey fan/sports management fan - 10/10, 2 thumbs up!

Great if you like oldskool shooters. Don't bother if you expect something slow-paced and story-driven.

Now, after few years I feel all refreshed about it, which is typical to happen. The story gets a bit too confusing later (2nd game), but that's very typical in ambitious projects, which Bioshock totally is, one of few really good onesev. review_text:
Before we get into this, I need to note, my review is influenced by an upcoming change, slated for Monday, 11/6/23, at 1 AM EST (or 11/5/23, 10 PM PST).

WOULD I RECOMMEND PSO2/New Genesis TO NEW PLAYERS?  Currently, ABSOLUTELY NOT.  While any game has its ups and downs, and deep down I do love the game / series, there's definitely pros and cons, and the upcoming change is a MAJOR addition to the cons list.

Pros:
- Combat flows very smoothly, and the attacks are very flashy
- The music is truly fantastic, some of the best songs I've heard in a game.
- Character creation is one of the most complex/full-bodied systems I've seen in an MMO -- while the face and body customization aren't quite on the level of BDO or better, the accessory system allows a LOT more freedom for end results.
- Beautiful and unique scenery
- What little bit of story is in NGS is decent.
- Hanging out with friends, like with any MMO, is a good time.
- Creative Spaces, one of the newer features, is a pretty great iteration on base/house building mechanics.

Cons:
- For as smooth as combat is, it gets very samey after a while.  Each weapon just has their optimal 1 or 2 attacks, and that ends up being basically all you use outside of very rare and specific situations.
- Rampant and greedy monetization.  Most content pumped out, over the last 2 and a half years, has been cosmetic gachas.  If you want to be able to sell anything, be it drops from said gachas, or drops you get after hundreds of hours of farming (that'll be the next point), you need to fork over roughly $15 USD per month, or use the single-time pass for 3 days of shop access that you get less than once per month.  Freemium currency is also used a lot, but sources of it in-game dry up very quickly, and sells for an absurdly inflated cash price if you cave (do not cave).
- Drop rates of anything of actual value in the game are ABSURDLY low.  We're talking lower than most MMO's END-GAME LOOT tables.  Quite literally, the last big set of weapons had, at the time, an estimated drop rate of 0.0000002%.  It's not fun or rewarding, it's a lottery.  Fans in both the Global and JP regions have given feedback on this multiple times, which has been acknowledged, but then completely disregarded / doubled-down upon.  This makes the game feel incredibly unrewarding, with most players never seeing BIS weapons before they become irrelevant again.
- Content updates at a snail's pace, and the last half a year has added no new MSQ battles, only a handful short 30-60 second cutscenes.  Basically no interaction in the main-story, in all that time.  First act of the game isn't even completed, we're just on Episode 1, Chapter 6 part 3, and the (actually exciting) plot hook at the end of chapter 5 hasn't gone anywhere yet (that was over 6 months ago).  Current content, outside of story, is just a level increase in older areas.  Which they've already done two previous times in the same maps.
- Mishandling by Sega has left the playerbase in a state of constant atrophy.  We're looking at less than 8k players per day, on average (and only roughly 2k players on steam per day), and that number has been in steady decline since Spring. 
 Thankfully it's cross-platform, but it does still result in the game feeling a bit like a ghost-town.  However, Sega's solution was to delete most blocks, forcing all these players into congested hubs instead, which ALSO negatively impacts game performance for many.  (Also, the game can only render 50 characters, at maximum, at one time, so, on days with very low block counts / higher than average online players, you might not be able to see most of your friends because strangers filled up the render limit when you load in)
- Lots of arbitrary limits -- limited accessory slots, seemingly random "point costs" assigned to them that can't go over another arbitrary point cost limit, limited build gauges in the creative spaces (but they give much larger limits in alliance(this game's version of a guild/free company) spaces, so it's not a hardware issue at all), caps on non-currency points you can earn per day/week, etc.  No reason behind some of them (accessories being the only one with some kind of reasoning, but the point costs still make no actual sense), Sega just likes limiting what you're allowed to do / your creativity.
- MOST IMPORTANTLY, the new change coming on the 5th/6th -- Sega is switching the anti-cheat from GameGuard (which isn't particularly great, to be fair) to the incredibly intrusive Wellbia XIGNCODE3.  While you can "opt out," it will still be downloaded and installed to your PC.  For those not in the know, XC3 has a reputation of running at all times in the background once installed, whether a game is using it or not  It also has been known to scan personal/unrelated files, transmit personal information (making it a potential violation of NDAs or HIPAA laws if you use your PC for both work and play -- also, on their part, their practices violate laws in much of Western Europe and the Americas), increasing CPU performance loads / power usage at all times, being an overall security risk for the consumer, etc.  It installs with kernel level access, too, which is far from great.  On top of that, it's been known to cause MANY false-positive reports, flagging AMD's anti-lag features, VPNs, Linux OSs, third party keyboard/mouse/fan management systems, etc., as attempts at cheating and automatically calling for a permanent ban of the player.  The constant intrusions of privacy, and consistent false-flagging, has led to most games in the western market that used Wellbia to scrap it in under a year and issue a massive apology, compensation, etc. but Sega seems to not know or not care.

If you work from home but only have the one PC, then, once Wellbia is implemented, even if you opt-out, this game will become a job / security liability, so uninstalling (or not even starting) is honestly your safest option until Sega walks this back.  If you use Linux (and therefore, Steam Deck), expect the game to barely work, and to eventually flag you as cheating because of your OS, resulting in a permanent account ban.  And know, their support/appeals team takes forever to respond, and usually assumes guilt even if you have indisputable and irrefutable proof to the contrary.  If you get banned, you're probably staying banned (unless they realize how many false-flags Wellbia makes and do a mass apology like so many MMOs before them -- but I doubt it).

All said, I love this game.  I usually WANT to recommend it, even in spite of its flaws -- which, it has MANY, and they really do need to fix them (most of these issues have been discussed in the official headline videos, solutions have been promised, corporate "apologies" have been made, but it has now been 2 and a half years, so, not feeling likely) -- but the change from GameGuard to Wellbia is the straw breaking this camel's back.  I strongly recommend avoiding this game like the plague until Sega takes this back -- if they ever do -- or letting it die like Sega seems to actually want, judging by their business decisions of late.  Or just play on console, if you have the option (where it performs much worse, and has way more limitations, but it's still an option).

review_text:
At first bonelabs was pretty alright in my opinion at launch, had pretty good time.
however thats not why im leaving a negative review, the reason why im leaving a negative review is due to the fact that the game came out with bare minimum.
What do i mean by that you may ask, well as the new additions are cool, like the new expanded hub, avatar system and drive able vehicles, thats pretty much about it, nothing really else is new for example the enemies or the improvements of the body physics, honestly it all feels like a copy and paste from boneworks but with half of its content removed, now i dont mean that literally i mean it metaphorically, meaning there is half of the content in bonelabs then in boneworks.

The other reason is the lack of updates from the devs themselves, gaps between each update is way to long, they allegedly promised 2 years of content and we only got one major update, it wouldnt even hurt if they gave us average development logs to let us know what they are working on, otherwise people will lose interest or people will complain and later become bored.
Now what things that also make this review negative:
-Most of the levels are just to show off the avatars physics and mobility, they are more like unnecessary puzzles or a walk through.
now i know boneworks has puzzles but they implemented them into the environment, however in bonelabs they "stick out like a sore thumb" and ruin the exploration of the first game.

review_text:
I've played this game since being a beta tester and while I do still enjoy it; you should have realistic expectations. As the only Star Trek game this gives it a big plus but often it rides on this very notion. This game could have been so much more but it is effectively a smash em up style MMO exactly the same as CO and NWN in terms of the gameplay. What we hoped for all those years ago was a refined tactical shooter; what we have presently is a combat game that is explosive to the point of it being OTT. 

My biggest gripes with STO are:
- Lack of ability to retain builds fully; the tedious detail you have to go into to switch between a build, or even a ship. You cannot save your skill points you have to spend money to respec them if you move from one ship type to another. Then you have your duty officers and traits on top to manually tweak to get the most out of your new choice of ship.

- Combat Gameplay: It's too erratic; not at all like the tactical shooting we see in Star Trek. Shield vectors matter little, this is effectively press space bar and unleash everything at once. Ground combat is also drawn out, and not even remotely fun.

- Things to do: I really wish the game had more going for it but after a while you're just logging in to see what new ships there are.

- Pay wall - So many ships are hidden behind a pay wall of some sort; a real shame that they don't allow players to access ships through ingame credits. 

I would love to see this game evolve into something it deserved to be.

review_text:
The game feels really great for the first couple hours, the guns look and sound amazing and the levels and enemies look pretty nice too, but before too long you're forced to interact with the progression systems and to put it simply they're really bad.

In-run progression takes the form of a choice of random perks every time you clear a group of enemies, but most of the perks  range from okay (a spell recharges faster) to effectively worthless (extra healing potion slot when you'll maybe see a potion drop once every five runs) with a much heavier lean towards the worthless side, and it'll be hours before you unlock any means to influence your choices. At no point did I ever really feel like I'd had a good build going.

Out-of-run progression comes from spending your two currencies on character levels that feel completely worthless (boosting max HP or stamina by roughly 1% at a time) and gold on starting random gun/spell/passive item unlocks that then require you to go into a run and basically just kill time until the unlock completes, all for an item that will feel not worth equipping until you spend 10 runs grinding out its own upgrade conditions (which are also gated behind items you have to spend gold and time on to accrue).  It's a whole lot of grinding and waiting for results that very much don't feel worth the time investment.

Lastly, the games difficulty ramps up pretty fast, much faster than any sort of power increase you're going to feel from the progression of your character both in and out of runs, which basically destroys that good feeling you got from the guns in the first few hours as your demon-empowered revolver with the muzzle report of a cannon loaded with saint blessed bullets starts taking multiple headshots to defeat peasants with pitchforks just because they started glowing red.

review_text:
I know this is going against the grain some. A lot of this game is very good. Visually very appealing. Very good controls (I played on the Steam Deck and had zero issues). Really distinct characters with unique mechanisms, nifty new twists in levels (I liked the disappearing snow footprints), and the combinations of the characters really changes how you play. I also liked the Shadow mode that lets you create a simultaneous string of actions to pull off big moves, though I am not sure I truly "got it" and ever truly took advantage of it.

But, the game starts to get really hard. I lost interest after I finished Mission 5 (assassinating Yobu at his castle). The level was so tightly patrolled that it felt like a very tedious, trial and error slog of slowly peeling back and onion to do anything. I spent 30 minutes after I finally assassinated the target just trying to sneak my characters out to the escape point as they added even more guards and patrols. When the game focused on cool powers and figuring out the fun way to do something? I enjoyed it. I liked the experiment. But, by level 5 it just went from "neat puzzle sandbox" to "tedious puzzle" and I put it down after completing the level.

I think the true way they want you to play this is going through the game to learn the levels and the mechanisms. Then, go BACK through to pull off more challenging requirements, or do it without killing or being seen. That all seems fun if you have infinite time and really want to invest. But, I wish the game's approach to difficulty went a different path and not just "infinite guards." It's very cheap, so I definitely got my money's worth the for the 7 hours I played. Still, if asked, I wouldn't recommend it. Not my favorite stealth game.

review_text:
Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is part one of a two part remake of the classic Hakuoki: Demon of the Fleeting Blossom dating sim. With six new bachelors to obtain, there is no shortage of engaging, well written content. While I do have qualms regarding this being released in two parts (Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds and Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms,) it is still well worth the time and money spent to relive the Hakuoki experience.

PROS
-12 Unique, likable bachelors with engaging, individual plotlines
-Gorgeous and consistent art
-Stunning soundtrack
-Excellent writing
-Tons of replay value

CONS
-Only half the story, to be continued in Hakuoki: Edo Blossoms
-An utterly massive amount of information overload regarding 1860s Japanese government systems. Truly, far too much information. If you're a real big historical fiction fan or history buff in general, you are in for a treat. Otherwise, buckle up, kiddo.
-Awkward user interface. Sometimes feels like a lazy PS Vita port.

If you're a fan of the original game, Hakuoki: Kyoto Winds is worth picking up for the new content. If you're a new player, and a fan of dating sims, it's a must play.

review_text:
“The year is 2007... the apocalypse has had an apocalypse.”
Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is what happens when a development team says, “What if we took everything from 1980s sci-fi action movies and crammed it into a game — and also made it funny as hell?” The result is a short but explosively fun standalone expansion that completely ditches Far Cry 3’s realism in favor of laser dinosaurs, cheesy one-liners, and VHS-fueled chaos.

You are Sergeant Rex “Power” Colt, a Mark IV cyber-commando voiced with maximum gravel by Michael Biehn (The Terminator, Aliens). After being dropped into a neon-soaked island crawling with mutants, killer robots, and dragons that shoot lasers from their eyes, you must stop your former commander from nuking the world… again.

The story is ridiculous on purpose, delivered in 8-bit cutscenes and overflowing with parody. It’s a love letter to ’80s B-movies and Saturday morning cartoons for adults — completely aware of how dumb it is, and loving every minute of it.

At its core, Blood Dragon is Far Cry 3 in a new skin — but what a skin it is.

Classic Gameplay, New Attitude: Expect open-world outposts, stealth takedowns, looting, and plenty of explosions — all wrapped in neon and synthwave.

No Crafting, No Grinding: You level up automatically, and weapon upgrades are earned through missions and side content. It’s streamlined, fast, and focused on fun.

Laser Guns & Explosive Bows: The arsenal is pure ‘80s excess — shotguns with explosive rounds, miniguns with infinite ammo, and sci-fi rifles that hum with power.

Blood Dragons: Giant neon reptiles that can be used as terrifying weapons… or terrifying enemies. You can even lure them into enemy bases using cyber-hearts.

Side missions include rescuing nerds, blowing up infrastructure, and liberating garrisons. It’s dumb, loud, and absurdly satisfying.

The art direction is intentionally retro-futuristic: purple skies, neon-lit rocks, glowing rivers, and scanning HUDs that wouldn’t look out of place in RoboCop. While built on the same engine as Far Cry 3, the visual overhaul gives Blood Dragon a distinct identity.

The synth-heavy soundtrack by Power Glove is phenomenal — pounding, catchy, and perfectly matched to the world’s vibe. Think John Carpenter meets Mega Man.

Voice acting leans hard into the satire, and Michael Biehn delivers every line with exactly the kind of gravelly, no-nonsense sarcasm the role demands.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a rare kind of spin-off — one that fully embraces its insanity, breaks the mold of its parent game, and becomes something completely unique. It may not be long (a focused 5–6 hour experience), but every second is packed with absurd fun, nostalgia-soaked style, and memorable moments.

This isn’t a “serious” Far Cry game — and that’s exactly why it works so well.

Recommended For:
Fans of 1980s action films, players who enjoy tongue-in-cheek humor, and those looking for a short, explosive, highly stylized shooter.

Avoid If:
You’re looking for realism, depth, or a serious story.

Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is a neon-drenched blast of retro insanity — short, sharp, and unforgettable.

Rating: 8/10

review_text:
If I had to compare this to any game, it'd be Football Manager 2007. EHM has always had a very similar layout and skin to the early FMs due to Sports Interactive's involvement, so anyone used to that kind of skin and general aesthetic feel to the game will feel right at home immediately.

EHM provides just enough depth for your hardcore players to immerse themselves in but is also very simple to pick up and play. The game has a hardcore community of fans and players who've played the game since its very first release and who also provide extra content and small modifications. A quick Google search will take you to a couple of forums I'm referring to.

Back in my time at uni, I found myself addicted to FM12 due to its healthy all-round balance of fun gameplay and vast database. EHM is no different, and at the ripe old age of 24 I regularly find myself slipping into comatose states at 3am instead of sleeping and performing appropriately at work later that very day. Even as I write this review, I am at work. The game is brilliant.

Unlike many management games, this has a 'pick up and play' quality to it and provides the option to manage a team 3 or 4 levels below the Elite League in the UK. Where tactics are concerned, you're able to give full instructions to your entire team, all lines and even individual players if you see fit, to a very specific level. If that doesn't emphasise depth, I'm not sure what does. The game is an absolute steal at £14.99 as well! Genuinely can't stop playing it.

review_text:
A puzzle game in which you construct various structures using shape-shifting goo balls.

[hr][/hr]
World of Goo drops you into a foreign world inhabited by different kinds of goo balls. The game comprises a series of levels, each of which contains a number of goo balls and an exit pipe which you'll have to help the creatures reach. To achieve this, you can grab any goo and attach it to others, leading to them being connected through trusses. Goo balls can slither along these trusses, allowing them to move across goo structures and towards the exit pipe.

The goo trusses are rather flexible, meaning you'll have to keep an eye on the integrity of the structures you create, lest they collapse. This is further complicated by the fact that each level requires a minimum amount of goo balls to reach the exit in order to be completed, so you'll have to strike a balance that allows for as many goo balls as possible to stay free. To push this concept even further, every level contains a bonus challenge, tasking you with completing it in a set amount of time or with an even greater number of goo balls escaping. These can be rather tricky to complete and provide some nice replay value.

As you progress, World of Goo gradually introduces different kinds of goo balls, such as floating or flammable ones as well as various stage hazards. Through this, the game's basic premise manages to stay interesting throughout its runtime while maintaining a fair difficulty curve. Every level also contains some observational monologues provided by an unseen character. This provides some background information on the world and events of the game, though stays rather vague throughout, leading to me personally not really caring too much about it.

For highscore hunters, the game also features leaderboards for each level, allowing you to push your solutions even further. Similarly, all goo balls you collect throughout the games' levels are placed in a separate area, where you can use them to assemble a tower, competing with other for the highest one.

Presentation-wise, World of goo goes for a charming cartoonish look that complements its overall tone. There's some decent music playing throughout the game, though it is mostly atmospheric and thus rarely memorable. Overall, I found the game's atmosphere to be a bit too bleak overall, which certainly matches the lore it contains, but can feel rather dreary.

[hr][/hr]
All in all, I enjoyed my time with world of goo, in large part thanks to its interesting premise.

What's there to say that hasn't been said yet? I think Act 2 of Hiveswap is phenomenal. It takes the game in a different direction, whereas Act 1 has mostly focused on locations, items and descriptions, Act 2 knocks it out of the park by focusing on what we all really wanted from the game. Trolls. And lots of them!

I think it's by no means an exaggeration when I say that what Act 2 puts into form is something every Homestuck fan has been wanting to see from day 1. More Trolls, more interactions. The train is a fantastic setting as well, allowing the player a highspeed hemospectrum tour that openly displays what has been canonically known for a long time, the way trolls interact with each other according to their social hierarchy dictated by blood.

And do not get me started on the music. While Act 1 had catchy tunes, Act 2 really knocked it out of the park with some absolute bangers (Quadrant Confusion) and some actually terrifying jams (Down with the Clown).

Overall, this is what we've been waiting for. All those years in the making, what Act 1 failed to deliver was realized in Act 2 and I'm very happy for it. It bodes well for future acts and it has me genuinely excited to see what's bound to come in the next 4 years.

review_text:
This review WILL contain some Spoilers to story and gameplay!
I don't write a review often, but for this it doesn't deserve the hate it gets.
For my part i sadly (Or probably luckily) got finally around to play it over 1 1/2 years after release so most on launch bugs and crashes most likely have been fixed (I didn't have a single crash in my 13,2 hours of game time.)

Let's start with the negatives.
Combat: Combat is.. very simple and I found a cheese very early on in the game if you continuously press A and D while meeleing you dodge pretty much every attack. I very often looked at my second monitor and reading or watching videos on the side while I just kept fighting against multiple enemies.
Enemies: There isn't a big variety of enemies. Overall there are like 5 different types of enemies (I count the "fat" and blind ones to the nomral ones). Which is fine but I believe the game would have benefitted from some more one off big monsters that you might not be able to really fight, the 2 Heads are put as a miniboss in too many stages of the game imo and after the first 2 times they were more annoying then adding to the game.

Now to the positives.
Story: It is a great story. All the elements for a "Stranded survival" experience are there. Isolated on a dying station. No way to get help other then helping yourself. A very interesting plot with backstories to how the place came to be and an ending that leaves many questions behind that need an explanation in the future projects!
Graphics and Perfomance: Game is running very stable on my PC (I5 Processor, 16Gbyte RAM and a 3060TI), graphics are very beautiful. A lot of gore and scenes that straight up reminded me of Dead Space (Which is a huge compliment imo). 
Weapons and Creativitiy: I really like the weapons, there aren't a lot but they show some creativity in design (Still simple tho) and I thought the "frame" for every weapon to then switch out the top part was fun. I sadly couldn't figure out the point of the tactical pistol until the end haha. The Alt fire modes are pretty fun.
Overal atmosphere: Game captured the atmosphere of what it wants to be very well. A stranded experienced no help from authorities, isolated with some very strong minded NPCs in the game.


Overall opinion:
Is it a masterpiece? Far from it. Is it a bad game? Not at all. 
It is a very solid start from what could turn into a really cool universe with a cult that controls government bodies that want's to bring Humanity to the next stage of evolution by any means necessary. A resistance group that wants to stop them. It is a great concept with A LOT of potential and I hope we can see more in this universe to build on top of this!

Admittedly, I was expecting more horror from Scorn. I guess it depends what kind of horror you enjoy, but there's barely any scares or tension in this game. Rather, it focuses mostly on gore and body horror, with some visuals that may disturb the trypophobic. The imagery honestly didn't disturb me as much as I was hoping it would. I think it's still really well done for what they were trying to accomplish, but unfortunately not scary in the least.

Rather, Scorn is an exploration of a uniquely disturbing, inscrutable world with a small amount of puzzles and basic combat sprinkled throughout. The puzzles were surprisingly satisfying but I was hoping for more. The combat was a bit of a bore but not too bad if you approach enemies more as an obstacle to avoid rather than confront. I was finished with the game in about 3.5 hours and I tend to be slow at completing games, so it's a pretty short experience.

The story is told entirely through the environment and was mostly indecipherable for me. I could piece together some bits, but not enough to satisfy my curiosity. The ending specifically was a major "what the fuck does this even mean" moment, and it left me pretty disappointed.

The art direction is where Scorn really shines, and it is mesmerizing. I would probably only recommend this game if you want to immerse yourself in its bizarre, fleshy world.

[h1]My Rating: 2/5[/h1]

Batman: Arkham City.. after I had finished Arkham Asylum I was convinced I had to buy the other 3 parts.

The first few hours were fine and even fun but the more i played the worse it got. 
It kinda feels like an expontential graph, that is decreasing.. 

Open World? true, it is bigger than in Arkham Asylum but manouvering through it is still a pain in the ass. Don't get me wrong, gliding has some nice mechanics... as long as batman doesn't get a mind of his own and just decides to grapple somewhere completely else or "get stuck" on a railing or something that he could have definitely glided over.

The Main Story is finished pretty fast. You play both Batman and Catwoman altough the time of catwomans appearance is still very short (story wise). 
The game is very monoton. Go from point A to point B, fight some guys, good job! now please return to point A, oh i forgot; please do this and that scattered all over the map! 

Batman Arkham City also has a way of putting you against Armed enemies which is sad as it highly determinds your playstyle. Want some action, yep no.. you ain't gonna find any here cuz if you don't play this stealth as an Assassins Creed game every enemy that is armed will fuck you over. Who's idea was it to call Batman Arkham City an Action game and then let Batman enter a gunfight unarmed without the intention to kill anybody. 

The rest:
-Side Missions
-Riddler Throphys 
-Challenges 

... make it very difficult to have fun. 
The Side Missions are flat, boring and poorly designed. Should have been longer with more variety to gameplay. Especially Szasz just annoyed the hell out of me with these phonecalls. The whole mission is literally about listening to this guy talk to himself and moving your mouse for several seconds just so he can hang up on you and call somewhere else. 10/10 good idea, very fun, lemau, gonna go cut my pulse artery now.

The Challenges are the purest form of horror for a completionist like me. Play more than like 20 levels on 4 different characters, but guess what, they changed the combat from Arkham Asylum and even managed to make that boring and annoying but not just because of their quantity noooo, it's literally the same.. over and over... you're gonna spend hours upon hours upon hours wasting your time on this game just so you can flex with those hard earned achievments. 
A grind that is supposed to drag out the length of the game but with that kind of game design i highly doubt a lot of people liked it.

All in all the game is highly overhyped, in my opinion, and you should be very careful what to expect!

You know what, I'm not even trying to be funny here. Over 1,000 hours on Steam version of PSO 2/NGS and even more when it was on the Microsoft Store only, as well as the original JP version. Here's what I have to say:

They BLEW IT. NGS could have been amazing, but they went so damn long without any significant content updates that tons of people fled the game. It's gorgeous, and the gameplay is good...when there's actually things to do.

Grinding is a core element of PSO/PSO 2 and other later Phantasy Star multiplayer games. But along with that, we've always had the thrill of rare drops, ranging from dumb things that are just fun for cosmetic purposes, to overpowered & ridiculous weapons with crazy effects. The gear game was where this series really shined, and being able to hunt items & have random crazy drops fall on you were things that personally drove me forward through countless hours of grinding. 

While PSO 2 had some of this initially (later turning into a grind for items to 'craft' endgame weapons...bleh but even then still had a lot of drops available!) NGS has pretty much anything but. What's with all the sets of garbage weapons that have been released over the years? 3-4 sets of 1-star, 2-star, 3-star & up weapons that barely have any differences between them. Nothing unique, cool or powerful randomly dropping from enemies (until way later, and even then, they eventually become easy to obtain) 

I don't know, man. I felt like expressing my disappointment. NGS has some good points, but it moved away from what made PSO addicting. 

Give us back:

Instanced areas (and like, MOSTLY these. This open area stuff is just padding!) dungeons and the like. I know NGS has a bit of this, but not enough! 

Drop in a plethora of new random/unique/interesting rare drops with cool and unusual effects. Assign nice and thicc drop tables to everything, as usual make only the best stuff drop for the highest level zones, but give the lower level areas some interesting things for newer players to find too!

Take us back to space! 

You know, after finding out Halpha was an experiment, I've been secretly hoping this game would just send us to some space colony/starship and be like SIKE!!! We're gonna A Realm Reborn this just and make it PSO 2 ver.2 but...I guess that won't be happening. Instead we got NGS ver.2 which...gave us housing. Hoooraaaaay.

Alright...I'm done. I'm just bitching at this point.

"Mom, can we stop for Dead Space?"
"No sweetie, we have Dead Space at home."

I really wanted to like this game, and after finishing the main story (still deciding if I'll go back for DLC) the best thing I can say about it is that I guess it was OK for $25 CAD for the Deluxe edition on sale. 

I had no issues with the performance all the way through, and the combat was mostly enjoyable, but WOW was the level design atrocious, almost all throughout. Your character's default walking speed was comically slow to begin with, but that's ok, because you spend most of your time crawling, sidling, and wading through forced slow-movement sections that, if used smartly, could have ramped up the tension, but there were entire sections of crawling through a duct, walking 8 feet, crawling through another duct, walking 10 feet, slowly squeezing through a narrow gap, walking 8 feet, and on, and on, and on. 

Then there was the unending "stealth" section where the game beats into you that the enemies are blind but have excellent hearing so you need to be silent. Turns out that excellent hearing doesn't apply when you're 6 feet away and perform a "stealth" kill wherein you loudly grunt while ramming a shiv through an enemy's skull, toss the body to the side, then stomp on it for the loot. But boy, if you stand up from a crouch, even for a second, get ready for every enemy in the room to come for you.

As someone who grew up with Mutant League Hockey and Hit the Ice as my go-to humour based hockey, this game has what it takes to join those legends.

review_text:
At first, Bioshock amazed me. The opening is very well done, the music just clicks with the amazement of any player looking at the wonder that is Rapture as first seen. The setting is fantastic at first: A utopia, as considered by the city's founder, would only be viable underwater in the middle of the pacific. And the buildings and neon lights, like a 60s city, but with whales and fish swimming around, reinforced glass tubes connecting the buildings... It's fantastic. And then, you start entering a building, and hear cries of distress: the inhabitants monitoring new arrivals didn't expect you, or anyone to arrive. And as you stop, someone tries to get to you and help you, they're killed by a mutated woman, with hooks instead of hands. 

She disappears, and slowly through the first level of the game, so did my amazement and wonder. One of the tubes connecting buildings has its glass broken and starts leaking while you're on it, but it doesn't convey a sense of distress. You kind of have the feeling that the water is barely rising so that any idiot can escape the tube. (Also, the pressure on the seabed would probably do a lot more damage.) The first plasmid (a genetic modification that reflects in magic, in this case Force Lightning) just feels like a basic attempt at emergent gameplay, and it's the best plasmid: You can stun splicers (mutated humans) and insta-kill them with a wrench, at least on the first levels, or temporarily disable turrets and other robotics to hack them and turn them against their allies. It's nice, but could have been used better, and the other plasmids are either mostly useless or the emergent gameplay created from them is more basic than this one: oil + fire, and ice + shatter foes with crossbow, basically.

Gunplay is pretty weak: the projectile speed for the machine gun doesn't feel right, the pistol is pretty much a Half-Life 2-like pistol that has a ridiculous recoil yet doesn't feel good, the shotgun is kinda meh, etc. The enemy variety is very low: There's turrets, whether stationary or flying on helicopters, 5 kinds of splicers that, even though they behave differently, they look pretty much the same and scream the same deranged stuff. Finally, there are the Big Daddies. They come in two flavors: Bouncer, who rushes at you like a bull, and Rosie, who will kick your ass with a proximity mine launcher. They feel good at the first times, but then you realize their HP is severely bloated and that's mostly why they're hard. But you keep on doing that because, whle you have a choice, it's much more beneficial to just kill them instead of ignoring them (they will ignore you unless you get too close to them or the Little Sisters.) There are no new enemies after the first third of the game or so, only elite versions with even more HP bloat.

The level design would be good if the objectives weren't so annoyingly placed. At least 7 of the 12 levels (not counting the first one or the final boss) consist of you being led to a nearby objective to keep going to the next level, find out the objective is blocked and you have to unlock it by exploring the entire level. It just feels wrong. The levels are "kinda open-ended" but with linear objectives, and in some cases ist's annoying as hell to get to an objective, backtrack to an area you were previously in and then, only then, to have to go through where you have just gone to, but farther into the level. With respawning enemies this just turns into a massive pain in the ass, and it's just you traversing through the same stuff 4 times.

The presentation is very good, the 50s art-deco style is very well presented. As for the story: It has some nice biopunk stuff, but it's pretty much about the plot twist, part of which they decide to shove in your face and make it obvious a few hours before and the other part a pleasant surprise: [spoiler] You're not playing Bioshock, Bioshock is making you play it.[/spoiler] After the plot twist halfway through, well, the game should have ended right there. The quality takes a nosedive into a pretty underwhelming final boss (though, underwhelming final bosses exist in most FPSs I've played so far) and an ending that depends on a certain choice: This choice makes you Jebus Lord and Saviour or LITERALLY WORSE THAN HITLER. It's even worse that Dishonored at that.

Buy it on sale, I guess?

review_text:
The game is sadly rather disappointing as from playing the game, it seems as if the art and world of the game was created first, and then the story and gameplay was added afterwards. 

Visually, it's a great combination of slzadizalv bekinski and H.R Gieger and brings us a unique, grotesque but intriguing world to explore.
The game has a "biomechanical" feel to everything, and is shown off to great work throughout the game, not to mention that it's HEAVY on the symbolism, that ties into the supposed interpretation of the game. 
One thing it does great, is the gore and bodyhorror, and it does not shy away from showing some genuienly grotesque things, which is shown throughout the game in the enviroment, but also in great animations. 

However the actual gameplay feels tacked on, the gunplay is fine and has punch to it, but is hardly used in the game and still feels clunky and underdeveloped.
The puzzles are never anything but basic and feels more like a blockade for you progress, than a genuine puzzle, in which it requires a button activated. 

The story is left completely open to interpretation, the actual explanation of the things that happends in the game is found inside the artbook, that supposedly don't work anymore.
Moreover the devs themselves have said that some places in the game didn't even make sense to them, and left it open to interpretation to the players, which sounds more like they didn't have a clue on what to 
create for the lore, and just said "let the players figure it out".
It is however one of those games you're left thinking about after you've completed it, either because you found it interesting, or that you're trying to figure out what anything meant.

So, it's hard to recommend the game, when the gameplay is mediocre, the story is pretty much inconsistent and the only thing the game has going for it, is the art.
However, if the game had no gameplay and was merely a simple walking simulator, idon't think a lot of people would have bought it.

look at the artwork online instead.

review_text:
Lucius could have been a great game. It could have been gruesome horror  fun but man... It's an absolute mess of a game.

- Story is as cookie cutter as they come. They pretty much picked up everything from the "Omen" series there's nothing new or interesting done here.
- Linear to a fault
- Controls that feel stiff and unresponsive
- I was constantly struggling to grasp what I'm supposed to do almost at all times.
- The powers are as cliche as they come: Mind control, Telekinesis, Pyrokinesis and there is a WHOLE SLOT in your powers list dedicated to what ultimately adds up to a simple Use button. Yes you have to choose USE first and then you can use stuff or open doors. When is this game from? 1986?!
- Gameplay Does NOTHING to differ itself from better, more revolutionary games in the genre (e.g. Messiah). To be frank, it's quite a miracle the game runs at all.
- It's janky and ugly but plus side is that the manor itself is a cool place to hang out in for a while
- Boring in every conceivable way
- Not even in the "so bad it's funny" gamut of titles out there (e.g. Goat Simulator). It's just a plain bad game that feels super dated and the gameplay is boring and too linear to have any real fun with.

Props to the music composer though some nice tunes in the menus and during gameplay. Voice acting is also kind of OK for a "B-horror" (or more like D-horror) game like this.

Anyway, you can safely pass on this title without feeling like you've missed anything remotely worthy of your time. The only thing this game does right is portray the potential for a kind of game in this style which would actually work and play decently.

review_text:
22 minutes was long enough for me to figure out that this game is, in its current state, just not worth its price tag at all.

I can forgive janky animations and gameplay in an early access title. What is laughably silly is the ugly, unfinished UI elements, the poorly labeled control scheme, the smudged textures, and the bland open world. The game is intended for multiplayer, so I understand that it's intended for people to fill out the role that AI creatures normally would - but the servers have very low populations for what feels like a MASSIVE map... which is also ugly and unfinished, with tons of jagged, uneven terrain to get stuck on. Though, that's par for the course for early access titles, so I won't harp on that too much.

Idk, I knew that getting this it was early access and it would be rough around the edges, but it just feels too rough around the edges to be worth its current price tag. There's no real gameplay that can be had unless you manage to convince friends to play this game with you (which might be a hard sell), or if you can convince randoms in the low populated servers to play with you (rather unlikely). 

I would also appreciate it if the solo mode... actually worked. Even when I got it to start, it's just, once again, a big, flat, empty open world with seemingly no AI spawns (if there were any, I lost patience with the walking simulator before finding them).

All in all, I wish the devs the best, it has a promising start, it's just not very... actually playable in its current state. I hope that when it is more stable or leaves early access, I can return and give it a much kinder review.

review_text:
I sadly wouldn't recommend Scon to the average player as its gameplay just doesn't feel fun to engage with but if you're looking for a beautiful world to look through and admire then Scorn might be for you.

To put it simply, Scorn is fundamentally a piece of artwork that has a game slapped onto it. Scorn involves elements of combat that feel out of place and unnecessary with enemies feeling like more of an inconvenience whether you engage with them or not. There are plenty of puzzles that usually feel fine and aren't too challenging to complete but feel used incorrectly as they tend to push you through a linear world when I feel they could have been used to feel like  they are opening up this strange world to you. HOWEVER Scorn is truly one of the best visual experiences I've had in a game as its clear inspiration from H.R Giger creates a disturbing and foreign world that ingolfs you in its atmosphere that unsettles you with the fear of the unknown in an alien world. There is little narrative or lore which I personally feel works in its favor as it feeds into this feeling of fear of a world that you don't understand. It's a world that clearly has a story to tell but wants you as a player to create your own understanding of the world that makes sense to you. Scorn is an extremely flawed masterpiece that tries to be something that it isn't and shouldn't be but still manages to be one of the most beautiful games i've ever played.

Just finished the game + the Final Transmission DLC now, clocking in at around 15-20 hours all up, and I gotta say - I actually really liked it.

The story is decent enough, evil corpo meddles with things that should not be meddled with, outbreak occurs, chaos ensues - standard stuff. In fact, it's pretty much much Dead Space without the Marker. If you go into it with that expectation, knowing that it's more of a status quo kinda narrative rather than one that pushes boundaries, then I think it's a great experience.

Josh Duhamel as the MC is awesome, stealing the show in basically every scene. The atmosphere is fantastic too, with the graphics being some of the best I've seen to date.

Combat is fairly enjoyable, especially with how weighty the impacts feel, though it's also a little jank at times due to the lock-on system.

I think if you're a fan of Sci-Fi horror then Callisto Protocol is absolutely worth a play, so long as you go in with the right expectations, though it's probably best to pickup on sale as full price is a lil' steep.

review_text:
[h3]Would you kindly stop scrolling and read this review[/h3]

Bioshock was groundbreaking in the way it introduced many gamers to an obscure art style and a niché political philosophy; namely art deco and objectivism. Both of these are weaved into the games DNA and helped to create its iconic look, deeply immersive and memorable world, and its well written story and characters.

The opening few minutes are also iconic and almost perfect in the way they introduce the player to these two concepts, as well as to one of the game's antagonists, Andrew Ryan. It is mostly on the rails and involves lots of delightful visual storytelling as well as a recorded speech from Ryan. As the haunting music sores your 'ride' culminates in a sudden reveal of Bioshock's underwater city, Rapture, a place founded by Ryan in the hopes it would become an objectivist utopia.

"[I]I am Andrew Ryan, and I'm here to ask you a question. Is a man not entitled to the sweat of his brow? 'No!' says the man in Washington, 'It belongs to the poor.' 'No!' says the man in the Vatican, 'It belongs to God.' 'No!' says the man in Moscow, 'It belongs to everyone.' I rejected those answers; instead, I chose something different. I chose the impossible. I chose... Rapture[/I]"

On arriving in the city it quickly becomes clear that Rapture is far from a utopia and that something has gone very, very wrong. 

Now I'm no political expert, but it's obvious from Andrew Ryan's opening monologue that this is a world built on objectivism. As I understand it, objectivism, a philosophy cooked up by Ayn Rand, is a form of right wing, hyper libertarianism, married to extreme capitalism. If selfish greed were a political philosophy, it would be objectivism. The needs of the few outweigh the needs of the many, as a mirror universe version of Spock might say.

Bioshock isn't a celebration of Rand's politics though; as you explore Rapture you'll quickly realise through the narrative that this is a critique of Ayn Rand's political philosophy. It turns out that in an underwater city where everyone is working for themselves, nothing useful or necessary gets done and there's no-one to do the menial, less 'creative and fulfilling' jobs; those jobs that are vital to maintaining and running a vast underwater city. There is also no money to pay the people who are needed to do those jobs, and no supervision.

The citizens of Rapture also discovered a substance called Adam. When refined into a Plasmid, Adam rewrites a person's genetic material, giving them superhuman abilities. One of the downsides of plasmids use is their addictive qualities and they can also cause mental and physical degradation when over used. The second 'person' you see in Rapture is a victim of Adam abuse and has lost their mind, becoming a murder happy Splicer. You see them through a small window, gutting the first person you see. So Plasmid use isn't healthy; luckily as the player you will inject yourself with many many plasmids!

In a democratic society, regulation, ethical considerations and/or law enforcement of some kind could have led to better safeguards and more thorough testing of Adam. But in Rapture that would be hampering creative genius.

Then some sort of conflict began on new years eve 1958, between factions loyal to Ryan and those loyal to somebody named Atlas. With plasmids added to the mix things clearly didn't go so well, and this becomes apparent soon after you 'land'. Things are fucked, to put it mildly.

You piece a lot of this together within the first hour or so through the visuals alone. Rapture's beautiful, clean, simple, symmetrical 1920's art deco face is cracking. The imposing bronze sculptures are tarnished and some are toppled; the gold plaques are grimy, and the green marble and ceramic tiles are pitted, shattered and broken. There are leaks everywhere too; maintenance having been largely abandoned. The city is flooding and large parts of it are without power. Machinery is malfunctioning and there are there are bodies all over the place. Many of the dead are in evening wear that is age worn and tattered. Some are wearing masks, like they died during a masked ball. The Splicers are similarly attired but those without masks are horrifyingly deformed. Mutated.

The atmosphere is unsettling and meloncholic, and sometimes, when the lights are flickering, casting strange shadows and the faint, nonsensical noises of one of Rapture's mad citizens are getting ever louder, and closer, the game is outright frightening.

This would be a decent way to tell a story but there are also audiologs made by the citizens before things went to shit, and NPCs that aren't currently trying to kill you. When taken together this is world building at its finest. Later on you'll start learning about the player character and their connection to Rapture, the two philosophies of Ryan and Atlas and the ultimate fate of the city. This is the game's story and it's wonderfully paced and told, and  incredibly immersive.

I'd be remiss if I didn't talk about the gameplay, but it's only important as a part of the whole, nothing about the FPS mechanics is outstanding. None of the guns are particularly memorable but they sound meaty enough and can be upgraded, as well as fitted out with different ammo types. You can also hack cameras and sentry bots to help you in combat, and these skills, along with heath and energy can be levelled up. You need the energy to use plasmids. There are a large number of plasmids, some of which you find and others you have to buy. They too can be levelled up and range from basic magical attacks like incinerate, winter blast and electrobolt, which are pretty self explanatory, to more tactical ones such as telekinesis, a decoy and one that charms enemies to fight for you. 

Enemy variety is a rather limited, there are only a few different types of Splicer, but each benefits from a slightly different approach to takedown, and there are generally plasmids that are better at countering certain Splicers. Encounters can be hectic if there are multiple Splicer types and then there are the big baddies. Not Splicers themselves, these armoured giants stomp around Rapture often in the footsteps of small girls. These little sisters are Adam gatherers* and you need Adam to buy plasmids, but before you can deal with the little sisters you have to get rid of daddy. Now you can just leave these pairings be when you encounter them, and as long as you don't get too close to the child the big daddy won't attack. It's always worth it though, and these fights can be some of the best, and worst when they're messy, in the game, requiring lots of ammo and plasmid use. 

This is where the game's morality system comes into play, you can 'harvest' the little sisters for a large amount of Adam, killing them, or release them from their drugged servitude, saving them for little material gain. It's one of those shit good/evil binary choices that video games do, that are never really choices because the good option is obviously the one to go, especially if it effects the ending. You're not even really punished for choosing the good option because after you've saved enough little sisters they'll drop off presents stuffed with Adam. It's definitely one of the most poorly thought out aspects of BioShock, along with the hacking mini game. Nothings perfect though. 

I've wasted enough of your time. Bioshock is a fantastic game worthy of its iconic status; it's beautiful, dark, deep,, smart, engrossing and unforgettable. Get it.

review_text: A pain in the ass. The gameplay is mostly there, but the terrible AI, absolutely disfunctional pathing, and the inability to stack commands or pause time (yes, this is an RTS, but the UI is too shoddy for the devs to get away with that) means that there are constant restarts because the characters won't do what you want them do. The quickload system is the only saving grace for this game, and the only reason its playable, but the fact that it NEEDS something like that is a poor fix to begin with. Not to mention that it gives you the number of quickloads at the end anyway, and throwing this game's mistake in your face, like it was the players fault to begin with, and not a bad design choice. I've long since lost count of the number of times that I've redone one specific point because my characters have a small window to perform, and won't do the commands correctly. The game allows you to check the guards changing viewcones, but only one can be highlighted at a time. If you need to run through several overlapping viewcones, the option given to you is to slap down a marker inside that area...that only tells you if a particular guard happens to be looking at that marker at any particular time. Useless. In short, the UI and AI really kills this game by just making it an excercise in frustration, and whoever was responsible for those departments should have been fired, because the rest of the team actually did a decent job. Shame.

Batman: Arkham City is a really underwhelming game. It honestly doesn’t succeed in any facet. Its gameplay is unengaging. Its story is abysmal. Its characters are uncompelling. It is needlessly padded out with tons of filler. It’s dragged down by a host of issues. The game does not deserve “Overwhelmingly positive” reviews. I can only imagine it received such widespread adulation because it is a Batman game and it certainly is a Batman game, but is it good? No. Is it terrible? No. It’s middling at best.

The combat is unsatisfying. It can be fun here and there, but there just isn’t any depth. It doesn’t feel earned. I didn’t come away from it feeling like Batman. I felt like I was just playing a very violent rhythm game. On top of that, it’s weird in practice, too. Sometimes Batman will leap across two screens to attack a bad guy, then he’ll fumble an attack on a bad guy right next to him. There’s no rhyme or logic to it. And you’ll be pissed off when it happens because you then lose your combo for no good reason.

The game is utterly filled with content, but that doesn’t mean it is good content. It is Filler City. It is seriously padded out with a lot of meaningless content that is either trifling at best or just atrocious at worst. It suffers all the pitfalls of a Ubisoft-style open-world and is no more compelling for it. The side activities are shoddily implemented and feel tacked on as a way to expose the player to more of Batman’s rogues gallery. Unfortunately, it just doesn’t work for creating a fun or interesting experience. Why would I care to see more of these characters when the experience is the same for every one of them? They aren’t interesting to see. They are window dressing. I feel like 75-85% of the game could have easily been cut. And the resources dedicated to more meaningful, interesting content. 


The story is just abysmal. Batman himself is completely uninteresting here and the central dilemma plaguing him and the world at large is equally uncompelling. He has zero personality beyond delivering gruff lines to everyone around him while all the characters you interact with are homicidal maniacs that would be better off dead. The villains are particularly heinous here and it beggars belief that Batman lets them live after the crap they pull off repeatedly in the game. Even the villains that aren’t wholly evil act idiotic here, too, and it drags the story down even further.

There are two massive drivers of events in the game and one is completely shrouded in mystery til the very end, so you have zero reason to care about it. And the other is much more immediate, but due to the flat performances and needlessly tacked on filler, it doesn’t feel urgent at all. It is barely a blip in your mind. And you feel there are no stakes whatsoever to what you are doing.

I know Batman is a gruff character with a somber demeanor, but he’s more than that. We have seen him across a large variety of media. And he can be so much more. And be more dynamic and interesting. He’s complex with a lot of issues that extend well beyond the surface. And we just don’t see any of that here. It’s just the most surface-level interpretation of Batman being Batman and that’s that. 

I came away from this game feeling like I may have enjoyed parts of it, but it was ultimately just a tedious experience and after playing other games, my opinion has been revised downwards. It just isn’t a good game. It wasn’t even a good game for its time. I’ve played a ton of games from its time period recently and it doesn’t measure up to any of them. I know my opinion is in the minority, but hey, it is what it is.

review_text:
If the developers' intention with Scorn was to create a visually striking, disturbing, and horrifying experience, then it's safe to say they've succeeded. Every single graphic element in the game conveys a sense of terror, with environments that seem to emerge from a nightmarish, dystopian world in decay. The aesthetics, inspired by the works of H.R. Giger, dominate the gameplay, constantly making the player feel uneasy as they're immersed in a deforming landscape where nothing is comforting.

The core of the experience lies in the puzzles, which increase in complexity as you progress. In Scorn, the absence of indicators or hints forces players to explore and understand the world through trial and intuition. There are no tutorials or explicit messages, making the progression both intriguing and challenging. You'll feel lost, just like the protagonist, inside a labyrinth of tunnels and rooms that all seem the same, but the compartmentalized structure of the game helps you make sense of each map and discover new corners of this alienating universe.

Unfortunately, the combat aspect represents the weak point of Scorn. While more powerful weapons are provided as you go, the combat system feels cumbersome and unrewarding. Ammunition is scarce and difficult to find, creating a constant sense of shortage. Additionally, health management is equally stingy, forcing players to remain vigilant at all times. The creatures that infest the environments are far from memorable enemies: instead of exciting challenges, they feel more like simple obstacles. This, combined with unforgiving checkpoints, can lead to frustrating moments, where you're forced to repeat lengthy and difficult sections, especially when health is low and resources are scarce.

In conclusion, Scorn is a game that stands out for its unique atmosphere, but falls short in several gameplay aspects. The enemies, unfortunately, are unremarkable, and while the environments are phenomenal, with claustrophobic architectures and desolate spaces that tell the story of a world devastated, the experience doesn't fully leverage its potential. The final "cathedral," with its perverse bas-reliefs, is a visual masterpiece that expresses the theme of the world's transformation into a hell, but it alone isn't enough to elevate the entire experience. In the end, Scorn is a visceral and disorienting journey, but with too many flaws in gameplay to be considered a complete masterpiece.

review_text:
While this game is certainly not bad, it's not exactly good either. But since most reviews are positive anyway, I might aswell tell you why it just didn't work for me.

-The story
In it's core I thought the overall concept was actually pretty original. You pay as two scientist who travel back through a dying man's memories in order to grant him his last wish artificially: taking him to the moon (roll credits). Though during the story, your original objective is often questioned, as you begin to understand that this wish is not what would make your patient truly happy.
So, it's really not the story that set me off, it's rather...
-The dialogue
You'd think that in a story that's supposed to make you sad and teary, you wouldn't need a character for comic relief. But damnit, the second main character suplied you with a steady ammount of jokes in all the wrong places. I just couldn't take the game serious anymore. At the first half of the story, whenever there was an emotional moment, that same guy, messed it up over an over again. And by the time the game was starting to get deep, it was just too late for me. 
You see, the sad moments of the game largely depend on how you attached you grow to the characters over time. And maybe it's just me, but I hated both of them.
-Gameplay
Well, interesting gameplay is virtually nonexistent. But that's really not an issue in a story driven game. As I mentioned before, it has a great outline, but it just feels so unrefined at some places that it just wasn't enjoyable for me.
-The length
You'll probably finish the game in 3-4 hours. And while I don't want to badmouth the content, you may think that it's been a short ride if you don't even have all the trading cards by the time you are done.

All in all, I'd say it's okay if you can pick it up during a sale. But I really don't think it's worth the full price if you take a look at what it offers. Just about 4 hours of gameplay which aren't even amazing. But I assume that most people have a far better time, given that they don't dislike the main characters as much as I do.

Imagine you are in the snow covered mountains of Northern Alberta. You find yourself inside of a hand built log cabin next to a crackling fire in a river rock stone hearth. You smell kerosene, pine sap and pipe smoke. At your feet you see fishing and trapping tackle along with wood shaving left by your host whittling during his lonesome nights that he fills with creative pondering. 

You look across from you and see an old rocking chair holding your host, a long chaw' stained grey beard runs from his weathered nose all the way down to his mid-chest. Looking at you through yellowed wire rimmed glasses he says to you: "Welcome to the tutorial of Rise to Ruins."

There are bugs galore in the code, Ping issues that cause headaches for both survivors and killers, a rather toxic community, and the new player experience is terrible.
