While getting up to speed you'll end up tunneled and slugged as someone in serious need of therapy humps your body as a newbie survivor or bullied with sabotage toolboxes and flashlights and t-bagged at the exit gate as a newbie killer. If you still persist be prepared for most of your friends to rage quit the game at some point and to be constantly disappointed at the devs inability to achieve any sort of balance in gameplay. Solo Queue for survivor is the seventh circle of hell, updates to counter certain OP killers turn other killers into a sad joke, and many of the most useful perks are locked on characters that require cash or in-game grinding to unlock. But Sable got a new $9 outfit so apparently all is right with the world.

The game is fairly unusual in design, in that it has superpower abilities that are sort of over the top in design, that allow you do things like ricochet the puck off off people's heads to knock them out or throw your stick like a tomahawk while having multiple hockey sticks strapped to your back as backup sticks. The game is also a roguelike game, which is actually a pretty cool idea where you keep trying to succeed at games until you lose, and then unlock different abilities and stats over time. Sounds good? There's one big problem: the rules of hockey were removed from the game. Big deal? Well, here's one example of a few problems:

The OFFSIDE rule doesn't exist in this game (where you can't pass the puck over the blue line of the opponent's zone if one of your teammates is already in the zone). This means any player (even the CPU goaltender, who will do this often) can flip the puck into the opponent's zone onto the stick of one of his teammates who is standing right next to the opponent's net, and then he'll have a free shot. There needs to be a defensive player dogging every opponent at all times because nothing is stopping them from standing a mile away from the action and waiting for the big lob pass across the arena that gives a free breakaway / slapshot into the net.

For the sake of not spoiling other surprise parts of the game, I won't go over all the different teams and the broken rules that get introduced and how they're abused, but this game essentially acts best as a reminder on why there are certain rules in hockey. The game design has taught me that hockey wouldn't become "more fun" if we took the rules away, with the experience being quite dull overall after playing a few games of such limited strategy.

With that said, the game has just released into early access, so there is still time for the design of the game to steer itself toward something more than an amazing hockey engine with wasted potential. I will change my review if the game manages to fix some of the oversights that rob the game of being enjoyable for me.

review_text:
This a solid game and a lot of fun to play. The combat is really good, the exploration is fun with stuff to find all over the maps. Games graphics, even at medium settings (I have a potato), are great and the art style is inspiring. The voice acting is really well done (I'm listening in Mandarin, with English sub-titles) and I've only run into very minor translation quibbles but even that's explainable because I tend to make assumptions too quickly lol. The soundtrack music is phenomenally good.

The fact that this is FTP without PTW is super nice for a change. The usual gacha is present, however it's purely cosmetics and purely optional. You can buy costumes for your character, if you like, and they run from reasonably cheap to very expensive- but they are simply skins and don't change the game by adding power etc. Be aware that there are also 'free' costumes you can find, and earn through questing, etc., in the game and they are absolutely cool too. So, yeah, no PTW. 

My only hang up, at the beginning when the game launched, was feeling overwhelmed by the amount of content and information being tossed at me…I felt like I couldn’t keep up with the menus (clunky, but the devs are working on that issue) and I'm one of those player types who likes to 'do'—teach me, let me actually practice for a bit to start some muscle memory, then throw me in the deep end lol. That and the terrain sometimes grabbing my character are my only gripes.

The various ways you can play Where Winds Meet is really interesting. Currently I'm playing the game solo, like a single player RPG. But I can easily group up with r/l friends who are playing for co-op. I could play it like an MMO too if I choose. I love the fact I have choice and am not being forced to play any particular way.

The questing (main, side) are actually interesting, not filled with agenda white noise, and many of them are actually fun to progress. I've yet to run into something I consider tedious. I also don't find the game grindy and I've played some grinders in the past (Lineage II anyone?). Getting materials to upgrade gear slots isn't difficult—the menu will tell you what you need and can show you the ways to obtain it, and even mark your map for you.

There is a crafting system that seems to work smoothly but I haven't spent much time with it, other than to make some potions and cook some meals.

Where Winds Meet is vast game. There is a lot to take in, a lot to learn, for sure. The best part is, this game really brings Wuxia and the Jiang hu world to life. Well worth the time. YMMV.

review_text:
I will say this. The game is fun. I do genuinely like it. I do think it is really cool.

Is it worth the price tag? Not yet. Keyword: yet. 

There is only one thing about this game that really bothers me and that is the Calamity mechanic that isn't really explained at all so it just sort of pops up at the worst time unless you are prone to looking things up.

This event comes into play once there are five marks in the top left. 

The way that you can accrue these are:
-Being seen by a specific entity
-Triggering a trap
-Picking up cursed stuff
-Taking damage

For the last one I do not think it is damage specifically it may be 'being hit' or it could have a value system. Being hit by a minion doesn't count as much as being hit by a boss or an elite. I've been hit by attacks that merely launched my character through the air without inflicting any visible damage that have increased the tally. 

What does it do? It creates one of several different events which all cause the sanity bar to deteriorate. In addition a threat will appear; sometimes directly on top of the player character, to make the event more lethal. As far as I have read the event can be defeated, but if you have been taking damage you likely are already in a bad spot to handle an additional higher level challenge than what you have already been facing. 

And that is where the problem I have with it arises. 

If you are having a bad time, this is here to make it worse. It makes it hard for new players to learn the game because if they flub a couple hits they suddenly have to run away from the boss of the level or die and then potentially lose out on progress.

Skilled people can farm it. That's nice, but that doesn't make the event better. It just means that it is effectively 'lose more' mechanic even if that wasn't the design intent. 

Truthfully I have nothing against the event in of itself, but instead with the triggers. If it is meant to be a punishment then it should be better defined and more easy to learn. Failing opt in challenges, intentionally provoking it, or taking too long on the map can all add points to provoke the Calamity. If you want to give it more of a real feel then you can increment it with time, by swiping valuable loot, and by killing important enemies. That way doing more provokes a more aggressive response from the antagonist. Being brazen or risky about it also should serve to further that building animosity. 

It also gives the players something to manage a bit more tangibly as well. 

I mean does it really make sense to 'go nuclear' and waste a bunch of supernatural juice on someone who is currently getting their butt kicked by one of your minions? I mean really... I mean it's all fun and ICBMs until you realize just how much they cost.

Game is constantly stopping you from logging in while they push updates in the middle of extra XP events.

Additionally there are quests with long-time bugs that update after update just don't get fixed.

Not to mention that a large portion of combat is dealt with via keyboard controls, but sometimes mid-fight (sometimes meaning a lot of the time) the game just decides to ignore your keyboard input.

That and it seems like in most missions the game is stopping you from just playing the game; whether that be with a short unnecessary cut scene, a few lines of meaningless unnecessary dialogue that serve no purpose, or the controls just flat out ignoring you.
I understand a certain amount of dialogue is needed to give context to what's going on, and the franchise revolves around diplomacy, but that shouldn't mean ripping control from the player every few seconds in some cases.

One issue I must make is multiple pop-up windows as soon as I boot-up the game trying to get me to take more bridge officers when I have no open slots for bridge officers.
It shouldn't take a huge coding change to say "if there are no open bridge officer slots, don't open these windows".

Top all that off with the fact this game makes it as hard as possible to report bugs or content not working as intended.

review_text:
The core gameplay loop, game mechanics, graphics, gunplay, audio and everything is pretty okay.

The only reason I do not recommend this game is due to the lack of polish in every seam of the game. It is not a finished product despite of coming out of early access. The game is very playable and fun if you have a group of people, but the frankly insane number of bugs (the software ones) in every single system within the gameplay makes it a frequently frustrating experience.

For example, movement is generally fine. The speed and responsiveness is all good, you feel like you have full control of your character. Until you are running on flat ground and for some unknown reason the collision on the ground bugs out and your character gets stuck on the tiniest elevation change.

Or you may be enjoying the most frantic battle with countless arachnids surrounding you, and you are battling them to the last blood. Until you pull out the health stim to heal yourself and magically the stim does not work, resulting in your death that is unwarranted.

Or you could be retreating from the pursuit of the arachnids and the arachnids starts teleporting. Or you could be throwing a resource canister to your teammate and suddenly physics nope out of existence and the canister starts to move erratically away from you.

The game is a conglomerate of implemented systems that have good concepts and design, but lack any amount of polishing to make the systems work as intended. In software dev 80% of the work is polishing. But this game shipped out 20% of the effort and called it a day.

So the game has nice mechanics and systems, good visuals and designs. But terrible implementation and absurd amount of bugs. Is it fun? Yes. Is it worth on a good sale? Yes. Is it frequently frustrating to play? Yes.

review_text:
I stumbled across Kingdom Come: Deliverance in 2023. I knew nothing of Steam at the time. Because of KCD, I returned to gaming after a hiatus of many years. The urban landscape in the first game was as beautiful as a museum and I found myself visiting city after city just to examine the different churches. As a college professor who studied fencing as an adolescent, I loved the combat, as well as the immersive, historically-grounded story. While fighting in the first installment of KCD was admittedly difficult and required more practice than most games, I thought it was fun to acquire genuine expertise at both the basics (blocking, slashing, stabbing) as well as the more skill-based, advanced moves that players acquire through experience and training. KCD1 was not a perfect game. The story -- which initially concerns Henry's quest to avenge his parents and to recover a lost sword -- gradually loses focus and becomes an increasingly solipsistic "journey of self-discovery." The disappointing (and profoundly derivative) revelation of Henry's true origins was a narrative nadir from which KCD1 never quite recovered. And the game was, as many have pointed out, swarming with bugs, especially in crowded fight scenes. I never had the patience to complete one of the buggier, final quests ("An Oath is an Oath") so watched the game's irresolute "conclusion" on YouTube. 

Despite these shortcomings, I liked KCD1 enough that I looked forward to the sequel for months. I regret that I was disappointed by it immediately. I happily grant that archery is easier in the new version (though I am not sure that making things "easier" is a net gain for a developer that prioritizes realism to the degree that Warhorse does). Yet I found the alleged "improvements" to melee combat to be simplifications and dilutions designed to please the mob of weekend button-mashers rather than serious attempts to refine the system in KCD1. As Warhorse's approach to combat in KCD has become less realistic, its treatment of other matters (such as potion making) is now governed by an obsessive and tedious verisimilitude.  As others have pointed out, there are enough chores to do in the real world without inventing virtual chores in a fantasy version of medieval Europe. 

KCD2, alas, did not work for me. But most players seem to disagree with me on this one, and I wish them well.

Don't buy this game at full price. In fact don't buy it at all if you value your time and money.
It is aggressively mediocre. It's not scary in the least. Bloober team's idea of a scary game is to barrage you with jump scares until you fall asleep of sheer boredom. Ambiance and atmosphere is replaced with blackness. Enemies are all the same - one big hand to kill you over and over. Make punch button react to boxes differently and implement dodge button, so she can dodge the stupid poison shit on the walls that is clearly there to be dodged. Make this bitch climb the ladders faster. She can run but can't climb fast? What is this fucking stupid ass logic?
The story is boring and boils down to "a man is abusive and bad and caused all the shit storm, i hate men".
Weapons are generic, nothing special about them. Another stupid mechanic is charge shots. Your regular shot is useless against monsters and is a waste of bullets, so you have to charge it. But charging isn't eternal, it releases when it's ready and if you're not aiming correctly at that second you're fucked. 
Art design is atrocious. Who came up with this vagina on the helmet thing? Fucking hell. And there's no visible progression to the suit when you upgrade it (since people compare it to Dead Space).
Characters are boring as shit. They supposed to be Pols but they sound like your regular americans. Only when they speak names they start to sound like some east european people. And the warden...man, fuck his memos..he speaks so slowly..you can watch the whole LOTR trilogy in the pauses he makes between sentences. 
All in all fuck this game. It's boring and uninspired.

review_text:
After spending more than sixty hours in Witchfire, I can confidently say it is one of the most satisfying shooter roguelites I have played. Developed by a small team, it delivers AAA‑quality visuals and a deep gameplay loop. As a preyer, I hunt witches with forbidden guns and pagan magic, and the game lets me decide whether to pick off enemies from afar, study encounters tactically, or combine firearms and spells into my own brand of mayhem. I am a long‑range enthusiast, and the time I have invested has been rewarded with memorable head-shots and tense cat‑and‑mouse encounters across the game’s richly detailed maps.

The July 2025 Webgrave update is the most transformative yet. It adds a brand‑new region called Velmorne, a blighted town full of secrets and new enemy types. This update introduces the Rosary, a system of passive skills that lets me tailor my build and share configurations with other players. The Workshop has been overhauled so I can control the research path of my gear, and the old stat categories have been replaced with an RPG‑style system using Flesh, Blood, Mind, Witchery, Arsenal and Faith. There are also new Gnosis levels and a redesigned Ascension Shrine, with a special item to reassign points if I am returning to the game. Webgrave even adds a proper tutorial via a prologue level and an in‑game handbook. For snipers like me, the highlight is the Oracle, a new sniper rifle that can ignore walls. There is also the lever‑action Nemesis and the quest‑locked Koschei. These additions, coupled with the Rosary and refined stats, make character builds more rewarding and combat more tactical.

This update builds on March 2025’s Witch Mountain update. That patch added a sprawling descent into Witch Mountain, the game’s largest level to date, and introduced Fallen Preyers 2.0, semi‑autonomous allies, Shadow Orbs that offer high‑risk, high‑reward challenges, and a suite of new gear. Earlier still, the Ghost Galleon update in April 2024 added souls‑style classes, new Calamities, a Calamity meter that teaches you to avoid mistakes, and the Gnosis system that lets you slightly over‑level and unlock hidden paths. These patches show that the Astronauts team listens to feedback from us and continually expands their world. They released a huge update just two weeks ago and released an updated patch today on Aug 13!

[b]The maps themselves are masterfully crafted and gorgeous to look at and run through.[/b] Early regions like Scarlet Coast are a study in melancholy; broken flotillas litter the shoreline, a blood‑stained beach and an abandoned fishing village give way to a quarry. Irongate Castle radiates corruption with its foul aura, labyrinthine dungeons and three separate ways into the castle! Witch Mountain’s labyrinth requires careful navigation and is filled with traps and Fallen Preyer allies. Velmorne offers narrow streets, blighted courtyards and new enemies that will surprise even veteran players. Each level feels like a mini‑dungeon; they are semi‑open but interconnected, giving me multiple angles to line up long‑range shots or retreat when calamities hit. The design encourages exploration with hidden Vaults, Shadow Orbs, Witchmarks, navigation charts and events that reward curiosity and precision.

[b]Weapons and sniping mechanics are a standout.[/b] The game already features excellent marksman rifles like Hailstorm, which has the highest base damage of any non‑demonic weapon. Landing three consecutive critical hits refunds bullets to the magazine and, at higher upgrade levels, improves handling, increases zoom distance and even unleashes a freezing shockwave. However, misses reset the buff and there is a stamina cost for aiming, so disciplined shooting is essential. Hypnosis, another bolt‑action rifle, rewards patience by charging extra damage the longer I aim. Now, with the Oracle’s ability to shoot through walls, snipers can set up truly spectacular shots in Velmorne or Witch Mountain. Mixing these rifles with spells, for example freezing cones to control mobs or shockwaves to knock enemies back, enhances the sniping loop and stacks the damage. Even demonic weapons like Vulture and Hailstorm act as panic buttons or boss‑busting tools, but I find myself returning to precision rifles because of how satisfying the critical‑hit system is. Stack that with electrical shock on top of fire...the damage numbers roll...

[b]Visually, Witchfire is jaw‑dropping.[/b] The game uses advanced photogrammetry and post‑processing to build gorgeous semi‑open world levels. The developers took their photogrammetry pipeline beyond The Vanishing of Ethan Carter, shooting objects at high resolution, using drones for large scans and compiling tens of thousands of photos to create assets. They then optimized these scans so the game looks stunning without sacrificing performance. Details like natural dirt, weathering and unique compositions give each environment authenticity. Even after dozens of hours, I still pause to admire the sun piercing through ruined arches or the way light dances off wet stones in Velmorne.

Witchfire has evolved into an exceptional roguelite FPS. The developers have continually expanded the game with new regions, systems and weapons, and the Webgrave update addresses onboarding while giving veterans deeper build options. If you enjoy sniping or methodical long‑range combat in atmospheric, dungeon‑like maps, Witchfire will scratch that itch. My 60+ hours have flown by, and with the Rosary system, new maps, gnosis levels to unlock and the Oracle in my hands, I'm not stopping.

review_text:
I loved SGW3, I know it was buggy, but I can live with getting stuck in a rock once in a while or on an elevator in the missile silo in exchange for the amazing open world go-anywhere-you-please-ability. If I wanted to get in my truck and spend 10 minutes driving to the top of a mountain across the valley from the target in order to take a long shot, I could. With this game the "open world-ness" is just an illusion, you are just funneled through the playing field with fences, mine fields, un-climbable rocks and cliffs on either side everywhere you go. If you do happen to find a spot to try to slip away, it immediately gives you a warning message that you have left the area and you have like two seconds to return or you just die.... The AI sucks, half the time the baddies just stand there and let you shoot them all, other times, you will be completely alone, nobody in sight, but then a camera spots you and thirty dudes are instantly on top of you. The other snipers rarely ever fire at you, they spot you from thirty miles away, but then just lay there... violently shaking for some reason.  In the whole game, 99% of the shots were at 200 yards or less. Most of the time the Desert Eagle pistol was the most effective way to clear a scene... The 12 gauges are useless unless you are three feet apart. Again, I loved SGW3, the only thing about this that was better was the ability to blow baddies arms, legs and heads off. I turned the "bullet cam" off right away because even though the footage was cool, it was like you were holding your breath the whole time and when you return to the scope view, you're out of breath and the baddies have all ran away.  I hated it compared to SGW3. 
Dear CI, please make more maps for SGW3, fix the getting-stuck-in-the-terrain bug and add the dismemberment stuff. 
 Thank you.

review_text:
NGS leaves a substantial amount to be desired. Stale content and combat, low drop rates, absurd amounts of RNG and monetization, absurd asking prices on the player market, and a low net income of the game's currency you receive by playing the game when compared to prices for upgrading equipment make for a low-to-non-existent return value to myself. It takes far too long to accomplish anything worth doing in-game, especially when you can just run copy-pasted seasonal events for decent gear every few months. 

Do your wallet a favor and pass on paying for anything in-game with real currency. Playing for free is very limited as well, because you only get a three day pass to sell your items on the player market from your mission pass (A.K.A. your dailies... which mostly involve food for some reason)... among other things. Its been a constant headache.

Overall, I feel like the game is bad. Had there been today's amount of content at launch.... I dunno'. review_text:
A massive bull with giant genitals derailed the train filled with coffins I was riding on. I can already tell it´s going to be a masterpiece because I got no clue what is going on and people are laughing at me as I am looting my fathers house. I am also afraid the kids in this place are going to shank me because I gave them a lot of stuff to shank me with.

EDIT:

So I now finished the game and jokes aside, I wouldn´t recommend it. This game isn´t fun - that´s the point, and that´s alright. It is trying to be miserable, it is trying to be oppressive, and it succeeds with that. The issue is that it is also trying not to be frustrating, and unfortunately it fails miserably at that. Some game mechanics are just badly implemented or don´t work well at all with the flow of the game. The gameplay overall just isn´t interesting at best, and frustrating at worst.

The story and the narrative didn´t resonate with me either. I read some posts on how it was "amazing" and how the emotional moments "hit so hard" or whatever, and I could not relate at all. By the end of it all I did not care in the least anymore. The story, the characters, it all seemed pointless by the end and nothing made me care about either of them. At some point when it became clear that there´d be at least two endings I thought that I´d try to see the other one as well when I was finished, but I couldn´t even summon the effort to play even half an hour more of this. That´s my final comment on this I suppose. Interesting at first, but it turns out to be a waste of time and money in the end.

It is also badly optimized and the save files are ridiculously large, so when you´re finished, maybe delete them if you´re running low on disk space.

EDIT 2:

Well, the game certainly keeps you thinking long after you finished it, you gotta give it that. It is interesting and unique in concept, after all. But I think I now have the perfect words to describe it: 20 hour long walking simulator without pay-off. You spend each day running around between people, while getting hit on the head every now and then, to PERHAPS get 3 lines of disconnected dialog once you arrive. Then you run off to your next stop.

You do so much running in this.

And then, at the end of it all, you get to choose between two endings, regardless of all you´ve done so far, both of which ultimately mean nothing. You then get another 3 lines of dialog with most of the characters you managed to save during your playthrough, and that´s it. It honestly didn´t feel rewarding enough for 20 hours of boring and frustrating gameplay. For a game that relies so heavily on dialog and story, there is precious little of it. There are no meaningful choices in conversations - There´s a few choices in what you can do, as in your actions, but it usually amounts to "Do thing" or "Don´t do thing", and again, it changes nothing ultimately. 

The game lured me in with an interesting premise, and the mystery was engaging at first, but after 10 hours of running around and the mystery becoming less and less engaging, I simply found nothing of value in this game anymore.

review_text: I loved the first game and am very experienced in its world. The sequel is similar to the first in that it’s not an RPG but a linear story with sandbox maps as areas to explore freely. The gameplay is fun, combat can be challenging, and I enjoy the survival mechanics of hunting and exploring the immersive world. I ran into numerous bugs and crashes. I watched many reviews praise this game for being polished, but I ran into issue after issue. Realism is still front and center,  but the sequel is more streamlined to reach a broader audience. If you played the first game, then you’ll enjoy this one as much as I did. My biggest gripe is that the storytelling in the sequel dragged down the overall experience for me. There’s not much in the way of action and consequence, but you're presented with the illusion of it. As the player, I figured things out before the game would allow characters to know such information, which would hinder any chance of me making any choices outside of what the writers wanted me to do. That's when I realized I was just along for the ride and had to accept everything for what it was. I stopped asking questions and went back into consume-product mode. The game is plagued by millennial writing and humor, making it difficult to take anything seriously. Act 2 crushed the momentum that Act 1 had going for it. Some jokes might appear funny, but I'm looking for a more mature theme in my realistic medieval game. A lot of the cutscenes felt like I was watching a bad movie filled with cliches and tropes. I was taken out of the experience many times due to the “Uh oh, whoops!” and “That just happened” type of humor. The only parts of the story I enjoyed were fulfilling Henry’s revenge quest, but the rest was a humiliation ritual for our boy. Characters, such as Musa, speak down to Henry. Even with a high scholarly skill, I could not retort to his blatant hypocrisy or lies. Then, the game has you solve a murder to clear Musa as a suspect. You’re forced to help him. Otherwise, you receive a game over screen. Another illusion of choice. It’s as if the writers were lecturing me with this character and others for no good reason. I didn't mind carrying sacks and being an errand boy, but now they’re just insulting our intelligence. The game is very loosely historically accurate. You can tell the writers had their own story to tell in history with their interpretation of what happened. I don't believe in buzzwords nor do I care about sides, but I see how people claim this game has woke elements. I saw the controversy regarding the creative director, and those elements bleed into the game. I rushed the story because, at a certain point, I gave up on the game when it gave up on me. I only stuck around to see Henry’s resolution across the finish line. I'm waiting for Hardcore mode to release because the decent enough gameplay pushes me through the rest of this game.

review_text:
Why on earth is this so childish?  I don't mean the graphics, either... cute graphics work in games.  But that's usually where the kid stuff stops.  But not in this game... it's so adolescent, it's not enjoyable.  

The vast majority of gamers who play games like this are adults.  If you look at games that this is clearly inspired by like Gungeon, those games had cute elements to them but they weren't made for children.

From the story, to the dialogue, to the characters themselves it's like sitting down as a full grown adult by yourself to watch old episodes of blues clues.  It's ridiculous, and I can't imagine how people enjoy that.  It's literally like watching a mediocre children's cartoon, and having to sit through all the characters talking and telling their children's humor jokes.

I get sitting with your kids to watch that stuff, but I cannot imagine why any adult would want to sit on their own time through a game like this that is so clearly out of touch with the age of its primary audience.

The achievement "Good Morning, Time Traveler" is awarded for completing the very first story mission.  5.8% of players have this achievement.  I guess I stuck around for the juvenile stuff longer than 94.2% of people did.

The gameplay is fine, it's actually decent enough if I'm honest.  That can't rescue the game from what it forces you to sit through and listen to, though.   If you can stomach the horrible 7 year old humor, characters, and conversations you may enjoy the game.  I cannot.

review_text:
If you like wide-scale community-driven co-op action with expansive buildcrafting and powerful metaprogression this is a game you don't want to miss. 

[h2] Wide scale: 16~20 players [/h2] 
Broken up into 4 player squads.


[h2] Community-Driven: The Galactic Front [/h2] 
The Galactic Front is like a global main objective which changes every major content drop. 

Join/Make a company, complete Company Operations (in other words join missions on the SPARTA), earn Victory Points which translate to global Galactic Front progress. 

When we've made enough progress, we start earning perks and cosmetics. 

So far the playerbase has unlocked 9 perks which everyone even new players can use, on any class, with 3 more on the way for this current sparta campaign.


[h2] Co-op Action: Gamemodes [/h2] 
Advance and Secure: Capture points, kill bug. Rinse repeat. Then run for evac!

ARC defense: Obtain materials to build and defend a base. Manage side objectives. Power up the cave scanner, hold them back, then run for evac!

Horde: 10 waves of bugs each harder than the last. Build a base and fight together to the end. Then run for evac!

Hive Hunt: Nuke bug holes. Then run for evac!

Critical Strike: Fight deep behind enemy lines. Reach the other side. Take on big bad bugs. Then run for evac!


[h2] Buildcrafting: Classes [/h2] 
Every class has a primary, secondary, grenade slot, up to 2 utility slots, and up to 3 perk slots. These "up to's" are not class specific restrictions, but slots you globally unlock after hitting certain career ranks. Weapons have up to 4 attachment slots- optics, magazine, internal (like barrels), ammo type.

Guardian: Take aggro, Tank damage, lock down ore drills. Deployable shield circle. Call squadmates into the circle when things get busy. Bash enemies back when you activate shield. Ignore knockback with shield to secure scuffed revives.

Demolisher: Blow stuff up, even yourself! Destroy bug holes. Nuke bug hives. Hold choke points. Cleanup Corpses. Shoot a cannon from your back. 

Sniper: Jetpack up high. Spot enemies first with VISR and scanner gun. Take down gunner bugs and big single targets.

Ranger: Kite and mark enemies. Take materials back to base. Place rally points for the whole team. Grab stims and fly in for risky revives.

Engineer: Team ammo supply. Build and repair faster. Make resource drill objectives faster. Active ability lets you build and repair anywhere, anytime. Only class that can build spotlights.

Medic: Revive from a distance with the active ability. Supply everyone with forms of healing. Heal gun, heal vendor, heal beacon. Trade first-aid for buffs with combat stimulants or offense with a guard drone. passive health regen nearby medics?


[h2] Metaprogression: Armory Unlock system, Prestige [/h2] 
Armory: Break free of class restrictions. When you level 10 a weapon, any class can use it. Demo with a flamethrower? Sure! Engineer with autoshotgun? Go ahead!

Prestige: Unlock a new loadout slot and various cosmetics. Class progression is reset but Career Rank unlocks are preserved (slots, cosmetics) and Weapon Progression is preserved. (attachments, camos) You just have to re-earn the base gear back (Weapons, Utilities, Class Perks)


[h2] Misc things I like [/h2] 
It runs great on linux, give it a look on ProtonDB.

Various objectives will have caches next to them. Once opened, they will contain any random weapon or utility from any class, AND ANY CLASS CAN TAKE THEM. IN ANY SLOT! AND YOU GET XP FOR USING THAT WEAPON EVEN IF IT ISN'T UNLOCKED! These little boxes are so much fun, you never know what's inside or maybe you just want to use another gun to shake things up.

There's two +1 util perks, which CAN BE STACKED, and even give +10 shots for stim gun and scanner gun utilities! EACH! I was ready to start a mission and say "meh I guess I have 12 stim shots now instead of 10" nope I have 30!! it's great!! these also up my stim stacks from 3 per stack to 4, or 5! and soon we will have a perk that starts us with 6 stims, will I get to reach 8 stims a stack with that new perk? we'll just have to find out!


[h2] Problems with the game [/h2]
The maps can be really confusing. SPARTA and Boreas especially.

Progression can be buggy sometimes, like I completed 3 missions that all told me I hit level 70 but only after the third mission did I properly rank up from level 69.

There is a nuke launcher in the game and with the right setup it can be spammed to the point of absurdity. You won't be able to shoot anything because your screen will be shaking so much.

Explosives in this game give off wet fart vibes. They practically have to be on top of enemies if not direct hits to deal good damage, and the VFX of these explosions leave a lot to be desired.

Customization menu is broken, the visors look worse here than they do in-mission. Olive visor straight up doesn't work correctly in this menu.

Server connection can really make-or-break the joy you get out of the game. When it's laggy, everyone suffers. Shoot early and this is mostly mitigated, but where it gets especially bad is when you are trying to mantle up something or climb ladders and it just warps you back down because it's struggling so much to keep up.

The UX for picking a spawn point feels too barebones and lacking in information, Ranger's rally beacons are the only reason I know this is a feature in the game. Critical Strike missions and Hive Hunts on the SPARTA really suffer for this where players who aren't in the know will just be single file line meat in the grinder until the mission fails for running out of respawns.

The game could use a ballbuster difficulty to really test the limits of 16 players.

Rico's portrait is obviously AI.

It gets a little too campy for my tastes especially because they arent even referencing it right. Would you like to build more? regarding a tutorial. Would you like to buy more? regarding cosmetic packs. Yeah sure "build more" and "buy more" make more sense but "know more" is fine IMO. 


[h2] How did I play up to this point? [/h2]
Medic -> Engineer -> Guardian -> Demolisher -> Ranger -> Sniper
Focused one class until they hit max (Lv16) and then moved to the next class.
I tried every weapon, utility, and perk in every class for at least one game as soon as I got them.
In the case of weapons or items that frustrated me, felt useless to me etc, I kept using them until either I figured it out or I unlocked what makes them good.


[h2] Final Verdict [/h2]
Prestiged.
Recommended.

review_text:
A good story mixed with a dreadful game. The gameplay is dull and the controls are awkward. In some sense, it's actually impressive how they managed to screw up the controls in such a simplistic game.

The story might be a bit cheesy and short, but good. Not worthy of any awards, but good. The story is the main selling point of the game, no two ways about it. The game is described as a "story-driven experience" and tagged as "story rich", so as you might expect the gameplay takes the back seat. But there's the problem: the game itself is so bad that it serves only as a distraction to the story. Every moment I spent actually playing the game was only so that I could continue the story. I would have prefered only the story, with no game at all. In other words, a movie.

So do I recommend it? Well, maybe. If you are willing to suffer through a bad game while being told a good story, then sure. If you want to support the developers, then sure. But if you want a good game, then stay far away from this one. Everything this game has to offer has been done much better. If you want a point-and-click game, there are plenty which are actually good as opposed to this one which is bad. If you want a puzzle game, same thing. And while the story is good, there are plenty of better ones. Just read a good book or watch a good movie. Even some games have better stories. This game is hilariously over-praised.

Visuals are cool, gunplay itself is pretty solid and the thematic of the game is real cool, but it's just not fun.
You can't shoot enemies further than 20 meters away without doing fuck-all damage wise, your melee and spell cooldowns are way too fucking long for how little they do, you can't dash mid-air, despite stamina already limiting your mobility anyways so I don't see why that limitation has to be there, the "roguelite" element of each run on the same map being "different" is laughable, the upgrades you get after clearing each enemy camp are boring and don't change your gameplay in meaningful ways, which is important cause the game expects you to clear the same set static maps over and over with the only variety being enemy camp setup and upgrade choices, especially early game where you have no other weapons or spells than you started with. Just an hour in and I was already getting bored, the game has very little depth despite trying to seem more complex than it is, with loads of different stat numbers for both your character and weapons.
There are so many other roguelite shooters than this, that aren't in early access(despite already being EA on EGS for over a year) and don't cost 40 US DOLLARS. This is a measly offering for that amount of money, buy a different game.

review_text:
Took me 30 hours from start to finish.

Ultimately, Witchfire is at its heart a soulslike, with a slight hint of extraction shooter.
Much like a soulslike, the class selection at the start just determines your starting stats and equipment. On death, you drop your belongings and need to recover them.
Pretty much most of the tropes you expect of a soulslike, you'll find here in an FPS format. 
The most unique aspects of the game, in my opinion, are the level design and the weapons. The game is split into a series of open maps, filled with secrets you have to find on your own. It is extremely compelling, and every map has a distinct layout and personality.
The weapons each have three tiers of progression, with each tier unlocking a core functionality of each weapon. Honestly, there are only two weapons I felt underperformed. All others were excellently-designed with unique niches and fantasies that are all useful and powerful. 
As far as critiques I could give, there aren't many. But there are a few key ones:
- There aren't enough bossfights in the game. Each map has a single named boss to fight. While it fits thematically, it does mean that there are only 4 unique bosses in the game as of writing, with at least 2 more still in development.
- The design ethos of the Calamity system eludes me. It is a system designed to punish you for taking damage by initiating an event in which you have to either kill a horde of enemies or destroy a circle of floating skulls elsewhere on the map within a time limit. In this game, healing is very limited initially, and enemies deal no small amounts of damage. So a system tacked on to punish taking damage even further seems a little... overkill, honestly. If there were a way to push back the calamity timer as a reward for finding secrets/performing well, I'd like it a little more, but as of now it's kinda a "kick the player while they're down" mechanic.

Overall, I found the game to be a lovely time with great gamefeel. What flaws this game does have are minor, and are already being worked on as part of Early Access. I greatly recommend!

review_text:
Not worth 40 bucks IMO. There may be a good amount of content here but the core gameplay loop gets ironically rather stale, with the game switching between exploration and tagging, then combo trials, then score attacks (which are comically easy), followed by a dream sequence, repeat, at least so far.

The game's visual style is pretty rad, give or take things very often clipping into each other. Call that part of the aesthetic choice if you will but I think it just looks bad. The music is extremely hit and miss, mostly miss, especially comparing directly to the JSR/F OST. Most of the tracks are ok at best, but nothing I'd listen to for fun outside of Naganuma's tracks, and at worst are grating enough that I preferred to play in silence. I wish more tracks were just there for me to manually put on, and not something I need to find, I'd just put Get Enuff on repeat. The story at least is interesting enough to justify the events, it's just a shame nothing else really holds up as much.

Worst offender is of course the cops and combat, not a new take I'm sure, but really worth driving home. I'm not sure what it is with indie platformers shoving in sub-par combat for the past few years (Hat in Time, Demon Turf, etc.) when they'd just benefit from putting me back into what the game excels at. Pacing is important but a bad pace breakers is worse than none at all.

Overall an ok game, some will love it, but I think 40 USD is just too much for what's on offer.

Wait for a $10 sale.

Atmosphere, graphics, ambiance, music - all of these are stellar. Unfortunately, the designers thought that adding frustration mechanics (combat, health, death) into this would improve it. They do not.

The combat is difficult and your weapons are slow. Your ammo is limited. Your health is limited. The enemies are way too strong and it is really easy to die. And when you die, you respawn somewhere, not sure where, and you have to figure out where you are and where you are going since everything in this game is impossible to navigate a second time. You don't respawn with full health either. Prepare yourself for infinite loops of being one hit from dying, dying, and then respawning one hit from dying.

Generally these sort of frustration mechanics are reserved for action games and Dark Souls. This is not the game for these mechanics. I don't want to learn how to be a combat master in Scorn. I want to be creeped out and experience the atmosphere. Pretty much ruined for me after I realized I needed to memorize enemy spawns and snipe them with headshots.

Edit - Just finished the game, that final boss battle was everything I said above that I hated all wrapped up into one giant wipefest. But the ending was cool. Still wait for $10.

review_text:
Have played the game for about 227 hours and had it since Early access and have 100% the achievements. With the amount of content that it has currently and considering that they've permanently reduced the price; I feel that the game is finally worth what it is priced and I can confidently recommend this game. 

Its a very fun straight to the point, action packed game. I love the class and weapon variety. The persistent Bug corpses really do change the landscape of the game and is definitely a spectacle to behold upon at the end of the battle. The base building mechanic is also very fun and throughout playing I have seen and played on many different effective base designs, it's an aspect of the shooter that makes it unique in its way. If you're a big enjoyer of the original film, you wont be disappointed. The current version (version 1.4) where you're able to wield the FedNet Camera is such a fun and mechanically practical for the gameplay, the potential for roleplay is also very good. Another plus is that the community is so passionate about the franchise aswell, making it fun for newer players first getting into the game.

You also have to bare in mind that the dev team working on the game is small and based on their actions like reducing the price of the game and making changes and actively listening to the community, I trust them. They've come a long way in development since early access despite the mistakes which were what I feel were that they released the game too early. The bug pathing for example is wayyyy better than what it used to be, they better represent the threat that they are. Either way I am looking forward to seeing future content being added by them, currently, updates seem to be coming at a monthly rate which is good!

At the moment I think Horde mode is the most refined mode out of all the bunch. ARC and AAS modes are fun which let you explore more of the map but I believe those modes still need more polish here and there. I think what would be cool for Hive Hunt mode, would be to have the lighting darker, forcing players to use a light attachment either on their suit or weapons; giving the mode a more claustrophobic kind of feeling.

What I would like to see:
Dismemberment for bugs and humans
Persistent Blood flow on the battlefield
Bullet holes that show up on bugs
ability to customise my trooper, eg different helmets, chest pieces etc not just a paint job change
Medals and Badges that can be earned and displayed on my trooper
In game Emotes and iconic voicelines from the films
Some sort of player hub 
Leaderboards for the company system
If possible a weapon wheel kind of system to easily cycle through each of your Utilities

Most importantly, This game NEEDS more tongue and cheek Federation Propaganda. For example on loading screens and the starting game menu, show a slideshow of artwork/propaganda posters. Before the mission start and you hear the Narrator speak with the FedNet News filter on screen, maybe have an animation of a News Reporter reporting on the location. It would really add to the game from a thematic sense.

review_text:
Where "Dead Space" is to "Resident Evil 4", as "Cronos: The New Dawn" is to "Dead Space".

This game isn't terrible. The setting and story are unique. The voice acting is also very cool, as I enjoy the Traveler's cold and almost automated sounding reactions to the world around her.

However, I will say that this game feels almost like a direct carbon copy of "Dead Space". You have designated buttons for punching and stomping melee attacks. Enemies are grotesque and strange. Only major difference is the overall setting and consumable/ammo crafting system.

Only gripes I have against this game so far is:
- Random Frame-rate Drops/Stuttering (Should be fixed in future patches)
- Combat feels ineffective. Enemies take multiple shots to take down and ammunition is scarce. Melee combat is lacking and attacks feel very under-powered. Wouldn't be much of an issue if a dodge mechanic was implemented, but melee is a death sentence if you are facing multiple enemies.
- Not enough checkpoints. I've found myself replaying significant chunks of gameplay due to deaths.
- Clunky and annoying inventory management. (May be better as game progresses and you unlock upgrades.)

I still recommend this game, but not at the current $60 price tag. It is worth buying if it goes on sale. I only picked this up because I had some interest in the title and I had a few spare Steam Cards laying around.
If you have played DeadSpace, you have literally played a better version of Cronos.

review_text:
I love the metroid-vania style of game, and I am a big fan of souls-like style games as well.

Unfortunately this game is not it. I understand that this game was meant to be punishing, but more then the game being punishing, it just feels bad to play. The combat is slow on clunky. Your swings are attacks are not only slow, even with a "faster" weapon, the attack animation locks you in place for a few frames before and after your swing. This makes it so you will be unable to use your dodge for longer periods of time to let the enemies just hit you. The timing of your attacks and slows take a bit of time to initiate, slightly delaying everything you try to do and messing up your timing. A huge example of when you try to do an attack while in the air. It does not trigger until you are already back on the ground. As much as I would like to call this an oversight that be patched, it is an intended feature - based on an item that locks you in place in the air for an attack. 

Don't get me wrong, you could just buy a bunch of magic rods and spam cast your way through some areas, or even just ignore a lot of the enemies all together, and that is another problem I have. There is no incentive to kill anything. You are punished, whether you mess up or not, the combat is slow and feels terrible, the hit boxes are inconsistent - at times hitting you even in your dodge, the dodge is short, slow and inconsistent, and there is no reason to really kill most of the enemies.

There are much better games to play in these genres, so I cannot recommend this one.

review_text:
Yet another game that tries to incorporate two genres at the same time and fails.

The puzzle side is pretty good - not too trivial to be boring, not too difficult to be annoying.

But the combat is absolutely awful, with a controller anyway, and why wouldn't I use a controller when the game is clearly designed for it, except when it's not.
The sensitivity option applies to both looking around and aiming, so if it's high enough to be able to quickly turn around and run away from a creature then it's difficult to aim (and there's no aim assist!), and if it's low enough to be able to aim then exploration becomes a chore and running away becomes almost impossible.
Reloading and switching weapons takes forever, so if you miss a shot then you're as good as dead because there's no time or room to retreat and reload. Which is especially a problem when some of the "stronger" creatures take an entire clip to kill.
And then when [i]you[/i] get killed for the n-th time - you have to watch this slooooow death animation before you're presented with "continue" button because apparently developers live in a parallel universe where skippable cutscenes were never invented.

I get that making combat more dynamic would've contradicted the general vibe of the game, but it should not have been added in the first place. The first weapon in the game also acts as a tool, and if the rest of them were also tools and the puzzles revolved around that - I think it would've been a more consistent experience.

Update:
The bossfight near the end is genuinely interesting, if played with a mouse.

review_text:
[h1] Retro Review[/h1] 
Now I bought this game a while ago mostly out of curiosity. Are people playing this game still? And is it the same as I remember?

[u] Gameplay[/u] 
I probably don’t have to explain the gameplay basics as its one of these games everyone already has played a lot or will never play as left for dead 2 exists. Most people playing this game do it solely for the nostalgia or achievements.

Now there is something I want to mention that I always disliked in this game. The enemy variety, gameplay itself was always fantastic but I always didn’t like in the first game the weapon balancing. There are only 5 weapons excluding the pistol. After a while in a map, you are usually given the choice of 3 weapon upgrades, either an assault rifle, automatic shotgun, or hunting rifles. I barely know anyone using the hunting rifle, and most of the time the automatic shotgun is better in almost every situation.

Anyways, I was really surprised that no matter which daytime I played I always found a single game or so going, albeit often people from far away countries, Brazil and such which makes the game kind of dead. For me the game had a weird bug on windows 10, making it a mess to play. Every once in a while, the game will freeze and I can continue playing like a couple minutes later usually being my death in a fight. Also, there are some griefers out there, outright abusing the console to join anytime and kicking people without votes. Weird that this isn’t fixed until this day making some weird spergs that solely want to go to other peoples games and kick everyone.

[u]Aesthetics [/u] 
Graphically I always had it way much better in mind. Some stuff like the fingers of the main characters or indoor models look really dated. On the other hand, player models itself, zombies (especially their ragdoll physics) and lighting effects are still really great. Animations itself are really neat and the more horror focused soundtrack is something that people liked more about the first game than the second.

[u]Conclusion/TL;DR [/u] 
Generally, you can still find people to play this game with without a problem. The thing is the game didn’t want to run that well for me, and I managed to encounter a griefer or two. Apart from nostalgia there is no reason to play this game tough. Left for dead 2 added all the maps from the first game and has a way much active community. Therefore I don’t really recommend to check it out.

Dead and overshadowed multiplayer coop fps by its successor

review_text:
Not the same game I used to play with my friend back in 2020. Take everything I saw with a grain of salt because I downloaded this game, played it, and quit because of my friend mostly. We had so much fun just mindlessly doing missions and talking over Discord. It was probably one of the best times in my whole life. Wake up, call friend, get on Phantasy Star Online 2, and looky here. He was already there an hour before waiting for me. Sorry man, sleep problems. Play the entire day until I have to do college classes. Leave class and get on Phantasy Star Online 2 so I could do my rainbow quests for EXP. That was my entire life for a while and I wouldn't have had it any other way.

Then New Genesis happened. We were excited for it. A lot of people were. Oh boy was it rough. My friend's laptop broke so I played alone and filled him in. Filled him in on what you may ask? Nothing. Because there was no content in New Genesis. Nothing at all. You did main quests and-oh sorry. Reach level 10 and come back to us. Fine. I reach level 10 to continue the main quests. I do a handful of missions and-OH SORRY REACH LEVEL 15 TO CONTINUE. Okay fine. I grind and reach level 15. Continue the main quest. Finish the main quest. What's next? Oh side quests? You mean THE ONES I ALREADY 100% COMPLETED TO MAKE UP FOR THE FACT YOU HAD REACHING A CERTAIN LEVEL AS A REQUIREMENT TO CONTINUE THE STORY? 

Fine. I get it. The game has daily and weekly quests too. I'll just do those. What are they? Kill X amount of Y. Kill X amount of Y. Collect X amount of Y. That's just the daily quests so the weekly quests can't be that bad right...put an item inside this tower. You can't be serious.

I mentioned before that there were side quests but at the time there were only a handful and they were basically what I'd consider just padding out game time which makes no sense since the game is free. Imagine buying Metal Gear Solid V and instead of completing side stories that gave you real rewards that HELP you, you had to enter a building that loaded you into a VR mission a la Metal Gear Solid 1 that only gives you EXP as a reward. Woah. Real rewarding.

*Note that's based on memory which could be wrong and you may have gotten rewards other than EXP but considering I may have forgotten then they probably didn't do much

Also why upgrade the graphics? The game didn't need an upgrade. My shitty HP laptop could handle the game fine but New Genesis melted it. The game looked fine so I don't see the point. Even now that I use a desktop PC which I admittedly spent too much money on I don't really see the difference. I only know the graphics are better from the devs stating they are and the performance getting worse. The performance is still worse on the original PSO2 server.

That's right you can go back to the original game but it's a pain in the ass to do and then you have to do the same process again to switch back to New Genesis. Plus you have to download save data from PSO2 which steam won't let me for some reason.

I admit this as well. They've updated the game a lot since I quit. I logged on the other day and there was a concert going on (with like no one attending it in my server) and 2 new areas and the combat is fine for what it tries to accomplish. The world itself is pretty good but I'm not a fan of open world so that's probably someone else's space to say if it's peak or not. For this amount of time it's been released I feel like we should have more since it still doesn't seem like there's a lot in the game. I'm not speaking from entitlement either. If you think the game does the have enough then delay it. I'd rather we had a slightly better than okay game that took longer than expected rather than what we had.

Whatever happened to the days where we'd have an entire lobby lining up to save our world from Omega Falz Luther? Seems those days are gone and I need to accept it.

Going to take time to finish what's been added since my last time playing. I'll get to it eventually and will update my review accordingly.

review_text:
This is a really tough one to review. Overall, I say "Recommend," because it's an audacious and quality work, and the makers deserve money for it. Do I think most people would enjoy this game, as a game? No.

It's not like HIVESWAP: Act 1, which was a straightforward point-n-click adventure game. That was standard--observe the environment, find the items, find the obstacles, use the items on the obstacles, progress. The setting and writing were quirky and neat, the puzzles fair.

Act 2 has a little of that, but only a very little. In Act 1, near the end, the game shifts into a new kind of game, that is almost straight-up visual novel told through dialogue, until the end. Act 2 carries this on. It is almost entirely dialogue-driven, with almost no point-n-click puzzling. The solutions are nearly all 1) Talk to character, 2) Talk to other character, 3) talk to original character.

Part of this is really impressive. While you're progressing, at every turn, every character--and there are a great many characters, each with a unique, consistent voice--has new things to say. For an adventure game, that is remarkable. Every one of them weighs in, helpfully or not, on every part of every puzzle. Huge amounts of dialogue.

Unfortunately, this ends up making the game-play a series of "talk to every character about everything," over and over again. This gets brainless and not fun.

A huge portion of the story is very similar to--to the point of near plagiarism--Snowpiercer. It's a shame that this is so shameless, because if it weren't for this piracy, it's a very-well-told cosmology of class distinction, class envy, class callousness, and class struggle. But it is far too close to Snowpiercer, complete with advancing-through-train-one-car-at-a-time, to give this game full credit.

Finally: The Phoenix Wright pastiche is *interminable.* It just goes on, and on, and on, and ON, AND ON, and the novelty wears out far, far before the sequence ends. The whole part is a joke, and an obvious one, but then it just refuses to let go, and this goes on for something like a half-hour of straight dialogue. This was a horrible choice.

I beat this because I almost never put a book aside once begun, and this really was a book. For adventure game puzzlers, I would recommend Act 1 but not Act 2. For fans of the setting and this writing, I say go for it.

kind of game, that is almost straight-up visual novel told through dialogue, until the end. act 2 carries this on. it is almost entirely dialogue-driven, with almost no point-n-click puzzling. the solutions are nearly all 1 talk to character, 2 talk to other character, 3 talk to original character. part of this is really impressive. while you're progressing, at every turn, every character--and there are a great many characters, each with a unique, consistent voice--has new things to say. for an adventure game, that is remarkable. every one of them weighs in, helpfully or not, on every part of every puzzle. huge amounts of dialogue. unfortunately, this ends up making the game-play a series of talk to every character about everything, over and over again. this gets brainless and not fun. a huge portion of the story is very similar to--to the point of near plagiarism--snowpiercer. it's a shame that this is so shameless, because if it weren't for this piracy, it's a very-well-told cosmology of class distinction, class envy, class callousness, and class struggle. but it is far too close to snowpiercer, complete with advancing-through-train-one-car-at-a-time, to give this game So.. I do recommended this game it does come with a slight warning - I do like this game, I had fun playing this game, I would say if you're one of the 5 people in the world who've been demanding more Ice Hockey games release on PC it's definitely one to buy. 

However, I do think this game has a serious Achilles heel that cannot be ignored and is holding the game back in a bad way: No Career/Franchise Mode.

Despite the game having great graphics, great physics, great gameplay and overall being very fun... it's painfully short, with those 2.8 hours on record I have already beaten the final team and 'completed the game'. I find the refusal to include a Franchise Mode baffling, especially for a Singleplayer only game.

I want to get hooked and go deep into seasons building a team or player, recruiting talent, watching them grow, dealing with the finances, having rival teams, or creating my own character starting as a young talent with potential and levelling them up over the seasons - it's the only reason I play sports games when I play those Offline but I cannot do that here and I feel that it's holding this game back.

It's fun and it's worth the money especially when it goes on sale, but I didn't hook me in for very long and I came away feeling very mixed - happy to have a good Ice Hockey game, frustrated that it doesn't fill the Career shaped hole EA Sports left when it became Console only.

review_text:
This game and it successor "Contracts 2" both suffer from game play defects. Most note worthy is the inability to transition from prone to crouch to stand from the prone position. The player is often left stuck prone from which there is no escape: often the character is frozen in place, leaving no option but to restart the mission; or in order to stand and run must crawl for 10m at which point you are killed. Other anomalies include bad contrast in the rifle scope view. The cross hairs are black and fade easily into the background leaving the player searching for them. In "Contacts" the enemy tag distance is in light red....very hard to see. There is also a quirk with the wind correction line in the scope (Contracts) that when the character holds his breath for a shot the correction line moves left requiring readjustment before the breath expires. Both games are deficient in the ability to resume from a point without having to replay the entire mission; contracts 2 gives an option to select a previous save to restart from at least, something the predecessor does not allow. 
There seems to be something about "game designer syndrome" that persists in most all games. It has to do with circa 1960 arcade games; where you loose and game over (for 25 cents!). Even exceptions there let you end the game with a score and you replayed if you chose to better it. It is unfathomable that a game today would be designed to have the player continually loose and have to replay the entire episode over and over ad nauseam. That aspect is the biggest gripe of players (older than 16) who just spent hours playing an episode. One of the other most frustrating things designers do is spawn enemies; particularly where there was none before; like right behind the player's character....surprise! "Sniper contracts" is full of this, plus not being able to escape being hit by enemy fire even when 300m away and behind a building or wall. Here again all for the propensity to have the player be defeated and have to play over. Somehow the thinking is that loosing depicts the difficulty of winning...duh! So if you don't care about any of this, then both games are for you. Good luck and enjoy!

review_text:
🎮 Game Experience – Phantasy Star Online 2: New Genesis Ver. 2
Playing NGS Ver. 2 has been a ride. The revamped visuals and fluid combat caught my eye immediately. I enjoyed exploring the open zones, especially when random events popped up—adds that MMO thrill. I spent time tweaking my character's look (the fashion system is still top-tier), and the photon dash and glide made traversal actually fun.

Combat felt smoother and more responsive compared to the original NGS launch. Whether soloing or partying up for urgent quests, the game kept me engaged, even if the grind can get repetitive. Some of the new creative space features are cool—though they take time to get used to. Met a few chill players along the way too, which definitely helped the experience.

✅ Pros
Massive Visual Upgrade: Gorgeous environments, improved lighting, and character detail really make the world pop.

Smoother Combat: Better responsiveness, more dynamic actions, and cool class synergy.

Open World Freedom: The large open zones and seamless exploration feel liberating.

Character Customization: Deep and stylish—your character can look exactly how you want.

Creative Space: A sandbox-style area to build and design your own zone (like a player housing system with freedom).

Frequent Events & Updates: Keeps things fresh with seasonal content and new gear.

Great for Solo or Party Play: You’re not punished for playing solo, but it’s more fun with others.

❌ Cons
Repetitive Grind: Content loops can get stale—grind for gear, level, repeat.

Sparse Story Content: The narrative can feel thin or stretched out over time.

Performance Issues: Some stutters or load times on older systems or during busy events.

Empty Areas: Sometimes zones feel lifeless unless an event is happening.

UI and Menus: Still a bit clunky and overwhelming, especially for new players.

Gacha System: Fashion and certain upgrades are locked behind scratch tickets and RNG.

TLDR: If you don't care about PvP, or if you do care about PvP but don't mind min-maxing via numerous restarts of your runs, then I'd recommend this game.

Ok hear me out.. it's easy to see the developer truly loves this game and dedicates their time to making it better. I hate leaving a "thumbs down" review on games that have a caring developer or dev team.
My review is coming from my personal experience with the game, not from whether or not you should buy it.

I think the game is a great idea, I like the classes, and roguelikes are my favorite genre.
If you remove "King of the Hill" from my experience, this game would get a thumbs up I think. KotH is the PvP mode you can play at the end of a PvE run. Whatever units you have at the end of the PvE run, and whatever upgrades you have, are what you take into PvP.
PvE isn't hard once you know how to play. My frustration is with PvP.

If you want to win PvP (place top 3, or especially finish a season in 1st place) you HAVE to min-max from the very very beginning of the PvE run (you have to restart over and over until you get the ideal augments). And there's typically only 1-2 comps that can place and hold top 3. You need to play them if you want top 3.
Once you know the comps that can place and hold top 3, you then have to get lucky in the PvE run and get all the perfect augments you need for your comp. It's also important to get the class-specific random events in PvE, that give your specific comp's class type a buff, and you need to win the random event, and then receive the correct reward.

I've played enough to finish 1st in a couple PvP seasons, and I've completed a PvE run in hardmode; I'm not just some frustrated new player. I feel like I have a strong grasp on mechanics and how to play.
I know roguelikes are "luck"-based. It's just... the amount of sub-par runs greatly outweighs good runs for me (bad or good being determined by upgrade choices and events/encounters).


----------------------------

Brawl mode feels the same way to me; if you don't have certain mutations, you'll only go so far. Like the +80% magic damage mutation. If you don't have that by a certain point, and you're playing a mag dmg comp, it's nigh hopeless.

I haven't been able to get past 7 trophies or so on Brawl. I don't really want to go on Discord and/or watch lots of YT videos just so I can play better. I've spent a couple hours watching YT videos, and it helped me learn, but my sentiments still stand. It still feels min-maxy. Although to be fair, Brawl does feel like a wider variety of comps exist. I've seen every race do well.

review_text:
The game very obviously walks in the footsteps of Dead Space and makes no apologies about it. Combat, inventory management, enemies, even major story elements all borrow heavily. However, that's not necessarily a bad thing. Dead Space hasn't really had any spiritual successors to speak of and it remains to this day such a functionally solid experience that even a game copying mostly 1:1 is destined to be good. The game runs well, has a banger soundtrack, spooky vibes, and cool weapons. In general it's just a very well put together experience.

My largest criticism is that for all it does to live up to the legacy of the games that came before it, the game and its story don't do much to try to genuinely stand apart. It spends so much time trying to be the next Dead Space that it doesn't manage to be anything but a game trying to be the next Dead Space. The story is serviceable, but nothing special. The enemies are good up to a point, but eventually become a bit predictable. The environments are mostly unique but only really cover classic horror story tropes (the spooky hospital, the industrial wasteland, the haunted church, etc.) For a game that markets itself as "a new breed of horror," it doesn't really do anything new, even with its great premise.

Where Cronos does stand out is the aesthetic. The game's protagonist, the Traveler, is just too freaking cool. From her bulky diving suit to her clipped and stoic dialogue, she radiates simultaneous calm and menace in every second she interacts with other characters. The technology of other Travelers, from their weapons to their time travel "anchors" to the breadcrumbs of ammo caches and anti-grav platforms seeded through the world, stand out from their Soviet-era surroundings in the absolute best way. It's just cool, and doesn't need any deeper justification than that.

All in all, a very solid (if flawed) title from Bloober Team. I very much enjoyed it and if scifi survival horror is your jam, you will too.

review_text:
Interesting take on a Metroidvania.

It diverges from the norm in a few ways:
- You do not heal at save points or checkpoints. You have to rely on consumable items, or gear you find later.
- Enemies don't respawn. Except when they do. Not really sure what the criteria is here, but it isn't screen transitions or hitting a save point.
- You do not gain new traversal abilities at any point. Walk, jump, and roll is all you get.
None of this is necessarily bad, just unusual.

Games had top-notch pixel art, is relatively difficulty, and pretty short at around 6 hours for a first playthrough.
Sound is a bit lacking - the sound effects are serviceable, but even having just finished the game I couldn't tell you if it even had music. Definitely no voice acting.
Gameplay is a little bit rough, but solid.

Decent 7/10 game. Worth checking out, but not likely to amaze you.

The visual depth of blinding bright lights of Destiny 2 aren't as bad as this since it isn't super consistent as "every hit you receive blinds you" that is present here.

Anyone confident that they won't have the same eye struggles as mentioned here, definitely give it a try.

review_text:
I feel so incredibly mixed about this game.

I think the dialogue and charm of Act 1 was mostly maintained here, as well as the pretty fucking great worldbuilding, but man there's just some things I outright hated about this.

I'm pretty sure the trial part took me a literal 3 hours to go through. I felt drained by it before the actual trial itself even started, and by the end I was trying to go through whatever motions would get it done and over as quickly as possible. It drags on so fucking badly I don't even know how to properly describe it. I'm sure other reviews can do that well enough though, as it seems like I'm not the only one who completely hated that part. Easily the worst part of the game, it's not even close.

Also I've seen next to no one talk about this, but I swear there was an entire forest section cut from the game. One moment you're at the edge of it, the next you're at the train station with the pair reminiscing about the things they saw there in like 3-4 text boxes. What's up with that? Surely that wasn't the original plan, I can't for the life of me imagine someone at WPG just going "hey what if we had this forest, okay, and the characters needed to find a thing to travel through the forest, but once that thing is found the player then sees none of what the forest has to offer and just ends up at the train station immediately after that thing is found." Whatever, guess it's not that big of a deal. Still jarring af though.

Oh yeah, there's a feeling of a lack of polish that persists throughout the game. Bugs, weird quirks like cutscene pop-in, a whole bunch of stuff that almost makes the game feel like it was rushed out just to have it finally release. And I can kinda understand considering it was a literal three years since Act 1 (and god knows when or if we'll ever see act 3) that they'd just want to get it out as soon as they could, but... really? I know for a fact these 3 years weren't spent on developing the game, there's no way that could've happened, but come on. The least they could've done was some adequate playtesting.

Also I swear that ending was even more abrupt than Act 1's was. I don't know whether to be impressed or upset about that.

My recommendation for this one is weird. I recommend it for reading through all the funny lines n stuff said there and to experience that great worldbuilding I mentioned, but I also really hope you're prepared for the bs this game with throw at you because if you aren't you will not have fun with the 2nd half of the train ride. Especially the trial section. Fuck that section.

review_text:
This game takes the fun out of auto-battlers.

First of all, food... What a boring concept whose goal is to restrict your ability to enjoy the army building aspect. You already lose units all the time via them dying. Why you have to add food to the mix is mind boggling.

Second, no enemy visibility. You can't strategize your line because you can't see the opponent or what they do. There's no good gameplay reason for this. It's artificial difficulty for the sake of it, which is sort of a running theme in the mechanics of this game.

Third, the art. The stick figure people all look so basic. You don't really get this cool army of heroes. You just have weird looking stick figures with tiny weapons.

I have played a LOOOOT of autobattle games and this just doesn't do the genre justice. It removes or dampens some of the key aspects that give the genre life. I looked forward to this for a long time, but as soon as I was finished with my first run I was just like "wtf..."
