review_text:
While people sing BioShock's praises, I'll have to wholeheartedly disagree with them. On one part, I do agree, the story is interesting and it's a shame that the other elements just don't do it justice.

The gameplay is... Just bad. The controls are clunky and counter intuitive, which leads to massive frustrations. A good example is when you fight the "Rosie" Big Daddy variants. These are long range types, who shoot at you with both a big-ass gun and grenades. One of the things your learn early on is "Use Telekinesis to throw the grenades back at the opponent". However, with this Big Daddy, you've got no chance of doing so.

For instance, if you keep your Telekinesis Plasmid active, it keeps on shooting its regular gun while you try to dodge the bullets to no success because for some reason, the bullets do still manage to hit you. When it finally DOES decide to throw a grenade, the Telekinesis Plasmid holds it in front of you (making it slightly see-through) but it still obscures the middle of the screen, making your throws INCREDIBLY innacurate.

If you manage to actually hit the Big Daddy and not something of the scenery (they're also "mine bombs", so when they land, they stay in place as a mine that can still hurt your ass which is so much fun...) the grenade does a marginally low amount of damage for the time that you've been shoving Med-Kits in your gaping wounds while jumping from side to side like a cartoon character that tries to dodge gunfire.

So, what do you do? You pull out your Tommy Gun to lay some smackdown on the mofo. You open fire, seeing that the damage you do is comparable to the damage an ant does to a plate of solid steel: almost jack-shit. However, for some reason, this makes the Big Daddy more inclined to throw grenades, so when you see the grenade fly towards you, you immediately go for your Telekinesis Plasmid and get hit in the face with the damn grenade. Wanna know why? THE PLASMIDS AREN'T ABLE TO BE ACTIVATED IMMEDIATELY! Yeah, so you see the grenade coming, you switch to the plasmid by pulling the left trigger, instinctively holding it because that'd make sense and activate the ability immediately, but no! It doesn't! You'd have to let go of the trigger first, then pull it again to activate the plasmid, hoping it does, but by the time it goes off, your ass is decorating several walls in the scenery already!

Another big problem: Enemies. Keep. Spawning. No matter what. Now, I'm a very thorough person, going through the entire map before heading to the objective marker because I want to explore every nook and cranny of the place and find everything that you can. However, this is hampered by enemies who suddenly appear out of fucking nowhere. Even though you've gone through the damn room 3 times already, there will ALWAYS be enemies that return. This takes away any sense of progression or accomplishment because it just makes you feel as if you're shoving your fingers in the holes in your boat to stop the leaking, and every time you close up one hole, another one pops up!

Compare this to Halo. In that, you'd murder an entire level and when you ran back for the supply drop you know you skipped on purpose to conserve ammo and grenades, you'd feel like an utter demon because, holy shit, you totally decimated their forces. Everything's dead, the place is silent, no suicide Grunts that pop out of nowhere, no Elites yelling "Wort Wort Wort" or anything. That made you feel awesome and creep you out because the levels felt so empty all of a sudden.

Here, you're backing up because a Big Daddy is closing in, only to get a grenade shoved up your ass by a guy who, logically, SHOULDN'T EVEN BE THERE!

Like, the Fishery level. You arrive there in a Bathysphere, the room you arrive in has no place for ANYONE to enter but through the bathysphere. You run through it, encounter your first Rosie Big Daddy, and you start backing up while firing your guns. All of a sudden, something explodes next to you, taking out a quarter of your health, and as you turn around, you realise that it's a damn fodder enemy that spawned in for the Hell of it. Good work there!

Then again, dying has no consequence either. With games like Halo, you're running when you're low on Health, hoping for that "Game Saved" pop up so you can keep your progress even if you die. Here, when you die, you just get back up, get to keep all your weapons, get to keep all your progression and most importantly you get to keep your enemy damage. So... Whatever, draw a Big Daddy to a Vita Chamber, then turn it into Swiss Cheese by turning into a steampunk version of Deadpool because you keep popping up without any repercussions.

Part of me is glad they did that, because if they didn't, this game would've been even worse than it is now...

As it stands, I don't see why people sing its praises so damn much. Sure, it's pretty, atmospheric and has a good story, but if the gameplay sucks, it's all for naught.

review_text:
I generally hate pay to win/buying power, but given that the only avenue for this was the battle pass which caps the power buying at a relatively low monetary number, I stomached it. I figured worse case scenario it's a free single player game of surprisingly good quality, given the graphics, storyline, cutscenes, boss design, etc.

However, the story quests are mostly boring, many of the puzzles are contrived, the menu and systems bloat is ridiculous, bugs aren't game breaking but ubiquitous, the localization is terrible, and the gear progression is full of chores that don't actually reward your time investment. Despite all of this, I was still kind of enjoying the game for awhile there. I put about 70 hours in the game and it didn't start feeling to stale until the last 10. Yet, I kept pushing. That is, until my encounter with the bounty system.

I got a bounty bc an npc I disguised myself as saw me. This caused me to be invaded, wasting my 2nd disguise (which aren't cheap) btw. I fought the invader for HALF AN HOUR before they gave up and left. I was frustrated at this point and logged off for a few days. I logged back on after my break only to be immediately invaded again. I nearly beat this invader, after a 10 minute fight, only to be killed by some geese I accidently agro'd during the fight. This caused me to be put in prison, where I have to wait 15 minutes in game without doing anything, or buying my way out, or crafting a bunch of stuff to "get on the warden's good side." The crafts would probably have taken me most of the 15 minutes to complete, but I didn't even get time to test that theory because you have to compete for access to a small number of workbenches that other players will want to use. You can not opt out of the bounty system btw.

So to recap, about 55 minutes of my time was wasted because I got caught wearing a disguise. I don't even know if winning the bounty fight would have ended the invades, because my fight was interrupted by a geese swarm. Having someone fight you for half an hour and leave does not reset your bounty. The prison system presents you with another useless crafting system, and all of that was a prolonged distraction from a game whose online functionality did nothing positive for my enjoyment of the game.

This crushed my last remaining bit of motivation to play this bloated game full of boring, basically mandatory elements (such as the oddity collection). The game is full of potential, but is ultimately a HUGE letdown.

review_text:
PSO2NGS is, in many ways, inferior to PSO2. This is because the game's direction is that there is no direction. The open world idea is great and all, but it plays more like a mode that would be attached to PSO2 than anything else. The core identity of PSO2 was the drop-in play and the quest lobbies. PSO2 was effectively an arcade game, which makes sense on why it had a couple of SEGA arcade collaborations. You drop in, play as much as you want, call it a day. Get loot, grind levels, so on. The idea of loot and power kept changing for the worst, unfortunately, and applies to PSO2 as a whole. 

How many f'ing stars will you add to your rarity before it's enough? 13 star items? Oh, now it turns out that 15 stars make 13 stars garbage.
... Of course, that's not the actual problem. The problem is that these stars are tied to time-gated events. PSO2 is basically what'll happen to NGS in terms of equipment.

The NGS story is set 1000 years later, but, APPARENTLY... ARKS fell during half that time.
Spoilers? Hardly. This is necessary knoweldge.
THE ARKS. You're telling me the ARKS, SET UP TO SAVE LIFEFORMS FROM EXTINCTION, FELL? We, the player character that happens to harness the power of Dark Falz a la DARK BLAST, was powerless on a new threat. The AIS against the Magatsu, the evolution of technology and the riders, the third/fourth/fifth new power that was Episode 6 in a nutshell.

All of that, for what?

Whoever the F was behind the story made PSO2NGS completely irrelevant as a story. There's no point in following it, and should be seen as an nonclinical what-if OR one of those alternate story-line generations from PSO2 EP6. ARKS is an acronym. Artificial Relict to Keep Species.
Now? 

We're conveniently, Artificial Relict to Keep Species Defenders. Yep. 'They' forgot their own acronym. 

The story content itself didn't matter, the overall story and idea was enough. PSO2 was about having a passable story, NGS is about trying to reset the legacy but unable to committing to a new game entirely. The original idea was nice, having both games run along each other and sharing data and even some items.

PSO2 was actually full of interesting ideas; when they added the fourth race... which was the same models as others but with a horn sticking out and other minor differences... they at least redid the opening and gave it a reasonable time/sci-fi explanation.

I actually have zero interest in NGS's story knowing that everything we did in PSO2 was worth less than nothing.
Unfortunately, it also made PSO2's story kind of worthless to invest in. The PSO2's Episode Oracle anime is good enough as a watchable summary. EP4 is mediocre, and 5 and 6 are enjoyable/whatever, if you can get to that point without burning out.

================
As an Open World, NGS has all the trademark garbage associated with it. Trash mobs that give next to no EXP, the ability to walk into enemies twice your level, and nothing rewarding. Shrines, a la BOTW, exist for Skill Points and other such. Why? How? Old MMOs actually let you grind in open fields with enemies that give EXP and drops.

The only plus is Ccombat is okay. Unfortunately, the basic idea for it is turning all base classes into PSO2's 'Scion' classes. PSO2's biggest problem was that the Scion classes ruined the game through high DPS, locking players into only a few choices once unlocked. They were the concept that became the gateway to NGS and why NGS plays quite differently. Thanks, team behind 'Scion'.

PSO2 itself is difficult to truly min/max in, as they locked all the speed leveling and gearing options away through time limits. Instead of having a repeating rotating cycle to still drop items, they decided to leave it with nothing.

Now, Both PSO2 and NGS (which people keep forgetting, it's not "base pso2", it's PSO2 & NGS), still contain some goodness to it, which is why I can still say it's okay to exist.

The character creator leads to creativity and fun creations, even though the pieces are likely absurdly expensive, and a few are even race-locked between CAST and fleshlings. It's still a great dress-up simulator with some fun combat.

PSO2 can still be played in 'Solo' mode, or rather, playable alone. The core of it shows that it's a game that can eventually be re-worked for a console offline version with peer-2-peer connectivity to keep it alive forever. (Even though we know SEGA will drop it once it ded.)

NGS, on the other hand, feels more like it is played alone due to the open structure. I know there are drastic differences between JP and US, such as economy, making NGS much more playable in Japan due to player economy alone.

PSO2 itself is still quite fun and still a unique experience, while NGS feels less new. PSO2 was about hitting big numbers in 'normal' amounts, depending on PA and class anyways, while NGS is hitting smaller numbers in big amounts, regardless of class choice.

While it'll take me a while to come to terms with NGS and like it, all the negativity stems from what people actually liked about PSO2 and now NGS gets all of those things wrong. NGS is basically the corporate version of PSO2. PSO2 was crafted with love, and players loved it from all over the world, even though it was in Japan for 8 years.

NGS is by no means 'bad', it's just... wrong. It's PSO2 gone wrong. It needs a FF14-styled revamp to give it it's identity back.
Sure, quests exist, but it's different in that they're only for a few specific things. Sure, Photon Arts exist, but that's also different.

Also, the terminally online troglodytes that can't be banned because they spend lots of money. That's a huge negative.
Seriously, the perpetually horny plebs who, for whatever reason, can't bring themselves to masturbate and get it out of their system, need to take it online and make it their entire identity. An issue in all forms of PSO2, including JP servers. They can be blacklisted to ignore, but the Symbol Arts stay in the cache.

It sucks, though, to see all these new enemies effectively be old reskins. I thought 'Sadinian?!' the moment I saw the "Pettas Sword". Why are there so many old enemies on this new planet? I might've missed the answer somewhere, or there isn't an answer. Regardless, I give NGS a solid half score, while PSO2 is a solid '7'. The core of PSO2 still exists and how it plays is still 'classic'. A good new game for free, should someone need something fresh without paying a cent.

But, SEGA is stupid as all hells, and that PSO2 is a separate DLC that is required to download alongside NGS IF you want to play classic PSO2 and not new NGS. That type of decision is why NGS is chock full of issues that frustrate long-time players and former PSO2 fanatics.

All said and done, if you're in the first world and can do the download, it's worth a try.

I mean, after all, they're both still free games, and NGS didn't shut PSO2 down directly. For a free game, it's quite surprising, and if you factor in the many years of love PSO2 had, it's a complete game available for free. Limitations apply here and there, but really, there's not much to lose if you're unable to pay for anything else.

review_text:
For being in EA for 700 years, the performance is ASS. The game, even for an early access game, is extremely underwhelming.

It's been out in EA for a long time which is what really worries me. It really is not even close to being releasable. It's a rough shell but there is a fantastic game somewhere underneath. Which is why it's hard to give it a thumbs down. Right now it's about maybe 40% done in my opinion. For it to be worth the $40 asking price it has a very long way to go, which is why I'm doubtful it can possibly make it since it has already been in EA for a hundred years.

Some major problems I've seen:

-Screen stutter jerking is a major issue and needs to be addressed before anything else. And no it's not me. I have a new Alienware system with a RTX 4070 that runs everything else perfectly.
-Running out of ammo is also a major game stopping issue because once you have no ammo and no ammo boxes are around, it's game over, and it can happen very easily on seemingly neverending fights.
-Getting stuck in bushes and not being able to move is a game killing bug that has happened twice to me so far,
-Lack of character sounds, including no sound when you land from a jump.
-Other than shooting enemies and opening chests there's nothing else to do besides upgrading a couple things at the base.
-Once you've seen every part of a map, which doesn't take too many runs to do, there doesn't feel like there's much incentive to keep replaying it other than to collect upgrade currency.

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a tactical stealth game developed by Mimimi Games and released in 2016. The game takes place in feudal Japan and follows a group of five assassins who are tasked with overthrowing a corrupt government. The game received critical acclaim for its challenging gameplay, detailed environments, and engaging storyline.

The game's visuals are stunning, with beautifully rendered environments and detailed character models. The attention to detail is impressive, with each character and environment feeling distinct and authentic to the game's setting. The game's soundtrack is also noteworthy, with a mix of traditional Japanese music and modern compositions that perfectly capture the game's tone.

The gameplay in Shadow Tactics is challenging and rewarding, with players taking control of a team of assassins and utilizing their unique skills to take down enemies and complete objectives. Each character has their own strengths and weaknesses, which players must learn to master in order to succeed. The game encourages players to think strategically and creatively, rewarding those who take the time to plan out their moves and execute them flawlessly.

One of the game's standout features is its emphasis on stealth. Players must avoid being detected by enemies, using cover and distractions to remain unseen. If an enemy does spot the player, they must act quickly to eliminate the threat or flee to safety. This creates a tense and thrilling gameplay experience that keeps players on their toes.

The game's storyline is engaging and well-written, with a mix of political intrigue and personal drama that keeps players invested in the game's outcome. The characters are all well-developed, with distinct personalities and motivations that make them feel like real people rather than just game characters.

Overall, Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a must-play for fans of tactical stealth games. With its stunning visuals, challenging gameplay, and engaging storyline, it is a standout title that should not be missed.

review_text:
I don't often write game reviews, but I have to for this one.

If you're a fan of atmospheric and narrative-heavy games where you have to piece the lore together, this one is a must play. It feels like a good mix between Dead Space and Resident Evil, but it also reminds me of games like Alan Wake 2, Control and Outer Wilds. It's quite authentic in its own way though.

The bleak environments, the minimalist yet effective audio, the overall dystopian and eerie design, and the fact that you have to worry more about managing your resources and inventory than engaging in particularly deep combat or puzzles really did it for me. Excellent job by the developers here.

On top of that, it runs pretty smoothly for me, and I've personally encountered no bugs. The controls felt slightly stiff for me at times, but they're quite functional for the most part.

The storytelling kinda leans can get a bit too cryptic, but that's not necessarily a bad thing. If you enjoy reading lore notes, this won't be an issue at all. 

This is a quite haunting game, sometimes a little frustrating, but definitely memorable for me. It gets a solid 9/10 from me. Totally recommend.

I realized that Lucius had problems when I was playing a side mission that involved repeatedly carrying dirty underwear through a sprawling mansion.  I'm the Antichrist, but I'm also a little kid.  That involves doing chores, which includes collecting dirty laundry.  So I have to wander up to the servants quarters, grab the maids panties, head back to the laundry room, and drop them in the correct basket (whites or colors).  This is not gameplay.  This is tedium.  

  
Lucius wants to be a creepy horror game.  Sadly, it can't maintain the atmosphere it would need to creep you out.  The soundtrack drones on all the time, which means it doesn't work to build tension.  Creepy music can help when you are sneaking around to murder your next victim.  It does not good when you are carrying around the previously mentioned dirty underwear.

Far too much time is spent wandering around a huge mansion, randomly clicking on things, trying to figure out what the developers decided was the single way to kill someone.  It's like Hitman, except instead of a hundred ways to kill someone, there's only the one.

With a lot more polish, Lucius could have been a good game.  Sadly, it's a tedious mess.  Any attempt to tell an interesting story is wasted.

[h2]Hakuoki: Fighting, Bleeding, Loving — In That Order[/h2]

You sit down, cigarette barely hanging on, scarf loose like your last shred of dignity.  
"Overwhelmingly positive?" you mutter. "Yeah, we’ll see about that."

Then you actually play it.  
And [i]merde,[/i] you get it.  
Lot of dudes? ✅  
None of them annoying? ✅  
Actual different vibes? ✅

You’re not flirting with strangers.  
You’re [i]living[/i] with them.  
Bleeding with them.  
Breathing the same dying Kyoto air.

Every path hits different.  
Every choice feels like you’re carving your initials into history with a dagger.

Saito.  
Okita.  
Harada.  
All ride-or-die material. 🥷  
I’d fistfight a government official for any of them.

The MC?  
She’s not a paper doll.  
She’s standing there with a blade in her hand like, "Try me."  
And you believe her.

Sure, the graphics are dusty. 🥀  
Sure, it’s old.  
But it’s got [b]guts.[/b]  
It’s got [b]grit.[/b]  
It’s got more raw goddamn heart than half the shiny new otome landfill pumped out today.

*I lean in. Flick ash at the floor. Jab a finger right at your chest.*

[b]This game is good, mon ami.[/b]  
I [i]was[/i] Chizuru.  
I [i]was[/i] living with the Shinsengumi.  
*Eyes wild, teeth bared, no lies between us.*  
[b]"I carved 'Souji is my ride or die' into the doors and I meant it."[/b]

Full price? Maybe.  
Sale? [b]RUN. CART IT. DON'T LOOK BACK.[/b]

[i]C’est la guerre, bébé.[/i]

review_text:
BioShock – A Masterpiece Beneath the Waves 

This isn’t just a game — it’s an experience, one that i highly recommend playing. From the haunting opening moments in the Atlantic Ocean to the first glimpse of the underwater city of Rapture, BioShock will grab your attention and never let it go.
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Narrative & Atmosphere:

This game redefined storytelling in gaming. With its dystopian, art-deco world, Rapture feels like a living, breathing city — decayed, deranged, and dripping (heh water pun) with atmosphere.  And let’s not forget that twist — one of the most shocking and well-executed in gaming history. 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Game-play:

Combat is fluid and engaging, blending weapons and plasmid elements (or powers whatever you wish to call it) in creative ways. The ability to set traps, freeze enemies, or unleash a swarm of bees keeps things nice and different as there is a wide variety of abilities. Enemy encounters, especially with the Big Daddies, are intense , rewarding, and horrifying. God knows how many times ive been jump-scared by these brutes lol.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Visuals/Sound Design:

Even through out the years, BioShock holds up artistically. The retro-futuristic design of Rapture is gorgeous and grotesque. The sound design is perfect — from the eerie audio logs to the echoes of Splicers muttering in the dark, every sound adds to the immersion. And that vintage soundtrack? Chef's kiss.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Final Verdict:

BioShock is a timeless classic that set a new standard for narrative-driven first-person shooters (in my honest opinion). It’s a game that will challenge your mind as much as it will your trigger finger. If you’ve never played it, you’re missing out on one of gaming’s true masterpieces.

Rating: 10/10 – Would you kindly play it?

review_text:
[b]A neat idea, but complicated execution.[/b]

Fractured Daydream brings 20 players into a raid, to take on parts of a dungeon, only to meet up fighting the end boss together. Only to finish what is a confusing conclusion of this game.

This game wants to be co-operative by working together within your groups and other 16 players, so you don't fail a mission together. Rarely this happens as the game teaches you to grind more, get better gear, and be competitive within the missions. These include getting last hit, highest damage, or better party scores to earn that "MVP" end of the game for more rank/stronger characters faster. So if there's a dead player on the ground that needs reviving, or no tower/STM objective being done before the boss, it's probably because the game wants the players to be competitive. 

I'm not sure to call this a PVE MOBA with competitive scores, or an MMO with lots of repeatable grind, or boss raids if everyone can't work together cause of conflicting objective interests.

When you go through parts of the story, or a couple multiplayer matches... you've done the entire game. The only thing different is having stronger gear (if you're lucky or you grinded it) for the same mission with slightly stronger enemies. There is no other variety in the game, for the price of $80 CAD it should be closer to $30-40. 

The flow of the game is to attack small monsters, gain exp throughout, then fight your way to the boss being 'Awakened level 20-25'. You can unlock skills similar to a MOBA when you level up. No other skills per character are different. Once you beat the boss, you get your fancy drops, some exp for the next dungeon or boss and do it again. 
While the grindy game may be a great way to chill and play with friends, there is not a lot for solo or variety combat to enjoy. 



[h1]The Good stuff;[/h1]
- Returning SAO fans will enjoy the story. Referencing previous games/characters and having good dialouge. 
- Environments look well done, models look good, lots of outfits to try on characters. 
- Daily and Monthly objectives for free battle pass rewards to give players incentive to try new roles.
- Crossplay. Didn't have issues playing with others.



[h1]The lots of bad;[/h1]
- Combat is very stiff, feels like this game is better for 2010 era. Using heavy and light attacks, it's not fluid when your attacks or abilities trying to hit targets. You could be swinging in the air for a while, or missing an entire ability, and not because the enemy moved. Most of the time you will be rushing up to the enemies in hopes to stagger them with your attacks before they can damage you. The auto targetting option does help alleviate some issues, but it makes it harder for flying combat or camera adjustments to prepare oncoming attacks for guard/dodges.

- Dungeons are not engaging, not balanced, and are intentionally frustrating. Since you play the same thing over and over to barely get rank exp, you'll be stuck on the same maps for a while. So you will see them 20-30 levels later again just to do the same tile sets.  
5 different groups are split into 5 starting areas, and they are all not fair or balanced. Some starting areas required more travel, or you have to do an escort, or you will have to travel blue boring teleporters, which result less awakening EXP for that match. So the 4 other groups will have a stronger lead on that. 
There's lots of downtime between rooms so most characters with better speeds have yet another advantage. Ontop of traps, bombs, or annoying "watch outs" that don't add value to the grind or complexity. The hitboxes of the shadow blades are extremely big and sometimes not where you think you see them. All they do is add a layer of frustration to players ontop of the hours of repeated dungeons to grind out gear and dailies for.
The pacing is also bad while you're trying to catch up to the other groups so you don't miss out on other objectives and exp for the missions. Adding onto the slow/stiff combat, it just favouring stronger gear so you spend less time on the first areas.

- Hit boxes from enemy indicators are very inconsistent. Seeing a red circle before a big enemy attack should indicate to the player to be ready, but often these attacks are too early, too late, or worst - show the indicator after the enemy has already attacked. Sometimes you can stand inside those red circle indicators and not take damage. While others when you try to dodge or guard correctly, may not register thus taking damage. 

- Net code for monsters and players. Good luck playing Sniper (Sinon/Sterben) for aiming boss weakpoints where there's a lot of visual effects and CHAIN-EXTENDED-DOWN pop ups in your screen. There's an objective to turn other players attacks off, but it's not enough. You can still see other buffs from support characters on you obscuring view. Ontop of if you rush into rooms too quickly in dungeons, the enemies and attacks will not render properly so there are often times you will get hit by bad hitboxes from attacks, or invisible enemies.

- Game is heavily unoptimized. Recommended is a RTX 2060, while my RTX 3070 on medium settings is at full throttle. The anti-aliasing option seems to be the biggest culprit. But the worst offender is the mouse sensitivity options for PC is TIED TO THE FRAME RATE. Playing at 144 FPS tightens your movement while 30 FPS turns your DPI to 999999. While you go into dungeons and loading areas, your mouse sensitivity continues to change and sometimes fixes itself throughout the run. 
Game also crashes a lot. Changing appearances/outfits before a raid can have a high chance of crashing your game, especially after playing for 3+ hours. Some other folks I played with crash randomly whether it be after 1 hour or 2 hours. 

- Currently there are 12 different queues for modes (except free Roam). So if you don't have 20 players game can fill them with bots. While that may be seem positive, it requires players to know ahead of time otherwise they will rush the boss being underleveled and have a much harder time defeating him.  Without a full group, you spend more time on that map farming enemies during the tower/STM objective. Which is unfair for solo groups cause they get matched with 3 bots. Less EXP for them, which means they will have to play the game more and longer to get rewards. Hopefully this gets fixed in the future or some adjustment with a catchup system.

- Roles are a joke. Having a Tank or a Support just have 1 dedicated skill to 'fit their role' which doesn't seem to fit their playstyles of a team. In reality, tanks and support characters often do as much damage as ranged or fighter role characters, ontop of the benefit/support they give to their team. Heathcliff and Yuna are AOE machines that will pretty much top majority of the time. 

- The UI is definitely made for console. Menus could be a lot better for finding stuff you need. The SAO memories for permanent buffs are placed very deep in the menus and is probably very important to level up to have stronger characters. Whilist items to enchant, move sphere effects, inviting friends, changing equipment or appearances, playing with funny stamps, etc. I'm not sure why most games are going horizontal on menus, when something vertical or lists would be effective and simple. 



[h1]Overall;[/h1]
Game is enjoyable to turn your brain off and grind and that's it. Once you ran a couple of dungeons... you've done pretty much the game. The rest is a cookie clicker and RNG fest for stronger equipment to get higher numbers.

For the price, no. This game needed another year of work. With only a couple of bosses, and reskinned dungeons you need to repeat - it's a conflict between co-operative and competitive gameplay, with no end goal or incentive for players.

review_text:
I really anticipated this game ever since it was first announced. I waited for it to be released. And then it did, and the reviews were not kind. I thought I will still like it, until I started the game. 19 minutes later I wrote this review.

It was the most boring opening I have ever seen. The background music was the most uninspired I have ever heard. The voice acting was jarring at best. Stiff and emotionless. The writing lies somewhere between banal and cliche, at times unapologetically indifferent, or unapologetically dumbass, for the lack of a better word. A woman died and the police concluded it was heart attack, and the detective who just arrived concurred, stating that it was typical of women her age, before he even set foot into the house. That was all I could take before I shut down the game.

Controls were unintuitive. Explanations were a mystery in itself. I spent 3 minutes trying to figure out how to use a lock when you don't have a way to select it even when you see it on screen. In the previous step, the game told you to pick it up, then it instructed you to 'holster' it. Then the game asked you to use it, without explaining that you need to 'unholster' it before you can use it. Brilliant. 

In the 19 minutes that I have played the game, I have probably played it for 5 minutes. I spent the other 14 waiting for the game to load, watching slow moving cutscenes that tells you what you already know, listening to words that hardly inspires, instill fear, or peak my interest in any way. It was more interesting watching paint dry.

Also, instead of opting for a first person perspective, the developers wanted to replicate a movie feel and go third person instead. I know, they are trying to recreate the tricycle scene of The Shinning, but ever wondered how awkward it is to control someone in-game like that? And that's not to mention how they always have to center the camera looking directly at Lucius, who admittedly looked creepy in the game. It's a wonder then, how no one suspected him.

Do I recommend this game? No. Will I continue to play it till the end? No. Will I buy Lucius II? No. Should you play this game? Depends. If you are patient and don't care about quality as much, you may enjoy it. If you are critical like I am, you will balk at the notion that this game was even made.

review_text:
I finally beat 5 a few days ago. I spent a whole weekend each racing, hunting, dancing, and hitting the batting cages. I've been trying to get through the series slowly. 5 is probably the strongest entry so far since my time with zero half a decade ago. Every time I outdrifted my opponents as Kiryu and then grinded the car like a madman I was grinning ear to ear. Hunting the demon bear could have been a little shorter, but I love this brand of stupid the series embraces. Akiyama and Sejima don't really change much from how they are presented in 4. Still fun to play as though and the plot is no slouch so they don't feel unnecessary. Having played the previous games I didn't mind spending time with Haruka and learning who she is and why she wants to become an idol. I can understand why this tonal and gameplay shift can be off putting if you haven't emotionally invested into Haruka across 4 games. Seeing happiness come into her life and then get snatched away made me pretty upset.

Shinada is probably tied with Tanimura as my least favorite fighting style. His grab focused moveset is probably the weakest of the 4 and the weapon leveling system tied to his unique weapon use sucks. It takes forever to level and better weapons are gated behind higher levels. That being said he has more personality than most of the cast. His batting cage story was ok. The mini game is stupid easy after you unlock heat eye. The supporting cast in his main story is fleshed out much better. Takasugi is probably one of the better written characters and Shinada's short attempt to leave town with Milky is probably one of my favorite moments in his story. They both know they are trapped and want to get away, but they are stuck as who they are. Shinada gets one extra ding for forcing me to play 9 ball for sub story progress. Overall I did enjoy my time in his story and the fact that he never shows up again in another game is a bummer.

I try to clear most of the side content in these games and I was able to clear about 95% of the substories. I'm glad I never have to talk to Tatsuya again. The finale chapter finally broke me and I booted up cheats to one shot some of the training fights. Fuck Leo and I really just didnt want to deal with any of Saigo's gun bullshit as Akiyama again. You want me to fight BOTH Komekis as Shinada!? How many times do I have to do IF7 to get all the souls orbs?! I have SIX more games after this. Ain't nobody got time for that.

I'm about a dozen hours into Yakuza 6. I usually take a few month break between games, but 6 takes place the day after the end of 5. It felt very natural to just continue where the last game left off. I may play Ishin in the future, but I think I'm done with the PS3 style of Yakuza games for now. Excited to get to 7 so I can start experiencing some new combat systems.

review_text:
The Hakuoki series is one of the most popular historical otoge in its genre and it deserves its popularity! Not only has Hakuoki its own anime, but it's now also playable on several platforms (PS, PC, Nintendo, Mobile). Wherever you are, you're now able to read the stories of /twelve/ bachelors and let them tug your heartstrings...

The MC, Chizuru Yukimura, heads to Kyoto to search for her father, finding herself attacked by mad men before they are cut down by members of the Shinsengumi who take her into custody for interrogation. Upon learning that she is a girl and the daughter of a doctor who developed the Water of Life elixir that turns those that drink it into invincible blood lusting berserkers called 'Rasetsu', the Shinsengumi decide to keep her as an aide in their search. During her stay with the Shinsengumi, she discovers that there is a lot more going on with the shogunate, but she also discovers secrets about her identity and those around her.

Kyoto Winds marks the beginning of Chizuru's journey. There exist spin-offs of the franchise, but unfortunately Steam offers Kyoto Winds and its sequel, Edo Blossoms, only.

I can definitely note that Hakuoki has amazing soundtracks. As a musician, I enjoyed the OSTs throughout the whole gameplay, even though it become repetitive when I played other routes. It's a shame that those soundtracks aren't for sale as DLC.

Also, the voice actors are wonderful as well. Maybe you'll be able to recognise a few voices from anime or other otoge! 

☯ Story ☯
☐ There is none
☐ Bad
☐ Alright
☐ Good
☑ Fantastic

Most otoge turn their routes into fairytales with minimal hardships. As for Hakuoki, I enjoyed the fact that [spoiler]main characters died and each of their sacrifice played a major role in every route (the writers are merciless!!!)[/spoiler]. This makes the experience quite bittersweet and mellow as I could really feel the angst. 

As for the MC, well, she was okay. As expected, the writers buttered up her fighting abilities, which she barely uses efficiently. Besides that being a shame, she was not overly naive or ignorant, which I can appreciate. I can appreciate otoge with decent MCs.

review_text:
Sucks, constantly crashes, gameplay is sluggish and the physics are incredibly basic, not letting me even stand on tree trunks and crates without slowly sliding off.

Edit, I decided I fancied a sniping binge after playing sniper elite 4 for a while so I redownloaded the game, and thought I would give it a proper go. Stealth games require two things to be fun, predictability and information. On this game you receive neither. You sneak up behind a big armor clad guy to cut his throat, and no matter how sneaky you are, it's impossible to kill them. Of course the game doesn't tell you this at any point so you have to figure it out through trail and error. Enemy corpses disappear if I respawn so I can simply kill a few guards, go back through a checkpoint, respawn then all the corpses have kindly hidden themselves the only problem then is that you desperately need those corpses for ammo, since in spite of this game being a sniping game, sniper ammo is about as common as unicorn turds, especially annoying if you are playing in a long range section since you usually don't have anywhere nearby to restock, and when you do, you get 10 bullets. You can walk past cameras 3 or 4 times and not get any feedback that they're there, then after you have been laid in front of them for a whole minute trying to get a kill, they suddenly spot you, that is when they're not somehow miraculously spotting you through walls. I've been in gunfights where the enemy have apparently decided to teleport in front of my very eyes to a position behind me. and I spent some of my hard earned money on a drone so I could spot targets without getting near them and it has a tiny 100m range. Although it gives you no indication that you're approaching this range, instead it just shuts off. The AI is just completely random, I've shot a barrel from across the map killing two guards, but then when I go over to the same spot to loot those guards, a stationary patrol who was previously oblivious to his exploding friends manages to spot me. I can shoot out cameras with complete disregard for the enemies realising because in this game the guards are watching the cameras so attentively that if I'm in front of a camera for more than 2 seconds, all hell breaks loose. But if I systematically disable every single camera on an entire level, then nobody bats an eyelid. Why does a throwing knife kill someone instantly if they're facing away from me, but if they spot me for even a moment, it doesn't kill them but bounces off even if I hit them in the face? Are they somehow able to catch knives in their teeth?

The sniping mechanics like windage and bullet drop are great, the world design and futuristic tech is great, but as a stealth game, and in many ways as a sniping game, this game falls flat on it's face.

review_text:
This game is ambitious as all hell, but it fails to deliver a bit in my opinion. First the pros:
-Excellent Graphics: very reminiscent of Paper Mario in the best way possible
-Fresh Premise: the idea of playing as your character's next of kin is VERY interesting
-A Few Welcome QoL things: Fast travel right off the bat, very customizable difficulty, not forced to pass out at 2AM

And then we come to the cons, and while there may be more later on in the game I don't know about these are the two I personally dealt with:
-It's very easy to move too soon and cancel your interactions (watering, picking things up, etc.) 
-By the nature of the system, it would be a TREMENDOUS (almost unthinkable) amount of effort to write interesting characters and dialogue for every character, as this is a multi-generational story with no guarantee that most of the characters you would have to write for will even be born in any particular game. This, unfortunately, leads to a lot of repetitious and procedural speech with very little to distinguish any of the characters besides their job and their physical description. This also bleeds into the quest system, which is, again, pretty much required to be able to give you any quest from any person on the list of possible townsfolk. I had 4 villagers send me a quest in the mail for a Pawpaw Fruit in first 4 days of being off my tutorial leash (which has its own problems, but I won't whine about how fast Pawpaw fruit rot as that's something you can customize in the difficulty settings) 

I'm willing to own the fact that I only played about 4 hours of this game, so some of my gripes might be addressed by later elements I didn't get to, but the fact of the matter is that I quickly came to feel like I was the only person in Plum Grove and I couldn't remember any of the character's names even a minute after meeting them. I'll be interested to see if something changes, because I REALLY want to like this one, but for now it's got to be a pass on this one from me.

review_text:
There was a time I enjoyed logging in to play but lately it just keeps rolling downhill.  There are people on and playing but most of the time they are simply raiding the boss in free roam which gets boring really fast.  For those of us in the higher levels, the T4 free roam is empty and the T3-T4 co-op quest are basically non-existent.  Of course, this is on the NA server and if hop over to the Asia server you don't really have a problem getting into a match for the higher levels but don't expect any kind of teamwork or symphony for players trying to enjoy the game.  

With every update they make, it just gets worse.  When season 2 hit they simply added tier 4 with one new location, zone bosses for free roam, and higher levels for a game already struggling with new players keeping up.  The cosmetics they added that can be unlocked were just as simple as the ones they gave away for free and they locked all the better outfits behind a paywall.  I mean, you do earn one ticket per month that can be used to buy 1 of 12 cosmetic packs every 2-3 months, at which point they will release another 12 packs.  It's more like a free to play game that never ends and never changes content that cost an upfront fee to play.

Match making is completely useless.  You need 5 to start a quest/raid and if one party has 3 players then I guess your playing by yourself as it will start the match that unbalanced.  On top of this, player rank has no effect on how teams are formed so you could have 2 max ranked players on one team even if the remaining players are below rank 100.  The characters are just as much out of balance with some clearing entire areas with one skill.  I mean, I love nothing more than going into a match and seeing 4 cheatcliffs in the waiting area.

Like I said, I do enjoy the game but it would be a rough ride for anyone just now picking it up and would likely just frustrate them into rage quitting.

review_text:
If you love devlogs and being behind the scenes of a game while it's in development, then GTTOD will be your bread and butter. As a game alone in its current state, it's hard to recommend. Off-Brand

Diving a bit deeper, I originally saw this being played by a YouTuber, the footage looked good, their commentary and recommendation was good, and I thought... movement shooter with some roguelite elements? I can get behind that! So I haphazardly bought the game on a whim, I mean, it's pretty cheap and when it's on sale it's really cheap. Even for an Early Access game.

But it's still really rough around the edges. I think most people, if they're not informed will buy it now and be disappointed (and I think that might be why the Steam rating is at 89% at the time of writing). I look at GTTOD, and think of it more as a promise, that one day, I'll go back through my Steam Library, find this game at its full 1.0(+) release, and have a blast. For players like me, it feels more like I've thrown down money as a pledge, and I'm happy to do so in order to support the project & the dev/s. I love the style, love the concept, hope it all gets realized. This is the main reason why I might recommend it.

Some players might be really into the idea of following this games progress along, and will be happy to know that the main developer is super active in their discord, and takes community feedback very seriously. Some people love seeing behind the curtain of a games development and having opportunities to possibly shape the direction of a game. If that's you, I think you'll love joining this game on its journey and being an active part of that community.

But I don't think the majority of people coming to this game will be in either of those mindsets and I believe for them it might be better to wait for this game to develop a bit more. Some of the games mechanics aren't flushed out entirely. The gunplay feels good enough, but gets stale after awhile, because the game just hasn't developed to that point yet. There is no real goal at the moment besides leveling up your character for marginal starting differences. The view bobbing and overall camera shaking is crazy... You can look through the reviews to find more of these kinds of complaints. GTTOD has potential around every corner, and promise at every horizon... it just might take a while in the oven to get there and it's important to realize that.

I think with all that information you can make an informed purchase. Don't buy into the exceptionally well done marketing or the words of YouTubers... and remember that you're not really buying a game right now... but rather the proof of your belief that the devs can put in the work to make and release a great game someday (with the added bonus of an ever changing alpha version of this game on the side).

review_text: Experience what it feels like to live in a plague ridden steppe town filled with superstition and misery. See first hand how the people of this odd community react to your actions and the plague itself through powerful world building elements and dialogue. Truly a masterpiece of a game and a hidden gem. The atmosphere is unmatched in many games compared to Pathologic 2. As soon as the first few minutes of this game there is a sense of dread. The steppe, barren as far as the eyes can see but also as if like maybe you are always being watched. The giant brutalist Termitary building that screams authority. The town that feels as though its living. The people you can listen to but perhaps not trust. The factory with the train station, I can imagine it smells like rust and iron. Even the plague itself feels like its just another natural phenomena. Everything about the atmosphere and world building is solid in this game and I wish i can go back and experience it again. At the beginning, new players to the game will be lost as I was. There's times where you will not know what anything means but fret not, you will understand as time passes with or without you and by the end it will all make sense. The game has heavy psychological and philosophical themes and touches on stuff like ego death, Idealism and metaphysics so if you're into that you will gain more value through the game however if you don't understand or not interested, the game is still brilliant in many ways. I recommend playing on the easier difficulty or at least find a good balance in difficulty options your first time as the game can be very punishing even if the game recommends playing on the true difficulty. Every death in the game is impactful, yourself included so it is still important to make sure the game isnt a cake walk. There are multiple endings depending on your choices and i found myself torn at times because of the choices I can make or have made. I don't really have any complaints about the game really except for I wish there was more. The whole experience was amazing and probably made the list for one of my favorite games of all time. The world and characters left a powerful impression on me and overall I highly recommend. 10/10 would suffer again.

review_text:
I grew up with the show and bought the manga once when I was little, so the game felt nostalgic and it was alright game. It’s just, I hated the main character and the story wasn’t believable and pretty dumb. This game actually put me to sleep a couple times. 


The Good
Nice old graphics.

There’s lots of animations and cutscenes in the game. Cutscenes will go on for 15 minutes. I think a lot of work went into the game and that’s cool.

The ui is nice. The presentation in general is very nice for the game.

There were videos that recapped the older games. They were like 15-17 minutes. 

There are parody videos that are like bloopers. They were short videos.

I think the main town was nice.

Good English voice acting.


The Bad
The story was the worst part for me. It had it problems and I tried to dismiss it to just enjoy a crappy anime. But the guy who was says that he protects players and works for CC corporation, (the company that owns the game) just told the main character player that they had no reason to stop the game even though he knows that the game put players in a coma. And he told the kid just because he was an epitaph user who had yet to awaken his avatar. The problem isn’t just that he told a player who can just sign out and tell people, it’s that it doesn’t make sense. So many players getting a coma from this one game? Seriously? You think I’m supposed to believe their stupid excuse that there was no correlation to the game and the players getting a coma. And he keeps the game online even though more people can get into a coma by this virus. And you are telling me that programmers would close the game to try and find the problem? I still think that the company would be in legal trouble in real world if this happened. It’s so dumb. Stupid story and writing.

Also, they main character keeps falling for clear suspicious traps. The second time he fell for it, was when he was searching for a 3rd teammate who could heal so he check the forum post. None of his friends pointed out that he was suspicious, we are just supposed to believe that a message on the forum that says to meet them alone in dungeon, would be safe. It’s so stupid. Brain dead stupid. Sigh.

And that part where the main character got mad at the girl for playing the game to enjoy the scenery and help is people is so dumb. He plays it only to fight to people and he couldn’t understand that not every plays a game like that. And the girl just kept being nice to him. Every time he calls her names or is mad at her in other scenes, she’s always nice and just takes it. Well, she did leave after he yelled at her and told her to leave, but she still was nice to him after. That one guild leader guy called out the main character for being so angry at Atoli (the girl) for helping him, and the guild leader didn’t even try to tell her to not hangout with that guy anymore or to block him. 

The email system and online aspect was cool but it was annoying. After every dungeon or cutscene, there will be another notification pop up that will tell you that you have new mail. So, you go to check and wait the load time to log out and get into the mail system. Then once in, another pop up shows up telling you that you have new mail. You check the mail and leave. It happens so much and just wish it was easier or not at all. Cause I remember making a party to do a dungeon for the story and then a mail pop happened and I had to check to see if it’s important for the story.

I liked being able to equip equipment but a ton of equipment doesn’t even work on your friends. You can’t give them anything or they are too underleveled. So, I guess you have to waste time leveling them too?

There were a lot of the same dungeons? I was so confused when I went to another area. I expected to see different things but the enemies just changed. Of course, the story for that part was different but it was weird.

I thought that there was too much choir music. Didn’t feel right for some scenes when they were just talking.

Some other characters annoyed me. Like the small creature in your guild.


Conclusion
I stopped playing at the part where you had to fight in the arena to fight that woman who keeps bothering you. I couldn’t understand how long it would take to be at number 2 to fight her. Did I really have to keep fighting teams? Grind out levels? I was only level 11 and the game put me against a level 17 team after facing a 12. Exp only went up a little and I barely moved up rank. 

Anyways, I tried to give the game a chance but it has too many problems for me to continue playing. If I had more time, I would have kept playing but I really want to try and drop games that I think, gives me red flags of being a bad story. I think 8 hours is enough time for me to know if a game is worth my time.

I wish the devs of this game wouldn't have released it

review_text:
"Pathologic 2" is a haunting and introspective masterpiece that defies traditional gaming conventions to deliver a deeply emotional and thought-provoking experience. Developed by Ice-Pick Lodge, this game is not just a narrative-driven adventure; it's a profound exploration of human nature, suffering, and the choices we make in dire circumstances.

At its core, "Pathologic 2" plunges players into a decaying town plagued by a mysterious and deadly disease. As the player assumes the role of one of three healers with unique perspectives, they navigate a web of interconnected stories, moral dilemmas, and existential crises amidst the town's impending demise.

The game's narrative is a labyrinth of emotions, ambiguity, and philosophical musings. Each character's journey intertwines with the lives of the townsfolk, revealing layers of despair, hope, desperation, and resilience. The writing is masterful, delving into themes of sacrifice, redemption, human frailty, and the fragility of life itself.

What sets "Pathologic 2" apart is its unflinching portrayal of suffering and the human condition. The game challenges players to confront difficult choices with no clear right or wrong answers, forcing them to grapple with ethical dilemmas, personal beliefs, and the consequences of their actions on others. The sense of moral weight and emotional depth permeates every decision, conversation, and interaction, creating a palpable atmosphere of tension and introspection.

The game's survival mechanics add layers of complexity and realism to the experience. Players must manage resources, maintain their character's health, hunger, and exhaustion, and navigate a harsh and unforgiving world. This adds a sense of urgency and immersion, mirroring the struggles of the townsfolk as they fight for survival amidst chaos and despair.

Visually, "Pathologic 2" is a hauntingly beautiful game, with a stark art style that captures the bleakness and decay of the town. The atmospheric sound design, haunting music, and environmental details enhance the sense of immersion, drawing players deeper into the game's haunting narrative and emotional landscape.

The game's pacing is deliberate and methodical, allowing moments of quiet introspection amidst the chaos and urgency of the unfolding events. This pacing invites players to reflect on their choices, relationships, and the broader themes of the game, creating a profound and personal connection to the narrative and characters.

In conclusion, "Pathologic 2" is a rare gem in gaming—a deeply emotional and intellectually stimulating experience that transcends the medium's boundaries. It challenges players to confront uncomfortable truths, wrestle with moral ambiguity, and explore the depths of human emotion and resilience in the face of adversity. For those seeking a profound and unforgettable journey into the human psyche, "Pathologic 2" is an absolute must-play.

review_text:
Really want to like this game but I just can't.

I feel like they really nailed the controls, gravity, and the graphical style of the "Jet Set Radio" games, but they really dropped the ball in some key areas.

The art style (like the character designs) doesn't live up to its inspiration, the soundtrack, while far from bad is a hodgepodge of different artists with sometimes radically different styles, the open maps in the vain of, but dissimilar to the likes of "Jet Set Radio Future" feel empty. 

Honestly, the whole game feels rather confused. Despite being a score boosting game, the trick system is woefully shallow and is essentially impossible to fail at. The maps are open, but the game's linear platforming segments feel the best to play. 

The graffiti and authoritarian police force in "Jet Set Radio" was a statement on freedom of expression. "Graffiti is art" (but vandalism is a crime, etc.). Nothing in this game's vapid, overly serious plot has anything to do with that message. It feels more like an homage. Or a formality. Or rather the game's going, "Hey, we're trying to be 'Jet Set Radio', do you get it?" 
(Although, I do like the graffiti system from a gameplay standpoint.)

It sucks because the core controls are everything I wanted while playing "Jet Set Radio", but even with an active modding scene, barebones platforming isn't going to keep your attention long past the end credits.


As an aside, you could say comparing this and JSR isn't entirely fair. You know, the game doesn't have to be exactly like JSR to be fun or good, but first of all, when the game is assuming JSR's identity it only makes sense to compare the two, and second, the game is doing its own unique spins on that identity badly as well.

review_text:
It took about 11 hours to beat the game for the first time. The Callisto Protocol really feels lacking in some areas, TLDR: Bought it for $19 on sale, and it felt about right for the quality. Not worth the $60 price tag.

Positives: 
-Offers big nostalgia for people who enjoyed Dead Space.

-More of a CINEMATIC style of game. lots of post processing effects, fixed animation elements, and cut-scenes. Less control over Jacob does make a lot of things look and feel immersive (even if you lose some control to accomplish the look)

Neutral points:
-Has a LOT of the jank associated with Dead Space (character feels slow but impactful, camera doesn't always prioritize visual clarity so jump scares come across better, etc.)

Negatives:
-It really loses points for lack of creativity. If you're going to basically swipe the entire idea of Dead Space, do it well. Striking distance really didn't add much to the formula other than a cinematic feeling. they removed probably the most fun mechanic of dead space (shooting a limb off immediately makes something less deadly) You KIND OF get the same thing when you knock off a limb, enemies shorten their combos. this really feels like a worse version of a game that came out almost 2 decades ago and somehow they couldn't figure out WHY it was good.
-It really isn't as scary as it should be. If its 90% jump-scares, it feels like only 10% effort. Aside from an early point where you're in  a small cave full of blood/goop and the mental asylum section of the Tower chapter, never really uncomfortable. 

-Really doesn't nail the difficulty well. Enemies are either brain dead easy (most enemies in the game) or near impossible to fight efficiently (anything that prevents you from fighting at close range) If you run out of ammo on the wrong part of the game, you can basically softlock yourself. ( I had half a mag RIGHT before a boss fight that you cant use melee attacks on, so I HAD TO cheese it by baiting it to an edge and provoking an attack so it would fall out of the map and die) They added special modes where they fix the guns (but make the game almost entirely too easy in the process) don't worry... bosses are still stupidly hard, since most bosses in the game will 1 or 2 shot you. and if that's not hard enough, you can play the game with next to no resources!

-Guns Feel bad at all points in the game. They never get better, and fail to capitalize on the fun part of survival horror (a gun that feels impact-ful with very limited use)

-so much content is LOCKED BEHIND A PAYWALL!!! you beat the game and OOPS, its still not over! only $20 to see what happens to Jacob!

Hoo boy, this game was mediocre.

one of the best games i've ever played...
kcd2 touches and evolves on every single one aspect and systems of it's predecessor, which already laid a solid groundwork for the sequel to achieve the level of polish it couldn't achieve.
The combat is realistic while still being very fun, almost every weapon feels different, though swords are a cut above the rest due to masterstrike being a thing.., the one on one duels are the highlites but now fighting multiple enemies is a lot of fun and not unfair as it used to be.

Each side quest has it's own unique story whether it just being a simple task to get a lucky stone for a lady or solving a murder mystery, some side quests even affecting the main story in some ways.
In a nutshell, games like these don't come very often.., and i wholeheartedly recommend this game to anyone and recommend them to pay attention to in-game tutorials and dialogue to have the fun like i had with this game..

review_text:
It is hard to recommend this game because although there are not many good metroidvanias out there, this is almost not worth it. This game is extremely frustrating. The difficulty does not gradually increase or jump up and stay consistent. Some parts are just stupidly hard for no good reason.

You don't level up. So you never do more damage unless you find better weapons. And you always take crazy amounts of damage unless you find an item that defends against ONE type of attack. Even then the other attack modifiers will easily kill you.

The worst is that you have no i-frames when you get hit. This makes it so that even early game enemies can combo you to death if they hit you right and there is nothing you can do about it.

For an endurance souls-like metroidvania there is almost no way to restore health. Save areas don't heal you. Health drops are infrequent or rare. You have to resort to cheesing two or three item abilities you find in the early game to heal yourself. It makes the whole exploration process unnecessarily slow and tedious.

You often will need to buy items to have a fighting chance or even progress in questlines that give you much needed items. However, money drops are rare. And enemies don't respawn when you just go to an adjacent room and come back. When they do drop money it is only 1-5 gold. Every useful item you need to buy costs 90-240 gold. This makes the mandatory grinding suck.

At least the character art is nice and the dialogue is a little funny. But due to the above mentioned problems, this game is hard to enjoy.

---

I went back and played 30 hours of this game to 100% it. My previous criticisms haven't changed much. I appreciate the care put into the game and all the extra modes. The heroine has different outfits. The dialgue changes based on the mode you are playing. And there is a hidden after-story. But in a way, those extra modes only confirm the previous problems of the game. 

The only way to win at combat is to cheese and abuse items/magic. When you figure out the trick combinations, you can blaze through anything. But it must be those combinations, otherwise it is like you hit a brick wall.

A boss can be made trivial by simply jumping in one spot to dodge and using a projectile over and over again. Another will be made into a joke by simply using an AOE spell and running circles around her. That same boss will kill you in literally 3 seconds if you try any other approach because you still have no i-frames, she has no cool-down between attacks, and her status aliments stack. review_text:
Lucius is a third-person adventure/puzzle game, in which you play as Lucifer's son and murder everyone in the manor you live in. The concept is interesting, since it's kinda like reverse horror, but unfortunately the execution is poor. 

The gameplay is pretty much just murdering the people in the house in a certain order and in a pre-determined way and watching a cutscene showing the murder. After the murder cutscene you get a new cutscene, which usually involves a detective, who is put on the case after your first murder. The game could have easily been a point-and-click game, because you just look for items and after using the right items you watch the murder commence.

The game let's you free roam around the fairly big manor between the murders, but there isn't much to do aside from some "fetch quests" called chores and looking for items needed in future murders. After doing enough chores you get some items, of which 2 just give hints for the murder puzzles and the last one is a tricycle. The tricycle let's you move around the manor a bit faster and also let's you use a glitched staircase to get out of the house. 

After each murder you get a new superpower or upgrades to the ones you already have. The game has 4 superpowers: telekinesis, mind control, memory erase and combustion. You will need all those superpowers for the murder puzzles and while you can use some of them for other purposes, they're not really fun. The combustion power is also used in the boss battles the game has and also in some extra mini-game, which seemed to involve priests chasing you (a child) with crosses in a dark forest. I didn't like the boss battles or that mini-game at all, because the combustion power isn't fun and felt a bit clunky to use.

Graphics-wise the game looks pretty good for an indie game, but the devs decided to occasionally use some post-processing effects, which actually made the game look a bit uglier. The lip-syncing seemed to be a bit off, but it didn't really bother me. The voice acting ranged from pretty good to quite awful. The game also has a pretty badly done sex, which looks quite funny as a result and there's some frontal 3D nudity as well. 

The story and dialogue is pretty bad and the ending was probably one of the worst endings ever.

It's a pretty bad game, which could have been so much more. I wouldn't really recommend playing it unless you want to experience some pretty funny glitches. The game is pretty short (took me 5 and a half hours to complete), so it's not like you'd waste a lot of time.

review_text:
[i]I turn a corner, and there it is again. The giggle, the unnerving noises, the shuffling of feet. I'm getting jumped again, I know it. I just know it. And I can't aim this stupid revolver right, not even to mention the tommy gun. I might as well throw the bullets, for what little good they'll do. Frantically, I look around, left to right, back and forth, up and down. They literally could be anywhere.[/i]

Bioshock is the game where the "recommended/not recommended" dichotomy loses its meaning. It's very well made, exceptionally well made. It's got the most gorgeous and interesting surroundings - an art deco dream of a city underneath the sea, frozen in time in the 1920s. It's got an interesting premise, telling the tale of a society free from all norms, creating itself away from all other interference. A veritable utopian experiment. So why don't I like it? Why don't I like it...

[i]My path is strewn with corpses, their sweet ADAM now coursing through my veins, giving me just enough strength to encounter the next enemy, and the one after that. This city is huge, and after a while, all the corridors seem to blend together into one large clownery of madness, filth and decay. How anyone survived here during the last 40 years is beyond me.[/i]

I guess the thing is that it's well set up, but leaves me feeling like I'm missing something. And I very well may be. Either that, or whatever it's trying to get across just doesn't... come across. A lot of people are praising the story, but compared to games whose story I thoroughly enjoyed (Deus Ex, System Shock, GTA) this one just isn't very well told. The encounters seem random, the locations feel like just an assortment of oddities and what little I learn about the events that led to the situation I find myself in leave me with more questions than answers. Because really: How DID anyone survive the 40 years between the collapse of Rapture's society and my arrival?

[i]Madness. Everyone has gone mad. Would this be my fate as well? Would I end up down here like anyone else, just a freak, a distorted image of my former self, bizarrely reflected in the waters? Or would I be just another source of ADAM for the little sisters? Because the longer I fight, the further I go, the deeper I dig into the veins of the city, the more it seems like there is no escape, no goal, no purpose, no end to it all. There's just madness.[/i]

The thing is: I can't really say anything bad about it, but still, after having finished it, I've been left deeply disappointed. Really, that was it? That's all there is to it? Don't get me wrong, it's pretty and all, and interesting, and varied, and... everything a lot of people seem to like. So I guess I just didn't get it.

review_text:
There will be some spoilers in this review. Read at your own risk.

Lucius is a murder centric puzzle game where you play as the titular Lucius Wagner, a child of Lucifer. The premise of the game is rather interesting. Lucifer visits Lucius in a dream and bestows him the unholy mission of garnering the souls of people around Dante Manor. This is done through rather unintuitive and lacking puzzles. 

The story takes place in the painfully large Dante Manor. From nearly the very beginning of the game, most of all of the manor is open to you. With the mechanics that exist in the game, this is NOT a good thing. It does not reward exploration (save for the aptly named "Explorer" achievement). Furthermore, the puzzle solutions are extremely unintuitive and, quite frankly, boring. At several points, there shows potential for many possible ways to kill the chapter's target, but as the game requires deaths to be the ones laid out for you, it does not help at all (for example, one kill requires you to set someone on fire, but simply setting them on fire does not work. You have to douse him in gasoline and then setting him on fire will allow the kill.). More than that, the way some of these events transpire, it will severely test your suspension of disbelief (if you were to light a ciagrette at a stove, would YOU stick your face into the stove fire?) and the game simply can't be taken seriously. 

Even worse still, this game at one (potentially two) point(s) tries to hopscotch between puzzle and action game. The controls and camera for this game are already pretty clunky as is and making it into a third person action game with a terrible camera does not help the game's case in the slightest. Lucius also suffers from having quite a few bugs (several things can go wrong during some chapters and will force you to restart the chapter) and collision issues (getting caught on nothing comes to mind).

Other bugs that come to mind are broken achievements. Some achievements do not work at times and can cause potential frustration.

All in all, this game is NOT worth your time or money. I got it on sale for 75% off ($4.99 instead of $19.99) and I still feel like I got ripped off.
