review_text:
I have seen many people recomend this game due to its emotional story, it is sort of sad sure but man it is not a good game in any way. Even as a means of storytelling it falls flat in almost every way. Gameplay wise it is not fun in any way, with poor controls on the mouse and the keyboard side the game just feels bad to play. I ran into 2 gamebreaking bugs along the way that prevented me from continuing, being fixed by a restart which lost some progress. The game also trys to pad itself to make it seem longer than a short 3act, 3 hour story.

[h1]Art[/h1]
The game has very sub indie pixel art. And a handful of digitially painted seens which looked rushed and pulled me out of the game world when they did appear. It seems that pixel artists just added a noise filter to everthing they could. It almost hurts to look at some objects. There are also several charecters in the game where they seemed to have applied a noise filter and not toned down the saturation of the noise, resulting in a few charecters being covered in rainbow speckles.
========================
The one redeeming aspect of the games art is the soundtrack which was one of the only things keeping me playing. It is the only thing that pulled emotion out of the dialog, which is very bad as well. But this was ruined several times by having a very hard transition to a different track often for the sake of comedic releif.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
It is a game so how does it play? Very poorly. For an rpgmaker game the keyboard controls feel slugish and the mouse controls are infuriating. For the amount of needless walking around the game makes you do the mouse controls feel like they are working against you. You left click to walk, very simple how could it be bad. When walking long distanced you need to click on an icon that takes you to a different scene. The problem lies with the screen always moving the camera is locked to the grid that the charecters walk making the camera jerk as the charecters change direction. There is no smoothness to it making it difficult to click on things while moving. This tied with the charecters slow walking speed and long padded distances makes it feel like you are just waiting and waiting to just get on with the task at hand. The keyboard controls for walking don't feel as bad but the distanced are so long and the speed so slow it is just easier to wait on the mouse.
========================
The puzzles which are placed through the entirety of the first Act are the only type of "gameplay" this game has. You walk around placing the mouse on random objects that act as puzzle pieces, after you collect the necessary amounts you play a really easy puzzle which can be won by randomly clicking around ten times. You do this around twenty times. It is just a time killer a very boring one at that.
========================
Object placement in this game is horrid as well there was one instance where I though my game was soft locked, you normally click on charecters to talk to them or listen to them. This speech icon was just placed on the ground in the middle of to spaced out charecters. Several times throughout the game I had trouble finding the puzzle piece because they didn't even have an icon. The game also pads itself with really long camera pans and slow movement speed on long backtracking paths. With many reused areas that made me hate walking along them again and again. 

[h1]Story and Dialog[/h1]
The game is well know for its sad story. I did not feel a strong enough connection to the charecters throughout the short 3 hours expierence. My connection to them was just barely strong enough for me to drudge through the awful two main charecters dialog to even finish the game. The reason I feel I had no connection the the charecters is due to half the game being a very bad puzzle game. I was hoping Acts 2 and 3 would payoff for waiting through Act 1 but it did not.
========================
I'm going to talk about the dialog now and oh is it bad. Even the non cheesy "comedic" dialog feels like a middle schooler's essay for english class. It is ok but not amazing. But the dialog between the main playable charecters is awful. The game was made in 2009 and it dates itself hard. The writers seemed to have a hard on for name dropping things. They talk about Doctor Who, Animorphs, Google, and many many others. It is just awful and makes the game feel straight out of Tumblr. The game told me to just google something about the Animorphs books after I answered incorrectly. It is so hard to take the sad story seriously when they through garbage references at you.

[h1]Summary[/h1]
The games cult-like following does not hold up, even when overlooking the dated nature of the game. It is not fun and its story simply is not good enough to make up for how awful it is to play. Its so short and filled with padding with its story loosley tossed throughout at 2009 meme and joke ridden trainwreck. This game is not fun, and its story not very good. It wanted to be sad but the only things I was sad about was wasting a few dollars on this. If you do want to expierence its still after reading this whole review just watch a long play on youtube, it wasn't worth my time.

[h1]Final Score:[/h1]
[h1]5/10 Didn't even make me cry[/h1]

review_text:
Normally I make fairly in-depth reviews, but I'm gonna skip that with this. There's a lot of fairly interesting design choices here and maybe a framework for a good game, but a city builder/sim this is not. This is a tower defense (despite what the game creator says) where you fight absurdly bloated HP monsters with very little actual strategy.

It's cool that there's a huge handcrafted island with different areas, but they all pretty much play the same.  There's mechanics to outfit your villagers with armor and weapons, but this is pointless as villagers barely fight and will instantly die later in the game.

The game, while not graphically ugly, makes it hard to identify what buildings are which without clicking on them. It feels like only the early game portion of this game was actually finished, and instead of introducing stronger towers, walls, golems, magic items or heroes, you just pick up enemies and drop them in instant death pits.

review_text:
keep in mind for any of you reading:
you need to understand all of the positive reviews are under the pretext of "for a SAO game"

in other words, the game is okay.... -for a SAO game-

Compared to other polished $60+ action RPG games? It's trash. Compared to a $30 indie game action RPG? It's playable.

Here are some of the things that no one will really talk about because they're fans of SAO and because most of the previous SAO game iterations were even worse, they'll gladly eat this one up despite its rather horrible faults:



-the camera lock on is absolute jank garbage. When you use a skill the camera zooms in on your character, making enemies above, below, and behind you out of your vision. When you do this during a boss fight, the boss will end up out of your camera EVEN WHEN YOU'RE LOCKED ON. And the camera does re-center the boss on your screen, but it feels like it takes forever.

-your characters feel animation locked and movement is generally very clunky. A couple of reasons why this happens is first, your characters do not actually move while attacking much. They feel static and locked in place during animation. Second, the game says you can cancel out of animation to do a dodge/block, but that's not really the case. Third: the game's dash, which also acts as a dodge, makes you dash forward when you do it without pressing any directional keys, instead of backwards. Most action games default dodge without a directional input is backwards, because common sense would let you believe you would dodge things backwards, not forwards. But this game wasn't made with much common sense, apparently.

-maps are rather bland and empty. There are things to collect in the maps during quests, but the game does rather a poor job (or rather, it doesn't do it at all) of actually guiding you towards them in one way or another. You literally have to just mindlessly run around the entire empty, bland map to find these. What they give you also is not well explained. After a quest is done, and you see those collectibles marked as incomplete, all you feel is a sense of conflict as to whether or not it's even worth running around 20 minutes again just to pick up that one data fragment you missed.

-not a lot of enemy and boss variety

-the bosses make no noise. They have no sound. No growl, roar, effect sound before a special move, nothing. Audio is a gigantic part of the immersion, and it's clear the devs have absolutely no understanding of it.

-virtually no sense of progression other than you unlocked the next quest for the story. You don't gain new skills, no passive skill tree of any kind, new gear is just practically the same gear just with higher levels. You can unlock characters to play in multiplayer as you do the quests, but that's only for multiplayer.



If there is one thing the game does well is that you can get a lot of outfits with no MTX just by playing the game, and the multiplayer seems to be decently functional, but that's about it.

The verdict seems to be pretty clear on this one: if you're a fan of SAO, you might enjoy it. If not, wait for a sale. If you really enjoyed Granblue Fantasy Relink like me, and you thought this might scratch your itch, prepare to be disappointed.

review_text:
This game is boring as hell. You're basically going to sit watching villagers chop wood for hours and not be able to do anything else because you are unable to expand. 

The reason being is that your population will basically never grow. Villagers won't reproduce unless they're assigned to doing nothing. Plus, after you do make a baby, it takes about three game days for it to grow up and enter the labor force, which turns out is quite a long time. 

Every building requires a dedicated workforce. You start with 40 villagers, so fine. You will have enough free villagers to assign them to work in your first buildings—say, a lumber mill. But the more you build—which you will want to do because you're going to want a population that is well fed and watered and well armed—the more you get spread thin. So then if you lose a villager to fighting zombies, you may well have lost the only person that smelts ore for all you know or who makes arrows for the ballistae.

You also don't really get nomads adding to your population from the outside. As game events go, notifications of nomads in the area are few and far between. Plus, after day four or so, it's unlikely they'll even be able to make it to your base because there will be so many graveyards and monster spawns on the map that they'll probably be killed en route with nothing you can do about it.

Plus, there's a fairly ungenerous building cap that requires you to continually expand your city center before you can add more buildings. Meaning more waiting and boredom while you watch your dwindling number of villagers chop wood. Your villagers are also very dumb. They will go all the way across town to chop wood instead of chopping the wood you've assigned right next to them/the building you told them to build. Also, don't try and build more than one structure at a time because they are so addlebrained that they will start one structure, get halfway through completing it, then go to the next one and start it until it's halfway done, then go back to the first one. So, more waiting.


So bored. Do not recommend.

review_text:
Where Winds Meet is a boring game.

Don't misunderstand, the game is beautiful and the gameplay is well choreographed.  However, it tries to be Dark Souls and ends up being Wo Long.  Gear is a pointless numbers-go-up grind and character development is simply a matter of higher levels giving you access to gear with bigger numbers.  All the depth and personality the Souls games allow through weapon selection, spell selection, and stat adjustment are simply lacking in Where Winds Meet.

What we're left with is a boring, one-note experience where combat relies first and foremost on a player's ability to memorize enemy attack strings and parry them perfectly to deplete their Qi bar and open them up to execution attacks.  A few of these execution attacks and the fight is over, and the piddling chip damage you do through your own attacks along the way doesn't amount to a shorter fight.  It's an infuriatingly reactive system and ultimately led me to quit the game with half the time still left on my battle pass because I was sick of standing there mashing parry until I was allowed to win.

review_text:
From the description: "Rise to Ruins is at heart a godlike village simulator, but it also throws in plenty of familiar game play mechanics from classic real-time strategy and resource management games like Black and White, Settlers, ActRaiser and many others."

I really wish it played that way.

Although the game is indeed a hybrid of several different genres, its implementation of each one is weak.

The village building mechanic: slow and plodding. There's a ton of support structures required for your village, and each one need to be manned by at least one person. Because population growth is slow, nomads aren't frequent, and the speed only goes to 2x before showing you a scary "hey this probably doesn't work" message, growing your city is kind of a boring slog. 

And, since you can't build freely on the map (you're limited to an area around your initial camp, which expands as you build), there's very little variety in the way you approach building a village. There's a bootleg strategy of building a chain of bonfires at the edge of your territory, which extends buildable radius dramatically, but not only is that approach just as slow and boring as the regular one, it also takes up limited building slots, so it feels like a crappy workaround for a crappy system.

At first the mindless slog is tempered somewhat by the introduction of "Corruption," a land-devouring plague. Its mysterious presence, and your slowly building influence meter, builds up anticipation for a Populous-style war: surely the idea is that I growth my village, and thus my influence, so I can use my divine powers to smite the corruption that plagues each region in the game, right?

Well, wrong.

The god system: weak and uninspired. You start off with several different spells in three different categories: loosely speaking you've got harmful spells, helpful spells, and neutral spells. Having said that, most spells are useless. Grab, which moves things around, seems the most interesting but has infrequent usage at best due to the resource drain. Labor Golem, a spell that summons a little stone helper to help move village resources, is invaluable due to the fact that you're always short-handed due to slow village growth (and not, say, any interesting gameplay mechanics).

The rest of the spells seem like they have promise but prove to be worthless. 

Motivate, a spell described as encouraging the regrowth of natural elements, caused an average of 3-4 trees to regrow -- that's nothing compared to your village's needs. 

Meteor, and some fire spell whose name I can't remember (Inferno?), aren't as exciting as they sound. Fires caused by Inferno go out almost immediately. Good luck trying to burn down a forest to keep the enemy from using those resources. In fact, it didn't destroy a single tree the last time I tried. _The fire spell, when cast on a forest, didn't cause a forest fire_.

To cap it all off, even if the spells were powerful and interesting to cast, the only place you'd want to bring down a rain of meteors on, the Corrupted lands, are off-limits to spell casting.

Instead, to deal with the encroaching threat, you...

...you play a tower defense game.

And not a very good one. Turrets have to be built like any other building, use up precious building slots, and have very little differences. There's 5-6 different physical tower types, but in ten hours I only found a use for 2 of them. The rest were of the "like that other turret, except I use stone as ammo!" variety.

The tower defense game has to exist, though, because there's no other way to deal with the Corruption. If you wall it off, they'll just attack your walls, so you need to make an awkward maze of walls and turrets to funnel the enemy though and kill them every night. Except that building the maze, and the turrets, is slow. And when night finally comes, its not even satisfying to watch plodding zombies turn into pincushions.

To sum it all up, much like this review none of the elements in the game really harmonize. The influence system is based on village population, but the spells that use influence are boring and neutered. The Corruption poses an omnipresent threat, but your villagers aren't meant to fight, and the golems you create aren't that interested in it either.

The whole goal of the game seems to be to slowly build-up a village and wait until you have enough villagers so you can colonize another region in the game, but why? The village building is boring. The spell system is boring. The Corruption is interesting, but you can't meaningfully interact with it, so it may as well be boring.

Maybe the game turns amazing during its 12th hour, but I only made it to 11.

In the end, thinking about what Rise to Ruins could have been feels more enjoyable than actually playing it.

NB: Although I did buy this game two years ago, I have not played any of the other iterations, having instead chosen to wait for the game to leave early access.

review_text:
You know, I've had longstanding opinion that PvP games have suffered from the common issue of players and developers alike assuming that bad sportsmanship and the zero-sum nature of the game are both not only inevitable, but necessary factors. Entirely too many people chase the wild goose that is balance, without affording any thought as to whether or not their game would even be fun were they to achieve the impossible. "Have any of them wondered," I ask myself, "if a 50% winrate truly feels like a 50% winrate?"

Games like Dead by Daylight help answer this conundrum for me. Here it is, standing out from the crowd; unlike most other game's I've played, this one is separate from them all, different to its core. It sits me down, leans over, and whispers sweetly into my ears: "You're completely fucking right actually! I hate people." Then it clubs me over the head and offers to sell me a fashionable bandage for $5.

Leave aside the issues of a horrible and punishing new player experience. Leave aside the richly awful new privacy policy. Do not worry yourself about the game's obsession with DLC and microtransactions, or the fact that interesting gameplay alterations are deliberately and pointlessly locked to time-limited events designed to generate a fear-of-missing-out. All of this pales by comparison.

This thing could scarcely be a better tool for engendering bitterness in its playerbase if it had been specifically engineered to do so. Every game, win or lose, ends up feeling like a hurdle that took something from you. The only people who truly thrive in this environment are the kind who specifically come to spit in the face of others—I ask someone why they enjoy playing Survivor, a role I find stressful and impossible, and you know what I was told? "I like to show killers their place." Call me crazy, but I don't think rampant mutual antagonism is a very healthy relationship for players to have with each other.

The role of a game designer is to create a mechanism by which players can explore various emotions. Frustration is a valid one, as games like Getting Over It have proved. But those were deliberate. This? This is callous negligence. As any other review can tell you, the toxicity is rampant. And I can't even blame people for it! How could I, when the game seems designed to [i]teach you[/i] to seek revenge on others and treat them as awfully as possible? I suppose it's at least on-brand for a game about a bunch of merciless bastards, if nothing else.

I feel bad for myself, because of the energy I've lost on games that made my day worse. I feel bad for other players, for having found an environment so rancid it ends up making them venomous just to feel sane. I feel bad for the players who I managed to thoroughly beat, since I know it's likely they had an awful time facing me. And I feel bad for my friends, who hoped that I could have fun playing this; though they too have left negative reviews, so at least I can know they will understand.

Mark my words, this game will never fix itself. Not because it can't be - the concept could be great, if enough work were done to fix it - but because Behavior Interactive is not interested in doing that. They're making money off of people, and that's all that matters. Considering this, and all the pain this game is prone to causing, I can recommend trying this game only in some hypothetical context wherein the publisher loses more money off you than they gain. No game that breeds this much hate deserves to turn a profit.

A word spared for the kind, though: There are a few occasions, and a few players, who when playing Killer will grant you leniency. They will not chase you relentlessly, thus giving you a chance to accomplish something. They will limit how many people they kill, so that at least some survivors can have a win. And especially as a new player, this was wonderful, and win or lose I enjoyed my time with them. Though it can't make up for the tremendous issues embedded in this game's execution, I greatly appreciate their considerate actions.

i suppose it's at least on-brand for a game about a bunch of merciless bastards, if nothing else. i feel bad for myself, because of the energy i've lost on games that made my day worse. i feel bad for other players, for having found an environment so rancid it ends up making them venomous just to feel sane. i feel bad for the players who i managed to thoroughly beat, since i know it's likely they had an awful time facing me. and i feel bad for my friends, who hoped that i could have fun playing this though they too have left negative reviews, so at least i can know they will understand. mark my words, this game will never fix itself. not because it can't be - the concept could be great, if enough work were done to fix it - but because behavior interactive is not interested in doing that. they're making money off of people, and that's all that matters. considering this, and all the pain this game is prone to causing, i can recommend trying this game only in some hypothetical context wherein the publisher loses more money off you than they gain. no game that breeds this much hate deserves to turn a profit. a word spared for the kind, though there are a few occasions, and a few players, who when playing killer will grant you leniency. they will not chase you relentlessly, thus giving you a chance to accomplish something. they will limit how many people they kill, so that at least some survivors can have a win. and especially as a new player, this was wonderful, and win or lose i enjoyed my time with them. though it can't make up for the tremendous issues embedded in this game's execution, i greatly appreciate their considerate actions.

The good
The story is engaging and the environment is properly terrifying. So if there would have been a properly story mode, with just placeholder combat, then I would have recommended this. 


The bad
* Movement you are stuck walking, there are running, but running is just walking faster, and whenever the game decies that the surface is to uneven, you cannot run, only walk. There are lots of places that are uneven in a smashed up big building... with broken stuff all over the place. When following an NPC, you are mostly prohibete from running, which makes looting large areas slow and teadious when following an NPC and there are loot to be find if you explore.
There is no jump, but you can climb over stuff, but only if you are properly aligned. there is no auto alignment that will nudge you character when you are just outside the alignement zone. so you can get stuck in a window and unable to jump out and then the monster you are moving away from catches up to you and you have a bad time. But you are severly restricted to which boxes you are allowed to jump up on. You are also restricted on what holes in the wall you are allowed to enter, despite monsters comming out of them and you have crawled into such hole before. 
Ladders, DO have a huge SNAP TO range. that override looting snap to, ie try to loot stuff on the ground under your cursor, and game thinks, hey, you are trying to go up that ladder behind you and thus you are now on the ladder. 


* Looting terrible, you can only a four kind of things, loose items, two special boxes you can open, one specuial box you can break, and monsters you have killed, to loot a dead monster, you have to stomp on them, so they drop the good stuff, everhting else you can basically not loot at all. 


* Terrible "action" scenes where you are moving fast with little control and you have to avoid stuff by moving left and right. These are mostly annoying. 


* Combat, the systems aims to be a stratetic combat system, where you take it slow, and react to what the monster is doing etc. but the implementation is terrible. Melee combat have a short range, and for some reason heavy melee attacks seems to have an even shorter range. There is blocking, but no special block button, on keyboad, it is the same button as moving backwards. You can dodge attacks, and that works mostly fine. 


* Force "glowe", think gravity gun, to use this thing you have to aim your GUN at the target, but instead of pressing fire, you scroll with you mouse wheel to pull or push the target. There are some strange forice field simulation that drops the target if you rotate to fast or something comes in between, so you drop the target. you cannot pick up dead bodies to throw at monsters, but you can pick other debri to throw at the monsters. There is a snapto to target. that makes you pick the wrong target/thing. 


* Game is divided into chapters and then each chapter is divided into checkpoints. You can save whenever you like, but when loading the save, it ill bring you to the latest checkpoint. You cannot go back and replay a specific chapter or checkpoint, unless you have made a manual save to load from that chapter/checkpoint. This makes the hunting of the recordings that tells much more of the story very tedious, as you have to start over if you missed something in a previous chapter. 


* Difficulty, what I can tell from the difficulty settings it affects how many hits you can tyake before you die, and how many hits the monsters can take before the die. even on the easiest difficulty, the boss fights are terrible, if you only want to experience the story. Took me quite a while to understand how to deal with the minibosses with two heads, as they behave very strange, even on easy mode. 


* 3rd person camery makes some stupid stuff, like most 3rd person cameras does... sometimes the game want to you to look at something important that happens for story reasons, but you are bussy doing your thing, so instead of realising that you are supposed to look where it turned you, you try to move the camera back to where you wanted to look...  and that can cause the camera to start spinning around. quite frustrating.

review_text:
É um j-rpg muito bom, ele é tão cheio de detalhes e tão cheio de interações entre personagens (npc) que você de fato se sente em um MMORPG (o jogo é offline e linear); Os personagens possuem características únicas e um ótimo desenvolvimento, como por exemplo o próprio protagonista, Haseo! 
- O jogo é linear, portanto não há escolhas mas a história é a mais linda que ja vi em jogos! Possui algumas sides além da missão principal, não se preocupe, há bastante coisas para se fazer no The World!!
- São 4 volumes, achei o remake dos 3 primeiros volumes muito bom, pois são idênticos aos de Playstation 2, porém nesta versão temos o Volume 4 que é uma novidade muito boa, e também alguns videos contando o que acontece nos games .Hack//IMOQ (também de playstation 2), assim dando informações sobre o universo de .hack aos jogadores!
- Você não precisa ter jogados os jogos anteriores nem ter visto os animes para compreender o que se passa neste game, mas por .hack ser uma obra excelente, lhes recomendo verem pelo menos .hack//roots antes de jogar este game!
- Como disse, são 4 volumes, e possui importação de save, ou seja, você pode começar o 4 volume a partir de onde parou no 3, começar o 3 a partir de onde terminou o segundo e por ai vai...Mas também pode começar qualquer volume sem importar os saves, o q é bem legal!
- Achei o ultimo volume bastante curto e limitado em relação aos anteriores, mas não deixa de ser bom, inclusive o 3* volume é o mais longo e mais cheio de missões e coisas a se fazer, não acho que seja um game enjoativo até porquê, eu zerei inúmeras vezes apesar de não ser um game curto, uma play normal leva em torno de 30 horas cada volume por ai, se você busca o 100%, obvio q levará mais tempo.
- Foi o game que me fez gostar de rpg, ele não é complexo como muitos outros que temos por ai, ele é dinâmico, mecânica simples, é mais fácil que a versão de play2 mas se você não farmar um xp, vai acabar apanhando nos boss kkkk que por sinal, são épicos e o jogo todo possui diversas OST's (músicas originais) que são de arrepiar!
- Sim, é meu game favorito, e se eu puder apresentar esta linda obra para alguém, saberei que minha missão foi cumprida com sucesso!! O game não é muito pesado, rodou de boa no meu amd 200ge sem placa de video, não está caro (até porque são 4 jogos) e com certeza será uma ótima experiência!! Obrigado!

review_text:
For as deep a discount as this game goes for a 3 to 4 hour story that tells a unique narrative that’s very likely to get a strong emotional response out of you, I think it’s very much worth the money. 

However, I recommend it with the caveat that you should please give the game some patience to properly get started. The first 30 to 45 minutes serve as a prologue before the narrative begins proper, and during this time the game is at its weakest in my opinion. 

Specifically, the game is setting up for an emotional narrative journey, and that’s what you expect from it when you buy it, but the first 30 to 45 minutes are spent with what is essentially a slapstick comedy duo slinging quips at each other with gags and language that make it hard to respect either of them as professional, rational adults, seeing as one of them says things like bro and epic even though he’s in his probably late 20s, and the other one says euphemisms for cursing that are awkward and unnatural, like what the potato. 

Once they start talking less and the characters the story is actually focusing on take the forefront, the  story becomes much more compelling in my opinion. So please don’t drop it 30 minutes in thinking the rest of the game will be like that, because it won’t be. And you’ll be missing out on a great story if you do.

review_text:
I still think Yakuza 3 is worse, but for a different reason. Yakuza 5 has good moments and redeeming features and it's not completely BAD per se, but it has many issues that make it one of the worst in the series and one that I will never go back to.

Basically you have 4 playable characters similar to Yakuza 4 and each has his own part with the main story and substories to deal with. But as it was in Y4 it strives further away from it been a story of Kiryu of it been someone else story whereas Kiryu is a kind of demigod bashing skulls and who, again is dragged into the story by "chance".

Kiryu part itself is fine, it shows him trying to move on to a different path in his life semi successfully and it's ok and makes sense, while in the background there is a Yakuza plot with a bunch of new faces you don't really know or care about and none of them has any proper charisma like those in earlier installments. Which is an issue. The minigame of Taxi driving is fun, it's mostly a parody on Initial D arcades and it's clearly that. Kiryu is semi efficient as a fighter from the beginning and takes much less time to regain his full power, which is good. Obviously you need Tiger Drop as it's the most useful skill against all bosses. No surprise here.

Saejima part is.. I didn't like it in Y4, but I could understand it plot wise, but here it's nonsensical, it does the same it did before it drags on forever, and it's a part where I have dropped the game for a couple of months. Saejima himself is as Meh as he always was. Slow, clunky, huge HP pool and all his style revolves around charged attacks which are not always useful. I dislike Saejima mostly for the way he himself is written as a character and everything that happens to him, I always want to skip it. His minigame of hunting is decent, but kinda slow paced as you have to move around the mountain hunting prey, and it's the one most profitable method in all of the game. There is an escape arcade sequence as well, that I should note is horribly made and honestly they should have simply made it a cutscene instead.

Haruka is a weird one. It's more of a minigame like Karaoke, but with a story line. Haruka is okay in this part until she does stupid things as part of a story and piss me off again. Let's leave it at that. No fighting here and frankly I don't even know anymore what is the reason of all the "Idol" stuff you are trying to do. It doesn't matter at all, so unless you can complete Story missions you can just do that. I thought that what you do as part of Idol job has meaning and I was surprised. Especially considering this is all there is to it.
Having Akiyama appear again is nice, as always he is a rather well written character who does the least amount of stupid stuff among all of them for whatever reason.

Shinada is a new addition, his story is more of a sports drama and doesn't exactly fit into the series too well. It's quite well done, but the way it's tied to one other character of the series is a stretch. His combat style is a weird one, but he is semi decent once you unlock throws during combos. He does the least damage of all of the characters with his attacks, unless you use weapons which is a drag. The story isn't that long to even bother. His minigame is a chicken run game which looks like an afterthought by the way the menus are made and how uninspiring it is. The fact that only 9% of players have completed 1 race of second tier championship tells all.

The Finale and the main plot once it starts accelerating towards the end becomes more and more nonsensical  and annoying. The writer/writers didn't care enough for many additional details that simply "happen" and explanations given are vague. Sometimes dialogues get to "we gotta do it" without proper discussions while at other times you will sit through ~10 minutes of dialogues trying to make sense of the story going in some excessive details about characters who you have barely seen before and usually it was somewhere in Part 1 of the game. The whole mastermind plot was cringe and showdowns happened for the sake of it. Haruka as always shines by making this story even more pointless than it already was. I somehow guess that it will affect Y6.

Overall I was pissed by the end of it and while I'm used to Yakuza in general been clumsy in it's storytelling and quite often having some dumb things happen "because" or having "Teh Drama", they hit a new level here. Yakuza 3 had issues with the focus of the story on the orphanage and the main plot was boring, something out of Tom Clancy, but in terms of character building it was still good, and here they lose in every single aspect, which is sad.
I heard polarizing opinions of Y6 so I guess I shouldn't expect any redemption from them.
I was originally sad that I didn't play Yakuza 5 on PS3, but I guess I didn't miss that much.

review_text:
Unrelated note - Don't change your vote from thumbs up to thumbs down AFTER you've written your review! Steam wipes the whole thing out! So thumbs down for steam!  Gahhh.  Anyway, back to SGW:C

I love sniper games.  I find them to be very stress relieving.  Stalking through the bushes carefully dispatching bad dudes with well placed digital lead can be very cathartic.  So, I wish I loved this entry in the SGW chapter, but I didn't.  I didn't hate it, but I think it is overall a big step backwards from its predecessor.

The pros: Sniping mechanics themselves are great imo, especially at higher difficulties, though it drives me crazy that I can't tag people through the scope, I have to use the binoculars to do it first.  This is supposed to add some level of 'realism' I guess, but its just extra steps.  But bullet drop, variable wind and bullet impact is all there, and it is satisfying to plan out your attack depending on your play style.  You can remain that ghost warrior and pick your way through enemies from afar trying not to raise suspicion, or you can go in and try to strangle everyone, or you can go in like rambo and shoot up the place.  Keep in mind that you're still a meat sponge and it doesn't take all that much to kill you, so your mileage may vary.

The graphics and environments are beautiful, and it all ran smoothly for me with my 5700XT at a 21:9 1440p, though I did experience spots here and there with an inexplicable stutter in performance.  

Negs: Well, SGW:Contracts is a bunch of, well, contracts.  They're a bunch of loosely tied together missions that reward you at the end with kind of a lame cutscene once you've completed everything.  I think its supposed to be some big aha moment, but it doesn't work.  I much enjoyed the story and atmosphere of the previous game much more.  You had a hideout! You could store and display your stuff! You could rest, or drive around the map looking for trouble and there was a day night cycle.  It was much more story based and immersive.  Contracts just feels disconnected, and that is really the least of its problems.  

Biggest problem for me is how limited you are by the maps and contract system.  Because each contract area is defined, you aren't totally free to find a perch or go your own way.  You're only able to climb up things they've designated (if you can get the damn controls to cooperate with you - which as an aside - movement in this game when you're trying to be athletic is clunky af.  Can't tell you how many times I just fell 50 feet for no damn reason), and this being a sniping game, I found it really hard to find really long shots. Heck, some of the optics range out to 500m but you'd be hard-pressed to find shots at 400m.  At least I couldn't. Most of my sniping seeming to take place between 100-200m.  I was able to get much longer shots out of Sniper Elite and that is set in WW2 with inferior equipment.  Also, once you're in this contract, you lose all sense of what you're trying to do.  The map is vague - you have a list of objectives, but nothing more than blue boxes indicating you should do something there.  Just kill everyone and eventually you'll succeed. 

Which leads me to UI/UX which is pretty abysmal.  Want to know what that 125,000 dollar sniper rifle does? Can it take heavy ammo? Can you add a suppressor? Will it blend a margarita? Well you have to buy it first to see that stuff.  Have you been playing for a couple of hours and have carefully picked through an amazing route to your objective, but the kitchen caught fire and you have to leave?  NO saving.  You'll start from a random checkpoint an hour before because we said so.  Just have one target or objective left in that contract? Too bad, you're still going to listen to and watch the details about the whole thing about 200 more times because that is our loading screen.  Hey, bullet cam is kinda neat the first 900 times, but its getting tedious.  Let me turn down the frequency.  Huh, that does nothing.  Also, when it kicks in, you completely lose your ability to make a follow on shot, so just turn it off.

The mask tech is supposedly the new hotness, but it is mostly gimmicky, and the key mapping to turn if on/off is the same as thermal vision.  I changed this mapping, but about 25% of the time, I turn on thermal vision anyway.  Which is particularly useless FYI. Kind of like most of the gadgets you buy in game. In general, you will be perfectly equipped for everything by like the second contract.  You need a slightly higher powered rifle and a couple of accessories.  50 cals are just loud, slow and pointless. Even things like the various grenade types are frustrating to use.  Apparently, once your throw is more than 10m from you, you no longer have a clue where it will land.  The target icon (which itself just blends in with the ground) just vanishes. It's like playing cornhole with a blindfold on.

Lastly, game length.  I put 25 very slow hours into this game. I'm a slow player in general and this seemed short to me.  I didn't 100% anything because the only way to do that is to complete silly achievements like 'gas 10 enemies' or 'troll 20 people on twitter'.  I'm not interested in playing the same map over and over a different way just to be a completionist.  So the game feels sort of phoned in from a content perspective.  

So in all, it has some fun parts, so it can be worth it at a good sale price, but don't go paying more than $10. It's a $10 game.

review_text:
I love sniper games and have previously purchased and played sniper ghost warrior 2 and 3. However, I cannot recommend ghost warrior contracts. This is due primarily to the absolutely horrible game saving system. It saves itself at certain intervals, so you have no control over the saves. Worse, however, is the fact that it only saves a single version. You cannot go back to prior saves except the most recent. I spent several hours executing a side mission "bounty". The game saved several times afterward. However upon exiting and restarting the game the bounty mission was still there and I got no credit for finishing it. Apparently I had not left the bounty area even though the game saved. So I then left the bounty area and when I did, the game stated that I had failed the bounty and it disappeared. The only option left for me was to start the entire mission over again loosing many hours of playing time.  This could have been easily remedied by the authors if the game retained even a couple past saved versions. This is inexcusable and demoralizing behavior for a game that makes me want to abandon it. In addition, there is no help feature or directions, so you make a lot of mistakes at first in attempts to learn how things work. Since there is only a single save, you are often screwed on accomplishments like the one previously described. The game was fun otherwise, but because of these horrible mechanics, I simply cannot recommend it.

After playing an additional 33 hours, the game is even worse than I previously described. Perhaps a half dozen times my character gets stuck in limbo on a branch or in between rocks or in the latest case simply backing up to a concrete block. You can't move, jump crouch or use any of your gadgets. The only alternative is to restart, loosing perhaps hours of playing time. Of course, if you could save the game when you want to, you might only loose a few minutes instead. Of the total time I've played, easily half of that is because of  bugs and lack of ability to save. I don't plan on buying another Sniper Ghost Warrior game unless these issues can be demonstrably fixed.

review_text: This is an intricate work of art first and foremost. It is one of the most important video games of all time for the current push of the idea that video games contain the prowess and ability that is needed to become a truly admired art medium. A medium which has the ability of telling stories which before these times were deemed impossible to tell, much like the impossibility of the fictitious world in which this game is set in. Coincidentally the condition of the gaming industry and the world of rapture share key similarities, both were brought to this world with great ambition and grandiose expectations, but due to the decisions of the very few who had the influence required to set forth a certain path, one was decided which tragically led to the corruption of the once fantasized idea. But it is natural, for a city underwater to slowly crumble (even if not directly by the water damaging the facility due to unopposable pressures, the political and phylosophical basis in which it was built were only possible by the unrivaled privacy and lack of power checks that being underwater enabled) due to it's absurd ambition, just at it is utterly juvenile to trust in the good side of humanity enough as if to expect that a man won't go for the lowest hanging fruit, even when having the ability of doing unfathomable progression within a medium with the ability to revolutionize mankind if taken with enough seriousness and devotion, with all needed resources at disposal. This is why I love this game, btw I only got 7 hours here cuz I played mostly on my xbox, but as I was saying, I love this game, not because the gameplay may have been my favorite ever, that goes to Cuphead, though it is in no sense of the word lackluster quite the opposite. But no, I love this game because it dared to dream, it dared to take the jump forward, and it has been truly pivotal in giving other developers the ability to dream and childishly ambition once more. I cannot add more commentary about the story or environment which hasn't been said already, and I am joyous that people have given it the praise it deserves. But I can say that those aspects of the game can be compared to many of the most important and revolutionizing moments in cinema, truly enlightening moments. I call this game the Napoleon (1927) of video games which utter confidence, and that classic "A man chooses, a slave obeys" moment to be as revealing to the potential of video game storytelling as the monkey scene in Stanley Kubrick's 2001 Space Oddysey was revealing to the potentials that cinema had, and still has, which are yet to be truly explored in grand scale, both in videogames and cinema. But games like Bioshock, and movies like Citizen Kane and 2001 Space oddysey make me dream.

review_text:
I bought this game for the aesthetic, but I have regrets.As you can tell by my profile picture, I'm a sucker for anything neon.

This game is _very_ unpolished. The movements feel super jank to me. It also doesn't have native controller support when it seems like there's no practical reason to exclude it. This also means no steam deck support, and no native Linux support. I place a very heavy weight on these things, but I was willing to look the other way.

Sadly, it gets worse... The game starts you in a huge open arena with zero instructions of what to do. There's a question mark that you can walk over. One might expect that walking over it would tell you something useful about the game. One would be wrong. Instead, you're greeted with a passive-aggressive note from the dev basically saying "people keep asking why you start in an empty arena, here's why I do that" and then it goes on to explain his strategy for developing the game that literally nobody cares about. Conspicuously missing is literally anything useful about what to do next to start playing the game.

I explored as much as I could stand, where I was greeted with what appeared to be chests that could be purchased with in-game currency that I could not purchase and no indication as to how currency is earned.

I'm sure the information on how this game is played in there, but I honestly have no patience for a game that doesn't just drop me into the action. People are asking why for a reason, pick up on it. Drop them into a tutorial like every other game, or at least into the first level where they can start killing crap. Very few people care enough about your game to have to read the manual before beginning, this isn't _actually_ 1980.

I'm certain I could have figured out what to do next, but I had no interest in doing so. In its current state, I don't recommend this game even though every part of me wanted to like it.

review_text:
An interesting experience, to say the least. The game has very similar vibes to Lust from Beyond, reason being that both of these games were inspired by the same artists (H. R. Giger and Zdzisław Beksiński), but unlike the other game, this game has more focus on gore, sexy stuff comes much later in the game.

The game just throws you into it's world, leaving you to figure out what's going on and what to do. No monologues, no dialogues, no story/backstory explanation, objectives, etc. Just you figuring stuff out, which in my opinion was really cool. A lot of puzzles, shooting, and very bizarre stuff. More bizarre than Lust from Beyond in my experience; At certain moments I was thinking what in the actual hell is going on in this game, and I loved that. It's more of an artistic, atmosphere experience rather than epic gameplay, and I'm okay with that.

The ONLY downside is that there are ZERO tutorials, which I kinda like, but at least there could've been popups as to which key to press on the keyboard for certain actions. What I ended up doing is just using the most common buttons which did work, but still, at least a popup that appears only once just so you know what to press would be really nice.

Regarding the ending, [spoiler] it was kinda lame. I know that the game has to end somehow, and after what you go through it is really difficult to come up with a good ending, but still. It would be really cool if at the end you fall into a pit of some sort and end up at the beginning of the game, so that it gives 
you the kind of "endless loop" feeling, where the character loses memory and then it starts all over. The actual ending was just him standing there looking like an abomination. But again, just my opinion. [/spoiler]

Also, it doesn't surprise me that this game was made by my fellow Serbians, because after all, we make similar gory/sexual media like "A Serbian Film". I was pleasantly surprised when I found that out by watching the credits, I didn't really know that when I started playing it.

So to close it out, if you like what you see in the screenshots, you're in for a good time! Just make sure to check the key bindings before playing so you can know what to press when the time for that comes.

At least 60% of my play time is me leaving the game open on pause.

9/10 story hamstrung by 3/10 combat system. The combat in this game is completely broken and works best when you engage with as few of its mechanics as you can. Here's a list of some of the things I've experienced:

- If you dodge backwards, enemies will do a slide-lunge several feet and land a free hit on you. (not hyperbole)

- The game doesn't always recognise when you're in combat an fails to lock onto enemies, even after user input. This causes you to swing through your enemy, sometimes indefinitely, giving them an opportunity to hit you first, until the game recognises you want to fight.

- Sometimes when you try to dodge in combat, you'll jump instead.

- It takes 3 second to change weapons in combat, during which time you're unable to dodge. Out of combat this takes 1 second.

- Enemies in full plate armor will outrun you even if you have no armor on and have all the sprinting/stamina perks.

- You can't stealth kill someone if they're doing anything besides walking, standing, sitting or sleeping. If they're doing any other action, the prompt to stealth kill disappears, even if you're part way into activating it.

- Arrows will sometimes go through their target.

The only time combat works is when you're 1v1 with a melee weapon, you don't try to dodge, and the game locks on to your target in time. I haven't even mentioned the corrupted saves, the constant crashing, or any of the stupid things the NPCs do outside combat, like inviting you into their home to teach a sword fighting lesson, then calling the guards on you for leaving through their home once the lesson is done. I'm only sticking this out because of the story is interesting.

DISCLAIMER: The lack of recommendation has nothing to do with the game being bad. There's very little I can say about it that's bad, mostly just that I didn't really personally enjoy it.
That being said, the one negative aspect this game does have is that there is a good degree of tedium involved. Some levels are painfully slow or repetitive, but not too many in the end. The level design is diverse, almost to the degree of being too much so as some ideas don't feel fully developed before the game ends. The graphics and music are wonderful and the story and humor present are pretty good too. This game mostly just fails for me on a gameplay level, as there's a bit of a luck factor involved in the harder levels, and no real difficulty curve to speak of. The level I found to be the most challenging (and one that put me off from playing for several days) was about at the halfway point of the game. There's also one World 1 level severely out of place, as well. And since you're required to beat every level to finish the game (well, you *could* skip them but where's the fun in that?) I could see that level being a real roadblock to many first-time players. There's also some metagame about bulding the tallest tower you can but there's not really any point to it. Like I said though, I can't say this is a bad game, just one I don't personally enjoy very much.

Came back after 2 years to start with NGS. Played PSO2 before for over two years on xbox (cross account save btw) and it is like night and day....

You learn pretty much your own style over time while leveling up and improving your gear. And the game rewards you for playing dailies with an EXP-Boost you can earn of 5%, adding up after 10 days to 50%, which can be hold up by just playing dailies. Urgend Quest are free for all Levels. Items for new gear can be earned by just playing the game. No cash grab what so ever. Just the usual random mechanics for cosmetics which is optional.

And NGS, New Genesis, wellllll....SEGA thought "Screw all of that!" No EXP-Boost for dailies, no skills to find, no real learning curce, more like a wall you hit. Learn to parry or die! 
positive side is more movement, and that's it. NGS lacks everything that was good in PSO2s combat system!
Classes are unballanced af! I started playing as a Waker (Summoner type class) and it was atrocious! The damage output of this class is straight out ridiculous compared to Braver (Katana melee class with Bows as an option for range) which I ended up playing.
The main reason why I quitted is simply the fact, that there is NOTHING to do! Only repetitive grind! I played two month with almost 200 hours and I have done literally everthing that NGS had to offer. I maxed out 6/10 character classes and I am at a Battle Power of 3832 which is by the way the barrier for content. Yes, not levels like in all Phantasy Star Online games before (Universe included), it is Battlepower this time, which calcultes itself over gear and class level. To make it short: This system sucks! True skill? Levelprogress? PAH! Who needs that? You have to flex with equip! Go grind for it you lazy maggot! The outgoing and incoming damage even get's calculated over battle power, which makes me question the need to levelup armor over +61....which brings me to the next aspect of the grind: Augments. The only thing they actually managed to do better in NGS. In PSO2 you had to find weapons with the same Augments multible times before you can augment the weapon you plan to end up with. it was overcomplicated. In NGS it is straight foreward. Find dat capsule muliple times, maybe gamble with the chances, get more UNLIMITED POWER! [insert plapatine meme here]

Another good thing in PSO2 and NGS is character creation and cosmetics. there are billions of opportunities until now. Many of the old stuff is hard to get and if it's worth it is up to you. This game is a paradise for weebs. They even call this aspect of the game Phashion.

So PSO2 is a good game, a bit dated but really really good and NGS sucks but! D:

review_text:
Even after almost 2 years, I still think back to this game. I honestly consider it one of my all time favorite games. Scorn has such a weirdly beautiful world that part of your brain is telling you to look away from, but you just can't. Discovering how to progress can sometimes be a challenge, but moving around the environment and seeing all the little details while trying to do so really helps show the morbid beauty of the game. 

While I think that the look and feel of the world is intoxicating and can go on and on about it, i don't think the game is completely infallible. At some point there will be combat and it feels out of place, and a little wonky. Don't let that discourage you. It may be a little tedious, but almost every combat encounter can be completely avoided by just sitting and waiting away from an enemy, and waiting for them to crawl into a hole or around a corner where they cant see you. I think that this approach to combat will help immerse you into the world and also helps in the long run by letting you conserve as much ammo as possible for the unavoidable combat encounters. 

Scorn is a genuinely interesting game that has a few hiccups when it comes to combat. With that being said it is absolutely well worth your time and will definitely be a game that sticks with you, just like it did for me.

review_text:
I DO NOT recommend this game (as of right now), however I can't bring myself to click "Not Recommended" due to the obvious amount of hard work the developer continues to pour into this game.

I remember the first time I played GTTOD. I had trouble understanding what the goal was, but the mechanics were there and it was pretty fun. When I played it again 6 months later, it was a completely different game. The primary objective had been changed so I no longer understood what to do, but I could tell the mechanics had been refined and that the game was making progress. When I played it again six months after that, it was once more a completely different game and I had to relearn what I needed to be doing in order to progress. Another 6 months later and you guessed it, everything has changed again and I have no idea how to play the game anymore.

GTTOD doesn't seem to understand exactly what it wants to be. While the core gameplay of extremely fast paced first-person combat with parkour elements has always been a constant, everything else seems to be stuck in a state of flux that leaves me confused each time I come back to the game. Is this a wave shooter? A roguelike? An arcade score attack? Are there bosses? Is there an ending? Can I unlock new weapons or abilities? I have no answers to any of these questions before playing the game.

As of right now, I have no idea what the core gameplay loop is or what my motivation to continue playing is. You shoot enemies, make it to an orange door, shoot enemies around the door until it opens, go through it into a new level, then repeat. It's structured similarly to a roguelike but doesn't have any of the clear progression that traditional roguelikes would have, such as multiple distinct level themes, multiple bosses, and an ending (usually with an option to either roll the credits or loop the run and keep playing). In fact, I would say it doesn't seem to have any progression whatsoever? Everything seems to be unlocked from the beginning (except for starter loadouts which are superfluous) and I don't feel rewarded or any kind of satisfaction for making it through levels.

Another issue is the game's lack of a good tutorial and arbitrary design choices that make it difficult to understand what certain items or abilities do, or even WHAT items or abilities you currently have because their icons aren't distinctive or descriptive. Weapons and items can be purchased from boxes in the environment but the environments are usually so large, the boxes so small, your movement so fast, and the lighting so dim that you often just fly past them (literally) without even registering their existence. This causes multiple problems, for one your gameplay style stagnates because you can't find any of the options to remedy that, and two when you run out of ammunition you're screwed because you simply have no idea where any other weapons are. Perhaps this wouldn't be as big of an issue if levels weren't as dark as they are, but as is every level I've seen (which is only 3 despite making it more than 3 levels) are all essentially pitch black.

I hope this game finds and becomes exactly what it wants to be, and becomes extremely successful. But right now, it's hard to recommend because of how frequently and drastically it feels like it changes, and how unclear the objective or point of the game really is. If at some point you fall in love with GTTOD, who's to say it will remain that way? It might be a completely different game in 6 months...

At its core, this is a mediocre FPS with bad controls.  You're in a boring, repetitive world with boring, repetitive weapons, fighting boring, repetitive enemies.  Upgrade your weapons by collecting pointless objects, or by doing pointless side-missions -- don't worry, there are two different types of side-mission for maximum entertainment value.  Even the protagonist of this mighty adventure uses the power of self-deprecating humor to crack wise about how tedious and boring the overwhelming majority of this game is.

I guess there's still the main storyline, but that's also complete garbage.  I get it -- it's supposed to be funny.  It isn't.  There's some attempt to invoke nostalgia for 1980s action movies, but they forgot to take the good parts of those movies, and instead just put in horrible dialog, neon colors, and music that is surely in violation of the Geneva Conventions. I hope this gets fixed in the future, because this really is a good game

review_text:
a great bridge between arcade tactical FPS, sniping simulator and stealth immersive sim, SGW:C puts you in the shoes of a mask-wearing goon by the name of seeker, who is tasked by a shadowy organisation to eliminate targets and perform key objectives across several sites located in siberia; ranging from snowstorm-ridden mountains to luxury forest estates to remote arctic islands and more.

 each area drops you in and has a list of key objectives you must complete in any order, mainly consisting of several assassination targets and a couple of intel-gathering/sabotage tasks; in classic im-sim fashion the maps are open-ended aside from the odd bottleneck in certain areas with many ways to proceed and eliminate your targets. do you wanna find a nice bush on a hill and wait for the perfect moment to deliver a half-mile sniper shot, do you wanna go chaotic-stealth and dive in with explosives and silenced automatics? do you wanna go full ninja mode, quietly plant a C4 by the target and blow 'em up from across the map while you wait by the exfil point? you can do all of those, provided the AI is generous enough to not look in your direction.

 Enemies are responsive and behave accordingly, taking cover and charging your position in a co-ordinated fashion; enemies' awareness is highly dependent on light level and atmospheric conditions; in a snowstorm you're nigh invisible, but on a calm sunny day there's a chance you'll get spotted from ways off, which can turn a routine stroll into a hectic game of katyn mouse when a whole squad of enemy snipers decides to clock you while you sneak through the middle of a valley.

 If you're here for story, maybe don't look too closely. The majority of the plot is deferred, meaning you'll only really get the picture if you go out of your way to interrogate your contract targets and grab collectible items, and even then there's not a lot to it.

i'd give it a 7.5 out of 10, fun game, doesn't overstay its welcome, plays nicely, only had a few minor bugs, ran pretty well on my old laptop. doesn't overdo it with content like your usual ubi cry nonsense. plot is mama's homemade weaksauce tho

review_text:
This game looks and plays similarly to the classic JGR, with a quirky, funky vibe and much needed improvement to controls and camera. So old fans might be satisfied with the loving homage and newcomers might enjoy something a little different. 

But I didn't like it. It just doesn't have the same kind of flow, and the world doesn't feel as alive. They've checked all the boxes, but the sauce just isn't there. I find I'm spending more time puzzling on what I need to do or struggling with a technical challenge, less time flowing around the stage. In my initial review, I referred to a particular graffiti spot... though having progressed and looked at some gameplay videos, it seems like this really is a general gameplay issue.

I'm not giving this a thumbs up because I really didn't like this game. But you might be more easy going, or maybe you'll just love it... or maybe not. This is a fresh and interesting game, and you'll definitely know after about an hour, so you can return it using Steam's generous policy. With that in mind, there's no reason not to give this a spin.

...Though if you are looking for a true spiritual successor to Jet Grind Radio, I would recommend Hi Fi Rush. The beauty of JGR was not that it was a cell shaded game about rollerblading and graffiti. It was its fresh style, unique gameplay mechanics, and bold artistic choices. It wasn't just a faithful homage to an old cult classic. In that regard, Hi Fi Rush is doing more of what JGR did, and it happens to be gorgeous and hella fun.

review_text:
First of all, let it be known i have not finished the game. I plan to and will, as i am sure the ending is worth it. The game is extremely unique, to the point i can confidently say i have never played anything similar. The atmosphere is brilliant, the story is great, the choice system is i think revolutionary and the way said choices are brought forth is very inteligent. Then why the negative review...two reasons:

First: I have backed this game when the project was announced back in 2014 i think, as i could already see the potential it held. and while news were scarce, the occasional email with an update on progress was always refreshing. and now 5 years down the line...the game doesnt run very well. the game is not big in term of ressources used, the graphics are fine but simple and the map is far from enormous, yet it barely scratched 60fps for me, and i know a lot of users are having worse performance. Also the game has the annoying tendency to crash in the middle of gameplay, like that, for no reason. When you know progress can only be saved at specific spots, this becomes frustrating really fast.

Second: Death...i have no problem with dying .. when its my fault, didnt eat >> starved, didnt rest >> collapses, ignore the plague >> dies of sickness. this is fair enough. The game has a mechanic where all your death are counted, even if you restore a previous save, and the game make it really clear that dying is NOT good on the long run. The main problem is that the combat system is so garbage you WILL die because of it, no matter how well equipped you are due to a few key points. Ennemies do not make noises, apart from occasional grunts on hit, they do not make noise, especially footsteps. I ahve died twice after engaging an ennemy and getting stabbed in the back by another who had sprinted behind me like a ninja. The stamina management is a disgraceful failure, the rate at which you lose max stamina is insane. sprinting for ten seconds with a full bar will make you lose 10% of it, and as soon as you start throwing punches it dives. trying to take on more than one guy in close combat is a nightmare as them hitting your guard cost stamina, and thus you cant attack, and they keep attacking, effectively stunlocking you. Running is not an option as they have infinite stamina. and the last nail in the coffin: if you get hit, your character will get all dizzy, spinning around like a drunkard, but they can tank uppercuts without flinching.
I can already hear the smartass guild telling me to use a gun, great idea, ammo management is difficult, but this is fine, i dont expect a village lost in the sticks to be sitting on crates of ammo, but in that case, make the bullet counts... even a headshot will not kill a guy, a guy who is sick with the plague to boot. And back to the previous point, hitting them with a bullet will barely make them flinch. Cherry on the cake, the revolver jams extremely often, even in near perfect condition.

So in short, great story, excellent story telling, garbage combat, i know it is not the main point of the game, but it is not avoidable. you HAVE to fight at some point. And the system is so simple it's incredible they managed to make it so bad, especially in this day and age where everybody before you has made such mistakes and you simply have to look at them to know what NOT to do.

PS: as mentionned before, i backed the game at the beginning, which normally entitles me to a free copy of the game on release...i never received it, one more reason to be disapointed.

review_text:
It's honestly mind-blowing to me that we can still get sports games like this in the 2020s, cheap and frustrating AI, half baked mechanics, and limited replay value.
First, the AI is way too unbalanced. You will dominate the game in shots on goal, time on attack, pass interceptions, and hits, and still somehow lose the game 2-1 or 3-0. The opponent goalie is way too strong, how many cross crease one-timers do I have to shoot in one possession, just for the AI to score on a lazy floater from the blue line that my goalie (whos usually in a bad position because the AI is terrible) helplessly watches fly past him? How many times do I have to poke check the opponent on defense until I can actually get the puck back? Why does the AI get frame-perfect body checks the moment one of your players touch the puck? If I had a quarter for every time the AI scored on a double tap deflect goal, I'd have enough money to hire a bigger dev team for this game. 
Your teammates are also another sore spot. They will go out of their way to make the game worse since the AI takes awful angles to loose pucks, rarely recovers defensive poke checks, and refuses to body check (more on this later) unless you put a powerup on them. Why are my teammates constantly skating towards me instead of taking a good offensive position to prepare for a pass? 
Speaking of passes... they are AWFUL. You can point your control stick or d-pad towards any teammate, and randomly your player will instead choose to fling the puck forward or at an opponent, ending your possession. The passing logic (if there is any) makes no sense, I've lost count on the amount of times I wanted to pass to the side and/or slightly behind me and the pass goes nowhere near where I aimed. This game could really use icon passing or some sort of improved logic. I don't know how many times I've said "I didn't aim my pass there!" when playing the campaign mode. 
The roguelike aspect of the game is okay, but it sometimes really hinders the hockey game underneath. Not being able to select any superstar teammate I want after I unlocked them is pretty crappy; I think choosing from a random pool of powerups can provide enough variability, but seeing the same 4 stars on rotation after I've unlocked all of them makes the game feel stale. When the run finally starts, I immediately feel a sense of dread looking at my benchwarmers since most of the time since their stats are abysmally low. Event spaces, while useful at times, are not often worth taking due to the potential downside most of the events give. It's much more useful to take a talent or raw stat boost over an event that sometimes provides a pure positive. 
I really REALLY want to give this game a chance, but I can't help but shake that weird feeling I get when I play any retro-like sports game with cheap AI. I don't want to get people the wrong idea though; for the casual couch co-op with friends (which is how I discovered the game), this game does enough to keep people entertained for a 40-60 minute session. Once you start to scratch a little further under the surface, however, the game's ugly underside really starts to show through.

review_text: I was confused when I first put the disc in all those years ago and was told I had to download something called Steam from some company called Valve. I was familiar with Half Life and Portal, but not with the company that made them. So the one good thing I can say about this game is that it introduced me to Steam, which I suspect was the whole point. I feel like this game was always just a virus to infect as many computers with Steam as possible. This is a very flawed game that for some reason is considered immune to criticism by its many fans. Simplistic. Minimalist. Repetitive. No character progression or customization. You do not unlock new characters, weapons, attachments, abilities, or anything. Every level is exactly the same with a linear path to follow and no real incentive to explore. A few hours of mindless fun, followed by a pointless grind. The excuse has always been, "It's meant to be multiplayer. You're supposed to play it with friends." Do you like doing the same thing over and over again? Because I sure don't. Neither do my friends. This game is one of many that represents a dark turning point in the history of the video game industry when things like offline and single player started to go out of style, when you needed to create an account and install a special program just to play, when developers once again began to use repetition in place of actual content. If you had told me ten years ago that this type of game would become the norm, I would have laughed in your face. I thought it was just a minor cold. Surely we could just take some medicine, get some sleep, and it would all disappear like a bad dream. But now, there is a plague of these kinds of games that provide about 10 minutes of content and put it on a dizzying, endless loop. I think I'm going to be sick. Excuse me while I throw up, question my life choices, have an existential crisis, and find a good single player game to wash this horrible taste out of my mouth.

review_text:
SGWC could have been the Sniper Ghost Warrior franchise's saving grace after CI Games decided to go full Ubisoft on its third mainline installment and made SGW3 an open world (which, nobody asked for).

I wanted to like this game. I like the Hitman repetition loop that offers something new when you try to play a different style. But the game's technical aspects bog it down for me.

--Auto-save--
Why tf does this game auto-save on fixed points of the map? As a game in which one mission session could last for at least two hours, this save system is disrespectful of the player's time. Why can't they just allow infinite saves? Or tie it to the difficulty. Say, give the player 15 saves in Marksman, 10 in Sniper, and 5, or maybe even 0 in Deadeye. Just, not this way.

--Terrain--
The terrain is fucking terrible. I find myself usually crouch-walking and prone-peeking angles and even the flattest, most innocuous-looking terrain will get the character stuck with no way out (except, by dropping a 'nade on your feet to kill yourself and choose to be booted to the last checkpoint, which, you have no control over, btw). The missions' environment and side objectives encourage you to play stealthily. Playing stealthily means crouch-walking most of the time. And with the navigation mesh as fucked up as it is, this takes the player out of the immersion and gives them a horrible experience.

--Respawn points--
When you force yourself to get to a save point, and then quit the game to finally do some irl stuff, when you return, you get placed to a default location of that save point region. Here I'm thinking I'll have a tactical advantage in this area that I know the game saved for me, yet, when I returned, I am placed somewhere else. WTF was that about?

CI Games is a Polish developer, but their games ain't polished, how ironic

review_text:
I didn't love it. It's not for people like me, but in all fairness had I taken the time to read the description instead of buying based of the title, I would have known that. I was hoping to grind up stats and leave a trail of bloody victims in my wake, as though this were silent storm set in ancient Japan. Instead I got a stealth game with shades of Dawn of War II. Leaving a bloody trail results in waves of guards spawning and putting a quick and bloodly end to my mission. Even wading into battle with the enemies usually results in a grisly end and a reload. 

That being said, I can see why it currently has a 98% positive rating. It's a landmark for the genre. If somebody gave me the design document and said, "we're absolutely set on creating the best stealth game possible, how can we make this better" I probably couldn't do more than a snide "change the genre".  If you like stealth based RTS this is the game you have been waiting for.  It has an engaging cast of characters with interesting mechanics and what seems to be a well written story.  Care has been paid to detail and new methods are constantly being presented, but the design still allows for multiple approaches to acheiving the missions. It's a testimate to the immaculate execution that I played it for 5 full missions before quitting, because, did I mention, I hate the genre? 

Still if, like me, you have certian expectations for games with "tactics" in the title, be aware that this is something totally different then the typical tactics game. I can't say that the name isn't justified given the nature of the game, but I can say that it doesn't scratch the itch I bought it for, or for that matter, any other itch, and for that reason, I'm putting it back in the box indefinatly.

Edit: 
Hey guys, I get it, I'm the guy outside the Norman Rockwell exhibit telling people it's full of cans. 

Half of you guys loved it and are on your way out. I'm not here for you. 40% of you are like, "No shit it's Norman Rockwell" I didn't come for you either. Some of you are indifferent about cans and just want to spend the day at the muesum. Go right ahead. However, once in a while somebody will look at me and say "Shit, I was about to spend my afternoon looking at cans?!" I'm here for you.
