review_text:
I don't usually write reviews, but this game is already so good and still has such great potential, coming from a die hard hockey fan, I love this game. 
Pros:
Scouting - Scouting mission details can be changed like player age, position, or ignore well known players/prospects, and it really helps you find the players you need, whether you're playing as Arizona stocking up on talent, or Detroit looking for a diamond in the rough, or Montreal and you are looking for some proven foreign skill to boulster your roster for the cup run, you can find the players you need. You can also generalize the scouting by assigning a scout to a continent, or country/nation, or you can assign him to individual leagues, you can even assign a scout to a particular player if you'd like.

Game simulation- You can choose to simply speed up games to get it over with, or you can watch the game real time and make tactical changes, line changes, etc. 

Line Changes/team tactics/unit tactics/player tactics- Wow. Just great. You can change defensive zone strategies, neutral zone defensive strategies/positioning, neutral zone offensive strategies/positioning, forecheck, breakout strategies, offensive zone strategies, and of course special team units like PP and PK. You can choose which player is le playmaker of the line, choose who takes faceoffs (which is great I'll explain further in), etc you have absolute control of your lines. You can also change individual tactics, so if you have two offensive players and a power forward on your first line, you can change the line to not body check often or hard, and not be aggressive, then go to your power forward individually and make him check hard, play aggressively and with a high tempo to balance out your line, or set a defensive type of player to shadow an opposing player and keep him in check.

You also have control over practice so you can train what coaches do what (coaches have attributes like coaching defensive players at 17/20, but then he might have 11/20 for coaching forwards and a poor goalie stat as well, so make him only handle defeinsive training. I believe it helps, clarification would be nice though. You can make certain player focus on an area of the game that maybe he is weak at, or boost what he's good at even more. You can have signing bonuses for games played, points, shut outs, etc.

Those are a few things that stuck out that I liked

Cons:

Now, I know you want it to be hardcore simulation, very in depth etc. But damn, it takes a looooong time to get through seasons. I want to go outside and do shit still, and have a life. I like it being in depth. Although I have quite a bit of time played, I find it extremely hard to get in to when it takes me like six hours or sometimes longer to finish the season. Just make an option to set a date a date simulate up to it. I know that's like EA NHL's simulaion, but it does work good. Or at least a quick sim game option. I know it might "dumb the game down" but the players that don't want it don't have to use it. Not everyone has time to play for six hours, although it's so good I have played for even longer in one session before. It may also interfere with game longevity, so I guess it's a choice the devs need to make. I really hope that isn't an option already that I haven't found lmao.

Player Overall and progression- (My only semi-major gripe about something wrong/broken with the game, not having quick sim is not wrong/broken, it's just not included)This is pretty simple to understand why it must change slightly... I will have great prospects for the future, but they are young and only really strong in the physical category on the far right like speed, strenghth etc. and since they are so strong in that category, they have a four star "current rating" so if he's playing in the AHL he will be unhappy because he's rated four stars, but then I call him up, and he's a complete liability on the ice, and he does poorly in the big league, and his potential may drop or he may not grow properly. The worst part is, if you don't call them up they will get unhappy and eventually request a trade and in some cases not resign a contract so you just lost out on a valuable draft pick simply because he was being a cocky bigot (imporper use of bigot ik) that thought he was the shit, then his hopes got crushed and blames it on me. If there's a way to fix this, I'd love some clarification, maybe I'm the only one with the problem. That being said, the rookies are in no way broken lol, this happened in a few particular cases. but maybe make it so that certain statistics count more towards your current rating and others less, physical category should have the "least say" in the current rating. Also, maybe have an overall stat or at least break up the stats into better catagories like defensive, offensive, physical, it is sort of like that but then teamwork is in defense (could be in both but offense makes more sense IMO) and stick checking and positioning is in offense so it's a bit odd when figuring out what type of player a player is. I don't really like the player type system either and how it changes. I draft a rookie and he is a playmaking offensive forward for 2 years, then he grew one year and he turned into a two-way. Maybe have a current player role and projected player role like what sort of player he will be at his peak (which you can alter using the practice system), and not just a comparison to an NHL player. I saw you did so in the most recent update, although I think the player/prospect progression could use some more tweaking. Although I have decent time played, I'm still learning so if I have gotten anything wrong I'd love an explanation on how a few mechanics work:) and I know it's early access so it's not fully complete, but it's already a great, complete game in my book. I recommend this 100% to anyone thinking about purchasing. My Vancouver Canucks did great in regular season, and got swept in the first round by a division rival. 8/8 realism. Love the game, looking forward to updates. Would continue to play even if you didn't update.:) Sorry for the long review. P.S. I'd rather spend 60$ on this rather then the 60$ I spent on NHL 15 on "Next-Gen" (lol) consoles.

review_text:
Dead by Daylight used to be a fun, flawed but chaotic "horror" game. 
Now it feels like Behaviour is running a “How Many Things Can We Break in One Patch” competition in their office and winning every-single-time.

Every update somehow manages to fix nothing and break five other things. New killer? Cool. Too bad half the perks get kill-switched, killers can walk over pallets and loops, survivors can't vault windows, and constant server issues that are even worse considering killers benefit from hit-registration that is STILL client sided.

If this game didn’t have Freddy, Michael Myers, Ghostface, Alien, Pyramid Head, Chucky, and every other horror icon they can slap into the store, the playerbase would’ve packed their bags years ago.
The core gameplay hasn’t evolved, the balance is non-existent, and yet the game keeps breathing because every few months they wheel out another nostalgia bomb to distract everyone from the trainwreck under the hood. People don’t log in because the gameplay is flawless they log in because “OMG they added my favorite character, TAKE MY MONEY!”

And yet… here I am. After all the bugs, the broken updates, the shameless reliance on licenses, and the balance that feels like it’s held together with duct tape and leftover perk icons I still come back like a relapsing heroin addict.

Because that’s the curse of Dead by Daylight today: it’s a sinking ship, holes everywhere, alarms blaring, water pouring in faster and faster, and Behaviour cannot keep up anymore. 

BUT HEY YOU CAN PLAY AS SPRINGTRAP RIGHT?!

review_text:
OK, yes.  I can, VERY tentatively say, "Yes, I recommend."  However, I am having several complaints that I am not entirely sure will ever be addressed.  And so, I am going to make a list of gripes, likely get hit with a "jester award" or fanboy wrath, and hopefully give someone who isn't "diehard" some insight.  I will start with....I am NOT a "Souls fan".  Personally, I find the entire genre to be, essentially, "unnecessarily difficult as a means to artificially pad your game".  That isn't to say I haven't played and enjoyed some.  I'm just saying they aren't my "first pick".

First off, the "souls-like" tag is pretty fairly earned, though not as bad as it could be.  If that seems like a problem to you, if it makes you "nervous"...probably move on.  However, I never felt like my ire was aimed at a "tough enemy".  Instead, it was aimed at terrain placement, or inconsistent AI, or poorly explained mechanics.  The game punishes you...fine...very "souls like".  However, it's got enough annoying me without being shot through walls or my dash being stopped short because of a small obstacle that shouldn't even be noticed in a gunfight.  It's infuriating enough to round a corner and get mowed down in one blast, losing all your loot.  Now imagine losing all your loot because a skull on the ground "blocked" you.

In that same vein, the camera has "its moments".  While it hasn't been frequent, it has been frequent enough that I made note of it.  Usually because of said "terrain", but the camera has gotten stuck in something several times or otherwise "glitched out"...spinning around and shaking with no way to see anything.  Again, in the midst of a heavy fight...not something that should be happening.

Secondly, the "familiars" or whatever the "boss-like" characters are....specifically the one of the Island of the Damned...are infuriating.  Not specifically because they are "hard".  Fine.  However, their behavior is inconsistent.  Some runs I'll come across him, spazzing out in his corner of the map and as long as I don't hit him; he's fine.  Other times, I'll be in a fight, nowhere near him, and he'll come over and "get involved"...usually wiping me out because I'm getting hit from behind and not at "full health".  Please do something about this.  It's really annoying to be doing some casual farming run and suddenly "Grunthok the Flatulent" comes out of left field and vaporizes you when you weren't even fighting the damn thing.

Thirdly, I feel like health drops need to be slightly more frequent.  I can go entire expeditions and not have one health serum drop.  Most I have ever seen is in one run is three (which admittedly for that run was PLENTY).  Still, to open 7 chests, kill every bad guy on that main map, and beat "Grunthok the Flatulent" and not get one health drop...even with the pitiful 1% Arcana boost chosen...seems a bit stingy.

Perhaps, there are all manner of explanations within some aspect of the game I haven't found.  The point is, these things are not exactly spelled out.  I still don't fully understand how "mysteriums" work and where to farm those.  The dungeon is annoying the crap out me with Sanity being introduced and I'm not entirely certain I understand THAT mechanic; but it seems to basically be just another way to drain your health in a game that is already doing it plenty....which just seems asinine.

I do enjoy the game.  And I can certainly hop online and find all manner of walk-throughs and guides.  The gunplay is pretty solid and the different guns I've used have each had their charms.  I WANT to like this game.  It's acting like that antisocial kid, though, berating you and being a general jerk every time you try to get close.

Maybe, instead of a "dash"...we can get a "teleport".  Perhaps make one of the traits tie in to "ease of traversing obstacles" so that, for instance, more mobile characters don't have small obstacles blocking them.  Give us more control over how "challenging" or "casual" we want a run to be (perhaps toggle if we want the extra bosses...and therefore extra loot chances....we've already beaten to be there on a certain run).  I saw another review mention tying calamities more into the loot you pick up and I can get behind that.  As it is, the game seems to either "kick you when you're down" or "let you roll over it".  "Feast" or "famine".

...And could we play "dress up" with our "Preyer"?  Sure, he looks badass; but, some customization would be "badasser".  Perhaps it's later and I haven't gotten there, yet.  I like making my character my own.  Sue me.

I really hope things get smoothed out on here because I am worried these issues I have will only get worse as I progress and fights get tougher.  I'll be PRAYING for the days that "Grunthok the Flatulent" was inexplicably getting drawn into fights a quarter map away; as I now curse "ZorZlub the Incontinent" for somehow nuking me across the map with a melee attack or something.  There is so much here and so much that COULD be here.  I just hope it doesn't end up alienating me and others before it can get there. with silly overlooks and mistakes.  As it is, while I can recommend it...I'm uncertain how long my own patience will hold out.

Edit:  I felt it was only fair to address my gripes with additional play time and research.  Firstly, I should NEVER [i]have[/i] to look up walk-throughs and forums for your game.  Much love and appreciation for the community that has stepped up to fill this gap; but, it was a task that the developer should have taken on.  This is a serious oversight.  There needs to be better explanation within the game.  Many of my complaints stem from the game not being clear about something and you either have to figure it out yourself or hope someone else has and is willing to explain it.

However, eventually, things do start clicking into place and, if you are willing to...the game is "eventually" a lot of frustrating fun.  Just be prepared, it almost feels like the first few stages and ascensions are nothing but a hazing.  The early game doesn't feel "right".  The "Gnosis" levels are the biggest walls and it isn't until Gnosis III and beyond that things seem to "normalize".  At least, that's how it was for me.  It wasn't until this point that things like "healing potions" began dropping with any frequency (though still, some runs, I'll have NONE......HOW?!) and my character has access to a mostly full compliment of abilities, skills, and weapons.

That's the biggest takeaway for me....this is a game that requires you to put the time in to experience it's best.  I'm 40 hours in an I still have only a "solid" grasp on everything (and there is still Gnosis IV and all that comes from that for me to learn).  I can say that, yes, small issues compound so if there is something that annoys you early that's a legitimate issue (say, the terrain posing serious problems)...it will only get worse as the hordes get nastier and bigger.  However, if you are willing to educate yourself a little and put in some extra work...this really IS a solid game.

review_text:
I would like to begin this review with this: you have to buy both Kyoto Winds and Edo Blossoms in order to get the full story. Kyoto Winds covers the first half of the original game +new routes of other characters +3 new characters that give you interesting perspectives. Edo Blossoms cover the individual routes and its full romances. What KW cover is 85% common route and the 15% being the start of the 'official' character route, hence, you need to get EB to finish the story completely.

This is my first 'commercial' otome game and I believe that Hakuoki as a whole lives up to its legacy. For what its worth, it's a good historical fantasy as it highlights the significant events of pre-meiji period and the fall of the Tokugawa Shogun. What I like most about this is how we are given the opportunity of different perspectives of these events through Chizuru's lens and each character. Particularly the introduction of the 3 new characters. Funnily enough, I seemed to have learned a few things about this part of Japan's history through this game.

I will say though, as some reviews have mentioned, romance is not the focus simply because KW covers the common route of the original game. Not to say that it is not romantic; the romance exists in a slow burn between shared moments with the characters and Chizuru. If I were to scale the level from romantic to platonic routes (in KW) then:
1. Iba
2. Yamazaki
3. Harada
4. Todou
5. Saito
6. Souji
7. Sakamoto
8. Sanan
9. Kazama
10. Hijikata
11. Souma
12. Nagakura
I mean, the scale is subjective depending on your taste, but the sequel game definitely covers the romantic parts of each route.

The issues I have with this game is perhaps the lack of exploiting Iba's and Sakamoto's perspective of the events of pre-Boshin war. Particularly the failing Shogunate and the dive in details of the oni clans. Because we are limited to Chizuru's perspective, we only catch glimpses of their point of view towards the two things.
Another issue was Nagakura's route, as the plot cannot decide whether it wanted him to be a platonic bro-sis dynamic or romantic. I would have been satisfied if it did go platonic, but by the end of KW it couldn't decide where it wanted to go.

The order of routes to play through? Honestly, go blind and see where the choices take you. I was surprised I landed on Iba first and did not regret it. Hijikata's route may not come off as romantic, but most of his route acts as a the main foundation of the game's storyline.
I do recommend it best to get the game in the full set on a steam sale. It's worth in both full and half-price, but it'd be better to buy it in a bundle.

review_text:
I don't have much to say besides that Hakuouki is a classic that must be played by all otome game lovers. I don't really understand why they split the game into two parts at all, so keep in mind I'm talking about the whole game (both halves) when I say this. 

The new characters are really charming, got my gripes with some bullshit storyline aspects in some of them both new and old actually, but they're amazing. Switching from other otome games to this I really felt this as more involving at least character-wise. Like for example Code:Realize's story is way better constructed than Hakuouki's but the characters aren't as layered as Hakuouki in the long run (and here I'm also speaking of the sequels/alternate stories), so the romances turn a bit too cringy and cheesy for my liking, because of how "perfect" (in different degrees, I really like Saint Germain and Impey, but Finis took the crown =w=), most of them seem to be, while characters in Hakuouki aren't dislikable by any means, but they got flaws, like Kazama's cynicism, Okita's sassiness and emotional dishonesty, Souma's tendency to always self-guilt, Sanan's ability to not talk and get misunderstood often (though some of his grey morals really ain't helping either) etc. 

This is also one of those old-fashioned otome games that tend to not be made as often anymore, where you have to really struggle to get the guy you want by using the trial and error of multiple choices adventures, you don't have a main menu where you can choose a route, and I really REALLY miss that gameplay aspect of it. (Edo Blossoms does but it's assumed you played Kyoto Winds which is where the work is mainly focused on)

Another thing I really like is how they made it easier to obtain all CGs and endings, not by save/load files that you had to make yourself at convenient places, but by allowing you to directly load the chapter you need with the stats you need. There's some charm in figuring it all out yourself, games like Heart no kuni no Alice heavily rely on save files, but that can become often tedious and most Hakuouki's endings aren't that worth it to go to that extent in my opinion (besides the Good ends obviously, with some exceptions, mainly Okita Souji. *insert a biased cough here*).

Some downsides would be the already mentioned bulshit storyline threads, like sometimes I just feel like the writers had no idea what to do with certain characters so they went on crack one day and were like "ah yeah, this totally makes sense!" (Hachiro and his whole arm situation comes to mind right now, like what. why. how??, Shinpachi to me was another problem, but in the opposite way, while Hachiro's route tended to be complicated and eyebrow raising af, Shinpachi had almost nothing going for him besides a "big bro/little sis" dynamic between him and Chizuru and while that doesn't necessarily have to be bad I also wondered why the story needed to be told in the first place besides just ticking him off the checklist of available samurai bachelors). 
That said, the second downside is Chizuru herself. While not entirely aggravating at all times, she unfortunately joins the dull, useless rank of otome heroines that expresses the wish to improve but she never does. Probably one of her best versions was in Yamazaki's route, where she expressed how while she found she was bad at fighting, she tried her best to fight in different ways, like using her medical skills and I could really see how hard she tried, besides just being the guy's emotional support as she's usually reduced to. I liked her attitude when in pair with Kazama or Okita too, maybe those sort of personalities just make her twitch enough to show that she's got character, which is always a plus for me lol.  However I think most of the guys and the story make up for it enough, especially if you're a history nerd or have interest in Japan's last samurai time period. 
 
Anyway, the game (+Edo blossoms) ain't that expensive at the time of this review, so I really recommend trying to go for it if you like otome games but never had the chance to try out Hakuouki. Also excuse my chaotic review, I'm really just writing this out of nostalgia and wanted to express myself somewhat. I might edit this later on. 

PS: I hope Idea Factory will stop milking this series. Unless they localize stuff like Hakuouki Reimeiroku and all the other Hakuouki mini games lol (Idea Factory, if you're reading this *wink wink*). But if they don't stop i'm sure we're gonna fall back into it like the trash we are. lol

review_text:
Given Bloober Team’s previous track record and initial showings of Cronos: The New Dawn, I was considering ignoring it entirely as it looked extremely mediocre at best. Yet, at release, the game started getting a lot of positive reviews from everywhere. It can’t be that so many people are praising a poor game, right? Wrong, apparently. Cronos turned out to be not just mediocre in ways that I predicted, but it also somehow managed to do poorly things, that Bloober Team usually does really well.

Cronos: The New Dawn claims to be a “survival horror” game, though for the initial 3 to 4 hours of my playtime I was fully willing to accept that it was yet another example of marketing gaslighting people into thinking linear third person shooters can be considered “survival horror”. However, as the game goes on, it does become a survival action, of sorts, with even some sections that indeed work as they would in a survival horror game. Which, unfortunately for Cronos, puts it into direct comparison with representatives of several genres, at all of which it is quite average at best.

As mentioned, the game functions as something that could be considered a survival action – think Resident Evil 4, – so it’s an action focused action adventure with horror theme for the story and setting and a mix of fully linear sections with some interconnected locations you get to explore and unlock more of. The team has previously attempted a similar approach in the quite adequate Silent Hill 2 remake last year, though this time around the “more linear” sections are extremely linear. Not that it’s a bad thing if the combat and locations are good, but sadly both are quite poor. The combat is far from the worst I’ve ever played – it functions and there are some nuances to it, like the ability to charge shots or the fact that enemies try to merge with other enemies to get stronger, which can be prevented. But it is exceedingly dull most of the time, except when it’s very poorly thought out and frustrating instead. There’s no real “difficulty” in the latter moments, nor does the game do what The Evil Within did – it doesn’t kill you for “playing wrong”, it’s just so messy that sometimes you get unlucky and start to slowly lose a battle of attrition. Boss fights are especially poorly designed, which is odd, since that was the only genuine combat highlight in Silent Hill 2 remake.

The biggest surprise, though, is in the visuals. I often said about Bloober Team’s games – they don’t know how to design a fun game, but their tech art and level art team are top notch. Their environments always looked interesting, transitions creatively used the Unreal Engine tech, they did a lot of genuinely impressive visual trickery all the time. But Cronos: The New Dawn is easily the ugliest Unreal Engine 5 game I’ve seen. Everything looks dull and boring and very reminiscent of the Unreal Engine 3 era at the end of 2000s, where games often looked hideous and you couldn’t tell one location from another. I feel like they were banking on the whole “alternate reality 1980s Poland after apocalyptic event” atmosphere being weird and unfamiliar to a lot of more English-speaking audience and maybe it is (it’s certainly not weird to me). But I do feel like if you want an interesting take on this whole “vibe”, there are far more visually interesting titles like You are EMPTY, STALKER or, heck, another Polish attempt at creating a Resident Evil 4 clone – Afterfall: Insanity. I can’t believe I am saying that Afterfall is more interesting than anything, but it is actually true.

Storytelling and the plot start very strongly, at least. There’s an interesting mystery and curious events that hook you in and make you wish to learn more. But even by the middle of the game it becomes clear that the most interesting ideas are never developed or followed up, some of the genuinely interesting mysteries are left hanging and the game, in typical Bloober Team fashion, is far less interesting in sci-fi, and more in “what if this was a metaphor about something” plot development that is, at the same time, so non-commital or surprising, that I can’t imagine anyone being interested in it. It’s told very poorly too, with utterly stupid dialogues and cutscenes, wild mood swings between moment to moment and plot points never organically developing or leading from one to another. Things just happen when the developers want them to happen, so there’s no flow to anything narrative or gameplay-related. All while somehow lasting for about 14-16 hours of playtime it absolutely does not deserve.

I’m surprised at this game. Cronos: The New Dawn is extremely mediocre at best, and poorly designed and put together as a game or a story at worst. Yet it is getting far better reception than, say, Post Trauma, which lands in the same range of quality overall. For some reason, people keep giving Bloober a pass and the clout from releasing a decent remake of a fantastic game probably didn’t hurt either. But really – just ignore this one. It’s not good at all and even the already mentioned Afterfall: Insanity is a more interesting project than this. At least it’s often unintentionally funny. This, however, is just boring and frustrating.

review_text:
[h1]A sequel to one of the best video games of all time, and it's even better now with OpenRCT2.[/h1]

Way back when, 8 year old me got this game in a cereal box, and it single-handedly changed my life. RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 is arguably the most iconic tycoon game ever made besides maybe the first game.

[b]NOTE:[/b] Just like the first game, this game tends to crash quite a bit on modern systems if you don't use OpenRCT2. This doesn't make the game unplayable by any means, but it does mean that you should save your game often, which you should ideally be doing anyway. If you plan on playing with OpenRCT2, you won't have this problem.

RollerCoaster Tycoon 2 is basically the first game, but with [i]more[/i]. Everything about the first game that was great (which is basically everything) carries over to this game as well. This game features a lot of new rides, a refined scenery building system, and new possibilities for coaster building. The first game didn't have a sandbox mode, and this game has got one even though it's not a true "sandbox" mode by its strictest definition. So far, this game sounds like a strict upgrade over the first game which I already thought was an 11/10 game, and that would be true...

... If the scenario design didn't take a back seat. The one true downside of RCT2 compared to the first game is that the scenario design and the difficulty curve of those scenarios is quite a bit weaker compared to the first game. Whereas every park in the first game felt like every single tile of terrain was thoughtfully considered to create the best looking landscape, there are quite a few parks in this game that were obviously made in about 5 minutes with the mountain tool from the Scenario Editor. The difficulty curve also takes massive spikes and drops as some scenarios are placed in the wrong difficulty section. review_text:
Just Cause 4 is much like the previous games in the series, with tons of vehicles, aircrafts, guns and all kinds of gadgets, including your trusted grappling hook, parachute and jet pack. All of this makes for a really cool and truly action filled game! All though the history is a bit thin, the missions are really cool, and you're almost free to do whatever you want with this game! There are even some secret things hidden in the game too! 

I have really enjoyed the games in the Just Cause 4 series, and all though they are all different, the goal is the same. Create chaos, destroy things, and make for a better place, wherever you are...at least for yourself!

With a great variety of challenges, missions and overall tons of things to do, I was really happy with what the game could offer. On the other hand, what I liked really much for the previous just cause games, were challenges that were actually challenging. I remember especially the wingsuit challenges in previous games, that had more than 3 rings, and required some practice to get through some times. 3 rings for the wingsuit challenges was not always simple to do, but I would rather have a long track, like with the hooverboard. I really enjoyed the achievements in Just Cause 4, because they were all mostly unique, and they were fun to do too!

There are only a couple of things that I disliked a bit in the start. You're taking over land, not bases, but I figured this worked out in the end, because to gain chaos, you still need to destroy things. I still found previous games where you actually took over bases more fun, even though it could sometimes be tedius to find the small thing you didn't blow up. On the other hand, taking over land, while destroying whatever you want to do, makes for faster progress, and that's not bad either. So not a big problem overall, with such a great game!

I was also a bit annoyed over that I was not able to change the keys of the wingsuit, because it was inverted, but as I had no choice other to deal with it, and live with, that is just what I did.

It wouldn't be fair to not recommend this game, but in all fairness, the earlier games were better. I saw my playtime for Just Cause 2, and it has 50 hour more time played, compared to this one. It's still worth playing, since it's in the series, and I do recommend it.

review_text:
This game is such a breath of fresh air.
The combat is fun and has a cinematic flow to it.
The movement is fluid and maxing your way from one part of the map to the other never feels like a chore.
The character creation system is the best in any mmorpg I have seen.
The story is captivating and the sidequests are a pleasure to do, they don't feel like just some exp/resource grind that you are forced to do in the side.
The world itself is captivating and the NPCs filling this world immerse you in their stories. You really start to feel for these characters, they are not just some props to fill in space.
Exploring the world itself never feels like a chore to explore. The maps feels full, with stuff to do, collect, or encounter.
The "gatcha" system is focused around cosmetics only, and the is no pay to win. However, cosmetics are not locked behind the draw system only. The game offers gorgeous free options and there are also cosmetics you can buy directly from the shop using irl money, for reasonable prices.
A final point I want to really commend this game for is the optimization. I locked my frames at 60 FPS because I have quite an old PC; however, the game is so well optimised that it feels I am playing at 100 fps. The graphics are breath-taking and the game ensures that you can fully enjoy every second of it.

This game is currently in the Humble Choice for April 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before May 7th, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.

Deader Space. 

The Callisto Protocol is a horror game that doesn’t even try to hide its inspiration on its sleeve, it shows it on the collar.  Everything about this game screams Dead Space. From the life bar on the back of your player’s neck to the inventory system floating in mid-air in the game world, The Callisto Protocol tries to evoke memories of Dead Space, which is good because that’s also how it was sold.

I can sum up my problem with the Callisto Protocol in one fact.  To dodge enemy attacks you hold left or right on the thumbstick, and then if they try to attack a second time, you hold the opposite direction.  Not hit it in time with the attack but just hold a direction.  If that doesn’t sound challenging, it’s not. 

There was a point also where you changed a club for a stun baton, and the combat didn’t feel like it changed at all.   Callisto Protocol also struggles to be scary, because most of its jump scares are pre-scripted.  But if you ever are afraid something is going to jump out, hold the stick to the Left just in case.   See it’s kind of dumb.

Also just saying I think the third person made it hard to be scared during several of the horror moments because you’re watching actions being done to the player’s avatars, not experiencing those actions.

Pick this up if you were waiting for a heavy discount.  This game got a lot of popularity leading up to release and then kind of disappeared quickly. I’m not the person to ask about a horror game, but I also just found this one to be more lacking than scary.

Review:
.hack//G.U. Last Recode is a collection of 3 substantial action-JRPGs all part of one contiguous storyline. The gameplay is reasonably deep; unfortunately, the game rarely provides enough challenge to players to force them to dig into the mechanics, even on hard difficulty. The story may not feel so unique and original in the age of Sword Art Online and its imitators, but it was pretty unusual at the time these games were first released, and the story is reasonably entertaining if you can ignore (or appreciate) some of the more cliched anime tropes. While nothing impressive for a modern game, the graphics are still decent and a significant improvement over the originals, and the game has an interesting aesthetic. In particular, some of the character designs are nice, although the models of some NPCs are reused excessively. The music ranges from decent to gorgeous, although a few pieces (such as the battle theme) recur so often that they can become a bit grating. And the dub for this game is mostly consistently good - enough so that it is probably worth playing with the dub for most people. Finally, as a port of console titles, the game appears to run quite well even on high settings and does not appear to have many issues.

Score:
Gameplay: 6/10
Graphics: 6/10
Audio: 7/10
Story: 6/10
Technical: 6/10
Overall: 62/100
Tilt: +3
Final Score: 65/100

Final thoughts:
Overall, I mostly enjoyed the time I spent playing this game. There's not a lot about the games that I would consider truly great, excepting some of the music. On the other hand, there's also not a lot that I would consider notably bad. Probably the weakest aspect of the games is the gameplay - while the games have decently robust gameplay mechanics for action-JRPGs, the games's relative ease means that there is little need to actually delve into those mechanics. For example, you character can learn many of the spells available to other classes, yet I only ever cast spells a handful of times during my playthrough and never encountered a situation were spells ever felt necessary. I will say I somewhat enjoyed the combat notwithstanding, but that was more from a sort of zen "watch me kick these guys asses" feeling rather than any sort of challenge.

You should probably avoid this game if the ease of gameplay would be a big frustration for you. Also, while it is somewhat different from your typical JRPG, it likely isn't so different that even JRPG detractors would enjoy it. With that said, I recommend the game to anyone who can overlook the ease of gameplay, and who enjoy JRPGs but are looking for something a little bit different.

Buggy disaster with one of the worst UIs of any game out there. Interesting idea, miserable execution.

As for the plot, what little exists of it reads like a 12 year old's Call of Duty fanfic. Each target is wholly interchangeable with every other target in any given mission. I really tried to like this game. I enjoy the genre, and applaud the attempt to create a hitman-esque open ended environment, but even in that they failed, as in every single mission there's really only one "correct" way to hit your target, and it might as well have flashing neon signs pointing the way. Everything about this game screams "THINK ABOUT IT FOR A DAY BEFORE IMPLEMENTING IT!", all the way down to the inane upgrade menus. So many times, the wrong choice in a simple decision was made. A real disappointment.

review_text: Well, I wasn't expecting a lot, but I got more overall enjoyment out of this game than Far Cry 3's main game. This game's very similar in most aspects, but certain mechanics make it a lot more fun to navigate. Increased speed, health, different guns, less time consuming and arbitrary leveling, it makes for a good, albeit, bite sized Far Cry experience. Again, just like Far Cry 3, this isn't anything ground breaking. The story is basically only there as a formality, the gameplay, at a point, is pretty repetitive, and the 100% is slightly annoying due to the grindy nature of it, but if you have something going on in the background, it doesn't feel like it. You ARE doing the same things over and over again, and you likely WILL do them ad nauseam, but if you just tune out the tedium of it, listen to some music, and let the guns do the talking, you fall into a decent rhythm. Collectathon elements will be what they are, and money is painful to get at a point, just like the base game, but the loop is enjoyable enough for me to not knock any points off for it. If you play just the story and be done with it, it's like a couple hours, max, but 100% will run you a bit longer if you aren't very proactive, like me. Overall, solid game, good soundtrack, bland story, but fun. 7/10.

review_text:
The game is interesting and innovative, speaking of shooting along with superpower, Bioshock is still one of the few games that matters. But this first game in franchise does give me so many problems compared to the third game Infinite. It is the first time I understand the importance of balance.

Minor Control Issue. We have to switch powers and guns instead of duel, it is the biggest flaw when it comes to basic control. It's not good but considering the tech problem is somehow hard to solve back to the days, I say it is only a minor issue after I get used to it.

And something I can't get used to is the game balance. I can't enjoy the game until the last few levels because the resources and abilities are so limited.

First few levels, I spend all the time collecting ammo, and even have some spare loot, but I don't dare to shoot Big Daddy because it is too hard even in normal difficulty, Mr.B can kill us in two shots. It is just torture, I have to leverage the environment like gun turret and oil drums. And guess what, after neptune's bounty, the ammo I struggle to save is robbed, fine, it is the setting, but why all special ammo is gone? I find people experiencing the same problems and someone says the remastered version has fixed this problem, haha, such big bug is not on their bug list until they need to milk new money.

I keep moving. The atmosphere is scary, enemies do scream and also make sound of footstep. I am sensitive to sound, such design is a little annoying because early days the sound design is not precise and distant sound could confuse me it is close. But the real problem is still lack of resources, or being afraid to use because we don't know whether we can survive later. The stifling game experience makes me decide to change my tactic, I should believe the game and have fun, enjoy the fight, well, the ammo indeed is not the problem, I don't have enough life. A big dilemma.

In another immersive sim Dishonored, where similarly we have to collect resources and keep saving progress, after I work hard on collecting, I can go with either assassination or fight, I have the confidence and I do enjoy it, I will not be reduced to a situation where I have no ammo or life.

Still, trust the game and carry on, finally after 20 hours, after enough upgrade and camera research, the enemies are not lethal anymore, I can actually see there is a way to do. This game costs me too much patience in the early stage, even more than Witcher 3. When I start to enjoy it, 30 hours has past, and there's only three levels left, the fun of exploration is gone because my resources are barely consumed.

In general, the game has no adaptive phase for players, we have to accept the harsh challenges and bear it, we survive as the protagonist does, it is pretty good in the term of immersive sim, but I don't enjoy such design, Tomb Raider is also a game where we start from the ground zero, but the challenge starts with a feasible level. The key difference is the irrational resource design, we are supposed to have more resources when we are weak, not after we are full of everything.

review_text:
I rarely write reviews but I just have to regarding this one. The fact that I am still recommending this title is perhaps quite weird given the following review, but I'll give it a solid 51/100 in favour of enjoyable gameplay despite the following WoT I am about to write.

I'm only some 20h into this game, so I really can't tell if I've done my part or not! However!

I bought the game in early access, I'd say it has paid itself by now in terms of entertainment value, but It had it's flaws like most EA titles. There are situations that really gets your blood pumping, but most of the time it is pretty frustrating. The only really viable way to amass some decent XP and fast leveling is through the game mode "Horde", and it gets pretty monotonous after a while. The worst bits are when your team is wiped out but the piles of corpses are so huge that the bugs themselves can't really find a way through the carnage and finish your HQ off, resulting in you quitting the game and recieving no XP whatsoever. This has happened several times by now.

The lack of players really shows sometimes (but I hope this will get sorted out with 1.0 and X-platform), with zero medics present most of the time the games get really hard, and to be honest, quite annoying. You can't really turn the tide as a lone wolf either.

As I suspected the active player base grew with the 1.0 patch, although it seems the game still struggles to fill 16 players for each game, either that or some or many of them gets kicked due to the current optimization issues, however these are issues which I am yet to enocunter for some reason as mentioned earlier. This makes finishing any match significantly harder than it should be, since you know, you're simply outgunned.

It was actually better before 1.0 as many have stated. The new "content" is locked behind companies, which really doesn't make any sense at all. Clans being all cool and all but really, even with a company there is rarely enough players online to do anything of real value.

As it stands, the game has way too many problems that weren't there just a few days ago.

The biggest issue is the bugged out bug counter in Horde (my favourite game mode, and I bet many others agree), which was the only viable way to gather some decent XP. The piles of corpses may look cool but in fact (I really don't have any performance issues btw, and no crashing problems) it makes the game more or less unplayable. You simply can't kill enough of 'em and unless you're blessed with a max level demolisher you can't even see what you're shooting at after wave 6 or something. To claim a victory on hard difficulty is now near impossble. On normal difficulty it more or less requires each and every player to amass 400+ (a number which is damn near impossible on low ranks) kills to even be remotely close to a win. It's gotten ridicilous.

Add to that, the early wave spawn sometimes happening right after another wave for some reason, where you don't even get 5 seconds to repair the base, come on! Give us a break.

Flamethrower is not working as intended, several weapons are reported that they don't register hits. The flamethrower is especially problematic, because this is where I actually encounter one of the few severe bugs I've heard of, and that's because whenever I use it it completely blackens my screen. I can see tracked bugs through the blackness but that's it. It takes a while before it wears off, it's comparable to being flashed in Counter-Strike, although the effect takes way longer to wear off. If this is an intended mechanic, it really is weird to say the least.

I've been getting stuck in walls and under things in general upon revival plenty of times, not nice.

I once got stuck in a pile of corpses and got 50+ kills with the knife from within the pile, as I was out of ammo i just kept swinging, but the bugs couldn't even touch me, and I couldn't get out. Let that sink in. So stupid, really.

I sacrificed myself as a Demolisher, resulting in a perma death and I couldn't spawn again the wave after, resulting in me sitting in the viewing screen for 45 minutes because the team was unable to finish the game (again, due to the broken bug counter), and the bugs had died in such numbers close to the HQ that they couldn't damage it either (again). Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts takes the popular-but-flawed Sniper Ghost Warrior series, and packages it into a much more enjoyable series of maps with precise objectives and great handcrafted content for each.  The game blends the importance of stealth and tactics with skill for sniping (particularly at the high end 'dead eye' difficult setting), where you have to use your own experience and judgment to snipe from long distances to attain a kill.  

I am on my third replay of this game having picked it up a couple of years ago, which is testament to the fact it is well produced, fun and has great sound and graphics that run well on even medium level PC's.  I really would love to see a Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts 3 from the studio in the future.  This is really a more high end/tech and first person version of Sniper Elite 5 for those familiar with that.  They're both good in their own specifics ways, but I personally love the use of turrets, drones, mines and decoys as I work through the complexities of taking out entire, heavily armed compounds solo.

For the low price too, I highly, highly recommend Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts, as well as the sequel.

I do not regret putting my money into it but will stop playing for now. 
I can just advise you to wait a couple of months or a year.

review_text:
Cronos: The New Dawn is one of those rare games that grab you from the very first minutes. I played it twice and a half just to see every ending, and each run remained just as gripping. The world is dark, oppressive, and beautifully designed - at times genuinely terrifying, yet always fascinating. It’s easy to draw parallels with the Dead Space remake, but the game confidently carves out its own identity.

The phylactery system, limited to three active at a time, adds a nice layer of strategy, even if it could have been explored in greater depth. I loved how the trapped souls occasionally whisper to you, sometimes at the worst possible moment, delivering perfect jump scares. The notes scattered throughout are worth reading for once, adding substance to a narrative filled with twists.

If there’s one drawback, it’s the final boss, a real bullet sponge that slightly dulls the finale’s impact. review_text:
I am on the fence with this review for sure, but here we go.

Pros: 
- The map seems pretty big all things considered, and there are really pretty areas if your PC can handle it.
-Lots of servers to choose from.
-A fun concept, amusing to run around as different animals.
- Lots of potential if the devs actually use it.
Cons:
-There isn't an in-game map to help navigate the damn place. No set migration routes for herbivores to follow, no ways to truly mark out different territories that has been "claimed" to either encourage people to stay away from the place or find the alpha and fight for it. 
-If you are trying to hide/blend into the foliage? There is a chance it's not there for players that have taken their graphics to a lower spec for performance, So you're just a dumbass standing out in the open to them.
- The servers are practically empty. No one is playing this game/the advertisement sucks so people don't even know about it.
-Better get used to lions, because that's all most people are. There is no limitation to how/when/who becomes a lion so they are overrunning the place. There's no sense of balance whatsoever which leads to:
-A review on here says it's an eat/drink/die sim. They are correct, there aren't any goals. Zero game play. Nothing to achieve, nothing to help shape experiences or build interest on. Hell, most people don't role-play out a basic ass child's game of "house" or "family" or any sort of pride/herd/group dynamic to make the game interesting.
-A review on here says it's irritating because people just want to sit around and talk. They are also correct. I spent time with a group for over an hour before I realized that we weren't just sitting around waiting for an admin to help out players or take care of problem players/server rule breakers. They were in a VC and just forgot to tell everyone else.
- The game is laggy, and buggy and I still haven't found out why. Animals clip through the rocks, but you can't see through the damn leaves if you're playing as a giraffe and get to close to a tree. You can be starving to death, or dying of dehydration but your button to eat/drink just refuses to work. Running with a herd -- or hell just a single other person playing the same species? Better get used to them jumping back and forth because the lag doesn't seem to know where they are either. That leopard over there? Yeah it looks weird because for some reason the body of it is vertical instead of horizontal. Game is a mess.

Somehow I enjoy the IDEA of playing this game, and even was excited each day after work this week to come home and give it a shot. The problem is my hopes have just fallen more and more each time I got on here. I found a pretty cool community in the discord I joined because of the server I found, But I can't say that the game itself is super great. If I wasn't an animal lover with a severe need to dissociate from the bs of real life there is no way I'd play this game so much. 

Tl,Dr; It's not worth the money. There is a lot of potential but this game just isn't there yet and I'm not sure why it was even released at this stage. I don't want to know what it was like a year ago.

review_text:
Game lacks basic QoL the genre invented decades ago.  Namely:

Click to drag the map.  No, too easy.  Instead, you right click to steer the map (in the opposite direction of dragging) in a floaty manner.

Pausing while navigating menus.  You can pause the game at any time.  But you can't pause while mousing over tooltips, placing buildings, or allocating jobs.  This isn't a necessary feature in your average competitive RTS (starcraft for example), but in a complicated PvE game - especially with a doom timer (They Are Billions, Rimworld, Dwarf Fortress) - the ability to pause and issue commands while paused is necessity for the average gamer.  

After encoutnering the above, I checked to see if I was missing something.  I wasn't.  The above issues aren't isolated incidents. Gameplay loops too complicated for the AI and pathfinding to solve, depressing gameplay loop where losing is inevitable, special abilities that quickly become micro intensive or outright useless, so on and so forth.  Moral of the story:  NEVER buy a game based off the positive reviews.  Check the negative reviews first!

review_text:
Most of the negative reviews I've seen are saying the PC port is bad, but the game is good. This is not one of those reveiws. 

I've never seen a more overrated game than this. Masterpiece? Please. Absolutely not. 

I went into this game blind. I had no idea any of the story, setting, gameplay... nothing. All I knew was that people are flipping out over how "amazing" and "perfect" this game is. Now I know never to make that mistake again. 

The first moments of the game, I was pretty into it. The underwater city is pretty awesome looking and I like the art deco style it's built in. It's very unique, as I've not seen any kind of environment like Rapture before. I was creeped out by the first splicer you encounter, and I love the moment you first see a Little Sister and Big Daddy. I was looking forward to the rest of the game, but alas, my emotional attachment was later shattered and I began to feel annoyed and irrated. 

The gameplay is downright awful. It's repetitive and bland. Every single time the story is advanced in some little way, or whevener you get a new plasmid, here comes a handful of splicers, yelling their insanity. At first, I was a bit on edge, but then it just became ridculous. Ugh, more enemies to fight. More annoying turrets and cameras. Moving around the levels is a chore. Dying has no penalty, it's just another annoyance. I got so freaking sick of listening to the splicers screaming and I wasn't even halfway through the game yet. (And the fact that enemies respawn made it 10x worse!) Then when you do get halfway through, the enemeis become even tougher for no reason. I ended up changing the difficulty to easy because I was not about to waste my time fighting and dying repeatedly. Any possible emotional attachement to the story was destroyed by how dreadful it was navigating and fighting through the levels. I reached a point where I couldn't wait to finish the game and uninstall it forever. 

The story is ok, but it's nothing special. Altering genetics and losing humanity is an interesting subject, but I thought it took way to long to get to anything remotely interesting, and there was just a bunch of filler that was unnecessary. Go kill these random nobodies and take their picture for this mural, go save these trees that were killed for no reason other than to make the game longer. Maybe I wouldn't be so critical of this game if I hadn't gone in expecting something truely amazing, I don't know. All I know is this game is horrificly overrated and I have no desire to ever play it again or any of the sequels. 

I suppose one could say I like the "concept" of this game, but the actual thing is very disappointing. If you're going to buy this game, would you kindly lower your expectations and get it on sale when it's only a couple dollars.

review_text:
Undoubtedly horrifically beautiful throughout, with the full-on Geiger-style alien biotech being juxtaposed against the rotting decay caused by the infection that's taken hold, there's some suitably brutal scenes peppered throughout your dystopian journey, and some better-than-the-norm puzzles to be solved as part of it. Despite being fairly linear, don't expect this game to hold your hand at any point - you're pretty much alone on this ship, and nothing's there that wants to guide or assist you.

The one weakness is the combat system - most encounters are highly repetitive given the lack of diversity in terms of enemy type, and it felt that they'd have been better served by being rarer and perhaps done without weapons (without wanting to give much away regarding the story, manually ripping some of these things apart in some way, and struggling to do so, would have felt more apt), then there's a battle towards the end which felt both unnecessary and frustrating, simply for the sake of being so. Rather than a sense of achievement, it was much more one of relief that it was finally out of the way, and I could continue with the story. On the plus side, accuracy counts, as this isn't a game to throw ammo boxes out there in every corner.

Scorn's stuck with me since playing, which is something I can't write about many games - the atmosphere is undeniably brilliant, and discovering the alien world plus fragments of the history *is* the experience - so on this basis i have to recommend it pretty wholeheartedly. Given the issues with combat, I still have to qualify this as being a highly unbalanced experience - removing the combat and leaving this as a 'walking-sim' with puzzles might have been a better option in retrospect - but overall it's left the right kind of impression on me, which is very much a good thing. Give me a unique, relatively short experience like this over something mundane that's typically also dragged out anytime.

review_text:
PSO2 and PSO2:NGS, I can say after first starting in the Japanese Server during the launch of Episode 4. I started out alone and with no prior knowledge going into the game. The game itself does what it offers, a vast customization system, flashy but a bit janky combat, expansive skill trees (that you now have to pay AC and SG to fix in the classic version, but completely free in NGS), and a wide array of players from across the global.

The classic version first is very unforgiving if you're a new player as many events and handouts are no longer existing. With most players being veterans who've already completed the game and the final quest HTPD (The Primordial Darkness Hard Mode), Masquerade depth 999, and the time attacks of Rondo to flex with each other on. However on the NGS side you can jump right in and pick up and put down at your leisure. The story will carry you throughout the early progression as you get handouts and things to help you along the way.

Towards the Starless first part quest is when everything in NGS has to offer for you is fully unlocked, so you can skip the remainder of the lackluster story if you want to jump right in to the "endgame". For F2Ps there are things like dailies, weeklies, dext farming, and alnothe farming to be your main source of N-Meseta. However dext farming requires a more specific set up to min/max in which in a good group or a private farm you make 1.5m-2m meseta per hour spent (with either meseta boosters or 100% Rare Drop Boosters + 1 Hour Auto Sell Passes as the drops there adds up to your meseta count when auto-sold.)

I will be real with you though, with the game pushed from the ESRB to T to M, there has always been a slew of extremely lewd and cursed players who are unhinged and ERP in the local town hubs. Central City being the main criminal for that. People can be either toxic or cringe depending on how you approach them, but there are always a good bunch around. Making friends and connections will do you wonders in the game, both Classic and NGS.

Though the game loop is lackluster at best, having friends and making small and big goals helps you continue to want to play this game. I myself have spent 12k hours into this game, yet still find enjoyment despite I am beyond burnt out, fed up with the toxicity and lewdity, and have completed most major content in the game including HTPD in Classic. Would I recommend this game I would say both "yes" and "no". Yes, if you are the fashionista who loves cosplay, looking cute or cool or both, taking screenies with friends, alliances, or yourself, or don't have much time to grind so to do dailies and weeklies then scoot off. No because the game though not completely finished in NGS is brutal when it comes to gearing. As most things boils down to overly expensive augments, preset abilities, and expensive upgrading. Being a loner type will only get you so far as you'll be limited to solo only content or try-harding to the point you drop grands on the game.

My TL;DR if you do decide to play, find your niche, make friends, make a cool unique avatar, and just be yourself. It's both the game I love and hate, and could have been potentially one of the best Anime MMORPGs of its time. But because of sega's greed, monetization, and poor management, the game falls short of what made Phantasy Star, Phantasy Star.

Dead by Daylight is the grandfather of the asymmetrical horror X survivors vs X killer game genre. It is unfortunately uncontested as with many other 'DBD killers' like Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Friday the 13th the game, etc shutting down, DBD remains a mainstay for those who enjoy that type of game. There is a reason I said unfortunately.

review_text:
To The Moon is a game I remember watching Pewdiepie play like, over a decade ago, but I had no real memory of what the story was or anything besides its introductory premise. Overall, I really enjoyed most if not all the aspects of this game that it presents itself as. It is able to balance itself between being a lighthearted and emotional human experience of a story of how love drives our existence, while also exploring more psychological affects like trauma, mental disabilities, and finding meaning in life. In some sense though, I wish the game treated mental disabilities with some more tact instead of utilizing the mystery behind them for senseless psychological horror.

I will admit that I'm jaded from playing way more RPG Maker games before completing To The Moon, but its age and technical limitations are extremely apparent when playing. Decisions from what the controls were on keyboard, the lack of any options, and children-level puzzles are what diminish this game's overall experience. It is unfortunately a short game because you're forced to walk for a lot of it, and the wide and detailed environments often lacked optional interactions for the many objects present. [i]Despite this[/i], the game has amazing emotional moments and was able to build up to it meaningfully; it was mostly near the last half-hour, but I had some tears in my eyes like three separate times.

This game feels foundational if you want to broaden your horizons for story games, but I struggle to say it definitively is. It's a short game regardless, and I think the story is broadly appealing for most people, but it has good moments. Pick it up if you like love stories.

review_text:
I tried. I really tried. It's a cool concept, and I like the general look of the game. But extremely poorly executed.
Everything is cool. Except the toon AI. It makes you want to stab your eyes out.

Example:
You have one building in progress on the west side of your base. Another on the east.
You have 5 builders and 10 organisers. And many lumberjacks and stone cutters.
The organisers supply the one building with some crystal which the other building does not need. It's higher priority than other buildings in progress.
So the builders ALL walk over to the building which now has some building material in a rush to progress the building by 5%. Only two make it and they quickly finish the 5%. Now ALL the builders are at or close to this building, but there's nothing more to do. So 3 turn around and head home, because the organisers have not supplied the other building with anything yet. 1 flirts with a random lumberjacks chick. 1 goes to sleep. One drinks some water. The other two are standing around having a good old chat.
Finally 2 minutes later a hero organiser somehow manages to deliver some wood to the other building while all the other organisers have just been supplying wood to the carpenters, or carrying wood around between your castle and various other storage buildings. Seemingly as the mood takes them.
By this time 1 building is eating food. 2 are in chats with some other toons. 1 starts to eventually make his way to the building. On the way he has a drink from a bottle. He eats something. Then he's confused for 2 minutes straight. And then oh dear. He notices you casting a spell close to him. He runs away in abject fear and awe.
2 other builders start making their way to the new building, but halfway there they start chatting. Then another champion of an organiser delivers some stone to the other building which happens to have a higher priority. So after they chat for a minute or so more. One eats a quick meal, and the other starts making his way there to progress another 5% on the building. 

If you're lucky he makes it there.

If the organisers could get their act together and just finish supplying one building at a time, and then building commences once all materials are supplied. That would be better.
Better yet. If builders could automatically distribute themselves among the highest priority buildings in progress and wait for material to arrive. That would be almost infinitely better.

But no. It's a god sim, that is also a toon walking, and time wasting simulator.
A warning that too many buildings are in progress? Really?
You can't even rotate buildings. Not that it matters. Whatever the buildings look like. An organiser that brings, say 4 wood to it, will walk around, and around it. Dropping off one wood at a time. It's like everything in the game is designed to make toons walk as much as possible, and waste as much time as possible.

Once you learn how to play the game, you are also thoroughly fed up. If you're lucky then yous till have your eyes.

review_text:
After playing this game and listening to what other people had to say about it, I find it really hard to understand why this game has been met with such positive feedback.   While the story of To the Moon -which is indisputably its strongest aspect- did have room for improvement, my biggest gripe is that telling the story through the medium of a  "video game" does not enhance the story at all.  Some other critics have said it is better for this game to be called a graphic/interactive novel, but I for one would have much rather to enjoyed reading this story in a short story / novella (in fact, this would have enhanced it quite a bit and allowed potential for a deeper plot).  The story might be worth telling / hearing if it weren't done through such a tedious and laborious manner [what gameplay there is, is clunky].  You would be much better off just watching a play through on YouTube.  

It's possible that it was the expectations of the game that I had going in that set it up for failure or maybe I just wasn't in the mood and felt overly cynical, but the game is a poor excuse for a game (and not just because of the lack of gameplay).  It does have its merits, but again, if you want to know the story, watch it on YouTube  

[b]I could rant about this for longer, but I will include just a few bonus points:[/b]
[list]
[*]The game is pretentious, not only because of the $10 price tag, but because the set-up of the game makes it seem as if the "emotional" story should justify its other shortcomings (e.g. the lack of gameplay).

[*]There were ample opportunities for the game to take advantage of gameplay, even indirectly, but it doesn't, as if the developers were too lazy to make the game deeper (such as incorporating player choice during the end).

[*]For similar reasons, it just seems unpolished.  I'm not sure how the silly banter between the doctors made it past the first draft of the script, but it seems like a 13 year old wrote it and thought it was funny and flirty.

review_text:
I will say that for the amount of time I waited for this game, it was honestly pretty lackluster. Taking nearly 3 years from the release of Act 1, and putting fans through thoughts that we weren't even going to get another part of the game, and that it was simply going to end on Act 1. The feeling of excitement that everyone felt as soon as we had a release date, and furthering that feeling once the game actually dropped was something that a lot of us expected to never feel. This being said, the final product after everything the developers put fans through, was honestly pretty mediocre from where the first part of the game stands. 

I remember when Act 1 first came out and spending my entire night beating it and being absolutely amazed at the art, characters, and story line that was coming out based on my favorite comic. So many times during that first game was I absolutely blown away at where the story line was taking me and the breathtaking art that only furthered the nostalgia. Needless to say, this was definitely not apart of the gaming experience that came with the second act of the game. Starting off rather strong with the adventure and breathtaking beauty off the art, and only getting less and less exciting as the game progressed. A majority of the tasks in this game giving me more anguish than entertainment at a few different points. Disappointingly enough, the only time during the play through of this game did I start to feel that rush of excitement within the plot was during the end of the games when the clowns came into play. Making it even more disappointing when the game ends exactly after that point, and the realization sets in that the only thing left to do is to sit and wait whoever knows how long for the third act to be released. 

All this being said, I understand games take a long time to make, especially ones with the quality of art that Hiveswap achieves. However, I do believe that this second act holds no light compared to the first one, and I am putting all of my hope into the third act being just as good, if not better than the first one. Hoping that Act 2 was strictly for story telling purposes and furthering of plot, and that future renditions of this game come out bigger and better than those preceding them. 

I spent a little over 13 hours and got every achievement in this game, just like I did the first game. Taking act 2 almost double the time and not nearly the fun and excitement that act 1 brought. I am not unhappy with the outcome of this second game; I am however, disappointed and only want the best of these games that mean a lot to me.

review_text:
A walking sim best summarized as an HR Giger designed continuous OSHA incident. 
[i]I think I might have Tetanus now.[/i]

In all seriousness, the visual design is [i]amazing[/i] - if you're into the HR Giger / bodyhorror / biomechanical aesthetic.
As is the soundscape, incidentally.

I still wouldn't call it a horror game though. 
It's rife with evocative body horror in all it's aspects, but it's not exactly tense or ... doing anything else "scary". 
More a gross-out & 'conceptual horror' walking sim I guess.

The puzzles are here or there - some are excellent and well tied into the environment, some are just glorified 'connect the dots'- or 'pull all the levers' puzzles. 

Combat is a bit icky and sticky, but then it's [i]not trying to be[/i] an action FPS, so it definitly fits the design brief. You can avoid a lot of enemies or just let them be, if you try.
The rest isn't too hard either, so far. Most of the enemies don't actively threaten you very much.

The game does occasionally struggle with sign-posting stuff well enough - partially because of the "overdesigned" nature of it's environments & assets I guess - but it's not a huge issue. Especially if you're somewhat well versed in how games like this (puzzle/light combat/walking sims) generally go, you should figure out what to do next. 
Since you can't box yourself into a corner / failstate either, you [i]can[/i] just push all the buttons until it clicks.

I do feel the game should've tried harder to not need a HUD & "non-diegetic" indicators at all - playing without [i]is[/i] possible, but you'll be in the dark about a lot of things (most importantly your HP) and you'll have to constantly flip the (admittedly well designed) 'inventory' up to check ammo and healing reserves
Still - a lot of games nowadays manage to put diegetic ammo counters and even sometimes healthbars onto the character- & weapon designs pretty front & center, without it becoming too overtly silly.
And even an artstyle this hyperfocused could've highlighted some things better.

I very much enjoyed it, but I also very much feel okay about waiting so long for a decent sale.

It's been really fun following the game mature more and more into what I imagine its final state to be; and every time the dev surprises me in pleasant ways as to which direction we're going in with this.

This mixes my favourite three genres together in a beautifully unique itch of God Game, RTS and Colony Sim, with some Tower Defence elements sprinkled in for good measure. It's got great humour, the music is fantastic, and the graphics have this unique and hand-crafted feel to them. Level design is unique, and there's a lot of maps! Plus, you get to design your own with the Map Editor (I can feel my pre-teen self from way back yonder cry out in joy). Finally, it has this Roguelite-esque / Idle Game progression system that I really enjoy, with some tongue-and-cheek references to loot box mechanics without falling victim to the predatory nature of those as often seen in AAA games.

Where the game is missing some polish is primarily in the UX department. The Level Editor primarily has some woes; eg. you can't erase a tile underneath a building without also getting rid of that building, and to switch from placing tiles to placing buildings, you have to completely switch contexts, which takes multiple clicks. This is the same in the base game too, where to switch between roads and buildings you have to perform the same action. Furthermore, the game doesn't remember your UI settings from playthrough to playthrough, so every time you start a new game, you have to do some initial setup, which could be streamlined. As far as criticism goes, I feel that's a rather minor (and personal) set of gripes. I've found in the past that using VoiceAttack to automate some of the frequent clicking / mouse movements away is a nice band-aid for me.

I have never in any playthrough experienced noticeably buggy behaviour, which makes this a unique game among all games I've ever played. Even the most polished and cared-for games I know, I can point out some exploit or bug. The only things I've noticed is one or two crashes in 372 hours of playtime (yeah really), and that the AI that drives the townspeople does things I can't necessarily predict. Eg. if I assign a new lumberjack task, it's not necessarily the lumberjack that's closest by who will pick up that job. But the behaviour *is* consistent; learning how to interact with the AI and work around its particular quirks is one of the learning curves of RtR for sure, but once you get good at that, you hardly notice it anymore.

On occasion, I've found myself a little bored waiting for things to happen. But I've come to learn over time, that this only ever happens when you've actually set something up inefficiently and/or made a mistake in your design. Every time you start a new map or use the Doom World option to reset all the maps (saving your unlockables!), you tackle the game slightly differently, slightly better, a little bit more interestingly. It's fun to experiment in this game, and there are many strategies that can work perfectly fine for you. My most recent playthrough involves very little base defences, no monster maze, a couple of golem spawners, and five Cullis Gates to drop monsters into if they overwhelm the defences.

I can only recommend Rise to Ruins. I've had nothing but fun with it for a really good amount of time. Well worth your money.

review_text:
Rise to Ruins is a fairly brutal village building god game, if played as intended. In fact its basically quite unfair, and the game pulls lots of tricks to ruin your village and any fun you're having building a village. There are thankfully modes of incremental difficulty for the less masochistic gamers, and the core difficulty curve can be learned in relative safety in a Traditional Mode. The issue is village AI is fairly dumb, and you have no control over them except in an obtuse sense. Villagers will walk into enemy land while "wandering" outside of the village, starve to death with a massive surplus of food, and generally bug out and not do their job even if you have set up everything to be as efficient as possible. And this is working as intended, apparently.

You build a little pixel village under threat from a spreading corruption that decays the land and spawns bad guys. You are a deity with a fairly comprehensive set of powers, both destructive, creative, healing, and utility in nature. You have no influence over land that is corrupted, so cannot attack it directly, and for the most part the corruption cannot be conquered or destroyed, only endured. The point of the game is to simply survive for as long as possible, through defenses and arming of your villagers and judicious use of magic. 

There is an overworld map, and each region on the overworld is a biome to survive in. The only primary victory condition is to survive a year in every region, which you have to spread to organically from each village you form via migrating villagers you select to leave for the new region.

And that is Rise to Ruins. You are a deity to a small group of people trying to simply survive an unstoppable, albeit partially containable, corruption. If you enjoy god games and village builders, and a have a taste for lite tower defense, this is a very fun and addicting game. Be warned, on Survival and higher difficulties it can be brutal, and even on Traditional difficulty a few too many mistakes and setbacks late into a village can doom it. There are many "features" to enemy AI that will essentially ignore established rules to circumvent your defenses, and added to this are "random" disasters like earthquakes and lighting storms that target your village. Pretend its just the corruptions angry god throwing its own spells at you if it helps justify it.
