review_text:
There's a lot of things wrong with this game tbh.

The story is confusing to follow along at the start, the pace is wacky, and I still don't even remember what happened plot-wise. It's just not that impactful. The voice acting is ok I guess.

The gameplay? There's no FEAR involved. When it comes to games like Dead Space and Resident Evil, there's always a fear of running out of resources and having to react in time for any jumpscares or surprises, and when you have to use melee, you need to create opportunities and even then the melee options aren't even that worth it. In this game? Melee is your best option and you don't run out of melee. Your worst option? Guns, and you run out of ammo. How does that make any sense??? The only time guns are useful is for the FINAL BOSS. I feel like because of all of this, any levels of fear is just thrown OUT the window.

The enemies? God I RESTARTED this game to play on the hardest difficulty just to prove a point. When you're using melee, you're safe 90% of the time. The enemies just LINE UP against you one by one. The only time when they gang up on you is when you're close to another enemy. Only ONE enemy is attacking you at a time. The melee attack patterns are so pathetically easy, you just need to remember to move left and right interchangeably, which is a strategy that the game TELLS you to do. And it ALWAYS works until the final boss. There is NO skill involved. 

Now, I rated this game as bad, but maybe this game just isn't for me. Whoever is reading this, you can either trust the reviews, or trust your own judgement. I'd prefer you trust your own judgement and play the game for yourself to see if it's to your liking. Otherwise, I wouldn't even recommend this game to my dog.

review_text:
First of all, this is a intermediate review and does not represent the full game nor will it be representative for all users - it's a very specific hardware set which I can write this review for, it's not for everyone.

Second of all, Boneworks is for me - together with Half-Life:Alyx - what I would describe as AAA VR title (quality/gameplay-wise). I won't go into detail why, but it will be obvious to everyone when looking at gameplay of it. Everything is physics-based, everything can be touched, there is a "free" way of interacting with stuff, everything has weight, etc. Most other VR titles are what you would call "point and click" compared to fully fledged which is great!

Sadly, playing this on a Pimax 5K Super and Index Controllers comes with a lot of caveats for this game (which weren't a problem in Boneworks):
- Native Pimax via SteamVR won't even load the menu (it just blackscreens)
- The work around does sort of work, but I didn't remember my Pimax to be that bad in blacks (might be a Pimax XR thing, which is necessary to play at all)
- The work around (and sort of without it as well as far as I've heard) requires Index Controller to Oculus Controller emulation. Those don't have 5 fingers, not even speaking about spatial tracking of them and thus feels very digital compared to an "analog" experience with native Index Controllers.

review_text:
🧟‍♂️ Overview
Left 4 Dead is a cooperative multiplayer FPS set in a post-apocalyptic world overrun by zombies. Developed by Valve, it emphasizes teamwork, survival, and replayability, using an AI system known as the “Director” to dynamically adjust the game’s pacing, enemy placement, and intensity.

🔫 Gameplay
Co-op Focused: You play as one of four survivors, working together to battle hordes of the infected across a series of campaigns.

AI Director: This innovative system changes item locations, zombie spawns, and difficulty in real-time to keep every playthrough unique.

Special Infected: Aside from standard zombies, players face unique enemies like the Hunter, Smoker, Boomer, Tank, and Witch — each with a distinct threat level and tactics required to defeat them.

Versus Mode: Players can also play as infected, adding variety and competition.

🎮 Controls and Mechanics
Classic FPS controls, smooth and responsive.

Friendly fire is enabled even in casual modes, emphasizing coordination.

Healing, reviving, and item sharing are all central to surviving, reinforcing the team-oriented design.

👥 Multiplayer Experience
Best enjoyed with friends or competent teammates.

While bots fill in for absent players, they lack the intelligence and nuance of humans.

Voice chat and teamwork are practically required on higher difficulties.

🎨 Graphics & Atmosphere
The Source engine delivers clean, moody visuals.

Lighting and sound design contribute heavily to a tense, horror-inspired atmosphere.

Campaigns are varied — from rural farmland to dense cities.

🔁 Replayability
High replay value thanks to the AI Director.

Custom campaigns and mods (on PC) expand the game far beyond its base content.

👎 Cons
Limited weapon variety compared to modern shooters.

No significant single-player narrative — the story is minimal and environmental.

Lacks depth in progression or unlocks (no XP or skill trees).

⭐ Verdict
Rating: 9/10
Left 4 Dead is a benchmark in co-op shooters. Its innovative AI Director and tight team mechanics make it a standout even today. Though it lacks modern polish in progression systems or graphics, the core gameplay remains thrilling and endlessly replayable. Best experienced with friends and a mic.

Cronos: The New Dawn is a very challenging survival horror game in which you awaken as a traveler, locating targets and paving the path for the travelers after you. Beforehand i want to say, first they released the perfect Silent Hill 2 Remake and now Cronos: The New Dawn, Bloober definitely stepped their game up these past years.

Cronos is a very polished game, in my 16 hours of total playtime i have encountered only 1 glitch, in which a orphan was stuck in a wall, that's it. The overall experience was really great and everything felt reactive and fluid.
As for the combat i had a good experience, it was really really challenging and they really managed to do a good balance of having too little ammo but always just enough to beat an encounter but i wish they wouldve added a small dodge or block mechanic as i was getting hit in some unavoidable situations but it was nothing unfun or demotivating.
The world/environments and sound design were absolutely stunning and beautiful, i was in awe at the snow apartments area just walking around taking in the ambience, 10/10 area.
As for the story i won't spoil anything but it has a very unexpected plot twist which i think was well made. The acting for the travelers was really good too, yet i found the acting for the humans to be kinda over the top but still passable.

Overall i can say that this became one of my fav. survival horror game of all time, it's really well made and i can only recommend it if you want a truly challenging survial horror game with beautiful environments and an interesting story.

review_text:
In response to the complaints of the game being too hard or certain units being imbalanced, I don't think that's true. This is a game you have to first learn and until you do, you will likely die on a run. All of your decisions matter and if you move around or spend your money carelessly, your run will fail. Once you figure it out, finishing a run becomes trivial and the challenge becomes being as efficient as possible to maximize your team's effectiveness for the king of the hill pvp battle that comes after (king of the hill pits you against a leaderboard of other players who have finished a run). 

My only complaint is I think there should be better in-game resources. There are some rules/interactions that are unclear to me. For example, does the food mechanic carry over into the king of the hill battles (i.e., does your army's hunger state in the last boss room also affect the king of the hill battles)? How does the trickster's team evasion mutation even work? I've picked it twice and it doesn't seem to ever impart a dodge to any other class.

Overall very satisfying and challenging auto-battler. Not for the faint of heart but also doesn't take that long to figure out if you have even a little bit of patience.

review_text:
This game is way too good to be free. Like, sure, there's an energy system which is annoying. But it's a lot less annoying as you get to the current level cap since you can get triple rewards and store over three days worth of energy, vs. Genshin where you can store like 18 hours or so. And you can't infinitely buy more energy either, just a few extra days per month from the battle pass.

There's surprisingly little pay-for-power. It's nearly all cosmetics plus the battle pass. There are a couple of mounts which can help you gather a little faster, for example, but it's not much of an improvement from what I understand. And that's really about it.

I'm playing on legend difficulty and the boss fights are like a Souls game, though easier and less punishing. But they're very well designed. Non-boss fights are hit and miss with most being trivial and a small number feeling a bit unfair. Otherwise, it plays like an exploration / collection simulator.

This is a game you can pour a ton of time into without paying a dime. I'm completely free-to-play right now and I'm only considering spending money because I feel like I'm ripping off the devs. You really do have to like exploration and collection though as it's basically mandatory to advance your character.

review_text:
If the complete game bundle is on a sale and you pay 20$ or Euros, you can purchase it.
If it's not on sale, keep your money.

The whole game is focused on melee, then they implement a "two headed" enemy who can be only killed with range weapons (or bugged). Smart game Idea you could think, but it's not. At least the game gives you ammo befor these 4 encounters start and they are in the last third of the game. Like one, after another, after another and then the end boss appears and the game ends.
This is where the DLC "Last Transmission" starts. It could have been possible to implement this DLC in the normal game and would be fine but not with this cash cow. In the DLC you get a new elee Weapon and your range attacks become more or less useless. This time you have to defeat new enemy types with melee, only another bad game design idea. The end boss of the DLC is the only enemy with a Health Bar shown to you. You can see how little dmg your "1 hit 1 kill" Hammer does on this enemy. Not sure why they implemented it, this DLC was more terrible with the forced "Hammertime" vs many enemys. You swing as fast as a snail and get hit. Maybe many ppl complained about the useless melee weapon vs "two head" in the original game and now they wanted to rage bait it with almost useless ranged weapons in the DLC.

This game took me 19,5 hours for two playthroughs on the highest difficulty. In the second run i skipped the cut scenes. The DLC took me 3,5 hours with like 30 minutes of try to kill 2 Robots in melee with my new Hammer friend. This was so interesting seeing how i combo 1 of the enemys while the other attacked me. After 3 Attacks i died from full health. That's what I call balanced or annoying.

I did not try the other modes but will try it.

The Story is okayish. I just don't understand where this "contagion" started. On "Eurpoa" or the Planet itself.
The DLC should have been a part of the main game from the beginning or be for free. The game ends and leaves you with a clif hanger. Stupid in my opinion.

The end game credits from the DLC are non existent but if you wait a couple of minutes you will get a funny cut scene.

I think this game was supposed to start a longer story. The Issue is that it will be burried after this DLC desaster. Cash Cow milking at it's finest.
60$ for the main game with only 12 hours playtime in the first playthrough is not ok!

The part with the blind enemys and "stab them in their back" was also pretty annoying in the main game. You kill 5 or more, the game spawns you 5 more in your face. Just because it can. If you alert on of them it's almost a reload.

You have the "grab and throw" thing whis can be usefl in the main game. You have plenty of "spikes" arounf you and can kill them that way pretty fast. The DLC didn't use this mechanic a lot. but it had "blades" you could grab an dthrow for a instant kill.

Long story short:
In my Opinion a possible purchase for 20 $/Euros in a sale for All contents of this game (like I did). Otherwise not worth the money and time. You can get a faster recap on Youtube and maybe there is a next game to this one which is worth the money from the start.

I would like to have a "neutral" Option with the Steam "Thumbs Up or Thumbs Down". Because for 20$ this would be a Neutral Thumb, for full price definetly Thumbs Down!

review_text:
This game has something for all fans of Star Trek. While the bulk of it might reference The Original Series, The Next Generation and it's spin-offs and Enterprise, there are definitely elements of the newer installations of Star Trek whether you as the fan, love it, hate it, or somewhere in between.

I will warn anyone considering to play this, that depending on how you game, this game can be difficult to learn without the proper guidance or research. While the in-game store makes it look like it's absolutely pay-to-win, it isn't.  However, the player can grind to achieve better builds for their ships if they decide to buy the latest Tier 6 ship, or stick with their free Tier 5 upon reaching level 61. It seems the PvP in this game died, but the PvE Task Force Operations are alive and well.

There are some glaring bugs that never got addressed, like the changeling in the "Jabberwocky" mission, the target in one of the Klingon missions for Klingon recruits (active during the KDF recruitment periods), and probably others as well. Depending on how your perception is, this may or may not turn you away from this game. Still, however, life persists in this game, and the community is live and well. Many things have changed over the years with Star Trek Online and unfortunately, I cannot share any experience to compare what type of game Star Trek Online was to the one of today. Be prepared to die a lot depending on your missions. If you're a masochist like me, but love Star Trek, then this game just might be for you.

As with many games, this one also comes with problems on top of bugs. As all die-hard Trekkies know, it should be possible to cross-faction or team up with different factions in this game, as cooperation is the foundation of the United Federation of Planets. Clearly, it isn't possible. Sure, if you want to play a Federation Klingon, you have to pay to unlock the option, but you cannot play a Klingon teaming up with a seemingly honorable Starfleet warrior or play a Starfleet Vucan who knows that it's logical to team up with Klingon Empire aligned people to face bigger threats, because that's the basis of Infinite Diversity in Infinite Combinations.

The space battles is where it's at in this game. If you pay attention to the detail of each ship and the writing, you can tell that the people who put time into this game love Star Trek, despite it's problems. At least, I can attest that this game is playable. If you want something fast-paced and something you don't want to put money into or a lot of time (or a bit of both), then this is not the game for you.

Easily 3/5 for me. It could be a lot worse and it can be better. The community still thrives and there's a lot of life in this game despite it's age. I recommend this game for any patient Star Trek fan who loves games.

I enjoyed my time in early access and could persevere as it was early days development on the bones of Squad. If this is what Offworld considers 1.0 good to go then avoid this like the plague.

I have a top of the range rig and suffer severe drops in performance, the desync is insane, the damage feedback both received and dealt is awful. 
Oh god the (literal)bug animations are dreadfully bad they just jankaly jitter or slide and stretch out to attack. 
(system)Bugs from the 0.1 release are still here like trying to ADS down the handle of your gun. 
The single player "tutorial" being nothing but caves with 0 interesting variation to objectives is laughable (it doesn't even train new players on how to play AAS or build fortifications). 
Not having licensed or at least tributes to the original score makes the music feel empty (I get it could be expensive and I think Klandathu Drop is in owner rights hell)

I cannot forgive you for getting Casper Robert Van Dien to replay Rico and accepting that performance as adequate, I get he isn't a VA but come on.

Nails the aesthetic and sounds though.

Last min edit: The price increase is far too hefty for what this is.

review_text:
This is the plot of the first Omen movie, but then
also taking place at a same location as in the second
movie, a mansion that is. Even the birthday party is
included right at the beginning. So this is simply
''Omen - The game'' (for those who are familiar with it).


Good stuff:

*Assuming it has been well tested or been worked on
by great programmers, seeing how I've never experienced
a single bug in it myself. 

*The atmosphere is probably what holds it up.
Like a weak and sole supporting beam. It makes the
game enjoyable enough to go on and see what the
next death is gonna be like.
Built up with the characters in the mansion getting
more and more tensed after every accident.
But other than that...


Bad stuff experienced (as feedback):

*Graphics are too dark in some areas to make out details.

*Music does not hold enough variety.

*The controls, or specifically in this case, the
camera perspective, is working against you when you
wish to highlight and interact with objects.

*The Gameplay offers very little to do other than
just progressing the story. Apart from being able
to acquire three more or less helpful items, after
doing minor tasks, there are no side quests at all
or alternative paths in the game. This makes it much
too linear and thereby cuts it down rather short.

*There is no challenge. The toughest part in the
game, is to control the telekinesis with your mouse
movement, in order to swing objects at people.
That's about it.


Conclusion:

I don't recommend purchasing this for more than
10 Euro/12 Dollar

review_text:
➤➤ Short Review: --Skip--

I "wasted" 4.7k hours in this game, hoping since launch (back in june 2021) that the game would improve as the foundation was really hitting that itch for me, but it's time to give up. After multiple world expansions (up to 3 new regions, 1 new randomized dungeon and a city exploration with timelimit), multiple class reworks, expansions and updates, after many "new enemies" to fight, player housing, a card minigame and after some new quest types, the game still isn't in an acceptable state. I played the game for this long mostly because of my alliance (guild) in the game and I had fun playing with them, even if the game itself wasn't good.

➤➤ Long Review:

- Story: The story of Base PSO2 is good, but it's majority cutscenes with some fights here and there. The story of NGS however, it's not great. It's slow, boring and somewhat predictable. It did however get somewhat decent with the latest story update, but it wasn't enough for me to say they redeemed the story.

- Gameplay: NGS gameplay originally was one of the stronger parts, but the longer you play it, the more you notice how empty it really is. It looks flashy, but there is no depth. The devs even realized this and added more customization to the attacks, trying the bare minimum to increase the build variety in the game, but for me, this is just a bandaid fix for deeper issues.. Another massive flaw was the overreliance on Dodge/Weapon Actions (A parry/counter unique for each weapon). The devs again realized this and added new mechanics to bosses such as Attacks that can't be avoided with dodge/weapon action, again, bandaid fix for deeper issues. Let's talk about the elements next. Usually, you would think Fire does something different than water or light, but in NGS, they all do the exact same. If the enemy has an elemental weakness, after hitting the enemy often times with that specific element, the enemy will go into "elemental down". That's it. There is no "fire deals damage over time" or "water decreases armor/damage resistance". Besides the "elemental down", there is also the "physical down", which is also the same as the elemental down, but it relies on physical attacks instead of elemental attacks. Now with all of the different classes available and lots of different weapons types, you could just play a different class/weapon combo to fight the boredom, but as mentioned above, the game heavily relies on Dodge/Weapon Action. Every fight with all melee weapons will be the same, the same goes for all ranged weapons and all tech (elemental) weapons. There are some minor differences for each weapons playstyle, but  these are really small. The gameplay also doesn't have the typical 3 roles system for the classes. Yes, you have classes that can "heal" or "buff/debuff", but they're extremely simple, Only 2 Skills that heal, either the same amount as a healing item or Full Life and Full PP (Mana) once with a massive cooldown and 1 buff skill. The Debuff isn't even a skill, instead it's a passive for one specific class which applies when you hit the enemy. Not to mention, all of the skills mentioned above aren't even necessary to clear any content. (Instead of them, the class called "Ranger" is necessary, as this class can apply an effect on an enemy that increases the damage of all people hitting the marked spot, basically making them necessary to have if you want to clear high end content when they launch.)

- Sound: The Soundtrack is actually decent and somewhat memorable. Doesn't feel out of place as well, but as with any soundtrack, you might start to hate them.

- Visuals: The game looks visually decent enough. The world looks nice and the effects are good, but the characters are bad. I don't understand how they thought this style for characters was in any way good. As an active player, you get used to the graphics, but for majority of new players, 90% of characters just look straight up awful and in some cases, it's not even the player's fault. They tried to "fix" this by adding a cel shading option to the game for all characters or just yours. This however isn't enough in my opinion. The foundation is already flawed and shows cracks. Just watch the reveal for the Atelier Ryza collab with NGS. The NGS versions of Ryza and co. look awful.

- Collabs: Yes, the game has collabs, quite a lot actually. From Eminence in shadow and Frieren to Atelier Ryza and Melty Blood, tons of collabs here, HOWEVER. The collabs are really barebones. In the beginning, all you got was "AC Scratch Tickets", (Real Money Gacha) for the cosmetics of the collab IPs. That's it. Now, You also get cardboard cutouts of these characters to place in your Creative Space (Player Housing), AMAZING! No quests, enemies, stories, nothing. The only exception being the Sonic "Collabs" if you want to call them that. Instead of "AC Scratch Tickets" with the cosmetics, we got Limited Time Quests somewhat Sonic themed. They were ok the first time, but they get boring really really fast.

- The only positive of NGS that no other MMO currently tops: Character Customization. The character creator in NGS is surprisingly deep and good. You have tons of sliders that actually change the character. You have the ability to mix and match outfit parts (which are separated into 3 layers, Outerwear, Base/Setwear and innerwear). You also can freely customize your whole character and change everything about it with no barriers. Want to change the Gender? Do it. Don't want to be a human anymore, change to a CAST (Robot). Now with all the years of NGS behind us, there are tons and tons of different outfits, hairstyles, accessories, motions and so on that you can use to create truly unique characters ... IF you either scratch (pay for the gacha) or grind yourself to death for the ingame money.

- I skipped so many other flaws and problems. There is no Trading between Players, the player market Search is horrendous, gear progression is boring, content gets repeated (especially normal enemies), the community is extremely horny and down bad, Rewards for "difficult" content is really demotivating, the game is p2w, the game punishes you if you play for free, The tutorials are bad (if there are even any tutorials explaining specific things), the open world isn't being used at all, majority of content gets obsolete in few months, and and and ...

review_text:
[b][i]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/i][/b] is a tactical stealth game in the Edo period setting (Japan). There are no RPG elements in story or gameplay - the characters' personalities and abilities are set in stone (except the early-acquired guns). The story follows a team of spies and assassins working for the local lord. 

The game is very well made - the team is diverse, from a teen hunter to a samurai, the levels are challenging (there are numerous optional challenges and difficulty settings), the controls are rebindable, saving is possible at any time. The graphics and visual design are gorgeous, the voice acting (English) and soundtrack are fitting. Additionally, the characters comment on the actions or events, though it does not change the general story (e.g. whether all hostiles were killed or not). 

In terms of audio and visual accessibility, there are settings for highlighting interactive objects and NPCs and enabling subtitles. The only drawbacks are the lack of the pause function, the inability to order the characters to run when executing the Shadow Mode commands, and the Mimimi logo. The latter is possible to solve by removing the video file.

review_text:
Dead Space for modern audiences.
It's alright, just manage your expectations: this isn't a game for players, it's a product for investors. It ticks the boxes but it doesn't innovate or respect you.

[hr][/hr]
Good bits:

- Lots of accessibility options: dyslexic font, color-coding for game items (enemies, hazards, etc.), subtitles font settings (size, color, background). Although, font settings apply only to subtitles, and not to other text such as item descriptions in the store which are barely readable.

- Interesting combat system: evading and chaining different melee and ranged attacks. But it gets really boring really fast, I started the game at medium difficulty and quickly dropped to low because having to hit each and every enemy a dozen or two times for them to go down is not that fun.

- Skippable cutscenes.

[hr][/hr]
Bad bits, in no particular order:

- Unskippable intro logos. Fortunately the movie files can be deleted or renamed.

- Stupid save system: there are auto-saves at plot checkpoints, and there are manual saves anywhere, except they also save only the checkpoints. And as far as I can tell, any checkpoint is saved only once, so if you stumble into an auto-save but then backtrack to pickup any leftover items - the only way to save that backtracking is to progress further to next checkpoint.

- Can't use GRP (kinesis) to pick up items like ammo and health.

- Enemies don't drop loot if killed with with certain types of environmental hazards like huge fans or other chopping/grinding things.

- Gamepad controls are not editable, and the default scheme is... suboptimal. Some buttons (d-pad) bind to several actions, while others (L3/R3) are completely unused.

- Ranged weapons are boring. There are 5 types, and they basically differ only in clip size and fire rate. Maybe in damage too but that's not noticeable. In general, they all shoot bullets in one way or another and they all have different ammo types so you have to carry every type separately, but they take extra time and attention to swap between them and keep them all reloaded.

- The "alt-fire" mode is pointless because it spends N times more ammo for N times more damage so it's not in fact an upgrade.

- Selling or otherwise handling items in the store requires long-press (which is good) but buying weapon upgrades is instant so if you accidentally click on wrong thing, you will spend a potentially sizable chunk of your cash on an upgrade that you might not have wanted.

- "Blind" enemies are a joke. You can cram a dozen of them into a room, and stealth-kill ALL of them. None of them will aggro as long as you do not exit crouching state and do not move closer to any of them than certain threshold, even though "stealth kill" itself is accompanied by a hefty amount of screaming and panting. However once they do get aggroed, they will chase you to the end of the [strike]Earth[/strike] Callisto even if you run away and try to hide.

- Closer to the end of the game they trick player by putting a puny enemy (a parasite larvae, found throughout the game) into a box that typically contains valuable loot. I guess the intent was to increase the suspense by breaking player's trust in loot containers, except they did it to three containers in a row, which completely defeats the purpose. Already after the 2nd container I couldn't care less if another slimy thing will jump on me or not, and the 3rd one drove the final nail in the coffin of horror and atmosphere.

- Final boss is impressive visually but poorly executed mechanically. He's invulnerable to bullets when he's in his first, weaker, human form. I unloaded all ammo from half the weapons in his face and the scene didn't change. The way to progress is to smack him a couple times with melee weapon. The logic left the room...

- Characters are pathetic. Kudos to the actors, they did their part well, but the writing is utterly flat. Saying farewell to Lucatiel of Mirrah was moving, watching Elias die was not. And they have roughly the same amount of interaction with their respective protagonists!

- For half of its duration, the game takes away your ability to run. Sometimes the plot "requires" that you walk and talk alongside another character, even though there's loot to gather on the other side of the (sometimes pretty big) room. Other times the main character just randomly slows to a walk. I guess it might have something to do with the terrain but if so then it's extremely unintuitive and inconsistent. Dead Space had a distinct sound and walking animation for "sticky" floor, this game does not. A game is supposed to be an interactive media; I, the player, am supposed to be in control of my actions; limiting that at random for no reason is [b]INFURIATING[/b].

[hr][/hr]
Update: spelling.

Most of my time was spent watching barely animated typical, trope-laden anime characters talking about an uninteresting story that moved at glacial pace. While the gameplay seemed to be at least somewhat improved from the original quartet of .hack games, only two (at most) of my six hours must have been spent actually controlling a character. The same sense of immersion from the first games was there, and I enjoyed reading through fictional forum posts, news stories, and even an entire website for the in-game MMO the story takes place in, but those all proved far more interesting than anything any character had to say. But in the end, the most unforgivable part of this is that basically every conversation can only go at the speed of voiced dialogue. review_text:
Perhaps all games which rely on physics simulations tend to amuse and frustrate in equal measure, but do keep in mind - this isn't much of a puzzle game but more a test of dexterity and mechanical skill with a mouse. 

The game is cute enough with its weird art and abstract meta-story, if somewhat trivial in terms of puzzle complexity. Gooballs come in different flavours - some are infinitely reusable, some can form flammable fuses, others are impervious to damage. Most levels feature little flies which allow undoing a limited number of moves by catching them with a mouse click. Through trial and error you will discover how to shape your creations so they do not topple over - at least until you need them to. Levels usually have a pipe you need to build towards, and set a fairly lax minimum amount of unused gooballs required to be extracted through it to progress.

However, most levels have optional challenge conditions - called "Obsessive Completion Distinctions" or OCDs here - which are genuinely pretty tough to figure out. These are of two types - a limit on moves, or a set amount of leftover gooballs to be extracted. Both call for building lean, efficient structures, and have corresponding achievements. Extra gooballs extracted from the levels are sent to the sandbox mode, where a tower can be built for fun. Unfortunately, the limit for this mode is 300, and it is indiscriminate to the kind of gooball saved - all of them will be converted to default black flavour.

Because the base game is pretty unremarkable as a puzzler, for some people it will only be worth playing for the challenges, but herein lies the problem. It manifests itself in a suboptimal user interface, which is too simplistic to be practical. Clearly designed for mobile platforms with one-finger touch controls in mind (there isn't even a settings menu to change screen resolution or volume), it lacks features as well as information for convenience, like the number of moves, the amount of gooballs available and how many have been used so far. The game doesn't feature controls to pick a flavour of gooball in levels where multiple are available, nor a modifier key to choose between a free gooball and an underlying reusable one to be disconnected from the structure. Satisfying the basic level completion goal removes undo-last-move flies and sometimes even the quick restart button, along with spawning a huge flushing handle, which has to be clicked on to continue and might get clicked by accident when the pipe is close by. If a cinematic is planned after a level, it has to be watched in its entirety every game session, and only after watching it once can it be skipped. While having to count moves or gooballs used, and losing ability to undo moves at the end of a level can be regarded as extra challenge, the rest simply adds unnecessary tedium.

all of them will be converted to default black flavour. because the base game is pretty unremarkable as a puzzler, for some people it will only be worth playing for the challenges, but herein lies the problem. it manifests itself in a suboptimal user interface, which is too simplistic to be practical. clearly designed for mobile platforms with one-finger touch controls in mind there isn't even a settings menu to change screen resolution or volume , it lacks features as well as information for convenience, like the number of moves, the amount of gooballs available and how many have been used so far. the game doesn't feature controls to pick a flavour of gooball in levels where multiple are available, nor a modifier key to choose between a free gooball and an underlying reusable one to be disconnected from the structure. satisfying the basic level completion goal removes undo-last-move flies and sometimes even the quick restart button, along with spawning a huge flushing handle, which has to be clicked on to continue and might get clicked by accident when the pipe is close by. if a cinematic is planned after a level, it has to be watched in its entirety every game session, and only after watching it once can it be skipped. while having to count moves or gooballs used, and losing ability to undo moves at the end of a level can be regarded as extra challenge, the rest simply adds unnecessary tedium.

It's a fun game. It's got a lot of puzzle variety and a pretty good amount of content. But it's so bare bones in certain areas that I was absolutely convinced it was a poorly done mobile port until somebody corrected me.

Dispite being a PC game first, it has no options menu of any kind, you can't correct the resolution, change the graphics (though I doubt you would need to) or even do something as simple as change the game volume. Distinguishing between the balls must be hell if you're colorblind, a menu option for that would have been really helpful for a lot of people. It does not lock the mouse to one screen if you have multiple monitors, but still requires that you move your mouse to the edge of the screen in order to pan the camera. It has no keyboard controls, even though it could have direly used some, such as the ablity to pan the camera with the arrow keys which would have delt with the mouse not locking issue, and a key for undo which would remove the need to click those stupid bugs (or more often, accidentally click one when you're trying to do a quick action).

Did I like it? I kept playing through the problems and beat it, so yeah I must have liked it dispite its problems. At the same time, would I recommend it? no, especially not at the normal $10 price tag. I found the missing features made it feel very unpolished and at the price point there are a lot of better games. Maybe on sale I'd recommend it, but that isn't an option.

review_text:
Fun little metroidvania! Recommended for fans of the genre who want something with some bite, or for those who like cute anime girls.

Takes a little bit to get the hang of the rhythm of combat, but once you do it's pretty smooth and not too terribly difficult, while still having some challenge. Has a good focus on resource management that a lot of metroidvanias lack. There's a ton of build variety, it's very fun to play around with different gameplay styles and it's fairly easy to swap between them at will. 

The pacing of the game does lack at times though - the ability to swap equipment in the middle of combat is both a good and bad thing. It provides lots of flexibility, but also slows things down as there's no reason NOT to constantly swap equipment in the middle of combat as the situation changes, which really slows the otherwise fast-paced combat down. If you don't like fiddling through menus, I'd maybe give this one a pass.

review_text:
A fundamental misunderstanding about this game is that is tagged as a "Story Rich - JRPG" - the thing is, this is not a JRPG, this a Visual Novel pretending to be a JRPG.
The reason for why it does this, is that the main character playing in an MMORPG is core to the story, and so to convey that and have you immerse better in this narrative, it needs for you to walk inside that MMORPG, however shallow and linear this representation of a MMORPG is. 
The gameplay being so linear, the "fields" being all identical randomly generated aggregation of few square rooms, the combat being so shallow and you so overpowered/overleveled all the time clearly hint to the fact this is not even trying to be a good JRPG, it needs that only as a background to tell the story of this Visual Novel.
Therefore is you, the player, that has to imagine that the MMORPG the Main Character is interacting with is far more rich, open world an immersive.

Ultimately, if you enjoy this game or not depends in which box/category you try to fit it in:
・if you consider this a JRPG, chances are you'll be disappointed by the lacking combat
・if you consider this a Visual Novel, the story is intriguing and it's quite enjoyable, I would say superior to other VN because it being 3D and animated, makes it feel like you're just watching an anime (with some interaction here and there, running from point A to B etc..) 

I'm considering this just an Anime on Steam, so it's a thumb up for me :)

review_text:
Get To The Orange Door is by and far the most fluid and fun shooter I have ever gotten my hands on. The game has changed over and over and over in its tumultuous development cycle, but at the moment, it's the best it's ever been. The new tutorial is perfect, full of expression, and beautiful viewmodels as always, something the game is absolutely no slouch on. Environments are stellar, gunplay is supreme, and the movement is incredibly open and easy to get a handle on. Remember; wallrun for speed, slide to keep it going.

The game is structured in a kind of "make your own difficulty" sense; you can rush to the end of the stage and fend off as best you can with what you have, or you can take your time killing and exploring to get more money and weapons. Later in the game when you're comfortable with what you have, just rushing to the end seems like a good way to progress. A lot of players might feel inclined to just meander around forever instead of going to the objective, but you can go there whenever you'd please. The game loops upon completion, so once you have a lot of good weapons and perks, it's pretty easy to just rush through the stages over and over and amass all the money and vines you'd like, especially when Dungeons are involved.

Get To The Orange Door is an easy instant purchase in my book if you're looking for something like Titanfall 2, and I personally don't think any other game comes close to its level of polish. Incredible movement, enemy design, gunplay, the amount of polish here is absolutely nuts.

review_text:
I don’t think this is a very good game.

First in order to be a good game you have to, well, be a game. I know it’s a point-and-click title but can they not at least make whatever extra puzzle/gameplay we have a little bit more interesting? The inclusion of these extra bits shows that clearly thought has been put into making things less monotonous than going to A, picking up B, going back to A, rinse and repeat. Yet they can’t go that extra mile to develop these much-needed gameplay bits more?

This first point would hardly be worth complaining about if the story is good. And a good story is more than a good premise, a good twist, or a good ending. Let me rip the band-aid off right now: The story is not well-written: There may be a good story in there somewhere but since it’s told from the focal points of two puerile scientists and written by someone with the sensibility of a Tik-tok-roaming Gen Z edgelord, whatever gravitas the story could’ve achieved is instead constantly sucked out by out-of-place jokes and awkward soppy dialogue transitions where characters would suddenly bring up topics out of the blue just to push the story forward and desperately make you feel something. I’m not saying every game needs to have subtle or edgy writing, only that if your goal is to create a heartfelt story, the last thing you want is to take the attempt so seriously that you lose sight of how it looks “from the outside”. The fact that this game’s writing is so totally inconsistent makes me wonder if it could really benefit from an editor’s input.

I can’t say I had a good time with this. The soundtrack can be lovely but mostly just sounds as cliche as a lot of the tricks the game pulls to elicit a reaction from the player.

review_text:
Preface: I love this game for what it is. More people need to go into the game knowing what to expect so as not to be disappointed because they wanted a completely different game.

This is a simple farming game in the style of Paper Mario, limited dialogue/relationship building, limited decorating, but lots of farming and quests to fulfill. Don't go in thinking this is a deeply involved relationship simulator with multiple story archs wildly different endings with whirlwind mysteries kind of game.

This game works best for people with a good imagination for headcanons & creating their own narratives for everyone because you won't get a solid backstory from any villagers, (aside from one very obvious one). I liken this to playing Sims for multiple generations, you invent personalities and backstories. 

The game is very simple in terms of story and dialogue. I can respect that because it also has a lot of gameplay accessibility options to make the game less of a grind which I like.  And there's controller support that's awesome.

The game advertises itself as "Cozy with Consequences" but I think they just mean "consequences for everyone who gets on your bad side." You can poison the whole town, no one grows suspicious, your relationship meters with everyone are unaffected, and everyone keeps accepting your Death Cake as gifts. The "consequences" are taxes, diseases, raising animals for food, and death. 

There are no negative social repercussions for decisions you make. You won't get price gouged for being rude to the shop keeper or get discounts for being sweet to the Mayor. There are weddings, funerals, festivals, farmers markets, and competitions. Zero consequences for not going to any of them. Your consequences are now you have no friends to give you gifts.

You only benefit from going to festivals and funerals is everyone gathering in one place so you're able to mass gift or talk to everyone at once. The more friends you have the more gifts you can get sent to your mailbox.

There is no deep mystery/lore to uncover about different towns people, there is *one* tidbit of lore about one very obvious person in town. Overall, you can expect all the townspeople are copy pastes of personality types and dialogue.

Villagers will say "Boy do I have some gossip for you!" then talk about how much they like the smell of bread from the bakery. Its got so much dialogue potential but it tends to fall a little flat. 

Imagine Animal Crossing level of limited dialogue based on personality and hobbies. There is no villager lore or backstory for 99% of the villagers. You invent and imagine whatever you like. You will see and hear the same dialogue from different villagers repeatedly.

Yes you can get married and have kids but there is zero relationship specific backstory dialogue. Other than your partner calling you darling and saying "I love you" at the end of a conversation.  

Your kids will call you mom/dad. Your family members can give you gifts every few days, sometimes its money, other times its sticks and dirt. You can send your kids to school to increase their skills but I've yet to see how that benefits you. You can send your kids to do apprenticeships and earn money, fun having one kid being a Blacksmith and the other a baker, you always have access to their shops by talking to your kids.

Marry any of the shop keepers/crafters you will not get a discount on any items, you will get to "collect" their wages every day which can be anywhere from 10 to 200 coins which may help. 

There is no family tree to look at and keep track of beyond the initial family.

Looking at villagers and their families they're all ordered randomly, it would make more sense for families to be grouped.



Gameplay:
The accessibility options is fine for gameplay. But I'd like to see some colorblind accessibility options. Just make things more distinct in for different colorblind types.

I love the gameplay accessibility. If you go to your settings and turn on and off settings that will make the game tedious or grindy such as taxes, hunger, energy, tool breaking, etc. No one judges you for settings that make the game more fun for you. I promise. 

I will say its a challenging game in terms of money. Earning money is ROUGH if you're unfamiliar what to focus your time on. I spent too much time floundering between trying to complete quests, buying items for crafting, and trying to pay the taxes every week and barely scraped by. Turn off Taxes in the Options Menu for the less stressful playing experience.


Decorating/Customizing:
You can decorate your cabin if you *really* want but honestly early game its a waste of money since there's limited room and so much you need to craft to even make a penny, invest in a flour mill, preserve bucket, drying rack, and candy maker (for autumn halloween)

Decorating is really lacking. 
For Wallpaper/Carpet: You can use the item ONCE and then its destroyed if you replace it. Place a red wallpaper, you get a fancy blue one and put it up to test it out dont like it and look back at your inventory and the red one is gone forever. Bye bye 120 gold. Good luck finding that specific wallpaper again. You should be able to preview wallpaper or be warned by using one you replace the other one forever.

You can buy a massive carpet, but not be able to place any furniture on it or very near it. Takes up too much space with zero benefit. A lot of the Craftable food prep items are *not* placable outside so you're stuck with having them inside your cabin if you want to make money.

Maybe this'll change in the future?

Making Money Tips:
For making money I suggest buying a fishing rod, lure, and lantern with lantern oil. Turn off taxes, energy and hunger and fish all through out the night from 9pm to 7am at the pond near your house. Collect fish to fill your inventory and sell them the next morning to which ever shop keeper you can find. Once you unlock the lagoon past the broken bridge fish there from 9pm to 8am. If you can preserve and dry your food items it'll sell for a *little* bit more.

You are limited at collecting wood from shaking all trees and what wood you clear from your farm initially, each piece of wood sells for 10 coins. 

Quality of Life Suggestions: 
-Automatic stacking: Often times placing items in your pocket or storage will just stack things beside one another instead of in the same stack via quality.
-Crafting from Storage: Maybe its an unlockable thing but it would make crafting simpler.
- Gates should open Inward instead of out: When playing the game by mouse clicks (instead of WASD or Arrows) has you spinning or walking in place quite a bit forcing you if you try to go through gates that open outward or at the Witch's Shack in the Bog.
- Craftable lanterns offer a small dot of light with zero glow around the lantern providing almost no benefit to crafting other than taking up a square on your farm maybe its a bug?
-Preview wallpapers on the walls before applying them. Once applied its fine if you lose the wallpaper you covered up. At least give us confirmation "adding this wallpaper permanently replaces the old one are you sure"

I'm really enjoying this, but Jesus is death so fucking annoying. For as fast you respawn after death, you'd think the game would autosave your inventory whenever you change it. You're constantly swapping items from room to room;

Okay, goblins in here, switch to the Shaman mask for 50% damage against goblins) 
This room is covered in water in, lets switch to the swimsuit so we can move through water normally.
Lightning-weak boss, let's switch to lightning weapons, etc.

Well, whenever you die, your inventory gets swapped back to whatever you were wearing prior. And since the autosave statues only autosave the FIRST TIME YOU ENCOUNTER THEM you never have a chance to resave your new loadout. So with each death comes having to switch all your shit again. And again. And again... if you suck like I do.

Imagine if everytime died in Dark Souls you appeared at the bonfire with whatever you were wearing the LAST TIME YOU VISITED IT. It's infuriating! The best part about these types of games is running at the obstacle over and over until you figure it out or force your way through it. Most of the obstacles in this game come with a pause just to swap out your loadout every single time.

Still. Great art, I'm digging the story. Just a little butthurt. If you like metroidvanias and anime you'll dig this.

review_text:
Rise to Ruins is a lovely city management/tower defence game that successfully blends the two genres into a very enjoyable game.

The basic premise is pretty simple; you place down building blueprints and then the pawns in your city try to build it. You then play a balancing act as you assign people to jobs freely (i.e. builder, farmer, lumberjack, etc.) in order to meet the needs of your city while also expanding, upgrading, and most importantly fortifying it.

The antagonist of the game is the Corruption which shows up after the first night and spawns monsters to attack you every night after that. The player can build an array of defensive towers and their support structures, walls and gates, as well as several different buildings that allow people to be assigned to a combat role or produce golems that protect the town.

The Corruption also expands its creep, allowing more graveyards to be built and thus more monsters to be spawned each night making it beneficial to contain it. The creep needed for graveyards to be built won't expand near your buildings so using torches, towers, or regular buildings you can build a wall where the enemies can't build (they can still come and destroy your buildings though) to limit how many they spawn. It's risky though, since the Corruption will actively try to build around this blockade if it can.

The game has a leveling system in place that rewards you periodically from milestones (like survive X days) with chests which you unlock with a currency generated by the pawns in your village doing things and building stuff. These chests reward you with powerful passive bonuses that apply permanently to your save game even if you reset the world map.

review_text:
I don't really understand the hype and positive reviews around this game.  If I could request a refund at this point, I would.

I spent the first 2 hours going through the intro sequences, with lots of scripted story to set the scene etc. and the dialogue was rather wooden and un-emotional, although the characters can be funny at points they seem to rely on lots of meaningless swearing.

After this, (and conveniently after Steam's refund timer), the real game begins, and there are many frustrations.

The save system leaves me questioning the design choices immediately, I'm not allowed to save unless I brew some potion that lets me, BUT I can "save and quit" at any point, leading to moments where I just need to quit to save and then load the game again.  Extremely pointless.

The combat is rather static, wooden, doesn't feel realistic or dynamic in any way.  It feels like something from the old era of gaming like Gothic etc.  It's just a matter of block/parry/attack rinse and repeat.

Then there's a forced first-person-view.  Why?  I want to see my character and the armour I've equipped, and I don't like all the forced camera movements in FPV when doing EVERY SINGLE ACTION.  it's like press a button, wait for 2 seconds while the camera moves around weirdly before you can do anything else.

As well as this, there are a lot of weird key binding choices, like sometimes I have to just press ESC to cancel something and other times I have to hold ESC for 1 second?  The same with E, or whatever.  Why?  This is confusing and un-intuitive and completely non-standard for PC key bindings.

And to top it all off, once I had managed to actually get to grips with some of the game systems and kill a small camp with 3 bandits in it near the starting area, I loaded myself up with their weapons and armour then proceeded down the hill to find 3 "wild dogs".  I got my ass absolutely beaten raw by these three wild dogs.  A man in armour, with swords, can't beat 3 dogs.  Right.

I also have issues with the stealth system, lockpicking, item equipping (you have 3 sets of equipment, and all of it ALSO stays in your inventory for maximum clutter), item stat comparison, and the combat system.  All of them feel clunky and at times like I'm not in control: the character and/or the UI feel unresponsive during actions quite a lot.

As a point of comparison with all of the above, I've been playing a lot of Mount & Blade 2 recently, and let me tell you that game does a lot of these things right, and overall has a MUCH better feel to playing it than KCD2.  It has a great first, and third-person views.  Amazing fluid and fast feel to the combat, 3 armour sets you can actually equip properly without cluttering up your inventory, and an easy to understand stat comparison for equipment.

So, I've modded this game now so I can save any time I want, and I have an optional TPV (which is pretty bad because the game hasn't been designed for it) but I'm hoping I can struggle my way through to find this supposedly "game of the year" content that people are going on about.

So far, it's very pretty, but every other thing about the game has frustrated me and feels clunky.  I will see how far I can get, but really not finding myself compelled to come back to play.  I unfortunately wouldn't find myself recommending this to my friends.

review_text:
I don't thumbs down because the game is not good. The town building and sense of urgency are great and there are unique twists on gameplay mechanics from all of the best games in this genre from decades back. that being said, The game tries really hard to be too many things which is at first engaging but eventually reveals a lack of substance. Once you figure out you're pretty much pidgeon-holed into a primarily tower defense game that eventually ends in a loss it's too late. Even if the eventual goal is too ultimately lose, there's no illusion of hope or progress. Simply put, there is ABSOLUTE ZERO offensive options for the player to use to beat back corruption inside the realm of what the developer ulitately designed the game for. To be fair, you can use the rules of the game to push your pixelites into corrupted territory to fight but it is very clear in practice this is not what the developer intended and as far as I can tell, he has no intention of implementing such a mechanic. I still think the game would be perfect for fans of peaceful townbuilding games that felt something like banished needed a more omnipresent threat than just the seasons and I think that the influences of games like simcity, rimworld, dwarf fortress, and other titles shine through brilliantly- especially with the use of god powers like black & white.
It is an absolutely killer townbuilder/tower defense game but the old school RTS gameplay advertised in my opinion only stretches as far as the GUI and overall aesthetic of the game. Offensive options just plain need to be there in some way to realize that specific ambition further. At the end of the day though, this game has no reason not to sell to its target audience and i believe that the developer has every right to make the game that he wants so thumbs down aside, great job man.

review_text:
*****SPOILERS*****
There are so many things that the game developers have done right I hate to say that I wouldn't recommend it, but the things that they did wrong are so glaring that it's frustrating.

First off, it's a beautiful game visually. The paper type graphics are really fun and overall make for a lovely asthetic. Occasionally the "thick outline" for things that you can gather isn't really thick enough but that's a small problem and I figured out what I could click and what I couldn't easily enough. Though watch out for the mushrooms, they're a little harder to spot sometimes. A minor issue at best. The seasonal changes of the environment are gorgeous.

The gameplay itself is where I have really mixed feelings and is ultimately why I can't recommend it. I love both the cozy game/farming style games, historical games, and survival games so I was super excited about this game when I first heard about it. Unfortunately there are some "quality of life" things that are super annoying like not being able to use three of an item to create dye because one of them is a gold star and the others are silver and bronze. It's not a big deal, you can stick the lower quality stuff in the fridge or somewhere to preserve them and stick the higher quality stuff in your bag to degrade but it's still an annoying aspect that gets even more annoying as you're desperately trying to craft things but can't because it takes two and you have one gold and one bronze item.

The second really big thing that frustrates me is that the game is HUGELY customizeable, they did such an amazing job of allowing people to play it the way they want to. I eventually turned off the fishing mini-game because I got tired of my keyboard feeling like it was going to break trying to follow the switchbacks on the fish that were so crazy. Where the frustration comes in is twofold, one, I get the desire to show support for the LGBT+ community but for a SURVIVAL style game, even in the cozy environment where survival is actually in part dependant on a. relationships and b. reproduction I was hugely disturbed to see that the game allows all the male characters to become pregnant. What frustrates me is that because reproduction is actually one of the survival functions of the game, being able to not only marry whoever you want but actually breed with whoever you want with no restrictions and no way to toggle it on and off actually turns that portion of the game SUPER easy. It's disappointing because one of the things they sell the game on is the relationships. If this were a fantasy game not advertised as a more historical game it wouldn't be a huge deal except that it STILL makes survival for the geneological side of things SUPER easy with no way to increase the difficulty.

Apparently it's fine to actually destroy the total social and physical function of women's bodies by making every animal male and still able to reproduce (Yes, I checked and so far have yet to see the female sign next to the animals ever). Again, if you want to make a game that totally destroys and makes invisible one half the species, that's up to you, but it ruins the survival aspect of the game because it doesn't matter if I kill them all off indiscriminately. So long as I have two animals of the same type, food, and space, they'll just keep impregnating each other and producing. This is a survival game, having male and female with their distinct characteristics mean that you are forced to actually look at that side of animal husbandry and not accidentally kill off the females or you don't get eggs OR progeny. I would love for this and the romantic relationships for people to be changed so there is the option for easy mode (gaytopia where everyone gets pregnant) or hard mode (biological reality).

They also really missed a goldmine of opportunity by not adding in the historical representation and attitudes surrounding Christianity. Instead the only religion is witchcraft and there is zero alternative except to engage with it because it's either miss out on huge content in the game or jump in and become a witch. Again, not something that by itself is bad, I get it's a game, but it's a game predicated on history that prides itself on that apsect, but then throws it out the window to portray that history in a light the developers prefer. The worst part of this is it takes a game that's trying very hard for inclusivity and tells people, "You're included unless you're not like me", which defeats the whole point of "inclusion" meaning everybody. When you go join the coven you're told to keep it quiet because there are people who don't like their witchcraft but there's actually zero option for anything else. There's a graveyard with a little masoleum in it with no indications that it's anything else but any reference to Christianity which was the prevelant religion at the time isn't there. It would be way more interesting from a survival side of things if the game had the church in it as an option with equivelent medicines and miracles as the witch's magic. Again, the game has mermaids so I know they're not really keeping to historical accuracy, but I think it would have been amazing.

Finally the travel distances. The village is HUGE. It can literally take you all day to walk from one end to the other. There are magic potions and stuff that can cut that down, sure, no problem there, but it feels like some of the distances are purely to ensure that you have to engage in the magic side of things. Not a problem but just seems like a time waster. Especially since the rewards for walking around the whole map and collecting resources are generally quite small. The mines drop very little ore for how long it takes to get there. It's beautiful but it gets super repetative very quickly.

Same with the relationships. If you just chat with everyone you meet along the way and show up for the market on sunday it's not really hard to build the relationships. There's very little interaction really and your spouse/family are useful if they're apprenticed somewhere handy, but it would be nice if making them a "farm helper" didn't totally tank their prospects until they move out of your house. For a game based on the social aspect it's surprisingly thin.

My HOPE is that if you play long enough from the 1700s then eventually you'll get to throw tea in the harbor, but I'm thinking that with how little actual story they've put into their game they probably haven't prepared things that far in advance, BUT I hope I'm wrong or that they add it in as late game content. Otherwise it's a very thin farming sim with some vaguely survivial-esque aspects (if you've ever played hardcore survival games this is very easy though the usual cozy youtubers that I'm watching are having a hard time with it so I guess it's not for people like me who enjoy both).

They do so many things well, but they could improve it substantially by getting a writer in (I'm available for longterm and character development if you're interested Devs) who knows how to create longterm and intricate stories that still allow players to play the game they want to play. I'm curious to hit my second generation after my first to see if taxes reset or not.

Overall it's a game that still has a lot of potential and is okay on it's own, but I wouldn't recommend it at this moment unless you're looking for a fairly flat game with a slightly interesting twist that doesn't quite allow you to take it all the way.

review_text:
I'm one of those people who got hooked by fans euphorically praising Pathologic 2 as a work of art, letting you experience feelings unknown in most video games. I was told to "skip doing research and just play it blindly".

Well, I dont think it worked out for me. Pathologic wants to be an interesting experiment on creating a specific dreadful experience. But it's also very much a video game. It has so many meters to keep track. And when it wants to raise tension, it just invents more meters. 

At some point, you're just not seeing the game world anymore, You're organizing your character like an excel sheet. There is so much distance between you and the game world. 

I feel like this would work better with it ditching a lot of systems, just experiencing the game world under the pressure of time and working out moral dilemmas. Focus more on that thick writing. As it is now I dont think Pathologic 2 was worth my time and I would only reccommend it to survival game fans.

Honestly not too happy doing Contracts.

[h1] Jet Set Radio's back babyyyyyyy!!! [/h1]

Bomb Rush Cyberfunk doesn't particularly do anything new, it basically tries to do what jet set radio did back in the day while trying to modernise controls and other QOL stuff, and I can't say it bothers me because this game is really fun.

[h2]Gameplay [/h2]
BRC has a very basic structure, get to a new aera, graph a few walls, challenge the local gang, get in a big "challenge", gain the territory as a reward. All of that with a lot of story in between, but the main fun of the game is controlling your character and doing bigall combos. The game felt pretty easy throughout it's total length, all the challenges aren't really hard and encourage more of a layed back exploration style of gameplay than an hardcore scoring arcade type of gameplay, but it's def very fun to explore the new aeras and try to get all the little collectibles and secrets here and there.

[h2]Graphics and overall Presentation [/h2]
This is where the game really hits the spot for me, the overall artistic direction, music, the overall vibe of the game is FANTASTIC (I Wanna Know by Two Mellow will probably be my most listened tune this year). The overall design of the aeras and character designs really hits the spot for me and for that alone I recommand playing this game!

[h1]Conclusion [/h1]
Bomb Rush Cyberfunk feels like a more modern and more accessible Jet Set Radio, and while i would of liked a little more challenge, the game is still fantastic!

That's what makes it tense and fun, because now you have to really focus and concentrate - It just works.

The game is simply brilliant, the graphics, story, sound, facial animations, variety of enemies, combat, boss-fights, jump-scares, the environment, attention to detail, the atmosphere, literally everything about it is superb. I have nothing bad to say about the Callisto Protocol, just high praise. Again, I say these things as my honest opinion, I simply take the game for what it is. What an awesome game!

The ambiance made me feel like i was playing a Fromsoft game (it's a compliment) you can sometimes feel dispair, sadness, but still find a lot of beauty behind some scenes, the aesthetic is great.
I recommand this game and will enjoy starting a fresh new save when 1.0 hit.

review_text:
Interesting premise but it fumbles the delivery.

The new-player experience is pretty bad, and I've seen some people say that the game is similar to Destiny 2, which it is because that game also has a terrible new-player experience. The shooting overall is pretty similar to Destiny, but the enemies feel a bit bullet spongey and the reloads take ages, leading to a game where you feel like everything takes ages to die.

The leveling mechanics are similar to Darksouls and other "Souls" like games, where you have to enter a somewhat open world, kill monsters, and then extract. The worlds themselves have nothing interesting in them, mostly lore messages and random obtuse sentences that mean nothing to the player. Unfortunately the game decided to copy Darksouls worst traits, which was having a story that made no sense, and edgy words written on paper because they seem "dark, and cool".

The level design feels very strange, as you'll be running around a dark-cave, accidentally falling because you can't see the ground due to how dark everything is, and then your run ends immediately after, and all of your hard work is lost. I ran through the games version of a Dungeon and got to the end, got a "You have completed the dungeon" message, and was unable to leave the instance and had to back track through the same traps I had to run through that were still active, ended up dying, and the run was over. Pretty frustrating experience.

The game has some good qualities, and there is a potential that it can get much better with some further patches, and providing brief explanation of game mechanics and what you should be doing. I would also like an option to see my current quest objectives for Gnosis instead of having to run through the hub over and over again. It's almost a yes on the recommend for me, but a few blunders make it a no right now. Wait for more patches and content before hopping into this one.

review_text:
If you are really interested in large-scale flesh contraptions and a despairing eldritch hellscape, then this game might be for you. The visuals and animations are fantastic, creating a very unique environment to wander through - but that's the game's only real strength... 

The combat should've been entirely removed from this game personally as it is more of a nuisance than anything else, just wasting the players' time between the puzzles. I would've much preferred an approach similar to SOMA, where enemies are given more interesting gimmicks and are instead avoided rather than fought directly.

The puzzles themselves are similarly annoying as the primary source of difficulty comes from figuring out the goal of the puzzle or trying not to get lost in a compact labyrinth of flesh tunnels. Once you actually get to solve them though, they can be kinda neat. They're just an exceedingly small portion of the total gameplay.

That being said, I am still giving a positive review because the visuals and animation work absolutely carry the game. If you are okay with the gameplay largely being that of a walking sim, then I'd suggest picking the it up when heavily discounted. But if you want actual combat, puzzle-solving, storytelling, or action horror elements, I'd suggest looking elsewhere.

review_text:
The idea is good but the execution is not to my taste. I hope that the dev will improve it such that I can recommend it.
The UI is pretty clunky, finding roles on the left pane was a pain almost every time, selecting a house to build was similarly painful. There are some useful stats but there is a lot of missing polish there. 
The game mechanics were pretty fun but left something to be desired in many places. The corruption encroaches rapidly at times and the methods I found to deal with it were not fun and not interesting. Mostly involving summoned walls and outposts.
The game is supposed to be challenging and unforgiving and I suspect that it's inspired by the idea of *fun* in Dwarf Fortress. Rise to Ruins is not fun, in the DF sense, at all. The reason DF is fun when you loose, often without any fault of your own, is that each loss tells a story which can be quite complex and nuanced.
Losing in Rise to Ruins was not fun at all as it just felt like I didn't manage the town well enough and no interesting story was being told. The game also doesn't tell you how to lose. You are probably supposed to just leave the region and reset the whole world if you lose but the game doesn't tell you this and just says that you are loosing all your progress by resetting the world.
The game is unforgiving in the worst of ways. I made the mistake of not preventing some corruption from entering a relatively thin strip of rock and the next thing I know, a very hard to reach part of a mountain had been corrupted. It would have been no effort at all to prevent this from happening but after it happened, It was going to take many hours to clean the corruption out of there. So I had a very successful town with a strong defense system practically ruined by not knowing the precise mechanics of the game, I didn't realize corruption went through rocks. Unforgiving punishments can be good game design but harsh punishments for rules that aren't explained nor obvious is not. 

I also think the game needs to be proofread. There are many strange sounding sentences like "Such a real shame." when someone dies.

I realize that It's just made by one guy but that doesn't make the game better or worse, it just explains why it is how it is.

review_text:
This is overall a recommend based on about 90 hours of gameplay combined between a Windows MiniPC (AMD Ryzen 7 5875U, 32GB RAM) and a SteamDeck OLED 1TB. For background, I only watched the .hack/sign anime series and played the first game in the PS2 series when I was a kid. I am doing this rating after completing all 4 games. 

Overall, I give this a RECOMMEND but barely. I’d overall say 7/10. 

THE GOOD:
- Nostalgia: I do appreciate some of the connections to my childhood (Mac Anu, Hidden Forbidden Holy Ground, layout features, etc.). 
- Leveling system: I personally think they do a good job of trying to find different types of maps as you level up and go from game to game, so it feels like the dungeons are different but the overall concept/mechanics are similar. 
- Story; Story is okay, though I think they could have put more into the last game. 
- Memoir system: You can never really not know what’s next between the map and memoir, though this further encourages mashing skip through the crazy number of cutscenes. 

THE MEH:
- Amount/Balance of Cutscenes: Way too much and what’s the point because you can skip through almost all of them very quickly. It almost became an instinct by the time I had played it for maybe 10-20 hours.
- Gift System; The stupidest way to equip your party members. Why??
- Party System: It doesn’t really give you much reason to consistently use all of the characters. Some come and go but there are a couple early on that can carry you through Game 4. 

THE BAD:
- No cloud saves: This alone is a big hit. I have yet to own another game that doesn’t have cloud saves. Just not forgivable and also keep in mind if you uninstall and haven’t backed up, your data is gone. 
- Optimization is terrible; The lag on my PC is the absolutely stupidest thing ever. Lumina Cloth was laggy as hell (and you spend a long time there, fun). All of the Skeith fights, including the final one, and many bosses were stupidly laggy. Imagine playing through 3/4 games on a laggy as hell PC only to  find out that the SteamDeck runs the game flawlessly, but have to cope and play the last game BECAUSE THERE ARE NO GD CLOUD SAVES!!!

So overall I think the game has a cool story (if you don’t fall into the temptation to skip the cutscenes). I would BUY IF ON SALE but NO WAY JOSÉ AT $50 PAL.

review_text:
Like many other reviews already said, great visually but whack gameplay.

The games setting can be described as disgusting and ruined alien facilities. Which is the perfect setting for a “biomechanical horror” type of game. The environments look really nice, as well as all the tools and contraptions you use, which have well-made animations. So it is no wonder that the atmosphere is also quite good, it really makes you feel like you are trapped in a place you want to get the hell out off. There is no clear narrative, and it's more of a game where you have to piece together your own meaning of what actually happened in the end.

Regarding the gameplay itself, the puzzles are more like small labyrinths where you need to find the right contraption to interact with, which allows you to interact with yet another contraption somewhere else. So, really a lot of walking around slowly and not much actual thinking. Sadly, the combat can't make up for the bad puzzles. Enemies are just an annoyance that makes solving the puzzles even less fun. The game also doesn't have a single textbox or something explaining anything, which can add a bit to the atmosphere, but it's also kinda annoying if you don't realize for half of the game that there actually is a healing or weapon switch mechanic. Admittedly thats somewhat my fault.

If you want to play this game for its visuals, it can be worth it, but if you want any fun with the gameplay itself, I cant recommend this.
