review_text:
This game simply reeks of "Dev Crunch". There was a very obvious attempt at making a genuinely enjoyable experience, holding the Dead Space franchise as a pedestal for its expected success... Sadly, there are a lot of moments in this game that make me doubt "Was there supposed to be a mechanic here?" Or incredibly frustrating gameplay elements that seemingly Ignored their source material for no apparent reason.

A lot of the issues with this game stem from the fact that... Modern Game Development requires developers to Heavily cut down on Ideas, Experimentation, and Creativity. With a lot of this game's playtime being spent in boring moments where the main character is slowed down by... Goop on the floor, Crawling through Vents, Shimmying through gaps, Waiting for blind enemies to turn their backs to you, etc.

In its DLC, they introduced "Puzzles"...  those of which only 3 exist in the entire DLC... but they feel as if they were meant to be introduced within the Main Game, as "Fixing Electronics" Puzzles were an essential part of Dead Space (the game of which Callisto Protocol was based on)

There are several other instances of interactions feeling Hollow, like something was Meant to be there, but was just... silently removed by the Developers. The incredible amount of Padding serving as its main way to increase how long the players will have to endure before they finish the game.

Most notably of all... This game is extremely easy, it holds your hand throughout every second. Even Combat!
Which makes every victory just feel even More Hollow than the rest of this game.
The best thing about The Callisto Protocol... are its graphics, who are now surprisingly well optimized, in comparison to its initial launch.

review_text:
Yakuza 5 really goes all in... for better or for worse.

Featuring a whole 5 character cast, 4 cities to explore, 4 substories with their own mechanics, more than a hundred side quests, tons of side content like gambling, fighting, training, the content this game offers is just, absolutely insane.

On the downside, that also means the game is bloated as all hell. Feature creep galore, all characters have their own combat mechanics, and it's not like you flip them all the time, in reality you play a character for like, 5-20 hours non-stop, before suddenly you swap to the 2nd character, and you do that until the finale.

Story wise, it's quite alright, but again, due to the amount of characters and stories, and the amount of time you spent with each character, the story feels absolutely disjointed. One character has like, 25% of the exposition, the other another 25%, another is just like 0% unrelated to everything that's going on, another gives a 25%, and then you have this character that is like, 10% connected, and then the finale for like the last 15%, which FINALLY has all characters involved. This is just... annoying. 

Overall, it's still, like, the biggest yakuza game out there. with 4 cities to explore and do stuff in, it's like your own travel guide to Japan. Good overall, but has some issues with how MUCH the game pushes the scope.

review_text:
Where Winds Meet could have been something, but almost every part of it feels designed to waste your time. The story and side quests are mind numbing. You follow slow NPCs who talk about nothing, and even though you can skip dialogue line by line or speed it up to x3, it still feels endless and pointless.

Quests force you into slow walking, carrying useless items, or staring at your character’s face because the camera zooms in for no reason. Exploration is hollow. You collect bugs and honey, repeat the same small set of activities and clear identical camps until your brain shuts off.

Combat is just as dull. Bosses look great but the fights are empty. You mostly stand still, parry and dodge while bosses spin around the arena in nonstop attack loops. There is barely any room for actual combat, and the whole thing becomes a boring cycle.

The UI is a complete trainwreck. It is ugly, chaotic and painful to navigate. Menus are stuffed with random icons and walls of useless text. The map is clunky and its filters barely work. Important info is hidden deep inside submenus, while irrelevant junk sits in plain sight. The inventory is a nightmare with messy categories, endless lists and zero clarity. Using the interface feels slow and outdated, like a bad mobile port.

Overall the game is full of wasted ideas buried under terrible design, boring content and one of the worst interfaces in the genre. It frustrates more than it entertains.

review_text:
Hello,
This is my first review, so I would like to ask for your indulgence and apologize in advance for any grammatical errors. 
In this article I would like to focus on Callisto Protocol in detail. Obviously, I can't do this without comparing it to the Dead Space series, so I'll spend some time on that part as well. The main reason I'm writing this review is to point out how horribly bad this game is and how much of a disappointment it is. I'd like to point out that while I'll try to be objective at first but I must say I grew up on the Dead Space franchise and have played all games(primarily Dead Space 1 and 3) + the remake several times as well. This review contains light spoilers. Let's get to it...

ACT I. - World without Dead Space:
Let's imagine for now that there is no Dead Space franchise and Striking Distance Studios is releasing a new unseen game in the survival horror genre. I must say that the audiovisual aspect of the game is amazing and immersive and it is clear that the authors know how to walk in this field. Unfortunately, I'm done with praise here.

COMBAT SYSTEM: totally worth a fuck. On paper it looks good that the combination of "melee" and "long range" duels will be fun, but the opposite is true in this case. The controls are incredibly insensitive and stupid since movement is on the same keys as dodging, and if you happen to decide to run away from the fight the next enemy will hit you immediately. There is no "roll" option in the game and the camera itself is pretty stupid when it comes to combat. It is literally a nightmare when you meet more than 2 enemies at the same time. At this point the game really becomes UNplayable. Generally there are few bullets in the game and the game FORCES you to combine "melee" and "longrange" style ergo forget about the choice. The only way to deal with multiple enemies afterwards is to use the "gravity gauntlet" to throw them all into pits or bayonets according to the level-design, which gets really BORING after 2h! It wouldn't even be that bad if you had more weapons to choose from than one electric baton and a couple of pistols. The weapons are boring and the upgrades are overpriced and don't even give you the feeling that you're gaining the upper hand.

STORY AND CHARACTERS: (if we still take into account that there is no Dead Space) is pretty good. The setting is interesting, but the characters are quite shallow and don't develop much.

PLAYABILITY: is terrible. If you are not moving from A to B you will encounter 3 types of challenges:
1) Find the "Fuse" to open the door.
2) Find the dead guy who has the key to open the door.
3) Kill everyone in the room.
And that's the end of it. Every now and then you get a BOSS FIGHT, but if you don't have enough bullets, it makes life pretty uncomfortable and the game just becomes frustrating again. Another drop in the frustration jug is the lack of any orientation. There is no map, no locator, no hint to tell you where to go and what to do. Main Character will only say, "I have to go along the red pipe.", "I have to go along the cables.", etc... it's incredibly easy to get lost in the game. And one more annoying little observation of mine. If you craft at a "station" weapon or ammo, you can only craft "1 pack"/component, and the animations are fucking long for my taste. So if you want, heaven forbid, 3 packs of cartridges and a first aid kit... Spend a good few minutes at the table :)

ENEMIES: they are quite stereotypical. You will encounter these types:
1) The common infected
3) "Babies" from The forest (toddlers)
2) "Clicker" from Last of Us (only hears)
3) "Spitter" from L4D2 (gases acid)
4) "Boss" he's variable

New!!! is a "head" that shoots and knocks you halfway across the room if you don't notice her fast enough.

The game contains quite long passages where there are so many clickers that you simply can't kill them all, but have to sneak past them. Their AI is extremely stupid, so if you want a realistic clicker experience, go play Last of Us.
It's admittedly subjective, but I'll say it anyway. Overall, I found the enemy design lazy and "not enough" scary than other titles such as: Evil Within , or Resident Evil. And there is no "pyramid" to filter the enemies by how dangerous they are. Even the most pathetic zombie has the potential to kill you in two shots.

ACT. II - Dead Space:
It's like chalk and cheese. Dead Space is better than Callisto Protocol in every way imaginable. Gameplay, level-design, audiovisual... No exaggeration, whatever you say, Dead Space is better in that regard (leaving aside the 2008 graphics), but it was great for the time.
In Deadspace you have: a locator that shows you where to go. A range of diversionary weapons. Enemies are intelligent, subversive and scary. The characters have purpose and depth. You have the freedom to deal with enemies and not be crushed by stupid camera and movement. Diverse level design and quests that make sense.

ACT. III - Review:
After reading the following lines, it's definitely obvious that I'm not going to become a Callisto Protocol worshipper. The optimization may be good a year after its release, but that doesn't change the fact that the game is a bad, unreasonably frustrating copy of Dead Space that will only piss off veterans of the series. DEFINITELY NOT WORTH THE 60€ PRICE TAG. I myself bought it for 20€ on sale and I didn't know what to expect. I was in for an incredible disappointment. The Callisto Protocol is definitely NOT THE SPIRITUAL REPLACEMENT to DEAD SPACE and unfortunately I can't recommend it to anyone.

EDIT: After almost 9 hours ive finished the game... im speechless. Everything so bad I dont want to write any more lines.

review_text:
Echoes of the Plum Grove, developed by Unwound Games and published by indie.io, is a beautifully melancholic and surprisingly complex take on the farming and life-simulation genre. At first glance, it looks like another cozy countryside game about planting crops, befriending villagers, and enjoying quiet days in a small town. Yet beneath its soft, watercolor aesthetic lies a system of survival, legacy, and mortality that turns this gentle world into something far more meaningful. It begins with a shipwreck that strands your character on the shores of Honeywood, a rural island village surrounded by forests and fields. What starts as a simple story of rebuilding a life slowly evolves into a generational saga in which time passes, families grow, and the choices you make ripple through decades of village history. The result is a game that feels both intimate and enduring—a blend of comfort and consequence rarely seen in its genre.

The foundation of Echoes of the Plum Grove rests on its blend of traditional farming sim mechanics and life-management systems. Players plant crops, tend livestock, gather resources, cook meals, craft tools, and build relationships with the townsfolk. The daily rhythm feels familiar to fans of Stardew Valley or Harvest Moon, but Echoes adds layers of realism and tension. Seasons are not just visual changes—they dictate the rhythm of survival. Crops wither if planted at the wrong time, and food spoils if hoarded carelessly. Winter, in particular, is an unforgiving season that tests how well you’ve prepared; without sufficient stockpiles of firewood, preserved food, and warm clothing, your character and their family can grow sick or even die. These mechanics give the game a grounded, almost historical tone—it’s less about endless productivity and more about sustainable living in a community that feels genuinely alive.

The game’s most distinctive feature is its generational system. Unlike many life sims that freeze time or loop endlessly, Echoes of the Plum Grove allows your character to age, fall ill, and eventually pass away. When that time comes, you continue the story through your descendants, inheriting the land, the family home, and the reputation your ancestor built. This sense of continuity transforms small decisions into lasting ones: how you treat your neighbors, how you manage your finances, or how you nurture your children all echo forward through the years. If you ignore your fields or neglect relationships, your descendants may face harder beginnings. If you leave behind wealth, strong social ties, and good health, they inherit an easier life. This mechanic turns what could have been a simple farming simulator into something contemplative and almost existential, making you consider not just how to live well, but how to be remembered.

Honeywood itself is one of the most charming and well-realized settings in recent simulation games. The village is filled with distinct characters, each with their own routines, preferences, and temperaments. Some are warm and friendly; others are prickly, gossipy, or downright unpleasant. Relationships must be nurtured through conversation, gift-giving, and mutual respect, but Echoes doesn’t shy away from friction. You can just as easily insult or alienate villagers as you can befriend them, and some quests even encourage mischievous or morally questionable behavior. This social realism keeps the world dynamic—people respond to your behavior, and friendships, rivalries, and even grudges can persist across generations. It’s a rare example of a cozy game that acknowledges that small-town life isn’t always idyllic. There’s gossip, jealousy, and tension, but also warmth and humor in equal measure.

The art and sound design elevate the game’s emotional tone. Visually, Echoes of the Plum Grove has the look of a handcrafted storybook—lush green fields, soft pastels, and charmingly simple character models. The gentle lighting shifts with the seasons, and the animation carries a quiet rhythm that mirrors the passage of time. It’s not flashy, but it’s evocative, managing to make even mundane actions like chopping wood or walking through the snow feel atmospheric. The music is equally understated, a collection of melodic and pastoral themes that shift with the mood of the season. Birds chirp in spring, wind howls in winter, and soft piano notes accompany your daily routines. The result is a world that feels warm but not saccharine, contemplative without being somber—a tone perfectly suited to the game’s themes of growth and transience.

While the core experience is rewarding, Echoes of the Plum Grove is not without its flaws. The social systems, though ambitious, can feel underdeveloped. NPC dialogue is often repetitive, and some villagers lack depth beyond a few simple lines or predictable routines. The AI behavior can be inconsistent—characters sometimes stand still for entire days or fail to react meaningfully to your presence. The quest design also wavers between inspired and underwhelming; while some storylines carry emotional weight, others feel like filler or lack satisfying resolution. The pacing can occasionally drag, particularly when managing the minutiae of daily survival, such as tool maintenance and illness recovery. These rough edges don’t break the experience, but they do reveal the growing pains of a small development team aiming for a deeply systemic world.

Yet, even with its imperfections, there is a sincerity to Echoes of the Plum Grove that makes it memorable. It does not rely on endless grinding or artificial goals to sustain engagement; instead, it encourages you to find meaning in small victories. Seeing your crops survive the winter, watching your children grow into adults, or witnessing your family’s home stand for generations carries a sense of permanence that most simulation games never attempt. It’s a quiet reflection on how lives unfold—how hardship, kindness, and resilience shape not only the present but the future as well. There’s a bittersweet pleasure in watching time pass, in knowing that every moment of prosperity is fleeting, yet still worth savoring.

Echoes of the Plum Grove succeeds because it understands that comfort and melancholy can coexist. It offers the joy of tending a garden, the satisfaction of building a home, and the sorrow of watching time take it all away. Its charm lies not in perfection but in the authenticity of its world—the feeling that you’re part of a living, breathing cycle of beginnings and endings. For players who want more than escapism, who crave a farming sim that values emotion and consequence as much as routine, it delivers something rare: a world that feels both cozy and alive, where the passage of time is not just a mechanic, but the heart of the experience.

Rating: 9/10

review_text:
I'll be honest, while this game looks deep, and maybe has some kind of message, or artistic value; it's not that great of a game. I'll elaborate further, but you can basically do a completionist run of this game in under 6 hrs. I say this because I beat it in 5.9, with slightly above average ability in shooters, and I died multiple times in Act V trying to figure out how to kill the last boss. Slight spoilers ahead.

I had been waiting for a while for this game, and I think I admittedly got it mixed up with Agony as far as some expectations were concerned; because I thought this was a game based on "a soul in hell trying to escape" with some shooter elements, but mostly horror. This had more or less no effect on my opinion, because I'm a fan of shooters and horror alike regardless. That being said:

I didn't really feel "scared" by anything in Scorn. It's just kind of gross and unsettling. I know it's based on H.R Giger's art, and I wanted to play a horror game for Halloween; but it wasn't very scary. It was just kind of disgusting and visually repulsive, because of all the flesh everywhere. Which, to some people, is scary. To me, it isn't; and most of my actual time playing, most of the game, was centered around these "diseased" biomechanical areas which make up most of the game. I thought the clean, biomechanical, alien looking areas in Act 5 were visually appealing. Everywhere else felt like I was walking through a shitty, gassy stomach.

Which kind of brings me to my point. Some people feel as though the fact that it's linear, and that it has no other endings is something of artistic value. Maybe? But it doesn't really add to my appreciation of it either. There are only 12 achievements to get in this game, and you get 11 of them based on a single choice you may or may not make at the beginning of your journey, before there is any danger. People love to criticize open-world games and games that aren't linear nowadays; and that's fair, but so is my own opinion:

The fact that there are no other endings and virtually no other content gives this game literally no replayability whatsoever. There is nothing you can change to fit a different playstyle, nothing you can do to alter the story (whatever the story is meant to be in the first place.), and no "actual" narrative. Even the most recent patch notes refer to a "getting stuck in the hurt machine." I looked at that, and said "which one?" There is no dialogue. It's so completely and utterly linear, that basically I found myself resigning any kind of critical thinking ability I had, to "Just find the interactable shit. You'll get through the story that way."

While some people think this is artistic, I feel as if it's kind of lazy. I don't even say this with any offense meant to the developers; it just feels unpolished. Making it so there is only one "outcome" that's meant to be depressing isn't profound to me, it's boring. Making it so that the protagonist seems to know where he's going and what he's doing while the player remains clueless doesn't necessitate being thoughtful to me. It feels like any deductive ability the player has is stifled by how narrow and linear it all is, including exploration. You don't really find anything that kind of clues you in. Even at the end, you don't even know where the hell you're going, if the portal you were intending to step through before Randall from Monster's Inc kills you goes anywhere that would've been able to repair your innards, or you'd start new life, etc. Most people don't find the shit in the can artistic, so giving people nothing doesn't really feel inspiring or anything either. It just kind of leaves a bad taste in your mouth where you're wondering why the hell it cost 40$.

I'll change my review if there's some kind of update, but I don't know or think there are any plans for one.

Lastly, the costs. My god, the costs. If I'm understanding their systems right, the cheapest of the expansions for this is $120. To get all of them would be almost a cool grand.

review_text:
Buying any game in early access is a risk, but sometimes your investment pays off. Once this game is finished it'll be better, right now it's good but there's only 3 arenas, limited enemies and gear. Yet within the limitations of this game there's still items that don't have a purpose somehow. Looking at you black salt.

Game runs well enough, although there are a lot of performance spikes, screen tearing, other graphical glitches where your textures become rubbery and move around. The enemy AI can just wander off and not be in it's designated zone.

Gameplay wise there's a lot of times when you are doing multiple encounters at once, and with the enemies wandering off it can lead to completely unfair encounters that weren't intended to be fought the way they are presented, while doable it's pretty annoying having 6 swordsmen who can teleport and become invincible just be on top of you. Although I will say, sound design and art design are great they did a good job on the gun sounds.

IDK how there isn't a reroll system implemented. So many times my manifestations are useless. I know there's more than 3 options in any given line. The merchant could sell something that lets you reroll your upgrades.

The incense is cool but there's only 1 option that's ever worth taking in any given run: The max health upgrade on clear. Every other incense option sucks, and that isn't my opinion it's a fact. You have finite healing, so healing an extra 5 health is the most negligible bonus you could ever receive.

Resources in this game are a real feast or famine sort of endeavor, you either have ammo or you don't, which turns out the merchant who just sort of appears with no dialogue sells you everything you need> Just really want notifications of things in your hub like that.

Also the game needs a better tutorial. I like figuring things out for myself but there's a bunch of nuanced crap that comes with encounters and progressing your runs and upgrading your preyer that, again, the game doesn't explain. (collectible mask shards, divine essence, debuff manifestations etc) So many things are just not explained, which again if you're intuitive it's fine probably but not every one is.

Lastly, your abilities don't always work as intended. For example I had a run with ice sphere which basically gives you an ice dome that freezes enemies that enter. BS swordsman can just walk through and kill you. Seriously the swordsmen have the most bugged code in the game and are ceaselessly annoying. Idk why they teleport. It's seriously unfun having a highly mobile regular dude that can just become invincible. BTW there's 6 of them... A lot of enemies will just straight up start running away from you once you engage them. We need things like this out of the game because it just adds to the overall time you spend in your run

Also why is the all seeing eye the absolute worst weapon in the game that thing needs a buff because it's absolute dogshit for a weapon. Absolutely no damage against single targets. Seriously, give that thing at least 70 power like every other weapon in its class. The disparity between how good weapons feel in this game is astronomical. It goes Striga at an S+ to all seeing eye at if you pick this you aren't finishing your run.

For an early access, 7/10. As a game in general it's a 5, maybe a 6. It's an unfinished shooter with a ton of bugs. Just wait til release since probably you'll run out of things to do in a couple of days.

review_text:
First off, let me start by saying that I am a hard person to please when it comes to MX/SX games. These games are my way to get a taste of racing after I got hurt and couldn't ride anymore... Like many people, I have been waiting for a game that not only provides the mechanics, physics, licensed products, etc.- but also the things that aren't usually focused on by these developers: exciting racing. Milestone has given me hope that this dream game will exist- sooner than later.

The usual MX game experience:
1) Ride a stock Chinabike while wearing ugly gear
2) Think to yourself "great- another floaty turd of a game"
3) Unlock some steezy threads
4) Grind the career to unlock tracks and a 450
5) Finish said career
6) Buy DLC name-brand bike(s)
7) Rinse and repeat
8) Do this all until you get bored of it and go back to a FPS shooter

This game does not provide any of that garbage. The new physics and features of this game add an excitment that I haven't had playing a motocross game since Reflex. What separates this game from the previous releases? The extreme career, paired with the improved physics and deformation (IMO). It's been a long time since I've raced, but I think that Milestone has done a really great job making the game as realistic as possible- without being impossible to make it through a race without biting the dirt. For once, I haven't won every race (unless I restart multiple times)- which is a welcomed improvement over past Milestone games (where you literally cannot lose to the AI unless you suck).

There is still much to do on the side of realism and the career (where did our official team sponsorships go Milestone?), which is lacking compared to previous MXGP games. I would also like to see:

- Popular MX fonts to customize our jerseys and number plates (so that we can look as cool as the official riders)
- Offical team rides (like there used to be in MXGP games)
- The ability to have sponsor's logos on your gear
- Further improvements to the new physics system (mainly ruts and deformation)
- Fix random crashes, incorrect timing/scoring/results
- Make the game not crash when I try to select a Yamaha 450 in career mode (literally cannot select this bike without the game crashing immediately)
- Improving the features added to this title- they're all great additions to these games!

All in all- I highly recommend this game. It's the best MX game (IMO) to date. Can't wait until the next SX game!!!

review_text: Firstly, writing a review for this game is extremely difficult. This act in the HIVESWAP series has a lot of good and bad attributes. Let’s start with the good. The art direction in this act is just as good as the first one, if not better. There are significantly more characters in this act than the first one. The decision to partially animate the character sprites was very clever. Partially animating the sprites helps the player keep track of which character are speaking, especially since there are numerous characters on screen at certain parts in the story, this drastically reduces confusion. That being said, the animation in this act is as good as the animation in the first act. However, the writing in this act is a mixed bag. The writing is pretty standard up until the player reaches the third train car, then the writing goes off the rails (no pun intended). The writing becomes very explicit, very quickly. Complete tonal whiplash compared to all the interactions and scenes before it. I’m not against that style of writing, but I wasn’t expecting it either, really caught me off guard. The gameplay is the same as the first act, with the exception of a few sections. The gameplay is slightly less linear than the first act, since there are alternative outcomes based off your choices. There’s more fail states in this act, so be careful. There’s a lot of unique optional character dialog throughout this act. Most character dialog changes as you progress through the story, which I found to be a really nice touch. Furthermore, this act is also composed by Toby Fox, which is just a short way of saying the music is still good, no surprise there. Now, the bad. The Ace Attorney segment that happens in the third train car is easily the worst part of the act. It feels like the developers didn’t understand why the Ace Attorney games worked mechanically. The developers knew this section of the game would be difficult and confusing for players, given the absurd amount of chances you’re granted and the generous hint system. Normally, with Ace Attorney games the player is given several statements and it’s the player’s job to spot the contradiction in one of the statements. Afterwards, the player would present “evidence” that proves the statement is a contradiction. If you are having trouble deciding which statement has a contradiction, you can “press” for more information. In rare cases, pressing statements is needed to progress the cross-examination. In this act, the contradictions in cross-examination statements aren’t always clear. Sometimes you’re not spotting a contradiction per se, just a statement you have to add more context to. If you have never played an Ace Attorney game before, you are going to struggle with that section of the game. Additionally, the writing in the third train car is very mature, explicit even. It’s like the section of the game was written by a completely different team. The whole trial in the third train car felt so surreal. I’m not entirely sure what happened during the development of that section, but it was insane. Luckily, the game returns to its normal self afterwards. Nonetheless, the section of game where Joey needs to challenge Nihkee to a theater brawl was also a little annoying. To complete that section of the game the player has to talk to Ardata, a character that will (optionally) endgame you with every interaction, after talking to Elwurd. There’s no indication that you have to talk to Ardata to progress the story. I ended up talking to Ardata and agreeing with her proposal after talking to every interactable character on the train up to that point (very risky). Then, there’s the final boss of the act. Some of the sequences are odd. For example, the player has to command Joey tap dance to shake the hula girl dashboard doll, which causes the dashboard doll to dance somehow. How does Joey generate enough force to cause this phenomenon when the moving train couldn’t? Not important. Why does a drone controlled vehicle need a dashboard doll? Doesn’t matter. Then the player has to command Joey to shine her flashlight at the dashboard doll, which causes it to shine and distract the drone. I’m not sure why the doll needs to be moving to accomplish this goal, but it’s what’s needed to solve the puzzle. The player, controlling Joey, needs to throw pet food at the train control panel, which causes Byers, the pigeon, to fly and land towards the drone. Then, the player, controlling Xefros, needs to use telekinesis to pull down the control lever. If the player uses Xefros’ telekinesis too early, it’s an immediate game over. I’m not sure why this is the case, but it needs to be done to solve the puzzle. Finally, at the time of writing this review, I am not a fan or familiar with the lore surrounding the Homestuck series. Therefore, I cannot commentate on how faithful the portrayal of certain characters are, the accuracy of the worldbuilding, or references in the game. Moreover, it’s obvious that there was a lot of work put into this act. Compared to act 1, act 2 feels lacking with all the effort put into it.

review_text:
Check out the other negative reviews for some valid criticism which I basically share. I'd like to highlight two things that bugged me about it.

First, the typesetting. For a game as text-heavy as this, more care should have been taken to make the text look good and readable. Instead, we get a hotch-potch of fonts and styles, for instance in the dialog boxes (emphases sometimes done in bold, sometimes italics etc), the character spacing is notably off quite often, and don't get me started about the memento preparation mini-game. I'm aware that this might be a limitation of the engine, but that's no excuse in my view. For a game that has great pixel graphics for the most part, the quality of the typesetting really stands out in contrast.

Second, the music. Yes, it's good, atmospheric, at times even original. But in some tracks, some instruments are painfully out of tune, as well as some parts of the voice in the ending song. It's probably been produced on a low budget, but it's still way too noticeable for me.

Other than that, it just didn't grip me as it apparently did a lot of other people. I found the storytelling, humor and background graphics enjoyable, but that's about it.

review_text:
This is a weird game. It's got great visuals, a great concept and the shooting isn't bad...but every system in the game comes off like a prototype from inexperienced developers. 

- No way to upgrade your gun stats
- Player upgrades have INCREDIBLE diminishing returns
- Difficulty settings are missing: you can't pick what difficulty map you want to run
- Guns have no range, but enemies have near infinite range
- Game forces you into close combat but cripples you with cooldowns and stamina limitations
- Very few guns that actually matter, and a small pool overall
- No melee weapons
- Very few options for loadouts, and 90% of the options won't apply to your playstyle
- No perk unlocks, and no perk selection in loadouts
- Calamity system which pretty much ends your game if you get hit too much regardless of health or healing
- Character carries almost no ammunition, consumables or healing items
- Game turns into a horde shooter with increased enemy spawns...but everything is bullet spongy and you have the ammo carrying capacity of a 7 year old child
- Very limited content

This game has been in development since 2015. I appreciate that it's a small team, but they have stop worrying about making the game so punishing and start thinking about making it worth playing beyond 8 hours. There's no content, there are no long term unlocks, there's no gain in player power for time spent, no cosmetics to chase, no loot system, nothing. And terrible design choices like making your guns have no range in your shooting game? And your shotguns feeling like nerf guns? And you character carrying almost nothing into combat?

I'm pretty sure this game isn't going to see much commercial success and won't really change beyond what we see today. So grab it on discount, play it for a few days, and then realise what a waste of potential it is.

review_text:
This game has major fundamental issues that result in a very poor experience.

TL;DR, the game tries to be a lot of games at once without really having an identity of its own. The result of this identity crisis is a game that feels slow, over complicated, and unrewarding. These are not Early Access issues, but instead core mechanics and design decisions that will almost certainly be carried on to full release.

The good:

1. The idea of the game is exactly as cool as it sounds. It's a dark fantasy FPS where you hunt down zombies and demons using magic and cool weapons. It does nail the atmosphere to a degree, especially in the latter maps and the weapon designs. This is pretty much what makes people be interested in the game in the first place, and the main selling point as you can see from the trailers and highlights. Notice how you get very short cuts of the fights in the videos above. This is meant to show the overall vibe of the game rather than prolonged pieces of gameplay.

The bad:

1. The gameplay loop is EXTREMELY repetitive and short of content. You basically spawn in a map, clear about 6 camps containing the same enemies in slightly different combinations, do that one puzzle, maybe kill that one boss, get the same 3 or 4 items and return. The thing you do on your first hour is the same thing you will be doing 6 hours later, no changes, no variation. You'd think this is the definition of a rouguelike, but the issue is there's virtually NO VARIATION between runs. Your build won't change from one run to the other. The changes are so minimal and so spread out that a vast majority of runs end up feeling the same way. If you want to get a new weapon / spell / item you have to complete a lot of runs to get the currency to then complete more runs to finish the research, to finally equip that ONE new item.

2. The maps. This game's level design is very bad. And I don't mean the atmosphere of course. I mean the actual design of the level. The layouts are bland, flat and empty. The first map is basically an island in the most basic sense of the word. It has a few trees, a few paths, and that's pretty much it. Then you unlock the second map, hoping it will be better, and it's so incredibly similar you think you selected the wrong map accidentally. The same coast, the same trees, the same paths. This is jarring because the few zones that take you indoors into dark corridors and castles are by far the best, but they're a minority. The levels feel like they're amateurishly crafted maps with a dark fantasy coat of paint. Once you get past the awe of the atmosphere, they feel uninspired and uninteresting. Not to mention that the maps play absolutely no role in the gameplay. No use of architecture or level design to make fights interesting or engaging. Enemies will spawn in random pieces of barren land and start swinging. The camps you're clearing? just a bunch of enemies that spawn in a spot, don't expect an actual camp or a building or anything.

The worst:

1. The progression system. The worst design decision that could have been made by far is the inclusion of this game's soulslike system. Get "souls", spend a million souls to upgrade a stat by an unnoticeable point, rinse and repeat. It makes progression feel completely unrewarding and pointless. The difference between vitality level 1 and level 2 is a tiny percentage of health. This makes your permanent upgrades and progress feel like a drop in a tall glass of boredom. If you compound this with the fact that there are only a handful of perks to pick inside the expeditions themselves, the result is an extremely slow and repetitive gameplay loop.

Summarizing, I wish this game had put more thought behind the gameplay loop and level design to make it an experience that remains fun after more than a couple of hours.

I would love to play this, but can't, due to it being just kind of inaccessable to me. 

I don't mean that in that it's difficult, I mean that in how i can't play it due to weird mouse sensitivity and a lack of FOV sliders.

Even on the lowest, the game is still too sensitive for me. I can't aim, a flick of the wrist and the camera's gone flying. However, the same is not true for the menus, as changing the sensitivity also turns down the pointer sensitivity used on the UI. This means that while the sensitivity in game is very sensitive, the sensitivity in the menus is way too slow. It also seems to have some weird angle snapping at the lowest sensitivity? I dunno.

I'd be able to look past that if the game offered a way to move through the menus via keyboard. But I can't. I have to deal with high sensitivity in game, but super low sensitivity in the menus. For me, that's unplayable. 

Oh there's also no FOV slider. You're locked to like 70(?) FOV, and it feels very weird and claustrophobic.

I'll give the remaster a go. Hopefully they're solved there. It does seem like a great game, but it's just completely inaccessable for me.

review_text:
I don't usually write reviews, but I feel like I have to say how amazing and underrated this game truly is. I tried playing previous SAO titles as they were coming out through the years, mind you they were on consoles and might I add not the greatest game series I have played. Which is why I have decided to write a review on this game.

[b] Story [/b] The story in this SAO title is a lot better than the last games. This time around the story takes place after the main anime, so they had a ton of freedom to really do something they wanted here, which really shows. The story is unique enough to have kept me quite engaged. As you progress through the story, you slowly unlock characters to use in the amazing multiplayer 20 man raid, which might I add is insanely addicting and very fun to play.

[b] Multiplayer [/b] This in my opinion is the main reason I am writing this review. I haven't played a game with such addicting multiplayer game-play in years. There are three different multiplayer options you can choose from after completing the main story, being free roam, co-op quests and boss raids. These three online modes are all extremely populated, which are always absolutely popping off no matter the time of day at the time of writing this review, mainly because this SAO game has cross-platform play, ignore steam charts as this game easily has 50,000 people playing at any given time. The combat feels insanely fluid, the mobs feel fleshed out, the zones are beautiful and the community in this game are very helpful. Even if on the very slight chance you find a quite game, you will wait max 60 seconds before you are placed into a co-op mode that fills the remaining player spots with bots until another minute later the lobby rapidly fills with players. 

I would rate this game a solid [b] 9.0/10 [/b]

IMO, most overrated game. 
I'd rather read Wiki for the original story than actually playing it. 
The original story is interesting, but way too epic and failed to be integrated into gameplay. 
While playing, I hardly follow and understand the events occurring in the game, and feel confused and meaningless. 
Until after reading Wifi for the original story, I got that the events in the game are just trivial tiny fragments within the original story. 

The actual gameplay feels very stiff and farfetched to the story. Sure in that world, its obvious Psychos are everywhere, so the whole game is about meeting some random psychos, knowing their respective little freaky anecdotes then killing them, but they don't contribute to the whole story. Little sisters cast you 2 same choices throughout the game to quantitize your morality, so there's actually nothing to be meshed and expected, right? Just counting your choices!! 

Its painful to play it like boring assignment to be done for what? Maybe for the hype and FPS training. 
However, as FPS, the shooting is utter disaster. Feels extremely plastic, no recoil, no weight, and lack of physic effects. The guns are jokes as toys. Enemy moves like flying as well as yours. 
Plus game stage/environment is pretty dull, dull as hell. 

1/10 for the yet inspiring and profound original story.

review_text:
I really can recommended Just Cause 4 even if there are many negative reviews. For those who like the franchise this will also be nice game with interesting content. Yes, after 20 hours it is becoming a little repetitive but that is similar to other games of this genre.

 - Action gameplay is still nice and interesting. Shooting is much better than in previous parts
- Hook is interesting to use with new modifications. Maybe there is strange behavior sometimes with the hook usage but it is still easy to pull things and do heavy stunts. 
- Graphics is excellent when everything is set on max details. Especially when you are in free flight across countryside. 
- Driving cars is better also than before.
- DLC packages were actually the main highlight of the JC4. I really enjoyed the racing DLC and Agency DLC. The one with aliens was kind of meh but still good because it was a little tough challenge.

But for sure there are also negative sides:
- Story is complete crap. With completely forgettable characters its almost B production. I mean it could have been better, because the plot is not so bad but scenario and performance is bad. 
- There is no clear indication how much progress is made on discovering events per region. Now you have one universal region and all locations are hidden there without knowing where is some that you missed. Very bad... because it is never done like that.
- Menu navigation is also bad. Its like for consoles but not easy to find anything without too much switching.
- Occasional crashes, which were on my side problem with high refresh rate. Once I limited to 160HZ I didn't experience crashes (like when it was set to almost 240HZ for my monitor native refresh)

But even with these negative sides, which are not game breaking, I find it nice to play and really enjoyed relaxing my mind when going through game world. This after all the main point of Just Cause series and I still can find that here and these 70 hours were very well invested. Honestly I would like JC5...

I don't understand the rave reviews for this game. I have played 5 hours and wanted to return it honestly.
The point and click for EVERYTHING is annoying. I feel like my mouse is going to give out, and heaven forbid if I click too early and have to pick the SAME FLOWER 5 times because it didn't finish its 2 second long animation of bending over.
The "survival" aspect of this could be cool if you actually had more than 1 recipe you could make in the beginning without needing 5 ingredients that weren't in your grasp. Making money seems horrible early game, the only thing that brings a good profit is wood but you need wood for everything.
FIshing would be great except the mini game glitches on corners all the time and I lose progress because the cursor doesn't want to actually go around the bends. Oh, and you have to repair all your tools constantly which costs money and are tool-less for the entire day.
You can mine for ore but so far I have no idea how to smelt it, I have not been given a quest or recipe for that and you cannot use the blacksmiths shop.
Who the hell am I supposed to romance? Everyone? Anyone? No one? Can I date married people, kids? Whats going on. There is no guidance.
The intro is extremely distressing and I would (hope) they dive more into that later in the gameplay, but after 5 hours I am only in season 1 day 12, after having to reload my game several times because I got sick and none of the medicine or medical advice helped me after days. 
I feel like it would be a good game if I knew what the hell was going on. I am sure they eluded to a story line for the game after night 5/6 when you're awoken by a sound and have to walk across the ENTIRE MAP when your character is dead tired after only having gone to bed.

review_text:
Game with a lot of potential, quite disappointing.

A lot of people complain about the lack of explanation to the story, but personally, I think it has a great appeal.
You're in a foreign world, nothing does make sense to you - so you push buttons, experiment around to figure out how things work. More and more you get a bit familiar with the vastly unfamiliar surroundings. There is nothing to explain, since you see the world through the eyes of a character who's also not familiar with the world around him.
It's great being thrown in there and solving puzzles or finding a way somewhere, but trying to figure out why you're doing what you're currently doing. I'd go as far and say there's a bit of a philosophical undertone.

To the game aspects:
Checkpoint system is broken, loading a save game makes you lose about 30 minutes progress.
The scripted loss of HP is just stupid, game auto-saved at a point where i constantly lose health, yet I have about 10% of HP left. Means i could load a savegame and repeat the tedious last 30 minutes again or i can run around with 5 seconds time and try to get somewhere over and over again (Which I did since I wanted to give it another chance). AI can easily be manipulated, or made disappear by just walking away and coming back or using an elevator.

Game seems to make you want to engage in combat at times (else they wouldn't have a boss fight), but the gameplay mechanics and movement are just frustrating. Scorn does not know what it wants to be - I have no problem with it being a walking simulator, the art style is quite impressive - but the scripted events, loss of HP over time (or at certain checkpoints) should have been fixed by now, since a lot of people mentioned it way before me, yet nothing has been done so far.

Come back in half a year when the game has been fixed, knows what it wants to be and they lowered the price. It's definitely not worth the 40 bucks they want for that thing.
There's a lot that has been done very good, but also a lot do be desired. Unfortunately it's not a game to come back to from time to time, more something you enjoy once or twice and that's been it, you've seen all it has to offer...

review_text:
If you've heard people call Battle Nations essentially a FaceBook game... it is. Sort of. Worth more than those things, but that comparison is not at all far off.

I would say that its strengths come from its characterization of the atmosphere. The actual characters in particular are written in fairly interesting ways and have vast amounts of dialogue. Some of it is quite funny, most of it quite engaging. Items and actions often have amusing descriptions, and there are a number of things to do during a play session. If you're a fan of resource-collecting, I suppose there's something you'll find here. There's lotsa that. The combat system was something I found to be very fun. If you've ever played Final Fantasy: Tactics or other tile-combat-ish games, they hold many similarities. Plus, if you like Team Fortress 2, apparently some of the more notable characters, i.e. the Heavy and the Pyro, are in Battle Nations. I suppose that's not much of a selling point, but I thought I'd mention it 'cause that's pretty much the only reason I got Battle Nations in the first place.

But weaknesses? There are a lot to be sure. While there's no arbitrary energy system like in many city-building FaceBook games, there are many moments when you just have to either wait and do absolutely jack-diddly or do a few repetitive tasks, i.e. waiting five minutes for cabbages. Yeah, it's a real-time game. Set something up and wait actual minutes for it to finish. I personally like those because of how I play games, but I know a lot of people don't. Granted, there are a lot of timers that are fairly short, taking literally what barely makes several seconds (building some things only takes three seconds), but there are a number of things that also take a whole ruddy day to finish. The humor, if you play it very often, can get wearing after a time. The art, while I appreciate its uniqueness, is kind of bizarre and definitely is not gonna be everyone's cuppa. I rather like it, but even then, it's more of an "Oh, it's neat that it looks like that" than an "I really like the way that looks." I'm talking mostly about the talking heads, but the rest of the art falls into this category too at times.

In addition, I don't know if anyone else has this problem, but I can't complete of the missions in the game because the game decides to have a crash whenever I look at the forces' Unit screen. I rarely run into game-breaking bugs, and I don't know if this qualifies as such as I can still play the rest of the game pretty alright, but that's a whole mission I can't complete. And because it's a whole screen I can't access without the game crashing, that's a whole level of functionality lost, which may indeed lead to game-breaking-esque issues, 'cause I can't level up my characters, at least not in this way. And missions often only show up after you've completed other missions, so whatever this particular mission (I don't remember the exact name, but it's something about promotions) is hiding will stay hidden for a good while longer, it seems.

Overall, I still enjoy playing Battle Nations. Probably will for a while to come, too. I like that it's more or less part of the TF2 universe and the fact that the vast majority of the characters look like specialized Pyros. It's neat to imagine that I'm building what BLU's HQ looks like or something. It's very much a casual game, not meant to be played for long periods of time, as far as I can tell. For what it is, it does its job quite acceptably. When it doesn't its job, it's bearable but only just. It's very close to being a FaceBook game but maybe a very well-executed FaceBook game yet a FaceBook game to the end. I can't whole-heartedly recommend it because of its issues, but I'd imagine it'd be worse just saying don't even check it out. I say get it. It's not a bad game at all and can be pretty enjoyable. It's free, anyhoo. Why not?

review_text:
Yakuza 5 my beloved.

You get to play as Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama, and Shinada.
All five were absolutely fun to play as.  Each having their own side stories.

On my first playthrough alone, I clocked in 88 hours, which was far longer than the 67 hours I did on my first playthrough on Yakuza 0.  And honestly, the sidestories were probably the reason I stayed so long, just as it was for 0.

Kiryu's at a debatable strongest here, as your bounding throws are completely free, Tiger Drop actually negates all damage through the ENTIRE animation, both attack and rewind.  And, you can negate all damage yourself by just entering dragons rage.

Saejima's still fun to play as and is great for crowd work. However, Tsukimino has a slightly minor problem where the map is so constricted that you'll likely fight a guy right as you get out of one fight.  I didn't have a problem with that though.  And, you can take a picture of Miku in there.

Haruka gets to be playable in game, basing it off as rhythm as she's now an Idol.  Doing various dance battles and the like.  And her music soundtrack is great.  It's got the songs that I'm willing to listen to outside of the game, among other ones.

Akiyama, he's still fun to play as.  He's got his kicks, and you can even do air combos with him.
Some people might say that having an air combo which apparently misses half the time was a waste on Akiyama, but I never had that problem.  He's either good, or he gets his ass kicked in by the Komaki duo.  

Shinada my beloved.  You get to have a baseball sidestory that is my personal favorite in here, rivaling that of Kiryu's Taxi Racing.  His combat is my favorite in the game, going above Kiryu simply because of "My Meteor Tackle" and his own version of a bounding throw.  He can get into grabs in multiple ways, and he's really good with weapons.
Continuing on that, some people say his weapons aren't very good, that being the sturdy metal pole, long pole, knife, and katana.        And to that, I say that you really shouldn't soley rely on his weapons.
Shinada already is great at fighting if you know how to use his overflowing amount of I-Frames.    I personally only pulled out weapons if I wanted to utilize the increased XP on enemy finish, or if I needed it as a solution to an enemy.  Just, don't be stupid with them and you'll get your use from them.


The story's fun, it has a lot of twists and turns, and the final boss has a lot of health, which I find to be refreshing.

But most importantly, Baka Mitai was introduced as a karaoke track for the first time in 5.   There's also Machine Gun Kiss, which is also amazing.

Anyways, Yakuza 5's a great game.  I'll be moving on to playing Isshin before I play 6.

review_text:
I bought this game years ago. Around 2021 I think. The moment I found it I knew that that it looked something that I will most probably like. The theme was right up my alley and top down stealth gameplay seemed well made. However for some reason I never brought myself to try it. Until few months ago.

I woke up with a terrible hangover and I wasn't planning to do anything productive that day. So I fired up my TV and picked up my controller. I wanted to try something new and I saw Shadow Tactics collecting digital dust in my library. I fired it up and got immediately hooked.

The game has quite advanced controls but It introduces them with a great pace with minimal learning curve. I played with the controller, however I imagine that using keyboard and mouse might be even more straightforward.

There are 13 levels that are big and beautifully crafted. Each took me 1-3 hours to beat. The final level took me a whooping 5 hours as it was a bit more challenging. Each level is generally an environment with different arrangement of enemies, places to hide and different team members. The cooperation between them is crucial as each member on your team has its strengths and weaknesses. Takuma is gameplay wise probably the most interesting character that you control. He is an old man that unlike other characters, can not jump, climb on vines or use hooks to pull himself on the roofs. He can't even backstab enemies. He of course has other talents, but given his disabilities he also becomes a part of the puzzle how to get all your characters to point A to point B. While everyone but him can jump, climb and easily kill enemies you need to use them to clear the path for Takuma.

An awesome feature of this game is also an ability give each character an instruction that is executed upon your command. For example, if you want to take down two enemies simultaneously, you can instruct two characters to do so. This mechanic opens up so many more possibilities like luring enemies or distracting them as other character can make a stealth kill.

And this is why this game is such a delightful time sink as you have so many options how will you tackle the problem. Will you kill the guard or try to distract him? Should you raise an alarm or is there another more sneaky way to proceed? The game also encourages replayability as it gives you various challenges on how should you complete a level. For example not using a specific skill, not being detected or complete a mission without the casualties.

This brilliant gameplay is packed in a beautiful art style. While the art style is not very unique, it is very well executed. Each level is memorable with different weather, color pallette and distinct level features. The music is also great and helps you immersing into edo period Japan.

Hands down this is one of the best games I played in recent years. Many tend to agree as game received overwhelmingly positive reviews. I can not recommend it enough.

There were a number of technical issues with the third and final puzzle of this game which soured my enjoyment of this game. For the octopus platforming puzzle, most of its difficulty stems not from figuring out which platforms to jump to based upon where they'll move, but rather, jumping a certain distance and hoping that a.) you don't collide with the lights, b.) you don't clip through the platform you're jumping to, and c.) that the platform moves quickly enough to follow you if you happened to be jumping to the same platform. One of the worst Games of the Current gaming era. The controls are clunky at the best of times. Most of the time the most important controls bug out "Mantling" over obstacles or climbing terrain and crouching under obstacles only for your character to not move or respond to direction inputs. The game more than once bugged out and wouldn't progress the quest line until you leave the area and re-enter it only then does the npc's tell you "you need to get the key from one of the guards" even though it was already painfully obvious as you had done this multiple times before... only to progress further you had to "trigger" the dialogue que to continue. The worst part was the terribly clunky combat that didn't work half of the time and when it did you would get swarmed by 5-10 mobs in certain areas. Achievements are bugged. I upgraded 2 weapons to max and  I only got the achievement for fully upgrading a weapon in the dlc mission "Final Transmission". 

The story was Average at best and terrible at worst. This was because, the gameplay was mostly a walking simulator with very typical jump scares, and combat which was supposed to be one of the main advantages of the game sucked. A fully upgraded shotgun took 3-5 shots to kill a "space Zombie" while my melee stun baton (More like club) as my character refused to use it's electrical options, took only 3-7 swings depending on the type of mob, making most ammunition worthless to keep and on the few bosses that appeared in the game the damage was god awful for the guns again. 

The reason i believe the combat was so bad was that the guns did barely any damage, you were swarmed by lots of space zombies often, and the main replay loop of the combat was press 'a' or 'd' to dodge damage when you tried to use 's' to block damage you get grabbed alot or swarmed by another space zombie further making gunplay feel bad. 

If you are on the fence about buying Callisto Protocol, do know that some of the developers that worked on dead space contributed to this game, and it did not help. Skip Callisto Protocol and buy Deadspace. This game its a "cheap" and "mediocre" game that tried and failed horribly at reproducing the great enjoyment and fear that deadspace had. 



Story 4-10 |      Decent enough, but far to easy to understand and i figured out the entire story when i saw the cargo container box in the tutorial mission.     
Weather effects 7-10 |    The snowy chapter was fun but you only saw these affects for that one mission.
Sound 6-10 |      (eery sounds effects which added to the atmosphere but most of the sound instantly notified you where the enemies were going to come from in advance, took away from the horror aspect greatly.)
Lighting 5-10 |      (Some times your guns flashlight didnt even work even through it did before you saved and exited the game.)

As for Final Transmission DLC: Just some of the worst content to play says you get to use your completed saved game data to keep your weapons... You dont, i lost all upgrades and most of my weapons except for my shotgun and pistol. The Powerhammer should have been in base game would have made much more sense and been more fun. The final boss of the DLC was terrible to fight did lots of teleporting and then would just spam fire Aoe explosives at you knocking you down then running at you to kill you, was infuriating. Darksouls, Eldenring and any other tough game had much better controls for fun and difficult boss fights, not just spam and kill. 

Overall rating I would give 3-10.

review_text:
I've been following this game since it came out and have played every time the game completely changes. Over the past FOUR YEARS of early access GTTOD has gone through a bunch of complete reworks of what the game is and everytime the reworks set the game back a year. Now, it's an underwhelming rougelite. To get upgrades and different weapons there are bunkers which act as rooms with many upgrades in them. To access these bunkers you have to find a key somewhere in the map, which is hard because every part of the map looks the exact same. Once you do find a key and are able to access the bunker, the upgrades aren't free, you have to buy them with shards, which is the currency you get in your run. The issue with this is you do NOT get enough shards to justify the prices of the upgrades are often are only able to either get a gun or upgrade a gun in a bunker. This would not be an issue if the higher tier threat levels (difficulty scalings) suck to play without proper equipment, and you often can't get the proper equipment in time. 

As I stated before, the level design sucks. Everything looks the same. I like the artstyle, but there needs to be a minimap for the levels to be any fun to traverse. Speaking of traversal, the movement has potential to emulate titanfall's movement but it falls short in every aspects. It just doesn't feel good to move around these levels. The gunplay is alright, nothing spectacular but it gets the job done.

If the dev had a clear goal for this game and worked towards it then it would be lightyears better than it is, but over the past four years it's gone through multiple complete game-changing updates that rework the literal core gameplay loop. The dev wants to do so many things at once but falls short of all of them. Wait another four years and the dev might change the entire game again. Don't buy this.

review_text:
This is a difficult game to review negatively, cause I love what it's going for and enjoy pretty much everything about it, *except* playing it. I'll try to cover my points as best I can.

The primary issue is simply the fact it's so repetitive. It's not that short of a game, it's about 10 to 12 hours, maybe more if you want a full 100%. Yet by the 3 hour mark you have seen pretty much everything it has to offer. There are 3 different "gear" types, skateboard, rollerblades, and bikes, but they all control exactly the same. And you'll be doing all the same stuff in every area you explore throughout the story. It's so boring in fact I can't get myself to finish it.

Alongside this the trick system feels completely superfluous. You get multipliers just by grinding on rails, and have exactly 3 tricks for every gear type. You press the button and it plays a canned animation, and it just feels very disconnected and floaty. They all chain into each other seamlessly but not really in a way that feels all-that cool because you only have THREE tricks! You also have a move that lets you keep your combo going quite generously even if you hit the floor, so there is virtually no challenge at all for any score attack sections of the game, and getting a high combo or score feels completely unrewarding because it's so absurdly easy to do. I'm so surprised that there is zero depth to this, like no combo tricks, or just, literally fricking anything to give it spice lol. The trick system feels like a prototype, it does not feel finished.

On an extra note about difficulty, the police system is completely pointless and provides zero threat. Which is a polar opposite to Jet Set Radio, feels like they really missed the mark there.

The story itself I did find interesting, the presentation is great and it has a fun mystery element. The visuals are also just gorgeous and the dream sequences especially are very fun. I actually enjoyed the linear sequences of platforming the most in this game because it feels like the only time it's trying to challenge you. And they are well designed challenges.

The music selection is *mostly* good but quite frankly some songs are obnoxious. "Hair Dun Nails Dun" might be the worst piece of music I have heard in my entire life and I absolutely hate it lol.

But yeah, it's an experience that feels overall very shallow. There is zero challenge besides the rare linear platforming sequence. The movement on its own feels nice, but doesn't really give you much room for player expression because the trick system is depressingly simple. And again, the other 2 gear types have no differences to them either. This does capture the *vibe* it's aiming for very well, but it needed more depth to really feel like it could stand on its own. As it is now, it just feels like an undercooked JSR fangame.

review_text:
Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts is a dotted line worth signing.

[b]DISCLAIMER: THIS REVIEW DOES NOT EVALUATE MULTIPLAYER MODE DUE TO LOW PLAYER POPULATION.[/b]

[h1]Story[/h1]
Set sometime in the near future, Contracts isn't so much a story as it is a series of things simply happening.  Players don the high tech mask of Seeker, an anonymous contract killer for hire who has entered a deal with an equally anonymous employer to assassinate several high profile targets in the newly formed Siberian Republic.  After a brief but bloody civil war, Siberia has split off from Russia to form its own independent nation.  Under the steady guidance of his contact known only as Handler, Seeker will work his way from target to target and eliminate them all as he goes.  There's very little in the way of characters here.  Handler is curt but professional, keeping most of his conversation on the mission at hand while Seeker is strangely unprofessional in that he simply won't stop asking Handler just who it is that he's working for no matter how many different ways he told to stop asking.  There is a reveal at the end, but the word "reveal" is far too generous for what you get out of it.  It's very clear that the story exists wholly to serve as context for the contract style the gameplay follows, and thus it is utterly devoid of any real merit to speak of.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
An FPS with an emphasis on sniping, SGWC drops players into five different areas of operation.  These maps are by no means open world environments but are each easily a square kilometer in size at a minimum.  Whether it's the twisting blizzard choked crags of Altai-24 or the serene greenery and cliffs of Sibirskaya-7, each map is filled with paths, tunnels, and open fields to navigate and enemies to kill or avoid.  Each area has a primary target for players to assassinate as well as secondary targets and tasks that they can fulfill to earn more cash.  Each map offers its own challenges, bounties, and collectibles to hunt down as well, which in turn, reward points for unlocking different equipment Seeker can use in future jobs.  A plethora of snipers, combat arms, handguns, attachments, gadgets, and abilities can be purchased to give players even more of an edge, though there are many items that feel outright useless compared to others.  You could remove the majority of weapons from the game and nothing would really change for the end user other than shorter menus.  Some upgrades are laughably overpriced for what little they do while other far more game changing abilities come earlier and at significantly less cost.  Each area of the game is filled with outposts large and small and players are given the freedom to tackle these places in any way they wish or even just avoid them.  Although sniping is your best tool as Seeker can fall to just a burst or two of concentrated fire, he's more than capable of holding his own in a stand up fight with the tools he has available if your aim is true.  The sniping itself feels fantastic.  Players can gauge target distance by instant instinct, a brief scope measurement, or taking the time to activate their mask's zoom and tag for the most accurate if slowest method of gauging range.  Meanwhile, the mask itself highlights how wind will affect the bullet at all ranges, but players are free to zero their sight if they wish for a more centered shot.  This ultimately turns sharp shooting into a little minigame all its own that rewards thorough preparation, good measuring skills, or good instincts equally.  Shots well past the 250 meter mark are a joy to watch as their tracer takes over a second to arc down directly into the skull of whichever poor guard you've pulled the trigger on.  Enemies are quick to alert and thus need to be dropped quickly.  If they catch sight of you, hear you, or find evidence of your work; you have mere seconds to silence them before the outpost goes into full alert; though thankfully neighboring outposts won't get the memo.  When inside an outpost, enemies will try to rush, frag, and flush Seeker out until he's dead; and they can be a genuine threat.  On the other hand, if you're sniping from outside, they can do little more than hide behind cover, spray bullets or mortars in your general direction, or be one of the brave few that tries to pull out their binoculars to slowly scan for you.  It's a shame they can't do much more than that but it does make you feel like a lead slinging force of nature that brings entire bases to their knees in fear.  The game can certainly feel repetitive at times and even frustrating when things go wrong in a way that might not feel fair, but overall the sense of freedom, the interconnected nature of the maps, and the solid shooting makes tackling each contract satisfying enough to enjoy doing it all the way to the end.

[h1]Presentation[/h1]
Fantastic but certainly not without deficiencies.  Visually speaking, Siberia's environments are stunning to behold thanks to the game's rich use of vegetation, rock, snow, and lighting.  Despite taking place across one country with mostly samey regional climates, each level feels distinct thanks to their topography and time of day.  Seeker's design stands out as a bit goofy though, and the mask only makes it worse.  He stands out poorly when set next to all of the highly realistic military gear the game surrounds him with.  Sound is equally satisfying to the visuals.  The harsh muted thud of a bullet blasting out of a silenced barrel doesn't get much better than it does here, and the bullet kill cams are simply excellent if a bit drawn out at times.  Animation as a whole is weighty and impactful with the exception of reload animations which feel stiff and awkward.  The music is a bit of a low point.  The game only seems to have a handful of songs which means you'll be hearing the same tracks over and over again.  At best, they're OK, but at worst they quickly become noise that you get tired of hearing and just want to shut off.  Voice acting is solid, though the actors are hardly performing roles that let them truly become a character.

Dead game.
Their slow development, weird design choices and worsening performance (due to engine switch from UE4 to UE5) basically scared off the last few players.
The player peak the last 30 days was 950, but the average is 370, if you spread that out over the entire day and all the timezones you're lucky if you can get an entire full match (probably the weekends only).

review_text:
I really want to love this game more than I do. As a huge fan of H.R. Giger this game should've been right up my alley. But the longer I played, the less and less I was afraid and the more I became annoyed.

The problem with this game fundamentally is that it feels like it has a bit of an identity crisis, specifically in terms of gameplay. The beginning of the game is a puzzle/walking simulator with some very cool and unique puzzles, but also some very frustrating ones. But later portions of the game are plagued with very underbaked combat that really bog down the experience.

The issue with some of the puzzles in Act 1 is that they rely on you just stumbling across the 'thing' that activates another 'thing.' But because of the very faithfully created Giger environments, you're gonna be crawling around at a snail's pace for hours just hoping to stumble across the correct 'thing.' But that isn't the majority of act 1 and I still very much enjoyed it for what it is. It's mostly there to get you acquainted with the world and the controls and it does so very well.

Next in Act 2, you're given two weapons, with a very unique ammo and health system. Like one in a robust shooter/horror game like Resident Evil. But this isn't that style of game. The actual combat is VERY underbaked. Fighting enemies feels like trying to kill small dinosaurs with a paintball gun and one of those electric thrusting dildo machines. I get making the player underpowered for the sake of tension, but this was just more annoying than tense. The reach on the dildo feels inconsistent, and missing even a single shot from the gun feels like a kick to the balls considering how scarce ammo is and how much HP the enemies have. Also dodging attacks is near impossible. The little chicken guys have near laser precision on their shots, and the big bulls are twice as fast as you and can kill you in two hits. The combat only starts to feel a bit better once you get the shotgun. But by then I felt like it was too little too late. Over all, Act 2 is by far the worst of the 3, and this is mostly due to its over reliance on the combat.

Act 3 was much better than 2, mostly because the combat is relegated to 2 simple boss fights that are actually pretty decent. Instead of being straight combat, the two bosses are more like two very similar puzzles, each with their own spin on how to solve it. The third act is overall much shorter and simpler than the first two, but after the utter frustration that was act 2, I actually welcomed this. The only problem with act 3 is that its actually possible to softlock yourself after a certain point. SPOILERS: [spoiler] at some point, the parasite that has attached to your character will start to grow mold on you. In order to continue the game, you need to activate certain machines that will break the mold for you, but you'll take damage OVER TIME from this. If you don't have enough health or medkits when you reach this part of the game you simply will not be able to move forward. [/spoiler] While I understand that this is supposed to create tension, I plainly just think this a bad idea and should've stayed on the cutting room floor.

As for everything else, the story, atmosphere, sound design, environment design, character design, etc. it's all a 10/10. Its really a shame that I found the actual 'game' part of this game very frustrating. I really REALLY  want to love this game, and its a story and world that I'm gonna think about a lot, and its even inspired me to do some more Giger style art myself. But This wasn't the game for me, and I can't recommend it either.
