review_text:
I have a flashing weak spot for looter shooters. They hit my critoris in just the right way. But it wasn’t until relic hunters legends that I realised theres practically no top down twin stick options that scratch the same itch that Destiny managed too back in it’s hayday.

I played the beta for legends a few months ago and I’ve been itching to tell you about it ever since. But I wanted to get a little further into this early access title before giving it my seal of approval just in case three hours into the campaign it tries to offer me NFTs or something.

Well fund the Taliban and call me a Clinton it turns out it’s actually pretty good.

For an early access title it sure feels finished to me. Shooting guns is finger licking good, the campaign feels all there and there’s enough to do every day to keep me entertained for a while.

So what have we got. A main hub area to trade with other players and test out weapons. A campaign. Various levelable relic hunters with stats and ults to level which all feel different. Instanced mission nodes. And Guns with more random buffs than a gay porno.

I particularly like the loadout screen which was lifted from Destiny, and you rely on a gear score to know whether or not a challenge is right for you. You can upgrade your favourite gear, and the games lets you know ahead of time to not be shy about upgrading parts your into, because you can always merge that gear into newly dropped stuff just fine.

It has drop in co-op and it isn’t rare to land into a public mission already underway. You can play solo just fine but it’s always sort of a relief to have random friendos helping you in a public match. Oh yeah there’s ingame chat and emotes too.

Levels have secondary goals of random resources sprinkled around and chests of extra loot tucked away as a reward for poking around.

Rogue Snail have managed to create a toit little product. I’ve heard about polishing turds before but they’ve managed to compress a turd into a diamond.

If you were wanting a new game to play with your 3 friends, or just something to turn your head off for as you get into the zone of dodge iframes and killing tons of dudes then you should probably check out relic hunters Legends.

review_text:
Scorn is an absolutely gorgeous art piece that, at its best, is moody, immersive, and completely a visual marvel. However, Scorn is also not just an art piece - it's a game; and the game part of Scorn brings it so very low that I'm not sure I can recommend the actual product.

Barring the lack of story and context - which is a bit of a shame but not a dealbreaker - the levels are pretty poorly paced, puzzle mechanics are "introduce ---> reuse until any semblance of uniqueness in its design is lost ---> repeat", and the combat is at once unsatisfying and unfair. The weapons themselves are actually fine and I think feel pretty good in isolation, but they're just not in a sandbox where they can shine.

Ultimately, you can buy the art book and witness the artistry of these guys at a much better pace - that is, at your *own* pace - with no distractingly convoluted level design, annoying enemy encounters, or nonsensical mechanics to draw you out of the experience. And I do think you should support these developers one way or another, because art like this is once in a generation and I would hate to not see more like it. I just think the medium of art is sometimes as important to consider as the art itself.

review_text:
This is an update on my review of GTTOD. My review was previously a negative one, and unfortunately, it's going to stay this way even after playing the update. I will also be talking about the developer's response to my negative review of the previous update.

I've been playing GTTOD since 2019, and I really, really had high hopes for the game. GTTOD used to be an endless shooter in a neon synthwave environment, and I believed that all the game needed was more content, because the gameplay and aesthetics were spot on. However, the developer decided that he hated the game, and wanted to completely rework the whole thing, and turn it into a completely different game. The biggest change is switching from a doom-style endless shooter to some Risk of Rain Roguelike FPS game. This new update is around the 3rd or 4th complete overhaul for GTTOD, where he completely changed the mechanics and alienating a lot of his older playerbase in the process.

Before getting into my issues with the game, I want to talk about the good things first. The movement is much better than it was before, in fact, it is the only thing keeping me from uninstalling the game. The animations are decent and the game looks better graphically than it did in previous updates. The new music is also good.

Now, for the stuff I personally dislike, I think with every update to this game, it loses more and more of what I enjoyed about the game in the previous version. Again, I'm not telling the developer what he can and cannot do, I'm just speaking from my own personal feelings towards the game.

In the previous update, the one thing that was keeping me entertained with this game is the Endless Mode, and although I complained about the Crevice map being completely broken and the game forcing me to play through some horribly designed parkour sequence every time I wanted to play a round of Endless Mode, it was still fun to be able to kill hordes of enemies, parkouring in a small arena, while grinding money to upgrade guns. For me, it was the closest the game's ever been since in rekindling what I really enjoyed about the old 2019 version.

With this new update, instead of improving Endless Mode and fixing the unplayable level, he decided to just completely remove Endless Mode entirely. In fact, now there's only one game mode in the game. Players who wanted something closer to the 2019 version would now have no choice but to play the main roguelike mode, which I also have some problems with.

The game tries really hard to be a roguelike, which is fine, but I think it is poorly executed. The game doesn't know what it wants to be. The movement is super fast, and the compass points RIGHT TOWARDS the exit door, which seems to encourage players to just disregard everything and run right towards the exit (and for the first few levels, there is no consequence for ignoring everything). This makes every level super fast to beat. The is no real incentive to doing anything else, the game barely teaches you what the mechanics are, you are just left to figure things out for yourself, which contradicts how the game encourages you to just ignore everything and get to the exit as fast as possible.

review_text:
I'm pretty sure the developer of this game enjoys the suffering of others. Basically, we have what appears to be on the surface a unique and interesting take on settlement survival with some wave/tower defense thrown in. However after trying and failing to keep one village alive for even 2 seasons, I have the absolute opinion that what this game really is, is a thinly veiled gacha game in which, even if you do everything right, build everything in the perfect order, place all the buildings in the perfect spots, you still will likely lose because A: you haven't suffered enough to open enough "god experience" chests to boost enough stats, and B: the 'random' events seem to absolutely favor causing you the most suffering possible. 

There's not nearly enough margin for the player to express any level of experimentation or creativity in building or defending. Basically, if you don't do everything just right - you doom yourself - often many days before you are even aware of it. Then you get to decide if you are going to spend the next hour slowly watching your village burn away because there's no possible recovery metric. The enemy just grows at a stupidly fast rate and you just die. That's it. That's the game. Personally, I'd rather go walk barefoot across a field of legos.

I don't think I can finish this one. Too many bugs are making it too frustrating. 89% most objectives on "Deadeye mode" but the bugs are driving me nuts. This is not a bad game on CryEngine, fairly good job. But it could have benefit massively from a polishing pass. Take a quick look below if interested in my experience on the hardest difficulty. (not bragging here but giving important context for feedback) There are fairly too many bugs to list as I didn't keep a running notepad next to me while playing, but here we gooooooooooo.

Bugs:
* crosshairs becoming decoupled from where bullet goes in CQB (like the recoil animation didn't fully reset to center screen)
* stuck on uneven terrain, rocks, pebbles, all the dang time
* stuck in midair when jumping over things and unable to do anything (restart checkpoint)
* when using gear or interacting with objects it seems to be possible to get stuck in between that and using your weapon leaving you unable to do anything
* blown up vehicles go to charred black and then walking up to them causes fire HUD but no fire is present
* screen flashes, whole patrols vanish in thin air and reappear sometimes, vehicles vanish in thin air etc

Negatives:
* CQB sights appear to be perma-glared making them worse than irons (most noticeable on pistols)
* character development is slow and requires a lot of mission redo which is fine, but system also treed which makes it hard to remember if you can still melee a heavy? or disarm a turret? nope DEAD again (must have switched skills uhhhhh this method of upgrading is so frustrating)
* super wonky movement and weapon cycling in CQB leaving you dead, its just wonky
* vault and falling animations like Deus Ex that take control and camera from player
* interrogating enemy is wonky, takes control and camera from player again, and occurs in real time which made a challenge incredibly frustrating to deal with, while interrogating enemies patrols can come up to you and kill you from around corners etc (while you are frozen in voice overs enemies can alert, run to you, and circle around waiting for cutscene to end and then DEAD again)
* enemies on Deadeye mode have aimbot across the map aim using full auto once loud gun fires or alerted
* enemies on Deadeye can soak incredible amounts of gunfire making CQB and LOUD guns fairly useless, even if you are topshot there is very little ammo to deal with it all, picking dead bodies for ammo uhhhhh, resupply gave 10 bullets uhhhhh
* player dies in what feels like one or two hits on Deadeye (in fairness there is armor upgrades but now you cant do the other important thing, etc the treed upgrade system)
* going loud is basically impossible on Deadeye so majority of weapons unable to be used, or enjoy playing whack a mole for a half hour behind concrete blocks
* massive map stutter out of nowhere when moving around the maps, oh a patrol, stutter, DEAD again 
* when getting bonked by that one enemy you forgot was hiding in the porta potty (not really), game resets you to a weird autosaved checkpoint a few minutes back where you have no ammo but decided to RESPAWN ALL THE DEAD ENEMIES like what the fudge, can haz ammo back?
* good grief the blindingly bright WHITE contracts screen, plz dark mode next time? playing at night is like getting a sun tan from the monitor holy cow, and my monitor brightness is way way way way down

Positives:
* satisfying sniping mechanics
* decent gun sounds and ambient world sounds (get close to creek and hear the water etc)

Summary:
Not terrible by any means, but do not take it serious or it will be constantly frustrating. The sniping is good, but just do not go loud. Silenced weapons only, man. Maps and targets remind me of Hitman, some elements like the character development remind me of Deus Ex HR. Played the contracts multiple times to unlock bounties and do challenges, which are required to get special tokens for upgrades. This part is super tedious due to the bugs and then basically cannot use any loud weapons and what with all of the wonky movement and the character upgrades are treed and uhhh most should be on your guy from the start? Not mad here just disappointed.

review_text:
After The Fall delivers a distinct take on the cooperative VR shooter formula by plunging players into a frozen, alternate-1980s Los Angeles overrun by mutated creatures known as Snowbreed. Rather than leaning on the usual sun-bleached apocalypse aesthetic, the game wraps its ruined world in ice, snow, and biting winds, creating a uniquely harsh atmosphere that immediately sets it apart. The backdrop of abandoned malls, skeletal high-rises, and buried streets adds a chilling sense of isolation even when playing with a full squad. From the first mission onward, the hostile setting works in tandem with the action to create a constant feeling of tension: every echo, every distant roar, and every frozen alleyway reminds you that survival here is earned through grit and coordination.

The gunplay and physical interaction are at the heart of what makes After The Fall compelling. Weapons feel substantial and responsive, rewarding players who enjoy the tactile rhythm of VR shooters—slamming a magazine into place, racking a slide, or dual-wielding against an onrushing horde feels satisfyingly grounded. Each firearm has its own personality, and upgrading them over time adds a sense of progression that keeps missions engaging. The game strikes a good balance between arcade-style accessibility and immersive realism; it never becomes overly complex, but it still demands enough physical involvement to make firefights feel thrilling and high-stakes. Facing a charging Snowbreed brute or a swarm erupting from the ice becomes a chaotic, sweaty moment where instinct mixes with muscle memory.

The cooperative design elevates the experience further. Missions are built around four-player squads, and the game’s difficulty scales in a way that makes teamwork essential. Reviving fallen allies, managing ammo under pressure, and coordinating defensive positions all prove crucial, especially on harder difficulty levels where enemy numbers swell dramatically. The social element gives After The Fall much of its longevity—playing with friends or an active online group transforms otherwise straightforward missions into dynamic, unpredictable encounters. Communication, even minimal, adds a sense of camaraderie that fits naturally with the desperate fight for survival. The hub area, where players meet between runs, reinforces the feeling of a small but determined survivor community carving out life in frozen ruins.

Progression is anchored by collectible floppy disks that unlock new weapon modifications, items, and upgrades. This system encourages repeated play, nudging you to refine your loadout and experiment with different weapon builds. While simple, it provides a steady reward loop that complements the game’s run-centric structure. Each completed mission brings new resources, pushing you to take on tougher routes, face more aggressive Snowbreed variants, and continuously improve your arsenal. Over time, the challenge ramps up in a satisfying way, making early missions feel dramatically different once you’re better equipped and more experienced.

The game does, however, show the limitations of its scope. Content variety is one of the main criticisms—mission layouts follow a similar pattern, enemy types are somewhat limited, and the absence of a strong narrative means the world’s backstory remains mostly implied rather than explored. While the moment-to-moment combat is engaging, players looking for a story-driven VR campaign or a vast sandbox may find the structure too repetitive. Technical issues, such as occasional matchmaking hiccups or minor graphical glitches, can also interrupt an otherwise fluid experience. Yet even with these limitations, the core loop remains enjoyable because it leans so heavily on atmosphere, gunplay, and the energy of cooperative action.

In the end, After The Fall succeeds by focusing on what VR does best: immersion, physical engagement, and shared adrenaline. It offers a polished cooperative shooter experience wrapped in a striking frozen-apocalypse aesthetic, delivering a steady stream of intense firefights and memorable co-op moments. While it may not offer deep narrative layers or expansive mission variety, it compensates with tight combat mechanics, strong social features, and the satisfying grind of upgrading weapons and tackling harder routes. For VR players seeking a reliable, action-packed co-op game with a distinctive atmosphere, it stands as one of the more memorable entries in the genre.

Rating: 7/10

I tried really hard to like IMSCARED. A game that has the player interacting with an entity that communicates with them by creating text files on the player's desktop is intriguing. The visual style, while not entirely original, feels dated, a commonly overlooked way to create unease with the player. The game's price point is also low and suitable for a game with this level of content. However, IMSCARED stumbles in a lot of areas and left me frustrated with it. I'll break down what I didn't like about the game.

1. I said in my introductory paragraph that I found the interaction between the player and the game to be intriguing. While it is, it's also a bit awkwardly implemented. There are several points in the game where you need to be reading a text file while playing the game. During these segments, you can put the game in windowed mode, but the window is incredibly tiny and the controls sometimes glitch out while you're trying to go back and forth between the text file and game.

2. The game "crashes" and closes itself on several occasions. This harkens back to Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem and the original Metal Gear Solid, where the game attempts to fool the player into thinking that the game is actually interacting with something in the real world. I initially didn't mind this, but the game began to abuse it. If you get caught by the monster at certain points in the game, the game will close and you'll be brought back to your desktop. There were points where you're required to solve puzzles with little to no conveyance as the monster chases you around the environment. If you get caught, you're brought back to your desktop, losing your progress up until the start of the puzzle. I actually took breaks from this fairly short game because I was so frustrated with my constant failures. I also imagine my Steam friends were getting annoyed, constantly seeing me start and stop playing the game. If the game maybe brought you back to the menu screen when you died rather than completely closing out, this wouldn't be so much of an issue.

3. Jump scares, jump scares, jump scares. I see a lot of reviews praising this game for being "truly scary", but I see very little criticism of its over-reliance on jump scares. While I'll admit that the game made me feel uneasy at times with its retro atmosphere and creepy ambience, there were way more occasions where something would pop out and make a loud noise at me for a cheap scare. There are points where an overlay will flash on the screen with a loud noise and the game will close, something entirely jumpy and even more forgettable. The worst offender, however, is a puzzle about 3/4 of the way through the game where the player is tasked with finding record players in a maze and destroying them. You're being chased by the monster during this segment, but weird figures will come down from the ceiling and screech at you for absolutely no reason. They add nothing to the experience at all and don't play into the puzzle in any way, just being added as cheap scares to make the situation less scary than it would have been if you were simply being chased.

4. The game is somewhat fragmented. There isn't really a hub location until the very end of the game, and the areas you're going through have little to nothing to do with one another. You go to a supermarket, a train station, a basement area and a hedgemaze throughout the course of the game. These areas aren't really connected to each other until the very end, and even then the game only connects them through a series of doors that teleport you to them. Some of the areas even require you to input different things into a text prompt, something that is vital near the end of the game if you didn't get all of the achievements (I'll expand on this later). Overall, you find yourself teleporting from area to area. The game will close, and you'll find yourself in an entirely new location without any explanation as to why. As a result, nothing feels familiar and the game feels stitched together, like a collection of different ideas.

5. Movement is awkard and actually somewhat buggy. It's fairly simple, being mapped to the WASD keys for moving, the Shift key for sprinting, and the Ctrl key for crouching. However, it's easy to get "caught" on objects, requiring you to reposition the camera in order to move again. If you want to try this, you simply need to walk along a wall and rotate the camera towards it. You'll eventually get stuck and won't be able to move unless you rotate the camera away from the wall. This wouldn't be so bad if there weren't actual segments where you need to get through cramped spaces and you're constantly getting stuck on both sides of the wall. There's also a segment where you're being chased through a hallway, and while I only got caught on a bookshelf once, it still exemplified how buggy the movement is. It's also worth noting that if you crouch next to certain objects, you can clip through them, which looks very awkward and allows you to peer inside some things.

6. Near the end of the game, the player is about to go through the last door when the game prompts them that they need to get all of the achievements in order to proceed. At first I thought this was a trick, but it's serious. Closing the game will bring you back to the start of the game, which has opened up some new doors to previous parts of the game where you can obtain these achievements. When I started this game, it was less than a week old. The achievement list gives absolutely no clues as to how the achievements are obtained and the discussion board was barren of help. This left me stumbling about, trying to figure out how to get the last few achievements so that I could actually finish the game. Some of these achievements are incredibly obscure, requiring you to do things like knock on a wall and set your system clock to certain times in order to get some items. Achievements are meant to entertain completionists, not frustrate people who just want to experience the game.

I truly, dearly wanted to enjoy IMSCARED. It does some really interesting things and has a very low price point. However, the times where I was wowed were undermined by the amount of times I was frustrated or disappointed. In the end, this is just a short indie horror game with lots of jump scares and a somewhat entertaining fourth-wall mechanic. It's not incredibly noteworthy and I can think of other games that do fourth-wall breaking better with less frustrations and more polish.

I clocked about 9 hours of this game on Xbox but I wanted to get it on PC as well. I don't know what's up with all the dislike on PC, but I wasn't an early access player, which is where a lot of the complains seem to come from. The performance is stable for me on PC, but I took the time to experiment with settings tweaks over a few games. I don't know what's up with the other players, because I didn't have to make all that many visual compromises either before things started running well. I don't have a top tier GPU either.

This game is great. The bug battles have a good sense of scale and feel like you're in the movie or the short lived TV show. I especially love the carnage system and how the piles of bugs change the terrain and how chaotic things can get. A lot of people compare this to HD2 and I see why, but it feels like it pulls more deliberate inspiration from Deep Rock Galactic. Overall I recommend the game and I hope the devs really nail the roadmap plans and build upon this game.

I love walking simulators and for two thirds of the game Scorn is just that. You explore a beautiful world, solve simple puzzles and try to fathom what on earth is going on. Is it even earth? Are we a human? Graphics are okay, the game mainly shines through the art style and liveliness of the environment. For some movement and progression might feel slow from time to time, but if you expect a game that is made for exploration this feels just right. Overall the game is a bit on the short side, less than 5 hours looking into every path there is. It definitely feels like there is more to tell and it was cut short.

But why isn't it recommendable? Well, sadly the middle part of the game brings combat. Some of the worst combat I've played in a long time. It's sluggish and just not fun. Reloading takes forever and switching the weapon takes forever, while some enemies spawn behind you or have attacks that track you around a corner before you can hit them. There is also a weird kill animation lock during which enemies can still attack you. I stopped playing the game twice during this part. I came back twice to finally finish it, as I wanted to see where it goes. If you're in it, the third part is worth going through the combat part (there is even a nice boss fight, which works way better than all the other combat in the game). But otherwise I cannot recommend to start playing this game. Frustration will hit you. Better watch a video of it.

review_text:
Disappointing.

Shadow Tactics is immensely well-designed and well-polished but nothing overcomes a fundamental flaw: The entire game is trying a tactic, then reloading a save when it fails. Now, many players do this in many types of games. A lot of stealth games are built on precision and people cheese it by reloading checkpoints. But Shadow Tactics is SPECIFICALLY DESIGNED for reloading checkpoints constantly.

I want to like the game but I can't help but feel like the solution to many issues is some insane rube goldberg equivalent of mechanics all stacked on top of each other and it requires at least 5-8 reloads before you figure that out. 

I didn't get very far, but it wore thin very quickly.

I'd wait a few more months to see if they manage to polish out the mechanics and the gameplay loop before recommending this.

review_text:
After several months i decided to give this game another chance and with that heres a new review on it:

Lets start with the positives:

The new holy potatoes and trees skill finally makes it possible to survive endless blight and all the nonsense this game can repeatedly throw on your settlement.

The god wall and tower lets you have defensive structures even if you are out of building slots.

The new crystal wall finally lets you have a fighting chance against specters, no more random specter wrecking town because it phased throught walls.

And thats pretty much all what changed since last year, the negatives stayed here with us to "enjoy".


Lets start with the minor annoyances:


The villager AI is still stupid as hell, you can observe Josh who is starving skip throught the entire town full of food to go home, sleep and die of starvation. They are still doing this full-stop everything nonsense whenever magic happens and the building priority is a wack.

The skeletons are still an overpowered enemy because the only way to stop them effectively is using rock tumbler towers which are the worst you can build ingame.

Phantom Dart towers are still a waste of resources and energy. Who needs a tower what deals 8-10 damage in a game where you fight swarms of 100-200hp enemies?

Building slots are still an issue where they dont feel like natural part of the game but more like another set of artifical difficulty made just to slow you down. I strongly recommend to mod it out if you want some fun.

Artifical difficulty wise the trash system is still something what was added for the sole purpose to get needless complexity ingame. It makes no sense and it just wastes away even more building slots.

Now for the major annoyances:

Theres no endgame, you cant beat the corruption at all. Even if you play to your best ability, its impossible to get corruption out of a region. You can make the most crafty, impossible to beat defense lines and such but you still cant win just turn the game from active management to idle play.


Several of the towers are too weak and their variety is not enough for a tower defense game, the fact that the enemy is even made in a way that you need to make short kill corridors otherwise they might decide to go around it is no fun at all. Your best strategy in all maps will be to find some natural borders and then make a corridor consisting of  3 lines (III) where the middle has static towers, the sides have the rest and thats it. No variation at all.


As the population numbers increase you will soon find out that the food ecomnomy is kind of busted. Water is easy to get but if you want them to eat normally you will need 1 farm per 20 villagers but there are lot of variables and nonsesnse here and if you are not spamming your motivate land on these farms you are going to need 2-3 farms per 20 villagers. My map has 162 villagers and i needed 8 established farms just so they dont start starving.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

My best advice right now is to wait for sale if you want this game and start modding it as soon as possible because it wont gonna fix itself.

+Great art style
+Excellent soundtrack
+Good story

cons:

-Animation isn't as good as Act 1

So yeah, there are definitely plenty of issues here and it's really not as good as the excellent Act 1, but I still think it's an solid enough game that's worth checking out. (Let's hope Act 3 and 4 will still come out)

review_text:
Blood Dragon is an absolute blast.

It takes everything that made Far Cry 3 great and cranks it up to 11 with a neon-drenched, 80s-inspired aesthetic that feels like a fever dream of everything awesome about that era. From the very first moment you step into the world, you're hit with a sense of pure, unapologetic fun, and it's clear that the developers embraced the over-the-top, action-packed, and absurd nature of the '80s.

The game's storyline is both ridiculous and brilliant. You play as cybernetic commando Rex 'Power' Colt, voiced by the great Michael Biehn. The dialogue is filled with cheesy one-liners and a sense of humour that never takes itself too seriously.

The world itself is an open playground of destruction, with enemies ranging from mutant animals to futuristic soldiers, all brought to life by the game's vibrant, pixelated graphics.

The sound design is top-notch, with a soundtrack that perfectly complements the over-the-top atmosphere.

Overall, Blood Dragon Retro-Fuelled masterpiece. A love letter to ‘80s action films and video games, offering a nostalgic, action-packed experience that’s equally thrilling and hilarious. Whether you're a fan of the Far Cry series or someone who loves a good, campy action romp, this game is a must-play.

review_text:
[b]“There is hope and a kind of beauty in there somewhere, if you look for it”[/b]
[i]-A certain artist artist[/i]
[hr][/hr]

“H.R.Geiger the Game” is the shortest way one could describe [b]Scorn[/b].

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
Of course, the main draw of this title is its aesthetic, everything is biomechanical, the environment, contraptions and creatures built with bone, flesh and sinew.

Also spotting Ambiental sounds rather than a full-on soundtrack to keep you immersed in its eerie world.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The shooter elements are light and focus on bullet economy, often pushing you to avoid enemies when you can.

The puzzles are what’s required to progress from one area to the other and showcase the many biological interfacing and animation of the aesthetics.

[h1]Story[/h1]
Is there one?
You tell me as it’s almost all ambiental storytelling where everything in the environment looks suspiciously like a phallus.

But it makes you feel immersed in an alien setting where these things may be the norm for them but quite strange for us.

[h1]Downsides[/h1]

The immersion is many times broken by how unnecessary the process to access the next area is.
For example I had to pick a shelled creature from a grid place it in a tray, attach a clamp to it, put it in another machine that would cut it out of its shell, drag the creature to a hole in a wall to give it another clamp on its hand, drag it into a room where I jammed its hand into a meat console.
Why did I do all of this?
Just to open a door...
Even worse, in many cases you could’ve just squeezed through the gaps that gate you of from the next section or vault over using a very climbable surface.

Another criticism is that it didn’t fully take advantage of the setting, many times I didn’t “feel” like I was inside a biomechanical being despite looking like one.
The many elevators, flat floors, consoles, handrails, and guns made it look like the game was set in a spaceship that just happens to have an organic look to it.

The creature variety that you can interact with in the shooter part of the game is almost nonexistent and some puzzles are poorly communicated.

Also a very blueballing ending to boot, I’m sure people wouldn’t mind much some of the flaws it Scorn had a satisfying conclusion
[hr][/hr]

I don’t recommend it as a game, but I do recommend it as a way to step inside a niche artistic style and the amazing artwork contained within this title.

Also the pricetag is absolutely not worth it for what you get, put this on your wishlist and wait for a substantial discount.

review_text:
I'm only really commenting because Steam forces me to when leaving a review. Keep in mind this isn't a bash, I actually see this game having a lot of promise.

While the movement is indeed fluid and fun, and the visuals are stunning, it still lacks a lot of quality of life features to make it worth coming back to.
For example: what is each enemy? All I see is their shots following me; the only one that stood out to me so far is the Mammoth, because of how distinct -- and annoying -- it is, with its large damage and being extremely tanky.

Why is the hub portal a consumable item instead of just having the pause menu allow us to quit to the hub? Why isn't there a button to see the objectives again instead of having us commit it to memory?

Is it normal to always be dying randomly because there is nothing like at least an indicator as to where shots and enemies are coming from? Everything being glowing means it's very hard to discern between enemies and props unless you look at them against the floor or against a wall.

Why are the resources so hard to come by in a mobility shooter? Having a nimble but frail character does nothing if I can't actually shoot back at the things I'm escaping from. More than once was I forced to retreat back to the usual 'shoot from cover' kind of gameplay one sees in other FPS games just because leaving it meant I would die immediately to the unrelenting horde that does not return enough health or take enough damage from melee to justify running through.

My biggest problem is the tutorial; it only really teaches you how to control your character. All other things are meant to be figured out normally -- which is not a problem for me, honestly -- but everything happens so all at once there is barely any time to look at items, enemies and resources as separate things instead of clumping them all in one box of "shoot everything and mash interact".

GTTOD has many merits and understands its references well, and I can see how it can become a great game in the future, but right now it falls short in understanding how to tie all of those together in an enjoyable way. Especially about progression; the game has so many weapons and I barely get to see any of them because the enemies get stronger each run, and the player doesn't unless they manage to farm enough shards or get lucky with a crate. It tries to do too many things at once, to its detriment.

I fought against the decision of asking for a refund, and now I continue to play the game to accompany its development and see for myself how far it has come from the skeletal stage it is in at the time of writing.

TL;DR: A gem that you knows looks pretty but it's in desperate need of polishing.

review_text:
Reading Witchfire's devlogs a few years after seeing the trailer at The Game Awards long ago, I felt confused that they were eager to make this game as a Destiny-derived roguelite.

Having finally played the game, I'm confused that they were eager to make this game as a Destiny-derived roguelite.

What caught my eye about the first trailer was, simply put, that the sell of a shooter with souls-y presentation and mechanics felt like a novelty in the genre. High-damage enemies that have to be consciously dodged, high-impact weapons, high-caliber environments and level design, you know- something that evokes that on-edge feeling of exploring something grand and dangerous, where it's satisfying just to progress. 

Witchfire still has some of that going on, but it feels blunted by the other aspects of its design. The very obvious affinity held for Destiny is especially confusing to me, as Destiny, to me, feels almost diametrically opposed to what a good Fromsoft-styled game can offer, where even normal encounters are consistently engaging. Gunfights in Destiny often feel more like pulling weeds than having a gunfight, and honestly, it's often the same here. You have battles with fodder that are utterly mind-numbing and THEN it throws something real at you and if you're sleeping at the wheel and die there, you have to deal with a ton of fodder again by virtue of the roguelite structure, and every time you return to a level after leaving it to save your not-souls. 

The game's art in general is gorgeous, the alt-colonial dark fantasy setting is neat, but while playing I just kept wishing that the game was a more traditional singleplayer game where individual battles and explorations felt meaningful as opposed to things that would be revisited without much joy over and over again. 

I'll note in fairness that I didn't get far in Witchfire, around two hours- but there was no point in those two hours where the game really clicked for me and I went "oh, now it's getting fun." I did hear that the game was made significantly easier between its initial launch on Epic and its launch on Steam, and I wonder if I would've liked it more back then- or perhaps the opening levels were always this way. Either way, I am interested in checking out the game again at some point, maybe when it's done- but likely with very different hopes.

review_text:
I geniunely could not find a single thing NGS improved over the base game. And I tried, really.
Combat is mindless clickfest with unsatisfying feedback and less depth. The progression is boring and extremely unfriendly to beginners too, as you get every skill and mechanic from the start, instead of unlocking it gradually.
"Story" is there just for the sake of one being there, characters are bland. Funny thing is the new NGS body models have more bones and support for better animations, yet in the cutscenes the characters are extremely stiff and just stand there. Voice acting sounds forced, not a single character sounds enthusiastic.
And the worst for me personally, the graphics. Everything is this washed out slop, with million generic post-process effects layered on top. The world and architecture is bland too and looks extremely artificial and unimmersive. The central CITY is just a big tower with few vendor stalls (that are just copypasted, they didn't even try to make each stall different like in base PSO2 lol, just one out of MANY instances where the NGS team doesn't care for details). Generaly the arstyle is uninspired and goes for this "realistic" anime look, which is an oxymoron by the way. If you jump high enough you can see the whole map too, that's how small it is.
On that note, the open world is completely pointless and just adds unnecessary walking and downtime. Hub based MMO worked, why change it?
Maybe the only positive change is the improved character models, but if you want to use the newer models you have to use NGS fashion too, you only get 3 free setwear and if you want to wear anything else you have to shill out money and pray to gacha gods you roll a new outfit. Oh and if you want to buy clothing from the player market for in-game currency, you can't, you need a premium to buy from the market. yet you can in base pso2, lol.

Don't touch PSO2 NGS, it's just garbage for whales who treat it as a dress up game. If you want a game with actual GAMEplay, try the base version or just look elsewhere.

etc

review_text: Samorost 2 is a point-and-click adventure game in which you play as a gnome trying to save his dog, who was kidnapped by aliens. As a sequel to the first Samorost game, Samorost 2 does a good job of "scaling up" the first game. Still, the game remains simple enough to be accessible to casual players. There was only one puzzle I found myself getting stuck on, and I believe it was due to a bug: [spoiler]In the room with the big alien, you need to push his chair forward so he traps himself with the sticky tendril that he initially trapped the gnome with. For some reason, I wasn't able to click on his chair, and had to restart the game to fix the issue.[/spoiler] Judging by some of the comments I've seen elsewhere, this appears to be a known issue with the Steam version of the game. Single bugged puzzle aside, I feel like Samorost 2 is a solid sequel to the original game, and definitely a worth a play.

review_text:
As I am roughly 5 hours into the game. I am starting to feel like this game isn't what I thought it was. There is a sense that all this game has to offer is surface level mechanics. The charge shot is a really cool mechanic on the gun, but past that, the incredible aesthetic and atmosphere, the game truly lacks. I really wanted to like this game, especially coming off of Silent Hill 2 from Bloober. For the "true" horror game fan, I can't recommend this.

First thing that bugged me was that these creatures can't chase you past certain points on the "track". I use the word track sarcastically, because that's what I feels like you are on for most of the game. A sequence of walking, finding a split path, one way leads to the main path but has an obstruction, the second path leads to the solution of said obstruction, which would be the second thing. It was just predictable and felt like filler. Whether it was restoring paths using that time mechanism, or wandering down the second path to find a key, to then be ambushed. It all felt so predictable. I see a lot of complaints about ammo being scarce, which I don't see at all. Unless you're senselessly shooting, or not charging your shots. Are you new to horror games? I will say in this, it just feels again like filler, not really strategic. I love scarcity, but not when it that's the only real component that is used to define the game as "survival horror". It really is just an action game. 

The difficulty isn't even a thing, it's so boring. 

Walk walk walk, solve obstruction encounter, repeat.

I may have had unreasonable expectations coming off Silent Hill 2, What I guess I was hoping for was something like a Silent Hill 2 or a RE2 Remake. The option to play with ink ribbons, using saves strategically adding to the suspense of moving from a known safe area, through a hell hole, to hopefully make it to the next safe area. Or strategically using Scarce ammo to create paths in order to backtrack more efficiently. In depth puzzles, exploration. The sense of relief you get when you survive your way through an area, and finally arrive at the save room.

There has been nothing that Cronos other than aesthetic, and atmosphere, (a cool gun play idea that I felt should have been expanded on more.)  That touches the RE2 or Silent Hill 2 remakes. I know that is a tough act to follow, but I feel like the door was open to take some of those ideas and expand on them.

Rather this game just delivers a very basic experience. The moat generous way I can describe it "Baby's first 'scawy' game". 

It sucks, I really wanted to like this game.

As someone of who really enjoys horror games, this ain't it.

A shame, I really expected it was better from the dozens the positive reviews I read before trying this out!

review_text:
Scorn is definitely a unique experience.  I say experience because it's less of a traditional game and more akin to an interactive movie in a sense.  There are high points and low points, and unfortunately I feel the lows outweigh the highs, so I cannot recommend Scorn for a few reasons.  I'd really like to, but it feels like the bad just barely edges out the good.

Let's start with the good first.  The visuals are fantastically done.  Scorn shines in the artistry.  The team nailed it there.  Everything looks fantastic.  The H.R. Geiger aesthetic has not been handled better since Aliens in my opinion, and you can see the attention to detail is present everywhere.  Performance is also fantastic.  I'm playing on outdated hardware and it's very smooth.  The team made Unreal Engine 4 behave very nicely.

Sound is a bit so-so.  The effects sounds are fine, but for an atmospheric game I feel there was not enough effort spent on the soundscape.  There is some immersive ambience as opposed to music, but It just felt a bit lacking in that department.

There are puzzles that must be solved for progression, and this has its upsides and downsides as well.  In one sense, some of the puzzles are very clever in their execution.  You have to move real-world objects around to progress, not just "find key to open door", though there certainly is an equivalent of that present here.  The only really annoying puzzle is found early on where you have to slide some "eggs" around on a wall to release the correct one into a machine.  It's just a tedious variation of a "slide the blocks" puzzle.  The other puzzles do not hold your hand in any way.  You MUST figure everything out on your own.  This might be a turn-off to some players as some of the puzzles are not entirely intuitive.  There's a bit of real-world problem solving involved.  On the other hand, the progression is fairly linear so if you're stuck on something it's not to far to backtrack to figure out what you're doing wrong, and once you've solved it, you know for certain that you've solved it.

Combat is where things start to get a bit lackluster.  There are only five types of enemies - including the "boss" fight near the end, and your weapons are woefully inadequate.  For the weapons, there's a melee weapon that doubles as a key.  It can "fire" two shots before needing to recharge.  It's basically a captive piston, and it's pretty weak.  There is a pistol that can hold six shots, and it takes a long time to aim it effectively, but it's also very weak.  The shotgun is VERY powerful, but holds only three shots, and finally there is a grenade launcher.  Unfortunately by the time you get the grenade launcher you use it in exactly one fight, which happens immediately after acquiring it, and after that it's really only used to solve three environmental puzzles.  You can carry only a very small amount of reserve ammo for any weapon, and the refilling stations for health and ammo are very scarce and typically become exhausted after a single interaction.

The enemy types consist of a stationary tentacle that can fling acid at you, a crawling meat sack that will try to vomit acid on you at close range, a smaller meat sack with... baby bird wings?... that will spit a glob of acid at you VERY accurately from a distance, a larger quadrupedal meat sack that will charge like a bull and takes a full magazine from anything to put down, and finally a cybernetic monstrosity that serves as the end boss.  

The combat overall is soured by the fact that the weapons are largely ineffective against the enemies, coupled with the fact that health and ammo is incredibly scarce, so there is zero margin for error.  To fire a weapon you must hold down an "aiming" key, and for the pistol to hit with any degree of accuracy you have to STAND COMPLETELY STILL while aiming, which gives the evil little chicken things plenty of time to land one or two shots on you, which severely depletes your health.  In addition, by the time you get the pistol you're likely to be facing three enemies at a time.  Aiming takes an eternity, reloading takes an eternity, and to avoid getting hit you MUST sprint, and guess what you can't do while sprinting?  Seasoned FPS players will find this frustrating beyond belief.  Combine that with the fact that there are specific cut scenes that involve your life being drained by a full bar as part of the story progression, and if you're left with almost no health after a fight the subsequent cinematic could end you.  Fighting the boss is a bit unintuitive as well, making it easy to waste precious ammo unnecessarily.

The worst bit, however, is the ending.  It's painfully clear how the game had to be cut and its ending tacked on.  Very little is explained or made clear as to why anything is happening, and from what I've read, some of this is explained in the art book as having been kept deliberately vague, but once you get to the ending it feels like the entire thing was a colossal waste of time.  It's not simply the fact that it is a negative ending - that's a common trope within the sci-fi horror genre.  What bothered me is that it felt lazy, or at least rushed, in its execution. It's a largely empty world with very difficult and tedious combat midway through and some puzzles that can be fairly tough at times.  If you can see past the downsides the visuals are fantastically executed.  That being said, it feels a bit unfinished.  Scorn definitely needed more time to complete and a lot more polish to be what it could have been.

It's a beautiful game. I wanted to enjoy the art and storytelling stuff, but a number of horrible gameplay design elements severely detracted/distracted from my ability to appreciate it.

I eventually "figured out" the "combat" (Protip: it's just patience and avoidance, always wait and/or run away. if you're having trouble so you're rage reading neg reviews, adopt a coward's tactics and see if that helps any), but not before becoming horribly frustrated, to the point where I was no longer paying attention to the environment/atmosphere/storytelling aspects of the game (just rage-playing, which isn't good for this kind of game), and even after that, there were a few unavoidable ambushes that killed me (after getting set back and returning to that point, the encounters were rendered trivial by the newfound forsight), and that kind of thing just feels bad. I feel like the frustration and slow uptake is because of how combat and the enemies are introduced to the player? idk, not fighting felt like it should have been intuitive (infact, I played very pacifistic at first, because I felt that suited the forlorn, ruined atmosphere/vibe of the game, until I died a few times because of misunderstanding enemy/game behavior, then coming to the logical, but wrong, conclusion that the game was asking me to fight better to progress).

I loved everything except for the greasy area with the fungus enemies (Act III), but perhaps due to the frustration that place caused me, it kind of overshadowed the rest and highlighted a bunch of other elements of the game that fall short, things I might not have otherwise noticed or cared about if it hadn't so effectively pissed me off.

My playtime is abnormally high because I play this kind of game super slow, died a bunch, and left it paused for an hour while I had lunch, and played the first area again to pick up the alternate act I achievement.

It started off really strong, though I expected more intricate/difficult environmental puzzles after the opening area, that it didn't have that is fine. I also felt like it had a really strong ending (note: you MUST [spoiler]have some healing charges left after the fight in the cathedral area[/spoiler] or you're basically sol because [spoiler]the puzzle solutions after that point require you to take a bunch of damage[/spoiler], which, is honestly a cool mechanic? and I think would have been a better use of your hitpoints than the combat if explored a little better/more, but is seriously unfair because if you're not ready for it you might basically get softlocked out of the ending and have to restart the area).

Leaving a no recommend mainly because the game has plenty of positive reviews. There was a lot I loved, but more I was disappointed by. Give it a go if you think you're interested, but maybe buy it on sale.

There's a great sentimental core but the game just lacks any sort of useful interactivity. It would almost be better as an indie movie or short story.

 The main gameplay consists of mainly being an item hunt and followed by clicking through dialogue and the occasional simple puzzle. It neither has the richness of writing to make it something like a visual novel like Analogue or provide enough interactivity to tell it's story through the mechanics of the game like Gone Home.

 The visual style often conflicts with the story's more emotional moments for instance because of the 16-bit graphics characters will give items to one another by lobbing the item on the floor infront of themselves. The 16-bit RPG style does not really benefit the story and the gameplay doesn't add to the emotion. It's not that you can't make something beautiful from a limited art style but you have to use those things to your advantage. The horror game Home takes the same art style and uses the vagueness pixels can cause to create a bone chilling atmosphere for instance. It's just that To The Moon never utilizes this art style and rather it seems like an art style the developer may just be used too or rely too much of nostalgia. 

There's a lot of heart but it lacks the substance and engagement to make To The Moon shine through.

review_text:
Only about a week in so far, so I'm in the honey moon phase, so keep that in mind. Also keep in mind the main selling point of the game is the multiplayer.

In terms of SAO games this one is a breath of fresh air.  DIMPS is now 2 for 2 on their track record for making games I enjoy in this IP.  Combat definitely takes some getting used to, you can dash cancel out of your normal attacks but can't cancel out of skills or ultimate.  Ultimate isn't a problem because you have Invulnerability during the animation.  For skills, you just need to be a bit careful and not lock yourself into one during an attack, or just put some effort into positioning.

Story was IMO pretty mid, it was inoffensive but nothing that hasn't been seen before and didn't take any risks.  I'd compare it to room temperature water.  It's not bad but it's not exciting either.

Progression I am super mixed on.  I like the amount of things there are for me to unlock, and I don't mind that it's pretty grindy and slow progression wise, but for a lote of people I imagine it might be a bit of a deal breaker.
Boss Raids, and Co-Op quests have unlock requirements.  You need to have the required Player Rank, and and clear the required Co-Op quests or Boss raid to move onto the next.  Assuming you play through the whole story first, you should be somewhere in the rank 20 range, so you should be able to do the first 3 co-op quests and the first boss raid.  The problem is that the Rank requirements DRASTICALLY increase later on.  If you get bored of running the same few quests over and over, you're not gonna last long enough to unlock the 3rd boss raid.  Which is a big downside because the first 2 boss raids are static, but the 3rd rotates through what the boss will be (I somehow can't remember if it changes daily or weekly).

Now if that sounded bad to you, I have more bad news, which for me is good news because I like grinding but I understand not all do.  Each character has two Passive slots.  Each character has their own passive by default.  Raising a character to Character Rank 30, unlocks that passive to be used on all characters.  This is a problem.  Not all passives are created equal, some are basically dogwater, and some are absurd once you find out the numbers.  You'll probably want passives that benefit whoever you want to main, and for some characters, that means both of those are from other characters.  That means you'll have to level two characters you might hate playing, to build your character the way you want to.  This is a baffling decision because this means you'll have to put in the time to level two characters other than the one you're intending to main.  You also get passive BASE STAT increases at certain character ranks, so two of the same character with exactly the same gear won't perform equally, and because of how multiplicative scaling works, base stats mean a lot.  The reason all of this is a problem is because you're gimping yourself by doing this.  You get extra EXP at end of mission for doing things like getting MVP, which will be harder for you to do against players who only focuses on their mains, because they will simply be doing more damage than you possibly can, and if you're not getting MVP you're getting less EXP and that means having to do more runs of quests, and that means wasting more time.

If you've read this far you're probably willing to read a bit more, and you also might be someone who'd be able to enjoy the game despite these issues, or you're literally just me.  I enjoy super grindy slow burn types of games, so this is actually perfect for me.  I don't know how this game will pan out longterm, but currently I'm having a lot of fun slowly chipping away at stuff, ticking boxes off my checklist of things to grind out.  First 3 dlc characters are funny greatsword girl and two more characters from GGO Alternative, which I really liked so I'm excited for that.  I am able to play as a funny magic lady with big hair who can fly, shoots big lazers, drops a funny sword man on people, and is voiced by Maaya Sakamoto (Jalter and DAO my beloved).  This game doesn't cater to everyone but it certainly caters to ME SPECIFICALLY.  Obviously the game has issues, but what game doesn't in current year.  My last hopes for games to be good were ground into the dirt, poured gasoline on, and burned, by SEGA when they killed PSO2 with the slap in the face that is NGS, which I still play on occasion because I have attachment issues and get overly invested in my MMO characters.  If you play on JP I might see you, if you play NA, still might see you but not as likely.

TL:DR Game grindy, Story Mid, Multiplayer focused, Not perfect but I like it.

I had played the game on PSP before (Hakuouki: Demon of the Fleeting Blossom) and when I heard and saw from the reviews that it's similar from that game, I was hesitant on buying the game. I ended up buying the game to see the differences (still playing the game at the moment) during the sale.

I'm not entirely pleased with how it was done, but I'm hoping that the other 2 will be better.

One thing that I'd like to point out is the affection animation. I feel that it could be better. SO MUCH better. I prefer the animation in the PSP game because it's less tacky and nicer? But on this game, it feels like they stamped an image, and a sound along it and it just doesn't look nice. It doesn't ruin the game per se, but it just makes me feel meh about it. If it could be better, the game would be better.

I really adore this game, it's a very neat experience with a nice story to back it. I recommend going in as blind as possible so i won't be listing too many pros, but I have to gush about the atmosphere and sound (and lack there of at times), this game is able to create dread just from sound design alone, with graphics that are reminiscent of an old ps1 game yet it is able to look unique and fresh despite that and if you're into "liminal" feeling games this one is a must play. It's short and sweet so you can finish it one session and I mean that in a good way, I feel if this game was any longer it would have been a worse experience.

My only cons for this game are:
- some of the elements don't work exactly as intended at times (nothing a quick minute or two fix doesn't fix), these problems aren't that common since the game has been updated to work with more modern machines but as with any game that messes with files things sometimes can go wrong (and in my case did) which can break some immersion
-  there isn't much replay value being a sort of "gimmicky" narrative driven game so once you've experienced the full game and story once there isn't much reason to go back. 

With that being said though, I highly recommend this especially for only $4 amazing experience. 
Make sure to play late at night with all the lights off 😈

review_text:
TLDR; The game is mediocre. Arizona and its DLCs were much better, quality wise. 

In Arizona the zombies felt like a threat and you felt like you a had purpose. Here the zombies (that look more like snow aliens with giant heads) are uninspired and are just cannon fodder, they are only a threat due to their numbers. The gameplay is not satisfying, you don't get any sense of achievement. You're just glad when the wave is over and can move to the next location where you'll just repeat the whole process, grinding your way through the waves of uninspired levels and enemies. 
It's pretty much the opposite of what Arizona was. Arizona had depth and charm due to its story, level design and sense of danger created by the enemies. The Devs should have improved on what made the first game a hit, expanding the story, the levels, weapon and enemy variation. This is just a bad L4D ripoff with zero innovation or interesting features. I'm not even addressing the grind required for the unlocks. The only good feature to me is the localized damage on the zombies, which is well done, but it's not nearly enough to compensate all the other flaws. 
If you want to shoot zombies solo or coop, you're much better of playing Arizona Sunshine, it's a much superior game at every level.

Edit: Just to make my point, after playing half an hour of Arizona, I stopped to buy all the DLCs, because I could already tell that the game was a lot of fun and that the devs succeeded at creating a really good zombie shooter. Playing After the fall, I couldn't even force myself to finish the first level as I was already bored after the second wave of enemies.  It's also important to note that it's not nostalgia, as I am a fairly new VR player.

I tried to give that game a chance. I tried to like it. But it has way too many cons to close eyes at. 

Pros:
1.Nice art style
2. You can switch off some annoying mechanics like food rotting or tools breaking.

Cons:
1.	Not much activities. Its not that much you can do in game. Crops, animals, cooking, fishing, tree shaking, gathering, speaking with NPC. And that’s it. It’s just not much things to be done. So, it leads to:
2.	Boring and repetitive. Wake up, water plants, walk around all locations shaking every tree, go to mine to hit 3 spots, speak with every NPC to find what in stock, optionally fish, rinse and repeat. Again. And again. EVERY. DAY. I feel like a hero of Groundhog Day. 
3.	For a game about “relations” NPCs are completely lacking of personality. They don’t have story arcs, intersecting quests, characteristics to remember, preferences etc. They are just paper dolls to move around. The only thing to remember about them is that they have so much personality that every playthrough then will marry random NPCs no matter their gender. For me that smashed game atmosphere to pieces that are beyond repair. 
4.	First attempt ended in spring year 1 with half village dead from disease that CANNOT BE CURED. On second attempt I nearly have half of village dead from disease until I switched that mechanics off. Because I got character whom I planned to marry ill. I tried loading earlier saves. Very earlier saves… No, result was always one and the same – after a market day everyone became ill. No matter what. And you cannot prevent that. You cannot even buy and give NPC a cure. Or they die, or you switch disease mechanics off. Very “funny” to play.

review_text:
Here are several of the critical issues I noticed in this game:
- Multiple currencies used for purchasing items in-game, AC and SG. Classic money-layering obfuscation tactic that should be illegal, with the sad industry standard practice for these things of having items cost just slightly more or less than the denominations of currency that are purchased to try getting you to buy more, and even worse many being basically gambling for a chance at an item.
- Being that this is an RPG it has a sort of talent or skill point system, many MMO players might expect some friction to respec-ing, but will be shocked this game will require you spend real-life money on an in-game currency (500 AC=$5 USD) to buy a secondary talent tree to then utilize for resetting talent trees by spending the other in-game currency (100SG=500ac=$5USD) for a reset pass on the newly purchased "un-set" tree and repeating the second step of this process-and payment-each time you need to reset a class' skill tree. That practice inexcusably abusive, and can only be somewhat overlooked by virtue of how universally shallow the skill trees are currently. SEGA gave out reset passes a few times in the past, but as of the last couple major updates has decided not to, so relying on them would really leave you out to dry if you were to mis-click and accept a bad spec or wanted to change things up when new skills are added in a big update.
- Nearly all the unique fashion/fashion accessories that allow for the much lauded character customization aspect of this game require "scratching" using one of the secondary currencies (AC + SG) for a chance at winning it from a pool of prizes in typical Gacha fashion. Similarly you must also spend money to obtain secondary currency (SG) to make adjustments to your character's physical appearance and the colors of your outfits each time (Color Change Pass, Salon Pass) 
-The market is established in such a way that the actual in-game, in-world currency of Meseta is primarily obtained by selling the fashion items bought with real money on the player market--a market which can only be accessed with purchase of a player shop pass which costs real money. The F2P experience is a 3day pass, once a month, obtained by completing dailies for approximately a week or two. Because doing activities in-game yields only slightly more than not playing the game altogether, your only real chance at obtaining the fashion items is spending real money for AC to then "scratch" aka Gacha RNG slot machine mechanics.
-The game is infected with RNG mechanics that are clearly deliberate as a means of impeding player progress to encourage real-money purchases.  Once you spend the often absurd amount of time to obtain 10x of a rare capsule obtained via RNG drops with extremely low rates, you'll see the max probability of success to affix it will sometimes be as low as 70%. Because of the nature of RNG, even at 95% you can fail multiple times losing the item and any success rate booster items, and aside from that, there's literally nothing to say the game isn't lying about this probability number either as they would have every incentive to do so, to get you "scratching" with real money for a chance at obtaining a 100% chance addi capsule relevant to your class, or maybe purchasing the augment protection by "recycling" the duplicates of items you spent real money on. There are also "add-on skills" in which you are effectively spending Meseta to gamble in hopes of getting a bonus level of what, in any other game including the base PSO2 game, would have been basic class stat bonuses or skill tree options. RNG to get the gear to drop(which you can improve by paying real money for "Rare Drop Rate +x% booster" items), RNG to get the capsules to upgrade the gear, RNG gamble to use the capsules to upgrade the gear, then more RNG gambling to upgrade base stats.
-Inventory is limited, with options for paid expansion. Any items dropped outside of Urgent/Limited/Trainia Quests, basically the majority of the game, will be automatically picked up with no -free- options to stop this from happening. Naturally, the game will drop such a plethora of items that often do not stack, and increase with each event and new region, so as to inconvenience and frustrate you into investing real money into expanding your inventory and storage. Fully upgrading your inventory will cost you about 40 USD. Fully upgrading your "Character Storage"-basically like a bank from WoW- will cost you around 120 USD. You can also rent storage blocks out for various time allotments, 30-90 days for 5 to 12 dollars, respectively. There's a lot of complexity to the storage situation but ultimately none of it would be necessary if not for the poor handling of item drops and forced pickup, which is clearly intentional. There's also a paid auto-sell feature, but it has been rendered useless twice (removal of most drops in Kvaris, then Introduction of Gold/Silver PSEf burst inv flood) and ultimately you're still going to need more storage for holding the various items you'll want/need or you will need to more regularly stop during combat to clear space to prevent potentially losing items.
-Almost every update consists of more gacha fashion items to gamble real money away for than any sort of meaningful content to play within the game, which is something the game desperately and glaringly needs. Watch any of the official PSO update videos they release to see this on full display. 
-There are clearly traps intended to have you spend money for poor/non-existent value items and services in the game. Every death you're offered the chance to buy a scape doll to revive for 100AC/$1USD, Rare Drop rate boosters starting from 800AC/$8USD which you have no way of knowing is actually doing anything-a placebo-since purported rate boost while seemingly large (+100%) is multiplicative against an infinitely minute number, although it's also believed by many to not directly improve the drop rate of rares specifically, and instead the rate chance of drops altogether which would to some degree as well increase the chance of a rare dropping--ultimately extremely convoluted and dishonest system of dubious benefit which expires even when you're doing nothing or logged out. Like a casino selling you a lucky rabbit's foot at the entrance for a few hours.
I'm sure I've missed some things, but I felt it was important that this was highlighted in a review for any would-be player. This is the product of companies hiring pyschologists onto dev teams and papers being published on how to manipulate vulnerable people into spending money. It has been woven into the fabric of this game, which by its lineage should simply have been a 3D verson of a Diablo clone in a sci-fi world inherited from the old Phantasy Star games like the original on Dreamcast. Apart from the critical issues I noted, the game has many glaring gameplay/user experience flaws all of which are probably due at least in part to this focus on monetization above all else. The idea of establishing a fun gameplay loop, with a rewarding payout for time invested as is typical of RPGs with character progression, is almost non-existent. Nothing as yet worth even trying to build a character up for, since the end-game can only be doing what you did to originally build the character up: best analogy would be like leveling up in WoW only to grind mobs in the open world and do dailies-no raids, no dungeons, no interesting loot or gear that comes from any specific place/boss or lore tying any of anything in the barren world together. Every kill just a pull on the slot machine, there aren't any unique named npcs or enemies anywhere in the open world and rare enemies are merely silver/gold colored normal enemies. Items you get are literally just stats, no flavor text, no descriptions whatsoever, no importance or value given to them. Complete degeneration, degredation of the PSO/Phantasy Star brand. Truly saddening.

review_text:
Scorn is an apt game given how the name makes me feel.

It's the perfect example of someone convincingly telling a team of environmental artists "Hey, let's make a Giger inspired game!" and everyone going "Yeah!". And that's about as far as it goes.
Off you go, crafting some genuinely stunning environments, full of Giger's bio-mechanical architecture and weirdly horrific sexual statues. Plus some gratuitous gore, deformed fleshy bodies, torture and lots of sphincter penetration.

The game plays out entirely as "there's this weird thing you see is interactable but can't interact with. Keep walking, find another weird thing you can interact with. Go back and interact with the thing. This opens a door with a long corridor with some more meaningless lever things. Repeat for 5 hours."; well, that, and absolutely atrocious combat, with needlessly slow and clunky walking, aiming and reloading. And don't get me going on the amount of time that the death animation takes and how the checkpoint is often before cutscenes.

The game is padded beyond description - which is a huge feat for a 5 hour game.

It's unfortunate that I am being so negative, but everything in the game was just a hurdle with no payoff. There's nothing interesting.

The game is beautiful, it's great to walk around in. But that's about it. 
And, honestly, it's not even the kind of art that benefits from having a full 3D environment. You can get about as much awe from the screenshots as you get from playing the game - I would say games like Manifold Garden or Naissance are the opposite, spaces in which walking around feels different from static screenshots.
The sound design is "ok", but nothing stellar or surprising.
And even the artstyle is entirely derivative of Giger. So... maybe go and get HR Giger ARh+ from OpenLibrary?

The gameplay is pure padding and the combat really terribly designed. Playing itself was seemingly unending frustration.

With that in mind, if you think that's okay and the screenshots appeal to you, go ahead and get it.

review_text:
I bought this game yeaaaars ago on the Sony PSP. It was my first ever otomege and it had a different name back then: Hakuoki: Demon of the Fleeting Blossom.

I'm glad to see that there are many more love interests in this revised version of Hakuoki. In the PSP version (Fleeting Blossom), you're able to play the entirety of the storylines within one game, rather than separating them into Kyoto Winds and Edo Blossoms. I do understand that if they didn't split it into a prequel and sequel, the gameplay length would be EXTREMELY long, due to the fact they added much more details to the characters and story backgrounds compared to Fleeting Blossoms. But it is precisely BECAUSE I played the storylines straight through in Fleeting Blossom, playing Kyoto Winds felt very not satisfying at all.

However, I have no doubt that if you're a first timer playing this game in general, you would be amazed with the beautiful characters, scenery, as well as the detailed history along with the fantastical element of Furies and Demons. 

 It is nice though to replay the OG LI routes though, because when I was playing, I kept remembering how I used to turn all my lights off, with my blanket hovered over my head, ready to pretend that I was sleeping if my hear my parents walking to the bathroom in the middle of the night. Very nostalgic haha. I have yet to play Kazue, Ryouma, and Chikage's routes because I've been playing this game for 40 hours straight. No doubt in my mind that I'll be done with these three routes if I were to spend 6-7 more hours on this, but I can't. I need a break from the heavy history hahahaha.

But as of now...
Best boy for me: Heisuke
Favorite routes to play: Saito and Heisuke

review_text:
Tape To Tape is an absolute gem and is probably the best hockey game on the market currently with a promising roadmap and passionate devs but there are definitely some things i would add/change.

- position lock camera that follows the player instead of the puck if they are position locked because i often find myself getting stuck when i am out of view of the camera since i pretty much exclusively play this way.

- would love a skill stick for toe drags, dekes, and other moves for more creative goals because currently it kinda feels like a 1 timer spam meta.

- AI needs improvement specifically defense because currently almost every play is an odd man rush and even if they do backcheck they just continuously skate backwards and won't even try to break up the play which leads to a point blank shot in the slot or a wide open cross crease

- offsides should be a rule in this game because every game there is always someone on the opposing team camping the offensive zone just waiting for a sauce pass from all the way up the ice which leads to way to many breakaways.

- more modes such as shootout mode, career mode, or maybe even some silly side modes such as zamboni mode or referee mode where you can sabotage the game.

- ONLINE CO-OP PLEASE!

Like i said this game is very promising and this is a very short list of negatives/wants next to a long list of positives. I can not wait to see how this game grows and i plan to be there every step of the way.
