review_text:
A mixed bag of a horror game. 

Created by Glen Schofield, the creator of Dead Space and developed by his new studio, Striking Distance, The Callisto Protocol was meant to be the spiritual successor to Dead Space, ushering in a brand new Triple-A horror IP in a era where survival horror is rarely seen in the Triple-A space. Unfortunately, we got Dead Space at home and after a disastrous PC launch and the fallout of both negative critic and player reviews, we are left with a horror title that could've been so much more but unfortunately ended up as a mediocre dud.

Pros:

Visuals are great across the board, the game runs on Unreal Engine 4 and there's been a incredible amount of care of bringing this world to life as everything from the cold, overwhelming darkness of Black Iron Prison, the game setting to the frozen wasteland of the prison's outside areas help to create a genuinely tense and horrifying atmosphere and with the right settings on PC, the game can look stunning at times. 

The all-star cast on display here is also great like Josh Duhamel who plays the game's main protagonist, Jacob Lee or Sam Witwer who plays one of the main antagonists in the story. Even the smaller roles still shine here, all delivering some good performances with the script that they're given here. 

Unfortunately, this is where the positives end. 

Cons: 

The gameplay of The Callisto Protocol is extremely dull and boring as hell as the game's central focus on melee combat with very little deviation of the formula itself makes every fight feel samey and not scary or tense in the slightest. Here's how most combat encounters go, you walk up to an enemy with your baton out, whack them with it, then they block it or dodge it then you have to evade their attacks using the A or D keys, it does not matter which direction it is, just hold these keys and then return back to whacking them until they fall over dead. Rinse and Repeat for 8 hours straight until the credits roll. Some fights may force you to use a gun every once in a while but the same strategy still remains of dodge attacks and then shoot them some more till they fall over dead. There's one part of the game where they reuse the same mini-boss four times in a single section and it's so BORING. Deadass, who thought that was a good idea? Due to this, combat gets extremely boring as the game rarely tries to spice things up or give you something more interesting to do like puzzles for example. There is a upgrade system but it only helps to make the combat even more dull with the benefit of making combat encounters go by faster. 

The story is everything you expect from a modern horror sc-fi game and with very little punches pulled and every twist you  can see coming from a mile away. While the acting is good, the characters here are bland with very little going on in their respective stories with everyone pretty much spelling out their motivations and with very little nuance or mystery behind their decisions. It's bad when I can relate to Issac Clarke, a silent protagonist from the 1st Dead Space more than a professionally voiced main character throughout the game's 8 hour playtime. It makes for a story that at it's best feels like everything you've seen before in much better games and movies and at it's worst, it's something that leaves you bored and wanting everything to end as fast as possible. 

The horror is extremely lacking here which is damning for any horror title. It's like forgetting your job description while you're still at work. Everything scary here feels like everything you've seen before and done better like the story. For example, Dead Space did space zombies better with the Necromorphs than the Callisto Protocol's Biophages. While the atmosphere here is great, the game's focus on lazy jumpscares, heavy focus on gore, and the extremely boring combat brings that atmosphere crashing down with not much else to replace it with. Nothing here feels distinct and that's my biggest problem with the entire game. It's this heavy feeling of "been there, "done that" that made me feel bored rather than tense and excited to see what the game had in store and that feeling sucks.

Verdict:
The Callisto Protocol was a big disappointment especially coming from someone who was excited for this game and wanted a developer to take up Dead Space's mantle again and give us something new in the sc-fi horror space. Instead we got Dead Space at home with a developer desperately trying to recapture that same spark that Dead Space had but with none of the quality that came with it. I really hope that someone else takes up the dead space mantle and gives something completely unique rather than a big, boring slog of a game to go through while failing to take notes from it's original source. 

5/10. P.S, Wait for a deep sale or buy Dead Space Remake if you're looking for a good sc-fi survival game.

review_text:
[i]Unique.

Adjective: being the only one of its kind; unlike anything else.
Particularly remarkable, special, or unusual.
Belonging or connected to one particular person, group, or place.

.....

"Belonging or connected".....

Connections.... Lines.... 

"Emshen"... He who sees the Lines... Draws the Lines... Makes connections.[/i]

.

When I started Pathologic 2, I thought I was playing the role of the character Artemy Burakh, and I took for granted the notion that this was a "role-playing game", and could affect a certain level of control over the world I was inhabiting by means of the choices I made--choices that were, as a surgeon, very literally matters of life and death... But eventually, I learned that even a doctor administering treatment to the sick (though he may very well determine whether his patient lives or dies) is still subject to the [i]Lines.
 
.

A line is a path, a direction, a singular course. From past to future, from here to there...

A line connects all points having a specified common property

A line is the precise demarcation of a boundary, a notional limit, a way of thinking...[/i]

.

He performs surgery by the very act of cutting [i]Lines[/i] into a body: Should he perform his Lines well, he will be known to the Steppe folk as [i]Emshen[/i]--"Knower of Lines"--or he can (both literally and figuratively) [i]butcher them[/i]. The Steppe folk have a word for this too: [i]Yargachin[/i]. It designates Artemy by his profession as a surgeon, but the word also means "butcher", as in, someone who simply cuts up the meat of a living being. And so the the distinction is made between cutting haphazardly into meat and performing surgery.
 
[i]A Line is drawn.[/i]

It's not an accident that the word chosen to refer the player's path (i.e. the [i]Line[/i] one follows through the unfolding of events)--is the very same word used to refer to an actor's dialogue within a theatrical production.

It turns out that Pathologic 2 is indeed a role-playing game, but only in the same way that an actor in a stage production also [i]plays a role[/i]: He has no real say in the unfolding of the events of the play, nor even in his own part therein, but he is nonetheless given the opportunity to embody the character and give expression to his part.

[i]Try not to butcher your Lines, Yargachin...[/i]

This, ultimately, is the lesson of Pathologic 2. In fact, this is the explicitly-stated philosophical underpinning of the entire game. The developers even tell you this directly through the fourth wall, via the character of Mark Immortell, the stage director. He literally tells you these things to your face--repeatedly, in fact, every time you die--but it wasn't until I had already sunk several dozen hours into the game before I fully considered the scope of what his words meant: that no matter what I did or what I said, the outcome would always be the same; that although I could not [i]overcome[/i] death, or [i]transcend[/i] it, I could [i]achieve mastery over it.[/i] The difference between performing surgery and cutting haphazardly into meat. 

[i].

He who follows the Lines needs not know of their existence; his path is still preordained.

The play remains the same. The role of an actor remains the same.
 
All he can do... is know the Lines.[/i]

.

Initially, I was disappointed with the lack of agency I had while playing, particularly when it came to dialogue interactions. I would save, enter into dialogue with a character, and come out of the interaction feeling like the choices I had made and the things I had said had produced a tangible outcome in the world. But when I would reload my file, re-enter the same conversation, and choose different dialogue options, I would [i]produce the exact same outcome[/i]. It bothered me that what we said to each other ultimately had no effect on what we did. It felt like what would otherwise be a source of agency, or even a system to be gamed in order to produce a desired outcome, was actually completely ineffectual.

Upon reflection, I'm not sure this is such a bad thing... Much of the game seems poised to instill a sense of futility; why should the dialogue sequences be any different? After all, the people who inhabit the world of Pathologic lie to you and mislead you and distract you with all kinds of wild goose chases and false promises.... So why should I believe that anything I could say could really make a difference here? Maybe this is the developer's commentary on the emptiness of words and the primacy of action; a slap in the face of players who believed that they could simply achieve their goals by assembling the right combination of utterances, the fools (like me) who tried to phrasemonger themselves into a happy ending...

It is through painstaking realizations such as this that Pathologic forces everyone it comes into contact with to re-evaluate their preconceived notions of what it means to play a video game.

[i]What even is a game?[/i]
 
At its most fundamental level, a game is just a closed system of variables with which players can interact in order to achieve a win state. Pathologic 2 fulfills this description, of course, but it is [i]so[/i] much more than that. On the surface, the system of variables that Pathologic employs are primarily immersive sim-style survival mechanics: Your character needs to eat, sleep, and take medicine when sick. This system is absolutely "gamed", but it is also simultaneously working on a deeper level: Pathologic uses these game elements as vehicles to force the player into simulating extreme, even apocalyptic survival situations. The moral weight of these situations are treated with an incredible level of acuity: Questions of the soul, morality, violence, trauma, desperation, perseverance, authority, truth... these are the real preoccupations of Pathologic 2.

I know what you're thinking: A walking simulator that's more concerned with getting the player to philosophize than to actually play a game sounds heavy-handed and pretentious as hell.
 
[i]But it isn't.[/i]
 
The game isn't pretentious, or pompous, or blowing hot air. Not even a little bit. In fact, much the opposite. It is frequently tongue-in-cheek, and well aware of its own absurdity. It asks only that the player make decisions and then deal with the consequences... or, worse yet, to reckon with the fact that the decisions they made had absolutely no effect whatsoever on the outcome.

I'm finalizing this review on the 10th of July, 2024--a full year after having last played Pathologic 2. And yet, I continue to think about this game. I'm writing this right now because, even 12 months later, I [i]can't help[/i] but think about it. It is completely unlike anything else within the gaming world, whether digital or tabletop, and has left an indelible mark upon me. Pathologic 2 is a work of art. It elevates video gaming as a form. 

It is completely unequaled in the world of video games for a work to be so high-minded and philosophically ambitious; to directly inform the player of its lofty goals through the fourth wall, and then achieve said goals in spectacular fashion.
 
Pathologic 2 is totally distinct among its peers.

A singular experience.

[i]Unique.[/i]

review_text:
Such a terrible step-down when comparing the game to Just Cause 3. 

The gameplay:
The controls FEEL terrible. They could've literally copy-paste 3's control's one to one and have the game handle itself much better. Something about this game feels very, very off. I can't really put this into words, but i'll describe at like this: In Just Cause 3 when you parachute, wing suit and grapple the game's world works with you and lets you glide across it smoothly. Here - to me, it feels like you have to fight it to move across. 
The game's world feels very bland to me and doesn't speak much volume as 3 did. feels like a bad redo of Just Cause 2's world and nothing is very unique. 
Explosions feel somehow worse than Just Cause 3 and 2 and the combat is about the same as 3's - though, enemies sometimes have insane aim hitting you with surgery precision in literal mud water or can't do anything standing there while you're in front of them.

Graphics: 
I don't know how they messed this up, really. The game again compared to 3's graphics looks TERRIBLE. As typing this will be very painful, I just recommend you see comparisons between 3 and 4, absolutely awful.

Performance: 
I have an RTX 3060Ti paired with an i7 12700f with 16Gb of 3200Mhz RAM.
This is by no means a top-notch setup, but it is well beyond to at least allow the game to run at 1440p, 120-100 FPS. But I can't, not at least at a steady 100. There's way too much stuttering and random FPS drops. The game slows to a crawl of 70-50 FPS at big fights, when shooting an RPG (I honestly don't know why) and at random. Weird.

And finally, the story: It's terrible.
The games takes itself way too seriously and most characters are completely forgettable and unfunny. step down from 3's action-comedy style story, It doesn't let you get as attached to characters here.
There aren't any funny tropes to characters that captivate you from the start or anything interesting really. Honestly skip the story when playing.

Overall, though - the game is fun at its core. It is just a huge step-down from 3 and If you don't have the money, don't buy this game and get 3 now instead, as when it is on sale, it's like 5-11 dollars.

review_text:
Difficult at first while your character's at a lower level, but once you learn how to use all of your movement abilities - double jump, slide, dodge - and find a couple guns that suit your playstyle, it's a genuinely incredible single-player FPS to pass time.

- Very well optimized, especially for its graphical fidelity
- Gunplay and weapon animations are butter smooth
- Movement system is remarkably well designed, especially the character inertia and air control.
- AI isn't perfect, but provides enough combat variety and genuinely interesting enemies to not feel lacking.
- Progression slows down as you level, but never feels too slow; in particular because your character level (the one that gets harder to level as it goes up) is independent from acquiring and upgrading items, neither of which take longer as you level, as well as world level (the thing that actually determines the in-game difficulty).

This game has the best atmosphere I have seen. A grotesque and strange world that is like a H.R. Giger fever dream. However this game is niche, and is primarily for those who would enjoy the world and atmosphere. the puzzles are just another way to interact with the world and see its strangeness, and the story purposely has a huge factor of unknown weirdness that is never solved. review_text:
[h1] The Best SAO Game [/h1]

[b] What I Liked [/b]

I'll start this off by saying the point of the game isn't the story.  The story isn't bad.  There are only so many ways stories in SAO can play out.  The story is the only way they could justify bringing in characters from the anime over.  That being said, if you're a fan of SAO, then you'll like the story.

The combat is where the game shines.  I've tried a few SAO games over the years, and none of them felt quite right.  This one though makes me feel like I'm in SAO.  The characters move and play like they would in SAO.  The enemies behave as if they are their counterparts in the anime.  The combat is great.

Of course, the point of the game is the grind.  It's a huge, huge grind.  It's all about leveling up and grinding for gear.  Doesn't make it bad at all.  With 21 characters, there is a ton to grind for.

The graphics are good, and again, I feel like I am in SAO.  I wish more locations from the anime were in the game, but it's good for what it does.

[b] What I Did Not Like [/b]

I'm an old guy, so the game hurts my hands after awhile.  There is a bunch of button mashing.  More than likely I'll have to give it up because it's too hard on my hands.

Playing online is the primary point of the game.  Doing co-op dungeons and boss fights.  The problem is that will get boring after awhile since there isn't a huge variety of areas.  The other issue is that the player population is low, and half the time bots filled in for a live person.  But, they were decent bots who fulfilled their role decently enough.

Day one DLC is also a downer, along with microtransactions.  They aren't required though.

[b] Why I Stopped Playing [/b]

Haven't yet, expect I will once it bothers my hands too much and I tire of the grind.

[b] Disclaimer [/b]

I have been a gamer for over 30 years.  I tend to play mostly PC games.  I also bounce around between games A LOT.  I may purchase a $60 game and play it for 2 hours or spend $10 on a game and spend 50 hours on it.  Even if I played a game a short time, it does not mean it is bad.  It just means another game caught my attention.  I also complain about flaws in games a lot, even about the littlest of things.  Keep that in mind when reading my reviews.  If I do not have a complaint, then the game must be special!

PSO2 Base: It is good to come back to this game and enjoy online play finally. My original intro to the series was on Gamecube for PSO.

I am an MMO player and a MOBA player. This game is very cool. I played the heck out of it, and as long as I am not focusing on 1 thing too much, i find the general growth pacing satisfying and rewarding.

NGS: I also feel that the System's and Utility features offered in the shop are valuable, and don't seem tacked on in any way. I am especially fond of Batch Movement and the re-done menus. Crafting has been revamped and makes a lot of sense now. The growth and pacing are balanced so that you're always going to find people who are willing to purchase your materials for their gear! And finishing a piece of equipment is also satisfying.

Combat feels very fluent and requires practice to utilize. There are always several more ways to increase your Battle Power. There's always something you can work on to get more and more power.

If you should decide to pay for in game currency, you aren't overwhelmed with so many different kinds of currencies as in other MMO's that the value of your Purchased Currency doesn't diminish with newer added types of currencies.

While it isn't perfect, yet... It is a very well put together game and borrows elements from both Phantasy Star RPG games and Phantasy Star Online games. The union of the 2 game styles hasn't been fully embraced by patrons of the PSO series, and you will get some variation in opinions of New Genesis. For me, coming from other MMO's and having been an avid RPG gamer for handhelds... I assure you this is a very polished concept for a game!

It has great potential. I can't wait to see what the Funding Boost is going to provide for us in the future!

review_text:
Oof, Lost Ruins is a Game alright.
But in my opinion not a good one.
This Game is kind of a Metroidvania Light with (badly implemented) Souls and "Survival" Elements and it just isn't fun, actually it is a frustrating mess.
I can forgive that a little bit because after seeing the Credits, I think only 2 people really worked on it (disregarding the Localization Teams here) but if a Game is bad, it's bad.

So the first thing you will notice is the extremely annoying sound the "Character Talk Box" makes. This is the first impression. Then you will notice good Pixel Art. It is just that, good, not the best ever but it kinda has it's own chunky style.

The next thing I personally noticed was extremely annoying. I played with a Gamepad, but when I switched to my Keyboard (for opening the Steam Overlay or for going to Desktop) the displayed controls in Game would switch constantly (!) between Gamepad and Keyboard and the only solution is to restart the Game and also: NEVER touch your Keyboard while playing.
Second thing I disliked (I at first thought the Game was buggy) was when an Achievement Notification would pop up but basically it only tells you, that you have fulfilled one step to get the full Achievement. Found it kind of annoying and also useless.

The Music was also kind of meh. More bad than good. More annoying than hooking me. (You see where this is going? There is so much ANNOYING stuff here and that's not all, the worst things I will tell you about next.)

I think this Game does not know what it wants to be, this is a perfect example of an identity crisis. 

- The Game has Souls Elements with slow and "deliberate" combat but it just feels clunky as hell. The Controls don't feel good. Then there are the enemies. Oh boy is this one frustrating Game. Normal enemies can be a pain to kill. I played most of the Game with a Zweihänder (yes, you write it like that) and the enemies are just unfair. The Zweihänder is VERY slow and in the time you attack, most enemies still have longer reach than you and can SPAM their attacks like CRAZY without ever stopping. Of course you are free to use other Weapons/Ranged Weapons/Spells, but everything feels kind of bad here.
Then there are the bosses which are laughably easy. Every Boss has 2-3 Phases (Normal Phase, Big B**b Phase and sometimes a "funny" Phase were you can just kill them easily) and most of them have only 3-4 Attack Patterns which are extremely easy to counter. Also they take a ton of Damage and are down real quick.

- Then there is the Metroidvania Element but the Game fails here as well. There is no real progression (apart from getting a LITTLE more health or getting new Items for new "Builds") here. No Double Jumps, no Dashes, no nothing. The Level Design is also extremely BORING and lazy. There are almost NO secrets to find and no branching paths and backtracking is also rarely if not ever needed. Basically you start on the left side, then go right aaaaall the way, then go up after a boss, go left aaaall the way, go up, go right and so on. This is the basic design here with VERY few variations (sometimes you go down also...).
Platforming when it happens: Also bad. Either you are in a very small space and bump your head or you are outside and jump on a few platforms, it's not really needed here but also not very well implemented.

I read some of the positive and some of the negative reviews on here and I actually agree with most of the negative reviews. 
Another thing: Savepoints and Checkpoints don't restore your health/mana, you have to consume items for that or just play like I did with a ton of regen-Gear.

Storywise it's stupid. So is the dialogue. Just wow, what is that even? Can't and don't want to describe this.
(And what's with all the big b**bs on the bosses?)

Well, my first playthrough took 5.9 hours, only got 12/40 Achievements. In good Games/Metroidvanias/Soulslikes I would want to jump back in to get more Achievements and to see a different ending. Not here. I am just glad it is over. Especially because for some Achievements you have to torture yourself through the whole Game again, grind/farm a lot and/or play different Game Modes.
I literally have 0 interest in that.

So yeah, if you are a REALLY REALLY big fan of Metroidvanias/Souls-Adjacent Games and you need to play everything, MAYBE you will get a kick out of this, for everyone else who just wants a good Game: Stay Away!

then there is the metroidvania element but the game fails here as well. there is no real progression apart from getting a little more health or getting new items for new builds here. no double jumps, no dashes, no nothing. the level design is also extremely boring and lazy. there are almost no secrets to find and no branching paths and backtracking is also rarely if not ever needed. basically you start on the left side, then go right aaaaall the way, then go up after a boss, go left aaaall the way, go up, go right and so on. this is the basic design here with very few variations sometimes you go down also... . platforming when it happens also bad. either you are in a very small space and bump your head or you are outside and jump on a few platforms, it's not really needed here but also not very well implemented. i read some of the positive and some of the negative reviews on here and i actually agree with most of the negative reviews. another thing savepoints and checkpoints don't restore your health mana, you have to consume items for that or just play like i did with a ton of regen-gear. storywise it's stupid. so is the dialogue. just wow, what is that even? can't and don't want to describe this. and what's with all the big b bs on the bosses? well, my first playthrough took 5.9 hours, only got 12 40 achievements. in good games metroidvanias soulslikes i would want to jump back in to get more achievements and to see a different ending. not here. i am just glad it is over. especially because for some achievements you have to torture yourself through the whole game again, grind farm a lot and or play different game modes. i literally have 0 interest in that. so yeah, if you are a really really big fan of metroidvanias souls-adjacent games and you need to play everything, maybe you will get a kick out of this, for everyone else who just wants a good game stay away!

The original BioShock is one of the greatest games ever made, a true work of art that remains just as powerful today as it was at release. Rapture is not just a setting, it is one of the most charismatic and iconic cities in gaming history, a decayed utopia dripping with atmosphere and personality. Exploring its ruined halls, listening to the echoes of its former glory, and piecing together its fall is an experience unlike any other.

The story is legendary, blending philosophy, morality, and power into a narrative that keeps you questioning everything. And then there is the plot twist, one of the most brilliant and unforgettable in the medium, a moment that redefined how storytelling in games could be done. It is practically insurmountable, even all these years later.

Gameplay mixes tense survival shooting with plasmid powers, giving you freedom to approach encounters creatively. It is not just about fighting, it is about experimenting, adapting, and surviving in a city that wants you dead at every turn. The balance of atmosphere, story, and mechanics is near perfect.

BioShock is not only a game, it is a landmark. A timeless piece of art that changed the medium forever.

Score: 10/10 - Atmospheric, innovative, and unforgettable.

Echos of Plum grove is a great game for the farming sim genre. It feels different and fresh, rather than a carbon copy of other great farming sims. Mechanics that really help this game shine are disease, death, funerals and marriages. Characters live independently from you, they get married, have children, and they die. Ugh.

review_text:
Pros:
- Great graphics and sound design. This to me does indeed look like a next gen game. I also really like the suit design.
- At times, the game can produce a nice sci-fi atmosphere. Unfortunately, it can also destroy its atmosphere very quickly as well (see below).

Cons:
- Lacklustre combat design. The game's combat is basically an animation based melee system that stops working entirely if more than one enemy is fought. In most scenarios, it makes the game very easy, which renders the gameplay towards the end rather boring. You also fight the same dead easy mini boss four times throughout the game.
There is also a distinct lack of enemy variety that really hurts the game as most of your enemy encounters will be against quasi-zombies (which is just boring)
- Flat story. The game's story is very strongly inspired by the one of Dead Space. However, whilst Dead Space had great lore supporting its story, CP's falls off here. The story is extremely predictable and uninspired. The characters are mostly uninteresting, unlikable and offer no depth such as an intriguing character development.
- Boring gameplay. Gameplay is ofc strongly impacted by the lacklustre combat design, however there is an equally important factor that brings it down: the incredibly high amount of time the player needs to climb ladders, crawl through vents and squeeze through narrow gaps. Certain areas feel like a walking sim because of that. I kid you not when I say that the player spends almost an hour doing these mind numbing bits that offer nothing. Together with long walk and talk sections, this makes the game simply tedious to play.
- Unsuitable environments. Certain areas in the game just do not make any sense from a design perspective. For instance, how likely is it that in 300 years someone builds a mining colony from shipping containers below ground? Another example: the game is set on Jupiter's moon Callisto, whose gravity is about 1.2% of the one of earth. This ofc would have a great impact on how you move on its surface (eg, think how the astronauts walked on the moon). However, in game the player just moves as if they would on earth. A small nitpick maybe but nonetheless an inconsistency in the game's setting.
Questionable environments (and there are a ton in the game) like these really affect the authenticity of the game's setting, which in horror title can immediately destroy the atmosphere.

Conclusion: If I had to describe the game with a single sentence, Id write: "Dead Space like survival horror action game with next gen graphics that is unfortunately brought down by tedious and boring gameplay".
The game is a 6/10 for me, where it makes it hard to choose whether to give a thumbs up or down. If you are into this sort of game or like sci-fi in general, I would recommend that you pick it up in a sale. If you are neither of those things, dont waste your time with it.
Ive recently read that Glen Schofield (the game's director) pitched a Dead Space 4 to EA, which was rejected by them. Having played CP, I am tempted to say that EA's refusal was for the better for the franchise...

review_text:
Gotta say, I wasn't expecting this much from this game:

It's an incredibly detailed Hockey simulator that says "Early Access" but besides some UI changes that could be made, looks like it could be a full-blown game right now. It's a game that is easy to lose yourself in and you know you want to come back to play it once you've shut it down. Even though right now the game doesn't have actual NHL rosters in, it is incredibly easily to download the real rosters and facepacks to go along with it. The Blueline website does a better job than EA has ever done on their NHL games at updating their rosters; you can expect an updated roster almost once a week during the regular season from the website. 

There are a couple of problems with the game right now, obviously. The trading in the game doesn't work very well. You never see a blockbuster trade in the game and teams are constantly sending good players that are underperforming through the waivers. On my simulation Dion Phaneuf had a 50 point season but when I put him on the block, the best trade offer I can expect is a couple of 3rd or 4th round draft picks. This could be because of his salary, but I still think the game's trading mechanics need to be a little reworked.

If you are looking for an extremely detailed GM simulator than Eastside Hockey Manager is the game to get. Don't let the "Early Access" deceive you, this is a game that is easy to waste hours on and is challenging and rewarding. Recommended to anyone that loves hockey and wants to know what goes on behind the scenes!

review_text:
95% positive?  I feel like I'm playing a different game than the rest of the community.  I was expecting a lot more with a score like that.

Shadow Tactics has a few good elements going for it that include the art design, along with a few interesting game play mechanics.  Apart from that it is a mediocre stealth game at best largely due to the horrific controls and lack of pause function.

Handling your characters in this game is an exercise in redundant frustration.  This is magnified by the lack of a pause function.  This game massively penalizes you for the slightest mistake, yet it is remarkably easy to click the ground right next to an enemy's feet.

The devs implemented a quick save option and actually put a timer on screen that is constantly reminding you to save the game.  There is even a part in the tutorial that suggests you quick save because you're about to take down an enemy.  So pause function bad but quick save crawl is good?

The devs have made it abundantly clear that there will never be a pause function, yet this game is in such deperate need for it that i found myself mashing the space bar out of "instinct".

Then there is the camera... Omg the camera is dreadful. It is kept at a terrible angle and the way it orbits makes it so you can never tell what the hell is actually going on


This game could be amazing, but it is brought down hard by some of the most clumsy controls i have ever seen in a top down game of any kind

Give it a shot at 75% off or better, but don't be fooled by the 95% positive rating like i was

review_text:
mixed feelings on this one: i wanted to like it, but i couldnt get myself to want to finish it, which is why i cant really recommend it although it is not an awful game either

audio is fine. There is no conversations, no vocal expressions, no inner monologue, just some groaning and walking, enemy sounds, environment sounds, machine sounds and a very backgroundy soundtrack. It is decent. good stuff, definitel elevates the experience, but doesnt carry it either.

visuals are style-wise exactly my thing: giger and some beksinski inspirations for sure.
But the muted earthy-grey-fleshy tones get a bit repetitive quite soon.
Same as with the animations where you put you arm or some device into some fleshy mound that is part of the construction

the riddles were okayish but a lot of walking involved and not really intuitive

i made a friend at the start, which i liked as a concept, and they followed me around despite me mistreating them after birthing them, but this friendship came to a sudden halt when i had to leave them behind, after walking through a gate that closed behind me

the game had some nice giger-style "tunnel of horror" "geisterbahn" in the beginning, which was nice. I wish the train puzzle was 1. more intuitive (less walking ,more doing) and i could ve spent way more time doing train related puzzles or going on a ride on these. This was over too quick

the reason i stopped playing is the repetitive backtracking and walking and the repetitive trial-and-error puzzling

i would have liked this game much more if it had either more action OR more _logical_ puzzling. They could even have had the same puzzle type multiple times in elevated difficulties, like the one with the nodes you had to move along this grid in the beginning, and i d be fine with that. However, the illogical adventure-style "try it out and see what happens" puzzles are not my thing, i have no patience to guess what a designer thought makes sense to them in the moment. And regarding the action: there is very little and that is fine but i d have also been ok with a System Shock 2 like experience, blasting creepy pitiful monsters away. I would also be okay if it was more of a "hide and seek" kind of thing where u dont fight at all. But it is in the end a little bit of everything but nothing really, except for the walking, which it really has enough of.

Not a bad game, i d recommend it to those who like adventure-like linear gameplay and like the style.

review_text:
[h1]
A Short Click and Play Game
[/h1]
Samorost was originally released in 2003 and it is still available on Amanita Design's website. This is the only game in the series that is available as a free game. I really love games by Amanita, with Machinarium currently being by favorite. They're quirky, they're cute, and they're fun to figure out. I highly recommend Samorost 2 if you're already fond of any other Amanita Design game. However, if you've never been introduced to the studio before (aside from Samorost 1) titles like Botanicula and Machinarium may prove for a smoother first ride. Samorost 2 isn’t really about the plot; the real content is the creativity. There is more of it present in the alien landscapes and all the little details they are filled with than in many large-budget AAA titles. And Samorost 2 manages to present it all under an hour, leading to a really concentrated experience. Sure, it has its price too, but if you like games a little more on the artistic side, then Amanita delivers yet again.

Although very short, Samorost is a great point-and-click adventure game which has a very unique artwork. The gameplay is very simple - we look for clickable objects on every screen and try to solve the puzzles that represent obstacles before Gnome could proceed any further to reach his goal. I really like the game's surrealistic world with its unique creatures - above all, Gnome itself, who lives on an asteroid full of plants.

[h1]
Story
[/h1]
We control a cute space gnome. In this game, we are trying to find our dog by going after those who came to our planet and kidnapped our dog. As we explore the planet they went to, we meet the people there and then we solve some puzzles to move forward. From then on, you'll encounter obstacles and puzzles in the form of, among other things, bug-eating creatures, flying seals and even wild dandelions. It doesn't take long to finish but it's a lovely little adventure and I think it's well worth experiencing.
 
[h1]
Pros and Cons
[/h1]
Pros:
+ Great music & sound effects
+ Cute graphics
+ Sweet puzzles
+ Weird, bizarre world and atmosphere
+ Cute main character
+ So sweet ending

+/- Maybe expensive for somebody but u can get it while on sale 

Cons:
- Short gameplay (i finished in 1 hour) 
- Too many mediocre puzzles
- Too many timing-based puzzles


My score for this game 8/10

Have a good game
Yours truly, Noyan...

review_text: I like this game. I have been following it's release. The art style really captivated me, as I love it's flat, cartoony look similar to a paper mario game. The idea to mesh together farming sim mechanics with the longevity of play of a life sim game is truly a combination I have been looking for. I love falling back into an easy routine, as  the small map and frequent teleportation points make traversing the island a real breeze. The game is packed with different mechanics that can diversify a playthrough. If you don't like farming, you can also: raise animals, fish, forage, mine, perform quests, cook, [spoiler] make potions [/spoiler], craft resources and furniture. The trading system is also a very unique change to the farming genre. Instead of a convenient shipping box, you have to go out to town and trade with the folks to get money, seeds, or any other resource which forces you to socialize and potentially find your favorite villager (and potential partner). Villagers have different professions which changes what items they trade, which further incentivises the player to talk with everyone. Another thing I like is the life sim mechanic of having a family legacy to play as when your character dies, as it promotes diversifyng your playthrough and money-making schemes without needing to start anew. One last thing that I love about this game is the LGBTQ+ friendly design. You can choose your pronouns (with a non-binary option) despite your looks, you can marry whatever gender you want, and when you are having a baby with your spouse, the game asks you whether you want to adopt or have a pregnancy, and then you can decide who in the couple gets pregnant (which is very inclusive if you decide that your character is trans... or if you want mpreg to be real, I don't judge). Overall, I recommend this game as a *insert cozy farming sim game* meets the sims type of game.

I really can't recommend this game much (maybe with exception of buying it for a very very low price). There is so much of unused potential it is sad. The basic idea is great but the execution is sadly lacking in almost every way.

You could think that in Lucius you will be placed in an open playground that lets you experiment with using environment for your intentions while there will be dynamic reaction of other people on your actions. But that is completely wrong. Instead of that you are forced to kill your victims in one and only exact fashion. No place for creativity or multiple ways to do that.

And the game is so unpolished. There is a load of bugs and glitches from the smaller (items in characters hands tend to move awkwardly during cutscenes) to really problematic (that can force you to repeat the whole mission). I can overlook some problems but there are just to many of them to be such benevolent with Lucius.

Also the core gameplay mechanics are poorly designed. For example you have paranormal abilities which you can use to manipulate others. To use them you have to switch to them...but then you can't use anything (open doors, search through drawers etc.) as that is also a separate ability. Or later in game you get a chance to conjure fireballs but when you begin to cast them the effect will cover your sight and you will not see what's ahead of you. There are also some "stealth" missions where you are forced to do them over and over again (and there are really long loadings) until you learn how to go through them step by step.

Well, Lucius is not a good game. But it is not so horrible as it can sound from my words either. The story is actually ok, the slowly deteriorating mental state of your family is for the most parts well done and the voice acting is nice. But the game has so many gameplay issues, bugs and other things. Also the replayability is almost none.

review_text:
I bought The Callisto Protocol on 85% sale for 8,84€, and here are my "no spoiler" thoughts on it after 3 hours...

Firstly... Callisto Protocol is a game that tries REALLY hard to mimic Dead Space in many ways, to a point where you might actually Google whether or not it is the same developer.

Most bad reviews you read, will call it "B-tier Dead Space", or criticize it because it's "not as good as Dead Space", and see the differences as a negative, rather than trying to rate it for what it actually tries to be. The main two differences between this game and Dead Space, is that combat is entirely different, and this game feels A LOT more linear.

And because of those two differences, people will see them as negatives because the only thing they can think is "is it Dead Space?"... Which is too bad, since Callisto Protocol is a pretty solid game that holds its own.

[b]THE GAME IS LINEAR[/b]

This is a big difference between Callisto Protocol and Dead Space, since Callisto Protocol is VERY linear, and has you basically go from A to B without much deviation. Same goes from exploring, which there is very little off besides a few "secrets", that you can find easily by simply checking out the area.

However... Callisto Protocol being linear isn't a bad thing, since it is obvious that the game tries to come off as a bit more of a "cinematic experience", than Dead Space did. Basically it half'n-half feels like playing a movie.

[b]"COMBAT IS BAD"[/b]

If you are looking for a challenging "survival horror game", then you might need to amp up the difficulty a bit in this game, since enemies basically just attack you one at a time, even when there are multiple around you. And this is obviously done to make the melee combat feel a bit more forgiving and satisfying. And combat DOES feel satisfying, but some might find it too easy.

While you DO have guns in Callisto Protocol, the combat is mainly focused around melee combat, with you dodging or blocking enemy attacks. This is very different from Dead Space, where combat is more centered around shooting.

The melee combat feels VERY satisfying in this game, but some might find it a bit too repetitive, since dodging and blocking is "half-automatic", where basically you just need to hold down a button, and not "tapping it at the right moment". 

So all in all, combat isn't bad. In fact, it's VERY satisfying. If anyone says it is bad, it's because they can't refrain from comparing it to Dead Space combat.

I personally enjoy the combat because I see it for what it is, and not what it's not.

[b]IS IT WORTH BUYING?[/b]

On the 8,84€ sale I got it on, it was an amazing buy. However the 58,99€ price tag it normally has, might be a bit steep.

The game IS good, but apparently people claim it takes 7 hours to beat, and because of how linear it is, it doesn't have much replay value. So I recommend getting it on sale. :) Not necessarily as cheap as me, but at least 25% off is a good price.

Honestly, I hate I am leaving a negative review for this game. Bonelab isn't atrocious, in fact it has a ton of potential. An openly moddable VR game a la gmod? Sounds  great, right? Well, at the moment of writing this, it's a bit more convoluted than that. 

First, the campaign. In short, it is horribly executed. It doesn't even feel like a campaign with how random it is. However, I can't really get into the criticism without getting into the meat and potatoes of the campaign. So, if you care about spoilers then skip ahead.[spoiler] Anyway, the game doesn't stay consistent within the first two levels of the campaign. First you start of with the hanging scene, which I will say really sets the tone and motivation for our story despite how brutal and sensitive a subject matter it is. Then it transitions into structures similar to Boneworks, its predecessor, which is cool to see the continuity. We approach the titular Bone Lab in the definitely-safe-to-use elevator, surrounded with... gamemodes? Huh? Ok, uh, we then progress by... hopping... through... different gamemodes? Wha- *ahem*. My dear reader, there is the continuity break, the first one at least. There's more? Oh yeah, later in the game you hop around different unrelated (and bland) levels collecting avatars with different stats so you can continue with the continuous part of the game. Why am I so frustrated about this? [/spoiler] Because Boneworks had a WAY better campaign that Bonelab, and Boneworks had that continuity to fuel that feeling of progression. Boneworks had visible landmarks getting closer by the level, keeping the rush of accomplishment lively. Bonelab has a body collectathon. Yikes. A majority of the store page goes over the content included with the game, the minority of it goes over-

Oh yea, the mods.

Um, how do I put this uh...

The SDK is still in development. 

It's last update was aboooout...

Six mo-

...

six months... ago...

...

WHAT?! IT'S BEEN THAT LONG!?

Oh boy, this is my absolute FAVORITE part of this game. The modding system is incomplete in a sandbox game about modding. How was this flubbed? HOW?! What if gmod added really basic features into the game you just couldn't mod in without a hackey workaround? What happened in the officially supported modding scene over the past six months? Nothing extraordinarily ground breaking. I think a group of modders was half way through porting Boneworks in the game, which just proves how desperate people are to play a different campaign. By the way, the mod makers for this game are awesome people for even putting up with these honestly silly limitations. Speaking of limitations, you can't search for specific mods. Nor can you link a mod.io account for the game. Y'know, this feels more like a Bethesda moment right here. Ship a incomplete mess and leave it to the community. What's even funnier is that most of these problems can be resolved by an external mod extender.

MelonLoader is a god send. What happened over the past six months with MelonLoader? Oh, just fully functional multiplayer and mod sync with mod.io, nothing too extreme for a single player game. A problem with MelonLoader is that it is PC exclusive at the moment (LemonLoader is the WIP quest port for MelonLoader that has issues with certain mods), leaving a massive chunk of the player-base on quest stranded.

The lack of SDK updates isn't the worst part. It's the lack of transparency. There has been no sign of life from the devs over the past six months. No official communication. If there was even a speck of reassurance that something was in the works, I would have been way less harsh on the game. Unfortunately, that isn't the state the game is in. I love the potential this game has, I love what this game CAN be. I hate what the game is, I hate what the game was left TO be. The modders can't just do all the heavy work SLZ, they need official support.

Well, here's to six months, and here's to possibly six more.

I'm going to try to keep the review as spoiler-free as I possibly can, because it's a game that the less you know about it, the better, but tldr; I would say IMSCARED is the best horror game I've played, but it's more like an incredibly unique experience that no other horror game I've seen has done, and is the FIRST horror game I would recommend to anyone interested in horror, outside of even just horror games as a whole.

review_text:
Lucius is an compelling complete mess of a game that sadly manages to sour itself right at the end.

The game is a point and click game where you play as Lucius, a 6 year old millionare child that for some reason is in leagues with Satan, and is tasked to kill the other people in his house discretely to harvest their souls. Everything in the game takes place within the giant open family mansion where you have to gather clues, find items and do your chores to figure out the solutions to puzzles involving killing people in more or less creative ways.

This is all conveyed in the style of a 70's B-horror movie akin to The Exorcist, only it seems to be somewhat aware (or charmingly unaware) of the goofyness of the situation and cranks up the cheese to hillarious degrees, with overuse of 666 symbolism, slow motion head explosions and cartoonishly unlikable house residents to murder. The game's attempts at horror falls incredibly flat out of the gate in other words, though it do manage to be bloody hillarious instead which is what got me hooked through the entire thing.

Because the thing is, the game itself is not very good. A lot of the time you are given very vague hints of what to do and it ends up with tons of walking around the house searching for interactive items, the magic powers you get such as levitation and mind control only seems to want to work half of the time, there is some horrible early 2000's license game style sneaking sections, and the final boss fight was completely broken for me until I reloaded a save. The game also has ludicrous loading times even on high end computers, and it looks like an upscaled PS2 game in a lot of regards despite seeming to use a surprising ammount of power to run.

However along with those bad things are a lot of fun "bad" things too. The physics engine is super wonky and makes doors and objects flip out at times, which is especially apparent with the ragdoll physics going into full Goat Simulator mode whenever they happen outside of cutscenes (if you get hold of the gun earlier than intended you can have a lot of fun with this). You can unlock a tricycle to help move around the house quicker, which breaks the laws of physics around stairs and other things. You sometimes spawn mid air or partway underground when starting a mission. Lots of weird unintended wacky things that is really funny whenever it do happen.

The truly bad parts really do tear it down a lot though, so even if I did enjoy big chunks of this game in a Troll 2 sort of way, the truly abysmal parts dragged it way too much down to outright recommend it. If you are interested in so bad it's good horror cheese and physics wackyness, grab it on a sale, but stay away at the current full price.

I will be making a more detailed review later.

But this was the first time i played this game, it is nearly 3am and i just played this for 11 hours straight.
So yes, i basically instantly fell in love with this and literally played it till i got to tired to play.

So much charm.

Additional info after 40 hours.

So, i have to say i really love this game but i can not recommend it.

While the combo of city builder and Tower defense at the start is very interesting, ultimately these two elements just collide with one another to strongly.

Matter of fact is that i am personally more of a city builder then tower defense guy.
So what i want is to build a nice and somewhat naturally grown city and protect it with naturally seeming turrets and walls. 

However in Rise ti Ruins you NEED to adhere very strictly and very fast to the codes of tower defense that in the end makes the city building unbefitting.

The problem here becomes that you need the rather abstract strategies of Tower defense or the Corruption will just flood you with rather harshly balanced (at points i'd like to say unbalanced) enemies.

Worst offenders here are Fire Elementals that just a few off can simply ruin an entire base and end even your best equipped settlers lives within seconds.

Second offender is the corruption creep which seems to follow no solid rules but changes behavior as they see fit. The game alludes t the corruption trying to end you the more the more you build up so you'd need to manage and balance how you spread and grow in comparison to said corruption. 

But corruption seemingly cheats, starts in totally different corners of the map and seems to pick up speed when spreading if you come close to cutting it off.

This is a good game, with tons of charm. But the balancing is in my humble opinion, not off, but weighted in a way that personally just frustrates me and that prevents the building of defenses that remind the observer  of actual castles and such and instead favors abstract and unwieldy mazes only. Which is a shame.

I did really want to like it, after all i put 40 hours into it.

I DO recommend trying it if tower defense is THE thing and you#d like top see a new an fresh approach to it.

I would NOT recommend it if you were looking to build more naturally functioning and looking settlements protected in a way you would protect a middleage or fantasy city.

review_text:
Let me be very blunt: this is an extraction shooter game, but single-player only. If you enjoy games like Helldivers II and Space Marine II, this is a decent game to play as well. However, the lack of multiplayer makes this a very repetitive and boring game, and I find that I can only play one or two runs before quitting out of frustration. I'll explain:

There are many aspects in this game that seem to contradict each other. It's a shooter game, but almost all the enemies don't drop ammunition. You can only obtain ammunition from ammo chests, which are scattered throughout the map, or by killing enemies specifically spawned from the portal. Now, there is also a melee attack, as well as spells you can use to further aid you in killing your enemies, but the main source of damage is your guns. As a result, ammunition is usually the limiting factor from advancing through the map or extracting early.

There are groups of enemies scattered throughout the map. These are alright. However, there seems to be an alert system that spawns more enemies when you kill one in a group, which can quickly get out of hand if you don't expect it. Furthermore, there seems to be no warning. You could kill ten enemies in a row without an alert, but all of a sudden you kill an enemy, and then enemies begin spawning all around you, even if you instakill them. It's annoying, especially because you NEED to kill enemies on the map to progress, so you can't avoid them either. 

The story of this game is very shallow, and it's clear the developers didn't intend on implementing storyline aspects in the game. You are introduced as a 'preyer', who is an agent of a Church. Your goal is to eliminate evil witches and their minions, using guns and spells. That's it. Nothing else. There is no insight into who you are, why you became a preyer, how the world changed around you, etc. Even the Steam description of this game has more story in it: "you play as a wicked inner turned witch hunter on his final mission to reach salvation." But when you get into the game, there is absolutely no mention of this through out the playthrough. You can see hints of the developers' efforts in a half-hearted story by reading the location descriptions and any notes around the maps you get, but the location descriptions are clearly flavor text, and the notes are used to describe the mechanics of the game more than actually providing a story.

In line with the issue of storyline, there is no end-game goal. Let's say you fully clear a map, get all the loot, and extract. Congratulations, you can level up, get new weapons, and go in again. There is no global impact. It doesn't feel rewarding at all. The map just shuffles a bit, and you go again. And again. And again. Eventually, only one clear of a map isn't enough to level up. So, without spending your witchfire (which is used to level up), you must go to another map. And if you die in this map, you drop ALL your loot. Of course, you can pick it up again by going back, but it just feels hopelessly endless without a goal. 

Lastly, there is no multiplayer. I understand that this game is marketed as a single player game, but without storyline, endgame goal, and with more and more enemies that get stronger as you progress, it just feels numbing. What feels worse is that on the developers' FAQ, they specifically stated that they have no plans to implement multiplayer even when fully released.

review_text:
Everyone harps on Arkham Origins, but to me, City is the odd one out in the series - the black sheep.

Honestly, this game feels like absolute garbage. The encounters are poor, the missions feel simplistic and above all else, the story is just awful, awful, awful. Origins had some issues with bland predator encounters, but combat felt really solid. In this game, both combat and stealth just suck and set up in ways that aren't interesting to play. I've started playing Arkham City 3 separate times since it's release and never made it to the end before I uninstalled out of boredom. This is in very stark contrast with the other 3 games, which had no problems in holding my interest aside from the boring Riddler stuff.

I cannot stress, however, how bad the story is. For example, Batman is infected with something and needs to find a cure, so he seeks out Mr. Freeze. He immediately starts bullying him even though he doesn't even have his suit. Then he goes to get his suit and what do you know, Freeze destroys his cure and attacks Batman immediately. You beat Freeze up, then they're both just standing next to eachother like they're buddies, even though Freeze still has his suit on. It's just weird as hell, and the entire game is permeated by these stupid feeling interactions between characters.

Even the ending feels dumb. Spoilers be damned. Joker is also infected and Batman is holding his cure. The idiot jumps Batman from the back and stabs his arm with some injector, causing Batman to drop the cure. Joker goes "waaah" and dies a minute later. What he injected Batman with is never shown or explained or even mentioned or anything. 

The whole game feels underwhelming in the same vein. Asylum, Origins and Knight are great. You can totally skip this one, there's just no point. All you need to know is Joker dies, the end.

If you want City's unique style as opposed to Asylum's or Knight's, then again, just play Origins. It's City, but better in almost every way, except for the open world traversal. VASTLY better plot, way more interesting bossfights and better encounter designs.

review_text:
The core combat in this game feels great: The movement and shooting feels smooth, and the looting is rewarding.
However, I have some grips with the gameplay of this game:

• The UI is cumbersome and sometimes annoying. Why can't I change characters while in the hub town? Why is the item inventory not just another tab in the menu? Why can't I claim all feats (achievements) at once? etc.

• The exploration in this game is honestly not fun. Some chests are locked behind some characters' abilities (why am I forced to pick Ace?), and having to stop the stage's mission to search for resource nodes or chests feels counter-intuitive and, unfortunately, annoying. Some chests are too well-hidden for a looter shooter, especially for their feeble rewards.

• The games forces you to use different characters too much. In addition to exploration, I'm being forced to constantly change characters for story quests, side-quests, feats. I honestly hate this. Let me use the characters that I want, give me more liberty.

• As you level up you unlock skill and stat points to spend. In my opinion, stat increases are too meager and the skill tree feels a little unimpactful. This is a trend with games like Borderlands I feel we could've escaped, but alas it stays with Relic Hunters.

Overall, I expected this game to be one I could binge and spend hours in, but these cons unfortunately bothered me more than I hoped. You can tell some features were added on top of the base game to increase its longevity (which is a great thing!), but the execution damaged the cohesion and flow of the game in general.

[h1] A Tale of Two Halves: Phantasy Star Online 2 vs. New Genesis [/h1]
Phantasy Star Online 2 (PSO2) and its successor, New Genesis, represent contrasting chapters in the iconic Phantasy Star franchise. While PSO2 has garnered praise for its rich content and engaging gameplay, New Genesis has faced criticism for what some perceive as a lackluster experience. Let's delve into the strengths and weaknesses of each to provide a balanced perspective.

[h3] Phantasy Star Online 2 - The Classic Jewel [/h3]
Phantasy Star Online 2 has been celebrated for its longevity, having sustained a dedicated player base since its initial release. The game's strength lies in its extensive content, featuring a plethora of diverse quests, challenging raids, and an intricate narrative that unfolds across various episodes. The combat system is dynamic and responsive, offering players a satisfying blend of strategy and action. Moreover, the character customization options and the variety of classes contribute to a deeply immersive gaming experience.

The game's graphics, while not cutting-edge, have aged well, maintaining a charming aesthetic that complements the sci-fi fantasy setting. The developers have consistently supported PSO2 with regular updates, events, and collaborations, ensuring that players always have something new to explore.

[h3] New Genesis - A Promising Concept, But Falling Short [/h3]
On the other hand, Phantasy Star Online 2: New Genesis has been met with mixed reviews, with many players expressing disappointment in various aspects. While the open-world concept brought a breath of fresh air, the execution left much to be desired. The game's visuals, though improved, have not matched the expectations set by contemporary standards, resulting in an experience that feels underwhelming compared to other titles in the genre.

The transition to a more action-oriented combat system in New Genesis was meant to enhance gameplay, but for some, it has led to a loss of the strategic depth that characterized PSO2. Additionally, the removal of traditional classes and the introduction of a skill tree system have polarized the community, with some applauding the flexibility and others lamenting the loss of class identity.

Furthermore, server stability issues and a perceived lack of endgame content at launch contributed to a rocky start for New Genesis, leaving players yearning for the depth and polish that defined its predecessor.

[h3] Conclusion [/h3]
In the world of Phantasy Star, the tale of PSO2 and New Genesis unfolds as a nuanced narrative. Phantasy Star Online 2 stands as a testament to the enduring appeal of its formula, with its wealth of content, engaging gameplay, and vibrant community. On the other hand, New Genesis, while introducing ambitious concepts, has struggled to live up to the legacy of its predecessor, facing criticism for technical issues and design choices that have left players wanting more.

[b]• ULTIMATELY[/b], the appreciation for each title hinges on individual preferences. Some may find solace in the familiar embrace of PSO2, while others may see the potential for improvement in New Genesis as it evolves with future updates and adjustments. Only time will tell whether New Genesis can carve out its own space in the Phantasy Star universe or if it will forever live in the shadow of its predecessor

review_text:
.hack//G.U.
I have so much to say about it... but I won't, because else it would take just as much time as cutscenes in this game do.
TL;DR: 6.5/10 game. I really want to recommend it, but I cannot do so, as it didn't age well. The snail's pacing of the gameplay, the pointless grind (due to the speed of XP gain), and every scene drawn out just a little bit longer than it should be all take away from the experience. Worth buying during the sales.

Let's start with the good things. The atmosphere is amazing. It ACTUALLY feels like you're immersed in the world of The World (haha... sorry, i'll see myself out)
Even though the console takes forever to load, I genuinely enjoyed launching the game and exiting it to read some emails in the system. I mean, come on, it's been what, 13 years and you still alttab to read some msgs outside of the game, there IS some truth in that.
OST is, well, hard to remember, but it's ok enough to pass. General sound design is decent, but definitely not remarkable in any way. Still, plays to the games' strengths, adding to the immersion quite well.
Writing is, well, not stellar, but gotta pay my respects to the fact that the franchise itself is like the granddaddy of a significant part of current media. Love it or hate it, forgot how the stupid meme goes, G.U. somehow makes you feel that stupid nostalgy even if you've never played it before, because it FEELS like a classic RPG experience. I was looking exactly for that and oh boy did it deliver. Keeping myself awake through the trainwreck of a story about a bunch of idiots unable to properly communicate was way over me though.

Somewhat of a middle ground are... The characters. DEAR LORD, how annoying almost everyone is, ESPECIALLY mc Haseo himself. I think it's the first time ever I've hated the protagonist so much. Fairly sure the writers had a competition of who's going to make the edgiest and asshole-est character possible, and I can say for sure they did deliver. I do know the full story of a game, I know all about his reasoning even though I never finished the trilogy, but even so controlling the most uninterested in video games angry online gamer ever felt like driving a car without brakes on a downhill road - the guy is so much of a jerk you can't relate to him even if you try.
Credit where credit's due: deuteragonists and other side characters you actually interact with fit all the tropes but still manage to feel like real people you would meet in an online game, each with their own personality, motivation and yadda-yadda... Buuuut even though they have some depth to them, it's still more like 2.5D with no real third dimension to them. For example, the twins are a good concept that was kinda poorly executed.

The worst part: gameplay. As I said in the beginning, every single scene is drawn out. Awkward pauses, repeated delivery of the same information, constant need to log out and log back in just because of some mail... Then there are the party members you don't actually need, relationship system (which, while well implemented outside of combat, still urges you to just hit those finishing strikes every single time just to max it out. like, come on, show me a single person who'll start loving me due to the fact i managed to pummel a virtual teapot), sidequests that require talking to every single character in the game (gotta be honest, i do that in JRPGs anyway, like talking to every single NPC i meet in Kiseki or Tales, but that's because they usually ARE interesting to talk to, not just "DID YOU KNOW THAT ENEMY CAN HAVE A WEAKNESS". damn, talking to people in FF is more interesting than those walking cardboard cutouts). 
The alchemy system is really not deep at all. The equipment all feels the same. The skills are... well, bland. Trading with other characters is great, but pretty much useless. Randomly generated dungeons are BOOOORING. Not like grindy boring, more like text-based games feel like they are filled with action next to those stupid corridors and square rooms populated with groups of three to five mobs.
How exactly do the players manage to play the game without gaining any levels at all? How does one walk around the world populated with enemies four levels above them and never get into a fight with any of them? What do they actually online if they don't participate in anything the game has to offer? G.U. doesn't appear to be written outside of the necessary world building and story canvas it needs to deliver the plot to the player.
It wasn't really a good RPG even for the time it was released. Damn, 2006 had Oblivion, Grandia, Suikoden, Kingdom Hearts 2, and so much more...

And yet even due to all the shortcomings, due to the fact the game feels outdated in 2017, it still is genuinely a good experience.
Buy it during the sales if you've never played it.
Buy it for full price if you played it some years ago and consider refreshing it in your mind.
Feel the nostalgy. Embrace The World.

review_text:
I was really looking forward to this game. It was at the top of my Wishlist for at least a year before seeing it on sale half off. So I bought it. It was fun for a little while...but then I had to fight a boss, and it went downhill from there. The combat in this game is atrocious! Feels like it was tacked on at the last minute as an afterthought. The first boss they pit you against flies around in the air, and since there's no lock-on feature, it's impossible to tell where they are half the time, making them very difficult to hit. And then when you DO hit them, it's hard to tell if you did, since they don't have a health bar.

As for the skating, while there is a boost feature, the gameplay feels very slow and you slow down significantly after you release the button (as opposed to JSR where the boost helped you reach top speed with very little slow down afterwards). Then there's the graffiti mechanic...what do I even say here? Each graffiti you unlock has a different pattern associated with it, so you're supposed to memorize the pattern for each one. However, since the game doesn't penalize you for messing up, you can just spin the control stick around until you eventually hit all the points. Which you'll end up doing a lot, since the game doesn't tell you which graffiti you're spraying in the moment.

The game isn't all bad. The graphics are sleek and colorful. And the music is perhaps the shining feature of the game with awesome tracks. But good music and graphics aren't enough to save this one for me. And finally, after a quick internet search, I found out there is no arcade mode. Jet Set Radio had a few arcade modes, like a time trial for getting a high trick score, or my favorite: seeing how fast you can tag all the graffiti spots. However, all this game seems to have is a story mode and then the ability to just roam around the city after. That might be fun for awhile, but eventually the replayability will run out. Looks like I'll have to get my JSR fix elsewhere. I do own Hover, maybe I should give that game another go...

review_text:
I reallllly wanted to love this game, but its definitely needs some work.

Don't get me wrong, it is very cute, lots of great concepts, and has serious potential -- but unfortunately for me the cons outweighed the pros. For example, time goes by insanely quick in this game. It is nearly impossible to complete more than one task a day because of how fast the days go by. There is also aging in the game, so trying to build relationships with how short the days are while still trying to get anything done is nearly impossible. The dialogue of the characters doesn't make much sense, and wouldn't unless you have played the game for some time. Planting crops takes forrrrever. It is very slow. It was also not possible for me, and I think it would be for anyone, to know who is who without referring to a wiki. To me it seems like you are stuck in a cycle with no real endpoint unless you get married and have kids to continue the game further, and even then it is the same cycle. I also played for a few days but got quite frustrated with it after a short period of time.

Overall, though this game has some great qualities and I am really interested in seeing it grow and what updates come in the future, I don't see myself playing until some changes are made. I enjoy the concepts of real life possibilities like disease, but again I think it could be executed better. I love the art style and hope the developers continue to work on this game because it has so, so much potential.

review_text:
Game is fun-ish but at the moment a very unpolished and potentially frustrating experience. Worth 30 tops if you are forgiving and willing to wait for some content. Only 5 maps that all look relatively similar was a huge bummer. Part of the problem is that everything looks the same when it's covered in snow. Expect to try 2-3 lobbies before getting an actual game going due to disconnects. You can't go into a game mid-match or even return to a lobby with a party. Which is really basic stuff that a game like this absolutely requires. The shooting itself is fun and satisfying, but the higher difficulties kind of kill that a bit by making all the enemies have armor and turning them into sponges.

Everyone's body models teleport all over, hunch over in awkward ways, and constantly spazz out regardless of how good your connection is. The presentation in general is kind of lacking in certain spots. Like when you see your teammates through walls I found that this hud element was distracting and messed with my depth perception. Turning off captions is an absolute MUST because they constantly float in your face. The characters themselves can't be customized and make constant non-stop generic commentary like "THEYRE HERE" "RELOADING" etc. This wouldn't be so bad except the voice acting is atrocious. Everyone sounds very generic and has the tonal cadence of an adult talking to an 8 year old child. It's a huge pet peeve of mine.

The upgrade system is a bit bland. Pretty much everything increases damage at the cost of recoil. Or decreases recoil. Some weapons don't even have upgrades in areas like you would expect. The shotty - you can't increase clip size in any way. Some things you can unlock but can't actually use yet like laser sights. You find floppy disks to get upgrades. But the game often screws you by randomly placing them in a spot where the level is coming to a close and they are impossible to redeem. The only items you can use are pipe bombs and heals. I feel like there should be a lot more variety in those consumables especially since the game encourages you to buy them between the levels. The specials are kinda meh too. You've got your standard exploder, and two tanky dudes that look different but behave in an almost identical way. The end of each match is a huge difficulty spike so often I'll be crushing it with a team only to get wiped at the end and lose all rewards.

At this point I'm just rambling. Part of the reason why this is frustrating is because it's so close to being a top tier VR must have title. But there's a plethora of smaller things that stack up and hold it back. You can definitely get 4 hours out of it. Beyond that - depends. Hopefully they support the title long term.

review_text:
Samorost 2 builds upon the quaint charm of its predecessor, expanding Amanita Design’s surreal universe while retaining the whimsical essence that made the original so endearing. The game invites players to once again guide the tiny gnome protagonist across mysterious planets, solving puzzles that feel both organic and imaginative, all within a compact, self-contained adventure.

In terms of storytelling, Samorost 2 continues the tradition of silent narrative. Without dialogue or text, the game conveys its tale through visual cues, animations and interactions. The journey remains delightfully abstract, but it’s emotionally resonant: small gestures, subtle humor and inventive world-building give the adventure personality and charm.

The gameplay is deceptively simple but cleverly designed. Point-and-click mechanics remain intuitive, yet puzzles have grown more intricate, often requiring multiple steps or lateral thinking. Each challenge is seamlessly integrated with the environment, encouraging players to explore every corner and experiment with interactive elements. The satisfaction comes from discovery, as solutions feel earned rather than handed to the player.

Aesthetically, Samorost 2 elevates the visual style of the first game. The combination of hand drawn art and photomontage is richer, with more layers and finer detail. The environments are alive with quirky, interactive objects, curious creatures and a palpable sense of place that invites lingering exploration. Complementing this is a playful and occasionally haunting soundtrack, perfectly attuned to the game’s dreamlike atmosphere.

Overall, Samorost 2 refines the formula of the original while adding depth and polish. It’s a brief but memorable experience that emphasizes creativity, curiosity and exploration. For those who value artistry and imagination in gaming, this title remains a shining example of how minimalism can deliver maximum impact.

review_text:
A nice stand alone experience that doesn't overstay it's welcome.

Enjoyable combat, completely optional collectibles and side missions and a neat '80's style dark future flair combine to make one of the few games I'd consider "must-play" gaming.

The only downsides aren't deal-breakers. The visuals can get same-y with the dark post-apocalypse meets neon look, but the game isn't long enough for it to really get old.

Yes, the game will occasionally attempt to connect to the now non-existent servers when you're in the start menu and that is annoying, having to wait thirty seconds, but I can't fault the actual game for that.
