review_text:
Simply put: This game fucking sucks. Desperados III is amazing but I have no idea why this weeb trash that preceded it is so highly-rated.

Firstly. The viewcones don't shrink when guards talk to each other so it doesn't logically hold up like it does in Desperados. The guards should be fixated most strongly on the person in front of them. In this game, they can basically see right through them.

Pathfinding is utter trash. For example, I wanted the two ninjas to drop down from the ledge and knife two guards while old man shoots a third. Impossible because they have to drop down via hook shot first, even though ledges of the same or greater height can be dropped down from elsewhere in the game. Throwing rocks are almost entirely useless and for some reason this ninja carries exactly ONE shuriken. Which leads me to the next thing: Shadow Mode.

Shadow mode is terrible. Unlike in Desperados, it does not pause the game. This renders it basically useless but many situations are of course set up where you need multiple things to happen at once. I suspect this was intended to make it "challenging" but it really just is inefficient and tedious; especially since only the fat Samurai is capable of taking out multiple enemies at one time and only via melee. Further, you can only issue the command to run and attack in Shadow Mode if the enemy is close by. This is inexcusable and makes no sense whatsoever. In Desperados, Showdown Mode feels rewarding because you can plan ahead multiple actions per character and then make a complex plan work. Here, you feel happy when they just did what you fing wanted the first time.

Speaking of tedious things: The game lacks a fast-forward key. So you can just sit and wait forever.

Characters also have abilities unsuited to their specific attributes; this was remedied in desperados 3 whereby the equivalent characters had abilities swapped around and some added. It makes more sense that a fast character like Yuki (why do they have British accents btw?) would have the saki bottle for example and fat sam would have the trap. Or, of course, old sniper man could also have the bottle.

Voice lines also tend to just pop up and repeat out of nowhere.

All in all — Just get Desperados III instead.

[h1]Doesn't feel finished. [/h1]
I like this game, I like a lot of the features that it has. The generational concept of the game play is fairly unique and well implemented. 
The world is cute. The ideas are all nice. The design is lovely. The problem is that it doesn't feel fleshed out.

 The NPC's all feel very much the same. They have "traits" but they don't seem to change much except the repetitive dialogue options that they have are a bit different than NPC's with other "traits". The family just sits on the stairs in my house instead of using the furniture or doing anything interesting. When someone dies you get an invitation to their funeral, but there is no indication of how they died and everyone at the funeral just has their regular interactions. review_text:
This game is beautiful in its own horrific way. However to compare this game's length to another recently popular release, [b]Stray[/b], it is relatively short. To compare this game to the semi-open world cat game is a stretch, but for [b]Stray[/b] being 29.99 USD being just as short if not a little longer with dialog that is not even voiced I found it much more enjoyable than the additional 10 USD I paid for [b]Scorn[/b].
I'll admit, I'm an idiot at times, but some of the puzzles that are required to progress in [b]Scorn[/b], aren't so much puzzles and more so "I'll just roam around until I can find the next thing I can Interact with to progress" style. Some rooms(two) added 30+50 minutes to my play-through simply because of map design or the vagueness of what I need to do next which is frustrating as a player because I'd like to learn more about my environment and dig into the lore of the game, not run through the same room 5-6 times trying to find the one room I may have overlooked or an object I could interact with. The ending, personally I expected right when I started playing and the seed of the end began, but ultimately ending as the story did; progressing to the end and those slight bumps of being lost for 30-50 minutes really made that ending feel like a slap in the face despite definitely knowing how it would end.
Not to continue to gush over [b]Stray[/b] just based on art style and the world design but [b]Stray[/b] being of similar length in playtime (if doing main story stuff only) the amount of direction in [b]Stray[/b] if being very little is all I could've asked for to fully enjoy a game like [b]Scorn[/b]. I'm sure if I knew exactly where to go and when to do it in [b]Scorn[/b] on my first play-through I'd recommend it to anyone, maybe at a slightly more reasonable price for the length of the game at 29.99 USD.
My last words being I would not recommend buying this game unless it was at half the price for maybe 19.99 USD. The frustrating moments of wandering the same areas to progress or generally no direction really made finishing this game more like a chore rather than an artful experience.
P.S In short; this game's art style and lore is deep and beautiful but uncovering it gets waived as soon as you get lost in an area to progress which can add much unneeded time to your play-through which ultimately made the game feel like it was dragging on for no reason for as short of a game it is.

review_text:
What do I dislike about this game?

The game frequently crashes during cutscenes, especially during ascensions, forcing me to skip them entirely. Thankfully, it doesn’t seem like you miss much, but it really breaks immersion.

Resources are incredibly scarce. You spend most of the game scraping by, surrounded by upgrade options but rarely able to afford any of them.

Any time you manage to gather a decent amount of supplies, a swarm of enemies shows up and drains them immediately.

The inventory space is far too limited, making resource management more frustrating than challenging.

I spent a lot of time running back and forth to the safe room to grab my “free” fire capsule (or whatever it’s called) just to clear bodies off the floor so low-level enemies didn’t turn into super beasts.

The church boss fight was incredibly annoying, constantly getting the boss to a sliver of health only to die because I ran out of heals was more exhausting than fun. It wasn't hard on the face of it, it was just awkward and poorly implemented.

[spoiler]Immediately after that fight, you’re thrown into another section where you’re basically forced to run from enemies with one arm, trying not to get hit, which felt cheap and poorly paced.[/spoiler]

Then it crashed again during the cutscene after escaping the church, meaning I had to redo the whole sequence and skip more cutscenes out of fear it would happen again.

By that point, I was done. The church segment drained any enjoyment I had left, and being tossed into more fights with barely any ammo felt like the game had overstayed its welcome.

I did make it to the final boss, but honestly, I had no motivation left to finish it. The fight’s move set includes some seemingly unavoidable attacks, and it’s a complete bullet sponge. Watching a video of someone else beating it was enough to confirm I wasn’t missing anything fun.

Conclusion:
The game clearly wants to be a modern-day Dead Space, but it just doesn’t get there. It feels more like a rough imitation than a tribute. I play games to enjoy myself, not to feel like I’m being trolled by poor design choices.

Just tone it down, jeeze. Why is it trendy to omit a difficulty slider? You aren't FromSoftware and this isn't Dark Souls.

The only genuinely enjoyable part? Collecting cats.

review_text:
Lucius is one of those games that has a very interesting idea, but executes it horribly. This game sounded like it was going to be waaay more fun then it turned out to be. 

I can't say much about Lucius, because as you can see I only have about an hour of playtime on record. I didn't choose to only play an hour, the game is just so buggy that I couldn't manage to get any farther. Half of the time I can't play because it glitches so much. 

On top of all that, the whole game is very linear. The entire gameplay consist of finding the item you are supposed to find and then using it on the objective. (ex: find screwdriver click stove, wait. Find lock, click freezer, wait.) There are no paths to branch onto, and no choices the come with the game. You have to do what the game wants you to do, and you have no free will to decide yourself. The most side missions you can do is to do your chores for money.That usually involves picking up blocks and putting them in a chest.

Even the powers in Lucius cannot be used freely. Towards the beginning of the game you are granted different powers. Sounds cool right? Not really... You are told when to use that power and you can't use it any other time then when you are prompted to. With how buggy the game is too, the powers can be a hassle to use. 

Another problem with Lucius is the voice acting. It's... pretty bad. Also Lucius himself lacks character. He doesn't show emotion, change his facial expression, say anything, or do anything to show that he is a character. Sure, he is possessed, but that's no excuse. I'd rather him do a cheesy evil grin then be a walking cardboard that is there to do one objective to the next. 

I may have only stated negative things about Lucius this whole review, but I will say that it could be worth it if hugely discounted or in a cheap bundle. The story can be somewhat interesting and the deaths are great to watch for the sadistic side that we all have. It's not a horrible game, but it's definitely not worth the $10 price tag. Especially with how buggy it can be. I say pick Lucius up on sale ONLY if you like very linear storytelling. Oh, and also pull up a walkthrough because the game is almost impossible to figure out without one.

review_text:
I started back when Wesker was first released and it seemed pretty fun. But over time I started to realize just how bad things were getting. Each content update was extremely buggy on release and it would take a ridiculous amount of time for the Devs to 'fix' the issues. Every attempt they made was just a band-aid on the original problem, which more often than not had to be reverted because each attempt made the game buggier or more unbalanced. The recent "health updates" to the gave have been a big failure and most of the content had to be reverted because it broke the game too much. So the Devs ended up wasting all these months just for one Quality of Life change to actually make it to the live servers...

Somehow BOTH roles both feel overpowered and underpowered because all the killers have widely different power levels and all perks for each role are wildly unbalanced. Both roles are extremely unfun to play right now unless you use meta stuff in every match. The toxicity in this game is worse than any other game i've played. You get called slurs and get death threats for ANYTHING sometimes.

TIme and time again the veteran players and content creators who know the game in and out seemingly more than the Devs do, have given suggestions on how to fix some of these root issues but in response they are ignored and pushed aside. The Devs have made several consultant-type programs over the years and each one has been abandoned and a new one created in its place. The neglect is pushing away these veteran players and content creators, and it's only going to hurt the game more. It's really obvious the Devs do not play test their own game and only make decisions based on their spreadsheet data and push those changes without realizing the effect it will have even if its a slight numbers tweak which they love to do.

This game is also extremely unfriendly to beginners. The tutorials are years out of date and don't accurately show you what to expect when playing a match. There's a lack of resources you can check to learn more about perks and status effects as nowadays there are way too many of them. Each DLC has introduced 3 survivor perks and 3 killer perks, which has led to an insane amount of bloat in the game. Most of the perks in the game, especially some of the really good ones, are locked behind DLC. In order for a new player to get all these perks which are basically required now, they have to shill out a ton of money on all the DLC packs, in-game currency for the licensed characters or grind for an eternity to get enough shards to buy them in the Shine of Secrets. This game is monetized to hell, more than some Free-to-Play games and it's crazy.

Don't waste your time buying this until the Devs actually wake up and fix all the glaring issues with this game, but don't hold your breath because in the past it has taken them literal years to fix certain issues.

review_text:
[b]The best & biggest of the three "Remasters".[/b]

Compared to the original Yakuza 5, the only changes made are with the translations, as well as a few very minor dialogue bits not even being subtitled at all for whatever reason. The pachinko minigame is still missing here like in Yakuza 4 Remastered due to potentially dumb reasons.

The game takes place a couple of years after the fourth game, and unlike the previous game, you start  off with Kiryu this time, only he's a taxi driver in a completely different town. Also like the last game, it features multiple characters each with their own stories, except for two of them who share a whole chapter. All the characters aside from one are familiar faces if you've played the previous game. There's Kiryu, Saejima, Haruka, Akiyama, and the new character, Shinada.
Once again, the characters' stories get really intriguing until big reveals & twists start happening near the end of the game, making a lot of emotional & dramatic story bits in earlier chapters seem pointless. All of a sudden some characters aren't who they say they are and they're actually connected to these people, their true motivations are actually this & that so you're just supposed to forget some of that exposition you heard before, and so on; it gets kind of annoying to follow along with how much of that there is, but it's not as crazy as the last game.

Just like with the previous "remasters", they did some "re-translating" for this game as well. Here though, it feels like it's the most obnoxious "re-translation" work so far, namely during the text-based cutscenes. Never mind not actually translating what the dialogue said, but so many times during these cutscenes, the text is way too long or way too short compared to what was just said, so you end up reading too fast or too slow before the next line comes. Other times, they add things like "haha" or "..." in the middle of sentences when you can clearly hear that the dialogue itself never even had those. It's really like they're re-writing the script or something.

The combat here's a bit improved from the last game overall. 
A lot of Heat Actions are a lot more lenient in their trigger requirements now. Enemies have far fewer animations where they're invulnerable so you're more free to attack and grab them without missing when something looked like it should have connected.
The three familiar characters play almost exactly the same as the previous game. Haruka's the most notable for being the only one who doesn't actually do any fighting in the game, but rather her gameplay being solely focused on minigames and substories. The new character, Shinada, may take some getting used to, at least on the harder difficulties where enemies dodge & block more often as Shinada's attacks are really slow and often not big enough to connect to enemies. His extremely improvised-looking fighting style is at least interesting once you upgrade his stuff and learn how to properly use his moves.

Compared to the previous "remasters", this is also the most optimized game of the three, at least with the fan-patch. In the previous games, the fan-patches barely did anything, whereas here I've only ever crashed once during my whole time with the game, and I've never had any frame skipping issues either.

If you got into the previous game, you'll most likely get into this game as well.

review_text:
[h1]An Absolutely Wonderful Isometric Ode to Borderlands[/h1]

Relic Hunters Legend - potentially one of the better shooter looters of the year!  Before we delve into the details of what makes Relic Hunters a worth while pickup, let's talk about something I found to put off a few people to the game - include myself, initially.  The over theatrical intro videos!!  The art style is fun, but whew, these videos are something else.  While you may think that you'll soon be thrust into a world of psychedelic colors and endless monologues, you'll actually find a vibrant tile set of levels spread across four major areas (Trash Sea, Desert, Ice, and City) - and the colorization and art style is fun!! 

Ok - maybe it was just me that didn't care for the intro videos; so, let's dive into the core mechanics and what makes the game fun.

Gear progression is spot on.  With four tiers (gated by levels) of gear at varying qualities, there's plenty of gear hunting to be had.  An upgrade system applies to each piece, and a transfer system is in place to encourage you to upgrade and trade out gear as you find better loot.  

Level diversity is pretty good, from capture objectives, kill all enemies (with a boss at the end), escort, exploration, and others - you won't find issues with variety.  The game also has harder special missions, delves (dungeons with multiple bosses), and a raid system.

Online multiplayer is well integrated, and it's easy to drop into quick matches through the 'help other players' feature, but if you're feeling introverted for a while there's an option to toggle from public to private.

Price point - I mean... when the game launches, it'll be free to play; so, you can't really lose out on that.  For early access, while on the launch sale, it's an easy ~$10, and worth every penny!!

If you've made it this long, thank you... but just go buy the game.  It's funner than reading my reviews.

review_text:
Rating: 6.5/10

The Callisto Protocol looks incredible — no doubt about it. The visuals are top-notch, from the eerie environments to the detailed character models. It really nails the horror atmosphere. The enemy designs are also varied and creative, which helps early on.

The story is one of the game's strongest points. It's actually pretty interesting and had me invested in figuring out what was going on. There's a solid sci-fi horror vibe that fans of the genre will appreciate.

Combat starts off feeling fresh, especially with the melee system and dodge mechanic. But after a few hours, it gets repetitive. Dodging is super easy to master, and once you do, it’s hard to die in combat. The challenge fades quickly, even for beginners.

One of the biggest frustrations is how the game handles multiple enemies. The camera locks onto the last enemy you hit, and there’s no way to change focus mid-fight. So if another enemy comes at you from off-screen, you’ll probably get hit — not because you messed up, but because the camera just won’t show you what’s happening. It’s clunky and unfair.

On the bright side, the telekinesis power is a lot of fun. It adds a cool dynamic to fights and helps make some tough encounters more manageable. I found myself using it often to control space and deal with enemies more efficiently.

The gunplay is fine, but I barely used it. Melee and telekinesis did most of the work, and I mostly saved bullets for specific moments.

Overall, despite its strong visuals, solid story, and fun powers, I can’t recommend The Callisto Protocol. It has too many frustrating design choices, and once I finished it, I didn’t feel any urge to come back. It’s a one-and-done experience for me.

I think this game has been around for awhile.  Seems like it anyway, but I am not about to do homework on that aspect.

The reason why I said no for this game to be a recommendation is because...

The game is confusing, daunting, and seemingly not very user friendly.  What I mean by this is that once you get past the tutorial and start to explore what other things you can do (like crafting, training, etc...), the questions of "How do I do this?" and "Why do I need to do this?" keeps popping up.  I am not one in favor of finding those answers repetitively over and over again.  And figuring out those things on your own seems to be an impracticality.

So, as often I run into this problem with other games, but a lot less in abundance, I often resort to the store to get what I need or want or like...whatever.  And that is where I really find this game disturbing.  Want a specific ship?  First you got to find it and remember exactly where it is, then when you want to buy it, find that it is exorbantly overpriced.  And I mean exorbantly!  Price can range from 30$ to over 100$  And you don't even know if you can put your current officers on it (because nothing is ever explained in plain language), current weapons, and/or what else.  Lifetime subscription price seems to be okay though, but not sure if it is worth it because of what I mentioned above about the confusion.  And the outfits you can buy for your characters seems to be at the right pricing area.  

I know there is a lot going on in the game.  But seriously, it does need to get simplified!  Because I believe the game has been around for awhile and is probably on the last legs, I don't think any serious investment is worth it.  I am afraid by the time I figure everything out and how to do everything, it's pretty much game over.

Spoiler ends.

review_text:
First, let me say that while i've only played this around 8 hours on Steam, I actually bought this game when it released more than a decade ago. I had played to maximum level back then, and watched the game decline from a monthly subscription game into a mobile-like money sucking free to play game.

So the first complaint I have about this game is its "free to play" nature. Like all games that claim to be free to play, there is a real money store integrated into the UI and it is basically where you purchase anything beyond the most absolute basics. This goes far, far beyond just being a cosmetic shop, it actually locks the overwhelming majority of ships, playable species, and bridge officer species behind a pay wall. You can technically play for free, but only playing basic races like humans, andorians, and a couple of others. As far as ships go, you're restricted to the free to play ships which there is basically 1 for each career path every 10 levels and the highest freebie ship I believe is tier 4, while the highest possible is tier 6.

Not only that, but the ships you buy with real money include special equipment and consoles that are very powerful and basically encourages you to buy entire ships just for access to the one specific piece of equipment it has so you can use all of these items together on your preferred ship. This is a pay to win tactic. You not only have to buy the best ship you can afford, but also have to buy other ships you may not even want if you want to be competitive with other players.

The worst part about it though is that all of these ships show up in the basic ship store, where free to play players go to purchase their ships. This means that when its time to upgrade your free to play ship to the next one, you have to go through this very long list of ships you have no access to and cannot buy before you finally get to the bottom of the list where the free ones are. It is also not immediately clear which ships you can and cannot purchase because there are like 3 different currencies, as well as random other items, needed to buy them. The whole system can be intensely confusing for new players.

My next gripe about the game is that everything feels extremely dated. Even when this game originally released back in 2010, the graphics and animations were rather subpar for the time, and in the decade + since then, they apparently haven't change any of it. Maybe the ships in space might look a bit better, they do look pretty clean, but all of the actual characters and away mission settings and maps look like something you would see from a game from 2005. I typically don't care a whole lot about graphics in games, but in this one it irks me particularly because you are required by the gameplay to spend so much time doing away missions. Everything is very awkwardly scaled with things like ship interior hallways being 20 feet wide, the bridges being 3 times larger than they should be and filled mostly with empty space. Away missions are almost universally linear in design where you basically just go in a straight line down hallways or pathways on planets with absolutely no ability to actually explore the area and there is nothing to see down there anyway but invisible walls.

Every mission follows the exact same formula. You fly up to a planet, usually destroy a handful of alien ships, press F near some random macguffins (typically satellites that need reprogramming or anomalies that need scanning or whatever, but you just move close and press F for everything), then beam to the planet or space station where you kill a handful of stationary pre-spawned enemies, press F on a few more items or people, then usually fight a few waves of enemies that spawn and rush at you. Every single mission plays out this way, these are the only elements of the game that exist. Then you beam back to your ship, and the mission is either over or sometimes you have to destroy a couple more ships, then its done.

It can be kind of fun, but it gets intensely repetitive very, very quickly. It's like they took the most mundane and boring aspects of a MMO and turned that into the only gameplay loop in the whole game. Feels like nothing but kill/fetch quests repeating indefinitely. Also, given that you flat out KILL all enemies in every mission and blow up multiple ships, your federation ship basically kills thousands of people every single mission which feels intensely unfederationlike.

On the plus side, I always enjoyed the customization of your bridge officers. You can make them look however you want, name them whatever you want, and change the powers they use both in space combat and as away team members. I always found that aspect to be neat, even though in reality most powers are rather useless and there are definitely optimal ways to set them up. Away teams were also unique in the sense that you and your bridge officers make up your own 5 person party, like most MMOs, except the other 4 characters are NPCs you control. So you can make a tank character, a healer character, and DPS characters to accompany you on away missions without relying on other players, and I did always think that was very cool.

But again, after the game went free to play they kind of fucked it all up because back when you payed $10 a month to play the game, EVERYTHING in game used Energy Credits as the currency. You could use that to buy officers, to change officer skills, to buy ships, to buy equipment, to do literally everything. Now that its "free to play" there are 3 different currencies shoehorned in to try to get you to spend real money to acquire anything. Now you have to figure out which currency you need for each thing and try to obtain it.

It is technically possibly to acquire the other currencies without paying any money, but it takes an absurd amount of time and is very convoluted. For example, you acquire the "Dilithium" resource in small amounts when completing missions. You can then refine it into "Refined Dilithium" but you can only convert a certain amount each day to put an artificial cap on the rate you can acquire it. Some things cost Refined Dilithium, but most of the things cost their "Zen Bucks" currency or whatever it is, and you can exchange Refined Dilithium for Zen Bucks at a horrible rate.

So you're basically looking at doing a handful of missions to get enough dilithium to convert the max amount in a single day, then you convert it. Repeat this process until you reach the maximum possible amount of refined dilithium you can acquire, then you trade ALL of it for a SINGLE zen buck. The ships usually cost something like 10,000 zen bucks. So you'd have to do that 10,000 times. It would take literally years to acquire a single ship for free. Absolute madness.

I think the game was alright back when it launched, but all the pay to win crap they added over the years made it horrific.

If you're a big fan of star trek, it might be worth getting to play sparingly. It can potentially be fun in very short bursts, but it is so intensely repetitive that really the only thing that ever changes are the types of ships you are blowing up and those are more or less randomized, no real sense of progression there. But you have to endure a lot of very dated mechanics and UI elements to play the game which makes it very unappealing as well.

I think if they remade this game from the ground up with better graphics, modern UI design, and remove all the pay to win nonsense, it could potentially be fun, but right now its a mildly amusing distraction from time to time at best and a complete waste of time at worst.

review_text:
Are you looking for a fun yet not too serious hockey game? Tired of playing hockey games that overcomplicate everything, and want to sit back and enjoy a unique hockey gaming experience? Looking for an entertaining hockey game to play co-op or against your friends?

Tape to Tape is the game you’re looking for. Initially, I was impressed by how much fun this game is, especially when played with friends. You’ll never play the same hockey game twice, as it features roguelite elements with unique hockey players, abilities, and even arenas. I’ve never played a hockey video game where you can play a game on a soccer field using soccer balls without hockey sticks, or a golf ball on a golf course.

It’s a fantastic hockey game, and even though it’s in Early Access at the time of this Steam Review, there is more than enough to keep you busy. The campaign mode is incredible, and even after beating it multiple times, it never got boring, since you’ll always get random players and abilities on every run.

Much respect to the developer, Excellent Rectangle, for creating such a magnificent game so far and continuing to implement smart updates based on all our feedback. This is how it should be done, and once the game officially launches, it should perform well. The foundation is there, and if they can continue building upon it, this will be a must-play arcade hockey game.

The graphics are outstanding, and it blew me away at how this sounds like a real hockey game. Chants, crowd noise, and the goal horns are all very well done. The gameplay is solid, and with those random abilities thrown in, you want to keep playing endlessly. Just hit the ice and have fun. That’s the beauty of keeping this game simple to play, but having a lot of depth in unique gameplay.

I give Tape to Tape a 10/10 at this stage in Early Access. I’ve played a plethora of sports games in my life, and this is up there as one of the best. It’s crazy to think this game isn’t even fully launched yet, but my goodness, the amount of fun, laughs, and everything else in between is worth buying this game alone. Throw in some great memories with friends in both co-op and versus, and you have the makings of a future hockey video game classic. If you love hockey as much as I do, buy this game. You won’t regret it because Tape to Tape is so addictive, you’ll be up late plenty of nights, saying just one more game.

review_text:
I've only played a couple of hours but I already had some quite dissappointing moments in the game.
Basically the game feels that it only can be fun if you've already played it and know every corner and secret beforehand. Experiencing it first time is not pleasant.

Bad level design. You can't backtrack and collect loot you were unable to take because you have a limited inventory. You have to know beforehand that there will be a shop soon to sell loot.
You have to know beforehand where to go first because you will be locked out of loot and secrets if you accidentially chose the main story path through the level. It's not really evident which passages are optional.
Enemies appear out of nowhere on script. You can't really see how many enemies you're fighting. Their number can increase midfight just because.
GRP throw an enemy will collide and stop midflight even with smallest collision. Looks unnatural. You lose energy on bad throws and it doesn't feels right.
Some enemy attacks are unavoidable and will damage you no matter what.
If you know beforehand that there will be an enemy you can cheat around it.
Enemy health is a mystery. Some times it takes 5 hits to kill sometimes more. You can't really see why.
Most fights are scripted so you can easily win them only if you know how to approach them. But level design is so poor that most times it's very unevident what was the intent of the level designer. So lots of reloads and experimentation which are not fun. Because you reload even on a slightest feeling that fight is going not good. Hard fights are fun to go through only a few first times. Some time into the game you understand that every fight is only hard if you have approached it wrong.
The most unnatural thing is when you fight multiple enemies they all wait their turn. They can easily rip you apart but they line up and wait while you go through them on at a time.
Game lightning is a physical strain for eyes. Even if you increase gamma.

This is a game built on an already successful core from EHM 2007.  Riz and the SI guys are not new at this, and SI is the company behind the super-popular, long-running Football Manager series.  EHM:EA marks essentially the 4th release in the EHM series after a hiatus of many years,

There is not a more-detailed, in-depth hockey management simulation game available on the market, period.  As with any sports management sim there is a learning curve.  But once you get it, you'll be willingly sinking a whole lot of time into it.

review_text:
I usually try my best to play games more and then give an honest review, but I feel like this game deserves it. When I was younger, I remember that one of my favorite Czech content creators GogomanTV made a video where he played this game. I immediately feel in love. It is very gory, violent and they use strong language (even though I didn't really understand a word I kind of knew what shit and fuck meant back then) ... what's not to love about this game when you are a kid? I remember when Gogo finished the game, I started to watch Pewdiepie how he plays it. And again, even though I didn't understand anything I enjoyed it. I even watch other content creators to play this game to this day (Call me Kevin, Flygun, Wedry...)

I owned this game for a while, but I always ended up stuck somewhere so I had to stop playing. But for some reason I remembered their other game Lucius 3 and I didn't really know what the game offers you, so I watched a gameplay of it... The best thing about it is that Penguinz0 was in it but that's about it. But it made me play this game and finished it. 

I immediately felt nostalgic, and I remembered a lot of deaths and a lot of details that I had to do. The house was big, so I was still lost all the time and I got used to it in like chapter 14 XD. Sometimes you just don't know what to do but maybe I’m just a dummy but I almost every time ended up wandering around the house trying to find a tool, I needed to kill someone. I just knew what to do and I remembered a lot of deaths, but I just couldn't find some stupid tool XD. 

I really adore the fact that you can see how the whole household is going insane. The NPCs dialogues changes through the gameplay. Nancy is going crazy and every time you see her, she's trying to calm you down. Then she starts to scream at you for no reason because she's stressed out about the whole situation... 

Sometimes it's buggy. For example, I got stuck because cutscenes didn't play in chapter 10 in the chamber. The whole chapter was awesome. I liked those sneaky peaky moments, but it was also very stressful, so I didn’t really enjoy playing this again. Then I got stuck in the cutscene in chapter 17... This game was released in 2012 so I get it, but you should be ready for some stupid bugs that will make you restart the whole chapter. 

It's sad that Lucius II was mid and not that fun to watch and I’m pretty sure that I will be even more bored playing it. The map is better but that's about it. I just didn't enjoy it as much and I won't even mention Lucius III. That was just downright awful. This will be my only classic. If you never played it before and you're thinking about it, then go ahead! I highly recommend! If you think that you're into these kinds of games, then you will have a blast!

8/10

review_text:
Pathologic begins at its end. You find yourself there, a failure, begging for another shot. [i] We just didn’t have enough time [/i] . It is not until you fail your first playthrough that this opening scene, or closing scene, really starts to make sense. What’s with the white masks, and the birds, and why has the theater been repurposed to a hospital? Step outside and find yourself walking through more than just foreshadowing; this is the end! Or is it? Can your actions change your fate? 

	Let me start with the criticisms. Pathologic is an unforgiving game. If you cannot embrace failure and tribulation it may not be your cup of twyrine. It is a beautiful game in many regards, but the animations leave much to be desired. There is not full voice acting, so get ready to read—a lot. When was the last time you read a good book? For those who played the first game, it may be disappointing to hear that of the three playable characters in the first one, each with a unique experience, only one is available in this game, and that is unlikely to change due to this games lukewarm commercial success. That being said, it is a fantastic game regardless, and gave me about 30 hours of content on my first playthrough. 

	If you are still reading, maybe you have not been turned away yet. This game has a lot to stay for, so let’s start with its story. The dialogue in this game can be a bit cryptic, but think of the dialogue as this game’s primary mechanic. Like any difficult game, it takes time to learn, but once you do it makes more sense. Characters can be unreliable and deceitful, and they will hold information from you. They speak in riddles, and metaphors, but it's not simply a bad translation or meaningless drivel. Some things may not make sense, even until a second playthrough, but they are important, and you must read everything if you want to have a clue what is going on. And, unlike the average AAA RPG, dialogue choices can carry enormous consequences, and even completely change the trajectory of the game. The narrative itself has elements of magic realism, mystery, horror, and theater. It synthesizes these genres well, into what is a very unique gaming experience. Overall, I really love it, but others may find its enigmatic style a bit grating. 

	Moving on, this game has a great visual art direction. This redeems any shortcomings in animations or mechanics for me. It is simply stunning. It combines the styles of gothic, macabre, and surreal art with a good dose of Russian industrialism. These are juxtaposed against what is likely the Siberian Steppe in a speculative past, along with a great soundtrack, to create something as unsettling as it is beautiful. 

	Finally, the gameplay itself. This is a mixed bag. I would not be writing this if I did not enjoy parts of it, but I do have some frustrations as well. There is a lot of walking in this game, and it can get kind of old. There are ferries that act as fast travel points, but the currency used to travel is sparse. The combat is exceptionally janky, but serviceable, and luckily can usually be avoided. But if you are looking for a game where combat and action are the main attraction, look elsewhere. 

	For me, Pathologic is one of the most memorable gaming experiences I’ve had. If you give this game a chance, I do not think you will be disappointed. This is a truly unique experience that pushes the boundaries of its medium. Whatever you do, don't listen to Aspity. Talk to [i] her [/i] first.

Instead of going against people with guns and wild animals, you will fight against cyborgs with laser guns and cyborg animals. In short, the whole game mocks the whole Far Cry idea and it does it in the most meta way possible, which is I've seen so many people enjoying it.
 Overall, it is definitely one of the best Far Crys ever created. It's an life-changing experience, so go play it, nerd.

Now, for the achievements:
 Really simple: do the intro gameplay, advance until the game tells you there's no going back making sure to headshot every enemy you can, then free all outposts, do all the missions and get all collectibles, kill a bunch of blood dragons and hide from at least one, buy every attachment and the finish the game. You can do it in a day if you're up for it.

I really wanted to love this game, but the gameplay is pretty fustrating. I have plenty of experience with 3rd person shooters and melee based games. Ive played thru dead space remake, jedi fallen order, jedi survivor and final fantasy 15. Easy mode in this game is what hard/hardcore mode would be in other games. Its too difficult to get resources to buy health, ammo, upgrades, etc. In the beginning the game doesn't do enough to ease you into its unique combat mechanism. You have to press left or right to dodge, and you cant press the same button during repeated attacks. Once you get the hang of things its not too bad till you get to the boss fights. The boss fights require you to use ammo instead of the baton, and the bosses are bullet sponges. So even if you think you have enough ammo there's a good chance you don't have enough and its very fustrating. Other than the gameplay being frustratingly challenging, the story and graphics were really good. The main villain of the game was pretty evil and there's lots of plot twists/having to trust bad people to get through the game. The graphics look pretty next gen, so you need a powerful computer to play the game. Its overall decently optimized I would say, it doesn't have the stuttering problem that dead space remake had.

I do hope the game studio still makes a sequel and they listen to the criticism of their poor combat mechanism and improve upon it in the sequel. If they make a sequel I will still buy it

review_text:
To preface, this game is easily one of the better free MMO's out there. It has an interesting dichotomy of ground based combat, and the real glean of the ship acquisition and gearing. The story is decent enough, though the co-op content (resource intensive fleet/guild system) are the main aspects of the game. I'd consider the first 20-200 hours to be reasonably fair, and the recruitment events offer amazing acceleration to endgame content. With it, in a few months you can be on your way to a T6 ship. 

Obviously, a free to play game comes with expensive caveats. A great deal of customization is paid for, and (arguably) many pay to win ships are also locked behing ZEN. You can spend a decent enough on this game and get what you want, and ZEN and most of the cash shop items go on sale on occasion, so I consider this to be an okay method, all things considered.

I really want to like this game. I really want to keep playing this game. But having experienced a 16 day outage during the recent Summer event, causing me to miss out on the T6 ship, completely buzzkilled this game for me. Having gotten 18/20 progress, having farmed the entire gear set, and gotten a 1000 favor floater all from scratch, to be hampered at the finish like was the absolute peak of frustration. I was strung along the whole time, then told with patronizing platitudes that they would not give me even the slightest recompense. With months of rubber-banding (Australia, I know), the game is close to unplayable and I have to call it quits.

review_text: I'm not sure that I would call Scorn a good game, but I don't regret playing it. The art of Scorn is phenomenal ranging from grotesque to arguably beautiful, especially in the final part of the game. I think that Scorn is best as an interactive art portfolio rather than a video game. Unfortunately whenever the game tries to step outside of being interactive art issues arise. This is most apparent in the combat which feels incredibly scuffed. There are only really three enemy types in the game followed by a mind numbingly boring 'boss' in the final act. Combat is very stiff and just generally awkward. I understand why this game did not get a great reception, it was marketed as a horror fps. The issue is that all of the fps elements feel like an afterthought that the devs added so the game would have broader appeal. If Scorn was just a puzzle game and scrapped the combat I think it would be a better experience. Even now the steam page claims that this game is 'open ended'. It is not. It is a completely linear walking sim/puzzle game with clunky combat thrown in. Despite all this, I still think Scorn is worth playing once to experience some fantastic digital art. I just think devs should not be afraid to market a walking sim as a walking sim.

review_text:
(***Minor Spoilers for Setting and Gameplay, tried to avoid story spoilers in my review as the game really benefits from a mostly blind play-though***)

Bloober continues to surprise, between The Medium, SH2 and now Cronos their catalog keeps getting better! Cronos wears its inspirations boldly on its sleeve and certainly isn't re-inventing the genre, but what it lacks in innovation it more than makes up for in an entertaining and consistent game play loop with a compelling story that had more than a few genuine surprises. Its settings benefit massively from the "temporal" nature of the plot, and seems to know just when to switch things up after being in an area for a while. The combat feels rewarding and seemed to favor a slower approach, as supplies (while not bone dry) are just limited enough to keep the tension up. A missed shot in a few of the more challenging sections can really sting, which is exactly what I want from a Survival Horror game. Its economy, crafting system (ammo/supplies ect.) and upgrade systems are very basic (with the genre staple "safe zones" for purchasing equipment and upgrades) but with its very limited inventory size and focus on careful timing with shots, I found myself engaged with its systems through-out. These mechanics in addition with items that take inventory space but don't provide an immediate combat need (sellables, keys, ect.) made inventory balancing land in a great spot for my tastes. 

Cronos is not the scariest game ever made and certainly won't keep you up at night if you enjoy this genre - but it had more than a few great segments that get the blood pumping. If you go in with the expectation of hair raising, sweat inducing segments like seen in the SH2 Remake and you may be let down. That being said, when it hits it really hits and got more than a few well timed jumps out of me without feeling cheap. The scripted sections are all eerie and have a great surreal quality, often making you think twice about if what you are seeing is what it seems. The enemy variety is for sure a weaker point, and I would have liked to have seen one or two more designs, but overall the look and sound of the enemies really grew on me as the game progressed. The merging mechanic is also excellent at making you snap from cautious defensive game play to a more aggressive approach, putting you in control of the difficulty during combat depending on resources and quick thinking. The boss encounters were also well done, but outside of one in particular a bit underwhelming. (*Minor Story Spoiler*) The way your "targets interact with you after you find them was a great boost to the psychological horror aspects, but this game is certainly tipping the scale more towards "combat" than "scary moments".

If you are a fan of Dead Space, RE4, The Evil Within or any of its contemporaries, Cronos is absolutely worth your time and a great addition to the genre. It is confident in its direction and commits to its theme fully, has excellent environmental story telling with an interesting and compelling plot, with some lightly designed but interesting game play gimmicks, and really solid overall foundations that made it a great ride from start to finish! Really excited to see what Bloober does next, they are a team to keep your eye on for sure! 

8.5/10

In the possitive aspects, the gameplay was very fun, the story line was great (and i reccomend it if you're going to play Burial at Sea), and the ending was good as well. There's a large variety of weapons so you have many ways to play and the game even leaves you with a few moral choices. I was able to run this on Max graphics on a video card with 1G of memory. Overall, the settings and the fact that my progress was not saved somehow (I may have uninstalled the game, should have backed the save up) led me to just watch a walkthrough on youtube to see the last third of the game. Should you get this game? It depends on if you're the type of person who will play Portal 1 before Portal 2; the storyline is so simple in Portal 1 and most of the time spent playing is spent playing a game mechanic: puzzles with portals. Sort of the same deal here.

review_text:
Samorost 2 have good visuals, sounds and music, both very closer to Machinarium.
But i can't recommend it because this game have too many negative points... a lot of them.

The first thing you notice is that you can't change resolution - you have to play it on a very tinny window. Being a Flash game, you can zoom in the image - and it's good - but you have to do it at every single new clip loaded. No Steam working layer, also.

The puzzles doesn't make much sense, so you have to pixel-hunt on your tinny screen, or bother yourself zooming every new screen. You'll fight to find the point to click many times, mostly places you need to enter or walking by, because they're not so visible, and considering the puzzles doesn't make much sense, it's always a waste of time and patience.

The game is very, very short. Not even 2 hours.
And part of this time you'll just watch your character slowly walking from a place to another, and since sometimes you have to do the same things more than once, it's very annoying. Also, you have not a save system, any of them. Instead, you receive codes every new level, and you can enter these codes if you want to play it later. If you don't realize the purpose of these codes to memorize them or take note, you'll have to play again from beginning, and considering what i said about slowly walking, you know what does it mean.

Finally, you don't have any real support from Amanita Design (developer). They're not present at Steam forums, and never patch their games to fix, improve or adapt them to continue to sell them. Although the asked price is low, it's not worth by any aspect, maybe for 1 dollar or so, and if you really like P&C games or the art style.

review_text:
TLDR: Don't buy this game, watch a Let's Play or a friend go through the game to see the visuals.
This game is interesting. A ton of thought went into the artstyle and how to make things alien yet still somewhat recognizable as a mechanism with a designed purpose. 
The environments, while somewhat repetitive, are still interesting as each area has its own theme. Its when you spend the entire area walking around nearly identical tunnels that the luster fades until you reach a new area with its own fresh design.
However, there are some issues that leads me to not recommend this game despite 100 percenting it (thought thats not much of an achievement). Firstly, is the false advertising. The store page as of this review, still claims that Scorn is an adventure game with regions that you can explore in a non linear fashion. This game is not non linear. There is only 1 decision point in the entire game and you can reach it in 20 minutes if you can solve the first puzzle pretty quickly. This decision has literally no ramifications on anything once you leave the room outside of which achievement you get. 
The combat is absolutely abysmal. Extremely clunky controls even by the standards of when the game first started development nearly a decade ago, let alone in 2022. Resources are punishingly rare leaidng to the possibilities o being stuck in deathloops, where you walked past a check point with low health forcing you to walk on a knife's edge until you stop dying and find more health. Speaking of checkpoints, their locations are rare, entirely arbitrary, and often many minutes of walking away from where you died, resulting in frequent backtracking to continue the game. No existing method of manual saving. Harping further on this section much longer isn't a good idea, as I can't put my thoughts on that very well. 
Movement around the game world is jerky at best. Character has a very strange level of momentum, though I have heard its much better on controller than keyboard and mouse. There is no jump button. Game is littered with invisible walls to prevent you from exploring too much and is frankly overzealous. In areas where they missed an invisible wall, you will wish they hadnt, because the game does not register fall damage and you will get stuck or fall into the void.
The puzzles are meh. Nuf said.
Overall, a very well done art piece, but not a game I would recommend you play. I recommend watching someone else play, so you can appreciate all the effort that went into visual and audio design while avoiding having to deal with the dreadful gameplay yourself.

review_text:
This game is really frustrating to play and the controls are generally counter intuitive, which paired with a style of level design that demands so much of the player while offering virtually no freedom of how to tackle a situation, is a recipe for disaster in my opinion. Shadow Tactics is excellent as a concept, has a passable story and great art direction, but the execution is possibly the worst I have ever seen in a game that demands so much of the player. 

I keep coming back to this game hoping to feel different and it just makes me wish I refunded it while I had the chance. The quick save feature, while brilliant in theory, just leads you to resent the game's level design even more. It makes it immediately clear that this game was designed in mind that even a single step outside of what exact action (or combination of actions) the game expects you to perform is immediate mission failure and having to quick load and try again. 

Expecting a player to bash their head against a wall over and over and clearly designing the game around that process is just not fun design. Overcoming challenging obstacles is a rewarding experience, I don't think anyone would challenge that claim. There are hundreds of games that exemplify this well. But when you finally succeed in Shadow Tactics, you're not left with euphoric celebration. You're left with a feeling of "Thank god that is finally over" only to watch a short, barely animated dialogue sequence and to be thrust into an even more absurdly designed level.

I really wanted to like this game but it's just not for me, I gave it several attempts and I will probably give it a few more because I have never left a game unfinished before, but I just don't think it's going to happen. Time and money are both precious and for CDN$ 47.99, plus paid DLC, there are thousands of better games to spend your time and money on.

review_text:
I might recommend this game if it were solely a historical visual novel (but that wouldn't remove the problem of historical revisionism and romanticization) but since Hakuoki is marketed as otome game, I cannot recommend it as such. It can be easy to fall for one or more of the love interests (I surely did) but the meaninglessness of the female MC that the narrative creates by always prioritizing the love interests and the lack of care given to her by both game and love interests, Hakuoki Kyoto Winds (and Edo Blossoms) fail(s) at romance.
[hr]Kyoto Winds is the first part of this edition of the Hakuoki franchise. The split into two is justified by the change in tone and game mechanics but even being half the full game's length, KW is still too long - mostly due to the abundance of love interests. Originally, the franchise had 6 love interests and while I do like two thirds of the new 6, I would have preferred it if some characters' routes were cut or the overall game were made less repetitive. This game is unplayable without a guide and if you look at one, it would seem there were many choices to make here. But when you look at their nature, you'll find that they only serve 3 functions: 1) getting MC to be in or avoid situations where she can interact with certain love interests, 2) making you choose between love interests and 3) gaining or not gaining the affection of a certain love interest. {In Edo Blossoms, the choices are only type 3) and an additional choice type which is completely redundant.} [b]If you like VNs where your choices matter (e.g. Amnesia: Memories, Heart Fragment), Hakuoki KW and EB are not for you.[/b] Another thing are the endings which, apart from the good endings, are mostly redundant and insignificant. The bad endings all end in either the MC or the love interest (LI) or both dying, whereas the unrequited love endings are either "LI leaves MC behind" or "LI sacrifices himself". [b]If you like VNs where each ending, good or otherwise, adds something to the game (experience) (e.g. Amnesia: Memories, Heart Fragment), Kyoto Winds isn't for you. [/b] {A similar thing can be said about Edo Blossoms where they added Game Over endings but those are just premature bad endings.} [/hr]
[hr]Aesthetically at least, this game does not disappoint. The art and CGs are great, the music is solid but can get on your nerves if you play through the whole game.[/hr]
[hr]Overall, if you're interested in this game, just watch playthroughs of it online. Neither KW nor EB are games that need to be played since they are linearly structured and probably the most literal definition of "visual novel" - a novel with visuals. And Hakuoki doesn't need your money, it's getting enough at home because everything Shinsengumi-related is highly popular in Japan (thanks to the romanticization of the past and yearning for a time where samurai still existed and were fighting against change).[/hr]
[hr]CWs (that I noticed): Mild depiction of blood, textual descriptions of violence and gore, use of alcohol and inebriation (by/of the love interests), verbal abuse & control of the MC (by love interests and others), sexism and conservative gender roles e.g. towards the MC (by love interests and others), familial mistreatment of the MC (by sibling and parent).[/hr]

review_text:
+ The economy in this game is well-developed and intricate. You have multiple ways to obtain resources, and you will have to find balance between money, reputation, and time. You will also have to think about what is better for you in the long term, but if you invest too much, you will be faced with setbacks and sometimes even death. 
+ It employs something that could be called nonlinear storytelling. You will be looking at a branching and interlinking mind map with multiple agendas for progressing. Sometimes small ideas could lead to huge discoveries, and you will have to decide which have importance and which are just dead ends and filler.
+ The map is really pretty and well laid out. No district place feels the same while still making navigating challenging. It does not lack detail, and you can experience so much by just walking around.
+ Stepee wives boobs.

- The art and music are really bland. It tries too hard to be dark/indigenous and have an eggy aesthetic. I think that the main point of the game is the balancing of different aspects of reality, so even though this one-dimensional representation of the world works from the point of view of a main character, it does not capture the complexity of the whole town.
- I really don't understand why every npc hates you so much. Is that just to feed more to the already depressive atmosphere? It mostly doesn't make sense in the story and serves just to humiliate the player. Then there are moments when everything treats you as the only savior and God of the universe. Yes, it is that inconsistent.
- There are so many fourth-wall breaks that it gets annoying really quick. It still uses a lot of theater/toy symbolism, but given the emphasis on more realistic gameplay, it just feels so forced just for the sake of being implemented to add more depth points with the critics.
- Time is the biggest enemy? More like we will not give you enough time to experience the whole story, so you will be forced to play the game for a second time. I think that is too much of a demand from a player in this economy of attention. 

It seems to me that the studio was not aware of what game they wanted to make. In the end we get a remake of the original game modernized, but now the problem is that the substance doesn't match its form. Sure, it is an experience, but it does not know who it was made for. It is supposed to be a "pain simulator," but that means that most average players will never give preference to this over any AAA title. The reason I would not recommend this game is simply because it betrays itself.

review_text: Hakuouki is such a great series, I wasnt sure how i'd like this series after I have played Amnesia, since of course this game is a different time period completely and has way more stories to it that I thought it may be hard to follow. I really enjoy this whole series, even though its mostly pictures and text its really worth while, gets you fangirling over characters and such. The characters are well designed as well, which I have seen some really bad art to a lot of series like this, which can sort of put you off. Of course this is a game directed towards females, and of course if you're a male and like romance sort of stories, this would count as well. The game tries to make you the protagonist and it is a game where your choices effect what happens, so you can play this game freely, or you can follow walkthroughs for the good endings, I enjoy doing both. It is pretty easy to follow, the only thing I recommend is having both games, since you can just continue the story on the next game and then come back to this game.

review_text:
After diving in and playing the prologue I suspected that this game may be a depressing slog... and it was. Well it was a depressing, disgusting, boring slog, actually. Ok, honestly I WAS having a little fun at around act two. But sincerely; this is potentially the worst gaming experience I have had in my life...

The game opens with lots of puzzle elements strewn across a large area and no hints or tutorials as how navigate the world. In fact you're given no dialogue, no UI hints, no direction whatsoever. The main mechanics do become clear, but the detection for interacting with important objects and / or elements is awful. What then results is a lot of running back-and-forth trying to figure out what the game wants of you, which is basically just opening a pathway to the next area. Once you've opened the way forwards, or upwards, or through something awful, you move on and then get to do it again. And again. In a more disgusting area...

And I think that's my gripe with the game. It was too gross and I had to spend too long there figuring out what the hell I had to interact with or where I had to go without dying - that's of the eventual drudgery OR the enemies with their superhuman aim.  That's not to say that the combat is actually difficult, mind you, just that you have to figure out how to play it yourself. Spoiler: You just WAIT for you character to aim. At monsters. And occasionally the environment. If you have the ammo to progress, of course. 

That said, I could have forgiven the game's flaws for some story development or a decent ending. I mean, I hated most of it, like how I was terrified of Silent Hill 2's first play-through and ran around in a panic. But Silent Hill was as compelling as it was terrifying. You just keep going back for more. Scorn on the other hand is more like an uncle letting out a wet fart after Christmas dinner. And everyone has to breathe it in. 

At least I don't have to throw the chair out after playing it, however, which was nice.

I have decent PC, but most loading screens can take at least 3-5 minutes to load in the map and it takes at least two loading screens to load into the game. After you play the intro of the game and you get hyped to continue playing. It makes you have to play each of the six side content first. There are six doors (most of which aren't gamemodes I would normally play) and you have enter every single one first to actually play the campaign. This doesn't sound so bad at first, but then you realize that for each of the doors, you have to wait for two loading screens. One for when you enter and one for when you leave. It took me over a half an hour of loading screens just to continue playing the campaign. After this the campaign is pretty good, but ever time I want to play it I have to wait at least 10 minutes of loading. And I am not the only person who having these long load times and in the first game it took no where near as long. The gameplay is really fun, but it feels like a chore to get to it. I haven't finished the game and I don't know if I will if they don't optimize the loading screens

review_text:
To be honest I can't understand why people like this game so much. In fact, I think this is out right an awful game. Now, I want to start by saying I don't care for Batman. I don't like him as a character nor do I dislike him. So 'being Batman' had no impact on my perception of the game. The game is bland at best and garbage at worst. The dialogue is annoying, stupid, and feel weird an unnatural. The story to what I can tell is poor and uninteresting. The characters are completely flat. The world is tiny and has basically nothing going on other than a bunch of guys walking around to beat up and useless little collectibles and 'side missions.' The combat is about the worst part of the game and makes up a majority of the game play; it has been copied by about 500 other games and all the other ones do it better. The combat has no complexity, nothing interesting happens, and the animations and movement have zero weight so the combat isn't even satisfying to perform well. The mini games are a huge hassle and none of them are properly explained. It also has that mission structure where every time you think you're getting something done some dumb BS gets in the way and distracts from the mission so the pacing is REALLY annoying. I really have no upsides to this game other than maybe some cool-looking architecture. Everything I've seen so far is either bland or bad and I don't want to play through 20 hours of bland or bad. 

Like I said I really can't understand why people like this game. Maybe it's because everyone these days has a huge, impractical hard-on for Batman. At it's core, though, mechanically, it is not a good game.

"RollerCoaster Tycoon 2" is the second instalment in the beloved RollerCoaster Tycoon series, a theme park simulation game developed by Chris Sawyer Productions and published by Atari. Released in 2002, it builds upon the success of the original game, offering enhanced features and more creative opportunities for players. Here's a review of "RollerCoaster Tycoon 2":

**Title: A Timeless Classic in Theme Park Simulation**

**Rating: ★★★★★**

**Pros:**

1. **Deep Gameplay:** "RollerCoaster Tycoon 2" offers a deep and engaging gameplay experience. Players take on the role of a theme park manager, tasked with building and managing their own amusement park. The game provides numerous tools and features to design, customise, and manage every aspect of your park.

2. **Variety of Rides and Attractions:** The game offers a wide variety of rides, roller coasters, and attractions to choose from. Building and customising these attractions, from gentle rides to intense coasters, allows for endless creativity.

3. **Scenarios and Objectives:** The game presents players with a series of scenarios, each with specific objectives and challenges to complete. These scenarios provide a sense of progression and purpose, encouraging players to expand and improve their parks.

4. **Sandbox Mode:** In addition to the scenarios, "RollerCoaster Tycoon 2" features a sandbox mode that allows players to build and experiment without the constraints of objectives. This mode is perfect for unleashing creativity and crafting your dream amusement park.

5. **Modding Community:** Over the years, the game has developed a strong modding community, which has created custom content, scenarios, and tools that extend the game's lifespan and add even more replay-ability.

**Cons:**

1. **Graphics:** While the game's graphics were decent for its time, they are somewhat dated by today's standards. Modern players may find the visuals less appealing compared to newer simulation games.

2. **Learning Curve:** "RollerCoaster Tycoon 2" has a learning curve, particularly for newcomers to the series or the simulation genre. Understanding the game's mechanics, optimizing ride designs, and managing finances effectively can take some time.

3. **Path Building:** Constructing and modifying paths and walkways can be a bit challenging and less intuitive than desired. This aspect of park design may require patience and practice.

4. **Limited Modern Features:** Compared to newer entries in the genre, "RollerCoaster Tycoon 2" lacks some modern features and conveniences, such as advanced AI behaviours and more sophisticated graphics.

In summary, "RollerCoaster Tycoon 2" is a classic and highly enjoyable theme park simulation game that has aged remarkably well. Its deep gameplay, creative opportunities, and scenario-driven progression provide a fulfilling and engaging experience for fans of simulation games. Despite its age and some minor shortcomings, it remains a timeless title in the genre and is a must-play for anyone who enjoys building and managing their own virtual theme park.

review_text:
A very good survival horror from the makers of the Silent Hill 2 remake.

Pros:
- Excellent, oppressive atmosphere.
- Amazing setting (post-apocalyptic 1980s Poland with sci-fi elements added).
- At times the visuals are really striking.
- I always felt the amount of ammo is just right to make things tense - I always felt that if I started missing more often, I would run out and get killed quickly as melee is not really a valid strategy.
- The enemies look really good and the joining mechanic makes things interesting.
- While the inspirations with Dead Space are obvious, the game is distinct enough not to be brushed off as a knock off.

Cons:
- Some plot points make no sense and the game does not even try to explain them (for example: who put the antigravity pads everywhere and why? And even how?).
- While I commend the creators for trying to be original, I didn't really like the electricity puzzles or the antigravity sections.
- That damn inventory management.
- The lack of Polish dubbing is jarring, seeing as not only this is a Polish game, it's also set in Poland.

review_text:
I see ACT 2 cynically. This game has a lot of interesting lore about Troll society, but that's because this game effectively exists to give non-Homestuck fans a crash course in Troll sociology for the later two ACTs. It was the moment that Xefros feeds Joey a full explanation (many times more concise than the original webcomic explanation by the way, this isn't a complaint) of the troll's quadrant system as opposed to being delivered more cleverly through dialogue and interaction that I felt this way. Joey isn't a moron except when she's entirely unable to derive meaning from context. I can only read dialogue to the effect of "huh? Weird alien word??" so many times before I start thinking that the character speaking it sounds dumb.

As far as the game itself goes, in most ways it's a step down from ACT 1. Great character moments and a good story continuation, but middling gameplay, and an extended Ace Attorney parody mini-game that manages to rapidly overstay its welcome and then drag on for about a couple of hours. The game starts, I get on a train, and it ends at the exact moment I get off the train that I've been wanting off for 5 hours because at this point I'm exhausted.

The most hopeful thing about ACT 2 is that it's hopefully the worst one. I think ACT 3 has a lot of potential to be good based on the conclusion of ACT 2, but part of that is going to have to be on What Pumpkin to make the gameplay more engaging and better paced. If ACT 3 comes out in three years and continues the trend that ACT 2 has started, it won't be worth buying.

review_text:
If I could recommend a "maybe" for this game I would. It's not a bad game, but after about 10 multiplayer missions you've pretty much seen everything the game has to offer. I don't even bother playing on hard because the bugs kill you pretty much instantly and they are bullet sponge tanks. I played as a grenadier for the entire time I've played except a few missions as heavy gunner. I would say the grenade launcher feels pretty good (although very inaccurate). The rest of the guns felt extremely weak to me. I wish they would make the guns feel stronger and give you more variety in your loadout because right now the bugs are much stronger than your weapons and your loadout choices are pretty limited per class (unless you grind a ton and rank up forever).

Playing as a explosives guy, I had a lot of issues placing remote bombs. I don't know if it was the server lag, but in the middle of combat sometimes my bombs just wouldn't place on the ground and I'd end up dying because I couldn't deploy my bombs. Kind of glitchy and frustrating. Just let us throw the bomb packs out instead of placing directly on a spot.

The base building is pretty good, but your defenses are fairly paper-thin when going up against the hordes. I would say they need to boost the defenses a little bit also. Most missions just devolve into everyone running around on fire and you not being able to see what's going on. The giant yellow tanks are insanely tanky, they killed me pretty much everytime and sometimes come in groups. Kind of annoying unloading 12 grenade rounds, 2 remote packs, and multiple hand gun rounds into it and not killing it.

I do feel a bit like the DLC is a cash-grab for skins & gun colors. Not really worth it in my opinion when you don't even really see your own character and most of the levels are pretty dark.

The solo missions are near unplayable. I got through about 4 and then just gave up on them. I dropped a canister I was carrying extremely far and it just disappeared. I wasn't about to run back the entire way for another (for the 3rd time). I would just stick to the tutorial and then straight to multiplayer to avoid frustration.

Matchmatching is a bit of a problem right now. It takes several minutes to find a server and you won't be able to really pick the exact mission type you want. You will eventually connect, but it's just totally random what server & game mode you get.

Overall, it was a fun nostalgic way to re-live the movie and play base horde for a while, but there are some problems with this game that make it not as fun as it could be. I wouldn't say it's a bad game at all, but needs improvement for more replay. It seems like the devs are actively working on it though, so I hope they make it better.

Overall 6/10

I can see where some of the positive reviews come. I really like the art style but I cannot in good conscience recommend this game to anyone. It's a pity I wasn't aware that there was a 2 week as well as 2 hour playtime refund policy because I would really like my money back...

My complaints are with the combat... I appreciate what the game devs were going for, I really do. It has an old school vibe with lots of consumable items and food to restore hp/mana. I can't get passed the first 30 minutes of the game though, it just feels so bad to me. It's old school in the fact that you attack in the air and fall like a rock. Holding forward and attacking in the air causes loss of momentum and you literally just fall with sword coming down with you. There is an item near the very front that gives you a brief "float" to be able to perform midair attacks. You still lose momentum and just fall down during the attack though, like an early Castlevania game... There is a duck and roll but it doesn't function as a dodge, nor the there a block button.

As I can't even get a refund for the game I'm deleting from my library permanently but not before I shared my thoughts on why this is not something I would recommend to anyone.

Titanfall 2 styled movement, with risk of rain styled gameplay loop. To be clear, this is not an item heavy, build crazy bullshit runs style rogue lite like RoR, but the same themes are at work. The more enemies you kill, the more shards you get to open vaults and buy upgrades, the higher the terror level rises, the more dangerous enemies become, until you clear the level and upgrade to the next zone along the way.

Vulgarity and gore does not a good game make.  I was sorely disappointed in Bioshock, and indeed, the entire series after finally playing through most of the games.  For years I had heard the praise of this series only to see that it was not that good. 

The story in Bioshock was disappointing - I had hoped for a much more interesting twist than what was unveiled.  

I did enjoy the character, weapon and level designs. This is the game's strongest part but rich steampunk, future-retro feel gets ruined by the bleak environments and constant blood letting violence.  

I actually did not finish the game as I encountered the well known and unfixed game breaking bug in the Sander Cohen level that does not let you advance; ended up watching a playthrough of the rest of the game from that point. I fell no loss for not having finished Bioshock myself.
