review_text:
This would actually be a solid 5/10 or maybe even 6/10 game if the execution was decent, but the game is overall of poor quality.
I will not include the story in my rating as I think it's irrelevant and almost non-existent in this title.

there's a couple of things that I like in this game, and it's the pretty decent equipment variety and side objectives/challenges, especially bounties, some of which have unique scenarios that keep things fresh. but that's all that's going for the game.

My biggest problem with this game is how clunky everything you do feels. Jumping, climbing, placing gadgets, throwing knives, ADS-ing etc. all feels off, and all of it has that very awkward split second where you feel like you can move on but the animation is not done yet. I think the biggest offender here are the throwing knives, which take 7 business days to allow another input in.
Another huge problem the game has is the AI and its hivemind like behaviour, where ALL of the enemies in the area suddenly know my location. What's weird is there are aspects that indicate some work has been done to make a proper AI for a stealth game, like a delayed alert state spread or enemies investigating bodies alone before alerting others, but it feels like the system was rushed and/or cut short.
The balance of weapons and mods is also atrocious, there's no reason not to slap a suppressor and a special mag on your heavy sniper rifle. Mobility is a cool stat, but it's not enough to deter people from using heavy SRs.

Overall, the game has a lot of problems that cripple it on every step of the way, souring the whole experience which could've been a not so bad casual shooter to boot up from time to time.
I'm guessing the game was on a strict schedule or just rushed in general because it feels like it desperately needs another month or two of development at the very least.

review_text:
This isn’t some frenzied, top-down action game; Shadow Tactics is strategic, methodical, and refreshingly hardcore. One of the best tactical strategy games i ve played. You’ve got hints of Metal Gear Solid and Hitman in there, infused with a bit of Tenchu and more than a little of the venerable Commandos series.

If you haven’t guessed already, the game takes place during Japan’s Edo period, a time of samurai, ninjas, and epic clan wars. Despite achieving unification and years of peace, the shogun senses a looming threat, enlisting an unlikely team of misfits and burdening them with the fate of Japan.

Led by the honour-bound Mugen, Shadow Tactics has you controlling a warrior, spy, shinobi, thief, and sharpshooter as they infiltrate and assassinate using a medley of unique skills. As the player, you will control them one at a time, sneaking past patrols, taking out targets, and completing a variety of objectives.

This is all done in real time, albeit from a top-down perspective, and although Shadow Tactics can be likened to other stealth action games, it comes out as something rather unique.

The game is at its best when combining character abilities to lure, distract, and take down guards without being seen. It can definitely feel a bit trial and error at times though this does little to diminish that sense of reward when a plan is executed perfectly. For those wanting to demonstrate some added flare, they can use Shadow Mode to assign orders to several party members, triggering multiple queued actions with a single button press.

WHAT’S GOOD:
Hardcore stealth action
Rewarding, tactical gameplay
Large environments that offer multiple approaches

WHAT’S BAD:
Some frustrating stealth sections
Levels can be long and exhausting

In short, the game is extremely satisfying and should definitely be played by strategy lovers.

review_text:
Probably the best immersion of atmosphere that I have ever experienced. It is not a "game" like the others; it is more of a simulation of solitude, with an atmospheric pressure so intense that it becomes difficult to think, hard to breathe, and hard not to get lost. The many landscapes of mechanical bodies blur love, war, procreation, the art of giving life, and taking it away. The enormous buildings induce vertigo—what are these nurseries, often transformed into slaughterhouses? By combining Zdzisław Beksiński's work with Hans Ruedi Giger's, a new dimension is created in their art, as if they were destined to meet, with one being nothing without the other, as if they were formed from the same skin.

The atmosphere in Scorn is suffocating, eerie, and profoundly alien. There is no dialogue, no guiding narration—only the sound of wet, pulsing textures, bone creaks, and distant groans. review_text:
The friendship is exactly what you are going to lose playing this ill designed game.

The game consist of 3 trials. Without spoiling anything:
- the 1st one is designed properly. You understand what is happening and the tutorial is good enough. You might not understand the time pressure at first, but restarting this trial is not tedious at all.
- the 2nd trial is a overcomplicated puzzle, which tutorial is inexistant. You will ultimately succeed, but the game forces you to finish your attempt despite knowing the outcome is already bad.
- the 3rd one is the worst of all. This is mostly a platforming trial with many mini challenges where communication is key. The tutorial for the main concept of that trial is innexistant, so you might first not understand what you need to do as the observer, and on the top of that, you will not understand why the observer is key in that trial. Actually, you might not even understand that you are an actual observer. The timings are too tight to feel fair for both players on the second mini challenge. And while this trial is about communication, you will restart it so often that the non-observer player will end up learning by heart what to do, and the communication is reduced to strict minimum. Oh, and the best is that if you have a disconnection, you are frozen... Did I mention the tight timmings?

I would really not recommend this episode, and after playing two of them I believe I wouldn't continue the "We were here" series.

For the record, I have played both games with a person I have excellent communication, with whom I have solved countless IRL and virtual escapes rooms.

review_text:
I so badly wanted to say this is good, but it just annoys me so much sometimes that it's lost all good faith I had. I don't care about the microtransactions (Escape Games are dip in games anyway and if you're stuck just use walkthroughs, save hint stars for skipping annoying puzzles) nor the episodes you need to buy (not that I'm happy about it, I came to 100% it and found out at least 9 achievements are locked behind a paywall. But so long as I get MOST of it, I can live with it at least). But the thing that makes me give this a bad review? The flip floppy nature of the puzzle difficulty. And no, I don't mean the fact it's "Beginner/Intermediate/Advanced", I mean the difficulty PER STORY.

Here's an example: I'm playing Death Dodgers. In one chapter, there's a puzzle where you count how many objects there are and that's the number on a code, one number for each code. The COLLECTIVE AMOUNT of this object equals the number (keep this in mind). Collective Amount codes are common fair in a lot of these puzzles. In the very next chapter, I see another puzzle with a similar motif: colour 1, colour 2, colour 3, colour 2, colour 1. I know images nearby have clues. Ergo, I do the usual, I add up the clues... Only it doesn't work. Nothing I can think of works. The answer, despite EVERY. SINGLE. GAME. I played THUS FAR (about 8 entire storylines) having "coloured things = collective number is code", this one is not that. This puzzle is "left number, left number, number, right number, right number".

And this isn't the first time the puzzle has been purposefully obtuse. People rip on Resident Evil for convoluted puzzles, but that's "use a thing, read a memo, find an object", they're basic. This? You can FEEL it was designed to force people to pay for hint stars. "The skeletons have directions on them", you mean the crook of the elbow that looks like an arrow for this arrow puzzle? "NO, MORON, IT'S THEIR NON-POINTY HANDS, OBVIOUSLY!". Not to mention, in Dark Ruins the rhythm game gives you notes that look exactly the same but one moves ahead of the other when you have two seconds to react and the forensics puzzle in Murder Inn has inaccurate readings. You know, forensics, the art of exact measurements, calculations and fact to determine who did what and how in law? Well, I got four different readings for the size of a bullet and the walkthrough I looked up showed a number I DIDN'T EVEN GET!!! It was a measuring tool WHICH MEASURED INCORRECTLY. And don't get me started on the fact that clicking an item will bring up a text box: You can't click anything pick-up-able while that text box is there. I clicked on the same god damn magnet 20 times and couldn't pick it up cos Kate yakked on about the board it was on. I solved the puzzle it was needed for with a little smarts (I tilted angled myself to see the outline of a creature in a fish tank then just tried the two possible combinations. Got it on the second one) but when I got bored of the tape puzzle that followed, went to a walkthrough to just get it out of the way, and then discovered you can, in fact, pick up the magnet, I was obviously aggravated.

Oh, but a time bomb? Getting shot at while pushing objects? Solving a puzzle that spanned an entire arcade? Piece of cake. All, btw, the final puzzle of the level. Same with the last Mirror Man puzzle. Same with Vanishing Act. Same with every. Single. Level. The annoying puzzles are the ones that are in the way, not the ones that matter. And I hate that the puzzles ruin this because there's glimmers of "Hey, that's a smart puzzle!", moments where the logic behind them is sound, where they do take some thinking but they're not impossible (again, even on Advanced, those difficulties mean nothing, puzzles flip flop). There's aspirations of a great Escape Game here, just like all the ones I played in the Flash era. Even the stories are good, I honestly like the writing and I was shocked to see so much death in these cos they give off the vibe of a teen game AT MOST, not something where you see a kid's parents die or a man turn into a skeleton.

But, no, the puzzles are clearly designed with hint money in mind. There's a difference between solving a Rubix Cube and solving it while on fire, blind, with your hands cut off, while falling off a cliff. And sadly the creators of these puzzles sometimes think the latter is the better choice...

Edit for later on: Having played more stories (as I mentioned, I'm achievement hunting), I am 100% firm in my belief they want your money, I found more purposefully obtuse puzzles and some broken ones too. Not broken as in unsolveable, broken as in the clues are practically useless to you and the instructions are so vague you may as well just say "Good luck, moron!" as a hint.

Edit two: Scratch that previous comment, one of the puzzles in final chapter of Cursed Crown is unplayable on PC cos it requires touch screen, so save 50 stars for that to skip it. I'm nearly done achievement hunting but, honestly, I think I'm put off Escape Games for life. I've reached a point of hate for these puzzles that I can totally understand why Bond villains would destroy the Earth over the pettiest of things. I don't want a gold star when I get a puzzle right, my reward will be never touching this ever again.

Edit three: I don't care if I don't have all the achievements (I'm not buying the Covenant nor playing this on mobile). I'm free! FREE, I TELL YOU! OH! It's so good to know I never need to touch this game again!

I haven´t finished the game yet, but I wanted to share my thoughts.
This is the first Yakuza Game I did not enjoy for the most part. I thought the pacing in Yakuza 4 was awful but this game takes the cake in that regard. Many boring parts and the Story is dragged out way too much. 

Of course this is still a Yakuza-Game, it has the humour and some really good parts. In regard of the Story-pacing and Mini-Games, Kiryus Chapter is the best in the entire Game. The Taxi-Sidemissions is the the best Mini-Game in the entire franchise, even better then cabaret club. Kiryus fight against the Tojo-Clan is one of the best in the entire Series (Kiryu doging a Missile is freaking awesome). 

I never was a fan of multiple characters in the Yakuza Games in the first Place. It dragges out the tension of the Story. This is the case especially after Kiryus part, where the game lets you run errands in the prison for 3 hours without any Mission-Markers. In Yakuza 4, the Prison was the worse part and now you can do the same shit again in Yakuza 5.

The reason I gave this game a thumps down is that they failed the balance between the serious stuff (Story) and the unserious parts (Side Missions, Mini-Games, etc.). I mostly enjoyed the Mini-Games, but if the other 50% of the game is poorly made, it is not fun anymore, especially if you played Yakuza not only for the Mini-Games, but also for the Story.

I know that Yakuza 6 will only have Kiryu as a Main-Character, on top of that, it is way more Story-focused then this Game, I will probably enjoy that Game more then Yakuza 5.

6/10

But that didn't detract from my enjoyment of these games. I played all of the Trapmaker trilogy and am now on the pirate one. If I had a criticism, it would be that it's not always clear what you are supposed to do. Sometimes I would get held up at one place and the "solution" would be that I needed to click on a certain part of the wall in order to open a panel, but the wall didn't look particularly "clickable." That is frustrating. Also, the interrogation process in the early games is really broken. You have to navigate your way through a dialogue tree, but if you make a mistake and have the wrong response, it starts you over at the complete beginning of the conversation. So you have to memorize every single answer you give because chances are, you will have to repeat the conversation multiple times in order to find the correct path. Later games seem to solve this, allowing you to just return to the previous question without forcing you to start all over again in the conversation.

Overall, I really enjoyed these games and wish that more of them were available on steam. The only way to play the rest of these games seems to be on mobile, and I don't game that way. Still, these ones were fun, and I highly recommend them.

Great game, love the concept, alright execution, good original sound track, Dev is committed though.

Rise to Ruins is a sort of Tower Defense/Colony sim type experience best summed up. You start, you have a colony centre, there's 10 people and work to be done, most of the social functions happen automatically but you can observe it real time and read the logs (they also react to your godly power which is nice). At first it's not too clear how the jobs section 'truly' functions but it gets easier to balance that when you understand the resource use, most people seem to complain the opposite though. Tower Defense is the other half of this: you need to build towers, upgrade them, maybe get some magic going, defensive golems, and walls. You continue this cycle as your colony space expands onto the map. Once you have enough people you can then migrate to different areas on the world map, there's some different biomes as well, keeps it fresh on a playthrough. (oh yeah there's trash too, heck that guy)

Overall completely worth it for the price imo, just that fun game to boot up every now and then and bust too many hours out in one session. There's been updates and roadmaps posted too, always a plus (as of this review)

review_text:
Honestly, 7 hours in I had lost all the will to continue, I was constantly hoping that it would end soon. 



Gameplay :

The stealth sections are way too easy, enemy being really dumb with extremely exploitable vantage point/grate takedown, alongside the extremely overpowered Detective vision just made it a matter of patience with barely any thinking required, since you can just hide easily because of their AI, there is usually no risk in getting caught cause you can just go inside a grate or repeteadly jump between vantage points, and rinse and repeat. 

The combat is really good and I played the entire game in hard difficulty, however the severe lack of enemy types just means that 3 hours into the game you've experienced the entire gameplay. There's the one armed thug, which I have no idea if they're supposed to make it harder, I mean, the only thing missing is for them to tell you when to dodge because you can't block it. Then the swinging "titan" which requires another different input to fight. Then the ones with the blade, which requires another different input to fight. Now these sounds good, but they were never really utilized in a way where they all perfectly work together to challenge the peak of the player's skill. I don't think they were willing to fully commit, which for me, really hurt the potential of the combat and almost made the game unbearably boring to finish. It was fun for sure, but after a while I stopped caring because I couldn't get engaged when the game barely throws anything my way that will require more than three brain cells to do.

The bossfights were decent if not bad, the entire point of the combat is a 360 degree combat, with emphasis on awareness. The bossfights being some sort of cuphead projectile dodging game was way too outside what the gameplay is about that it felt jarring, this isn't Dark Souls where'd you spam roll to dodge, doing that in the Clayface and R'as al ghul fight was just too awkward. However, the bit in the bossfights where you'd have to dodge Clayface while fighting off multiple small clayface was good. Because you know, it challenges the skill you've been honing during the game. Uniqueness and variety is good, but doing it for the sake of just doing something differently even thought the entire core of your game does not support it is not. This is the equivalent of platforming with suddenly breaking floor and dying instantly as Bed Of Chaos in a game about learning your enemies' moveset, dodging and counterattacking which is Dark Souls.  The Mister Freeze fight was tedious, you only need to take him down twice, to know all that you need to do. Doing it 8 more times was boring. He's extremely smart and dumb at the same time, adapting so that a trick will not work twice, but not learning to change his approach. 


And there's the hacking part, if you can call that gameplay. They exist to slow down the game, they're not engaging in any way. A few of them is fine, but they are way too prevalent in the entire game. 


STORY 

Story is decent, held down at being good because of Hugo,  I just couldn't get myself invested with the whole Hugo Thing, how he speak is just so annoying, he has zero charisma, and he speak so "smart" but doesn't sound threatening, he's so one dimensional in his dialogues and delivery that it was painful. The Joker part was better, his lines were good, delivery was good and when he talks you want to listen. It's because of his attitude, how he acts and carries himself, which if you put Hugo Strange in there, is a statute when it comes to being alive so I have no idea why he was even there. The twist was eh. There's another one, great. Totally didn't see that one coming because of the Joker looking deathly sick and healthy as a horse in another scene. Let's be honest, There being two doesn't matter. In detective stories, twists are good, because throughout the story, you're not just given clues, but you are also given misdirection. So when the reveal happens, you think yourself an idiot, not because there's a twin brother that you didn't catch up on, but because you suspected his sister. In Arkham City, the twist is just that there's a twin brother. Even if you pick upped on the clues, the only question you ask is "Wait, is there a different Joker or something?" You don't ask yourself the why. because there is no why, he just did it. That could be the real Joker holding down Talia, but instead of all that stuff, he just shoot her down instantly. Which would result in the same thing, no twin twist needed. 

Overall, I'd give it a 6/10. With the Joker and the combat being the sole good parts of the game

The game is basically a Facebook or mobile game where you have to pay to speed up the progress or wait X amount of time before you can advance by earning more "nanotechs". A few of the missions even require that you use the nanotechs in order to finish the mission, well guess what, if you don't have them available and you want to advance you can always pay this small fee to buy them.. Gee Thanks! The TF2 characters aren't unlockable until you're a lvl 10 or roughly 5.5 hrs into the game. I decided that even though I love TF2 I can't sink more time into this trite game than I already have. review_text:
When I first started playing Dead by Daylight, I genuinely thought I’d found one of the most exciting multiplayer horror games ever made. The first 100 hours or so were a blast, running from killers with friends, pulling off clutch saves, and feeling that rush of tension as the exit gates opened. But once your MMR starts to climb, that fun quickly evaporates. The game goes from thrilling to downright miserable, and it’s honestly shocking how steep the falloff in enjoyment is.

At higher MMR, the game feels completely unbalanced. Killers suddenly move faster, hit from ridiculous distances, and seem to have a supernatural ability to track you no matter what. The supposed “skill based” matchmaking doesn’t really feel like it takes into account teamwork or playstyle; you just get thrown against sweaty killers with pinpoint accuracy and map knowledge that make most matches feel hopeless.

And the tools survivors get to fight back? Practically useless. Flashlights almost never work properly; you can aim dead on and still get nothing. Pallet stuns feel inconsistent, sometimes they register, other times the killer just powers through like nothing happened. Even perks that are meant to help counter killer pressure barely make a difference at high levels because of how oppressive killer perks and add ons have become.

The worst part is how predictable the experience becomes. If the killer isn’t brand new, they will catch you, it’s only a matter of time. There’s no real comeback potential unless the killer makes a huge mistake or decides to give you a pity escape. That feeling of tension that once made the game fun is replaced by frustration, because it’s not about skill anymore, it’s about how long you can delay the inevitable.

Dead by Daylight has a solid foundation, and for casual players or newcomers, it can still be enjoyable. But for anyone who plays long enough to get decent, the experience becomes punishing and unrewarding. It’s like the game actively punishes you for improving. Until the developers seriously rework MMR and address balance issues between killers and survivors, I can’t recommend it beyond the first few dozen hours. It’s fun until it isn’t. Then it’s just pain.

review_text:
I do not recommend this game~ 🌹

Most people who pick this game up will want to play Multiplayer.
But here's the thing... You have to play the single player campaign to unlock characters.
The single player Missions take place on very large maps, which are obviously set up in a way for multiplayer.
So you spend so much time in single player running/dashing just to get to the next objectives.

Even crazier still, once you slog through all of the campaign missions and finally decide to go into Multiplayer, there are currently only 6 multiplayer maps (Will they add more later? Probably.) 
But here's the next kicker!!!!

Those maps are arranged by Player Level. That means if you want to gain the most exp for your Account, you'll always want to do the latest mission. Once you reach "end game," they decided to pair up two missions together in a single queue. So if you select it, it's random which of the two maps you get.
At first you'd think that's good for variety, but this also means you have to stare at the loading screens to figure out which map you are playing on in order to select the right element weapon for that mission. Even worse, some characters don't have access to certain elements. Klein for example, doesn't have access to the Electric element, so if you pick him and the map switches to the forest, there's nothing you can do about it and you are forced to play that mission suboptimally. 

Not only that, but as you progress through the player ranks, it gets harder and harder to gain experience for your Account. Which means you end up running the same 2 quests or bosses (which there are currently only 3, maybe 4 because they switch out the last remaining boss from only a queue of 3 bosses). 

Which again, You need to be a very high player rank just to select the highest boss to fight.
Think about that. You are stuck farming the same boss over and over again. 

The game is also EXTREMELY grindy, which wouldn't be a problem if the game was fun.
But some characters are just broken. For example, with Asuna it's almost always best to just spam Triangle while held down. Some characters play best just spamming Square. Completely nullifying their entire kit. 
The combat is also extremely clunky imo.

Even with it's own faults you might get some fun out of it for awhile.
But I personally believe that Alicization was the last best SAO game out of the entire series.
Even better than Fatal Bullet.

This game just needs to be fleshed out with more content to be worth $60.

review_text:
Finished JC3 up to 100%, loved it for the crazy stunts and overall mayhem you can cause with your tethers, bavarium wingsuit and various explosives. I bought JC4 expecting a decent sequel and after a couple of hours posted this critic so... Let's see what I got.

[h1]Loyal to its older brother : 8/10[/h1]
JC3 was all about having fun with the unrealistic physics, grappling around and using your wingsuit to jump unsuspecting ennemies and destroy their whole base without them being able to do anything against you. And JC4 does it quite well. It even jump starts and bypasses the lengthy upgrading system in JC3 by giving you, right at the start of the game, 10 tethers (more than the 6 tethers limit in JC3) and in a couple of missions (less than 30 minutes of gameplay) provides you with the boosters and the air lifter. Overall, the reason I "only" gave it an 8/10 is because they unnecessarily changed the way you free the areas of the map. In JC3 you have to find several spots in each area, destroy all chaos objects and you were done. Here there is a bit less destruction involved and it is more like about completing certain missions, then ordering your "troops" to move in another area in which you will repeat the process. I think the idea was to make it feel like Rico needs the island's people to win but it sounds silly considering that the NPCs are just as useless as they were in JC3. Seriously, I just did a mission for which I need to take two NPCs with me drive in a car for several kilometers to destroy 4 boxes. It took me almost 10 minutes to get it done whereas doing it by myself with the wingsuit would have taken me less than 2 minutes. Basically you are still a one man army and you could install a mod that removes every member of the resistance and you wouldn't feel any difference. I think JC5, if it is made one day, should take this one man army seriously : the cutscenes should be about NPCs telling Rico that he needs their help to kill the evil dictator and Rico answering "Hey, I just destroyed 5 ennemy bases by myself without a scratch, don't worry about me, just stand back and enjoy the show".
Anyway, overall it is enjoyable, fun to play and the feeling is similar to what you had in JC3 between the gunfights, the wingsuit/parachute combo, the tethers and the handling of the fun and unrealistic physics.

[h1]Chaos mechanics : 4/10[/h1]
In JC3, the usual way you free an area was : head to this area, discover the N settlements in it (small bases, big bases, outposts...), destroy every chaos object in these settlements and the area becomes yours and the rebels now occupy these settlements.
In JC4, they removed this idea that you had to cause mayhem and destruction. Basically you do the 2 or 3 missions you can find in an area, during which you will have to kill black hand's soldiers, which generates chaos which grants you "rebel squads". These squads are "stored" somewhere in your... Inventory ? Whatever, basically you accumulate squads and once you have enough (between 2 and 4 for most areas) you click on the map to say "hey, rebels, go free this area", at which point the rebels establish a frontline where the constantly fight the black hand on the borders of this area. Then you do the missions in this area, accumulate a few more squads and proceeed to the next area. I do not like this idea, not only is it a fake way of pushing the idea that "Rico is just a man, he can't take the black hand by himself, he need help from the rebels who can't even kill a single foot-soldier in 5vs1 in less than 1 minute" even though you can move around freely on the whole map and utterly destroy any black hand squad you encounter. I really feel like the devs saw a few videos on youtube of players utterly destroying some black hand military bases and decided that "oh no, we can't have that, we need the player to work hand in hand with the rebels, it's much more realistic than a single man freeing a country !". I'm not exactly sure what was the motivation here, but it is a big failure, the amount of chaos you have to generate in "roaming" when you just mess with the black hand is absurd, i litterally spent 15 minutes destroying almost 50 helicopters and 50 armed cars and killing several soldiers, it only granted me 1/10th of a squad.

I don't get it. I also do not want to have to go through the 13 different menus to see what action is the 'X' key bound to if I want to use it for something. Binding keys should not be that hard : you double click on an action, you press the key you want to attribute to this action, and if it is already bound the game either highlights the conflict or switches both keys. Then you display every action in the same menu with categories, you do not split it between 13 submenus.
While we are talking about the menus, if you have the sound and the sensitivity set as values between 0 and 100 (it goes even beyond 100 for the sensitivity, I don't understand how scales work in your minds but whatever), you either use a slider or provide us with an input to quickly change it, I don't want to hold my right arrow for 30 seconds to reach the value I want.

The second part in [i]Samorost[/i] trilogy. This time a little bit longer than the first game, but still fairly short. The graphics are yet again very peculiar, it's a combination of real photographs and hand-drawn images – the world has thanks to it a mysterious and surreal atmosphere. The music is very charming. As he won't abandon his friend in need, he bravely follows the aliens to their home planet! On his journey, he needs to be rather resourceful and use every wit to get both of them safely home.

Puzzles are pretty straightforward although some can be a little bit obscure to realize (also the final puzzle with seals can be sadly somewhat tedious). There is no penalty if you do something wrongly, so if you don't know what to do next just try clicking on everything on the screen!

All in all it's a very pleasant game and I can only recommend it. :3

review_text:
When I first started up this game I was absolutely mesmerized. The visuals, the sound design, the whole morbid atmosphere simply blew me away. It felt like a dream playing this game. There are so many details to admire and the whole art style is one of the most unique things that I've seen in my 29 years of gaming.
Every single action in the game has a hand crafted animation to it. You don't simply push a button, instead you insert your fingers into this construction of skin and artifice to pull a lever that opens a door.
Besides this amazing art style, I cannot recommend Scorn, as it is still supposed to be a video game, not an art project.

While the whole presentation is absolutely astonishing, it just gets stale after walking around for two hours as everything looks "kinda the same". 
Scorn also suffers from a big navigating issue. Since everything looks very alike, it is hard to remember where you've been or where you have to go. Combined with a very long process of puzzle solving, it's more of a chore than fun to play. 
I did enjoy the puzzles, as you have to figure out everything by yourself. The devs did a good job at transferring that feeling of working with an unknown technology but beyond that, the game feels rather hollow, like a skeleton without much flesh on its bones if that makes sense.

I still appreciate the work that the devs have done but from a video game perspective, I cannot recommend Scorn.

review_text:
I almost wish Steam had a "recommend if on sale for xx%", but since not I had to vote No. This one was frustrating, as there are clear improvements that are overshadowed by confusing downgrades. 
[u]PROS[/u]
- gunplay feels quicker and a little more frantic
- enemies move around more, especially helicopters, feel a bit more aggressive
- visuals are pretty, if oversaturated
- the tether is a little snappier when transitioning to a landing

[u]CONS[/u]
- no more base liberation (this was what I did the most JC3; re-oppress and fast travel to capture bases again, it was the main challenge of the game)
- challenges are basically gone. Instead of a full, beautiful wingsuit course, you have literally have "fly through 3 rings in less than 9 seconds". Instead of a race, you have "pass through this ring over 150 km/h". These are a joke I would expect from a single-person indie game, especially after JC3
- no longer have remote mines
- only two weapons can be equipped at once; no longer have dual-wield pistols/smgs

[u]OTHER[/u]
- control changes, the most subjective part:
 -- the d-pad no longer handles weapons. Left/Right now swap between your three tether loadouts, and Up to trigger effects
 -- weapon swapping is handled by holding Reload, hence only having two weapons now
 -- zoom-in moved from R3 to L2, and now must be held down, fine with me 
- you now have three different tether effects:
 -- Air Lift: attaches a lift balloon
 -- Retractor: auto-retracts once attached to two things
 -- Booster: is booster
 -- You can set 0-3 effects on each loadout
 -- You can set these effects to trigger automatically, or by pressing d-pad up, or holding it. You can also set the intensity/strength or each effect
 -- There are also mods, such as making the balloons fly in a direction instead of hover, or pop when they reach full altitude, or change booster direction, etc

review_text:
Turbo Golf Racing is a fantastic game that I admittedly would never have tried if not for the free weekend that was running when I purchased. This game is heavily compared to rocket league which is honestly not my thing.

The reviews that compare this game to rocket league are a little off in my opinion. Sure, you are driving a car, hitting a ball. But the similarities pretty much end there. Turbo golf is mostly a time trial type game. You can shoot rockets at your opponents but there is no collision with other players or their balls. Your score is purely based on your performance, even if playing in a group. The party system is just to ensure you get into the same match as your friends.

There is a ton of customisation in this game with a whole heap of different parts to customise the look of your car, as well as power cores to let you activate abilities to help complete the courses. The season progression is nowhere near as grindy as other games, even ones where the season pass is paid. No buying a battle pass with this game each season has been free and I don't see that changing. With playing for the free play weekend and playing casually for a couple of weeks I completed it no problem. Probably 10 hours max.

The one downfall of Turbo Golf Racing is the low player base. You can still get into matches as they fill the spots with bots after a couple of minutes of waiting. Generally you will be up against 2-4 other players and the rest of the slots (8 "players" per match) will be filled by bots. I only play casual matches so playing bots doesn't bother me. However, ranked play can be an issue for some with a the low pop.

Overall I would say this game is definitely worth a try. You will know if it's for you within the two hour refund window for sure.

review_text:
Bioshock is one of the most overrated games in the history of FPS. First, the only good thing of this game is level design: it is clear that the people from 2k put a lot of effort and detail in map design, this is evident in the Medical Pavillion map.

Now for all the flaws:
a) Vita-chambers: lots of players argue that it removes all tension and difficulty from the game. they are used for free and turn Bioshock from a complex-FPS-with-hard-enemies-wannabe into a kill-until-I-die-and-then-resurrect game.
b) Unoriginal weapons: let's see, pistol, shotgun, machine gun, grenade launcher, sniper (crossbow). Meh.
c) Enemy splicers do not use their plasmids: yup, I have 6 plasmids under my sleeve and the r-tards of my enemies who are sinking in ADAM overdose do not even use electric bolt.
d) Useless weapon powerups and false sense of "choice": so, you apparently get a dozen weapon powerups that put you in a difficult position to choose. Yeah, right. It makes a lot of sense to have high fire rate in a 4-shell shotgun (sarcasm), or an extended mag in a pistol in a game where I can use a machine gun.
e) Side characters I could not care less: so, through the game you pick recordings that supposedly tell you stuff about what happened in Rapture. Who cares? A woman complains she got spliced until becoming Quasimodo... why would I care? At least if it had a video, but nope. Audios are supposed to create a "story" (note the "") for side characters who have no relevance at all.
f) Useless plasmids: face it, from all the plasmids you can choose from, you will only use and need electrobolt (paralyze and kill Big Daddys), incendiary (not necessary anymore after you get the flamethrower), hypnotize big Daddy (to fight against the other big Daddys), decoy (to draw Big Daddys to groups of proximity mines) and that's it. The rest are completely useless and irrelevant. Which leads me to the next three points.
g) Lack of compromise in decissions: you can change your plasmids anytime you want in a gene station,. This allows you to equip yourself as you want before a fight, thus relieving you from facing the compromise of plasmids that are good against splicers but useless against powerful enemies.
h) Redundancy and false sense of choice: most powers granted by plasmids do not add anything new other than the "fun" of killing an enemy in a "fun" way (why use freeze, when you can use electrobolt? no good reason) and can be obtained through weapons (why upgrade freeze when you can use your nitrogen in the flame thrower?).
i) Useless ADAM: ADAM is supposed to be the ultimate reward. Thing is, several of the plasmids or powerups you buy with ADAM can be created by crafting things in the "U invent machine". As a result, you get to a the 60% of the game and wonder what to dowith ADAM as you got all you need.
j) Useless powerups: why use "hack expert" powerups to have reduced alarm tiles when hacking if you can use the "camouflage" powerup and become invisible to everyone by standing still while hacking? I escaped 80% of the alarms of a failed hacking by standing still, becoming invisible, and watching the bots flying while I took pictures of them (added bonus of increased damage to bots).
k) Lack of compromise 2: as 75% of plasmids and powerups are redundant, your quest for ADAM becomes a horse with 5 legs (who would want to buy one?), removing all tension from decisions. Rescuing little sisters should put you in a position to decide where you will be selfish and harvest ADAM to get "awesome?" powerups or save innocent children. FAIL.
l) Boring, cliched and I-couldn't-care-less endings: both endings were written by a 5 year old kid.
m) No gibbing: seriously? yout game required a top notch computer and I can blow a guy's arm off? A Big Daddy pushes a drill through the rib cage of a splicer and no hole in it? give me a break!!!!

I could keep going and going, but I think I made my point. I paid 4 euro for this load of rubbish, the only thing that justifies my "investment" was the splicing screaming "Ay.... me muerooo!" every time I used incendiary on it.

Do not buy it, do not play it. This game makes the Modern Warfare franchise look like top notch art.

review_text:
There Are many things good with the original Bioshock game, but there a few gripes I have with the game. During the main story there are a few glitches and bugs (I was playing the non-remastered edition) but nothing major, mostly just rare occasional crashes, too intense for the physics engine to handle (same with the 2nd game, but more on that over there).
The introduction of the plasmids and weapons were very fluid and intuitive and at the ADAM stations, the prices for ammo, plasmids, and tonics were very balanced the entire course of the game. The Game is also very well put together story-wise, aside from at the ending of the game. In which (at least the good ending, I haven't played the other ending) seems very forced onto the player, you get a happy ever after with all the Little Sisters, and not more of a realistic ending where it works out, but some things don't. 

One good thing in the game are the Plasmids; they are the genetic encoding power-ups you get throughout your journey in Rapture. Some are unlocked through Story progression, meanwhile others are rewards for harvesting ADAM, or even just exploring the different rooms in the game, although most are just bought at the ADAM vending machine. They are pretty balanced, being you as the player needs to be able to use plasmids, as well as using the Weapons in order to fairly get through the game. They need to work together, not seperate power systems throughout the game. for example you can get the frost blast plasmid and then freeze a big daddy stunning him. Then you can shoot him with other weapons while he is frozen, which they balance with the incinerate ability (fire blast). which if you use ice and then fire, it just melts the ice, not being able to have both active on an enemy. Another Good aspect of the game is the Weapons; during my play-through I mostly used the Shotgun, Wrench, and Tommy Gun. Throughout the game you can upgrade your weapons, but only up to 7~ times throughout the game collectively, across all your weapons, so you must choose wisely. Even on easy mode, you will want those upgrades. 

Another positive element about the Original Bioshock is the story. You are the sole survivor (or so you think) of a plane crash and stumble upon a lighthouse, bringing you to the great underwater city of RAPTURE. Here, you find your first plasmid on the surface, and are communicating with someone known as Atlas; in which he asks you to help him with helping out in recovering someone/something he needs from the city. "Would you kindly?". Where it leads to you going around a relatively small portion of rapture, searching, finding out what ADAM is, seeing the remaining residents of the broken city; and most of all Andrew Ryan, the supposed crooked villain of the story. But all is revealed throughout the story, As you collect ADAM and grow stronger. In order to escape you will have to turn into a Big Daddy, in order to both, lure the Little Sisters to help you (in the good ending), and it adds an extra layer of defence, armour, and protection to you for the Final Boss fight. Although this is a good game, there are some plot-holes that arise and are never acknowledged in the subsequent games being Bioshock 2 and Infinite. 

All in all, Bioshock 1 is a pretty solid game, story and game-play-wise, but overall does lack just that extra oomph that is to be desired.

review_text:
Every positive review is correct, the experience of playing and the plot cooperate to take full advantage of 'games' as a medium of storytelling and is a delight. However, the optimisation of the actual game leaves a lot to be desired. 

Playing on recommended hardware, there is often minute long loading screens between entering doors from inside to outside and sometimes within the same building. Combat is not intended to be anything like a natural FPS, but the unique flavour of jank when anybody hits anybody feels unfair in an unintended way and has caused a lot of deaths. 
While Pathologic does make normally boring things like walking and buying food nerve wracking to the most engaging degree, I think there is a difference between that and being put in time out staring at a half loaded door for most of play. Of course if those things don't bother you/hardware isn't an issue and other positive reviews capture you, you'll probably have an interesting time. 

But for those whom this warning applies, I cannot recommend this wonderful game.

review_text:
I'm not a fan of classic RPG style game to begin with. But eventhough I believe that beautiful audio and visual are crucial in storytelling, I know the story itself is the most crucial part. Plus the overwehlmingly positive review has encouraged me to give this game a go.

I agree with everyone else that this game has a beutiful story. But there are some factors that bother me:

1. Characters
This game has some notable characters with distinct personality and role, but there are some that are lacking both. This game jumps from one plot to another without giving us enough time to be introduced to the characters. I sometimes forgot the significance of a character. This problem even occurs with main characters. This problem also makes me less 'bonded' with the characters.

2.  The conflict
The conflict, or I should say, the important plot points seem to be stretched. This makes them giving me less impact on each of the plot points. 

3. The details
There are some important details scatered around the story. All of those details supposed to help building the story. But unfortunately, this game isn't so good at 'connecting those dots'. Eventually, those details became some sort of distractions.

4. The mechanics 
The controls seem to be a little floaty. And, within the game, there are mini games that are supposed to be the connectors from one plot point to another. But unfortunately those mini games felt unnecessary and distracting for me.

5. The jokes
To touch the heart through a story, one should make the player laugh and cry. This game has failed me at the laughing part. 

I know there are countless positive aspect of this game. But at the end, those things above can't get out of my head. It's a little bit unfogiving, but I couldn't aprove myself to give this game a thumbs up with those things unimproved.

review_text:
SGWC(1) was somewhat enjoyable at first.  It's like a mashup of Sniper Elite and parts of Far Cry Blood Dragon in a way.  But after playing thru it, I started discovering it's major flaws.  I would not waste my time playing thru it again.  The controls are poorly planned out, and are sometimes unresponsive.

-- I'll start with the most annoying thing.  You CANNOT adjust your position via the movement keys while in scope view.

You can change your stance, but you absolutely cannot move left/right (or forward/back) to adjust your shot.  That's just dumb.  If you need to adjust for objects in between you and the target, you can't.  You would have to leave scope view, adjust without being able to see, then go back into scope view to see if you adjusted enough.  By the time you get the right positioning, the target has moved on.  Major fail on that one devs.

-- Picking up a body and melee are the same control. (and the game does not prioritise melee over picking up.)

So if you are sneaking up on someone that was hiding, and his dead buddies are around him, your character would rather pick up a nearby body, getting spotted by the target you were trying to sneak up on in the process, and you're dead because you can't use your weapons while holding a body,  This one just made me shake my head.  It's so stupid.

-- The challenges are set up in a way that forces you to do multiple playthroughs.

Meaning, some of the challenges contradict each other.  No need for examples.  I'm pretty sure you know what I mean.

-- Some seriously bad hitboxes on the final map/mission.  (The one the devs should have put the most time into.)

I lost count of the number of times I had a perfect shot, especially someone standing in the open, and my shot would be deflected off of an invisible hitbox from an object 3 feet away.  I got so frustrated with the last mission, I didn't even worry about the challenges.

All I can say in conclusion is that I hope SGWC2 is way better than this.  The SGW series is, after all, the same game as Sniper Elite. (same menu format, same interface, same HUD/interface sounds offset in tone, etc.) i.e. SGWC is based off of SE3, although I enjoyed SE3 immensely.  And supposedly SGWC2 is based off of SE4.  We'll see.

so being a VR title with natural compromises, for being in VR, we have an ok game, but with the draw backs but none of the benefits or bonus's of being in VR, no immersion, no physicality, no object interaction....so all this makes it an objectively bad game.

which is especially erroneous, considering this is one of the few companies with as much experience and time in the VR space...it seems they learned nothing, and that's really disappointing.

After playing through 1/3 of the main story content over the last week and getting to level 55 (of 65), I had to give up. From missions that can't be completed to massive bugs and glitches that have seemingly been there since the content first came out. Combine that with an extremely grindy and predatory "micro"transaction system that has you either grinding for months on end to unlock a ship for one character versus dropping the equivalent amount of money as TWO FULL PRICED GAMES for a specific ship (because the tier 6 'big name' ships are all in bundles and you can't buy them by themselves) for all your characters.

If you're in it for the aesthetics and 'space barbie' aspect, then be prepared to make it your second job (or take up a second job to cover your purchases). If you're in it for the story, be prepared for dropped plot lines due to quests being removed for tuning and never returned, and a bunch of broken quests.

If you're like me and wanted to just fly a Constitution-class (TOS Enterprise-class) around the galaxy while you go through the story content,  then I'll save you the research time: You'll have to pay $150USD at full price for it as part of a bundle (it's never by itself) plus another $20 for the bridge aesthetics, grind out resourced for the next 8 months (less if you grind resources on multiple characters), or wait until next year's year-long event chain and grind that out over the course of the year (which will give you a token to unlock a ship of your choice for one character)

Overall, I find the game to be fun and the story to have its good moments, but the fact that I had more fun in the 23rd Century tutorial area than anything afterwards should've been enough of a warning to not push through as far as I did.

To start this review, i'm gonna give my biggest gripe about this game.

The save system

I know there were a lot of launch-day issues with it being laggy and buggy and that's why it got so poorly reviewed at the start, but all of that's fixed now as far as i can tell, besides some chunk-loading lag.

The combat system still feels like Dead Space, but it's got it's own spin on it. My dislike for the lack of damage dealt by melee swings in Dead Space isn't present here, because both guns and the baton are equally useful! 

The Cinematography is great, and the story is really good. I'd give this game a solid 9/10.

review_text:
I played this game yeaaaaaaars ago, so this might be outdated as I did not really keep up. I am not even sure this game works on new systems anymore but I will try to write a review from what I remember. 

Being a satan child out to murder all the residents and family was pretty good. This is more of a puzzle game than horror or anything else really. Your main objectives include killing, acting normal, killing, sneaking and snitching, killing, invoking the powers of the devil by directly talking to him, acting normal and killing again. Yeee this game really doesnt have many different quest options. You have chores which are these side quests like clean your room or do this thing but nothing else. If you are here for something more dynamic, then I would say go find something else. 

Now going from the feel lets go to how this actually plays. You are literal offspring of devil whose powers are just awakening. Your daddy comes in and wants you to kill everyone. Since you are still pretty powerless, you are expected to kill silently. You are a hitman essentially, without choking people and throwing them in closets. Most of the kills will look like freak accidents. This game really is just a puzzle game on that aspect. With more murder, comes more power. Eventually, you will be able to even toss fireballs. Its fun, but you are still a midget, so do sneaky burning. 

For visuals, this game doesnt look all that bad, but there are definitely better looking games from that time. 

As for sounds, they are nothing too special. Maybe except the demonic powers. Where the greatness of sound design lies is in the games music. Its great. The chanting during murders is still stuck in my head even till this day. Its great OST.

What I remember, is this game has a lot of bugs. Some items not spawning, getting stuck, AIs pathfinding was sometimes fucked and some other bugs.

Overall? I do recommend this game, pretty cool experience but do be aware of its age.

review_text:
Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a game that draws too much inspiration from its 1 source and fails to do anything to call its own.

It's been 23 years since Jet Set Radio came out, you really couldn't create anything unique to your own game? The game-play is amateur at best, the story is uninteresting and the characters likewise, there really isn't anything here that I really would call worthy of praise or attention outside of the game's ability to recreate and capture the appearance & vibe of a style. The music and visuals absolutely kick ass, but, once you're done appreciating those BRC doesn't do anything to really hook the players in.

Game-play as stated earlier is very bare-bones and unimaginative. Each form of mobility is mechanically the same, save for the bicycle which grants you access to 2 new areas as part of the story. The combat as necessitated from part of the story handles very poorly and seriously misses out on the opportunity to involve the players transportation option as a usable combat tool. You got 3 buttons for performing tricks & combat moves but there's no skill ceiling for how they function or really any way to get better at the game. Pulling a manual is done at the press of a button and absolutely cheapens the game's score system basically allowing you to infinitely keep up a combo so long as you have a brain. The additional player characters are all reskins but they're locked to their respective modes of transport.

On the topic of performing tricks, they're all incredibly absolutely underwhelming. There's little to no impact on actually performing anything. Sound effects are so quiet or even just tame and the visuals don't really do much to emphasize anything. The experience of handling the game from minute 1 to hour 10 is exactly the same. The game-play loop no different. Go to area, spray paint, fight whoever, go to the next area. The actual gang battles I was excited for because it actually lent some use to the scoring system but every gang fight is incredibly easy with absolutely little to no challenge whatsoever.

review_text:
THIRD REVIEW:

So, the main story finally started picking up last night. It was quite satisfying to take out an antagonist from the first game that well frankly, is annoying as hell. You also have a friend in the game I'd love to kill even more because he's friggin whiny as hell but anyway .... this review is not for diehard KCD fans. I've a feeling that like the roughly 40% (from what I gather from achievements) with this game that gave up, many also gave up on the first game QUITE EARLY. Then ... even more gave up later. Finally, some of us stuck it out. You'll see quite a vocal community online as with any game that'll make it seem quite great and it can be fun at times but I leave my reviews for the average gamer. If I were reviewing Dark Souls, I would choose "No" to "Would you recommend this game to other players?" because well, it's Dark Souls. 

Unlike DS, combat on here takes even longer to get used to. I finally found the one idiot that teaches the "master strike" except now it only applies to swords. Don't ask me why. Blocking doesn't work half the time. I'll have full stamina and no matter which way I'm aiming or "aiming" (as in, the red in the recticle), Henry simply will not lift his shield. I had a lot easier time with combat in the first KCD. By this point in #1, I could take on a group of enemies no problem. I wouldn't pick "Yes" to that game either however as I believe many players would have quit it and wasted their money.

That's the simple truth. The game is picking up. I'm starting to enjoy it but, I do not believe this is a game for the average player. It can be grindy, repetitive and down-right hard at times if not straight-up annoying. If you're not really into the setting and/or story or have some other major draw, you'll probably quit.

At the very least, spend a good amount of time watching some youtube videos. Not ones where someone is OP and killing hoards of enemies at once. The real ones where they are dying over and over. I've beat the first KCD on hardcore twice and still struggle with this one. The pacing of this one ... I still don't know how I feel about it. I'm not the only one either. It's all over Reddit. Some quests still seem bugged depending on the player also.

I'll leave this a "No", while I boot it up for myself.

If you liked the first KCD, you'll probably be a bit annoyed by this one for a while but then it'll grow on you.

If you're new to KCD, you can start with just this one but, I'd be cautious. The introduction is too long for a refund on here.

Happy Gaming!


ADDENDUM:

It's finally picking up ... We'll see.
Still though, 30+ hours to get going. I spent maybe 10 or so brewing potions. I don't know where the time went. The sack carrying and stuff really stands out. I also skipped the first DLC. I'd google it. Fetch quests.

SECOND REVIEW:

My original review is below. This is not KCD1 and unlike others, I'm not complaining about the combat being "too easy" because unlike KCD1, I'm still getting my ass handed to me. I find it harder actually. It's taking a lot longer to get some skill (training). That's not my gripe. Much of my time has been leveling alchemy, yes. Basically the rest of my time has been carrying sacks and doing other labor. This game has become a labor simulator. The story ... each part of the story is just do this labor task, do that labor task.... The side quests, suck. Sorry but they do. 

Some drunk up in a tree that again, I have to carry back and forth? What is it with the obsession of having me carry crap back and forth all game? I'm seriously about to electronically shred this game just for the satisfaction. I'll change this if there actually becomes something to it. As of now, it's just a bunch of whiny-ass Hans and slave-labor.

I'd like to point out that while they brag about 4 million copies sold... I've a steam achievement that is required to progress the game early on. Required. Less than 60 percent of people have it. I'm telling you, they kinda shit the bed with the beginning of this game at the very least. I truly hope it gets better. Looks like A LOT of people simply quit the thing. 


FIRST REVIEW:

There's simply too much to say about this game. Honestly, I really suggest reading Reddit or such. Combat was hard in number one (until you leveled up and got used to it). People say it's easier in this one but I've died a lot more. Maybe I'm just rusty. To me, it seems very familiar. Like a continuation of the story with way better graphics. Also, I love that there's an alchemy station right near the start so you can start earning some money early without having to kill bandits (or get killed). 

It's KCD2. I'm not a shill. I'm probably not it's biggest fan but, it's a pretty damn solid game so far. You just have to get used to it. The first KCD I almost gave up on and this is as a hardcore souls-like fan. The combat is simply different. I cannot think of anything I've ever played that is similar. Give it a try .. just know that unfortunately the first two hours won't give you an idea of what the game is like so if you don't like it, you won't be able to return it on here. There needs to be a policy change for games like this. I won't be returning it though.

review_text:
Pros: 

Nice community of players but that's about it.

Cons:

The gameplay gets dull after a certain amount of hours

The "pay-to-win" of this is that you can buy items with real money then sell them for a very high price so you could buy some high level gear from the profits you make.

Rare items may take a while to drop, at which point it becomes like working a job where you don't get paid.

The battles are very repetitive and the open world is very boring to explore.

The gear gets released in seasonal intervals which take a while and most people end up spending real money to get it every season, so its a good strategy for the business but very predatory towards the consumer.

It seems any game published by Sega is heavily divided into micro-transactions(ex Total War series)

The "End Game" of this is "fashion" according to most players, and that consists of you either spending real cash or a very high amount of in game currency for an item that gets bound to a character and cannot be sold to others.

If you want to change or customize your character you'll need a "Salon Pass"

It feels more like a chatroom vs an actual game

Conclusion:
You can still enjoy this but very minimally, if you stay longer you'll end up wasting money on mediocre lootboxes. Unless you're broke then you'd probably going to be grinding for this like its a real job lol.  Also, if you're looking to play this because of PSU like I did, don't bother. The company is not what it used to be.

Just Cause 4 is an explosive open-world action game that delivers on the franchise’s promise of chaotic fun and over-the-top stunts, though it arrives with a mixed bag of improvements and noticeable flaws. Developed by Avalanche Studios, the game thrusts players into the vibrant, yet dangerous world of Solis, a fictional South American country beset by extreme weather, political turmoil, and a powerful private militia known as the Black Hand. As Rico Rodriguez, the iconic protagonist, players are tasked with dismantling the regime of an oppressive villain while navigating massive landscapes filled with opportunities for destruction and mayhem.

One of Just Cause 4’s most impressive features is its dynamic weather system, which introduces tornadoes, thunderstorms, and sandstorms that drastically affect gameplay and add a layer of unpredictability to the already chaotic combat scenarios. These natural disasters not only provide visually stunning moments but also influence tactics — tornadoes can throw vehicles and enemies into the air, while lightning storms might cause explosive chain reactions. This weather mechanic enriches the open-world experience, making exploration feel fresh and challenging. The map itself is vast and diverse, ranging from dense jungles and snowy peaks to arid deserts and sprawling urban areas, each offering unique environmental hazards and mission types.

Gameplay remains true to the series’ DNA, focusing on fast-paced, destructive action combined with Rico’s signature grapple hook, parachute, and wingsuit. These traversal tools enable incredible freedom of movement, allowing players to chain together jaw-dropping stunts and creative takedowns. The combat is highly customizable thanks to the ability to upgrade weapons, gadgets, and vehicles, encouraging experimentation with different playstyles. Missions often revolve around sabotage, base assaults, and high-speed chases, all designed to maximize player creativity and destruction. However, despite the freedom, some missions feel repetitive, relying heavily on similar objectives that can dampen the overall momentum after extended play.

Graphically, Just Cause 4 offers beautiful vistas and detailed environments, though it occasionally suffers from technical issues such as pop-in textures, frame rate drops, and clipping. The weather effects are particularly well-executed, showcasing the game’s ambition in visual design. Audio design complements the chaos, with explosive sound effects, an energetic soundtrack, and solid voice acting that bring the world of Solis to life. While the story itself is relatively straightforward and sometimes predictable, it provides enough motivation to push through the campaign and engage with the world.

Despite its strengths, Just Cause 4 has drawn criticism for a number of bugs and glitches present at launch, some of which persist, impacting immersion and gameplay smoothness. The AI can also feel inconsistent — enemy behavior ranges from overly aggressive to strangely passive, reducing tactical challenge in certain encounters. Additionally, the multiplayer absence and lack of significant innovation compared to previous entries leave some players wanting more. Nevertheless, the core experience of chaos, destruction, and freedom remains intact, and for fans of the franchise, these shortcomings are often outweighed by the sheer fun of wreaking havoc in an open world.

In conclusion, Just Cause 4 is a thrilling, if somewhat flawed, open-world action game that delivers spectacular weather effects, expansive environments, and the trademark explosive gameplay that the series is known for. review_text:
[2017/07/19 Update]
I'm leaving my original review below, but tl;dr:
This version of the game is broken on newer systems. Grab the Remaster instead.



Disclaimer: My playtime didn't register for reasons explained near the end of this review.
I actually completed the game twice (a Normal run with all audio logs and Little Sisters collected, and a Hard run with Vita Chambers disabled), so I know more than enough about this game to make a proper review of it.

Welcome to Rapture, a once thriving underwater city that fell to insanity and complete chaos after its inhabitants got addicted to ADAM, a substance granting super-powers and enhanced healing capabilities. You play as Jack, the token silent dood who's unlucky enough to plane crash in the middle of the sea and find himself in Rapture in the aftermath of the war confronting Andrew Ryan, the visionary leader of Rapture, to Atlas and his band of rebels, who are desperately struggling to stop Ryan's madness. From there, you'll embark on a grim journey in the depths of the ocean, fighting your way through underwater buildings and corridors infested with the deranged splicers, as well as the infamous Big Daddies, pedophiles in diving suits moaning like whales and stalking 8-year old little girls with giant syringes and glowing eyes.

Without spoiling anything, the story of the game is interesting and complex enough (for a FPS) to follow till the end, with its fair share of plot twists and excellent voice acting, although the endings were in my opinion slightly disappointing. Visually, the game aged quite well and the various steampunk environments of Rapture are a real treat to explore, which you'll have to do if you're interested in the background story of the city, distilled through audio logs scattered around the levels. The musical score is quite discreet but comes at the right moments, and the soundscape is well done. Atmosphere-wise, the game clearly takes inspirations from classics like System Shock 2 (the insane splicers from BioShock and the enraged infected from System Shock share some similarities) and the game certainly got its lots of creepy moments, from your first encounter with the splicers to your stroll through the medical ward, without forgetting your stay in Fort Frolic, the depraved home of the equally depraved Sander Cohen. Don't expect however visceral horror that will make you soil your pants as you would in games like Outlast or DreadOut. BioShock barely rely on jump scares or stuff of the sort, and while there's gory scenery here and there, the fear it tries to instill is more subtle, often mixing the awe-inspiring marvels of Rapture with a dose of creepiness to strike a chord of the uneasy kind.

Gameplay-wise, I'd hardly say the game has RPG elements, unless you count ADAM as experience points. However, it allows you to customize your experience in three different ways: Plasmids, Tonics, and weapons. Plasmids are kind of the equivalent of spells and come in many sorts (elemental attacks, ability to create a decoy or to mind control a Big Daddy to make it temporarily your ally...) - you use a "mana" bar (EVE) to use them, and you acquire most of them by spending the ADAM you will collect from the Little Sisters you encounter in the various levels. Tonics are passive abilities that you can equip on your character to give yourself various bonuses (see that as rings or amulets maybe?). You can find many hidden off the beaten trail in the levels, while others are bought with ADAM or offered as rewards for performing certain actions in the game. Finally, there is a variety of different weapons which all come with three types of different ammunitions whose effectiveness act on a rock-paper-scissors basis on ennemies depending on their weaknesses. You can also enhance permanently your weapons in different ways in specific stations scattered throughout the game which can be used only once for each. There are some other ways to customize your character, as ADAM also allows you to buy more Plasmid or Tonic slots to equip them, and to increase your Health or EVE bar. Later in the game is also introduced a crafting system were you can create your own ammo with materials you find on ennemies or in containers.

Now if we have to talk about the flaws, I'd say there are two main ones in this game. The first is that you're actually more limited than you think when it comes to customization. You'll quickly learn that some Plasmids and Tonics are must-haves, while others are completely useless (I'm looking at you, Natural Camouflage), which substantially reduces your options, as a lot of Plasmids and Tonics also have synergies between them. Same goes for the weapons: I found myself never using certain types of weapons or ammunitions because they proved utterly ineffective even when fully upgraded compared to other ones, and the weapon enhancing part with the previously mentioned stations also only gives you the illusion of choice, as you will eventually get all the upgrades anyways if you manage to find them all (which isn't that hard). It only comes down to which ones you take first. The second flaw for me is that the difficulty wasn't balanced very well. review_text:
I had heard nothing but good things about this game, I’m also a sucker for quirky indie games. Unfortunately, I hated this game. Let me tell you why.

Johnny’s story, as seen by the doctors in his memories was actually quite poignant and moving. It dealt with all kinds of interesting themes like old age, mental health, regret, memory, love, secrets. And it dealt with them all fairly well. So what was the problem? It was the doctors. Johnny’s memories on their own were a lovely story experience, but then we have these annoying doctors, cracking jokes, making comments, being jaded. Dr. Watts especially was a dick. They just didn’t shut up. Reading their dialogue got old really quick.

Though the doctors were the most egregious problem they weren’t the only one. The controls were bad. Sometimes clicking an object would move you to it, sometimes it wouldn’t. The cursor placement was weird. Of course, controls weren’t a huge deal since 90% of the game was just clicking though dialogue. I don’t have a problem with games being more about narrative than gameplay, but in this case I felt that watching this like a movie would have been move rewarding than having to move and click. There are completely inconsequential tile flipping puzzles that you need to do to travel from memory to memory. Near the end of the game I guess the developers felt like they needed to jam some gameplay in and there was a short frogger-like shooting sequence which seemed entirely out of place. 

If they could have told Johnny’s story without the annoying doctors making quips all the way through, I’m sure I would have liked this game more. As it was, I was just wanting it to end from about the 2 hour mark onward.

review_text:
I was initially optimistic for this game, patiently waiting for 1.0. I was hoping that, despite its unfinished state, it would offer enough content to enjoy and revisit once fully launched, but no. I would consider this game almost good. It almost has its gameplay right, but OH, how it fumbled so badly in design.

Firstly, the gunplay feels great, BUT the guns themselves feel very underwhelming in combat. The damage in the vast majority is weak, requiring so many shots on a single enemy that it feels like it's going into the Borderlands style of bullet sponge territory (bolt-action rifle headshots only take 3-5 shots to kill a common enemy for example).

While there are weapon upgrades, these involve tedious chores like killing a 100 enemies to improve each individual weapon. Not only does this drag out the experience, but the upgrades don’t make the guns feel significantly more powerful or rewarding. Like really, why do I have to do this arbitrary chore of using the weak version of the gun and do it for every individual weapon and spell in the game? It doesn't add anything to the gameplay whatsoever other than wasting time. I also want to mention leveling up your character is completely needless, apart from the Gnosis thing, all you do is level up witchery, as nothing else is better. You could remove this mechanic entirely, as it does not add anything.

Stamina also exists. Now I wouldn't mind stamina, as it limits how much you can dash or jump around so much, except for the fact that when an enemy hits you, it drains all of it. It completely halts your movement, which causes more hits, which then again halts your movement and finally dying. Not all the time, but it feels like the only cheap way for the game to kill you. There's no recovery you can do to get out of it or skill. You simply don't get hit. It's not a fun way to get punished. 

Secondly, it's a very weak roguelite, if any. There is virtually zero replayability. I came to the impression that part of the gameplay will mix things up to make stuff feel fresh, but no, the map doesn't change at all, and the enemies don't either. The only things that change are the locations of enemies and the chests. You do get perks during the map, but nothing fancy, just some percentage damage increase or a reload when dodging. You can completely ignore this mechanic, as it won't impact your style, unlike many other far better roguelites tend to do. 

I wanted to like Witchfire, but its design flaws and lack of substance make it feel like an so close yet so far experience rather than the compelling game it could have been.
