review_text:
This JRPG 4-pack is an incredible journey; very few games can take this many hours of my life without garnering a sense of resentment, but this was special.  I can't say that I was left wanting more, but it didn't wear out its welcome, either.  Keep in mind that as big a fan of the genre as I was back in the Fourth and Fifth Generation (I didn't play much else back then), I've really fallen out of love with the genre, so there may very well be better ones out there that I just never picked up.  I also probably didn't play this the way that I was supposed to, so keep that in mind, but that also means that I had the freedom to even do that in the first place.  With most of my biases out of the way, let's get started.

The gameplay was pretty refreshing, and I don't know why more games of the era aren't like this.  Devil May Cry came around and revolutionized 3D Action, but it took other genres a while to try their hand at this type of combat system.  Like my beloved Rogue Galaxy, these games have a similar, but watered-down type of combat; you run around and slash at things in real-time, and the mechanics, while not all that deep, are pretty solid.  You've got your standard combo, your charge attack, and your over-the-top specials, and while that's mostly it, you can get enemies into a special state where your special moves do more damage and give everyone a bonus in experience.  Doing all that, you also fill a bar that lets you go into berserker mode.  There are tons of options, and your main character's warrior class is a jack of all trades, so you'll have access to several different weapon types over the course of the 4 games.  Your companions are controlled by AI, and you have a few basic guidelines to give them, which isn't a whole lot of control, but they mostly act intelligently.

The basic structure of the game allows you to dial in an address out of hundreds or thousands of possible combinations; dial it in to a level appropriate to your party, and go on an adventure!  There isn't a lot of variety - most of the areas are pretty cookie cutter - but all of the outside areas have different times of day, and what's there is designed beautifully.  Even though a lot of the areas look the same, I found myself getting really absorbed into the scenery, though mostly outside; the dungeons are neat, but not as pretty, and they're a lot longer.  Each area gives you a rank once you finish, but thankfully, how quickly you cleared it is not a factor; you can just take your time and do a good job.  Most equipment can be customized with extra goodies that give you benefits such as status ailments, elemental damage, and HP drain.  You don't really have to worry about grinding, either, because your levels skyrocket with little provocation; if you're looking for a challenge, keep on walking.  That said, there is so much to do: the game keeps track of which items you've possessed, which monsters you've battled, etc., and the more you do, the more your guild grows, which gives you extra benefits.  With that and all of the different quests available, there's plenty to do, and honestly, I found it fun just going on adventures to random areas, maybe even more than the story missions.

The actual story... well, it grew on me.  At first, I hated all of the characters (except the one who established early on that she's just OVER IT), but by the end of the third game, I found myself even getting attached to random NPCs that wandered around town.  I became genuinely happy for my extremely stereotypical shounen protagonist when people showed a genuine interest in his wellbeing.  Even some of the more annoying characters grew on me by the end, and with a cast this big, and an attitude as cynical as mine, that's no small task.  The actual plot has a lot of weird things happening, and not having played the other games or watched any of the anime, I was pretty lost at times, but almost everything comes together in the end.  If nothing else, it's a thematic departure from the usual settings of a game like this.

The environments, as I've said are beautiful, and the more unique elements of the game generally look pretty cool.  Most characters have some form of tribal tattoo on them, and they all look pretty neat.  In typical anime fashion, the main character's outfits get progressively more ridiculous, as do the weapons, but once I started to lean into that, I began to enjoy myself.  The monsters look very unique, especially the avatars, and even though some of them are a bit outlandish, they are very creatively designed.  Special attacks, spells, etc. are all appropriately flashy, and usually not too hilariously over-the-top.

The audio is pretty good; nothing really blew me away, but there's a lot to like here.  I didn't notice too much of the music, but the fields have appropriately serene music by day, and somewhat unsettling music at sunset.  A really nice touch is that at night or in the rain, there is no music, and you can just enjoy the atmosphere.  Most of the voice acting is good and not only fits the characters, but also frames them in a way that makes them work, not to mention that Liam O'Brien plays one of them, and that man is a national treasure.  You have a couple of duds now and again - one character sounds like a little girl making fun of how little boys talk [b]all the time[/b] - but they aren't too common.

If you're looking for something that's going to let you just pick up and go on an adventure at a whim, this might be up your alley.  I'm not a big anime fan, and despite that, I found myself really getting really into it.  I can't recommend it just for the extra fourth game that's never been released before; it introduces a few cool new things, but it's shorter than 5 hours, and in terms of plot, it doesn't add much.  That said, if you're looking to play these again, or are a newcomer (like I was), it's a pretty good value, and is pretty fun once you finally get into it.  See you in The World.

most characters have some form of tribal tattoo on them, and they all look pretty neat. in typical anime fashion, the main character's outfits get progressively more ridiculous, as do the weapons, but once i started to lean into that, i began to enjoy myself. the monsters look very unique, especially the avatars, and even though some of them are a bit outlandish, they are very creatively designed. special attacks, spells, etc. are all appropriately flashy, and usually not too hilariously over-the-top. the audio is pretty good nothing really blew me away, but there's a lot to like here. i didn't notice too much of the music, but the fields have appropriately serene music by day, and somewhat unsettling music at sunset. a really nice touch is that at night or in the rain, there is no music, and you can just enjoy the atmosphere. most of the voice acting is good and not only fits the characters, but also frames them in a way that makes them work, not to mention that liam o'brien plays one of them, and that man is a national treasure. you have a couple of duds now and again - one character sounds like a little girl making fun of how little boys talk b all the time b - but they aren't too common. if you're looking for something that's going to let you just pick up and go on an adventure at a whim, this might be up your alley. i'm not a big anime fan, and despite that, i found myself really getting really into it. i can't recommend it just for the extra fourth game that's never been released before it introduces a few cool new things, but it's shorter than 5 hours, and in terms of plot, it doesn't add much. that said, if you're looking to play these again, or are a newcomer like i was , it's a pretty good value, and is pretty fun once you finally get into it. see you in the world.

I spent near to no money on it, so no harm done there, but damn don't bother with this.

The Story, While not stated outright, is really fun to figure out yourself. I love a game that doesn't make itself obvious and doesn't treat their players like infants. It feeds you just enough info to make you think on what just happened. Its a great message too at that. I love how emotional the story is combined along with the music. The MOM sections especially, which i consider some of the best parts of the game in terms of Storytelling.

Overall, A Great game. Not Perfect but its still worth a good go if it ever goes on sale. Its def not worth the 15 bucks if im being 100% honest. Worth 10 at most.

review_text:
EDIT (26/7/2019):
The inclusion of sliders for most of the game's mechanics has made Pathologic 2 a more fair and balanced experience. Sadly, I am hesitant about giving it a thumbs up, because the performance even after 2 months from its release, remains a mess...


[h1]INITIAL STEAM REVIEW (5/6/2019)[/h1]
First things first:

- Get it only if you know what you'll be dealing with.
- I'd recommend the 1st game over this one.

Pathologic 2 does many things right but makes some mistakes that the first game didn't, 14 years ago.

It's ironic how the original game felt esoteric and cryptic due to its story and narrative, whereas Pathologic 2 tries not to ostracize players from its world by hinting a bit too much at the greater picture (even the death mechanic could be considered sort of a  giveaway) and inevitably does so with its unrefined mechanics, while it should be the other way around.

Example of balanced system -> Infection :
In Pathologic: easy to get infected, antibiotics are largely available
In Pathologogic 2: not that easy to get infected as long as you have even a bit of immunity left, less antibiotics to be found.

Example of unbalanced system -> Exhaustion:
In Pathologic: exhaustion gauge is full after ~ 10 hours, you can stock 3-4 coffee beans and 1 lemon a day without having to scour the whole town
In Pathologic 2: bar fills faster, lemons and especially coffee are not that easy to procure.

Pathologic 2 is a weird and unique experience, but at its current state it is besmeared by optimization and balance issues. Its narrative, story and atmosphere are suffocating under the weight of its mechanics and I’m pretty sure that heavy reliance on meta-gaming to avoid hitting a roadblock wasn’t something its creators intended.

I'm waiting for the performance and difficulty customization patch and  I'd be happy to give the game a thumbs up if said issues are mended.

I had high hopes for Witchfire. The concept looked intriguing, and I’ve been eagerly anticipating its release for quite some time. Unfortunately, what I found was a game that fell short in almost every aspect.

First off, the crashes. It’s incredibly frustrating to be all set to dive into an expedition, only for the game to crash repeatedly. I lost count of how many times I tried to start, only to be thrown back to the desktop. It’s a major issue that really hampers the experience.

Then there’s the combat. I expected fast-paced, engaging action, but instead, I found the gameplay to be slow and lackluster. The gunplay felt uninspired, making every encounter a chore rather than an adrenaline rush. What I expected to be well thought out fights, was just a series of repetitive battles that lacked any real challenge or thrill.

Speaking of repetition, the worlds feel empty and uninspired. I was hoping for rich, immersive environments, but instead, I encountered vast, dull landscapes. The lack of variety made exploration feel pointless, as if I were running in circles through the same uninspired scenery.

Overall, Witchfire had so much potential, but it ultimately leaves a lot to be desired. It’s disappointing to see a concept I loved turned into such a frustrating experience. I really wanted to enjoy this game, but it just didn’t deliver. In it's current state, despite being early access, feels like a $35 demo. Buy hades 2 for a cheaper and better roguelite experience.

A pretty off-the-wall game that wasn't exactly done well. At first I had some problems with the game, and I even posted about a bug which got fixed in a quick response. But despite the developer's response showing that they cared about the bugs, it does not mean that the game as a whole was made into something that great.

Despite how evil the premise is, I was looking forward to the game. Sadly, it wasn't executed as well as I expected it to be. It seemed cheaply thrown together into an over-the-top B-movie format. I genuinely think if the game had even more work done on it, it could've been a higher-level game than it is now. And according to many reviews, the sequel to this was made even worse, disappointingly.

I would've liked if the story was actually more serious and if the characters weren't as silly. The gameplay as a whole isn't necessarily horrible, but many things are really easy or quick to do, and nothing got exciting at any point in the game. You can even get half of the items needed in the game just by running around and picking things up right away. I got through multiple "missions" really quickly because I had picked up all of the items needed for them earlier on.

The fact that the "missions" simply mean "Go pick up item X / Go to room Y / Use random skill" goes to show how cheaply the game is done. Yes, as I said, I understand the premise, but playing the game didn't really do the idea justice. Besides that, the graphics were nothing special, nor was the voice acting (and lip sync didn't exist really). All in all, a rather lackluster game that I wish was made better.

review_text:
Great classic online game with a lot of content but has minor issues.
Rather than say what is great about it, i'll say what isn't as I'm pretty sure plenty of reviews note the good things already.
So I will focus on what might make/break it for some people in rather situational & specific ways.

1. Limited compatibility with lower end pcs due to inability to configure many vital things and no "potato mode"
(While this might seem petty, the base game is crazy old and should run fine on a lower end modern pc but doesn't so it is in fact terribly optimized)

2. A bit convoluted and isn't completely true to the jp version, many things were reworked in negative ways.

3. Dated combat mechanics, it was shortly after we learned we wouldn't get a global version of PSO2 games like tera online released in example which had much higher tier combat quality. The former being 2012 and the latter being 2014, it's safe to say we should be in another league in 2024. Especially considering how hard they try to monetize the title.
(More-so if we consider NGS is like a pseudo pso3 which we might not get for another 10-20 years if ever! The mistake here is a simple underlying factor of not splitting base pso2 from ngs)

4. Steam/epic dependency, this hurts lower end pcs even more and over-complicates getting the game working well. Steam has an astronomical amount of issues and hardly any redeeming factor beyond marketability.

5. Some minor p2w, not purely to the definition of p2w as everything is reasonably achievable by playing. Cashers will undoubtedly have an advantage but it actually doesn't matter much because their gameplay isn't yours. 

If you can look past all of these minor issues and like what you've seen--
You'll have a great time on PSO2, notably I would add if you use an HDD it will cause many issues.
The cheapest upgrades you can perform to get it to run better are:
SDD
Ram modules
Cheap gfx card

Those 3 things can get the oldest junker toasters running it decently but won't fix everything as this game is again very poorly optimized.

review_text:
Game has decent foundations, but even as a big fan of Destiny, Hunt: Showdown, roguelites, and all the other games people can't stop comparing Witchfire to--it really is just OKAY right now.

This game is very far from finished. It works fine on a technical level, but charging $40 for this right now feels pretty shitty. 

You are basically running the same 3 stages over and over with only minor variation in enemy spawns to grind currency and research (the main system of unlocking new gear/spells which for some reason is literally tied to in-mission time instead of something you can earn or fast-track with skill). There are some cool hidden bosses and gauntlets to reveal as you progress, but you'll also quickly find yourself getting bored of running those same encounters over and over as well.

The audioscape is also utterly barren and hollow (ironic given the Hunt comparisons) and this actively hurts the combat and enemy design--it feels like audio should and will become a bigger part of combat and avoiding damage as development progresses.

To be clear: I don't dislike the game, but I'm downvoting this so people who are weighing a purchase can see this and understand that it is a tough value proposition at the moment. Consider wishlisting it and returning later after some major updates and/or full release.

P.S. glazers: before you comment "nO sHiT iTs UnFiNiShEd It SaYs eArLy AcCeSs" idgaf they're asking $40 for a game that is barely more than a demo rn. For that you could go buy an actually great, feature-complete game like Hunt: Showdown, Helldivers 2, or two-thirds of a copy of Space Marine 2.

review_text: This game is pure 80's cheese and I love it. Blood Dragon is like Far Cry 3 but without any filler, it knows that all you care about is the gameplay which holds up quite well from start to finish. It begins with a funny "drawn out" tutorial section and then leads into the rest of the game where the story does exist, but due to it's corny action movie nature, does not stop the gameplay in its tracks to tell. Everything out of the protagonist's mouth is cringey action movie lines that fit with the 80's aesthetic that I believe will make this game timeless. The difficulty was the highest at the beginning for me, then the rest of the game became a breeze once stealth and upgrades came rolling in. The game does have some of that copy-paste side content with there being a number of bases you have to take down like in Far Cry 3, but unlike that game, there are a reasonable amount of them that completing them and their side missions are never a bore. You could blow through this game in one long sitting because this game gives you gameplay not tedium, and personality in place of realistic visuals; something that the other games in the series could learn from. Overall I had really fun time playing this and would recomend it to anyone who enjoys retro shooters or appreciates 80's vibes.

review_text:
I really like sniper games and am willing to forgive some shortcomings.  The graphics were so-so, the story lines ... well it IS about contracts so nothing is really related.   It's fun to spot and shoot people from a distance, but the long range gun mechanics were a little sketchy ... you could shoot two guys standing beside each other, same distance, same windage, but the shot would act differently for each.  When you adjust for wind or bullet drop the graphics shows this huge ribbon of a turn not a fade in.  Kind of annoying.  I was on a rooftop, almost 400 yards away, shooting down from behind a doorway in the dark, and was killed by small-arms fire.  400 yards away.  From the ground.  Really. 

My biggest complaint is the lack of automatic saves ... not complaining that you can't save it yourself, but the checkpoint saves are very far and few between.  You can get quite a bit of distance into a mission, get killed and lose 2 hours of play.  That shouldn't happen ... the save points need to be more evenly spaced, especially since the maps are so big.  Which feeds into my second complaint ... glitches.  Getting stuck, unable to move forward or back, up or down, movement keys stop responding.   Happended several times.  So I have to get out and revert to my last checkpoint.  From two hours ago.  I have what appears to be a lot of hours in the game, but much of it is because I am replaying portions of missions again and again because the checkpoint saves suck.  I don't think this is what you mean when you say "replayability".

Pros: 

Fun spotting people from a distance and shooting them.

Cons:

Glitches
So-so graphics
Shooting mechanics
Lack of checkpoint saves

Overall the game just doesn't look look or feel sharp.  I got in on sale ... if I would have paid full price I would have been ticked.

review_text:
Pros : 
          - It's star trek!
          - There's actually kind of a story. Some of it not bad at all.
          - they made a pretty decent effort with their character creation elements.
          - you kinda get to make a whole party, and can customise their appearances, so yes, you can have a pretty female bridge crew wearing skirts


Cons:
          - terrible, dated graphics that kinda feel like PS2/PS3 era.
          - Story & immersion is undone by MMORPG elements, i.e.: no failure states, respawning, reliance on gear etc.
         - Immersion is ruined by the faction system butting up against what should be the plot, this is best explained with examples, for instance, Romulans and Jem'Hadar must join starfleet or the klingon empire, which can now use ships from these races. The klingon missions are often about honour and klingon society and such, but your character may not be a klingon. Also, federation content is reused for much of the klingon stuff.
        - Whilst you can technically get premium currency for free, you can get roughly 22 premium currency a day as you are limited to the amount of dilithium you can refine. The things you want cost 3,000 premium currency. It's designed to make you want to spend real world money.
       - It feels very strange for star trek models to be shooting at one another, chewing through masses of shields and hit points or hull integrity, this is very unlike the franchise.
      - a lot of the game can be played solo, so the game doesn't seem very social to me, I'm only 70+ hours in, but haven't spoken to another player yet.
     - this raises the crux of my problem with this game, it would have been a much, much better experience if it was made as a single player game, the content trimmed down into higher quality stuff, rather than needing to produce the mounds of chaff that MMORPGs need, and so on, but, well, MMORPGs must be more profitable.
      - the endgame is gruellingly hard, and requires ruthless management of equipment, with only specific playstyles and loadouts and such being playable. In fact, many missions are best done when you are low level, as the enemies if anything over-scale as you level up. Yeah, the endgame really saps the joy out of it for me, and makes me want to stop playing with my max level characters.
      - absolutely chock full of bugs, I encounter one every 2-5 hours. Most of the time you can fix them by dropping the quest and then re-acquiring it, but it's still a pain in the ass. (and this game is 10 years old!)
     - you have to wait for background tasks to complete, just like Neverwinter.
-they're stopping support for windows 7 soon, won't be able to play any more soon, I can go to hell it would seem.

Overall, play only if you're a megafan like myself, and don't expect this game to leave a huge impression on you.

Edit : yeah, the endgame is just too punishingly difficult, try a mission at levels 45 - 55 and then the same thing at 65 and the 65 mission is just too difficult. It seems to me to be a way to encourage you to buy premium currency, but I'm uninstalling instead. Games shouldn't become un-playable in difficulty as you increase in level.

This is my in-depth review directed towards the "New Genesis" Game, not the legacy game hidden behind it. Steam state's that I played this game 4,6k+ hours, but in actuality I've clocked in double, heck even triple the amount of time since I played during the Microsoft launch BETA. 

:Pros:

- [Great graphics that can be further enhanced with re-shading and other third party methods.]

- [Combat controls are fluid and intuitive.]

- [Very easy to pick up mechanics regarding gear/leveling up.]

- [Variety of different Races to choose from Human, Newman, Deuman, Cast.] Doesn't matter now, race is "free-form" 

- [Game pacing is very quick, you can be gone for months and catch up fairly quickly.]

- [In-depth character creator with many facet's of customization that's arguably "one of the best" on the market.]

- [Fantastic Fashion for your player avatar]

- [Personal Quarters Customization is quite complex and actually really fun to play with.]

- [Space faring aesthetic] 

- [Makes a great "side game" If you can stomach existing along side the player-base.] Wow that's a pro?

:Cons:

- [Lacks meaningful content and poorly designed endgame.] Main content to this day is STILL PSE farming. Purple Triggers are boring once you subject yourself to artificially inflated difficulty that doesn't help you learn anything new to gain true mastery over anything except being "optimally perfect". Boss trigger content such as Dark Falz Aegis, Dark Falz ll, etc are well done, however still falls short due to being repetitive with bad reward structure. Enemy cannon fodder still feel like DPS sponges that take forever to kill making it feel like a really bad dynasty warriors game compared to base, despite having above average gear or hell even the best gear. Game doesn't respect your time. Not much else to say, let's move on.

- [Combat rewards are extremely unrewarding.] This one is a HUGE one for me. There is nothing more debilitating than watching last or current season's gear fall right into your inventory, only for it to be scrapped into a measily 80 meseta or however much it's worth. The only way for gear bit's to be worth any shread of Meseta, would be via Fixa's, but at that point you're just asking yourself if you want to slave away for copium drops. You can spend hours, days, weeks, even MONTHS, before you can even see something viable to even sell in the shop. The way I can see them fixing this, is by bringing back the system in base ps02, where you can exchange "useless" obsolete gear for things like ex-cubes, etc mats. I'd love to have some form of material progression, that won't require me to go out into the world shooting rocks all day like genshin impact.

- [Poor Story] The character's are easily forgotten. Poorly written dialogue that does not make any sense. Things just happen too fast, with little to no context or build up. If you're interested for the story alone, turn back. Many other games execute this better. There is nothing entertaining about these characters to make you care about them. The writing between base game and NGS is night and day.

- [Final con is the community.] I've been around for a very long time since base game in Japan to the beta of NGS. Traveled on 3 ships [Primary ship is 2], under different aliases. All of this is being said based on my own experiences, which is subjective to some if not most people. This game has some of the most mentally unhealthy/degenerate/heinous groups of people I've ever had the displeasure to be associated with. As with most anime games, it was going to be inevitable that such groups like this would exist within an MMO space. It's very hard to describe this community without stating the obvious facts. It's weird, horny, and you got some of the most mentally stunted adults I've ever seen in a video game period. 


Despite it's flaws, I love this game franchise to death as a long time fan and wish it nothing but success. It has SO much potential as an MMO and the proof shows with the previous iteration of the game despite the legacy game having it's own share of major problems that hindered it's development. However that is still no excuse for a game that was built on the ashes of that success only to heavily fall short. It sadden's me that I can't recommend this game to anyone. It's a badge of embarrassment and shame in it's current form. 

Phantasy Star, a franchise that was ahead of it's time that paved the way for other games to exist and be successful. SEGA should be ashamed of the legacy that is now stained. A lot of us waited 8 year's for the original MMO game to come to the west only for them to abandon it a year later to chase souless open world gaming trend with NGS. What a damn shame SEGA.

review_text:
A distinctive and reasonably compelling experience. Although it is not consistently challenging the gameplay loop remains fairly entertaining and presents a solid variety of features.


The combat system is relatively well-rounded and simple, but includes a tangible amount of room for strategy and player input. Unfortunately the threat of many early missions is quite low; and so while players can be tactical in the early stages they often do not need to be. The game does have multiple difficulty modes although how difficult they really are remains to be seen, as reaching such content takes a decent amount of investment.

There is a distinct amount of customization between the cosmetics, unlockable perks and gear bonuses that clearly outline how players can work towards creating unique builds as a long term goal. Between the story mode, regular missions, dungeons, faction tasks, higher difficulties and achievement unlocks the game presents a great variety of progression mechanics to juggle. There are a decent amount of unique areas, characters and enemies but it definitely does not stand out much beyond satisfying a baseline level of content variety.

Overall the presentation of this game feels effortful and well-rounded as well. The music, art and voice-acting all give it a polished vibe; although the selective absence of voice-acting is awkward. The story and writing is somewhat hit-or-miss. It does eventually build an okay plot with okay characters, but there are definitely moments of shallow or otherwise unsatisfying writing. In the same way there are moments where the writing particularly excels.

The story has a sparse but relatively clear agenda with regards to the lesson it's trying to teach, but it largely fails to do so in a very convincing or fluid manner. The moments where the writing attempts to implement a lesson are tactlessly obvious and put forward absurdly hyperbolic scenarios to make a point, which only make the developer's view look infantile. While elements of these lessons are reasonable at the deepest level, they are taken to such a zealous extreme that it makes the entire sentiment contemptible; if not outright insulting. According to the developers, [spoiler]if a plainly selfish and malicious person is trying to destroy your life and the lives of everyone you care about; mocking that person even a single time is extremely uncool and merits a personal crisis[/spoiler]. It's just ridiculously overblown, and thus incredibly unconstructive to anyone actually facing such problems in their life.


Although this experience is not particularly ground-breaking in its mechanics, the developers have clearly put a lot of work into giving the game a substantial amount of features and identity. The gameplay may not be especially engaging in terms of its difficulty at first but the story and progression mechanics help compensate. Hopefully the later difficulties present more of a daunting challenge as that is what the experience really lacks in its beginning. It certainly has quite a lot of playability given the price. 

If you're interested in finding more games like this I've probably reviewed quite a few on my curator page [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/38950844-Anoemalous/] here [/url].

review_text:
I wanted to recommend this game; I really did. 

A lot can be said about Scorn. It's visuals are stunning, the art direction is uniquely horrifying, the puzzles were simple yet compelling, and it's atmosphere is one of a kind. I have never played a game quite like it. I felt that the inventory system was immersive, and it seemed like the game knew exactly what it wanted to accomplish. It didn't overstay it's welcome (literally).

Now, reading that above, I could understand why you - the reader - may be mildly confused to why I don't recommend this game. I'll be honest; Scorn is an okay game, but it still left so much to be desired.

I feel for the people who have followed this project since it's conception. I didn't learn about Scorn until late 2021, so I didn't wait in anticipation for 8 long years for its release. Although I enjoyed this game, I felt like the game doesn't deserve a $40 price tag. Even at the 10% off price that I bought it, I still felt like I was a bit scammed out of $35. I can't believe that the deluxe version is $50! Yes, the art direction of the game was fantastic, but the level design was quite poor in multiple areas. There were a few times were I found myself getting turned around in the linear labyrinth that is Scorn. Just because you make the area look good doesn't mean you throw level design out the window. On top of that, the combat was lackluster, the "boss fight" (if you want to call it that) at the end of the game was slightly frustrating, and the overall fun factor of the game was relatively low.

Sure, make a cool art horror experience, but maybe if it's gonna be 5 - 6 hours long make it about $15 - $20 cheaper? 

TL;DR - Get Scorn on a Summer/Winter Steam Sale; otherwise it's not worth it and overall disappointing for the price.

review_text:
Sometimes it is difficult to rate a Steam game by the score of whether you want to recommend it or not.

Because although I definitely [i] felt [/i] emotions and it made me cry a couple times there are quite a lot of things holding it back.

First of all, I do want to say what I like. I liked the premise of revisiting the life story of a dying man which feed into the gameplay of looking for moments in memories and the emotional depth certain items can hold throughout a lifetime. It is a novel concept that for especially the first half I liked a lot to explore.

It’s however the way this story is being told I have a problem with.

[Spoiler] And it all has to do with the characterisation of River.

For people that don’t know, I am autistic myself and that means the vast majority of my social circle is neurodivergent. I’m incredibly familiar with what makes an autistic person tic and what they’re like.

And I barely saw any of that back in River.

In fact, it actually falls into a lot of stereotypical, Rainman-like traits that alienated me. Because let me tell you, from all the autistic people I’ve met throughout my life (which like I said are a lot), not even one closely resembled River. In fact, it makes it even worse by also portraying her as mentally unstable and almost insane which I find maddening and pulled me out of the story.

Which is a shame because this whole part of the story feels unnescary and only muddles the theme of wishing your life went different with other people who were taken away from you which is a hell of a lot more powerful message.

Combine that with writing that, although very pure in its authenticity, has a tendency to remark its own story beats as cheesy and corny [i] while still wanting us to care deeply about said payoffs, [/i] and there are story moments that just either fall flat, actively annoyed me or both. [/spoiler]

Overall, although I do think To the Moon has something going for it, the novelty of its gameplay and story however wears off to a point that halfway through I really wanted this to end, especially since Before Your Eyes tells a much more focused and impactful story in half of To the Moon’s runtime.

review_text:
When PSO2 first came to the west it was something special, something new, people had been waiting on the game to come to the west for 8 years and the wait was worth it. The game had come out with Episodes 1-3 with Episodes 4-6 being released later. The game even whilst being released in a technically incomplete state in the west was still filled with hundred of hours worth of content with the quality of said content ranging from standard MMO to just straight up mind boggling and there was always something to work towards. PSO2 wasn't perfect by any means, but is wasnt bad either and had  extremely strong foundations and additions that would make it very easy for SEGA to keep adding or improving upon for whatever would come next for Phantasy Star as a series or so you would think.

PSO2 NGS would get announced. SEGA showcases a complete refresh/new game using a whole new game engine, revamped Character customization, and the game is no longer separated by multiples maps with instances within them, NGS instead has and open world. NGS releases and its just okay, the first couple hours felt amazing, but the more you played the more empty the game felt and it just didn't feel as good as PSO2, sure the combat was more fluid, but its felt like it was missing something. it is now 2025 and while the game hasn't been abandoned i might as well be. Content roll out for NGS was always slow and too be honest i don't see a problem with it being slow, it's the contents of the updates that have absolutely killed this game for me and many others. For some reason SEGA has decided to take a page out of bungie's book and they consistently choose to release mediocre content updates and under deliver constantly. The game will not have a meaningful update for MONTHS and then when they do update it, they either release a small mediocre content drop that only lasts hours, give us another recycled seasonal event for the trillionth time or release another pay-to-win/ cosmetic gacha. The game as it is is a shadow of its former self and now shares more in common with Barbie Fashion Designer than the game it used to be. 

Until SEGA decides to open their eyes and actually take the development of this game seriously then i can't see myself recommending this game to ANYONE long-term or short-term unless they like throwing them selves into the empty hobby of whaling out on every gacha for "fun".

review_text:
I find it difficult to call this a horror game even if on paper it hits all the right notes. Yes it is about a young antichrist killing all the occupants of the household in a gorey fashion but I only ever found myself exasperated by the game mechanics or laughing at the stilted voice acting and the underwhelmingly cliched story. 

Personally I think it would have been just fine if it was only the story that underwhelmed me. The real attraction of this type of game is the gameplay. An Omen-Hitman style crossover sounds really cool and one day I hope we get to see that game fully realised but as it stands what we have is a nonsensical linear puzzle game that isn’t particularly impressive. 

It’s also buggy as hell. 

You’re assigned a target each chapter, with a cutscene playing when you interact with them. Not only was it not always clear who you’d be killing at the beginning of each level, sometimes the wrong cutscene would trigger a few chapters early for a character. Leaving the player to run around trying to figure out how to kill them until they accidentally bump into their true target. For example: [spoiler]Agnes’s cutscene triggered before Jed’s.[/spoiler]

I’d clip into walls frequently and found that the ending of the game was broken. I looked up a tutorial to see if I was doing something wrong but no, I’d done everything I was supposed to and yet [spoiler]my father was still beating me to death with a fire extinguisher[/spoiler]. Thankfully, the game also managed to bug it’s way into ending with my sweet little antichrist clipping into the door and into the final cutscene. So, there’s that. 

In my experience Lucius is more fun to watch someone else play than to actually play yourself and so with that in mind, I cannot recommend it. 

TLDR: I got this game on sale and still feel like I paid too much for it. It’s very reminiscent of an old B-Horror movie, cheesy and a little dated.

review_text:
This review is going to make me a hypocrite. But hey, we’re all hypocritical once in a while, right? Oh well, here we go.

This metroidvania is pretty heavy on the “-vania”: there are some really heavy RPG elements that, depending on your level of enjoyment of those mechanics, will make or break this game. Elemental damage and status effects abound here and only the right combination of equipment will make life easier for the player. Depending on the player’s gear, a puddle of oil on the floor can either lead to a quick death to the player or a helpful weapon against any baddies standing in the middle of it. At first, this caused me some really aggravating deaths until I started to get a better grasp of the system. Also, it might be worth noting that the menuing can be a little annoying as the player switches equipment in and out for different obstacles, but all-in-all it’s really fun.

The story is pretty silly, despite some twists here and there. But the characters you meet along the way are pretty great. The psychotic butcher schoolgirl, the zombie fangirls, the katana-wielding goblin slayer: they’re all fantastic. On top of that, the enemies the player faces are memorable as well and each poses a different threat while being vulnerable to different damage types. This game constantly mixes things up and keeps things interesting.

Where this game makes me a hypocrite is that it’s very linear – which is precisely the same reason why I didn’t like [i]Guacamelee 2[/i] and why I didn’t recommend that one. Any real exploration is locked behind sidequests, so if the player isn’t paying attention to those, there is no real reason to roam around the world. On top of that, items needed to complete those quests are marked on the map, eliminating any need to do any real searching. The thing that makes this game more interesting than [i]Guacamelee 2[/i] is that the limited exploration usually leads to a unique piece of equipment or a new spell or something. In [i]Guacamelee 2[/i], exploration lead to either a health pick-up, a stamina pick-up, or (eventually useless) money, and that’s pretty much it. [i]Lost Ruins[/i] does it better, is what I’m trying to say.

In the end, I really had a blast with this game. From the characters, to the maps, to the combat, everything came together to make this one a memorable stand-out. If you’re willing to muscle your way through this often-challenging game, you’re likely to find something you like in here. I know I did!

review_text:
If you consider yourself a fan of the first person shooter genre, buy this game. Period. Most innovative, cohesive vision of a single player FPS in the last decade.

Incredible presentation. Sound design is flawless. Movement and controls are slick, intuitive and reactive. Level design is tremendous and ingenious. Seriously, the level design deserves a second mention of praise. Right down to the bones, they are soaked with atmosphere and tone, and every single one presents uniquely while conjuring its own vibe and feel. Progression is fun and rewarding and never feels like a slog. The arsenal is devilishly satisfying with some excellent gun play, mechanics and perks. Replayability also punches well above normal because of the looter shooter RPG aspect. I'm 50 hours in and haven't beaten the game yet. 

I've been playing shooters since Wolfenstein. It's hard to impress and innovate on one of the oldest computer game genres. Let me say with complete honesty, Witchfire impresses me. This game is quality, better than any "qUaDruPLe A" title you can buy right now.

review_text:
TLDR; I do not recommend it, but only barely. Game is slow and rewards a methodical play-style, and I'm hesitant to continue because of how the devs prioritize gun-play over spells, in addition to boring rogue-like boons that don't affect game-play much throughout each expedition. Each run feels almost the same. 

A pretty decent rogue-like extraction shooter combo, it has a lot of gun-play inspired aspects from Destiny (that is a good thing) like weapon frames. They do, however, also use a lot of "rogue-like" boons similar to destiny (that is a bad thing).

A lot of boons you earn throughout a play-through are pretty mild, and don't affect game-play all that much (including a whole whopping 1% extra drop rate for healing elixirs, wow), which makes each run feel nearly identical. Similarly, there is an emphasis on gun-play compared with the spells we earn and use, which I'm not a huge fan of. 

The spells feel pretty weak, and seem to be secondary to guns (even though ammo is also sparse), as they have pretty large cooldowns and very low damage. None of the heavy spells I've gotten so far are very satisfying or useful, especially for how long they take to recharge, and very few light spells are very useful either. Mostly they seem to be used for staggering enemies, or afflicting them with an elemental affix, which isn't bad in and of itself, but if that's their main purpose, their CDs should definitely be reduced imo. If their damage is so low, I don't understand why their cooldown isn't lower either. I'm sure it has to do with the balance they want with how fast-paced the game feels, since it definitely feels like a conscious decision, I just don't think it's a very good one.

Speaking of pace, the game is pretty slow. I saw someone else mention how it's a very dad-game, if that makes sense, and I can understand that view. It's not a bad thing, but man oh man I wish the game was faster. Even just a little, but more than a little would be better. I really really wish stamina consumption was not a thing out of combat, and everything generally feels very slow/sluggish once you get used to the dance of things. I'm not going to speak on the balance of weapons, but some certainly feel stronger than others. 

Ammo consumption is directly linked to how good at the stun mechanics you are, which is a great idea in concept, but feels kind of bad when you realize you're going to be doing 1/2 damage and losing ammo unless you're constantly abusing the stun mechanics, even when it doesn't feel necessary.

I'm not sure how often the devs update the game, although it's been one or two months since last I played and everything has been the same since then, and it's difficult to want to continue just because of how unbalanced the game feels with guns vs. spells. Maybe the later game is different, I don't know, but 7 hrs in and it isn't looking like it, even after unlocking the other inventory slots.

Falling off a cliff into void/depths also immediately ends your run, which generally I wouldn't mind, if it was my own fault. However usually, the circumstances are questionable. More often am I pushed horizontally by a projectile coming at me from a perpendicular angle than running off of my own volition. Projectiles *pulling* me forward and thus into an abyss is also an issue I have, especially when they look identical to all other projectiles and just behave differently for some reason. Or at least I assume they look identical, maybe they don't, but I've never noticed a difference.- look, I don't mind losing player autonomy, especially when it's purposeful, however when it happens for some willy-nilly, not-so-easily-identifiable reason, over and over again, it really knocks the wind out of your sails. Especially when that reason ends a long winded run unceremoniously. I'm not saying to remove the mechanic, but at least give only a specific enemy enemy the ability, or maybe give the projectile a very obvious look about it compared to the other projectiles. Something that allows players to know when there's a different threat to be aware of. Readability in games is a legitimate issue and one that isn't always obvious. When a unit that you've been fighting begins behaving differently when only in certain locations, maybe just make it a different enemy instead.

Sorry, I got lost in the sauce. It's a decent game, although there's a lot I'm left wanting for. Maybe once it's out of EA it'll be better, but it's difficult to recommend atm.

review_text:
What seems like a sort of dungeon crawling roguelike take on the ideas of Domina ultimately feels a little unnecessarily punishing. The fact that units can level at all runs counter to the notion that everything is expendable, and of the many classes, one is explicitly required to play the game: the healer, which you do not start with and might not ever find any of. On top of this, your classes can only upgrade their abilities (including that necessary healing ability) if you have different weapons per character of that class... in a roguelike, where you might not have a choice in whether you're getting duplicates or not.

It's really not my thing. Maybe someone else will like this more; there's plenty to enjoy and I'm sure it's a good game, but with these issues and the knowledge that they're intended parts of the game, I'm too annoyed to play more.

review_text:
If you really like autobattlers this game might be for you. I didn’t put many hours into it but there seems to be a decent variety of classes / weapons to choose from. The difficulty is challenging, and the flavor text / narrative is pretty entertaining. I’m a sucker for pixel graphics, and the animations on units, attacks, and pretty much everything else are nice. The backgrounds are pretty boring though: steel, steel, and more steel. 

The gameplay loop unfortunately gets stale very fast, at least for me as a generalist gamer. Jump into a match, arm up your pinks, and watch them fight. Make occasional decisions for events which have varying impacts such as giving extra resources or items / killing your dudes. And finally deciding on what items or upgrades to buy, so you can stack bonuses.

It’s got pretty much all of the qualities needed to be an autobattler, but it lacks the visual flare of say Team Fight Tactics, Hearthstone’s Battlegrounds, etc. 

All in all, I feel like the game is a bit expensive for what it is and offers, especially since other titles offer the same archetype of gameplay for free. There are some great positives, but for me, the average gamer, the gameplay loop gets repetitive quickly, and does not justify the $15 price point.

Again, if you like autobattlers, this game might be for you.  But if you are like me and just want to try a new game, you might want to hold off and wait for a sale.

review_text:
I really want to like this game. I want to like it so much that I played through the whole thing, despite realizing how bad it was going to be 20 minutes in. It's right up my alley with its grizley subject matter and over-the top style. Everything is lovably purple, with the number 666 showing up pretty much anywhere any kind of number is called for. On that level the game is brilliant. 

But aside from a lovable style, there's not actually much of a game here. There's no freedom, no challenge. Each level drops you into the house, where you follow a line on a map until you run into a certain NPC. The game shouts "There! That's the person you're trying to kill on this level!" Then you check your notebook for some hint at how the game wants you to get that job done. You follow that hint until you reach another hint, then follow that hint, and so on, until someone dies. There's never more than a single path towards killing any given target, so there's no decisions to be made. The only thing that might actually be considered a challenge is figuring out what the hints mean. The hints oscilate between so obvious as to be trivial, and so obtuse as to be useless. There's no happy middle between the two. No sense of satisfaction in figuring stuff out.  

Then there are the times when you need a tool that isn't already in your inventory. Some specific item, like a screwdriver. Your first instinct is to go look for where you'd keep a screwdriver in your own home. Is it in the garage? The tool shed? Nope. It's on a table in the sitting room. You just have to wander around aimlessly, scanning every drawer and surface while you wonder if you're missing something that would make this fun. 

The demonic powers are also a little annoying. I could ignore the fact that the telekenisis never feels right, or that the fireballs are basically only available in pre-scripted sections of the game. That stuff, to a degree, makes sense. But the ability to make people forget seeing you doesn't even work! The moment your seen, all of the controls go completely dead, so there's no opportunity to use it. I went so far as intentionally getting caught multiple times in a row just to try and figure out what I was doing wrong, but it's no use. 

The game's cutscenes are too numerous and too boring. And even as numerous as they are, they often fail to explain things. Without spoiling anything, the game's story makes a few strange leaps forward that I still don't really understand. Several characters apparently come out of nowhere. Halfway through the game everyone starts talking about my uncle. Your mom even tells you to stop bothering your uncle, because he's been complaining about you lately. Meanwhile I'm left to wonder who or where my uncle is, because it's the first time I'm hearing about him. 

I'm disappointed that the game wound up being as bland and boring as it is. The graphics are nice and clear, the controls are mostly pretty solid, the deaths are reasonably creative. In most respects the game is a competently assembled thing. But there are just too many problems for me to give it a blanket recommendation. 

I'd say you should buy it only if you meet two criteria:
1. You, like me, think the premise is AWESOME. 
2. It's on sale for less than $3. 

Otherwise, give this a pass.

review_text: This game is almost there. I love the concept - the RPG pieces, the roguelike components, all of that is great. However, the actual hockey gameplay mechanics are not there yet. The defense boils down 100% to throwing hits. There is no stick checking or anything like that to break up plays, so if you miss a check (and 90% of the time, you will in this game), that's it. On top of that, switching to other players doesn't seem to have any kind of consistency. Sometimes it switches to the next closest player, sometimes it switches to someone random. I've also run into a few times where switching to another player seemingly freezes that player for a few seconds which is just enough time to let the other team score. It almost seems at time that the game punishes you for playing hockey versus playing into the RPG/roguelike components. I'd love to revisit this game if some of those can get fixed in the future, but as of right now it's more frustrating than fun for me.

review_text: Started as a free flash web-browser game in 2003, the "Samorost " was a fun little, point and click adventure game with gimmicky puzzles. "Samorost 2" the award winning sequel definetly surpassed the first. Samorost 2 is pretty much the same as the first, but much more improved, better grahpics, harder puzzles and an awesome soundtrack by Tomas Dvorak. However, the puzzles are much much harder... which can easily frustrate some not-so-patient gamers, you need to squint and try to click on every tiny detail in some stages.. which kind of damages the beautiful graphic experience. There is no inventory or lots of gathering like in most adventure games, instead you solve puzzles at every stage and proceed to an another. Collage-esque graphics are rare in video games, but Jakub Dvorsky definetly knows how to make some very lovely and astonishing backgrounds and artistic graphics in general. If you are looking for a challenging, lovely and a bit weird experience. Samorost2 is a great choice.

review_text:
I feel like it's important to note that I'm a huge fan of Dead Space, Resident Evil - OG and the more modern action focused entries, scifi in general, and Silent Hill.

Cronos draws inspiration from a bunch of different scifi and horror material, namely Twelve Monkeys and Dead Space. The soundtrack is pretty good and the story isn't bad. Every other aspect of the game is mediocre at best. The combat wants to be Dead Space but it's *so* slow and supremely predictable. Every combat encounter is punctuated with reusable explosive barrels that take away any potential surprise. "Reusable explosive barrels?" you ask.. due to time travel shenanigans you can reassemble barrels to blow them up again. You do this after running in circles with your last bullet because ammo is constantly a scarcity. You begin the game with what you think is going to be a really cool heavy handgun that can morph into brass knuckles.. and who knows what else?! I do, I know what else. It morphs into every generic firearm archetype you can imagine and that's about it. You have a flamethrower built into your wrist.. awesome! Not really, it consumes charges that you can only carry one of at a time for most of the game and it basically only serves to stun enemies even though they make it clear that fire is the ultimate weapon against the infected. Enemies are bullet sponges and the "don't let them merge" marketing is essentially moot, if you can hit the broadside of a barn from a few feet away they will never merge. I played for 5 hours and honestly I'm not sure what even happens when they do. The story unfolds as slowly as the combat, and after those 5 hours I had enough and watched the rest of the relevant cut scenes on Youtube. The scariest thing about the game is the unpredictable framerate, tried all sorts of settings and nothing could maintain a decent FPS during combat, and it doesn't even look that great. The enemies are really uninspired and so are the fleshy environments that just look blurry and generic - especially up close. 

All of that said, if you could pick it up on sale for $9.99 I'd recommend it.

review_text:
You run around shooting things that used to be people but are so messed up that they aren't really anymore. While you yourself have to use the same "plasmids" they do in order to survive against these monsters, you need to be just as strong if not more so! With these new powers you can shoot lightning out of your hands and other fun things. The concept of big daddy and little sister encounters I think are pretty cool. The imagery of the game is really cool with it's steampunk style. But then you realize how really truely annoying this game is.

I can't stand to play this game more then about 30 minutes to an hour. 90% of this game is hacking things: safes, robots, vending machines, etc. Everytime you hack something it's the same mini game - moving pipes around to get the fluid from one side to another, usually with obstacles. The first time I encountered this I thought "oh this is interesting" now I look at the analog gauge that shows the difficulty and if it's a hard one I think "this one's going to be literally impossible or at least really obnoxious". It gives you a shock and you have to try again. Again and again and again. Then you are successful and guess what... you go around the corner and there's another thing to hack.

Now back to Big Daddy. This big guy has a few different attacks, once you figure out the pattern, it's pretty boring and repeatitive. Even if you don't even really care to try you can just keep running into him guns blazing and just die and keep respawning and do it again and again until he dies. There isn't really any punishment to dying, You don't have to reload your game, just pop out of some respawn machine.

The story seems pretty interesting though, so I'll play through it and see how it ends, then I'll uninstall it and never look at it again.

review_text:
Game struggles to find balance between the enemies and the characters you control. No matter WHAT you do, you will make a mistake and be forced to "Quick Load" multiple times to hopefully have an enemy who saw you the first 12 times to finally not register your movements and allows you to proceed. The game is designed for repetition, which it why they shove the "Quick Save" down your throat LITERALLY every minute reminding you that you haven't saved in the last minute! review_text:
Just Cause 4 was a bit improved compared with the previous game.
But still it wasn't amazing, atleast not if you play it on mouse & keyboard. The control of bikes, planes is pretty horrible. But I can appreciate the fact that the wingsuit was way more enjoyable on keyboard compared with Just Cause 3.

In the beginning I hated that they removed liberations and the challenges seem pretty hard, but after a few hours I started to LOVE the new challenges. In this one you have a lot of towns / military bases and in each you have 2 - 7 challenges, depends how bit the location is.

+ Wingsuit was improved and much controllable.
+ Challenges revamped which made the game even more fun, no more leaderboards.
+ Pretty interesting weapons and enemies.
+ Garland, Sargento & Javi your new buddies asking you to do different jobs for them, and complete all their taks was interesting.
+ The Graphic was improved a bit, probably a new engine but this will go on CONS aswell and you'll see why.
+ New tools, grapling hook that can tether in 2 points and lift stuff, the baloon tool was interesting and we have some boost tools but i never used it.
+ The story was pretty good and theres a big chance that you'll get attached a lot of characters. They were well done.

- Graphics are improved but in same time made some characters to look dead inside. Bulgy eyes and no light behind them.
- I encountered some problems with the water. Most of times when I plunge into water game fully crash and get some weird error.
- The game needs to be set in Full Screen and 50 FPS otherwise on a mission where you have to go underwater for some generator the game will crash non stop if you are not locked on 50 FPS.
- During game I plunged into water from helicopters and with cars and the bug reappeared even with 50 FPS locked.
- With new engine the hair and the character details sometimes looked weird.
- When you fully finish the game, they dont show on map everything, so you'll have to waste a lot of hours to search for hidden towns if you wanna make all stunt challenges.

I played this game on my YouTube channel took me 30 episodes and a total of 43 hours, 7 minutes, 13 seconds, and I didn't made it 100%. Still missed a good portion of challenges and all those Rampage races + 11 statues for Javi.

The game is good and I recommend it, is worth playing and offer a lot of content if you want to waste lots of hours to complete everything. 

P.S.: YouTube in Steam bio if you are interested.
Happy gaming!

review_text: Dear god, how is this game so much worse than Boneworks? All the things that are shit: automatic crouching, crouch in real life and don't crouch in-game, climbing ladder uses legs, hands get stuck in stuff more than the previous game, reloading on larger characters is almost impossible, can't see below boobs/pecs, climbing up ledges throws you. How come when I lie down on the ground in real life my character doesn't follow me past a certain point, but I can use the crouch stick to go to the pov of an ant? Attempting to climb as I did in Boneworks (acting out the motion of pulling myself up in real life) is impossible because character height isn't correlated to real-life headset height, presumably for seamless seated/standing gameplay. Who even wants seamless seated/standing gameplay anyways, just make separate options like in Boneworks. Climbing up ladders and ledges is a pain in the ass because they decided it would be a good idea to use legs/feet that you can't control. My feet get stuck on the rungs of a ladder trying to get to the next rung and my pushed against the wall of a ledge I'm climbing just pushes me further from the ledge. The amount of times hands get stuck in/on things is ungodly annoying, fuck the physics I'd rather my hands clip through my body so they can line up with my hands irl than get stuck on every little thing because it would be unrealistic for them to clip through something. Attempting to reload on larger characters is literally impossible presumably because the mags don't get close enough to hitboxes to snap to gun. I don't have huge tits but I'd believe you should be able to look at your waistline and underarms to see ammo and guns even with the pecs or boobs in the game. Sometimes climbing up a ledge, I will be launched forward, (similar to how the zombies were when climbing in Boneworks) and be thrown off the object I just climbed. Maybe this one is just me, but the difference between characters' strength, height, speed, etc is an insignificant amount to the point where there is no need to ever change characters. There's the Boneworks level of jank where it's easier to climb a door knob than open the door with the knob, but this game just made things worse. Forgot that Valve takes refunds up to 2 hours until 2.5 hours. I'm still going to finish it but hate it 90% of the time. Still not worth even on sale. If you don't have Boneworks get that first, then seriously consider not purchasing this even if you enjoyed Boneworks as much as I did.

TL;DR for lazy people: Boring, confusing, horrible stealth mechanics. Decent story.

This game sounded a whole lot better on paper than it is in practice. You're a creepy mute kid who is apparently the son of Lucifer and you have to kill everybody in your house so your father can have souls, using diverse methods to knock off your targets one by one while making it look like an accident.

Unfortunately, finding how to do it is a hassle, there's only one way to kill each target and it's not always obvious. there are few clues and if some of them are usually simple and clear, you never know where to find the item, you have to search a huge, confusing manner to find said item and use it. Even after you found the thing, it's not always clear where and how you're supposed to use it. This game doesn't hold you by the hand.

Despite those problems, the game is rather interesting to follow as some drama starts because everybody's stumped and the detective in charge has no idea how all these deaths happen. But then comes ... The Betrayal. The one chapter that manages to ruin what little fun this game managed to offer. You have to cause a power outage so you can sneak around to get in the garage, which is on the ground floor, on the absolute opposite of your starting point. Here, you have to contend with locked doors and horrible stealth mechanics that barely work coherently. you can't see a thing but you don't dare use the flashlight in case this game actually makes you easier to spot when your light's on. All you do is try just about every door in the frickin' house while avoiding the adults patrolling with flashlight for no obvious reasons while your remaining satanic powers are drained because you manage to get spotted by someone who's at the far opposite of you in the corridor or by people you couldn't see or hear and open the exact same door you were planning to open.

This, this is what killed the game, that was barely alive in the first place. It'll probably end up being one of those curios I bought for a buck that I'll never finish, let alone re-install and that's too bad 'cause I'm rather curious about how the story ends. Oh well.

review_text:
Like so many people I've wanted a sequel to Jet Set Radio for years, not a sequel to it's flabby, unfocused sequel Jet Set Radio future. This unfortunately isn't even that, it's basically a Tony Hawk type thing with low budget Jet Set Radio Future inspired visuals. 

The game game is mostly concerned with forcing the player to do tricks for points, with some light graffiti here and there. There's little pressure to do anything in a hurry or even at all, and it all feels very loose and frankly becomes tedious quickly. 

The visuals are a mixed bag, with reasonable if overly open and empty JSRF style environments and incredibly purely done character models. I get it that they're going for a low poly aesthetic, but these are just ugly. And the cut scenes, I haven't seen cut scenes this bad since the PlayStation 1. 

Then there's the music. There are some Naganuma tracks and they much evoke the classic JSR funk. Then there are the rest and my goodness they're terrible. Repetitive, tuneless, and there is even some god awful rap (!!!!) "music" in here.  Overall it's pretty dire stuff.  

This isn't the JSR sequel you're looking for.  I wish it was, but it really isn't.

review_text:
Key thing to remember is "Free to Play" = "Pay to Win"

All the best ships and equipment are behind paywalls so you won't get any T6 ships without paying $$$ to open loot boxes or buying Zen credits.

That said, the game is ok but very dated. It certainly looks and feels like it was made in the early 2000's, gameplay is rather basic, NPC "AI" is primitive at best. The episode missions feature good stories, but some of the later missions just go on and on and on and get quite tiresome. Mission difficulty scales with player level which is good, until you hit the top levels (65) when the scaling seems to assume that you are using top tier ships and equipment (from loot boxes which cost $ to open). This means that they become very difficult if you aren't paying to win.

Some missions are bugged, usually involving scripted events not firing or unresponsive NPC's which can usually be got around by aborting the mission and retrying from the beginning. Very frustrating when you spend an hour getting to the final boss. Frequent issues with loadouts disappearing, traits resettings, bumping into invisible "forcefields", rubberbanding, and other lag based effects. Daily extended maintenance issues which seem to fail to address issues.

Away mission controls are horrendous out the box. I remapped the WASD keys to match every other game and using B to enter shooter mode makes it tolerable. Space combat I was imagining something like EVE Online, but instead its more like the old Star Trek Starfleet Command of the late 90's and hasn't been improved upon.

If you're really interested in Star Trek and want to explore the stories and lore then go ahead, if you're looking for a space based MMORPG or single player shooter experience then there are much better alternatives.

Oh, and there are no Steam achievements despite what the store page says.

review_text:
There are a lot of things this game has potential for, however, there are plenty more problems the game needs to address before it can really shine as being a good and fun game for me.

The game tries too hard to be too many things, it has the movement elements of titanfall 2, has a lot of weapon variety like doom, has meta progression and rogue like elements, which has potential to be good, but none of it really works well together. there are too many things never explained to you, no tutorial is actively presented to you, other than basic movement. the rogue like elements arent ever really explained well, and plenty of stuff just left me asking "what purpose does this serve?" 

another issue is the art direction. while it is good, and is visually pleasing, incorporating it into the enemy designs makes it near impossible to tell enemies apart from one another, as well as making it difficult to discern what enemy does what. it all becomes a bit orange yellow glowing mess once a few minutes have passed, making it hard to judge what is a priority target amongst the horde. Which leads into my next point, the weapons presented to you, especially in the early game, do NOT clear the hordes well. youre stuck with weapons that are primarily single target, while youre put up against 30-40 enemies as early on as the first stage. theres no real satisfaction to slowly chipping away at one enemy's hp bar, just for 3 more to spawn behind it as soon as you take it. when i saw this game, i assumed it was a fun game to clear out hordes with with lots of weapons, but it felt hard to enjoy that power trip with the lackluster early game. 

some final issues i have are the crosshair not being customizeable (especially considering how bad the default one is) the enemy hitboxes being absurdly small (the lack of bullet tracers also makes this annoying, due to you sometimes having your crosshair right over an enemy and the shot missing) and the overall lack of a clear goal, (should i sprint for the door right away? should i loot some more? do i kill some enemies?) 

all in all, the game has potential, but needs to figure out what it wants to be rather than trying to combine too many different elements without explaining them well enough. ill definitely keep an eye on it for future updates, and the eventual release, but in its current state, i cant really recommend it due to the lack of clear vision of what it wants to be, and what it wants you to do.

I like it. I had fun and I'm still having fun at 101 hours in. Some of the people criticizing this game are trying to shame fans for being "numb" to the flaws of the game. They say that they're only saying it's good because it's a "good SAO game". But my experience says otherwise. I'm having a blast.

The Pros:

-The animations are nice.
-Having 20 players to play with every raid or dungeon crawl feels good.
-The loot system is triggering my addiction.
-The stats restrictions on characters and weapons on lower dungeons makes it so that newbies don't feel left out. You're not going to see someone do 20k per hit, while you deal 20 per hit.
-The raid bosses feel great to fight.
-Didn't try to break my graphics card or overheat my PC on launch unlike another certain game that haters keep comparing this to.
-LLENN, Shinohara Miyu (I'm using her real name because STEAM thinks her game name should be censored for some reason), Sinon. Playing as a ranged character just feels amazing.

The cons:

-The camera man has ADHD and will randomly spin 180 sometimes.
-Playing as melee needs getting used to.
-The costumes aka Appearance Items' drop rates are abysmal. I'm not sure what's the rate, but I've been farming the final coop dungeon for 2 days now but I still haven't gotten the item.
-The price feel a bit steep.
-Story mode isn't something to be excited for.
-Some characters can only be unlocked in doing certain chapters of the story mode. Because story mode isn't too good, it becomes a bit of a drag.
-Items called 'mods' are sometimes hard to find, and getting the one you want is even harder. I wish I would get a "crit rate up" every time but instead I get a "guard damage reduction up" on a character THAT DOESN'T HAVE A GUARD FUNCTION. Your luck will really be a big factor in your coop experience.
-Some dungeons encourage speed running the entire thing because if you get left behind, other groups will take all the experience for themselves which means now you're fighting a boss at level 10.

As you see there are more cons than pros so maybe you'd think I won't recommend this game. But... no. It's fun. What can I do? I know many of you hate the anime. There are probably some of you reading this who decided to just hate on the game because it had "SAO" on the title. But the truth is that it's just fun. The feeling of spamming emotes after finishing a dungeon beside others who revived you because you carelessly stood in front of a 1-hit kill mechanic is wholesome. It feels like you're a part of a community who's just enjoying the game for what it is without trying to min max anything. If you're the kind of person who likes competition there's also a ranking page after runs. Being in a 20 player raid gives a different feeling that other games that only allow up to 4 players just can't give. If that's a feeling you're looking for and want to share in, then this game is for you. If it isn't, then go buy Sparking Zero. Either way you'd be giving money to the same company lol.

You probably already know if you want EHM or not. If you aren't a hockey fan, and if you don't like pretty deep simulation-based games, there's nothing for you here.
However, if you like those two things, EHM isn't perfect, but it is the best option in the genre. Sports Interactive know what they're doing, and EHM is no different, although it is a little barebones. It's a shame that, for what is ostensibly a new game, there's no modern features such as achievements. Thankfully it does have Workshop support, and it's here we see EHM's trump card.
EHM's modding community is what, for me, pushes the game from standard sports-sim to something engrossing. Real-world rosters and clubs, as well as facepacks, allow for something more realistic - and thus, fun. For me, trying to turn my beloved Calgary Flames from perennial bottom-feeders into an actual force is far more enjoyable than doing it with a fantasy club, with fake players. Without these mods, EHM is pretty sparse.
On its own, EHM is a tough sell. Even with it's fantastic mod support, it caters to a pretty small niche. If that niche includes you, though, you'll be treated to a game that demands time and patience, but yields great reward.
