review_text:
[h1] A Very Solid VR Experience That Feels Unfinished [/h1]

The game has a great foundation, super solid gunplay with good dual wielding implementation and simple yet fun gameplay, graphics are good for the most part with an atmospheric feel and the weapon customisation is very well done, headshots are satisfying, the difficulties feel very well balanced overall, floppy disks are a great way to do unlocks and the sound design is fantastic. A genuinely brilliant VR game, but only for a few hours.


Unfortunately that's where my praise for the game ends. the foundation isn't built on. There's only 5 levels currently, with 2 of them being particularly short and one being a gimmicky final level, very little changes on replays and the only thing to aim for is weapon modifications. The game peaks in it's first level and I blame this on the games biggest flaw; a lack of variety, with only 6 weapons, a handful of enemy types, one reused boss and little change in where you fight enemies (overall themes are different but it just boils down to large empty spaces, the game gets stale. Fast. There is also the PvP but it's weak and not popular enough to regularly find full lobbies. Enemies don't really take into account your hitboxes with attacks and moreso just hit unless you interrupt their clunky animations. I understand why this is the case but it still feels dirty when you get hit by it, not to mention it completely breaks immersion.

The game is also littered with QoL issues and bugs, the party system is dreadful, manual grip doesnt let you swap guns from holsters, enabling hand swapping prioritises grabbing guns over ammo so you end up having trouble reloading, the shotgun feels uncomfortably short, the black screen whenever you SLIGHTLY clip with something is infuriating and completely breaks immersion, the jump downs are done poorly, you either instantly transition down, or put on the more immersive option and risk clipping out of bounds. Guns disappear for no real reason, the MT-47 bolt occasionally has a misplaced hitbox, doors can just be walked through, the one NPC in the game that you regularly see can become unresponsive and stop you progressing the game until you leave and come back, the shooting range refuses to give new guns ammo until you reload the area, the A.I. (as well as being completely stupid) gets buggy dealing with being frozen, corpses regularly get stuck in walls and ceilings, multiple spots where world boundaries/flat textures can be seen, I could go on but you get the idea.

The game has a lot of potential, like a hell of a lot, but it feels like an early access game, or a proof of concept, but considering that these are the guys who made arizona sunshine, and we're far enough into VR where that isn't needed in this capacity AND it's a whopping 30 quid, that's not even close to being worth the money. It ends too quick, there's not enough variety in anything in the game and it needs a lot of tweaking. 

I know the developers have a long roadmap for the game and plan on a lot of updates but come on. This is genuinely pitiful for a game that costs so much, with that price, it has to compete with games like Pavlov, Beat Saber, Blade and Sorcery, Saints and Sinners etc. and it doesn't come close to comparing. 

I really enjoyed my time with this game, truly, but now I'm just craving more, which the game doesn't provide, it's really good with friends despite the awful party system and could go on to become one of the better VR titles available, it just needs to be much more fleshed out. I look forward to seeing where this game goes but unfortunately, at it's current price, and the state that it's in, I just can't recommend it. 

tl;dr Has a lot of potential but feels unfinished, definitely keep an eye out after a few big updates but nowhere near worth the £30.

review_text:
Eastside Hockey Manager, developed by Sports Interactive and available on Steam, is a deep and comprehensive simulation game that puts players in full control of managing a professional ice hockey team. For fans of the sport who relish the behind-the-scenes decision-making—from roster building and scouting to financial management and tactical planning—this title offers an unmatched level of depth. Though it lacks the glossy presentation and mass-market appeal of mainstream sports titles, it more than makes up for it with its authenticity and meticulous attention to detail. It’s a spiritual sibling to Football Manager, built around the same philosophy of realism and strategic control.

At its core, Eastside Hockey Manager allows players to take charge of nearly any professional or junior team from a wide range of leagues around the world, including the NHL, AHL, SHL, Liiga, KHL, and countless others. The breadth of leagues and player databases is staggering, and Sports Interactive has clearly made a concerted effort to reflect the real-world structures and dynamics of global hockey. Whether you're managing a perennial NHL contender or a small-market European team, the game adapts to your environment, with different rules, financial constraints, and player development paths. This global authenticity provides significant replay value, allowing players to test their managerial skills in vastly different hockey cultures.

Gameplay is structured around daily team management tasks. You’ll be handling contract negotiations, training schedules, scouting reports, player morale, and even media interactions. The game features an in-depth scouting system that mimics real-world evaluation techniques, including tracking player potential, mental attributes, and developmental ceilings over time. Drafting young prospects and nurturing them into first-line stars years down the line is one of the most rewarding aspects of the game. It requires patience, long-term vision, and strategic roster balancing, especially under salary cap constraints or when dealing with injuries to key players. The level of micromanagement can be overwhelming for newcomers, but for experienced sim players, it's a dream come true.

The tactical aspect of Eastside Hockey Manager is equally complex. You're not just setting lines—you’re building chemistry, creating power play and penalty kill strategies, deciding on forechecking intensity, and adapting your style to your roster’s strengths. Matches can be simulated quickly or watched play-by-play, with commentary that reflects real-time decisions and player performances. While the in-game visuals are limited to 2D representations and text-based feedback, they provide enough context to understand what’s working and what’s failing. The tactical feedback loop is robust, with detailed statistics, form trends, and opposition analysis allowing you to refine your approach game by game.

Visually, the game is utilitarian. The interface is dense and packed with data, with hundreds of screens dedicated to stats, reports, and rosters. While it can feel dated and intimidating at first glance, the design favors function over flair. Once you're familiar with the layout, navigation becomes second nature, and the sheer amount of available information becomes one of the game’s greatest strengths. However, this no-frills presentation may deter casual players or those expecting a more dynamic graphical interface. Still, for the hardcore hockey strategist, the spreadsheets and data tables are part of the appeal.

One of the standout aspects of Eastside Hockey Manager is its community and modding support. The game’s built-in database is already extensive, but player-made updates, real-world rosters, and even custom leagues add tremendous value. The user-driven updates help keep the game relevant long after official patches slow down. Community forums are active, offering advice, guides, and tools that help new players overcome the steep learning curve. Whether you're adding junior leagues, tweaking league rules, or importing historical data, the modding flexibility opens up near-limitless possibilities for long-term play.

That said, Eastside Hockey Manager is not without shortcomings. Its learning curve is steep, and the game does little hand-holding for newcomers. Tutorials are limited, and much of your early experience will involve trial and error. The lack of dynamic media narratives, visual flair, or player personalities—features that titles like Football Manager have increasingly embraced—can make some seasons feel clinical or detached. Additionally, the game occasionally suffers from user interface lag or minor bugs, especially when managing large databases or simulating multiple leagues.

Despite these limitations, Eastside Hockey Manager remains the definitive experience for players who want total control over a hockey franchise. Its unmatched realism, strategic complexity, and deep customization tools offer a uniquely satisfying simulation experience. It demands time, attention, and a love for the minutiae of the sport, but rewards that investment with a gameplay loop that feels endlessly rich. For hockey fans looking for a cerebral, spreadsheet-driven experience rather than arcade thrills or quick wins, Eastside Hockey Manager is not just a game—it’s a long-term project that captures the soul of managing a team in one of the world’s most dynamic sports.

Rating: 8/10

review_text:
I am 32 years old.

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and we adopted our son together. Both are now 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I felt lost and unhappy. I was self-destructive. One day, I was so angry with everything spiraling out of control that I punched a concrete wall in a moment of overwhelming emotion. This resulted in breaking my fifth metacarpal in my right hand—the hand I worked with, played games with, and used to carry my children to bed—the hand I desperately needed to ensure I could continue providing.

Upon learning the severity of the self-inflicted damage, I became almost suicidal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man, with no history of depression or anxiety. I had never experienced anger outbursts, nor was I the type to break down and cry, but I was in a tough situation that truly prevented me from seeing the light on the other side.

With nothing better to do, I looked for a game I could play WITH ONE HAND while recovering. Somehow, I stumbled upon this game and read some of the comments. I decided it was worth a try... I must admit I didn't beat the game, nor did I play as much as some of you. In fact, I may have played this game for only a day or two. That being said, after doing so, I had a new joy and hope for life. I managed to leave behind the pain and suffering that had been thrust upon me. I could experience the joy and happiness of other people. I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥ minutes listening to this music, long enough to realize that I would be okay.

After realizing this, I turned off the game and went back to work. My hand hurt a lot, but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so sorry for myself and became the father I needed to be at that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving like.

Today, I am close friends with the mother of my children. We don't fight, argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents and friends.

Now I have 3 children. My third child is, wait, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my separation, and we just unexpectedly stumbled into each other's lives. We have been dating for a year and are very happy together.

Moral of the story: you never know what life has in store for you, and if I had given up when all odds were against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you.

review_text:
[h1]Review of Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon[/h1]
Pure 1980's action flick cheese mixed with a high octane twist on the base of Far Cry 3's open world fundamentals? Yeah it's no wonder Blood Dragon spawned a community of its own. 

Blood Dragon started a trend with the Ubisoft Far Cry titles, where we'd see a spin off game released in between the mainline titles every other year. Or at least, that's how it was for a while. From Blood Dragon prior to FC4, Primal prior to FC5, to New Dawn prior to FC6. As someone who started playing the series in 2012 with the third game, I've followed every release since. 

[u]"You know, I'm starting to actually like this.."[/u]
I'm going to be completely honest, when I first played this game many years ago, I wasn't really a fan. I replayed it a couple times back when, but it got to the point I'd consider skipping it when doing a franchise playthrough. However, my experience after replaying it just recently was completely different. I had a total blast, and I think I know why. Normally I prefer to play Ubi Far Cry titles on the hardest difficulty, Blood Dragon included. This time I decided to try Blood Dragon on a lower difficulty, and suddenly I was living my own VHS tape action movie. It's clear I found my personal sweet spot for enjoying the game after all these years. 

Blood Dragon is a 1980's synth inspired spinoff title, that heavily parodies movies of that decade. Tropes & all (Even a training & sex montage!). The story is as simple as go kill big bad & save the girl while serving lady liberty. All the while the protagonist is spouting the cheesiest one liners known to man, these of which I find hilarious. Rex "Power" Colt is a Mk.IV Cyber Commando, and he's sent to investigate Colonel Sloan, a rogue operative. Along the way he brings down Sloan's entire operation by eliminating key targets and capturing strongholds for the scientist nerds. The distant nuclear wasteland of 2007 is at threat of being reduced even further by Sloan's desire to return Humanity to a Stone Age-like existence. The key to this vision? Blood dragons. 

[u]"He said 'blow me'. So I did."[/u]
Easily the most enjoyable part of Blood Dragon for me is its gameplay. A majority of Far Cry 3's open world mechanics remain here, but most things have been tweaked in favor of a sort of power fantasy. Rex is capable of running & swimming faster than a normal Human, nor does he take fall damage. This allows you to run about the new, albeit small & somewhat bland, island with minimal restriction. 

I think my favorite part is the way leveling and weaponry works. The standard arsenal is much smaller than Far Cry 3 itself, at only 5 core weapons, and 3 additional ones you can find later on. Though this time you unlock new attachments by completing optional missions from your scientist buddies. This was an addicting process because every upgrade you obtain adds or changes something with your weapon. Visually & mechanically. The SMG going from a burst fire ballistic weapon, to a fully automatic pulse rifle with a badass reload animation was ecstasy. Or your Terminator 2 inspired lever action shotgun gaining extra barrels and new ammunition that completely deletes anything at close range. You also have the A.J.M.9, inspired by Robocop, which serves as one of your go-to stealth weapons, a sniper rifle capable of firing explosive rounds, and the classic unchanged recurve bow. The bow can't be upgraded unfortunately, however. Later you'll be able to make use of a laser minigun, flamethrower, and the greatest thing to bless our little souls.. the Killstar. Meanwhile leveling works in a more traditional sense. You don't have a skill tree, and instead obtain character upgrades as you level up to 30.

Combat works nearly identically to Far Cry 3. Enemy types are cyber variants of the archetypes you find in the base game. For better or worse. I say for worse because in my opinion this actually makes stealth harder, as the standard cyber soldiers have this giant ball shaped helmet. Even a fully upgraded burst from the handgun at point blank range can fail to pop the dome sometimes, and because this is an older FC, you'll alert the entire base failing to do so. I think that's another reason I struggled to enjoy the game originally. Opting for loud approaches here was so much fun in comparison. 

After capturing strongholds, you get a collection of side missions to do. Hunting down important targets, protecting/rescuing scientists, or the odd completely unique one like taking on a bunch of mutated sewer turtles with a taste for pizza. Hmm.. seems familiar. Scattered across the open world are also your usual fare of collectibles. This time being data notes, TV's & VHS tapes. Because of course. Hunting the cybernetic animals is also required for all unlocks and 100% completion. 

Then to the selling point of this game, the blood dragons. These big giant beasts that fire beams of destruction from their eyeballs, roam around random parts of the map. They're conceptually exciting. You can even lure them around using thrown cyber hearts, and they'll wipe out camps all on their own. Unfortunately though, these guys are a little buggy in my experience.. I'll leave that for the below section.

[u]"Come down and face me you rusty cum buckets."[/u]
Alright, so I'll briefly go over some of my issues with Blood Dragon. Even after finding a lot to enjoy, there's still some things I'm either mixed or unhappy with. 

The first and probably biggest issue I have, is the CRT filter. The entire game has this filter present. It's obviously an aesthetic choice, but it genuinely causes my eyes to strain after a while. There's no way to turn it off ingame. I've heard you can disable it in the files, so at least there's that I guess. 

Blood dragons are buggy. The most common attack they have is to blast you with their eye lasers, but every time I killed one, I would get blasted by phantom lasers every single time after their body was turned to a pile of dragon goo. 

"Service Not Available" .. ugh. After Ubisoft ended online services for various games, Blood Dragon included, you get this obnoxious pop up nearly every time you open the menu. You're forced to sit for like 30 seconds to a minute before you're given control again, and can't look at what you were trying to. I'm happy we can still play the game, but what's so hard about just putting a little pop up in the top corner when you launch that reminds you services are shut down, and not impede the pacing of gameplay with this? 

Lastly, the game is insanely short. We're talking 3-4 hours to 100% the game on high difficulties. That's not necessarily a bad thing, I just prefer games to be much longer. Thankfully, I will enjoy replaying this from now on, so I'll get to keep having fun with it. I could also add here, that there's this "Annoying Tutorial" joke at the beginning of the game, that's suppose to spoof how hand holding and interrupting game tutorials can be, which can be funny on a first time playthrough, On subsequent playthroughs it actually just is annoying because you can't skip it. A minor gripe though.

[h1]Conclusion (Pros & Cons)[/h1]
All in all, it's a great little package after enjoying Far Cry 3, or just wanting more Far Cry in general even if it's whacky and full of entertaining cheese. I'm happy I was able to find enjoyment with the game after so many years.

[b]Pros:[/b]
+Hilarious one liners
+Addicting upgrade system
+1980's "future" aesthetic
+Steam achievements

[b]Neutral:[/b]
~Super short

[b]Cons:[/b]
-Forced CRT filter

[h1]Disclaimer[/h1]
Thank you for taking the time to read my review. Please remember, that this is just my opinion. We don't have to agree, one thing I love you may hate, and one thing I hate you may love. Hopefully this gave you an idea of what to expect. 

[b]Review lengths have been greatly compressed due to the character limit.[/b]

review_text:
Ever since I've first heard of this game, which was a long time ago. I've always considered this to be the scariest game, why, you may ask? Despite the fact I've never even played or watched it to the very end, only seeing YouTubers play it for a couple of minutes before inevitably leaving out of pure fear like a big dumb crying baby, I've heard lots of what it can do, not necessarily the plot or major spoilers, but what it *can* be like, or what it *tries* to be like. I've seen some couple of clips here and there, but it's mostly because of how terrifying the art style was, back then, when I've first seen this game, it was my number one fear already, just because of how terrifying the characters even looked.

I've preached that idea ever since, day after day, exclaiming on the top of my voice, that THIS game is the most terrifying game ever to exist, I've played MANY horror games ever since, and it still remains to be the one that makes me scared the most. It is SO scary that I'm not even willing to TOUCH the game, or interact with it in ANY way whatsoever, that's how scary it is to me, despite how sad and foolish that may sound, but I do mean it.

People asked me what is the scariest game ever for me, and I, with no hesitation, say this, I've had it on my mind multiple times until I gave in and tried it.

I bought it, and there.



And I was right.
I was right all along.

Playing this game made it even more terrifying for me.
Everything about it was just an absolute scarefest.
And I love it.
Something that I can't say I've ever really seen from any other game, at least tried to replicate but never succeeded on doing so.
The unique setting, the ambience, and overall the feel for the game.
It is AMAZING.

I'd go as far as to saying that this game isn't even a game, it's a full-on experience.
I don't think there's going to be anything in this world that won't make love this game.
This. Is. THE BEST. Horror game ever.

I've went from calling this the "Scariest Game Ever" to the: "The Best (Scary) Game Ever."

This was such a wild ride and I wish to have more games like these, this is one of the games where I simply just can't ever describe how amazing this game is with just words.
This is just something you'd have to see.

Ever since playing this game, I find it hard to even be scared of any other game.
This game put me in emotions and fear that I've never felt before, in levels I've never seen before.
It is amazing.

review_text:
[h1]A short and sweet point-n-click puzzler.[/h1]

In Samorost 2 you guide a space gnome on a quest across a couple of bizarre asteroids in order to rescue your dog from some aliens who dognapped him. As you explore the asteroids and meet their wacky inhabitants, you'll have to solve a few puzzles in order to progress. It's not overly difficult, certainly more straightforward than their other games that I've tried, but it's challenging enough to be engaging and personally I prefer not to be left scratching my head anyway. It doesn't take long to finish but it's a lovely little adventure and I think it's well worth experiencing.

It originally came out in 2005 and received a 15th anniversary update this year to improve the graphics, add achievements and tweak/improve a few other minor things. I believe this the earliest of Amanita's games available on Steam, and the first Samorost game is only available online. 

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list][*]Lovely art.
[*]Humorous sound effects.
[*]Short and sweet.
[*]Engaging puzzles.[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list][*]None that I can think of.[/list]

If you found this review helpful, please check out my other reviews over at [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/33633486/]Kemo's Corner.[/url]

It's fun, but not very. It's a good time waster. The city builder aspect is weak. You have a priority system but your little villagers seem to view your priorities as more of a suggestion than instruction. Your towers are weak. The enemy pathfinding seems to arbitrarily decide what it figures the path of least resistance is.

You'll get to a point where you're good at the game, you've got it figured out but then one morning your villagers wake up and refuse to survive. They do something foolish and after a chain reaction, your settlement is destroyed for no real reason.

Buy any other city builder.

review_text:
I wish Steam had a better rating system than like or dislike.
The game captures the Resident Evil feel it was going for pretty well ('cause that's basically what it is, a well made RE clone).

Atmosphere 9/10
Level design 9/10
Systems: 3/10
Horror: 5/10
Story: 6/10
Value at €60: 5/10

[b]What it did well:[/b]
- Graphics: one of the best looking games I've played
- Level Design: Very detailed settings, very well designed environments that don't really force you to backtrack (but the inventory system does), very well designed and placed props.
- Voice acting: Very good.
- Music/Audio: Perfect, it really helps set the atmosphere. Both audio effects and music are really well made.

[b]What it didn't do well[/b]:
- The inventory and storage system - tries to emulate RE, but ends up as constant, unfun juggling.
- Overused cheap jump scares. Towards the end it's just annoying, since the game keeps doing the same thing over and over again.
- The Story: Feels like it was written by multiple people. Someone started a very good, compelling story. And someone else, not so talented, finished it.
I felt let down at the end. Even though I liked playing it, the second half was so frustrating, with the ending and the constant inventory frustration, that I felt cheated of my time somewhat.
It's an ok game, could have been a masterpiece, but it landed just off the mark. It doesn't deserve the "Very Positive" review. Bloober Team can do better.

Ending Spoiler ahead:
[spoiler]By the end, the game feels like LOST - the videogame. The finale leans on a shadowy mastermind + time-loop reveal overused trope, without addressing the bigger mysteries (collective/travelers/virus), which left me cold.[/spoiler]

If it was €30, I would have recommended it. But for 60, it does too many things wrong, in the worst ways, at the worst time.

The game honestly was really good with really fun combat. At times it really did try it's hardest to be Dead Space and thought not being able to reach that mark the game has it's own unique strengths and quirks.

All 3 Dead Space games I played on their respective "medium" or "standard" difficulties and they where walks in the parks with a difficult section here and there. This game downright felt brutal and unforgiving at some times. Though this difficulty did come with some annoyances like when the enemies start to sprout these tentacles and failing to hit them makes them transform into more powerful enemies as well as once you start to frequently encounter the 2 headed enemies, they are absolute bullet sponges and kill in one or two hits.

This game was also a lot more graphics and gory compared to Dead Space. Sure Dead Space had it's gruesome  sections it really doesn't compare to the type of Mortal Combat-esque death animations you get in this game.

In the game you get these chests that give you ton of loot, but towards the end it's just these parasite things coming out there to jumpscare you. The story felt like something of a mess and as soon as you feel like you are making progress the game throws something at you that feel so forced but I guess the game needs to go on. 

The ending does somewhat feel like it's setting itself up for a sequel as well as it ends almost exactly like Dead Space where Nicole jumpscares you. 

The game is good, if you are a fan of Dead Space, play it, if you are not a fan of Dead Space, still play it, unless you don't want to.

review_text:
[h1][i]"New breed of Survival Horror"[/i] ~ No. It's not.[/h1]
[h2]PSA: Disable Panini in Display Settings - Helps Cutscene crashes[/h2]

Gosh Bloober Team, I was rooting for you. I still am, the story to Cronos is.. intriguing albeit thin right now but their capacity with optimising UE5 is very concerning. 

[h2]Tldr on: [b]Not recommend[/b][/h2]
- Terrible performance (9800X3D x 4070ti @ 3440x1440)
- Poor UE5 optimisation ~ Consistent choppy drops below 60fps
- Crashing (Particularly during cutscenes)
- Update: About the half way point, incredibly underwhelmed.

[h2]First Impressions[/h2]
The story is thin at this stage, outside a plague that has seemingly wiped out humanity current day, there's not much detail as to what you're doing, what your importance is and the community of other travellers. However, the notion of time travel through rifts is certainly curious on how these events might uncover why the Earth is in the state that it is. So more to come and I'm at least invested to learn more. If the game actually works.. more on that later.

Gameplay is akin to Dead Space weight and combat, with early Resident Evil inventory management torture. You won't be shooting limbs but rather aiming for the head or the glowy fleshy bits. You're encouraged to prime your weapon with a charge before shooting for maximum damage which gives your enemy the chance to close the gap, get a range attack in or complete a wind-up within range. Picking to finish your charge can be tight sometimes to stagger them which is welcome intensity. Along with a flame stun emergency tool, you can also choose to stun and run instead which allows for more evasive play. 

Addressing the resource complaints - It's still early but honestly I've not felt any problems at all and you can opt to avoid combat since enemies don't know how to walk through doors or leave the areas they're clearly attuned to. Running back into the apartments and watching half a dozen enemies along with the big "merged" fatty decide "Welp. Never mind I guess" whilst the door is wide open is hilarious. It does allow for the notion of "Pick your battles" but at the same time, it's 2025 and this is kinda pathetic and ruins any sense of danger.

[h2]"Don't let them merge"[/h2]
Speaking of danger - the enemies are.. uninspired. 
The gimmick for this "New breed of Survival Horror" is a twist on Crimson Heads from Resident Evil 1. Back in 2002... Everything is an inspiration from something, it's tough to be original these days but.. this isn't strictly new guys, come on.

The tag line you'll see in the trailers "Don't let them merge" is the star mechanic here, cautiously choosing how to leave the battlefield: torched or littered. In RE with Crimson heads, you had an option to burn corpses since they could get up after meeting death a second time and come back meaner and faster than ever. The.. *googles* Orphans are closer to Necromorphs with their horrific transformations as previously expressed but if you want to see the real horrors of Cronos, it's almost to suggest.. not to play correctly? Huh?

Great idea on paper but so far, either the area is pimped out with explosive terrain to deal damage or even outright kill enemies (these explosions need more umpf) in the action set-pieces or you can just run. If you play conservatively (which is the whole point) you won't have problems stopping them from merging so..... mute marketing? I do hope more variety comes but so far I'm rather concerned that pressure comes from poor play, which is an odd choice. 

That said, I have chosen to reload an autosave if things aren't going in my favour or I know I could do better to save resources. However, I don't consider this penalising my experience to feel "the merged" since the nature of Survival Horror is coming out on top as best as you can. 

Reserving complete judgement but so far, consider me unimpressed.

[h2]The bad[/h2] 
You know the story for UE5, it's a gorgeous engine with horrendous performance. And the implementation here is no different at all. 

You'll experience frame drops in areas for seemingly no reason, the area doesn't change or events don't occur in the area and you'll consistently drop in the same places. I experienced this several times, the one I can recall is on the landing amongst one of the first buildings you enter and it's a warning sign for things to come. It's not a deal breaker as for where it counts, the drops are absent during combat, so there's that at least. 

Then there's hitching when things are dynamically loading (I assume). Silent Hill 2, Bloober Team's previous project, had this also which ruins the seamless worlds we've come to expect. I don't mind the elevator sequences or forced walking exposition if it means the world can load, 2018's God of War was the first game I truly appreciated this. When the game hitches for a second or two, it just breaks immersion and becomes a blemish rather than a refined work of art. Anything that brings the user out the experience is markedly a problem, an irrefutable fact.

You know what truly breaks immersion? And incites frustration? Crashing. 
In my time with the game so far, I've crashed 3 times. All during cutscenes:
1x when encountering [spoiler]Edward[/spoiler]
2x during the ascendance sequence, ironic and utterly hilarious.

There's no defence for this, when you're ejected from the experience, it takes effort and a desire to see it through to offer up more of my time for your product, giving it fair shake before condemning it. 

After it immediately crashed again initiating the first ascendance sequence in the same place, here I am with this first impression and opposition in a recommendation. I truly ascended as I'm no longer in your crafted world. [i]Ba dum tssssh![/i]

I'll be trying again without streaming to my friends in discord to see if that improves things but if that's a solution, that will only further display the poor experience on show here. 

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]
Outside an obscure plot, there's not much innovation here and wouldn't recommend full retail. Even at £40 via Fanatical (great authorised retailer), I'm not impressed and only further frustrated with the performance issues. Take that away, Cronos The New Dawn early hours are nothing more than: okay. 

If you're into Survival Horror, yeah it's gonna be your bread and butter. We're not always in it for the plot and these games are typically more gameplay driven which is to say... it's more of the same. I don't know how Bloober can push this experience as a "new breed". Maybe its intention is to be frustrating and artificial as here comes an additional nitpick:

A key takes up a single inventory slot but so does my Boltcutters? 
If they were limited use, I'd understand but there's seemingly no end to these padlocked doors so it's more of an integral tool. So why the f*ck am I having to juggle this? I also notably have an empty carabiner on my belt. I couldn't use that in some capacity to carry my Boltcutters? I'm an old RE Veteran, this is not new but pushing it imo. 

After all this, pardon my gall here, but I can't help question Bloober Team's competency with the UE5 engine. 

I recently walked away from Virtuous's work on Metal Gear Solid Delta in UE5 and it was seamless. No stutters, hiccups or crashing for the 30 hours to 100% achievements and 4 playthroughs. Therefore I refuse to believe it's impossible to have a good UE5 experience. Especially since Delta is close to 30% cutscenes.

Being this was an in-house project with no outside partners interfering, they had complete control being their own product. Sorry guys, but this has made me doubt you yet again like I did with the Medium and will be choosing cautiously to investigate your projects with more scrutiny here on out. 

Here's to hoping more updates and actually able to progress. Do better.

Update: Added PSA line. 
Also, I've somehow unlocked the "To Pave The Path" with only 5 recipes unlocked. *facepalm*

review_text:
So I've played this game for a bit and I've run into a few issues. It gives you the option for what type of movement you want, the walking movement or the teleportation movement. That's great! But there is no option for turning. When I use my remote to turn it will always be a snap 90 degree turn. It is kinda jarring when you want to look around a room and you're turning your head. You want to see more than just what turning your head does, you want to turn your body 45 degrees so your body is now facing where your head is. Well you can't really do that. You can move your physical body sure, but I think it would be better if the game had that smooth turning option too.

The other issue I'm having is I'm playing this game standing up. I put the belt where the game suggests where I should put it. Yet no matter what I do, adjusting my height in the in-game options, standing on something irl, or anything else, the facial scanner in the game is a head taller than I am. So I can't play solo. I did a Co-Op run with a random person and they were showing me the ropes. They couldn't understand why I couldn't use the scanner to unlock the door. To them I must have looked like a troll. To me, I am desperately trying to gain the extra 6 to 8 inches so I can progress through the game. I have no idea what to do to fix it. 

Its a really fun game. People comparing it to L4D are correct. This just feels kinda buggy. The facial scan for me is a game breaking bug since I can't even progress without Co-Op and hope someone else doesn't have the same problem. I had height issues with Arizona Sunshine as well, so I dunno if there is an issue with my height and where they suggest to put the belt somehow throws off something.

review_text:
There's an episode of Star Trek the Next Generation where Commander Riker pretends to be Sherlock Holmes in the Holodeck. However, he makes a critical mistake when he asks the Holodeck for a puzzle that would prove difficult for "Riker", and not "Holmes". This enables the Holodeck to create an experience that starts to mess with his mind by convincing him he is in other areas of the ship. This is similar to the experience of Imscared. The game has elements outside of just running the application that are necessary for the story to progress, and a player has to keep an open mind to succeed.
A pleasant surprise from this game is it manages to be scary while giving your character a reasonable movement speed, and avoiding artificial game lengtheners. The experience is short only because it respects your time. This game absolutely nails getting to the fun, scary, exploration constantly.
There are parts of the game that I definitely had to reference a walk through to understand, but I also lack patience and that's how I experience most horror games.
The game contains a variety of jump scares, but I wouldn't describe them as cheap shots. Some have complained about the volume of them, but I would just suggest playing without headphones.

TLDR:
Great, short, scary game. Contains jumpscares.

review_text:
"Samorost 2" is a point-and-click game that tells a surreal story of a space gnome whose dog just got kidnapped by mischievous aliens. You will help the gnome to find its dog by solving different kind of puzzles. This game has an interesting plot, enhanced graphics with full-screen support, beautiful art, humouros sound effects, engaging puzzles and 13 achievements.
It's a short game as it took me only 20 minutes to finish it and get all the achievements (all the achievements can be acquired in one sitting). It has only one ending and there is a save feature, so you can restart or continue the game from a selected chapter. I would give it a 2/10 difficulty rating as the gameplay is minimal and the instructions are pretty clear during the whole game (you need to solve the puzzles and finish the story).
After playing "Samorost 1", which is a free-to-play game on Steam (you can find it here - https://store.steampowered.com/app/1580970/Samorost_1/), I decided to try more games from this developer. 
"Samorost 2", released in 2009, is the second game from the trilogy (you can find the third game on Steam as well) and it  has been developed by Amanita Design (Jakub Dvorsky's indie game studio), same company responsible for other well-known titles such as "Machinarium" or "CHUCHEL". In this game you will need to guide a space gnome on a quest across a couple of bizarre asteroids in order to rescue your dog from some aliens who kidnapped him. As you explore the asteroids and meet their strange inhabitants, you'll have to solve a few puzzles in order to progress. 
I didn't encounter any issues while playing the game and I was very much impressed by the beautiful visuals. The game's backgrounds often combine organic with inorganic elements and each scene in the game contains movement. The music (composed by Tomáš Dvořák) was extremely relaxing and created a wonderful atmosphere to just sit back and relax while solving the puzzles. The puzzles were not too difficult, although difficult enough that it presented a bit of a challenge. The story was really cute and well represented without the use of any word dialogue (there is only a little voice-acting in form of non-legible utterances).
As a recommendation for developer, I would like to suggest adding a hint button which may improve the experience for a lot of players. I would also like to mention that I got this game on a sale (for 99 eurocents) and I think that its initial price (of 4.99 euros) is a little too high for 20 minutes of gameplay.  
All things considered, I will definitely try more games from this developer and I would recommend this game to players that like surreal games or to the casual players that are trying new games/doing playthroughs.
If you want, you can check my full game playthrough here:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JjnsCRI9WEM&ab_channel=Spartakus

This game may be 17 years old, but it’s still a blast to play. The gameplay is smooth and enjoyable, with modes like Survivors vs. Zombies and Survival keeping things fresh. The ability for players to jump in and control bots adds a fun, dynamic twist, and the custom mod support breathes new life into it. Surprisingly, the cutscenes are visually stunning even by today’s standards, adding extra immersion to the experience.
That said, it’s not without its quirks. The terrain can be confusing, and the game lacks clear direction, which can make navigation frustrating. There’s also little distinction between difficulty settings, and the final campaign feels near impossible to finish with bot teammates. The base content is limited compared to modern games, but mods help fill the gap.
The player base may have faded over the years (expired), but this game still delivers plenty of fun for those willing to give it a try. If you enjoy nostalgic gems or are open to experimenting with mods, this one’s worth your time!

👎 Cons: Confusing terrain, lacks direction, tough final mission, and limited base content.

review_text: Honestly, Yakuza 5 just doesn't cut it as a good Yakuza game. I tried it out because I had played 0 first, and this game inspired 0, so I expected much more from it, but this game feels so drag-on, tutorial-filled, and non-action-packed. By the time I got to Part 2 I just thought it was uninteresting, and returned to it after 2 years, and the story really didn't pick up until the Finale, apart from Haruka and Akiyama's part. I just thought this game was too packed with side stuff. This is usually where Yakuza games shine for most people but it can get repetitive and boring fast doing the same thing over and over again, and especially you'll have to do these things 5 times each because each character has something new for them to do. There also is no CP or unlockable abilities like earlier games so everything has to be done by constant trips and while walking, bottomless stomach, sprinting, or anything. This means that for each new character you play as there will be the same "Learn from Masters, Do Side Story, See all Revelations, Visit all Restaurants, Do Touring, Increase Weapon Skill, Play Minigames, Fight In Victory Road, Complete Hostess, repeat." for each character all while being hounded by the numerous fighting encounters that they can drag you into, as well as the countless backtracking and trips you'll have to do. The Level Ups also are so strange and disorganized. The fights also give out pretty cheap rewards, and also And the story? Ok but a bit underperforming in my opinion. Every time you get into the city there's always many things hounding you from progression, such as a substory or a revelation, or a certain enemy that sneaks up on you causing needless encounters, and there are far too many of these. And, even when it LOOKS like something interesting will happen, there are needless dialogue scenes between story events to make the game feel longer than it actually should be. The characters are also not bad, but a lot of them were a bit off to me, especially with the way they changed during the story, and some of the plot twists that occured for certain characters. There are returning ones like Yuya, Majima, Kamiyama, and Komaki, but everyone just feels so "meh". And I feel like the story just is poorly written, and replaying this to completion has showed me why I have stopped playing this, because it just is a long, gruelling journey with no satisfaction or reward. It's not a action-packed, immense story-telling game like the first 3 games (0,1,2) are. Instead, they were more content-hungry and less action and adventure here than ever. Maybe if you're a die-hard Yakuza fan you'll love this, but me, it wasn't as great just because it had the most content. I finished it but still my opinion hasn't changed. I don't know if i'd say I wish I never bought it, because I think this one is just ok, but it's nothing too special, although it's definitely better than Yakuza 3/4. After the Yakuza 0 Trilogy (0,K1,K2) it's the best of the remastered collection given it has 0 unnecessary changes from the original game unlike the other two games with an ok story and the biggest number of protagonists, but there are some other notable flaws that keep it from being as good.

review_text:
Personally I wouldnt recommend this game. All the movement feels...off for otherwise decent gameplay. Gave it a shot, not for me. Maybe later?

April 15th Review Update: So its been almost a year and ive rebought the game for the new update that overhauls the movement and I do have some thoughts

The movement is better...ish. I feel like I can do things however ive identified my main gripe/quirk with the movement and its how you detach from walls. It gives you a huge boost in a sideways direction that is opposite of the wall. Now this may be like a momentum thing or realism it makes playing the game awkward. I try to correct by holding the appropriate direction but then i overshoot the direction I want to go. In comparison to titanfall 2 im confident when im jump off a wall that ill go where or near I intend not so much here which is detrimental to gameplay. It could be that im just bad and have to get good but im fighting the controls and obstacles at the same time which is a frustrating thing. It seems more so that aiming movement is more determined by wasd than camera which makes it not as intuitive for me 

As for moment to moment combat it feels good but I notice that aim isnt very needed. Its just hordes and Im not sure if I like that. So you have a bunch of enemies and it doesnt feel rewarding to hit a headshot and more so just sorta shoot the enemies till they are dead. Dont get me wrong the weapons feel good to use just not in this context. Again maybe its just me but slower firing weapons feel weaker than faster firing cause without benefits to good aim you can just pump more bullets into the horde. Slower firing weapons should atleast one tap mobs or something cause slow reload + fire rate feels not fluid but again in this context of horde style gameplay. Maybe I just need more time under my belt but this is my gut feeling. When I die in combat im really unsure of what I did wrong despite my best efforts to keep moving. 

The last problem is that not much is explained, I stumbled into the dungeons thing by accident and have no clue how to save shards between runs for the shop in the hub. There are objectives I have no idea how to complete. I understand wanting people to explore but when i feel handicapped by not having all the mechanics its not very fun. I literally didnt know dungeons lead into the main mode which makes me feel like starting the main mode feels like youre not playing the game right especially when the dungeons give you shards, gear, keys, and jade for fairly easy challenges. Either dungeons needs to be separated or made more prominent as part of the gameplay loop. Also dying takes too long for a game about speed, why do i die for longer than it takes to start a new run? 

I wanna say that despite how negative I am i truly want to like this game and see it for all the potential its worth. I think the game is getting there but just a couple more tweaks are needed. As of now ive crossed the 2 hour threshold so Im just in it for the long haul now and just hope that the game changes as needed. I dont think I recommend it but its closer now than before.

review_text:
[h1]Not quite Sniper Elite, but pretty close.[/h1]

The first of the five big open-world-missions in Sniper Ghost Warrior Contracts was admittedly rough. The second one went significantly smoother, and in the third one i was sniping dudes from 300 meter distances like it was nothing and had a blast for the remainder of the game.

Don't know if you could call the sniping mechanics and physics realistic (Sniper Elite seems to be slightly more so, it seems to me), but it is a bit tough to learn how to use your scope properly and it will take one or two missions until you get the feeling for it, so I guess you could call this a proper sniper simulation. Anyways, even on the easiest difficulty setting the game is absolutely no cakewalk and if you are one of the impatient kind who just tries to go in all Rambo, running and gunning your way through, you'll get your ass kicked. SGWC is more of a thinking man's game where you have to plan ahead and try to stay as stealthy as possible.

Unfortunately, the mostly fair challenge flips into unfair territory now and then, because the enemy AI is dumb as dogsh*t and they have to compensate their lack of intelligence by having impossible accuracy: Those b*st*rds can hit you with a common assault rifle from 200 meters away, even if you're prone in high grass on top of a hill.

But that's basically the only thing to really complain about. The rest ist just nitpicking. The gore effects are slightly exagerated (this is the kind of game where you can take a half face off with a small 9mm pistol), but overall the presentation is solid. The "story" is far from a masterpiece, but at least it gives you a decent enough explanation why you are doing what you are doing. Five missions seem a bit short and the replay value is relatively low if you are not a completionist, but even on the easiest difficulty the longest of the missions can take up to 3 hours so you'll be occupied for at least 8 to 10 hours if you just focus on the main missions alone.

In the end SGWC is a fun game for people who like their First-Person-Shooters with a balanced mix of casual gameplay and challenging realism and a good dose of stealth on top. If the historical WWII setting of Sniper Elite is not for you, the Sniper Ghost Warrior series is the next best thing.

review_text:
There needs to be more simple, generic, just games like this. It's an open level base infiltration game with outposts sprinkled in across the map, their layout is fine, fun to sneak through. As for sniping, it feels like the sequel to this sacrificed the areas you can actually infiltrate to enable the meme over 1000m shots, which is fine for a flash game or a separate type of small side content, but I'd rather have actual levels like here than shooting galleries. If sniping from around 300m doesn't satisfy your sniper fantasy, just zoom out and pretend your range finder shows you 10km, Jesus. 

The AI is fine if you ghost, but if you try to go panther, as in eliminate enemies quietly but hard, leave the bodies etc. then it kinda falls apart. They have very short "suspicious state", and if one enemy gets alerted, suddenly the whole area is, instantly, and they know where you are. Would be much better if, for example, after finding the body, the AI first alarm the nearest squad members, run a search, and then call it in by radio and alert the base. It's gamey, but it's a game, it would give the player a chance to react and correct his mistake instead of loading a badly placed checkpoint.

I really like that this game knows exactly what it is, no patronizing, no deep message, no forced gaming tropes like open world, the devs clearly learned from SGW3 and found the type of game they are comfortable with making. Thematically enemy installations are just soldier camps and post-soviet bases but there is a suprising amount of soul here. Each level has some nice vistas and clearly takes place in a different region, with different weather and time of day that suits the area best. First level is cool, mountains at night, a slight blizzard and northern lights in the sky.

Should be way longer though, same as the sequel. Devs claim it has replayability like Hitman, but that's BS, after running a map once you've seen every path you can take, no reason to replay, first time is nice though.

review_text:
MXGP Pro: Tokyo Drift is not worth your £40.

Gameplay

Yes it's more challenging than previous iterations with pro physics enabled, but 90% of this percieved difficulty seems to come from constantly trying not to slide out the back end. I can see what they are trying to do but it's too far. You can no longer case jumps and just keep riding like nothing happened but again it's completely unbalanced. Theres basically an arbitrary number that once exceeded you will crash upon impact. Theres never a scenario where you almost crash and manage to recover.. its either you keep on riding or you collapse off your bike instantly.  

AI seems unchanged, they still take more or less the same line and only seem more difficult since the game is now harder for the player. I'm playing on medium for now and usually play realistic.

Very little interaction with ruts, they seem mostly shallow and inconsequential. 

Whips are schocking. Worst yet in any iteration of the game. They look horrible and unless you land perfectly straight, which is awkward and clunky, will basically ping you off sideways.

Graphics

The same as GP3 from what I can tell. Some pop in in menus while stuff is loading. No complaints.

Audio

Bikes Good enough, seem a bit samey but haven't yet ridden all the bikes to compare. Hitting 2" puddles for some bizarre reason is the loudest sound effect in the game, far louder than your bike or the crowd. No matter how tiny or short they are you get a loud splash.. easily patched but annoying.

I've yet to play multiplayer. The compound is fun for 10 minutes.

No Matterley Basin which was disappointing!

Don't buy it unless they do some serious patching.

review_text:
I'm going to review each separate part of the game

I recommend playing the main story and the non-tedious side missions only if you do buy this game. The whole package I don't recommend in general though because the other parts of the game aren't that great. Especially the boring-as-hell challenges.

Main Story

I hate the combat in these games with a passion. Mainly because your character's movements are mostly arbitrary and you have no idea what exactly they will do other than "attack" or "counter". You don't know which direction they will counter in, which enemy they will target next, you have little agency in movement during combat. Battles last forever. It feels like crap. It's easy too, but when you "lose" ever it's because of the above issues, not because you made some sort of mistake. After all, all you have to do is press A to attack and Y occasionally when you need to counter. Whether the game allows those attacks to connect with an optimal enemy or one with 50 other enemies around them is up to the game though. You have other techniques you can do, but no real way of indicating which enemy to do any of them on for sure, so it feels like you just hope the game does it on the right enemy for all your attacks and actions. Enemy about to shoot you? Sorry you targeted a different enemy and got shot and died. You couldn't do anything about it - it's just the game's decision. WHY CAN'T I HIT MULTIPLE ENEMIES AT ONCE WITH SWEEPING KICKS OR SOMETHING IF THEY SURROUND ME? You have no agency in combat other than punch one guy, counter the guy who ran up behind you - maybe use a gadget and hope it targets the right enemy. Dealing with multiple enemies at once is out of the question outside of some special attacks you can occasionally use that stun them, you can never kill multiple enemies in one go, that'd be a fun and quicker. You have to suffer through punching each enemy one-by-one to kill them. Or spend 200 years creeping up on each enemy like it's dishonored (much better game) if the room layout lets you.

The graphics are great. The story is quite interesting, and the exploration of the city and light puzzle solving elements are fun. This game isn't all that long so the reliance on "bat-vision" isn't too annoying. I actively just avoid combat since it's such a drag. At least the game gives you options to take out opponents without having to start another brainless boring brawl session. Great voice acting and the appearance of each superhero/supervillain look fairly accurate to their original designs. I appreciate that aspect. I'm not much of a superhero fan but it was interesting seeing all these supervillains in the game.

There are simply too many riddler collectibles. I got all of them, but it gets to be a drag after a while. Rather than pepper the world with things that give you a tiny amount of EXP that look exactly the same, pepper the world with actual interesting experiences and encounters. Focus on side missions with actual interactions with characters, and if you need collectibles, have a smaller amount that give you something particularly useful like a new optional gadget or skill or something.

Challenge pack DLC / Riddler's Revenge

Absolutely abysmal DLC / extra content that is just "fight some enemies" times one million. The combat in these games is the most boring part. The exploration is more interesting and the light puzzle solving as well. No I don't care about getting a combo of two million (mashing A and Y and maybe B for fun) for three hours to get a medal and an achievement. F*** off with this garbage. I'm glad this fad of "attack and wait to counter and no enemy lock-on" went out of style eventually. Arkham Asylum, Shadow of Mordor, and this game are the ones with that combat style I've played and I'm already completely sick of it. There's a reason the achievement rates for this part of the game are the lowest out of the whole package. It's not fun and takes forever.

Harley Quinn's revenge

It's a small DLC that focuses on story and combat. It's essentially another mission that adds on to the main story, and is pretty good just like the rest of the main game but honestly if I bought this dlc separately I would feel like it isn't worth whatever you could charge because it's such a small thing and is almost completely reuse of assets in the steel mill area of the main game's map. Nothing much to it, and almost entirely just fighting trash normal enemies too.

Overall this whole Arkham City game would have been recommendable if it wasn't padded with so many awful combat sessions. If you play the game just for the story it's more fun than trying to do the soul-sucking challenges. So I'd recommend if you just play the story, but don't recommend the other parts.

review_text:
Writing this after 2 hours of actual play time cause playing this game after completing the 3rd one is legitimately depressing. My first hour of playing the campaign of Just Cause 3 consisted of a brief exposition dump about characters you're made to care about like Dimah and Mario along with some exploring and capturing of the early outposts which was generally really fun. My first hour of Just Cause 4 was was being introduced to 'Bad Corporate Guy #1' and 'Bad General Woman #1' along with 'Rebel Woman with Vendetta against Bad General Woman'. After the least memorable intro to a game I've ever had the displeasure to sit through, I was immediately put off by the tether mods that i found to be more of an annoyance than anything, the next 10 minutes was "wow a tornado!", and then i spent the last 30 minutes of my first hour searching the wind outpost for breakers that would've taken 5 minutes had they been directly marked (like they would've been in the last game). I genuinely remember more of my first hour of the 3rd game than this one and I just started playing this 4 hours ago. I would 100% refund this game if i didn't go AFK and put myself over the 2 hour mark, which says a lot considering i got the game at a 90% discount, I'd honestly rather have my $10 back than subject myself to playing and finishing this game but it's in my library now so its gonna get finished, will edit review when done.
Edit: the mission based regions instead of the destructible outposts really doomed this game from the start. Progressing by blowing up outposts is something nobody wanted changed from the last game. The concept of front lines is cool but the execution just wasn't there. The fact that there are actual battles on the front line would be cool if these battles weren't just static battlefields, the line doesn't move to either side as you kill enemies they just endlessly spawn on one side of these big fields on the border of predetermined provinces. If they would've had outpost based progression like JC3 and implemented the frontline mechanic with an actual moving front that you could manually interact with instead of taking preset regions, this would be a better and more successful game than JC3. Also idk what happened between JC3 and 4 but Rico just seems so much more bitter in this game. His mood and tone in both games really mirrors my experience with either of the games, in JC3 Rico was making jokes and seemed to be having fun as I was enjoying the experience, in this game it just feels like he's doing this cause he has to, as opposed to doing it 'Just Cause'
TLDR: Play the 3rd game this is too repetitive, if i had a dollar every time they asked me to flip a breaker or hack a console id have enough money to buy the Just Cause IP and make a better game myself

Well, reaching that 100 hour mark, it's finally time for me to write that review. And let me put clearly, as a fan of Starship Troopers for 20 years, ever since I killed my first bug in the 2005 Starship Troopers game....

Its worth it. Even Full Price.

review_text:
I absolutely loved this game! It was a fun time and reminds me a lot of RE and Dead Space. It's a proper survival horror game that asks the player to be alert at all times and to be mindful with their limited resources. The story quite good and had me eager to see what it will turn out like in the end. The overall atmosphere of this game is incredibly immersive. The sound design is solid all-around with good surround sound support and a wide sound stage. The soundtrack is a banger and feels both retro and futuristic, which is a nice way to compliment the time-traveling aspect of the story. Graphics-wise, this game is beautiful much like SH2R that Bloober released a year ago. The budget difference between this game and the last is a bit noticeable in cutscenes. They are still very well done, but the quality of the animation is a bit lower than that of SH2R. But, in the grand scheme of things, the artists did an absolutely fantastic job with this game's overall graphical presentation. The only real complaint I have with the visuals is the horrendous black level floor when HDR is turned on. Seriously, it makes the game a lot more bright than it should be in the shadows and overall dark areas. Thankfully, using Ultra+ Mod Manager from Nexus Mods helped fix the black level floor issue and even allowed me to tweak the graphics settings further and really push the image quality to the max. The gameplay is my favorite part of this game because it knows how to make my survival horror-loving heart happy. Having to line up your shots with the enemies' heads as you charge every bullet makes the combat pretty intense. Missing a charged shot, or even not shooting for the head, can cause you to waste resources and risk the enemy getting too close to you. Enemies hit quite hard so even taking damage once from a small enemy at the beginning of your first run can mean you die a lot earlier than you'd like. Personally, I didn't have a tough time with the game likely due to playing survival horror games like the RE series since I was a kid. If you've played a Resident Evil game or even Dead Space before, you'll likely have a fun challenge ahead of you that won't make you frustrated when you inevitably make your first mistake. I am beginning my New Game+ run immediately because of how much fun I had. I really recommend this game to anyone looking for a solid survival horror experience that won't stray too far from the pack, but it can stand on its own if need to. 

Such is our calling.

review_text:
I consider this game to be an improvement over Hiveswap Act 1, but ultimately it should still appeal to the same people (and most of those people will want to play act 1 first).

As before, it's effectively a visual novel disguised as a point and click adventure. However, despite most of it being literally on-rails this one has more legitimate puzzles and requires you to think a bit. The focus is almost entirely on social interactions with the trolls you meet, rather than "use item X on background object Y", which is a great change from traditional point-and-click fare and really plays to the author's strengths.

And yes, Andrew Hussie is in peak form here. The characters you meet are all fun and quite varied, the scenarios they place you in are creative, and several puzzles have more than one solution you can find. The story is focused on the parts of Homestuck's lore that everyone already found most interesting. The worldbuilding holds up with or without knowledge of the prior work. The comedy and character development is on point. There's plenty of silly secret remarks you can get from using every item on every person or talking to people at different points in the story, but since you're actually TALKING to people it doesn't hurt the pacing much this time. And the change in format renders it 100% immune to the pacing problems that Homestuck itself suffered from.

That being said, the brief portion at the start of the game where there AREN'T a lot of characters around suffers from the same slow pacing as Act 1. Maybe even worse since not much is happening.

Don't worry about difficulty. Most puzzles can eventually be solved by just talking to everyone about everything, and the one section with deeper puzzles (the trial) has a hint button that starts vague but will hand you the answer if you hit it enough times. There's no other skill-based minigames (one got removed and if it gets readded it'll probably be skippable) so anyone should be able to beat this game.

The game is longer than Act 1. Took me about 13 hours to complete (with moderate reloading to explore other options), compared to 8 on the first game. For replay value, there's a lot of hidden achievements based on the multiple ways of solving certain puzzles, on preserving certain items for the whole run, etc. In fact you'd need several full playthroughs to get all acheivements since some are mutually exclusive. But since you can't fast forward dialog I have a hard time imagining myself doing more than just a second playthrough (not counting reloads just before a part I want to retry).

Some people on the forums complained about bugs and softlocks, but I didn't see a single one in my play experience.

Overall, anyone who liked Homestuck, or even liked parts of Homestuck, will probably love this game. And Act 2 is better than Act 1. But I'd still suggest playing Act 1 before Act 2.

review_text: Great game, dated but fun none the less. If you enjoy older arpg games and don't mind some ps2 graphics this is a good buy. The game also appeals to fans of mmo games as the story centers around an mmorpg. I'd suggest the game if you found the idea of shows such as sword art online interesting, but were let down by the lack of writing quality. .Hack in a way feels to me like what SAO should have been. However, if a high amount of cutscenes, extreme levels of jank, and a healthy dose of mid 2000's anime angst sound like turn offs, .Hack might not be for you. Base PSO2 died for this hollow husk of an MMO. Anything New Genesis has done Base PSO2 had done better, the only good thing New Genesis did was make force better and made the fremium currency more available.
As a PSO2 fan I am deeply crushed that, that masterpiece of an MMO was killed for a game that acts more like a mobile gatcha game or a screenshot simulator.

Edit: I'd like to add more to how New Genesis is such a husk of the game it killed, the live performances for starters Nadereh, will never beat Quna in her current iteration. Maybe Quna's ep4 songs were spammed a little too much but even then the spectacle of them were so much greater then hearing the "song of mourning" or the battle song, When Quna came back in base PSO2 for a special event due to the PlayStation players getting a hold of the game was the most people and most community traffic talking that I've seen before and after a live performance since before New genesis released. The amount of "I missed this"'s that i saw.
And dont get me started on the ARKS festival people, the community singing in chat to "We're ARKS and Rare drop koi koi" almost brought a tear to my eye, then when its all over seeing those same players in NGS just sitting and waiting during a Nadereh concert to end so they can get their concert boost and leave.

Instead of two anime's that base PSO2 had with PSO2: Episode Oracle and PSO2COMI, we get what? A VTuber from IDOLA (IDOLA another thing that just died thanks to NGS) that you can tell shes trying her heart out but feels like she's getting not enough support from SEGA or the Phantasy Star team.

Everything in NGS runs off this weird battle power system, instead of how it was in base, oh a emergency quest is up and you just started playing the game? thats fine join the level bracket that you can join. Not in NGS you have to be the minimum battle power level requirement or else you cant play, and if you can play your reward is a choice of three EQs of a mining rig defense, fighting a bigger version of an enemy you've already beaten a handful of times while pse burst farming or maybe if it came around the mediocre dark falz fight, that is the closest you'll get to feeling like you're still playing pso and not a genshin ripoff.
Yet base PSO2 had all these special eqs over the years that they gave us, if you didn't like the one that was currently up, thats fine, im sure that the Yamato fight, or Magatsu fight will be back again sooner or later or an EXP EQ, or an equipment farming one, or an armada of annihilation just to name a few, and ANYONE could participate in those you didnt have this thing of playing with a friend and seeing an EQ pop up and just shrugging going "sorry you aren't the power level."

I recently started playing Phantasy Star Online Blue Burst for the first time, a Dreamcast game and while rough around the edges to someone who got so used to the qol stuff we got in more modern games, the game feels plays and still looks like pso.
I can't really say that about NGS, the stuff that looks the most PSO are the people still using the old faces on their characters.

I feel like you have to gaslight yourself into liking new genesis, you best hope to liking this game is that, or never have played or seen anything else of Phantasy Star before you played this.The best way to play this game is to not play it and just wait for the catch up events or a quest that just gives 20 million exp to come up which will give you literally everything you need to do whatever you want in here.
Which just invalidates any reason to grind, why should we spend hours grinding for the new gear if in a month a catch up event shows up giving gear of the same rarity that's slightly worse then the gear you worked for?

Combat is nothing but a glorified hit the red button sim, the classes don't feel nearly as special as they did in base, I really hope i never see Hero, Luster, Phantom, or Luster added to NGS as I don't think I can handle seeing those classes gutted like the others were.
And I havent felt remotely attached to my gear or any of the characters besides my own.
Most of my Phantasy Star Online 2 time was on xbox having an absolute blast doing everything offered, going to the in game casino or decorating my room, and hanging out in our alliance quarters.Seeing the decorations in the main lobby, shopping plaza and the cafe during events was also really nice.
My time on this game on steam, has been mindbogglingly boring doing the NGS stuff and unbelievably saddning walking around the graveyard that is base PSO2.

If this was a review on Phantasy Star Online 2? 10/10 game it made me fall in love with gaming again.

But this is Phantasy Star Online 2 New Genesis, we are talking about and i couldnt give it higher then maybe a 3/10. This game perfectly replicates why modern gaming has become so bleak.

review_text:
Star Trek Online is something you can enjoy, but you should also consider its value.

As a fan of the Star Trek universe, you're guaranteed to find something you like here.

The possibilities are there, but not accessible to everyone.

There are tons of starships from all over the galaxy, a large number of story missions with excellent voice acting, and a wide variety of customization options for your captain, bridge officers, and ship.

On top of that, there are PvE and PvP events, seasonal events, fleets with bases, different factions, and much more.

So basically, it's a complete package for all Trekkies.

However, we also have to consider the Gorn in the room: 
FOMO, gacha, pay2win, bugs, and slow hotfixes (if they happen at all).

I'm not someone you can just milk, but I've met many players who, without hesitation, shell out a hundred euros for a ship bundle just to get a single, specific console.

And that's insane, because it's profiting off the backs of people who are ultimately being blackmailed.

It's about maximizing digital "performance," hidden behind a massive paywall.

If it were just about cosmetics, it wouldn't be so problematic in my eyes, but these are items that significantly impact the gameplay experience.

And if enough people have purchased the package, a small patch will often be released to mitigate the "accidentally" overpowered item... 
What a surprise!

The rabbit hole you can climb here is deep if you're looking for optimizing your experience.

Very, very deep.

I mean - watch some videos about top tier builds.

And now, after 15 years of STO, I have to say that the still clunky interface, the truly awful character animations, the disproportionately expensive items in the shop, the terrible communication from the developers (last Steam post from April 25, 2017), the bugs that have persisted for years, the pay-to-win mechanics, and much more,
show how little respect they really have for the fan and player community.

/peace

Fairly short game that some have called a Metroidvania. It feels like more of a puzzler at the beginning, but then you get equipment that can cheese bosses. As I am pretty low skill level, this was nice. Due to the low hp of your character, it seems intended that your repeatedly die and retry.

Scaling: The game starts out quite hard, but then gets relatively easy. The hp scaling of enemies is too flat. While you can still die from a single enemy, the regular enemy battles are still pretty quick. 

Weapons/Spells: I like the variety. There's a multitude of ways you can get through the game after you've run the past the first area. However, there are significant issues the speed variation in the weapons make many weapons next to useless unless you really like handicapping yourself to hone your skills. The enemy reactions make many slower weapons unusable.  While it's intended that you use specific weapons/spells for different areas of the game, you can eventually cheese through with 3 or 4 after the first half of the game, especially if you pick ranged weapons. 

Bosses: I do like most of the bosses, and definitely died the first try on most phases, but felt some satisfaction in getting the timing down. It's weird that they have the order of the items from the bosses that they do. 

It definitely could have done with more balancing, but was still worth playing.
