Really fun game, and thankfully there's a bit more to do now since launch, when there was practically nothing to do after completing the story at the time.

Some pros and cons...

Pros:

- Looks great, and the gameplay is really fun, the combat feels great and smooth(To me personally as a Jet Boots user at least!) Getting those perfect dodges and parries feel really satisfying, and just soaring through the air while kicking butt is oh so fun!

- Good character customization, lots of cosmetics to get, both through drops, and scratches(gacha. Both paid and free, more about this in cons :v)
It's fun seeing what people come up with for their designs, and how some accessories get used in unintended, but creative ways(ie. using visors as chestplates, tails as hair etc.. Totally didn't do that myself, nope!... not at all!...) The game has a Lookbook system, where you can register your look for others to see, and for you to see their looks. It's not updated automatically, so you can register one look while using the other still.

- Surprisingly easy to socialize with others in the hub, and getting groups going. I say that cause personally I do have issues with social anxiety and whatnot. I guess it's easier to talk to fellow degenerates :v
There's a lot of nice people in this game. There's those that love phashion, RP'ers, and those who just likes playing and punching things. 

- Creative spaces! This new feature has some great potential. Basically, Creative Space is your own little playground. You can build obstacle courses, wacky statues, gardens, houses, clubs, pixel art... If you can think it, you can prooooobably make it. There's some incredibly talented builders in this game, and seeing what they've made is just stunning! So much creativity!

cons:

- Back to the topic of [b] scratches[/b] (gacha)! The game loooves it's scratches, and for most of these you need AC(ARKS Cash - Premium currency). These scratches give you anything from clothing, accessories, hair, CAST parts, color change passes, augment aid's etc... The game gets new scratches more than it does actual story content, which is a minus in a way. Drip's nice, but you know... 
There is a daily free scratch poll, as well as an SG scratch poll (SG is a currency you can earn through playing the game). The free and SG scratch polls have been updated with new stuff through updates, so some of the things in it are actually nice now. 

- The game is not very new-player friendly still, with the confusing UI layout, menus, hotbars, etc... Granted, NGS is a lot easier for newcomers compared to base PSO2 thanks to the dumbing down of certain aspects, such as having to time your attacks, MAG feeding, etc.

Also...

Please SEGA, give us new concerts! Nadereh is great, but we need moar! Concerts are fun, and a great way to get together! The interactive concerts in base were so much fun! Please SEGA QuQ

review_text:
The .hack series has been one of my favorite series since childhood. Although the anime and movies aren't the greatest there has always been something about the games that have kept me coming back. The original .hack IMOQ series unfortunately doesn't stand the test of time so I understand why G.U. was remade first but I still wish they would port that series to Steam just to have the joy of grinding through it again.

As for Last Recode I think they did a great job making this game true to the original while also providing easier ways for new players to enter the series via things like cheat mode to have a decent amount of money and items to start your playthrough. Although Mass Effect is the first series that comes to mind for most people when you think about a playable save being ported game to game I always think of .hack first and it was just such a fun and innovative concept when playing through the series back in the day that continues with Last Recode.

If there is one recommendation I could make for people buying the game is to not use cheat mode unless you feel like you aren't good at these type of games. It is VERY easy to over level everything in this game and you can often clear content 4+ levels higher than your actual level to expedite the process. Between "The World" that you spend your time in, CrimsonVS, the party system, or just the fun and enjoyable story I think this will continue to remain one of my favorite games of all time and I would highly recommend this game to anyone!

Id love to recommend this game almost purely on the basis that Im a HUGE Starship Troopers fan since I was like 14.

The game for the most part is quite fun, gunplay feels good albeit somewhat floaty, the building aspect is also a nice addition. 
However the game starts to fall flat fairly quickly when you come to realise the servers the game utilises simply cannot handle the amount of enemies it spawns in. 

By round 4-5 of a horde game you will start to notice teleporting enemies and friendlies, either delays in shot registry or no registry at all and any sort of movement ability stutters so badly its hard to tell where you landed. (Admittedly my internet is not at all fast, I have 0 issues with other games like this e.g. Helldivers or LFD2 hordes so the issue seems to lie predominately in this game. Also my ping is usually never above 40 at max, commonly sits around 15-20)

Personal suggestion would be to maybe lower the render distance of bug bodies after they've been killed or perhaps limit/negate the amount of bodies outside of a certain render distance, could help reduce the server loads somewhat but otherwise the game starts to become unplayable.

review_text:
This is a tricky one. As a Jet Set Radio Future obsessive, and later, Jet Set Radio, (the two left-field rollerblading, spraying, future-grinding games that Bomb Rush Cyberfunk is a direct homage to), I put off playing this for a bit. The possibility of disappointment was too great! But turns out this is a super fun game that kept me plugged in, and not just because of mis-placed nostalgia. That said, it has a high bar to live up to, and I don't think it quite clears it.

The start of this game is a goddamn slog. The game *does* have fun characters, but they sure aren't around at the start. The starting areas are drab and the cut-scenes are SLOW. The music hadn't grown on me at this stage, and I was pretty mad that they didn't just get 2 Mello (absolutely jammin' JSR-style music producer) to do the whole soundtrack. And skateboards? This is a goofy game, and having "cool" skateboards and bikes (with no futuristic add-ons) is jarring. For the first couple of hours I was having a pretty grumpy - but not terrible - time. I was sure that it was going to be nostalgia that pulled me through.

Then, not too far in, the game opened up, I'm unlocking tags, new areas, and hooking together combos like nobody's business. There are improvements in this game! The tag system is great. The flip-phone map and camera system is GENIUS. The cut-scenes are still boring, but you get to meet a claustrophobic masochist, who is always in tight spaces having a terribly good time. The police enemies are annoying (on brand for JSR). The main thing is that the flow is gooooood. I maintain that some of the level design is very poor, with some unlockables requiring specific backtracking or annoying hidden access points, but if you find yourself going for the unlockables and achievements that require combos, you will be in for a treat as you start to flow through the large levels. The soundtrack grew on me, and I have the soundtrack LP on order...

Overall, an incredible achievement. The team put this together with a lot of love, and without a big budget. Nailing the look, getting the soundtrack together, the tags, the amount of characters... an absolute lifetime achievement. It's not perfect, but I'll be damned if I would give this a thumbs down - if only because I want Bomb Rush Cyberfunk Future so badly! Get this, and get the Jet Set Radio remaster, and fall in love with a absolutely unique vibe.

Reviewing this after finishing the game. One of the best stealth experiences that initially reminded me of the Commandos games with the enemy view-cones, movement patterns, reaction and alert systems, but this game stands on its own. Mimimi's execution is top-notch, the voice acting is amazing in Japanese (which I played in), the story is gripping - humor, sadness, happiness, anger, everything a story should have! 

I'm a trial-and-error player and I found the gameplay is addictive. I spent a lot of time (over 2 hours per level) solving tactical puzzles and not once was I frustrated or felt like giving up because the combinations in which to approach solutions with the characters is up to the player's imagination.

I'm not the type of gamer who generally finishes all his games, but this game got me hooked right till the very end and I highly recommend Shadow Tactics even if you are new to this genre.

p.s. That kuma is amazing!

I'm eagerly waiting for the Mimimi's next game "Shadow Gambit" - The demo was amazing!

The game itself feels very floaty, slow, arcadey with huge AUDIOVISUAL indicators for enemy attacks. 

I don't recommend.

review_text:
Game is good, story is interesting so far (few missions in), feels like a semi-fresh start for the game series. Runs well, polished (no bugs or connection issues out of the gate), and combat is that of a third-person character action game, with soft-roles you would see in any other MMO-like game. Menus are a tad on the heavy side, and Campaign has two difficulties.

For people interested; look up Havian on YouTube and look at his impressions video. If you bought into the game for the Advanced Access, either you were impressed by the Open Beta to buy in or you were already a fan.

For cosmetics, the co-op quests and boss raids have a chance to drop one of several cosmetics (as in, theres a handful per specific quest/raid) upon completion. There are also cosmetics in campaign missions (they look like the exact same ones in the cash shop so maybe reskins?) that give a bit more replay-ability. You can permanently upgrade characters the more you use them or by spending in-game earned currency on memories. There IS a lot here on display and with a roadmap planned for the next bit, for people invested it will be worth it. My wife says the only gripe in the first few missions is "we don't know whats going on" but believes more story beats will hit when we clear more.

Yes there is a cash slop shop, and it looks like every 30 days, if you run the course of the single-track battle pass, you get enough tickets to get a single set of cosmetics. There is NO gatcha to this. I would even say play the campaign and get all of the cosmetics to show off.
I am a slut for SAO so shelling out enough for me and my wife to get all the cosmetics out of the gate is par for the course, but I ABSOLUTELY understand that those more conscious with their funds will get more value spending elsewhere on a game they enjoy.

TL;DR
If you are a SAO fan, it will be fun.

review_text:
Good MMO in a sea of shite, it's a Whale's paradise but still very F2P friendly. 

Star Trek Online is made with love and passion from the developers, they've got the original actors from the TV shows to reprise their roles and voice act in well written story. There are plenty of story arc for the players to play through and explore more of the Star Trek universe. Most of them are written very well and kept interesting enough to hold the players' attention at all times. 

You gotta love this game's music, the main character selection screen has got the BEST background music ever. I have looped the game in the background over the years just for the music. 

The graphics has not aged well, you can see that most evidently on ground where the textures are disgustingly bad to the human eye. However, an advantage of low resolution texture is the extreme fast loading times between areas. It takes no more than 30 seconds for me to load from one area to the next.

Now, combat in this game is unlike anything you've played. Space combat where you pilot your starship is one of the best PvE combat system in anything similar. you can move in a 3D environment (3 axies XYZ) and position your ship for a broadside barrage of lasers. Your starship can be further customised with different weapons and loadouts to varied styles. It's glorious, Beam Boats to Cannon Volleys and Torpedoes build.

Now for what you have waited for. Is the game P2W?

Yes. Like all MMOs, STO has been alive for 14 years. You don't have a MMO running for 14 years without massive player's whaling. Most of the best DPS consoles and traits(captain and ship) in the game are obtained from Lockboxes(Lootbox) or from Zen Store ships.

Fortunately for you F2Ps, it is not all lost. You can reach very competitive DPS numbers by just spending time in the game and reaching Lvl 50 to unlock the Reputation system which has BiS gear for free. Some of the story mission also award you with very good end game scalable gear. Every story basically give enough for 1 level up each time, so you can reach max level (65) in a few days if you grind long.

This game is still good, you're be joining a friendly and knowledgeable community. Besides, this is the ONLY good Star Trek game out there.

Playing this since 2015 - started on JP base game... and since then some aspects which making me sick didn't changed at all.

First con is a graphics. It became better since then but still simplified pastgen one with ugly poligonized player models.

Second con is an annoying, stressfull and not relaxing combat system with neverending incoming attacks and tight defence timings (Slayer class step-dodge I-frame window for example is only 0.34 seconds), And it became even worse with recent updates because new bosses got overlapped attacks with uncertain hitboxes and timings.

Next con is also about combat system - a targeting marker which sticking to different spots on an enemy... yet you can play in fully targetless mode but without hitting it you'll never get good results. And this targeting maker's behaviour is just awful because it tend to jump between these spots like a crazy.

Another con of this game is a damn camera which didn't changed at all since from a very beginning. It have only 5 zoom levels and can't be put away from a character enough for a comfortable MMO gameplay experience (like World of Warcraft released about same time for example).
Moreover during combat it's feeling free to zoom in and out whenever IT wishes to and not a player...

review_text:
"Don't mind me, just disposing of a body."

This game is a ton of fun with impossible amounts of enemies around forcing you to employ stealth mechanics and tactics and also sniping skills. Crucial weapon unlocks are tied to challenges which ensure you must play each level at least twice and each level is a huge open map with a half dozen missions.

That said the draw backs of the game mostly come from the limits of the AI. Patrolling guards are so regular you can time your movements to the second, getting spotted is tied to proximity to a hit box rather than line of sight of the NPC's face, and some sounds are easily heard while others sound just for the player. Alarms and explosions are not reacted to more than a few hundred meters out even if the call goes out over the radio, and NPCs will never leave their AO even if they see you sniping from a tower. And once the alarm goes out the guard's ability to detect your sniping spot becomes superhuman. Once you know the exploits you can pull off impossible stealth missions, knifing guards and hiding their bodies in the bushes IN PLAIN SIGHT.

Other potential downsides are the graphics are good enough this game won't work on an ordinary PC, you'll need a gaming PC or console. Also it gets glitchy sometimes with weird lag spikes but nothing major.

What I'd recommend for the game is instead of a barebones multiplayer they do a PvPvE match where first man to get the bounty target's dog tags wins.

review_text:
EHM has really evolved since the old days. I last played it in the early-mid 2000s and was only marginally impressed. At the time my impression was "ok, this is nice but not what I'm looking for."

Fast forward some 15 or so years: WOW - the game is like night and day different! Loads of fun and very realistic. Taking it to the next level by bringing in Sega was a very smart move. Bringing more of the Football Manager element that allows for multi-player and really solid tactical customization right down to the individual player level brings about a level of hockey not seen elsewhere on the market. I like the fact that the styles of play can be customized to simulate anything from today's more "sanitized" NHL to the classic "old-time" hockey of the 70s, 80s and early 90s when brawls were common. By increasing player aggressiveness and selecting "encourage" as the fighting selection, I have seen some games that much more closely resembled the rough and tumble, bump and shove, drop the gloves hockey I grew up with 40-50 years ago. That level of customization - plus all the great mods that are available for rosters, logos, face packs, etc., make this the must-have hockey game for any serious PC sports gamer.

I'd love it if more classic seasons become available via the community. It would be a blast to play the Big Badd Bruins of the early 70s or the French Connection Habs of the late 70s or the Broad Street Bullies or Gretzky's high-flying Oilers. This game sets up perfectly for these kinds  of mods.

review_text:
This is my favorite game in the series tied with Arkham Origins.

It feels like everything that was great about the first game was improved on and refined to perfection, and some of the rougher bits were rounded out.

The world is much bigger than the first game, and it's absolutely full of great missions, including both side missions AND main story missions. It feels like this game has just the right scale for an open world. Big enough to not get boring, but small enough to not feel daunting or overwhelming. Because of this, the game feels alive, and like you can find a completely unique interaction anywhere.

The character writing is at some of its best in the whole franchise. Some of the weird characterization bits from the previous game have been whittled down by a LOT! The stakes are much bigger than the previous game, and the characters, although they're still recognizable to their comic and animated counterparts, feel much more realistic and believable than the last game.

This game has some of the best art direction I've ever seen from this series. With notes of Tim Burton's influence, the architecture of the city feels exactly like how I'd picture my ideal version of Gotham City. I absolutely love the graphics in this game. The character designs are also FANTASTIC.

The story and gameplay is much more dynamic than the last game. The combat flows fantastically, and there's a learning curve that makes it really fun to keep on coming back to. You switch between playing as multiple characters throughout the game, which keeps things fresh.

Overall, I would say that this game is ABSOLUTELY worth playing and has nearly zero flaws whatsoever.

review_text:
TL;DR.
If Dark Souls and Destiny 2 merged in the best possible way — you’d get Witchfire.
Incredible gunfeel, moody atmosphere, and endless replayability. Worth every cent.

 Gameplay

The shooting feels phenomenal — easily on Destiny 2’s level of precision and impact. Every weapon hits hard, and just firing feels satisfying.
Each gun comes with unique perks and upgrades, keeping combat fresh. The balance is perfect: no overpowered builds, no useless ones — you’re always just slightly weaker, which makes fights intense and strategic.

It combines Destiny’s silky-smooth gunplay with Dark Souls’ deliberate rhythm and risk–reward feeling. The result? Combat that’s both thoughtful and thrilling.

 Balance & Challenge

Witchfire keeps you alert at all times. You can’t just rush through — timing, movement, and cooldowns actually matter.
Bosses hit hard but fair, rewarding focus and adaptability. The game punishes carelessness but never feels unfair — it’s always your fault, and that’s what makes it fun.

 Visual Design

Absolutely stunning art direction. Even the base area looks beautiful — you just want to stop and take it in. Every environment feels handcrafted, detailed, and alive. The atmosphere is dark and oppressive, but not horror — just the right amount of tension.

Exploring

Exploration is genuinely rewarding.
Hidden doors, events, minibosses, puzzles, and those little glowing fireflies leading to loot — there’s always something new to find. The game constantly rewards curiosity and careful observation.

 Sound Design

The sound work is exceptional.
You can pinpoint enemies by footsteps, locate secrets through distant whispers, and feel the tension build through ambient noise.
Play with good headphones — it’s immersive on another level.

 Verdict

Witchfire blends Destiny 2’s perfect gunfeel with Dark Souls’ challenge and atmosphere.
Every system — shooting, balance, exploration, sound — fits together flawlessly.

As an SAO fan, I was lucky to get to try the game early in the Closed Beta Test, and from that I immediately knew that I wanted this game badly. Fast forward to now, I would say that this game did not disappoint me, despite its quirks. The character rigging is weird during cutscenes, blocking and dodging can be hard due to the delay and stuff, the map doesn't show the edge of the map makes exploration a tad bit more annoying, the way you start at level 1 on every coop game can get tiring, etc. It's definitely nowhere near perfect, but in a way, that's the charm of SAO games. It basically hits all the marks I expect from an SAO game.

With that being said, this game is definitely not for everyone. If you're one of the people who tells people to buy Grandblue Fantasy Relink instead, you're kinda missing the point of this game. We play and like it because it's SAO, and to me, this is one of the better games in this IP. It kinda has the vibes of Fatal Bullet, but with SAO elements and uncapped fps. If you're not into SAO or you only just knew about SAO, I wouldn't really recommend this game especially at these prices, and you're probably be better off buying that other game or play earlier SAO games to familiarize yourself with SAO games as I personally think this isn't the best game to start the journey. I might be biased, but that's kinda the whole point with games based off of IPs.

Updating after playing for 30 more hours.
If I could describe PSO2, It's a game that took everything wrong with black desert and everything wrong with genshin impact and put them together, in a game which forgot its origins and its identity, have no proper content and only rely on thirsty anime fans and collaborations to make a buck.

PROS:
-the combat is quite fun and quite smooth, action packed
-character customization is among the bests
-free housing right from the start and massive customization of housing
-able to skip any cutscene (this is generally a good thing to have even when the story is not bad; foreshadowing)

CONS
-there is no content; yeah the fighting is fun, but everything will always die too fast; there is no proper raids or hard enemies; no dungeons, no raids, no ever reason to interact and play with other people; it's an MMO that play as a singleplayer where you gather around to chat only to show off your characters, your houses or to do ERP (lots of NSFW stuff in common areas)
--to add to it, the game throw experience at you like crazy. I reached level cap within 20 hours. This would be great, if there was anything to do at level cap.
-the story is trash, there were very few moments where the dialogues made any sense or where I felt attached or invested in what was going on; you most of the time jump from one area to the other and suddenly become the local hero, without interacting more than maybe 5 main quests per area. I suppose on one side of the coin, it's good that there's no "filler", but the quality is so poor it might as well be considered filler all of it.
-aina
-items, clothes, inventory are generally extremely confusing, where sometimes wearing a piece of clothes will change your entire bone structure without proper indicators of that being the case before hand
-ui and navigation is awful
-camera is awful
-keybinds and what is allowed to rebind is awful
-the game flood your 100 slot inventory with roughly 5 different items everytime you kill an enemy so after half a minute of playing you will find yourself struggling with the UI and struggling to manage your inventory which will already be full, when you won't really know how the inventory works or which items are useful and which not, because you launched the game for the first time 10 minutes ago;
-lack of proper chat filters or customization means if you want to read what your party members are saying, then you are also forced to read what the NPC party members are saying, and they just keep.on.talking.on.and.on.and.on. Nonstop.
-the only reason I managed to play as much is because I am not kidding in the pros in saying the combat is fun, but after you reach the level cap and endgame and there is no endgame other than doing houses and "afk in limsa lominsa" then it's just disappointing.
-had forgot to mention the absurd amount of gachas and premium and transactions within the game;


Original review and indepth about UI, keybinds and camera:
The UI, camera and control schemes are a crime against videogames.
Control scheme is meh, but with the biggest offender being the most obtuse re-bindable settings. ALT is forced to be an "emote wheel", and you have no way of changing it. CTRL also cannot be rebinded. Hotbar buttons are also not rebindable and stuck on being numbers 1 til 9, meaning anything beyond 5 is hard to reach and never used without being extremely awkward during battles. 
The UI has ZERO customization, except of "make it bigger". And I don't mean "make this element bigger, this one smaller", no, just make everything big, or make everything small. No change in opacity, no change in location, no change in what is even active and what not on screen, no change in what is where.
Plenty of games do this, but extremely rare to have MMO's not allowing this. And you know, it wouldn't be too bad, if only the UI elements were designed with user experience in mind. Instead, you get popups, tutorials, character dialogues, everything and anything, taking the center of the screen, where all the action is happening, mid fight, and because this game also has a 1990 camera controls of course the UI will be covering 90% of the enemy. Unless you use the free camera, in which case you will miss 90% of the attacks. Unless you use the "camera on shoulder", which look like a 2006 game where 1/3 of the screen is the character, the FOV is awful, and you have no idea of what is going on to your left, to your right, to your feet, to your back, no, you can only see the front.

And all of these awful choices would have been a super minor problem if ONLY they had customization for UI, controls, and a proper camera.
They are so bad, that the aggressive monetization and gachas and the 20 lotteries you are spammed with the moment you finish the prologue before being able to breathe once and the ADS you see during loading screens, are NOTHING compared to the issues with controls camera and UI.

The only positives I have reached and experienced are character customization (despite the awful menus and ambiguity of the equipments) and movement being smooth and satisfying for it being an MMO.

review_text:
This game has great vibes, fantastic lore, and a beautiful aesthetic. The team that put this together should be proud of their work. My review here is based entirely upon my own game preferences and should not reflect negatively on their work.

Witchfire is very Dark Souls-esque in its gameplay and level of basic difficulty. You are given a basic tutorial and thrown into the deep end, with enemies that are too strong for you, ready to fight even in the prologue. You are left to find your own way through your various expeditions, with no guarantee of a safe path to your destinations, and no checkpoints to pick you back up where you croak (and you will croak).

Some people find that game style fun. If you're one of them, I actually would recommend giving this game a try. There's a neat story brewing wrapped up in a very well-realised world that offers a lot of exploration and a steep survival challenge.

I play games to relax and I don't find that particular style of play relaxing. If you're in that same boat, you probably won't enjoy this one.

review_text:
I've only just scratched the surface of what this game has to offer, but I can give it a thumbs up reccomendation without hesitation or doubt already.

What an experience!

Comparing it to Left 4 Dead or Back 4 Blood are not comparisons without merit, but being VR, the immersion is brought to a whole new level.
And the VR aspect is done extraordinarily well, and in a fashion that will suit just about every VR user!

For example, when it comes to motion, you can use teleport movement ala Half Life Alyx, or you can use regular movement via the toggles. Both have their drawbacks and positives, both suit different players.

The firearm handling is fantastic for a game like this, and again, is designed to suit all players.
You can use your off hand to steady a weapon, even one handed weapons such as pistols, or duel wield pistols, or use consumables ect.
Weapons have weight, recoil is noticeable and reloading has been handled perfectly. There are two settings, manual and easy.
Easy is where, to reload you just bring bring your firearm to the ammo on your rig and bam, magically reload your weapon - in the same vein as a lot of wave shooters.
Or you can manually reload your firearm - eject the magazine, push in a new one, rack the slide ect. As a bonus for taking the harder route and extra steps of manual, you gain a 35% damage increase to balance it out against easy reloading, which is just fantastic and opens the game to everyone.
Again, with weapon storage, you can choose to have holsters like in Saints and Sinners, or you can go for a traditional gaming weapon select wheel.

TLDR: The devs have really taken the time to make After the Fall as approachable as possible for every type of VR gamer, whether they come from Pavlov, Half-Life, Saints and Sinners or obscure wave defence games.
Firearms are fun to use, they have weight, oomph, recoil and can be operated realistically or not.

Graphics are pretty nice! If it was a PC title, not so much, but in VR they look fantastic and are very atmospheric. 

There are a large number of unlocks, a hub area, you can play solo with bots or group up with friends or strangers to tackle different difficulties or even game modes.

I don't (yet) have the playtime to declare this a must play title for VR gamers, but I'm close to doing so.

review_text:
I wish there was a mixed option.

This was an enjoyable experience, the problem is value for money.

This game is about 15 hours long on a first playthrough if you're competent at survival horror games.

The game is not particularly scary. There's a couple of flashing image + audio jumpscares, but otherwise you're fighting spaghetti people for most of the game. 

There isn't a lot of enemy variety. If we don't count variants of the same enemy, there's 3 enemy types in the game, and 5 boss types in the game.

The charged shot mechanic is fun to play with, and the gunplay is satisfying. Just the starting pistol feels like a pocket railgun which is great. But the movement is clunky, which is on purpose so you can't avoid damage easily, and there's no additional mechanics to the combat gameplay loop. Shoot enemy, throw explosive at enemy, shoot explosive barrel next to enemy. That's it.

The merging mechanic is easy to ignore since any merging enemy can be stunned out of merging with a charged headshot. Burning bodies is not a viable strategy most of the time because of the limited ammo on your personal flamer, and the fact having flamer ammo on you takes inventory space when you have such limited inventory.

There's melee buttons but I don't think you're meant to use them. Outside of when you're in NG+ or late in your first playthrough, if you've figured out enemy health breakpoints there's -sometimes- you can use it safely, but most of the time the melee button might as well not exist.

No dodge, no parry, no Stasis, no Kinesis, nothing. Its a survival horror game from the mid 2010s. It does nothing particularly new.

And I know what some people are going to say. If you give the player more ways to fight back you make the game less scary. Taking away player agency, player options, and making the player feel weak is how you build tension and make a good horror game.

I'd agree with you if I wasn't 1-shotting every basic enemy with the starting handgun once I fully upgraded its firepower.

I'd agree with you if I wasn't 2-shotting wall crawlers, which ambush you in large numbers and from odd angles and are clearly meant to be an actual scary enemy with it too.

The game doesn't give you the power fantasy but it doesn't do enough to be scary either.

And more frustrating than all of that, is that it leaves too many questions unanswered to instead focus on a personal drama storyline. All the parts of the game that are interesting to me, are left vague. Who/what are the collective? Who made them? Who made the tech we're using? How does the time travel work? What started the change?

We can only speculate with vague snipets of information left on notes and audio logs. There is no concrete evidence, which means the game's biggest most interesting misteries never go answered.

Buy it for half price.

review_text:
During the installation process, along with the DirectX libraries, another program will be installed called AMD Dual-Core Optimizer which was meant to improve the performance on systems that run Windows XP and use old AMD Dual-Core CPUs.

On PCs that run Windows Vista and later and/or an Intel CPU, you won't need that program because it will impact the performance and cause other issues.

Unfortunately when you launch the game for the first time you don't get the choice to decline the installation of AMD Dual-Core Optimizer (that's why I left a negative review).
In order to stop that program from being installed, do as follows:

If the program is already installed, you should uninstall it. Go to "Programs and Features", select "AMD Dual-Core Optimizer" and click "Uninstall" (perhaps it will take a while, do not cancel the process and wait); afterwords, reboot the PC.

1) Go to the installation folder of the game (right click on the game title -> properties -> local files tab -> browse local files)
2) Open "installscript.vdf" (right click -> open with -> use Notepad)
3) Scroll down until you see the word "AMD", followed by a bunch of code between the two perpendicular { and } brackets; delete that portion of code, beginning from the word "AMD" to the last perpendicular bracket (note that you must leave the brackets on the left side and everything else)
4) Save the file. Make sure you didn't delete anything that has to do with DXSetup, VCRedist_x86 and DotNetFx35
5) When you're done, go to the "Setup" folder and delete "amd_dc_opt.exe" (this is an optional step, just to be safe)

If you've done everything correctly, when you launch the game the installation of AMD Dual-Core Optimizer won't start.

REMEMBER TO NOT VERIFY THE INTEGRITY OF GAME FILES, OTHERWISE YOU MUST REPEAT THE PROCEDURE

Old Genesis enemy design is great, and New Genesis design is great too dont get me wrong, but my first reaction to the new Starless enemy is "Ahh, it's another pallete swap of that one enemy since launch, isn't it?". review_text:
World of Goo is a game that has followed me through my entire life. I first played it on Wiiware and fell in love with it immediately. This is the debut game from publisher 2D Boy, (now known as the Tomorrow Corporation) and despite it's rough edges is a wonderful example of the creativity of the puzzle game genre. In this game, you are tasked with navigating a group of goo balls to a pipe, usually on the other side of the level. You can tether the goo balls to each other to create a tower to the pipe which allows the stray goo to exit. As the game goes on you'll meet new varieties of goo that create new and interesting puzzles. The game is a perfect length, at four chapters and an epilogue. It's story is short and straight to the point. I look back fondly on key parts of the story, especially chapter four. It goes in a direction visually and in it's puzzles that is wildly unique and unexpected. All throughout the game Kyle Gabler's compositions complement the interesting world and storytelling, though I wish there were a few more tracks. The OST is a good length, at 27 pieces, but several levels reuse the same tracks and it'd be fun if this didn't have to be the case. On top of this some of the tracks feel a little unpolished, but this can be overlooked considering the conditions the game was developed under. 2D Boy, especially at the game's release in 2008, was a very small indie team. I still think the music is beautiful, even nostalgia aside. I recommend tracks like "Are You Coming Home, Love MOM," "Ode To The Bridge Builder," "The Goo Filled Hills," and "Tumbler" to see the wide range of styles this game covers. The soundtrack is free on Steam and easily accessible on youtube, Kyle Gabler's blog, and other platforms :)
Overall, World of Goo is an excellent puzzle game, an excellent indie game, and well worth it's low price tag. Please give this game a chance if you somehow haven't in the last decade.

review_text:
Scorn is probably going to be a pretty hard game to recommend for most people, because the thing it struggles the most with is actually being, yenno, a [i]videogame[/i]. It kind of meanders between being an environmental puzzle game, and a survival horror - but with such scant gameplay, it's often even labelled a walking simulator. Although at least in those moments of downtime, the horror dressing still poses a persistent sense of tension and threat.

But with Scorn, if you get it then you GET it. It's primarily going to appeal to the kinds of people who have taken one look at its presentation - the promotional art, screenshots, videos, and so on - and decided that they [i]need[/i] to experience this, no matter what form it takes. Unlike the gameplay, which can leave much to be desired, it completely delivers elsewhere in its style and atmosphere. Scorn is absolutely a triumph of artistic direction and execution.

A fairly short experience, my playtime here covered two somewhat leisurely playthroughs. If you're into more artsy gameplay experiences, and are keen on the idea of some kind of gruesomely interactive artpiece experience (in the style of greats like H.R. Giger or Zdzisław Beksiński), then Scorn is going to be right up your alley. But whilst the puzzles can get you thinking, and the combat encounters can keep you on your toes, those who require a more robust and well-rounded gameplay experience will probably want to give this a miss.

★★★★✰

review_text:
This is a stealth sniping game.
A bit rough around the edges but still a pleasant experience.

The biggest positive this game has is that it is pleasant to interact with.
The visuals are very good and pleasant to look at, the sniper gun play is good.
It is pretty easy to figure out how the bullets will fly, so you can hit the shots with relative ease.
There are usually decent options for vantage points so you can plan your hits out and clear some bases without even raising an alarm.
It is possible to mark every single enemy to get full information about the level and sometimes clear entire bases without anyone noticing that someone is dead (though, that is rare and you usually get an alarm at some point)

The negatives are less severe than the positives, but definitely noticeable.
To put it roughly - the game is a bit buggy, especially when loading a save or an area is involved.
It is very clear that the game works on an area-based loading system, there are some predefined areas that, once you enter enemies spawn, and despawn once you leave.
While it is understandable that there is no need to load things that player is not looking at, it should not be this noticeable.
This is further highlighted by the numerous bugs that I noticed without going out of my way that relate just to this loading mechanism, specifically: electronics breaking in sync when you re-enter an area, marks on electronics just vanishing, broken electronics sometimes working despite being broken, drone not triggering the enemy loading so you can scout ahead an empty field only to see it magically spawn enemies once you get close.
The geometry is also a bit bugged, I could constantly hear the "jumped on metal" sound as NPCs kept on getting stuck.
I also got stuck like 3 times and had to reload.
Scout drone jammers feel really buggy - it is not clear where it will work and it seems that sometimes it mixes up whether it is supposed to be jammed or not (area I know should be okay was heavily jammed, jammed area had no distortion and just broke the drone)
Supposedly there are towers that block it, but I could launch near some just fine or had my drone break without any close, it is just confusing.

There is a slight identity crisis where this game can not decide whether it wants to be a "Sniper Ghost" or "Ghost Warrior".
Longest shot I think I got in this game was around 450m and most of them are at around 200-150m range.
That's fine, but at least I would have liked to see some "snipe important target from a kilometer away and get out" kind of deal.
One mission has a challenge of "complete everything with a knife" which implies it is possible to do so and the level has a completion path like that.
That's not bad per se, but the game kinda markets itself as sniper game so I would expect me to challenge on sniping (like kill targets without entering the compound) or stealth (like every level having a "complete everything without alarm", which, admitted one contract had but I would have wanted to see it on all) instead.

To summarize, this is a very decent game.
There is nothing exceptional about it, and it comes across as somewhat bugged, but the gameplay feels good.
Nice, slow, relaxing experience.

I find this game extremely difficult, I cannot play it for too long in one sitting. Due to my own personal mix of traumas and mental health issues, this game is emotionally taxing to power on through. I am perpetually afraid of making the tinest mistake, I am perpetually filled with dread over what is next to come. It is punishing, too: If you die, it will make it permanently harder to play the game.

It is also an incredible game that I think everyone should give a go at least once. You do not need to have played the first game to understand this. In fact, I would go so far as to specifically recommend that you avoid the first game and any spoilers related to it. Your experience with the game will be better for it. This game makes you care about people by placing you and them under hardship. The game will immerse you through hardship. Without that hardship, it would simply be a game about wandering from place to place in an odd town. Instead, it is a game about survival, about failure, about misery, about the deaths of those in your care, about progress vs tradition, about idealism vs realism, about plague and Utopia.

It's good. But it's very heavy, it's very difficult, it's frustrating, it's harrowing, it's dense, it's gruelling... and that's the point. It is not a pleasant experience, but it is a powerful one. I hate it. It's incredible. Play it. It's good. Extremely good.

review_text:
Lucius is about the son of Satan. He’s come back to take over the world. In order to go concur the world he, for some reason, has to kill off his family. While he’s killing off whoever the family slowly starts getting paranoid as to whos killing everyone. Some have emotional breakdowns and then the police get involved. The lead detective bumbles about and tries to piece it all together. Every once in a while Satan will drop by and give Lucius power ups.
This is one the few games I really really wanted to like. For once you play the ultimate bad guy and there are weird justifications for doing tons of gory bad things. Then you get to read his journal entries and shows the mindset of a terrible person for once. However it doesn’t do much else. The story is so frail that it doesn’t really explain why its a good idea to kill off your family, nor how he was going to go about ruling the world. Think about it. If he kills off his family he’ll be a penniless orphan and will only go on to kill other families. On top of that there is zero time for character development to make the player care about the people who are being killed and much less why they are killed.
Now murdering them all is a mixture of grotesque and unique. This portion of the game is pretty much a stealth puzzle mixture and all the combinations are interesting to figure out. Although some do die in cliché ways, although the setup is always different. This gameplay as a whole isn’t too difficult. It’s a lot like some of the older point and click games where you take everything that isn’t nailed to the floor. After that you explore the house to find the special spot to use it.
Also some of the best power ups that Satan gives you come really late in the game and you won’t be able to use them except maybe once. Like it you eventually get to wipe peoples memory after they catch you doing something bad, which would be hella useful in earlier parts of the game. But it’s only introduced after 3/ 4 ths of the game is complete and since you’ve already killed some 10+ people there are less people in the house to catch you. So it doesn’t really serve a purpose unless you really suck at stealth. Or better yet, you don’t get the ability to conjure fireballs till the second to last level. How awesome would it have been to just go around smokin mofos left and right with this ability? Well guess what? It isn’t happening.
This wasn’t a great game and it wasn’t what I hoped it would be. The graphics are OK, but not great for this generation. The voice acting is sometimes just terrible, or feels like a bad B movie. The characters are sometimes completely cliché, like the only butler in the game is British. On top of all that a lot of the story is just stupid. It basically amount to “go out and kill everyone just because!” and then it doesn’t give you a option not to kill them or give you a better explanation.
So if you do pick it up try to find it cheap. It’s a short experience and there is little replay value. Sure there are two bonus levels, but they’re hard, boring and serve no purpose. Also the story is going to be too bland for some people. Hopefully they’ll make a sequel seeing as they could easily fix things and adjust the story and game mechanics.
4.5/10

review_text:
I've always had a soft spot for the .hack series of anime, especially .hack//SIGN and .hack//Roots. While I don't consider either of them to be amazing, they are conceptually original and it's interesting how they were delivered to complement their video game counterparts. And in the case of .hack//G.U. Last Recode, .hack//Roots is the anime counterpart - I'll refer to them as GU and Roots from here onwards for brevity.

It's hard for me to decide whether to recommend this title or not given my slight bias towards the anime series. So instead, I've decided not to recommend based on the fact that this game hasn't aged well (at all). The graphics and 3D models look very dated; and the action combat is clunky and not very engaging. This doesn't mean it's a bad game, it's just not good by modern standards for a video game - but it's definitely more than just playable as long as you can tolerate the gameplay of older console games. 

You'll be playing as an unnamed main character who plays an MMO game, "The World", and whose in-game character name goes by "Haseo" - it's a "game-within-the-game" concept. You'll have access to in-game mail, forums, news site and the MMO, with which you'll often be switching to and fro as the story progresses - much like a simulation of real-world (but without multiple displays because you're gonna need to logout from the MMO just to read mails, etc!). When you logout of the MMO, you are presented with a desktop screen (a simulation of an operating system) which is used to access said features. The story revolves around mysterious incidents of players (of The World) falling into comatose (in the real life) which is somehow connected to the game.

Despite my not recommending it (I'm really on the fence here), I think there's something that can help you decide more easily. You will be thrown into time 8 months later shortly after you begin playing GU. The anime, Roots, is about what happens during this time gap (as a prologue) and you can watch it to see if you're invested in the storyline - youtube has some dubbed episodes (but might not be a complete collection). A word of caution, however, is that the anime is more philosophical than action-oriented. I've actually rewatched Roots just to recap the earlier story. While it's often said that .hack popularized the "Isekai" genre in animes, it isn't parallel/alternate worlds and is very similar to Sword Art Online but with a more extensive backstory (though I don't think either series had inspired each other).

If you liked the anime, I recommend getting the game for a continuation of the storyline as it is well-delivered in the game. The voice-acting (both Japanese and English dub) and pacing is pretty good although it can feel like a slow burn and text/cutscene heavy. The game consists of 4 volumes and is down to 90% discount when on sale. I should also mention that the game includes video summaries of the quadrilogy before GU (referred to as "IMOQ"), to provide some context relating to The World up to this point.

If what you care about in a JRPG is primarily story and immersion (i.e. everything else is secondary, or can be overlooked), I think GU is an above-the-average JRPG title. The story is good and still holds up well, with a balanced focus on both plot and characters. If you liked the type of stories in Persona series, I find the story in this game to be pretty similar. If you're acquainted with the .hack series, you'll also find characters in the game that connect back to earlier games/animes, which I found to be a nice touch. There's also humour every now and then which can be easily appreciated by any self-respecting weeb (disclaimer: I play on Japanese dub). The music is good too where immersion is concerned, though not at the level of its earlier anime counterparts, which without a doubt, had contributed greatly to the popularity of the series - like "Key of the Twilight" by Yuki Kajiura, or "Dwindled Bible" by ALI Project, as examples. My favorite song in GU is "Gentle Hands" and a couple of other BGMs that stood out to me are "Eternal City Mac Anu" and "Celestial City Dol Dona" which are played when in town. As a side note, if you found "Gentle Hands" pleasing to your ears, you should definitely also check out "You smiled kindly" and "Carl's theme" - I rotate between these 3 as BGMs played when in the desktop screen.

Now, if you didn't like the anime (or don't like anime at all), then I suggest skipping it because the main attraction here is the story and world-building, the rest are pretty mediocre. It's also filled with anime tropes which most people either love or hate.

Regardless, I am having fun with GU because I've watched the anime long time ago (and liked it) but have never played the game. But I feel that both GU and IMOQ deserves modern remakes; especially IMOQ, which I feel is far superior (story-wise) but is even clunkier in terms of the gameplay. So here's hoping that Bandai Namco would one day decide to remake the 2, so that I no longer need to hesitate about recommending them. Ironically, for a game that I didn't recommend due to its aged graphics and gameplay, it's a new entry in my favorites list.

P.S. There's something about Haseo that is neither explained in the game nor in the anime. However, he does have a relationship to past series (as with many characters you meet in the game) which I'll leave to you to find out on your own. ;)

like key of the twilight by yuki kajiura, or dwindled bible by ali project, as examples. my favorite song in gu is gentle hands and a couple of other bgms that stood out to me are eternal city mac anu and celestial city dol dona which are played when in town. as a side note, if you found gentle hands pleasing to your ears, you should definitely also check out you smiled kindly and carl's theme - i rotate between these 3 as bgms played when in the desktop screen. now, if you didn't like the anime or don't like anime at all , then i suggest skipping it because the main attraction here is the story and world-building, the rest are pretty mediocre. it's also filled with anime tropes which most people either love or hate. regardless, i am having fun with gu because i've watched the anime long time ago and liked it but have never played the game. but i feel that both gu and imoq deserves modern remakes especially imoq, which i feel is far superior story-wise but is even clunkier in terms of the gameplay. so here's hoping that bandai namco would one day decide to remake the 2, so that i no longer need to hesitate about recommending them. ironically, for a game that i didn't recommend due to its aged graphics and gameplay, it's a new entry in my favorites list. p.s. there's something about haseo that is neither explained in the game nor in the anime. however, he does have a relationship to past series as with many characters you meet in the game which i'll leave to you to find out on your own.

review_text:
A very clunky, awkward, stressful game that I can't really recommend to everyone, but that I think is definitely worth playing for people who want to experience something unique. I'll try not to give anything important away while still giving a decent summary of what to expect.

You play as a doctor in a town that gets ravaged by a plague and the entire gameplay loop is essentially trying to balance saving people around you, doing objectives (some of which might save people's lives or work towards solving problems), all while making sure you don't get sick or die of hunger/sleep deprivation. You can't do everything, so time management is basically the entire game. It makes you feel pretty awful and I was stressed for what feels like 95% of my play time. That being said, I enjoyed it and will likely give it another go when I have the time. I appreciate how it doesn't pull any punches, it never says "oh well he was doing a big objective that took all day, we'll give him a pass and not let this character die." No, you wasted your day, or you chose your priorities, you live with the consequences. Not many games are willing to do that and potentially piss off the player to such a harsh extent. 

I also appreciate how unclear everything is. A lesser game would just say outright "work on the cure today or go out and help people?" Instead, you get a cluster fuck of "What objectives should I go after? How can I make a cure in a town in the middle of nowhere with so little technology? Will this objective even help me find a cure or is it a waste of time? Will it be beneficial in other ways? This character says there's something important I need to see way outside of town which will take time to get to, do I go to him or do I spend that time making and distributing immunity boosters?" etc. It's an absolutely crazy, unforgiving, horrible mess in the best way.

If any of this sounds interesting to you then give it a go, just make sure you get past the weird prologue (really turned me off tbh) and into the actual game itself. Once you're there you'll know if it's something you'll like or absolutely hate.

review_text:
One of the first MMOs that I've spent so much time on. I enjoyed it quite a bit initially. I am an anime fan and the anime aesthetic immediately caught my attention. The combat system is engaging and the community is very welcoming and helpful. The story starts off with a bang and it seemed like I was finally going to get into an MMO after trying and not liking a couple of the big ones. That's all it is though. A good start to get me into the game and then a slog afterwards.

The main way this game keeps a hold of its player-base is fashion, like most online games. You can customise your character to a crazy deep level and there's a massive variety of clothes and gear to obtain. A lot of the end-game and events are oriented around getting new clothing items or emotes. The issue is that the grind to get these outfits is HEAVY. As a free-to-play player, the main way to get the currencies to unlock said outfits is by completing daily and weekly quests which require you to log in for about 1.5 hours everyday. I don't like the idea of games incentivizing logging in everyday. On days that I didn't log in, I felt like I was missing out on something. I avoided starting new games because that would mean that I can't log in on this game.

Speaking to some long term members of the community, I learned that a substantial number of them either do whale or have whaled on this game before. Of course it's possible to be a free-to-play player and still gain the same things that pay-to-win players get, but the paying players will get the newest items a lot faster and the free players will be left with a feeling of FOMO and a massive grind to get these items. At it's core this game is trying to frustrate you into spending your money. People said things akin to "Good luck, enjoy the game, but try not to spend money on it". That's never a good sign.

As someone who enjoys the process of trying out a variety of games and discovering indie gems, I realised that playing this game, or any game like it, is counter-productive for this hobby. I'm obviously not the target audience of this game and I'm glad I realised this before I got sucked into the sunken cost fallacy grind that these kinds of games instil in their player-base.

If you're anything like me, I suggest you avoid this game. 
If you enjoy creating and dressing up your anime waifu or husbando, go nuts.

"A DEEP, EMOTIONAL, WELL-WRITTEN STORY."

"IT MADE ME CRY."

"ONE OF THE GREATEST INDIE GAMES EVER MADE."

"A MASTERPIECE."


...And it was with words like these that I dove into 'To The Moon' with very high expectations. I prepared myself for a mind-blowing experience...with all the overwhelming positive reviews, how could it not be? This game was going to OWN, I was convinced. So when I saw this in an attractively priced bundle, I didn't hesitate to snap it up. Unfortunately, the actual game didn't live up to the hype.

GOOD 
+ Graphics are decent for this style of game
+ Music is good, though repetitive
+ Interesting concept for the storyline (scientists going back into a dying patient's memories and recreating them to match the patient's one true desire, like granting a wish)


BAD
- Clunky controls. Imagine playing an old school SNES JRPG with a mouse. 
- Lack of ENGAGING gameplay. Finding the 'mementos' and completing the ensuing simple flip puzzle got tiresome fast, and having to complete a bunch of them to advance the storyline made me feel like I was slogging through the game after a while. This is pretty much all there is as far as gameplay, other than moving your character around and clicking through dialogue boxes. 
- Slow performance. This game wasn't optimized for modern machines. But that's due mostly to the engine it was built on, from what I've read.
- Overrated story. It had its moments, but too much cheese and seemed forced. Characters weren't fleshed out enough. Ending...was typical. And predictable.
- Not enough feels. At least for me. I was really hoping the story and characters were gonna grip me and make me bawl my eyes out, like all the reviews said. My eyes remained dry throughout.
- Zero replay value. No alternate endings. No secrets to find. No extra or hidden characters. No bonuses. You get NOTHING.

Overall...."meh". I finished the game, but it felt like a chore most of the time. With an engaging storyline, which is this game's main selling point, it would have been different. I bought this game in a bundle, and dividing the cost of the bundle with the number of games in it, 'To The Moon' came to about .60 cents; a good deal any way you slice it. Full price = hell no. At $1.99 or less = worth a shot. Still, despite all its positively glowing reviews, I can't give this my full recommendation.

review_text:
It's safe to say that I gave it a very fair chance, considering the fact that I completed the whole game in under 60~70 hours. I really tried to like this game. It's beautiful, but it has way too many shortcomings. 

The documentation in this game is really poor, even for a Chinese people like me. I've dealt with many confusing interface across the games and irl too, but this game really tops it off for me. The most important settings are hidden behind 7~8 pages of interfaces and I have to really look where I need to click to find it, and the help function is useless, it doesn't let you type more than a handful of characters in, probably because it's made with Chinese character limits in mind. The inventory section is poorly sorted and the icons are hard to decipher, and a lot of the things I've collected either serve no purpose or doesn't have a clear purpose, clogging up inventory and making it hard to read. I don't know. There are three main classes namely tank, DPS, healer, but the definition of the classes in this game is extremely blurry or nonexistent because anyone can be a healer and do an absurdly high amount of damage and take a lot of damage, it does not reward you and make you feel that you're getting better at any role, in fact it gets more punishing as the enemy balance continues to worsen the more bosses you encounter. If I have to search the Internet for "how-to" videos / wiki articles just to manage the basics, this is an entirely fundamental problem in this game. Even if I had the privilege to understand Chinese, I looked up multiple sites to find what I need help with, but there are either no guides, or anything relevant to this game's topic, even though this game has been out for more than a year at this point.

It feels the developers were so busy pouring in all of these "cool" features that they overlooked providing information to players about how to use / manage those features. And there are endless screens of stuff - constantly presented with new screens. Impossible to keep track of so much data.

The game feigns complexity by adding a bunch of jargon and word salad, even hard for a Chinese to understand. - it's just frustrating when there doesn't appear to be any path to understanding the complexity. Also the sickness system doesn't really do anything, it's just a bunch of added jargon to scare the players and all you need to do is either visit a clinic or have a player heal it for you, this system in particular lacks a lot of depth.

I play games for an obvious reason, either the gameplay is good, or the story presented is good, this game fails to achieve in both fronts. Everyone is very familiar with how buggy this game is and I'll skip over this part. The story however...not a lot talk about it, because it is genuinely not interesting, and there really isn't a character worth getting attached to nor remember about because they all act like an npc and act upon a very stupid reason, for each and every one of them, including the main character of this game.

这款游戏的文档实在太差劲了，即使像我这样的中国人也难以理解。我在游戏和现实生活中都遇到过很多令人困惑的界面，但这款游戏绝对是其中最混乱的一个。最重要的设置竟然藏在七八页的界面后面，我必须仔细查找才能找到，而且帮助功能也形同虚设，输入的字数限制非常严格，可能是因为它是按照中文的字数限制设计的。物品栏的分类也很混乱，图标难以辨认，很多我收集到的东西要么毫无用处，或者用途不明，堆满了物品栏，很难阅读。我真是无语了。游戏里有三大职业：坦克、输出和治疗。但这些职业的定义极其模糊，甚至可以说是不存在的，因为任何人都可以治疗，而且输出伤害高得离谱，也能够承受很多伤害，一个火车砸下去都不会死的那种。这种设计既不会让你觉得自己在任何角色上有所进步，反而会随着遇到越多的怪平衡越来越差，觉得自己在游戏里没什么成长。如果我需要上网搜索教程视频/维基百科才能掌握基本操作，这绝对是游戏的一个根本性问题。即使我懂中文，我也查了很多网站，但要么找不到攻略，要么找不到任何与游戏相关的资料，而这款游戏已经上线一年多了。

这款游戏试图通过堆砌大量术语和晦涩难懂的文字来营造复杂性，就连中国人也难以理解。最令人沮丧的是，玩家似乎找不到任何理解这种复杂性的方法。此外，疾病系统也没有意思，只是用一堆术语吓唬玩家，玩家只需要去诊所或让其他玩家帮忙治疗即可。这个系统尤其缺乏深度。

我不是一遇到什么就退坑的人，但如果游戏之后继续让我失望，而且没有任何改进，我会立刻弃坑。

review_text:
7.5 / 10
Already played it once on PS3 nearly 10 years ago, and I enjoyed replaying this today.
GOODS
--- Good solid arcade style gameplay, not much different from the usual FAR CRY game experience, but still enjoyable in its own right.
--- Plenty of very good humour and a nice neon retro visual style.
--- The excellent underrated actor Michael Biehn voices the main character.

MIXED FEELINGS
--- On Hard Mode, it’s too easy, mainly because of the overpowered weapon mods. But then again, part of the charm of this game is the retro arcade gameplay and over the top humour.
--- There is a bit more variety of enemies than usual for a FAR CRY game because of the massive Blood Dragons, but enemies could’ve been more varied.
--- I do like its visual style, but the darkness especially in the wilderness does get in the way of the gameplay every now and then. Me getting confused of where I am in the middle of an intense fight.

FLAWS
--- I know it’s a spinoff game, but this game could’ve been double the length.
--- I wished the game had proper boss fights in the spirit of old school games.

I think that if the Ubisoft devs knew that this game was going to become a hit that it became, they probably could have spent more time expanding the game. Personally, I'd like to see a good expanded remake of this incorporating the gameplay elements of the latest FAR CRY games and add some new things to do. It's still a good game as it is.

review_text:
I did like this game. The first hour of it was an absolute delight, the first few puzzles were a blast to solve, but as I continued playing I couldn't help but to feel like something was missing.  There are a ton of bugs and performance issues that for a relatively short game that they have been working on for years are actually unacceptable. Cutscenes would lag, interrupt each other, sound effects would happen sometimes, and sometimes they wouldn't. 

I understand the development of this game has a rocky history, but come on. It's been a little over three years since Act 1, which in of itself was a really short game, there is no reason to hype it up as much as the What Pumpkin team has been and then just let it be a buggy mess.

SPOILERS FOR THE END

The story itself was super engaging, but the bugs caused performance issues that killed a lot of the pacing, especially near the end. A lot of the puzzles felt like they weren't at all telegraphed to the player. The Ace Attorney segment was fun for a little bit and then it just dragged on, and a lot of the clues in that segment felt like it was random bullshit, rather than something you would naturally consider. The "final boss" had some solutions that were debunked earlier. For instance, after breaking the window, I tried throwing treats into the room, but it failed by bouncing back towards Joey because it wasn't the right sequence, but when it was time to throw the treat in it magically worked. Pressing the final switch is a game over if you don't get rid of the body, but there's no indication to what that means to the player, forcing them to use trial and error or the hint system until they eventually get it. After all of that, we're treated to a lukewarm ending that is supposed to hype us up for Act 3, but that's gonna take another 3 years at this rate.

I really really wanted this game to be good. The characters and writing were pretty solid, and interacting them was fun. I know that is the main draw of this game, but everything else was so lacking that I can't say that I recommend this to anyone who isn't engaged in the overarching narrative.

One more game I wish I could give a neutral review, since it always sucks to thumbs down an indie. 

I love Rise to Ruins, but it feels more like a prototype. The bones from which the game was meant to flourish with continual expansions and mods. The former are rare and far between, the latter do not really exist. The game might feature a workshop, but you'll see that there's no real content other than translations - I don't know if it just failed to catch on, or the game doesn't feature any sort of mod support to build mods to begin with, but the result is unfortunate regardless.  

As it stands right now, it offers an anemic lack of content, a shallow endgame experience, and nothing worth the repetition to say that at least the rest of the game stands by itself.

review_text:
I remember the original .hack very fondly.  This game seems to be doing everything in it's power to wipe away that nostalgia and replace it with frustration and horror.  I have heard some games described as love letters to players.  .hack//G.U. is hate mail.  
The first time a dungeon door locks behind you could be an opportunity for a tiny jump scare followed by minimalist puzzle solving.  Nope. Stop the game, slow pan to the place to unlock it, put up a word balloon with instructions for unlocking it, leave it up long enough that someone translating from a dictionary can read it with no option to skip, then slow pan back to the PC.  Doing that once is annoying.  But this game does it EVERY SINGLE TIME.  
Going into "Avatar mode" for the first time? Pop up a panel to show the controls.  But wait! Gamers are lazy and stupid, we'd better show those controls every bloody time so they don't forget from literally two minutes ago!  
Going through a dungeon with a "puzzle" layout that wouldn't fool a four year old? Anyone playing a video game is too stupid to figure it out for themselves, we'll give hints as the enter every room.  Going through a dungeon with EXACTLY THE SAME LAYOUT on the very next quest? review_text:
As a huge fan of the first game (it's one of my favorite VR games), I gotta say... This game really doesn't live up to the first and in many ways feels like a downgrade.

For starters, let's talk about the engine. I know Boneworks has a reputation for being janky but this game seems just slightly worse in this regard than the first one. Half the time when you go to grab a mag, you will pull out your belt item, or grab nothing. Shotgun pumps work maybe 50% of the time. When you grab certain guns, your hands will sometimes freak out and spaz all over the place (try grabbing the AK on the front and you'll see what I mean). The worst of all is sometimes you'll just get completely stuck in geometry and have to restart the level. It's annoying and maybe I have "rose tinted glasses" for the first game but I don't ever remember it being as janky as it is here. Hopefully it can be fleshed out with future patches but as for right now, it doesn't really work that well.

In terms of the story, well... There isn't really one, or if there is, its a complete cluster(expletive). You have basically a tutorial showing you how the different player models work (will get into that later), then you have a few minigames and then 1-2 missions to finish it off. If there was a story, then it completely flew over my head. It just feels like a bunch of disjointed missions and then it ends. Granted, the story in the first game wasn't mindblowing or anything like that but it was leaps and bounds better than whatever this is. Also, I ran into multiple bugs that required me to restart the level to pass. Stuff like doors getting stuck, my hands and legs getting stuck in geometry, stuff like that. [spoiler] Also, there's a part in level 13 where you're in a tunnel, and you have to use launch pads to catapult yourself through the tunnel. This barely worked for me, and it took like 10 minutes to finally get it to work and not bug out [/spoiler] Honestly, if you are going to buy this for the custom content, I wouldn't waste your time with the meager story offerings here. Just download a 100% save and spare yourself the time and headaches.

You can now drive vehicles around. Sounds great on paper but in practice these are literal headache/stomachache machines. I've never once gotten sick while playing VR (aside from the first few times I've played it) and I legit had to take breaks every lap I did on the karting level. I very much doubt you will use any vehicle ever again after trying it and being nauseated by it the first time.

You can also now easily switch out your player model, and these player models all have different traits that you have to use to complete the story. Let's go over each of them:
- Strong: Probably the only one that actually feels right. Like the base character but can roll bigger boulders/pick up heavier stuff more easily.
- Fast: Honestly doesn't really feel much different to the base character model. I hardly even notice a speed difference.
- Heavy: His body takes up way too much of the FOV and his tutorial mission revolves around melee combat, which feels awful in this game (TBF it is also pretty bad in the first game)
- Small: Kind of pointless honestly. There's like one part of the game he's actually useful, and that part isn't even in his tutorial level.
- Light: Again, pretty much feels almost exactly the same as the base character model.
- Tall: Probably the worst in terms of jankiness, and also has the absolute worst mission in the game as his tutorial.
It is kinda neat that it's really easy to switch between all your player models.

In terms of modding, yes it's way easier than the first game. But, the problem is that the first game already had a solid base game underneath. It didn't rely on community made content to be great. This feels like the opposite of that. You pretty much have to put mods in to get your money's worth. Also, it begs the question: why didn't they just implement these modding tools into the original game?

The new guns are a plus. More variety is always welcome.

Idk. I honestly say just go get the original game and skip on this. Unless you really want/need a VR gmod-esque sandbox and you're willing to put up with all the issues, the first game has more to offer. I don't think I would be as upset if this was a $15-20 DLC for the original Boneworks, but as it stands now, I don't think it's worth the money and I'm not sure if it will ever be.

review_text:
The idea of a company offering a service that consists of manipulating your memories through the use of technology in order to give you experiences you didn't actually have or forget those you had is not exactly new. Decades ago I read a short story by Phlip K. D*ck (the guy's last name is censored, WTF) called "We Can Remember It For You Wholesale" that dealt with such a concept, and that would years later be adapted almost beyond recognition to film as Arnold Schwarzennegger's "Total Recall"  (later remade again). The film "Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" is also about a similar concept. 

But what if you told a story about such a company but not focusing on the client having their memories modified, but on the actual technicians/specialists doing the job and that job consists on giving a dying person fake memories that grant a life-long wish or resolve a life-long regret? That's basically what this game is, packaged in retro pixel art and injected with enough humor and sincerity to make the emotional beats pay off. 

Stuff like this proves that a good story that is told effectively can make a very simple game with retro graphics hit as hard as any modern offering with complicated gameplay and mind-blowing hyper-realistic visuals.

Edit: The two mini-sodes centerd around the office's Christmas party further develop the company and Neil and Eva's characters and relationship, though they hint at something not being exactly what it seems. I especially liked the detail about people protesting outside the building because they disapprove of the service they provide. Seemed oddly realistic.

review_text:
A fun enough survival horror with strong (if not simplistic) brawler element that works well in a three-dimensional space, The Callisto Protocol is rightfully a divisive game, though one worth buying at a discount. This is a shame since the game play of the melee combat is actually good, or at the very least promising if there is to be a sequel. However, do not go expecting a Dead Space experience in terms of either combat or storytelling or comparable atmosphere.

Pros:
+Genuinely fun melee system incorporating weaves, combos, and firearms in a way that works far better than what was expected.

+Atmospheric setting that comes with being in a prison on an icy and dead moon.

+Environmental kills with the GRP are very satisfying.

+Enemy mutation adds a level of danger and depth to the combat.

Cons:
+Awful boss fights (Two-headed, Ferris) require a very different play style in terms of combat outside of the melee system that defines over 90% of the game, turning the game into a mediocre 3rd person shooter. 

Note to all prospective game developers: If the bosses of your games have a different playstyles than the rest of the enemies, then it is likely a bad boss battle. Don't make most of your bosses be platformers in a turn-based game.

+Nonsensical environmental storytelling that makes for an uninteresting world to explore. Like really, the prison went to shit in like what, a few hours tops? Compare this to Dead Space where it is implied (albeit inconsistently) that it took around a few days for the USG Ishimura to reach a similar level of destruction, or even weeks in the remake. It makes no sense why there are barricades, why there are widespread fires.

Uninteresting world. We learn very little about how the prison operates beyond it is just a front for experimentation, but we hardly hear from the prisoners themselves or even most of the workers about the day to day. By the time the game proper starts, most everyone is dead. For a gameplay mean to evoke the brawling and gritty aspects of prison life, this game merely takes place in a prison setting, but not a prison.

+Story leaves much to be desired in terms of its characters (Jacob's underdeveloped character arc regarding guilt, Dani's entire character, Elias' entire character)

+Making the ending of the game actual DLC.

+Lack of a good range of enemy design and game play that adds to the base gameplay.
